From the images captured through SEM and digital camera, and the data gathered from the deconvolution of GPC chromatograms, it can be concluded that the degrading polymers had undergone bulk erosion. Pore formation was detected at about the same time as when three molecular weights appeared in the chromatograms. Three peaks in the chromatogram started to show up after 18.96 hr1/2 (2 weeks), 25.90 hr1/2 (4 weeks), and 32.90 hr1/2 (7 weeks) of incubation for PLA1, PLA2 and PLA3, respectively. This simultaneous emergence of a trimodal molecular weight distribution and porosity could represent the commencement of bulk erosion. The SEM data during the latter part of degradation further supports this mechanism of degradation, as larger pores are seen within the polymer matrix. Such pore formation throughout the samples suggests the occurrence of autocatalytic degradation where the oligomeric hydrolysis products are trapped within the bulk that causes the localized increase in acidity, thus further accelerating the degradation rate. The self-catalyzed hydrolytic degradation results to the formation of large pores or hollow structures that then leads to an enhanced deterioration of the mechanical properties of the bulk polymer and eventual loss of its structural integrity.44 The dimensions of the polymer matrix have also been known to govern the resorption behavior of biodegradable polymers, in addition to the rate of hydrolysis of the functional groups in their backbone chain and the rate of water uptake into the bulk.44 For poly(α-hydroxy esters) such as PLA, the critical thickness (Lcritical) below which the hydrolytic resorption mechanism favors bulk erosion has been measured to be 7.4 cm.57 This further supports our observations since the dimensions of the 3D-printed milliprojections are much smaller than the Lcritical. This suggests that the printed models will favor bulk erosion as the primary degradation mechanism. At the latter part of the degradation process, it is reasonable to expect a hollow structure rather than a thin layer of material left (as opposed to surface erosion). This happens when the rate of water diffusion into the polymer matrix is much faster than the degradation rate. In this case, hydrolysis is not restricted to the surface but rather occurs within the polymer structure.44, 57 Figure 17 illustrates the difference between the two erosion mechanisms during the course of degradation. The biodegradation of three grades of 3D-printed PLA in PBS at pH 7.4 and 37°C has demonstrated bulk erosion as the main mechanism of degradation. The biodegradation profile also indicates two stages of degradation, which includes the decrease of molecular weight followed by weight loss. The decrease in molecular weight occurred prior to bulk erosion, while the weight loss commenced during bulk erosion. The critical molecular weights of the polymers have also been recorded as 9,702.54 g/mol, 12,515.77 g/mol, and 8,007.72 g/mol for PLA1, PLA2, and PLA3, respectively. It was observed that the rate of degradation of the polymers is inversely proportional to molecular weight, with the amorphous PLA degrading more rapidly than the semicrystalline PLA samples. An analysis of the polymer crystallinity during the course of the degradation process also demonstrated the preferential degradation of the amorphous regions over the crystalline domains. Bulk erosion became apparent as porosity starts to occur until the bulk polymer starts to disintegrate. Although pore formation was seen throughout the samples, the layer interfaces were identified as favorable breakage points that initiate the bulk polymer fragmentation. During bulk erosion, multimodal molecular weight distribution was observed, suggesting further fragmentation of the polymer chains within the matrix. The results of the study provide a useful idea on how the drugs can be administered through the printed system. Different drugs can be loaded in different projections and the delivery can be controlled by using polymers of varying molecular weights and crystallinity. Future investigations involving polymers that degrade or dissolve faster and processed at lower temperatures such as polyethylene glycol are of interest. This will extend its potential application to drugs that need to be delivered at a faster rate and to sensitive drugs that degrade at demanding processing conditions.

Kenley et al.28 decribed three major features of PLGA degradation curves: 1) Induction period where mass and molecular weight values are unchanged; 2) onset of molecular weight loss becoming exponential with time; and 3) erosion onset. Several factors contribute to the hydrolytic degradation (molecular weight loss) of aliphatic polyesters. Among these are molecular weight, composition (monomer selection, ratios for copolymers), initiator selection, and morphology. Hydrolytic degradation of biodegradable polyesters occurs by random or nonrandom chain scission. Hydrolysis of linear PLLA and PLGA is generally considered to proceed by random cleavage of ester bonds. However, nonrandom ester cleavage of PLGA arms from a PEG block has been observed in 2-arm PEG-PLGA.29, 30 The chain scission mechanism in multiarm PLLA and PLGA has been shown to be dependent on the backbone material.20, 29 Random chain scission of the PLLA and PLGA branches has been observed in polymers with a backbone of diethyaminoethyl dextran chloride20 and nonrandom chain scission when the backbone was dextran sulfate sodium,20 4-arm PEO, or 8-arm PEO.29 Cleavage of the branches from the core material was followed by the degradation of the resulting linear polyester fragments via the random scission mechanism until the molecular weight was low enough for the fragments to be water-soluble. When the polymer fragments are small enough to be water-soluble then erosion (mass loss) is observed. Polymer mass loss may occur via a surface or a bulk erosion mechanism. Polymers that undergo bulk erosion absorb water into the polymer matrix and undergo hydrolysis uniformly throughout the sample. Surface-eroding polymers do not absorb water into the matrix rather, erode from the outer layer in. Bulk erosion is considered to be the primary erosion mechanism for PLA and PLGA, however, it has been shown that PLA and PLGA erode in a nonuniform manner with faster degradation in the center of implants than at the surface.31 This heterogeneous bulk erosion is caused by autocatalysis, accelerated degradation inside the polymer matrix by trapped acidic degradation products. It is expected that the 2-arm PEG-polyesters and the multiarm PG-polyesters in this study demonstrate similar degradation behavior to the 2-arm, 4-arm, and 8-arm PEG/PEO polymers discussed above. Degradation and erosion behavior of linear and branched poly(L-lactide)s and poly(L-lactide-co-glycolide)s were investigated. Normalized molecular weight loss versus time is reported in Figure 4 and follows the order PLLA35 < PG4-PLLA2 < PEG-PLLA7 < PG2-PLGA2 < PEG-PLGA6 < PLGA20 ≈ PLGA12. Figure 5 shows the normalized erosion versus time for the polymers studied. Normalized erosion rates followed the order of PLLA35 < PEG-PLLA7 ≈ PG4-PLLA2 ≪ PEG-PLGA6 ≈ PLGA20 < PG2-PLGA2 < PLGA12. Erosion and MW loss for the semicrystalline polymers (PLLA35, PEG-PLLA7, and PG4-PLLA2) was significantly slower than that of the amorphous polymers (PLGA12, PLGA20, PEG-PLGA6, and PG2-PLGA2). This was expected as polymers containing PLLA are more hydrophobic than the polymers containing PLGA. Hydrophobicity of PLLA slows the diffusion rate of water into the sample and the crystallinity of PLLA reduces the amount of free volume in the sample therefore less water is absorbed affecting the amount of water available for hydrolysis. Erosion lags behind MW loss for all of the polymers tested. The lag implies that hydrolysis proceeds throughout the polymer bulk. Degradation by the surface erosion mechanism requires mass loss precede MW loss.

The degradation mechanism of polymer involves bulk erosion and surface erosion.54 Surface erosion is believed to occur when surface of sample is eroded and its interior remains nearly unchanged. The almost constant degradation rate in Figure 9(a) implies that the enzymatic degradation of PLLA composites may proceed via surface erosion. In order to further clarify erosion mechanism, the morphologies of degraded samples were examined by SEM. Figures 10 and 11 show the surface and cross-sectional morphologies of stretched samples with a stretch ratio of 6 after degradation, respectively. Video micrographs in Figure 10 suggest the changes in surface morphology as a result of enzymatic degradation. Exposure to the activated inoculum causes removal of material from surface, leading to an increase in sheets surface roughness with increasing degradation time. Even though degradation models are similar, the surface of degraded composites is much coarser compared with that of neat PLLA, and increasing porosity leads to a transformation of degraded surface from coarser to porous. This means that the surface erosion proceeds slower in neat PLLA due to no micropores formation during stretching. Degradation rates depend primarily on porosity, and increase with increasing porosity. On the other hand, surface erosion seems to be much affected by the ES content in composites. After PLLA chains on surface are degraded, the dispersed ES particles may fall off from PLLA matrix, leading to a larger surface area. Therefore, in process of degradation, greater ES particles also contribute to larger surface area, consequently causing a further increase in degradation rate. As a result, PLLA70/ES30 composite exhibits the highest degradation rate, 0.39 mg cm−2 h−1, which is approximately eight times larger than that of neat PLLA. Figure 11 shows the cross-sectional morphologies of stretched samples after degradation for 48 h. No obvious morphological change in the interior bulk and thinning of samples thickness further demonstrate that the enzymatic degradation proceeds by surface erosion. It is worth noting that the surface degradation occurs in stretched PLLA composites even though there are many micropores generated by stretching in PLLA matrix, indicating that the micropores do not connect to each other, but form a closed-cell structure. In the present work, we fabricated biodegradable PLLA/ES composite sheets constructed by crystal networks with highly degree of crystallinity, orientation of amorphous regions, and closed micropores by uniaxial stretching, successfully obtaining preferable thermomechanical properties, and controllable biodegradation rate combined with superior ductility and strength. Based on morphological observations, it demonstrated that the deformed PLLA composites produced micropores due to debonding. The size and numbers of micropores increase with increasing stretch ratios and ES content. The microcellular structure in PLLA composites resulted in a decrease of density. Moreover, on the basis of thermal behaviors and WAXD analysis of this system, it was found that α crystals were formed by strain-induced crystallization, while the crystallinity and amorphous orientation increase with the increase of stretch ratios. The enhancement in thermomechanical properties and mechanical properties, and the controllable degradation rate were obtained by constructing this superstructure. The elastic modulus at 80 °C and degradation rate of stretched PLLA70/ES30 composites could be increased by more than 140 and 8 times, respectively, compared with that of neat PLLA. Furthermore, the strength and stiffness of stretched composites increased with increasing stretch ratios. It could be exemplified by the rise of breaking strength and modulus up to 140.8 and 3810 MPA for PLLA90/ES10 composites with a stretch ratio of 6, showing a remarkable increase of 148 and 190% compared to neat PLLA. Unexpectedly, the ductility (35.2%) had also increased by 507%. Moreover, the degradation rate, stiffness, strength, and ductility can be effectively tailored over a wide range by adjusting ES contents and stretch ratios and expanding the application of PLLA.

Both enzymatic and chemical catalyzed hydrolytic degradation of PCL have been extensively investigated, showing that several lipases accelerate the degradation significantly,13-15 while hydrolytic degradation usually needs several years.16 Next to the mechanism of the hydrolytic degradation the erosion profiles of the polymers are of crucial importance for the successful implementation of these polymers in biomedical applications.17,18 The main steps involved in the erosion process are: (i) the diffusion of water into the bulk polymer, which is strongly affected by its porosity and might be accompanied by swelling of the material, (ii) the polymer degradation leading to the formation of cyclic oligomers and monomers which are water soluble at low concentration, and (iii) the weight loss via diffusion of degradation products from the bulk material. Concerning the erosion process, two types are distinguished, either heterogeneous surface or homogeneous bulk erosion.18 Crucial parameters are the diffusivity of water inside the matrix, the degradation rate of the functional groups of the back bone and the matrix dimensions respectively its porosity. Surface erosion occurs when the diffusion of water into the polymer is slower than the degradation of the polymer. In this case, only the region close to the surface of polymer matrix is affected by hydrolysis. In course of this process, the hydrolysis front advances towards the material core, since the surface is eroded and removed continuously. This type of erosion behavior is generally shown by poly(ortho ester)s, poly(anhydride)s and some poly(carbonate)s.19,20 In the case of bulk erosion, water penetrates throughout the entire polymer matrix before hydrolysis occurs. Consequently, chain cleavage happens uniformly throughout the entire material. The mechanical properties change from the very beginning, in parallel with mass loss and the decrease of the molecular weight. Typical polymers following this erosion mechanism are poly(lactic acid) and poly(ε-caprolactone). The degradation rate is influenced by various factors. It is generally accepted that hydrolysis of ester groups initially occurs in the amorphous domains of the polymer. The degradation rate increases when the crystallinity of the polymer decreases. An increasing molecular weight results in a lower degradation rate. Furthermore the hydrophilicity of the material, crosslinking density, porosity and surface chemistry may influence the degradation rate.21-23 This high number of parameters influencing the degradation rate of polymers results in a wide range of possibilities to tailor this rate. For demonstration some examples are given: (i) incorporation of a hydrophilic monomer into a hydrophobic polyester increases the rate of degradation; this was achieved by copolymerization of 1,5-dioxepan-2-one with ε-caprolactone. (ii) By using a hydrophilic macroinitiator for the polymerization of ε-caprolactone, e.g. a hydroxy-telechelic poly(ethylene oxide), amphiphilic block copolymers with enhanced degradation rate are obtained.24-26 (iii) Changing the microstructure and architecture of PCLs by preparation of block or graft copolymers, star-shaped polymers, porous scaffolds and crosslinked networks, leads to a decrease in crystallinity and an increase of the degradation rate.27-29 (iv) Modification of the end groups, e.g. by attaching carboxylic acid groups at the chain end enhances moisture uptake and hence accelerates the degradation.30-32
Further examples of potentially biodegradable bio-based PET mimic could be found in the literature, although their hydrolytic degradation has not been fully studied. Some examples include poly(dihydroferulic acid) (PHFA), whose hydrolytic degradation yields the antioxidant dihydroferulic acid as a product, which can be found in tea, coffee and whole grains. However, no insights on the time required to undergo through chain scission has been provided in its invention, which is protected by a US Patent [282]. Similarly, the synthetic approach for the development of the bio-based semiaromatic poly(ethylene vanillate) (PEV) together with its thermal and mechanical properties was provided by Gioia et al., although no reference was done to its degradability [181]. Although the hydrolytic degradation of poly(2-(2-hydroxyethoxy)benzoate) (P2HEB) was not studied, its degradation was investigated in the presence of aluminium salen 1 by Lizundia et al [178]. It was reported that after 1 h in toluene at 70 °C, the molecular weight was reduced by 80%.Very interestingly, the depolymerisation was found to be selective as the cyclic monomer of P2HEB was the only product formed during degradation. Such rapid recycling to the monomer emerges as a novel and promising way to rethink the polymer life-cycle as the cyclic monomer obtained upon degradation could be prospectively used for repolymerisation without additional processing. In the light of reported results, eco-toxicity studies on the degradation products of polyesters need to be carried out to get a bigger picture on the environmental impact of such polymers and ensure that no harmful products are released [283]. Despite to the generally observed pH drop and high oxygen demand (due to an increased microbial activity) during degradation that could present some minor negative impacts [284], overall no relevant harmful effects of the degradation products arising from polyesters such as PBAT or PBSu are detected [285], [286]. However, polyesters releasing low pKa species may yield to cytotoxic/genotoxic effects. In this sense, PLA degradation products have been found to have an aneugenic action onto common onion, resulting in slightly cytotoxic/genotoxic effects [287]. Other aspect that has traditionally limited the applicability of biodegradable polyesters is their tendency to undergo through bulk degradation reactions, resulting in non-linear release of by-products with burst-release characteristics and sudden changes in mechanical properties. On the contrary, poly(ortho esters) and poly(anhydrides) are able to undergo surface erosion [143], [288]. Since the primary driving force for bulk erosion of polyesters is their hydrophilicity (DT > tc), a plausible approach to develop surface eroding polyesters and expand their applicability would be the modification of the water penetration kinetics. Accordingly, Xu et al. synthesized a library of over 50 surface eroding polyesters derived from poly(α-hydroxy acids) with a Mw ranging from 20.000 to 130.000 g·mol−1 by increasing the hydrophobicity of the polymer backbone [289]. Using a two step synthetic approach by macromer formation and a coupling step, building blocks with differing hydrophilic-lipophilic balance (HLB) were synthesized. The newly obtained polyesters showed steady and linear mass loss profiles upon hydrolytic degradation (37 °C; pH:10), while morphological observations revealed porous surface and dense bulk structures indicative of surface erosion mechanisms (i.e. hydrolytic reactions are limited to the surface). Some naturally occurring polymers such as PHAs are biodegradable as they are susceptible to enzymatic degradation. Tokiwa and Suzuki showed back in 1977 that apart from such natural polymers, other synthetic polymers also have the ability of being degraded by some isolated enzymes [298]. Afterwards, lipases extracted from hog pancreas and Rhizopus arrihzus were used by Tokiwa et al. to investigate the degradation behavior of several aliphatic polyesters [299], [300]. Since this pioneering work carried out using lipases, a plethora of works have studied the degradation of both aliphatic and aliphatic/aromatic polyesters using different enzymes [301], [302], [303], which opened the door to the synthetic design of polymers capable to undergo depolymerisation reactions under microbial attack.

Physical erosion accompanies hydrolysis aiding in degradation. Physical erosion can be either (a) bulk erosion or (b) surface erosion. Based on the provided context evidence, the distinction between bulk erosion and surface erosion in aliphatic polyester degradation is defined by the relative rates of water diffusion into the polymer versus the hydrolysis rate of the ester bonds, leading to fundamentally different degradation profiles:

1.  **Mechanism Trigger**: Bulk erosion occurs when the rate of water diffusion into the polymer matrix is **faster** than the rate of ester bond hydrolysis. This allows water to penetrate the entire bulk before significant hydrolysis occurs, leading to degradation throughout the material. Surface erosion occurs when the rate of ester bond hydrolysis is **faster** than the rate of water diffusion. Hydrolysis is then confined to the surface layers as water cannot readily penetrate deeper before the surface erodes. [1], [8], [13]

2.  **Degradation Location**: In **bulk erosion**, hydrolysis and chain scission occur relatively uniformly throughout the entire volume of the polymer matrix (*homogeneous degradation*). In **surface erosion**, hydrolysis and mass loss are restricted to the outer surfaces of the material, with the interior remaining largely unchanged initially. Degradation progresses via an advancing erosion front moving inward. [1], [6], [7], [8], [10], [13]

3.  **Morphological Changes**: **Bulk erosion** is characterized by the formation of pores, cavities, or hollow structures throughout the bulk of the material as degradation proceeds internally. This eventually leads to the loss of structural integrity from the inside out. **Surface erosion** is characterized by surface roughening, thinning of the material without significant internal pore formation (unless inherent porosity exists), and the creation of pits or irregularities on the exposed surface as material is removed layer by layer. [1], [2], [3], [6], [7], [10]

4.  **Molecular Weight (Mw) Loss vs. Mass Loss**: For **bulk erosion**, a significant decrease in molecular weight (due to chain scission throughout the bulk) occurs **before** observable mass loss (erosion). Mass loss commences later as fragments become small enough to diffuse out. For **surface erosion**, mass loss (erosion of the surface layer) precedes any significant loss in the molecular weight of the remaining bulk material. [4], [5], [8], [13], [14], [15]

5.  **Autocatalysis**: **Bulk erosion** is strongly associated with autocatalysis, where acidic degradation products (e.g., carboxylic acids) become trapped within the bulk, lowering the local pH and accelerating the hydrolysis rate internally, often leading to faster degradation in the core than at the surface (*heterogeneous bulk erosion*). This autocatalytic effect is less prominent or absent in **surface erosion** as acidic by-products are readily removed from the eroding surface. [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [14], [15]

6.  **Influence of Dimensions/Geometry**: Sample thickness critically influences the dominant mechanism. Thin samples (below a critical thickness, e.g., <7.4 cm for PLA) favor **bulk erosion** because water can readily diffuse throughout the entire volume quickly. Thicker samples can exhibit bulk erosion but are more prone to autocatalytic effects internally. High surface area-to-volume ratios (e.g., microparticles) favor **surface erosion** due to the increased availability of chains at the surface. [1], [2], [3], [13]

Erosion of polymeric implants is typically defined by two different modes: surface and bulk. Surface erosion occurs when a solid polymer loses mass from the surface of the structure and then erodes towards the center of the body. Conversely, bulk erosion occurs when a polymer loses mass such that outward diffusion of monomers occurs in a uniform manner. If water diffusions into the polymer faster than the macromolecular chains can degrade then the polymer will exhibit bulk erosion. If the degradation proceeds at a faster rate than water can diffuse into the body then the polymer will exhibit surface erosion [12]. However, surface and bulk erosion are ideal cases as most polymers often experience a combination of both [13]. In polymeric implants the balance of these two processes in combination with the geometric features of the scaffold determine the final shape and material characteristics of the implant. During the degradation process, the chemical, physical, and mechanical properties of biodegradable materials change over time, and as erosion takes place the geometrical shapes and sizes of the implants also change over time. Physical and chemical properties of biodegradable polymers during degradation have been widely studied, for a range of polymeric materials and compositions, that span the analysis of the overall (macroscopic) change of molecular weight, fluid concentration, monomer concentration, crystallinity, and porosity [4,12,[17], [18], [19], [20]]; etc.). Similarly, macroscopic mechanical properties have been investigated to understand the overall behavior of these biodegradable polymers and scaffolding structures over the course of degradation [[7], [8], [17], [18], [21], [22], [23], [24]]. However, the understanding of local (microscopic) material properties remains to be a challenge. The understanding of localized changes in the physical, chemical, and mechanical properties during the implant degradation is crucial to guarantee a proper load bearing is met and for the prediction and tuning of engineered polymeric implant degradation. In summary, degradation induces heterogeneous changes in the mechanical, chemical, and physical properties of a polymeric body that is initially considered as homogenous with regards to its mechanical, chemical, and physical properties (see a detailed discussion in Ref. [13]. This heterogeneity in the material properties and changes in the geometrical shape and size will influence the overall structural integrity of the implant as well as tissue growth. There have been computational models developed to describe the spatial and temporal changes in the chemical and physical characteristics of biodegradable polymer solids during degradation and erosion process. Casalini et al. [11] presented a statistical modeling approach within coupled partial differential equations for the degradation and drug releases of PLGA micro-spheres. The models consider reaction kinetics involving concentrations of water, monomer, and oligomer during the hydrolytic degradation. In addition, governing differential equations for control drug releases (erosion) are also presented. The coupling between the degradation and erosion are considered by having the diffusivity constants for both water and drug to depend on changes in the molecular weight as the polymer degrades. Gopferich [13] discussed a different approach in capturing polymer erosion, moving away from setting up partial differential equations. He considered a probability of the erosion of small polymer segments, which were modeled as grids within a polymer body. Each grid contains binary pixels representing amorphous and crystalline phases that differ by the erosion rates. The erosion was modeled by a Poisson process and as the pixels were in contact with the buffer medium, pixels were removed to simulation the erosion. Similar to the probability approach in Gopferich, Yu et al. (2008)[25] use a cellular automata technique to simulate drug release in three-dimensional multilayer biodegradable polymers. The studies by Sevin and Pan [26] and Chen et al. [10] combined the stochastic and differential equations in describing hydrolytic degradation and erosion in drug delivery systems. The mass balance and diffusion of the constituents were modeled by the differential equations and the erosion process followed the probability approach of Gopferich [13]. Chen et al. [10] focused on understanding the spatial distribution of autocatalysis on the pathway and size of polymers at different degradation time. Wang et al. [27] presented a phenomenological approach in capturing the degradation in biodegradable polymers by considering the reaction-diffusion processes involving the concentration of ester bonds of the amorphous polymers, monomers, and crystallinity. The spatial and temporal variations of the above constituents in 3D polymers were investigated. However, the model did not include the erosion process where changes in the shape and size of the polymers can be incorporated.

Concerning the erosion process, two types are distinguished, either heterogeneous surface or homogeneous bulk erosion.18 Crucial parameters are the diffusivity of water inside the matrix, the degradation rate of the functional groups of the back bone and the matrix dimensions respectively its porosity. Surface erosion occurs when the diffusion of water into the polymer is slower than the degradation of the polymer. In this case, only the region close to the surface of polymer matrix is affected by hydrolysis. In course of this process, the hydrolysis front advances towards the material core, since the surface is eroded and removed continuously. This type of erosion behavior is generally shown by poly(ortho ester)s, poly(anhydride)s and some poly(carbonate)s.19,20 In the case of bulk erosion, water penetrates throughout the entire polymer matrix before hydrolysis occurs. Consequently, chain cleavage happens uniformly throughout the entire material. The mechanical properties change from the very beginning, in parallel with mass loss and the decrease of the molecular weight. Bulk erosion and surface erosion in aliphatic polyesters are distinguished by the spatial and temporal progression of degradation. **Bulk erosion** occurs when water penetrates the entire polymer matrix faster than the rate of hydrolysis, leading to homogeneous degradation throughout the material. This results in molecular weight reduction prior to significant mass loss, internal pore formation, and eventual structural disintegration due to autocatalytic hydrolysis (trapped acidic byproducts accelerating core degradation) [3], [6], [7], [10]. Polymers like PLA and PCL typically exhibit bulk erosion when their thickness is below a critical value (~7.4 cm for PLA), allowing rapid water diffusion [6], [7], [10].

**Surface erosion** involves degradation confined to the polymer’s exterior, with minimal interior changes. Enzymes or hydrolysis preferentially attack the surface, causing linear mass loss and increased surface roughness, while the bulk retains molecular integrity until later stages [1], [2], [11], [14]. This mechanism dominates when degradation outpaces water diffusion, often observed in composites (e.g., PLLA/ES) or enzymatically catalyzed systems (e.g., PHBV) [1], [2], [11]. Surface erosion is influenced by additives (e.g., ES particles) that increase porosity or surface area, accelerating material removal [1], [2]. 

Key distinctions include:  
1. **Degradation locus**: Bulk erosion is homogeneous; surface erosion is localized to the exterior [1], [3], [5].  
2. **Mass loss vs. molecular weight loss**: Bulk erosion shows early molecular weight decline followed by mass loss; surface erosion exhibits linear mass loss with delayed molecular weight changes [3], [6], [11].  
3. **Critical thickness**: Bulk erosion dominates in thinner polymers (< Lcritical), while surface erosion persists in thicker systems until critical thickness is reached [6], [14].  
4. **Role of autocatalysis**: Bulk erosion is accelerated by acidic byproduct accumulation, whereas surface erosion lacks this feedback [3], [7].

In light of the substantial environmental repercussions associated with the production of conventional petroleum-based polymers, there has been a burgeoning interest in biodegradable polymers derived from renewable resources. These biomaterials are held in high esteem for their environmentally beneficial characteristics [1-4]. Among these, polylactic acid (PLA) has emerged as one of the most extensively studied polymers in the current year, owing to its remarkable tensile strength, favorable processability, and biocompatibility. PLA is mainly produced from renewable resources such as sugarcane, potatoes, or maize, which makes it sustainable [5, 6]. Notwithstanding these beneficial attributes, the inherent brittleness of PLA poses limitations on its application in various domains [7-9]. To mitigate the shortcomings associated with PLA, poly (atopic acid)/butylene terephthalate (PBAT) has been identified as a highly viable toughening agent, characterized by significant elongation at break and low modulus of elasticity, akin to the properties observed in thermoplastic elastomers. Consequently, PLA and PBAT are perceived as complementary materials [10, 11]. However, the pronounced discrepancy in solubility parameters between PLA and PBAT results in suboptimal interfacial adhesion within the resultant blends; thus, achieving robust interfacial compatibility between PLA and PBAT is critical for obtaining composites with superior properties. In this context, reactive blending stands out as one of the most effective and convenient methodologies [12, 13]. Chain extenders are multifunctional additives that bind to the ends of different macromolecular fragments, thereby increasing the average molar mass of the polymer, and can also be used as reactive bulking agents in the blends. The use of chain extenders in blends promotes the formation of copolymers in the molten state. In this framework, Joncryl ADR-4468 is utilized as a chain extender due to its abundance of epoxy groups [14, 15].
In recent years, the literature has reported on the use of chain extenders as compatibilizers to improve the mechanical properties of biodegradable polymer blends.[96-98] Isocyanate chain extenders, such as l-lysine triisocyanate (LTI), 1,4-lysine diisocyanate, methylene diphenyl diisocyanate, phenylene diisocyanate, 1,3,5-tris(6-isocyanatohexyl)biuret (Duranate 24A-100), and 1,3,5-tris(6-isocyanatohexyl) 1,3,5-triazinane-2,4,6-trione (Duranate TPA-100), have been applied in PLA/PCL blend systems as reactive compatibilizers. However, due to its high reactivity with hydroxyl and amine groups, LTI is the most efficient chain extender that can be used as a compatibilizer.[45, 49] Apart from isocyanates, the literature has reported on other chain extenders, such as Joncryl, triphenyl phosphite, tris(nonyl-phenyl) phosphate, and polycarbodiimide which have been used to improve the performance of polymer blends.[55, 99, 100] Joncryl consists of multiple epoxy groups that react with the hydroxyl and/or carboxyl groups of the polymer. It has been successfully used as a reactive compatibilizer in several immiscible blends.[49] Joncryl has been incorporated into many biodegradable polymer blends as a compatibilizer. However, it should be noted that there are limited studies that highlight the incorporation of Joncryl into PLA/PCL blends. Recently, Matumba et al.[70] have shown that 0.5 wt% Joncryl can effectively improve the compatibility of the PLA/PCL 70/30 w/w blend, resulting in greater toughness. Wang et al.[76] observed a similar effect with 1 wt% Joncryl, showing a high elongation-at-break when the PCL content is increased to 30 wt%. It is evident that Joncryl has a sufficient compatibilization effect and can play a significant role in improving the mechanical properties of PLA/PCL blend. Therefore, the use of Joncryl should be considered to provide new insight toward materials development where PLA/PCL blends are concerned. Likewise, reactive LTI compatibilizer is used to increase interfacial bonding of the two phases, thereby improving the compatibility and interfacial adhesion of the PLA/PCL blend.[101] Visco et al.[102] added 0.5 and 1.0 phr LTI to the PLA/PCL blends and reported an improvement in ductility, which improved the maximum deformation and breakage. Therefore, the improvement in mechanical strength was evidence of the improvement in yield stress and the ultimate tensile strength of the blends. In a separate study, Visco et al.[25] reported that 1.0 phr LTI was sufficient to reasonably improve the ductility of the PLA/PCL 50/50 wt% blend. This is caused by a prominent reaction with the epoxy groups that promotes cross-linked chains in the blend. It is noteworthy that a low LTI content can sufficiently improve the compatibility of the PLA/PCL blend, resulting in improved mechanical properties. In general, the incorporation of compatibilizers into their various contents improves the mechanical properties of the blend. Compatibilizers facilitate efficient stress transfer through interfacial adhesion in the PLA/PCL blend. Other compatibilizers should be considered as potential materials to improve the mechanical properties of PLA/PCL polymer blends. Nanofillers have recently been used as compatibilizers to balance and modify the properties of polymer blends required for specific applications.[103, 104] Studies on the incorporation of nanofillers into PLA/PCL blends are summarized in Table 3. In this case, to improve mechanical properties, the filler must be well dispersed within the blend.[105] This depends on the localization of the filler in the blend.[106, 107] Preferential localization of the filler in polymer nanocomposite is influenced by factors such as the viscosity ratio of the two polymers and the enthalpic interactions between the polymers and the filler.[108] Regarding the PLA/PCL blend, the localization of nanoparticles in the PCL phase is attributed to enthalpic interactions. This is because the melt viscosity properties of PCL are higher than those of PLA.[109] This assumption is based on the fact that fillers prefer to localize in the phase with lower viscosity.[61, 110] In contrast, fillers located at the interface can increase stress transfer in the blend and thus improve the final mechanical properties.
The mechanism underlying the enhancement of chemical reaction capacity lies in the melt blending of the chain extender or crosslinker with PBAT and PLA. Through chemical reactions, chemical bonds are formed among the components of the copolymer. This process effectively improves the adhesion and compatibility at the two-phase interface of PLA and PBAT [22]. Currently, the epoxy chain extender is the most widely used type of chain extender, such as chain extender of Joncryl® series (ADR) [23], glycidyl methacrylate polymer [24], epoxy soybean oil (ESO) [25], etc. Specifically, ADR series chain extenders consist of aromatic vinyl monomers (e.g., ethylene, styrene (St)) and acrylate monomers (e.g., glycidyl methacrylate (GMA)). The aromatic vinyl monomers serve as the structural backbone units, while the acrylate monomers supply active epoxy groups. These epoxy groups can chemically react with the end hydroxyl group and end carboxyl group of the polymer to form a cross-linked structure, effectively improving the compatibility of the polymer matrix. For examples, Li et al. [26] explored the effect of ADR chain extender (ADR-4370F) on the physical properties of PLA/PBAT blend; when ADR-4370F content was 0.15 phr, the elongation at break of PLA/PBAT blend rose from 23.5 % to 410.3 %. Han et al. [27] found that ESO could react with end groups of polymers to enhance compatibility; the elongation at break and the gap impact strength of PLA/PBAT blend containing 5 phr ESO were significantly increased. However, these traditional chain extenders lack biodegradability. Despite their ability to effectively enhance the mechanical properties of polymer blends, they have an adverse impact on the biodegradability of PBAT/PLA blends [28]. In this work, a biodegradable epoxy-based terpolymer (SHG), which consisted of GMA (serving as the source of active epoxy groups), 1,6-hexadiol diacrylate (HDDA; providing the ester groups), and St (functioning as the structural backbone units), was synthesized via the solution polymerization method. With this design, the SHG, which integrated both biodegradability and high reactivity, was employed as a reactive interface compatibilizer or chain extender of PBAT/PLA blends. The effects of polymerization reaction duration, the molar ratio of monomer, and amount of chain transfer agent on copolymer conversion, molecular weight, and epoxy value were investigated in detail. The effect of SHG on the interface compatibility, strength, toughness, heat resistance and processability of PBAT/PLA blends was explored, and its strengthening/toughening mechanisms were also investigated. In the study of chain extension of polyethylene terephthalate (PET), a di- or poly-functional low MW compound is reacted with PET carboxyl and hydroxyl end groups to reconnect broken chains caused by PET chain scissions during melt processing. A branching reaction is unavoidable alternatively. Branching and cross-linking occur throughout the chain expansion process. [13]. The use of a chain extender in the form of acrylic epoxy resin (Joncryl® ADR-4380) enhanced the molecular weight of recycled PET while also broadening the molecular weight distribution. The amount of gel content of formed crosslink-materials was dependent on the amount of chain extender used. The use of a chain extender enhanced the shear and elongational viscosity as well as tensile properties of recycled PET [14]. For bioplastics which are quite sensitive to thermal processing, some studies have focused on improving the properties of bioplastic products by using chain extenders in the compounding and thermal forming process. The intention of Yu et al [15] is to improve compatibilizer performance by controlled distribution in hydrophobic PLA/hydrophilic starch blends. Pre-blend processing can be used to control the distribution of methylenediphenyl diisocyanate (MDI) in either the PLA or starch phase. Thermal characteristics and mechanical properties such as modulus, yield strength, and impact strength of the blends were enhanced when MDI was dispersed in the PLA phase owning to the improvement of interfaces between PLA and starch. These enhancements may have resulted from the creation of a block copolymer with compatibilizing properties between isocyanate groups in MDI and hydroxy groups in starch and polyester. Baimark and Cheerarot [16] focused on the investigation of influences of a styrene-acrylic multifunctional oligomeric chain extender (Joncryl® ADR 4368) on the thermal properties of poly(L-lactide) (PLL). It was found that the chain extension process proceeded more efficiently at 190 °C than at 170 °C. When the Joncryl® ADR 4368 ratio was raised, the molecular weights of the chain extended PLLs increased while the melt flow indices dropped. The chain extender influenced the thermal characteristics and crystallinity of the PLL. When the Joncryl® ADR 4368 ratio and blending temperature were raised, the branched PLL content went up. The thermal stability of the shorter linear and branching PLLs was lower than that of the longer linear PLL. In another work about Joncryl® ADR 4368, Wutisart [17] found that this chain extender can improve morphology and enhance mechanical characteristics of polybutylene succinate (PBS) and polycaprolactone (PCL) blend. However, Joncryl® ADR 4368 need to process at high temperature, therefore it is not appropriate to PCL which has very low melting temperature. For PLA polymer blends, Khankrua et al [18] study about the effect of two chain extenders as Joncryl® ADR 4368 and polycarbodiimide trade name BioadimideTM on thermal and mechanical characteristics of PLA at high processing temperatures for blending with polyamide 6 (PA6). They illustrated that when processing temperatures were increased, the processed PLA’s molecular weight (Mw) tended to decrease, and its molecular weight distribution (MWD) shifted towards to lower molecular weights zone, whereas Mw of chain extended PLA increased, and MWD displayed bimodal distribution and shifted slightly towards to higher molecular weight zone. Epoxy chain extenders are commonly used to improve the interfacial compatibilization of bio-polyesters The production process plays a crucial role in determining the effectiveness of the chain extender. Soleymani Eil Bakhtiari et al. evaluated the effect of an epoxy chain extender on PLA-PBAT blends produced via film extrusion, compression molding and injection molding. The most effective compatibilization was achieved when the chain extender was pre-mixed with either PLA or PBAT using single-screw extrusion. However, reactive extrusion is more commonly carried out with twin-screw extruders [8]. The presence of mixing elements in twin-screw extruders facilitates a uniform melt composition through the combined effects of distributive and dispersive mixing [9]. In addition, the shear rate achievable in a twin-screw extruder is higher than that in a single-screw extruder [10]. The potential for producing compatibilized PLA-PHBH blends with an epoxy chain extender was previously investigated by Zhou et al. The incorporation of the chain extender increased the elongation at break and impact strength of the PHBH/PLA blends, promoted a uniform distribution of the polymeric phases, and reduced the particle size of the dispersed phase [11]. The price of bioplastics is generally higher than that of fossil-based polymer. The price of PLA, among the least expensive bio-polymers, is around 2.3-2.9 $/kg while the price of PHBH can reach up to 6 €/kg. Currently, most single-use trays are made of polypropylene or polystyrene, whose market prices are around 1-1.6 €/kg, significantly lower than those of bioplastics. This cost disparity remains one of the main barriers to the large-scale industrial adoption of these polymers [12]. Over time, the optimization of the production process and the improvement of production technologies can lead to a decrease in the cost of these materials and potentially meet market demands [13]. A well-known strategy to reduce product cost is the incorporation of mineral fillers into formulations. Beyond cost reduction, fillers are also used in the packaging industry to improve processability [14] and to enhance certain mechanical properties, such as stiffness and strength ([15]). Additionally, PHBH has a very slow crystallization rate and requires nucleating agents to enhance its processability. Talc exhibits excellent nucleating properties for conventional polymers and can increase the crystallization rate of a wide range of polyhydroxyalkanoates [16]. For potential industrialization and scale-up, reducing thermal crystallization time is a key factor in improving production efficiency ([17]). The extrusion of polyhydroxyalkanoates requires careful control of processing parameters, as their degradation temperature is close to their melting point, making them susceptible to chain scission [18]. PHBH exhibits a broader processing window compared to other polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs), due to the presence of 3HH units, which also reduce crystallinity and enhance flexibility [19]. However, the shear stress generated during twin-screw extrusion can further reduce the molecular weight of polyhydroxyalkanoates [20]. The introduction of mineral fillers at high concentrations increases overall shear stress during extrusion. Post et al. reported a significant decrease in the molecular weight of PHBH when compounded with talc or calcium carbonate [12]. In this context, the use of a reactive epoxy chain extender may also help mitigate the degradation of bio-polyesters during extrusion [21], in addition to compatibilizing different polymer phases. At the same time, the use of a chain extender has a detrimental effect on the cycle time, as it decreases the crystallization rate [22]. Future developments of this research field may concern the study of the combined effect of chain extender and talc in PLA/PHBH compounds through the use of micromechanical models [23-25]. The present study investigates the combined effects of reactive epoxy chain extenders and mineral fillers on PLA-PHBH blends, with the aim of assessing their suitability for producing single-use trays via thermoforming. The blends were compounded using twin-screw extrusion, followed by cast film production and thermoforming. The functional properties of the resulting products were then evaluated. In view of industrialization, the main requirements are a cost lower than €0.03 per tray, equivalent to polypropylene, a cycle time shorter than 5 s, and greater than 90% PHBH molecular-weight retention after processing at 150°C. Talc acts as a strong nucleating agent [16] and increases thermal diffusivity [26], thereby reducing cooling times and shortening the thermoforming cycle. The chain extender blocks terminal acid groups and stabilizes PHBH [27], maintaining molecular weight provided that the moisture content remains below 250-300 ppm and the residence time stays under 3 min. Polypropylene (PP) costs €1.5/kg, and a typical tray weighs 20 g. To achieve the same cost per tray, the mass of the bioplastic blend must be less than 13 g, assuming a blend cost of ~€2.3/kg. A 30%-35% weight reduction is technically achievable if the processability of the sheet is confirmed at low thicknesses, since 20% talc doubles the flexural modulus of the blend compared to neat PLA [28].
PLA is an excellent candidate for blown film products such as carry-out bags, wrapping films, and waste bags/bin liners. The blown film process requires polymer melts to exhibit a certain level of melt strength as well as nonlinear viscoelastic properties like strain hardening. However, PLA exhibits low melt strength and does not show strain hardening behavior. Long-chain branching or a small fraction of high-molecular-weight polymer can be introduced to neat PLA to improve these rheological properties.2, 3 Chain extenders have been widely used to improve the rheological properties of polyesters by reacting with either the carboxylic acid and/or hydroxyl end groups. For example, diisocyanates have proven to be an effective chain extender of PLA and improve its rheological properties.4, 5 However, the toxicity of isocyanates as well as the high propensity to form gels have limited its application. Epoxy-based chain extenders, like the one used in this study, can increase the molecular weight of polyesters and introduce long-chain branching.6-12 These chain extenders can be available in both solid and liquid forms allowing for easier processing. They show low toxicity and can be introduced via reactive extrusion. The chemistry involves reaction of the carboxylic acid or the hydroxyl chain ends of PLA with its epoxy groups to form an ether or an ester linkage.13-16 Very few studies have focused on the reactivity difference between the hydroxyl and carboxylic acid chain ends. In the need to prevent undesirable cross-linking, previous studies have “avoided” using high concentrations of chain extenders. The epoxy-based chain extender used in this study is a copolymer consisting of styrene, acrylic, and glycidyl methacrylate blocks. There are multiple poly(glycidyl methacrylate) blocks per polymer chain and these blocks contain primary epoxide rings which make it an excellent modifier for fast processes such as reactive extrusion. In this study, we exploit the reactivity difference between the carboxylic acid and the hydroxyl end groups of PLA to synthesize epoxy functionalized PLA (EF-PLA) molecules by reaction with a multifunctional epoxy polymer (MEP). Model compound studies helped establish the reactivity difference between the end groups, and the process parameters driving the chemistry. A series of EF-PLA compounds containing 1-10% MEP content were prepared with no gel formation. These new epoxy modified PLA polymers function not only as chain extenders but also as rheology modifiers and compatibilizers in PLA and other biodegradable polyesters to give resin formulations that have the required melt strength and strain hardening properties to be blown into films and foams. Molecular weight and rheological studies are presented to help understand and establish the improved properties and processability. A statistical simulation was created to model the properties of the EF-PLA materials at various MEP content, to support the results presented. PLA 3051D resin pellets with a molecular weight of ∼130,000 and 8% meso-lactide content were purchased from NatureWorks, LLC (NE, USA). The MEP (Joncryl 4368F) was purchased from BASF (MI, USA). Reagent grade stearic acid and Poly(ethylene glycol) with a molecular weight of 400 were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (MO, USA).
The chain end groups, carboxylic acid, in PLA and PBAT are often used for reactive extrusion with chain extenders for compatibilization.13 For example, 2,2′-(1,3-phenylene)bis(2-oxazoline) and phthalic acid were used in tandem in a PLA/PBAT (80/20, wt. %) blend demonstrated high strain (516%) and high strength (45.3 MPa). The increased interfacial adhesion between PLA and PBAT, as well as a decrease in the crystallinity of the blend was attributed to the enhanced mechanical performance. Furthermore, trans-esterification of PLA/PBAT via 0.4 wt. % tetrabutyl titanate led to a PLA/PBAT (70/30, wt. %) blend demonstrating high strength and elongation through enhanced interface compatibility.14 PLA and PBAT blends were also compatibilized using cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs). CNCs had stronger thermodynamical affinity towards the PBAT phase, while with higher CNC loadings (3 wt. % and 5 wt. %), the CNCs were found mainly at the interface and in the PLA phase. This led to an appreciable Young's modulus for the composite but low extension at break of 4% for 5 wt. % CNC loading.15 In other work, Cardolite®NC-514, a bio-based epoxy-cardanol pre-polymer (ECP) was used for compatibilizing PLA/PBAT blends. It was observed that the ECP content of less than 3 wt. % could effectively compatibilize the blend and showed significant improvement in elongation at break and a slight increment in tensile strength compared to the non-compatibilized blends. The ECP showed better interfacial compatibilization for PLA/PBAT blends than for Joncryl ADR 4300 (a multi- functional epoxy chain extender by BASF) for the same concentration.16 Abdelwahab et al. used glycidyl methacrylate monomer as a toughening agent for PLA and organosolv lignin based polymer blends. It was observed that by blending glycidyl methacrylate with PLA, the elongation at break was enhanced from 3.3% to 401%.17 This result suggests that epoxy-based compatibilizers may also work for compatibilizing PGA and PBAT blends. In this work, we investigate the compatibilization of EMA-GMA, a commercial terpolymer of ethylene, methyl acrylate, and glycidyl methacrylate for PGA/PBAT (50/50, wt. %) blends prepared by melt-extrusion. The phase morphology, rheology, thermal and mechanical properties were studied, the moisture and oxygen barrier performance evaluated at 23°C and 65% RH and, 23°C, 0% and 50% RH, respectively. The results revealed that these blends were effectively compatibilized and can be suitably used in flexible packaging films.

Epoxy-functionalized chain extenders like Joncryl® play a **multifunctional role** in PLA/PBAT blends by:  
1. **Compatibilization**: Reacting with terminal carboxyl/hydroxyl groups of PLA and PBAT to form **non-linear copolymers** (e.g., PLA-co-PBAT) at the interface, reducing phase separation and refining morphology [1], [2], [5]. This enhances interfacial adhesion and stress transfer, improving mechanical properties like toughness and elongation at break [2], [10].  
2. **Melt strength enhancement**: Introducing long-chain branching or cross-linking in PLA via epoxy reactions, which improves rheological properties (e.g., strain hardening) critical for processing methods like blown film extrusion [1], [9], [11].  
3. **Thermal stability**: Stabilizing PLA against thermal degradation by reconnecting broken chains during melt processing [1], [7].  
4. **Crystallization modulation**: Increasing nuclei density in PLA, enhancing crystallizability and heat resistance [1], [5].  
5. **Degradation mitigation**: Reducing hydrolytic degradation during processing by blocking reactive terminal acid groups of polyesters like PLA and PBAT [8], [13].  

The epoxy groups in Joncryl® enable these effects through covalent bonding with polymer end groups, creating interfacial bridges and branched architectures without gelation at optimal concentrations [1], [2], [5].

Multifunctional epoxy-based chain extenders such as Joncryl® ADR 4368 (Joncryl) have been shown to help alter the topology of PLA from linear to a non-linear long chain branched PLA. This has the effect of tremendously improving the melt strength [30], [31], improving thermal stability [32], and increasing nuclei density and thus the crystallizability of PLA [33], [34], [35], [36]. More importantly, the addition of Joncryl could compatibilize PLA with other polymers such as PBAT [37], [38]. Joncryl is a styrene-acrylic multifunctional oligomer chain extender that was designed to reverse the degradation of condensation polymers [39] and has epoxy as the functional group, which would react with the terminal carboxyl and hydroxyl. The present work reports on the development of new PLA-based blend material with significantly superior qualities. PBSA, environmentally benign biodegradable polyester, chemically synthesized by polycondensation of 1,4-butanediol with succinic and adipic acids [40] was used as a model soft polymer to confer PLA with toughness. Joncryl was used to not only compatibilize PLA/PBSA blends but also to improve the thermal stability, melt strength and crystallizability of the PLA. It was hypothesized that at the interphase of the two polymers, there are in situ generated copolymers, which are non-linear due to the multi-functionality of the Joncryl. The objective of the study was to demonstrate the role played by the intricate non-linear copolymer interfacial architecture in controlling a vast number of properties of the resultant blend material, including super-toughening, unique morphology and melt flow behavior. The PLA used in the study was of a commercial grade (PLA 2002D) and was obtained from Natureworks, LLC (USA). The PLA had a d-isomer content of approximately 4%, a density of 1.24 g/cm3, a glass transition temperature Tg of approximately 60 °C and a melting temperature Tm of approximately 153 °C. According to the supplier, it had Mw = 190 kg/mol, density = 1.23 g/cm3 (ASTM 1238), Tg = −43.8 °C and Tm = 83.1 °C (first) and 94.5 °C (second). The multi-functional oligomeric chain extender used in the study, Joncryl® ADR 4368 CS, was kindly donated by BASF, South Africa. The mechanism underlying the enhancement of chemical reaction capacity lies in the melt blending of the chain extender or crosslinker with PBAT and PLA. Through chemical reactions, chemical bonds are formed among the components of the copolymer. This process effectively improves the adhesion and compatibility at the two-phase interface of PLA and PBAT [22]. Currently, the epoxy chain extender is the most widely used type of chain extender, such as chain extender of Joncryl® series (ADR) [23], glycidyl methacrylate polymer [24], epoxy soybean oil (ESO) [25], etc. Specifically, ADR series chain extenders consist of aromatic vinyl monomers (e.g., ethylene, styrene (St)) and acrylate monomers (e.g., glycidyl methacrylate (GMA)). The aromatic vinyl monomers serve as the structural backbone units, while the acrylate monomers supply active epoxy groups. These epoxy groups can chemically react with the end hydroxyl group and end carboxyl group of the polymer to form a cross-linked structure, effectively improving the compatibility of the polymer matrix. For examples, Li et al. [26] explored the effect of ADR chain extender (ADR-4370F) on the physical properties of PLA/PBAT blend; when ADR-4370F content was 0.15 phr, the elongation at break of PLA/PBAT blend rose from 23.5 % to 410.3 %. Han et al. [27] found that ESO could react with end groups of polymers to enhance compatibility; the elongation at break and the gap impact strength of PLA/PBAT blend containing 5 phr ESO were significantly increased. However, these traditional chain extenders lack biodegradability. Despite their ability to effectively enhance the mechanical properties of polymer blends, they have an adverse impact on the biodegradability of PBAT/PLA blends [28]. In this work, a biodegradable epoxy-based terpolymer (SHG), which consisted of GMA (serving as the source of active epoxy groups), 1,6-hexadiol diacrylate (HDDA; providing the ester groups), and St (functioning as the structural backbone units), was synthesized via the solution polymerization method. With this design, the SHG, which integrated both biodegradability and high reactivity, was employed as a reactive interface compatibilizer or chain extender of PBAT/PLA blends. The effects of polymerization reaction duration, the molar ratio of monomer, and amount of chain transfer agent on copolymer conversion, molecular weight, and epoxy value were investigated in detail. The effect of SHG on the interface compatibility, strength, toughness, heat resistance and processability of PBAT/PLA blends was explored, and its strengthening/toughening mechanisms were also investigated. PLA (2003D; density: 1.24 g/cm3; weight-average molecular weight (Mw): 217000 g/mol; d-isomer content: approximately 4.4 %; melt flow rate (MFR): 7 g/10 min at 210 °C) and PBAT (801T; density: 1.23 g/cm3; Mw: 126000 g/mol; MFR: 5 g/10 min at 190 °C) were sourced from Nature Works (USA) and Tunhe Polyester Co., LTD. (China), respectively.
The effects of ethylene-vinyl acetate copolymer (EVA) and multi-component epoxy chain expander (ADR) on the performance of PLA/PBAT blend were investigated by preparing PLA/PBAT/EVA blends and PLA/PBAT/EVA/ADR blends through melt blending method. The mechanical properties, morphology, thermal behavior, and rheological properties were studied. The addition of EVA had a slight improvement on the impact strength of PLA, while the tensile strength had a decrease and elongation at break had significant increase. The microstructure of PLA/PBAT/EVA also showed a sea-island morphology, the EVA had a small impact on the rheological property of PLA/PBAT blend. When introduced ADR in the PLA/PBAT/EVA blend, the morphology showed that the interface interaction of the blends was been significantly improved. As a result, the rheological property, including the complex viscosity, storage modulus and loss modulus increased remarkably compared with PLA. The impact strength of PLA/PBAT/EVA/ADR blends had a significant improvement, the highest impact strength reaches 51.99 kJ/m2, which is 22.3 times higher than that of PLA. Furthermore, the PLA/PBAT/EVA/ADR blends also showed an improved of heat resistance and thermostability compared with PLA. In light of the substantial environmental repercussions associated with the production of conventional petroleum-based polymers, there has been a burgeoning interest in biodegradable polymers derived from renewable resources. These biomaterials are held in high esteem for their environmentally beneficial characteristics [1-4]. Among these, polylactic acid (PLA) has emerged as one of the most extensively studied polymers in the current year, owing to its remarkable tensile strength, favorable processability, and biocompatibility. PLA is mainly produced from renewable resources such as sugarcane, potatoes, or maize, which makes it sustainable [5, 6]. Notwithstanding these beneficial attributes, the inherent brittleness of PLA poses limitations on its application in various domains [7-9]. To mitigate the shortcomings associated with PLA, poly (atopic acid)/butylene terephthalate (PBAT) has been identified as a highly viable toughening agent, characterized by significant elongation at break and low modulus of elasticity, akin to the properties observed in thermoplastic elastomers. Consequently, PLA and PBAT are perceived as complementary materials [10, 11]. However, the pronounced discrepancy in solubility parameters between PLA and PBAT results in suboptimal interfacial adhesion within the resultant blends; thus, achieving robust interfacial compatibility between PLA and PBAT is critical for obtaining composites with superior properties. In this context, reactive blending stands out as one of the most effective and convenient methodologies [12, 13]. Chain extenders are multifunctional additives that bind to the ends of different macromolecular fragments, thereby increasing the average molar mass of the polymer, and can also be used as reactive bulking agents in the blends. The use of chain extenders in blends promotes the formation of copolymers in the molten state. In this framework, Joncryl ADR-4468 is utilized as a chain extender due to its abundance of epoxy groups [14, 15].

These findings gave important implications for designing and manufacturing polymer packaging materials. The large use of plastics in the packaging industry is increasing the interest in using biodegradable polymers to replace conventional polymers in order to reduce the environmental pollution caused by the inappropriate disposal of conventional polymers.1, 2 Development of consumer products from biodegradable and renewable materials is currently an area of great interest for researchers.3 Poly(lactide acid) (PLA) has become one of the most promising biodegradable polymers due to its excellent properties, such as nontoxicity, easy processability, gas permeability, fully biodegradation within a few weeks, high mechanical strength, and transparency.4-6 According to these advantages, it can be used for different applications such as drug delivery system, food container, resorbable, automobile, and film packaging.7-9 However, PLA's weak melt strength due to its highly linear structure hinders its use in blown film applications.10 Another inherent weakness such as inherent brittleness, narrow processing window, low thermal stability, and high price in comparison with polyolefins limits their large scale applications.11, 12 To overcome these drawbacks, the processability of film blowing and the mechanical properties of the PLA can be improved through copolymerization or blending with other polymers.13-16 Melt-blending PLA in an extruder with other flexible polymers is an excellent method to modify PLA. Environmental pollution poses a serious challenge to sustainable development, with packaging waste in landfills contributing significantly to environmental harm. The development of biodegradable polymers from renewable sources is seen as an effective solution to plastic waste, and their adoption as a substitute for petroleum-based plastics is increasingly recognized worldwide.[1-4] The problem of white pollution caused by conventional non-biodegradable plastics has attracted global concern for decades.[5-7] In response, many countries are now actively encouraging the use of eco-friendly polymers. The adoption of biodegradable polymers is widely regarded as an effective solution to this issue.[8-11] Polylactic acid (PLA) and polybutylene adipate-co-terephthalate (PBAT) are two of the most widely studied biodegradable polymers due to their complementary properties. PLA, a bio-based polyester, is characterized by its high stiffness, strength, and biodegradability, but suffers from inherent brittleness and poor flexibility.[3, 12-15] In contrast, PBAT, a synthetic aliphatic-aromatic copolyester, exhibits excellent ductility and flexibility but lacks sufficient mechanical strength for high-performance applications. To overcome these individual limitations, blending PLA and PBAT has been explored as an effective approach to developing balanced biodegradable materials with improved mechanical properties, biodegradability, and processability.[9, 16-20] Despite the potential of PLA/PBAT blends, the inherent immiscibility between PLA and PBAT due to their different polarities and molecular structures results in poor interfacial adhesion, leading to phase-separated morphologies with compromised mechanical properties.[9, 21, 22] Therefore, compatibilization strategies have been widely investigated to enhance the interfacial interaction between these polymers, ensuring improved mechanical performance and structural stability.[23] Compatibilization affects polymer blends through two key mechanisms: i) preventing droplet coalescence and ii) lowering interfacial tension, both leading to reduced droplet sizes. These effects are most pronounced when the compatibilizer is located at the interface.[24, 25] In the absence of compatibilizers, polymer blend properties are notably inferior to those of the individual polymers. Common compatibilization strategies include i) non-reactive approaches using co-solvents or copolymers, ii) reactive methods that create copolymers in situ, and iii) nanofiller-assisted techniques incorporating small amounts of nanofillers. The selection of a method depends on factors such as cost, performance, recyclability, and biodegradability.[26-28] One common route involves the use of reactive compatibilizers, such as multifunctional chain extenders, which promote in situ reactions between PLA and PBAT to improve interfacial adhesion.[16, 29-31] Among these, epoxide-based chain extenders like Joncryl have been extensively studied for their ability to react with carboxyl (─COOH) and hydroxyl (─OH) groups, extending polymer chains and reducing phase separation.[16, 29, 32] Research has demonstrated that incorporating various types of Joncryl ADR, such as 4468, 4368, and 4370, into PLA/PBAT blends enhances tensile strength, elongation at break, and impact resistance. These improvements are attributed to better interfacial adhesion and an increase in molecular weight due to chain extension. For example, Wang et al.[33] developed high-strength, high-toughness PLA/PBAT (60/40) blends using a melt-reactive blending approach. By introducing Joncryl ADR-4370S as a compatibilizer through an in situ compatibilization reaction, its epoxy groups and the terminal carboxyl and hydroxyl groups of PLA and PBAT, forming a PLA-g-PBAT copolymer linking the two segments. This reaction notably reduced the interfacial tension between the phases. They achieved enhanced mechanical properties across all blends.[33] In another study, Al-Itry et al.[34] evaluated the effect of multifunctional epoxide (Joncryl;ADR-4368) on the interfacial properties of biopolymer blends based on PLA/PBAT. The results indicated a decrease in interfacial tension in the modified/compatibilized PLA/PBAT blend and the formation of the PLA-Joncryl-PBAT copolymer, leading to enhanced mechanical properties.[34] Arruda et al.[16] studied the influence of Joncryl ADR 4368 on PLA/PBAT blend and found that for the 60 PLA blend, the addition of a chain extender resulted in a 900% increase in elongation at break compared to the 60PLA blend without it. Additionally, it exhibited a 1200% increase relative to neat PLA, significantly enhancing ductility. Moreover, in the 60 PLA blends containing a chain extender, the dispersed phase was refined, transitioning from coarse sheets or platelets to elongated PBAT fibrils. This morphological transformation is likely responsible for the increased elongation at break. Additionally, a notable enhancement in stress at break was observed, rising from 22.3 MPa (without a chain extender) to 34-35 MPa with its addition.[16] However, the effectiveness of Joncryl in modifying PLA/PBAT blends is highly dependent on processing conditions. Previous research has primarily focused on single-step blending methods, where all components are processed simultaneously. While this method can enhance interfacial adhesion to some extent, limitations such as incomplete reactions and phase inhomogeneity still persist.

Through SEM and mechanical property tests, it is found that the addition of ADR makes the molecular chain form a micro-crosslinked structure, thereby improving the tensile strength of PLA. Nowadays, with the goal of “Carbon neutrality, carbon footprint” and the promulgation of a “plastic ban order”, it is urgent to develop easily degradable materials with excellent comprehensive performance.1-4 In recent years, polylactic acid (PLA) has obtained increasing attention because of their excellent mechanical properties, outstanding biocompatibility and good biodegradability.5 Besides, it does not use oil, and other chemical raw materials. Epoxy chain extenders are commonly used to improve the interfacial compatibilization of bio-polyesters The production process plays a crucial role in determining the effectiveness of the chain extender. Soleymani Eil Bakhtiari et al. evaluated the effect of an epoxy chain extender on PLA-PBAT blends produced via film extrusion, compression molding and injection molding. The most effective compatibilization was achieved when the chain extender was pre-mixed with either PLA or PBAT using single-screw extrusion. However, reactive extrusion is more commonly carried out with twin-screw extruders [8]. The presence of mixing elements in twin-screw extruders facilitates a uniform melt composition through the combined effects of distributive and dispersive mixing [9]. In addition, the shear rate achievable in a twin-screw extruder is higher than that in a single-screw extruder [10]. The potential for producing compatibilized PLA-PHBH blends with an epoxy chain extender was previously investigated by Zhou et al. The incorporation of the chain extender increased the elongation at break and impact strength of the PHBH/PLA blends, promoted a uniform distribution of the polymeric phases, and reduced the particle size of the dispersed phase [11]. The price of bioplastics is generally higher than that of fossil-based polymer. The price of PLA, among the least expensive bio-polymers, is around 2.3-2.9 $/kg while the price of PHBH can reach up to 6 €/kg. Currently, most single-use trays are made of polypropylene or polystyrene, whose market prices are around 1-1.6 €/kg, significantly lower than those of bioplastics. This cost disparity remains one of the main barriers to the large-scale industrial adoption of these polymers [12]. Over time, the optimization of the production process and the improvement of production technologies can lead to a decrease in the cost of these materials and potentially meet market demands [13]. A well-known strategy to reduce product cost is the incorporation of mineral fillers into formulations. Beyond cost reduction, fillers are also used in the packaging industry to improve processability [14] and to enhance certain mechanical properties, such as stiffness and strength ([15]). Additionally, PHBH has a very slow crystallization rate and requires nucleating agents to enhance its processability. Talc exhibits excellent nucleating properties for conventional polymers and can increase the crystallization rate of a wide range of polyhydroxyalkanoates [16]. For potential industrialization and scale-up, reducing thermal crystallization time is a key factor in improving production efficiency ([17]). The extrusion of polyhydroxyalkanoates requires careful control of processing parameters, as their degradation temperature is close to their melting point, making them susceptible to chain scission [18]. PHBH exhibits a broader processing window compared to other polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs), due to the presence of 3HH units, which also reduce crystallinity and enhance flexibility [19]. However, the shear stress generated during twin-screw extrusion can further reduce the molecular weight of polyhydroxyalkanoates [20]. The introduction of mineral fillers at high concentrations increases overall shear stress during extrusion. Post et al. reported a significant decrease in the molecular weight of PHBH when compounded with talc or calcium carbonate [12]. In this context, the use of a reactive epoxy chain extender may also help mitigate the degradation of bio-polyesters during extrusion [21], in addition to compatibilizing different polymer phases. At the same time, the use of a chain extender has a detrimental effect on the cycle time, as it decreases the crystallization rate [22]. Chain extenders have been proposed to be added during processing of PLA so as to minimize the drop of molecular weight through reconstructing the low-molecular weight PLA chains induced by the degradation, and combining the cleavage chains by reacting with terminal carboxyl and hydroxyl groups of the PLA. Three main groups of chain extenders have been suggested for PLA processing stabilization: multifunctional epoxides,17, 18 polycarbodiimide,17, 19 and phosphites.20, 21 Joncryl ADR (styrene-glycidyl acrylate copolymer) which consists of 3-9 epoxide groups, is one of the most widely used chain extenders for PLA. With the addition of 1 wt% Joncryl, the loss of molecular weight of PLA during processing successfully reduced.17, 21-23 The PLA with branching or crosslink structure was possibly formed as a result of chain extension reaction.18 Polycarbodiimides have also been examined and they are recommended as good chain extender for durable PLA but should be avoided in the applications that require fast degradation. Porfyris and coworkers compared the influence of carbodiimides and epoxide-based chain extenders on the PLA hydrolysis reaction and found that all aliphatic and aromatic carbodiimide-based additives restricted the hydrolysis reaction of amorphous grade PLA efficiently.23 Phosphites are extensively used in a large scale as stabilizers to prevent transesterification during melt processing of several polymers such as poly (butylene terephthalate)24 and poly (ethylene terephthalate).25-27 They are also commonly used in combination with hindered phenols for stabilizing poly(amide 6) composites28 and polyolefins.29, 30 In addition, phosphites are capable of limiting the color development that is induced during processing of polyolefins.31 The influence of triphenyl phosphite (TPP) on chain extension and oxidation stability of PLA in the melt processing has been discussed in literature.20 The addition of 2 wt% TPP increased the molecular weight of PLA up to 50%, however, as the amount of TPP increased to 3 wt% the stabilization dropped.20 Some studies have focused on the efficacy of tris(nonylphenyl) phosphite (TNPP) on stabilizing the molecular weight of PLA. Specifically, at the temperature above the glass transition but below the melting temperature (Tm), the effect of phosphites on the degradation characteristics of PLA is not well studied. Hence, this study aims to explore the effect of phosphite structure on thermal stabilization of PLA during melt processing in a twin-screw extruder, and its impact on hydrolytic degradation ability of compressed PLA film products. Furthermore, the crystallization and mechanical behaviors of the stabilized PLA in terms of tensile and flexural properties are also discussed.
