IntroductionPoly(lactic acid) (PLA) is a biopolymer from renewable agricultural resources which is on the expectation to substitute petroleum-based polymers, due to its physico-chemical properties such as high modulus, strength, thermoplasticity, as well as the easy processability to create various types of products. However, the fact that PLA is brittle due to its slow crystallization behavior, the improvement of PLA-based product is still required. As the crystallization of PLA in terms of the rate and the extent of crystallization can be enhanced by nucleating agents, the mechanical properties can be improved whereas the cycle period in injection molding processes becomes shorten [1], [2]. Nucleating agents are typically either low molecular weight organic or inorganic additives. Talc is a good inorganic nucleating agent for crystallization of polycaprolactone [3], [4], poly(ethylene terephthalate) [5], and PLA [6], [7], [8], as evidenced from a decrease of crystallization temperature upon heating as well as a decrease in spherulite size. Jiang et al. [9] investigated the crystallization behavior of PLA nanocomposites with montmorillonite clay and found the crystallization temperature (Tc) was shifted to lower temperature leading to an enhanced crystallinity. For organic nucleating agents, Nam et al. [10] reported that aliphatic amide such as N,N′-ethylenebis(12-hydroxystearamide) increased an overall crystallization rate of PLA whereas the average spherulite size was found to decrease as the number of nuclei increased. Blending PLA with other polymers can also modify the crystallization behavior. For example poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) [11], poly(butylene succinate) [12], and poly(ethylene oxide) [13] shifted the cold crystallization temperature of PLA to lower temperature and increased the crystallization rate. Stereocomplexation between PLLA and PDLA is accepted as the most effective methods to enhance the thermal properties of PLA-based materials [14], [15], [16]. Dendritic hyperbranched polymer (DHP) was reported about its nucleation effect as it significantly increased crystallization rate and crystallinity of PLA and simultaneously improved mechanical properties [17]. Although various nucleating agents for PLA were reported, most still showed phase separation with PLA. In addition, the price is also the condition for the practical nucleating agents.It should be noted that the organic molecules with a certain chain length such as dibenzoylhydrazide compounds [18] or carboxylamide derivatives [19] were reported for enhancement of crystallization of PLA. This leads us to an idea of short chain polymer to initiate the crystallization of PLA. Here, we consider the multi-branched short chain PLLA (m-PLLAs) as an effective nucleating agent which not only can be expected for the acceleration of PLA crystallization in multi-directions but also the good miscibility with PLA. Up to the present, only few reports are about the synthesis of the m-PLLA. For example, Miao et al. [20] reported the preparation of m-PLLA in star form using carbohydrate derivatives as the multi-functional cores. Hao et al. studied the syntheses of 3- to 6-armed star PLLA with natural sugar alcohols of glycerol, erythritol, xylitol, and sorbitol as initiators [21]. It should be noted that all of those star PLLAs were prepared through a ring-opening polymerization of l-lactide. In this work, l-lactic acid was applied as the monomer to prepare poly(lactic acid) via polycondensation. We propose a simple preparation of m-PLLAs by using core molecules containing multi-functional groups for the functionalization with l-LA. The use of succinic acid (SA), malic acid (MA), and citric acid (CA) allows us to vary the branch number for two, three, and four, respectively (Scheme 1). Microcellular injection molding, which employs a supercritical fluid (SCF; usually nitrogen or carbon dioxide) as a physical blowing agent, can fabricate lightweight, dimensionally stable plastic parts while using less material and energy [1], [2], [3]. The SCF is capable of plasticizing the polymer, as well as decreasing its melt viscosity and processing temperature. In the microcellular injection molding process, supercritical CO2 or N2 is accurately metered into the barrel and quickly dissolves into the polymer melt to form a single-phase polymer/gas solution due to the high shear generated by the screw. Upon injection, the thermodynamic instability triggers homogeneous and/or heterogeneous cell nucleation, followed by cell growth that helps foamed parts to fill the entire mold cavity. Micro- and nano-fillers (e.g., nanoclay [4], talc [5], [6]) are sometimes used as nucleating agents to refine and stabilize the cell structure, which can enhance the tensile strength and modulus, and even the toughness and impact strength, as a result of a synergistic effect of combining the microcellular process with nanofillers. Cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) are a new class of biorenewable nanofillers that hold promise as a nucleating agent for micro-cellular injection molding. CNCs are derived from native cellulose, an abundant polysaccharide that is the main structural component of trees, plants, and marine creatures like tunicates, certain bacteria, and algae [7]. CNCs have great potential as biorenewable fillers for polymers due to their abundance in nature and their high mechanical performance. They are prepared by hydrolyzing amorphous cellulose with concentrated acid while leaving behind the crystalline portions. This results in a highly crystalline, high modulus fiber, which is not surprising given that the modulus of native cellulose I crystals is typically about 138 GPa [8]. The actual modulus of the CNCs depends on the source of the cellulose and the specifics of the extraction method. In addition to high mechanical performance, CNCs have been found to nucleate biodegradable polymers with relatively low melting temperatures like poly(ε-caprolactone) [9] through the microcellular foaming process.

Plastics are synthetic polymer compounds made substantially from petrochemical materials extracted from coal, oil, and natural gas.[1] In general, fossil fuel plastics achieve high mechanical and fluid barrier properties by packing their chains into specific crystalline and amorphous regions. However, its hydrophobic and long-chain structural features make it lack bio-accessible organic chemical groups, limiting the ability of microorganisms to break them down.[2] The accumulation of fossil fuel plastics in the environment has severely affected soil quality, the aquatic environment, flora, and fauna.[3] The depletion of fossil fuels and environmental pollution have prompted researchers to develop eco-friendly biodegradable polymers to replace petrochemical-based polymers. In this context, bioplastics appear as a promising alternative. A bioplastic is often considered bio-based and/or biodegradable material[4, 5] such as polyvinyl alcohol, polylactic acid, polybutylene succinate, as well as carbohydrate derivatives and blends based on protein, starch, chitin, and cellulose. The global market size for bioplastics is considered to burgeon every day. The global production capacity of bioplastics in 2023 was ≈2.18 million tonnes, which is projected to expand to 7.43 million tonnes by 2028.[6] This shows that bioplastics have great application value and development prospects in various fields of modern society. Currently, PLA is the most important among the biobased biodegradable plastics because of its zero toxicity, biodegradability, and good mechanical attributes.[7] PLA is produced by the polymerization of lactides or lactic acid monomers fermented from starch, mainly used in 3D printing, food packaging, transport, agriculture, and textile industries.[8] Upon biodegradation, PLA releases CO2, water, and decomposed organic matter without leaving any visible and toxic residues.[7] These substances are absorbed by plants, thus imparting less carbon footprint. Although, compared to fossil fuel plastics, neat PLA has some disadvantages such as brittleness and low crystallization rate, which restricts commercial usage.[9] The mechanical performance of PLA is greatly affected by the crystallinity degree, which depends on the source and processing conditions.[10, 11] For example, the oriented samples of PLA were prepared by being heated and mechanically drawn, the tensile strength and crystallinity increased significantly with the increase in draw ratio.[12] In addition, there is also a study on increasing the crystallinity of PLA by adding nucleating agents (Zinc PhenylPhosphonate, Ecopromote, and EcopromoteHD) to improve its mechanical properties.[13] Heterogeneous nucleation is a frequently encountered phenomenon in the crystallization of composite systems.[14] By adding inorganic compounds,[15] polysaccharide polymers,[16] carbon-based materials,[17] and other substances[18] as nucleation sites, the heterogeneous nucleation rate of the matrix can be effectively promoted.[19] For instance, lignin was used as a heterogeneous nucleating agent to increase the crystallinity of PLA, which also results in the enhancements of PLA tensile strength and gas barrier properties.[20] However, the heterogeneous nucleation effect of proteins as nucleating agents is rarely reported. Blending the protein with biodegradable synthetic polymers has been shown to be an effective strategy to improve performances,[21-23] but whether this is related to nucleation effects still remains unclear. Proteins are commonly used for biocomposite materials owing to their abundance, biodegradability, low price, and better film development capability. In 2023, worldwide protein meal production reached 369.79 million metric tons, of which ≈4% were cottonseed meal.[24] Cottonseed meal is one of the most important sources of plant protein, but little research has been carried out on its high value-added value, especially cottonseed protein bioplastics. According to the report, cottonseed proteins (CP) have almost the same primary amino acid components as soy protein.[25] The excellent processing properties and plasticizer efficiency make CP a smart choice for bioplastic production.[26] Nevertheless, hydrophobic PLA is incompatible with amphiphilic CP, so interfacial compatibility between PLA and CP needs to be improved by adding compatibilizers. MA is typically used as a compatibilizer agent.[27] MA is highly reactive with a variety of polymer chains and biomacromolecules such as proteins, lipids, and glucose, increasing the polarity of the thermoplastic polymer for better adhesion with biofillers that have polar groups on their surfaces.[28]

The development of sustainable and environmentally benign polymers from renewable feedstocks is important to reduce the dependence of most engineering and commodity plastics on fossil-based resources [[36], [37], [38]]. Moreover, the global shift from reusable containment and packaging to single-use contributed to an extraordinary growth in the plastics market [39]. For instance, the global plastic production reached about 407 million tonnes in 2017 [39]. The most extensively produced commodity plastics such as low density poly (ethylene) (LDPE), linear low density poly (ethylene) (LLDPE), high density poly (ethylene) (HDPE), poly (propylene) (PP), poly (ethylene terephthalate) (PET), poly (styrene) (PS) and poly (vinyl chloride) (PVC) constitute close to 70% of the overall production as shown in Fig. 3a [39]. Overall, about 38% of all plastics produced are employed in packaging applications (Fig. 3b), mainly because of the appealing cost structure and excellent packaging attributes of plastics [40] over other materials such as metals or glasses. In addition to their prevalent use, the stable carbon - carbon bond in the backbone of most of these polyolefin and polyolefin derivative plastics that withstand biodegradation, resulted in a tremendous increase in the share of plastics in municipal solid waste. In middle - and high income - countries, plastic waste increase was estimated from less than 1% in 1960 to more than 10% by 2005 [39,41]. The geographic distribution limitation and unstable and unpredictable prices of fossil fuel feedstock for such plastics coupled with the alarming waste accumulation and pollution associated with non-biodegradable plastic caused an increasing research interest in sustainable polymers. In the quest for an alternative raw material to fossil derived resources, agricultural feedstock such as polysaccharides, proteins, chitosan, lignin, algae, glycerol, and lipids are being extensively studied [11,[42], [43], [44], [45]]. More recently, research and development efforts in catalysis, process development, and polymer science and engineering put a spotlight on CO2 based polymers. However, the kinetic and thermodynamic stability of CO2 has limited its extensive utilization as a feedstock for polymers. Many reactions pathways for the conversion of CO2 into useful polymers involve positive change in enthalpy (ΔH) and thus they are endothermic. Consequently, a substantial input of energy, effective reaction conditions, and often active catalysts, are necessary for such conversions [46]. Despite these challenges, methods to overcome the high energy barriers based on reduction, oxidative coupling with unsaturated compounds on low valent metal complexes, and increasing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon are being developed [23].
There are various origins for natural polymers, where as far as the biomaterials field is concerned, natural polymers are sourced from microorganisms, plants, and animals. Due to the benefits, natural polymers offer, especially environmentally, they are a considered good substitute for fiber production, especially for biomedical-related applications. Some of the major benefits of utilizing natural polymers are the fast integration onto wounded sites and resemblance to the host tissue, along with its biocompatibility and biodegradation. It also has the potential to degrade by enzymes and the capacity to react with biological structures in a controlled method.[94] At present, there are a large number of natural polymers that are compatible with current polymer fiber manufacturing methods, which have been extensively researched in the recent past.[37] In general, biopolymers are thought to be ecofriendlier than traditional polymers. However, a 2010 study by the University of Pittsburgh concluded that this is not particularly factual when the entire material life cycle was analyzed.[95] The research contrasted seven traditional plastics, along with four bioplastics and a single plastic produced from both fossil fuels and renewable resources. The investigators discovered that bioplastics manufacture produced a larger quantity of pollutants when fertilizers and pesticides were taken into account. These chemicals are utilized in growing crops and chemical processing which are required to convert organic material into bioplastic. It was also found that bioplastics promote ozone depletion more than regular plastics and also require large-scale land use. However, bioplastics do emit a remarkably lower amount of greenhouse gas emissions in comparison to traditional plastics. There is no resulting increase in carbon dioxide when bioplastics break down as they are produced from the same quantity of carbon dioxide. A 2017 report concluded that substituting traditional plastics with corn-based PLA would reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 25% in the USA.[92] The report also determined that the production of traditional plastics from only renewable energy sources can reduce emissions by 50-75%. Although the biodegradability of biopolymers is beneficial, most of these biopolymers require high-temperature industrial compositing provisions, which is uncommon and only a few cities seem to possess such provisions. Subsequently, these biopolymers culminate in landfills, where there is risk of methane being released from them, a greenhouse gas known to be 23 times more potent than carbon dioxide. Solar UV radiation is necessary to trigger the photo-oxidation degradation process of most polymers, which occurs through a radical chain mechanism that results in bond cleavage and a reduction in molecular weight.[4] Polymers discarded in landfills are unlikely to have enough access to UV radiation. Bioplastics (and biodegradable) when discarded incorrectly can contaminate recycled plastics and can impair recycling infrastructure. For instance, if PET (polyethylene terephthalate) which is common plastic utilized to produce bottles, is exposed to bioplastics, the whole lot may be declined and end up in a landfill. Therefore, there is need for separate streams to appropriately discard both biodegradable plastics and bioplastics. Bioplastics are produced from natural materials and hence, composting of bioplastic components can make soil fertile, due to the absence of artificial chemicals.[96] The land need for the production of bioplastics may hinder food production, as the crops that are used to manufacture these plastics can be utilized for food which is known to be in a shortage. In 2017, a joint report of European environmental organizations, estimated that the area of land required to keep up with global demand would equate to more than 1.3 million acres of land by 2019.[97] This is an area larger than Denmark, the Netherlands and Belgium put together. It can also be noted that the petroleum required to maneuver farming machinery will also emit greenhouse gases. Bioplastics can also be relatively costly. For instance, PLA can be up to 50% more expensive in comparison to similar traditional plastics due to the intricate method utilized to convert corn or sugarcane into the building blocks for PLA.[93] Regardless, the costs of bioplastics have slowly reduced as businesses and researchers evolve more greener and efficient techniques for manufacturing bioplastics. The production of bioplastics such as PLA, commonly used to make nanofibers for various applications, does not require the process of discovery, acquisition, and transportation of hydrocarbons. This results in the use of fewer fossil fuels and produces up to 67% less greenhouse gases during manufacture.[98] The manufacture of biodegradable plastics can be costly. However, considering the clean-up costs along with the lower negative environmental effects, biodegradable polymers are the better option. They also require less energy for production in comparison to regular plastics. Crude oil (petroleum) is a major element in the production of traditional plastics. The extraction and refinement of crude oil significantly affect the environment. According to the British Plastic Federation, it is believed that 4-6% of oil is used in the manufacture of plastics in Europe alone.[99] Biodegradable plastics use up to 20% renewable materials in its production when compared to traditional plastics. Current research is being undertaken on biodegradable plastics, where in the future, these plastics will only release the same quantity of energy used in manufactur.[100] Nonpetroleum-based plastics such as PLA, that are made from plants such as corn and sugarcane also curtail carbon dioxide as they do not emit an excess amount of CO2 during decomposition.[101] The use of plant oil as renewable feedstock for the synthesis of polymers has also been recently researched for development.[102]

The use of bio-based polymers has environmental benefits including lower greenhouse gas emissions, reduce the quantity of harmful chemicals/pollutants and conserve ecosystems and biodiversity, among others.17-20 Poly(lactic acid) (PLA), polybutylene succinate (PBS), polyethylene furanoate (PEF), or polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA) are examples of bio-based polymers, which global production was estimated to increase from around 2.11 million tons in 2019 to approximately 2.43 million tons in 2024.21 Being probably the most known bio-based polymer, PLA which is derived from starch by a fermentation process, is a renewable, microbial derived biodegradable polyester that can be processed similar to various commodity products.22, 23 Moreover, due to its outstanding properties, is used as high-value applications, such as tissue engineering and drug delivery,24 orthopedic regenerative engineering,25 shape memory hydrogels26 among many others. Furthermore, the use of PLA in packaging is not a recent subject,27 in fact, Changwichan1 conducted a comparative life cycle assessment of plastic and bioplastic derived cups, reporting that the bio-based cups exhibit lower global warming and fossil depletion impacts than the petroleum-based plastics. Likewise, the use of recycled raw-materials can enhance the eco-efficiency of the plastic products.28 Recently, it was reported that the use of 25% of recycled materials, reduced the environmental impacts of plastic cups in the range of 35%-56%.1 In that sense, the use of recycled materials, that is, residues from coffee beverages are excellent sources to produce new products. Nagarajan et al.28 prepared cellulose nanomaterials from used disposal paper cups, while Silva et al.29 used coffee grounds oil to produce radiolytic stabilized PVC. Likewise, Tong et al.30 studied the properties of recycled fiber from waste newspaper/PLA composites. It was reported that the modification of the fibers using alkali treatment effectively improved the compatibility between fibers and PLA, the mechanical properties and water absorbency of composite materials. Similarly, Elina Pääkkönen et al.31 used recycled fibers and fiber sludge as reinforcement materials in injection molded PP and PLA composites. It was reported that the recycled fibers provided comparable, or even higher, reinforcement effect than virgin softwood fibers. Hence, the possibility to use low-cost materials like recovered paper to produce composites is an interesting option for future sustainable applications. Aiming the enhancement of the environmental impact of plastic products, in this work, recycled cellulosic fibers from paper coffee cups were used as reinforcement material in PLA composites. The paper cups were milled and the fibers obtained were modified using lactic acid to enhance their compatibility with PLA. In parallel, coffee oil was extract from spent coffee grounds (SCG) and used as plasticizer. The obtained composites containing the biofiller and bioplasticizer were exhaustively characterized in terms of structural morphology, physical properties and eventual processability and biodegradability.
Due to its advantages, such as formability, high strength, and lightweight, the plastic-based materials are used extensively in many areas, such as packaging, agricultural films, clothing, and biomedical and engineering products [1]. For almost a decade, the rise in global production of plastics is seriously increasing. According to Plastic Europe: Association of Plastic Manufacturers Report (2019), the global plastic production in 2018 is 359 million metric tons. It is predicted that the compound annual growth rate for 2020-2027 is 3.2%. Most of these plastic products are designed to be thrown away after being used, which resulted in serious disposable plastics waste accumulation. Most of the plastic wastes ended up in landfills or dumps or are thrown in the open environment, which led to serious environmental pollution. It is estimated that 80% of plastic wastes from land activity is carried by winds and rivers that finally ended up into the sea and oceans. The accumulation and progressive fragmentation of plastic wastes in the sea and ocean has led to dramatic consequences to the marine wildlife [2]. Recently, a shocking report has revealed that at least 180 kinds of marine organisms were detected to eat plastics by mistake [3]. Majority of the plastic wastes were derived from commercial plastic materials that were mainly produced from petroleum-based polymers. These plastics are known to be very resistant to microbial attacks and required a long time for degradation, which took approximately 10-1000 years to degrade. Public pressure against waste and its disposal are seen to be the main inspirations for the development of biodegradable plastics [4]. Biodegradability is defined as the propensity of a material to break down its constituent molecules by natural processes often by microbial digestion [5]. It has a unique advantage over commercial plastic, where it reduces the dependency on limited fossil resources and diminishes greenhouse gas emissions [6]. Biodegradable plastic is produced from natural biopolymers that are easy to degrade and occurred in the natural mechanism. The natural microorganisms influence abiotic degradation through physical, chemical, and enzymatic reactions [7]. Degradation of biodegradable plastic started by hydrolyzing biodegradable plastic and followed by the microorganisms’ actions on the fragmented residues. One of the most attractive biodegradable plastics is polylactic acid (PLA). PLA is a green thermoplastic polyester derived from renewable resources, such as starch, sugarcane, corn, beets, rice, and carbohydrates from other crops [8, 9]. It exhibits favorable mechanical properties, superior transparency, and satisfactory gas barrier properties [4, 10]. Under suitable condition, PLA can be completely decomposed by microorganisms. Of note, landfilling of PLA takes less time than that of commercial plastic, between approximately 6 and 24 months [11]. Despite many paybacks of PLA, poor toughness, high brittleness, low glass transition, heat distortion temperature, and high cost have restricted its usage in many applications [10].
Despite advancements in plastic waste management strategies including mechanical and chemical recycling, thermal treatments, and microbial biodegradation a substantial fraction of plastic waste continues to be openly burned or relegated to landfills without adequate treatment. Open burning releases carbon monoxide and other hazardous pollutants, exacerbating air quality issues [68]. Moreover, plastics and their additives can infiltrate food chains via ingestion or inhalation by wildlife feeding on contaminated sites, adversely impacting human and ecological health. Landfilling compromises soil fertility, Rendering land barren and unsuitable for agriculture. Alarmingly, an estimated 10 million metric tons of plastic debris enter marine environments annually through Riverine pathways, inflicting lethal harm on aquatic organisms and promoting biomagnification of toxic constituents such as heavy metals and flame Retardants. In 2019 alone, plastic production and disposal accounted for approximately 1.8 billion metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions, significantly intensifying climate change [185]. Thus, the pervasive use and improper disposal of plastics threaten global sustainability objectives, necessitating urgent exploration of environmentally benign alternatives. Bioplastics offer a promising solution. These are polymers that are either bio-based, biodegradable, or both (European Bioplastics). “Bio-based” refers to their derivation from renewable biomass sources such as corn, sugarcane, or lignocellulosic feedstocks while “biodegradable” denotes their capacity to be decomposed by microbial action into benign end-products like CO₂, methane, water, and compost. The biodegradability of bioplastics is governed by factors including their chemical structure, degree of crystallinity, chain length, and prevailing environmental conditions such as humidity and temperature [106]. Generally, bioplastics with simpler chemical architectures and shorter chains degrade more readily. The dual attributes of renewability and biodegradability endow bioplastics with a circular life cycle, thereby substantially reducing environmental impacts. Life cycle assessments indicate that bioplastics can lower CO₂ emissions by up to 70% compared to conventional plastics [21]. Consequently, bioplastics are gaining traction as sustainable alternatives in diverse applications, including food packaging, sanitary products (e.g., diaper films, disposable gloves), biomedical materials (e.g., binders, drug delivery nanocarriers), agricultural films, construction components, textiles, and other consumer goods [45, 118]. Nonetheless, transitioning from petrochemical plastics to bioplastics faces considerable economic hurdles, primarily due to the higher production costs of bioplastics, which arise from the price of raw materials and processing complexities [83]. This economic barrier also dampens investor interest. Ongoing research is focused on alleviating these constraints by utilizing cost-effective, locally available substrates such as lignocellulosic biomass, agro-industrial residues, food processing by-products, and carbon-rich crops like maize and sugarcane [114]. Additionally, microalgae-based systems are being investigated for their rapid growth rates, minimal nutrient demands, and ability to utilize light and even industrial wastewater to biosynthesize bioplastics in a scalable, economically attractive manner. For instance, Hempel et al. [71] demonstrated polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) production in genetically engineered microalgae Phaeodactylum tricornutum, highlighting the feasibility of such approaches. Harnessing biomass resources including starch, corn, sugarcane, and lignocellulosic materials for bioplastic production supports a transition to a circular bioeconomy, curtails fossil resource extraction, and lowers carbon footprints. This paradigm shift holds significant promise for mitigating the environmental burdens associated with the end-of-life management of plastics.
The worldwide production of commodity conventional plastics reached 367 Mtons in 2020, with a European contribution of 55 Mtons1 and a decline in the production for the plastics industry due to the coronavirus pandemic in the first half of 2020.2 These fossil fuel-based polymers have several advantages as their light weight and low cost. However, they present drawbacks as their dependence on oil prices and their non-renewable nature. In 2020, more than 29 million tons of plastic post-consumer waste was collected in the EU27 + 3. More than one third was sent to recycling facilities inside and outside the EU27 + 3 but over 23% was still sent to landfill and more than 40% was sent to energy recovery operations.1 The use of bio-based plastics as alternative materials is continuously increasing in several applications as packaging, automobile manufacturing, agricultural equipment or household and toys, among other. This will lead to an unavoidable need of searching for adequate end-of-life strategies for these materials. Currently, bioplastics represent less than 1% of the global plastics production which capacity is set to increase from around 2.1 million tons in 2020 to 2.8 million tons in 2025 (https://plasticseurope.org/). Polylactide (PLA) is a bio-based and biodegradable polymer receiving much attention because of its versatility in many applications as packaging and disposal bottles/cutlery3 or biomedical materials and drug delivery systems.4 Properties as good processing capacity and the ability to biodegrade under specific conditions minimize its environmental print with respect to conventional polymers. One of its limits is its poor mechanical stability, exhibiting less than 10% elongation at break and relatively poor impact strength (1.9-2.6 KJ/m2)5 that it is surpassed by the addition of reinforcements as natural6, 7 or glass fibers8 in the polymeric matrix. Another limit remains the relatively little knowledge about degradation behavior in different aqueous environments and the combined effect with the degradation temperature. Previous works have dealt with the aging of PLA-based biocomposites. PLA was immersed in distilled9 and sea water10, 11 at room temperature, where natural aging was characterized by a slow degradation rate even after 10 weeks of immersion time. Temperature was employed to accelerate aging by Deroine et al.,12 who immersed PLA samples in distilled water and seawater at temperatures up to 50°C to evaluate its influence on the kinetics of degradation observing a deviation from Fickian behavior and morphological changes of the samples at higher temperatures.12 Gil-Castell et al.13 tested the hydrothermal aging of PLA/sisal biocomposites below and above the glass transition (around 70°C) and observed that at tests below 70°C the polymer chains maintained their morphology and structure whereas above this temperature some changes in the internal structure of the biocomposite might occur.13 Few works can be found testing the stability of PLA after immersion on different media (acidic and alkaline solutions) as shown in the review by Gorrasi and Pantani,14 where tests at varying pH and their influence on the degradation mechanisms are described. Elsawy et al. showed that pH, temperature, and the autocatalytic behavior of PLA were the key parameters controlling the PLA degradation process.15 PLA was tested at different pH and temperatures mimicking biomedical applications16 obtaining high degradation rates in extreme alkaline conditions. Understanding nanofibrous membranes’ mechanics is essential when evaluating their mechanical properties at various structural levels, both during processing and final applications. Computer modeling of electrospun nanofiber membranes is a difficult task because of the randomness of the mesostructure of the fiber web and its sophisticated mechanical response. These responses often involve large deformations and rotations, bonding and fiber fracture, fiber slippage, and the continuous recombination of the fiber network topology. The literature shows that the mechanical properties of an electrospun mat are tunable by changing the characteristics of the polymer,9 the diameter of the constituent fibers,10 fiber alignment,11 porosity,12 and bonding at the cross-points of the fibers.13 Wei et al.14 showed that the fusion between fibers affects the tensile strength of fiber membranes. More fusion points can increase the strength of the membrane, while over-fusing may decrease the fracture energy. However, this study was only at the nanoscale, not in a multi-stage medium. It could not explain why excessive fusion of fiber bonding points did not significantly affect the tensile strength of the membranes. The study of Chavoshnejad et al.15 shows that a large percentage of interfiber bonding at a predefined porosity of a mat does not increase the elastic modulus of the mat, nor does it have considerable effects on the failure behavior. Moreover, the effect of interfiber bonding increases with a mat’s porosity. Even after considering those parameters, it remains challenging to link the overall bulk material behavior to the small-scale constituent elements. In recent years, many researchers have investigated the uniaxial mechanics of polymer nanofibers and membranes.16-21 However, the force of nanofibrous membranes in practical applications is mainly a two-dimensional plane force. Uniaxial stress analysis cannot entirely reflect the actual stress state of the material. Therefore, double-axis mechanical tensile analysis must be conducted on the electrospun nanofibrous mats. Yin and Xiong22 established the biaxial tensile relationship between the fiber and fiber membrane according to the microstructure characteristics of the electrospinning nanofiber membrane, which was verified by the biaxial tensile experiment of the silk fibroin/polycaprolactone composite nanofiber membrane. The results of the study confirmed that the model developed for the biaxial tensile relationship could better explain the elastic-plastic tensile mechanical behavior of the polymer. Chavoshnejad and Razavi23 studied the tensile mechanical behavior of the membranes by considering the microstructure of the electrostatically spun fiber membranes and the percentage of intersections that were bonded, and they developed three finite element models with no interactions between fibers, half of the intersections acting, and all of the intersections acting, respectively, assuming that the distribution of fibers in the fiber membranes was uniform. The biaxial tensile mechanical properties of the fiber membranes showed that at a fiber membrane porosity of 0.25, inter-fiber fusion could increase the nanofiber membranes’ stiffness, independent of the tensile loading mode and the mechanical properties of the individual fibers. However, as the porosity of the fiber film increases, the inter-fiber bonding will be weakened. These studies, in some aspects, elucidated the relationship between the composition, structure, and properties of the electrostatically spun nanofiber membranes under external tension. However, these studies are more or less complicated with derivation calculations and high operating costs, which are not conducive to the microstructural design and practical application of electrostatically spun nanofiber membranes. It is envisaged that this work will provide insights to understand the biaxial mechanical characteristics of nanofibrous membranes in applications.

The Weibull distribution is a great way to model the tensile properties of natural fibres because it accurately shows how heterogeneities, size effects, brittle failures, and irregularities affect the mechanical behaviour of materials. This distribution is commonly used for both synthetic fiber [31] and natural fibers [32] as well as composite yarns [33]. This model is founded on the concept of chain failure, where the rupture is determined by the weakest link. It has been useful in describing tensile test results prediction at a certain gauge lengths. The Weibull distribution is categorised as linear law model (two- or three-parameter Weibull model) and power law model (modified Weibull). In two parameter (2P) Weibull model, the goal is to find the scale and shape parameters that best fit the experimental results, such as diameters, strength, Young modulus, and strain distribution. However, this model was shown to be insufficient for some fibers (ceramic fibers and other natural fibers), prompting to the development of three-parameter (3P) model which is described by three parameters: the shape parameter, the scale parameter and the location parameter. Considerable effort was undertaken in the various studies on Weibull distribution analysis for different natural fibers to predict their physical properties. Amroune et al. [34] utilized the 2P Weibull model to assess the variability in strength, failure strain, and Young modulus of flax fibers across different gauge lengths, demonstrating that it yielded results more consistent with experimental data than the 3P model. Naik and Fronk [35] reported that the 3P-Weibull model for Kenaf fiber showed a 26-46% error in parameter estimation. However, the anticipated average strength differed by 3-7% when compared to experimental data. Wang et al. [36, 37] proposed that the linear-law model is not necessarily accurate for describing variability in brittle fiber properties and their dependence on gauge length size. So, they investigated the effect of variation in bamboo fiber gauge length and diameter size on tensile strength using a modified Weibull model which was firstly introduced by Watson and Smith [38]. Some of the recent studies using different Weibull distribution on newly extracted various fibers can be found in literatures [39,40,41,42,43]. While the traditional Griffith and Weibull models are effective in predicting variability in fiber tensile properties, more advanced statistical models and machine learning techniques [44], such as generalized extreme value (GEV) distributions, neural networks [45], data-driven approaches, support vector machines, and decision trees, offer the potential for even more accurate and nuanced predictions. These sophisticated models have the capability to process large as well as small size datasets, uncovering complex patterns and insights that traditional models may miss [46]. MW stem fibres (MWSFs) are among the most durable natural fibres in saline environments, known for their mechanical qualities, salt stress tolerance [47], insecticidal and antibacterial properties [48], antioxidant potential [49], medicinal value [49], and somatic hybridization [50], low density, and widespread availability [51], making them unique among various natural fibers. MWSFs exhibit a high cellulose content (60-76%), which is higher than many commonly used natural fibers such as hemp (74%), bamboo (26-43%), sea grass (57%), coir (37%), rice husk (38-45%), oil palm (65%), jute (45-71%), bagasse (45%). With a lower density range of 800-1171 kg/m3 compared to synthetic and other natural fibers like carbon fiber (1400-1800 kg/m3), E-glass (2560 kg/m3), jute (1460 kg/m3), and hemp (1500 kg/m3), MW fibers offer a significant advantage for producing lightweight composites [51, 52]. MW stems (MWSs) belong to the Poaceae family and are abundant in Southeast Asian countries such as India, Bangladesh, Thailand, and Myanmar. These tall and uncultivated plants grow naturally on tidal riverbanks and mudflat soils along the coastal line. The MW stems have a multi-celled structure with many lumens next to each other. Sahu et al. [6] have conducted significant research on MW stems, highlighting their economic importance, ecology, distribution, and morphology, particularly among artisans. Rashid et al. [53] focused on the anatomical features of MW plants, revealing their adaptations for salt tolerance due to the structural adaptive features such as salt secreting pores, a thick epidermis, abundant metaxylem, large phloem in the stem and leaves, and sclerenchymatous vascular tissue. Kumar et al. [47] explored the salt adaptation mechanisms and identified the proteins responsible for salt tolerance in MW plants. Their proteomic analysis revealed proteins that promote the growth and development of MW plants in saline conditions as opposed to fresh water. Understanding these salt-responsive proteins is crucial for research aimed at enhancing salt resistance in rice and other crops. Kumar et al. [50] advanced this research by creating salt-resistant callus cultures through somatic hybridisation between Oryza sativa and MW plants, demonstrating improved salt tolerance in rice. The studies show that MW fiber have the ability to withstand in saline environment. Experimental studies have shown that MW stem mats and MW stem short microfibres work as reinforcement in polymer composite [54]. Retting MW stems involves weakening the fibre linkages, followed by mechanical or manual separation of micro fibers present in the stem. In our previous studies [51, 52], we have employed two extraction methods (alkaline and water retting) for the first time to successfully obtain micro MW fibers (MWSFs) from MW stems for composite applications. Yet, there remains vast scope to understand the fiber quality by exploring a range of extraction techniques [55, 56], including dew retting, stand retting, warm/cold water retting, ultrasound retting, steam explosion, duralin retting, enzyme retting, mechanical and physical retting, as well as ammonia, acidic, and oxidative delignification. Each of these methods holds unique promise for optimizing fiber strength, uniformity, and qualities. Additionally, employing various surface and chemical treatments [57, 58] on the retted fibers could further elevate their quality, paving the way for superior fiber performance in composites. Researchers have focused on analysing the mechanical properties of MWSFs, which address the intrinsic variability of the stem fibers caused by factors such as processing techniques, growing conditions, irregularities, and retting techniques. However, insufficient attention has been given to thoroughly assessing the uncertainties associated with the inherent variability in strength, diameter, modulus, and strain at break in MWSFs. A deep understanding of these properties using statistical tools is essential to accurately defining the mechanical properties of composite structures that utilize natural fiber with intrinsic variability [59, 60]. The use of MWSFs in structural polymer composites is currently receiving interest as a feasible substitute for traditional fibers like glass, jute, sisal, hemp, banana, etc. [54]. However, the significant variability in the physical properties like diameter, density, strength, Young modulus and strain at break of the fiber have been identified, which raised serious concerns for its industrial use. MWSFs show noticeably larger diameter fluctuations both between individual fibers and within a single fiber than the synthetic fibers. Due to large variation in mechanical properties of the fiber, an attempt was made to analyse it statistically using Griffith and Weibull model to evaluate the inherent variability of mechanical properties of MWSFs. In accordance with these statistical analysis, the current study compares the tensile behaviour of MWSFs extracted from both chemical retting [52] and water retting [51] processes. A comparative analysis of the Griffith model as a function of fiber diameter, along with 2P and 3P-Weibull models using the Least Square (LS) approach for parameter estimation, is used to statistically analyse the fiber’s physical characteristics. As per the author’s knowledge, this is the first time that the physical properties of MWSFs have been predicted and validated with experimental results utilizing the aforementioned two statistical models. The study also shows the effect of retting methods on the fiber surface morphology, mechanical behaviour and statistical prediction.

Much attention has been paid to biodegradable polymers in recent years on account of the continuous decrease of petroleum resources and environmental concerns.1-3 In particular, the commercially available polyester, poly(lactic acid) (PLA), which is derived from plant sugars, has been extensively investigated for its high strength and high stiffness.4-7 Currently, PLA is mainly used as drug delivery devices and sutures for biomedical applications, mainly on account of its biodegradable and biocompatible nature. Actually, the derivation from renewable resource makes PLA even more valuable from environmental viewpoint. PLA could predictably turn into an alternative to traditional commodity plastics. Fatally, the much higher cost than petroleum-based plastics makes the extensive use of PLA still far from reality. Also, low melt viscosity, low toughness, and low heat distortion temperature are usually dissatisfied for various long-term applications. Blending techniques have been proved to be an efficient method to improve the properties of PLA. Isotactic polypropylene (iPP) has been compounded with PLA to enhance the physical properties and also to develop novel materials. Complementary to PLA, iPP is not biodegradable or biocompatible, but it possesses superior mechanical strength, high tensile toughness, excellent abrasion resistance, and high heat resistance. Reddy et al8 prepared iPP/PLA fibers, and they aimed to improve the resistance of PLA to hydrolysis and raise its dyeability. Kotiba et al9 investigated the rheological and mechanical properties of iPP/PLA blends; however, either the tensile strength or elongation at break was much lower than that of each component polymer, and the immiscibility between the component polymers is the primal problem. Compatibilizers, such as polypropylene-g-maleic anhydride (iPP-g-MAH), styrene-ethylene-butylene-styrene-g-maleic anhydride (SEBS-g-MAH),10 glycidyl methacrylate-g-iPP (PP-g-GMA),11 and polyethylene-g-glycidyl methacrylate (PE-g-GMA),12 were used to improve the compatibility between PLA and iPP. However, the mechanical properties of iPP/PLA blends were still much lower than the theoretical prediction of rule-of-mixtures. Noticeably, the earlier mentioned iPP/PLA blends display ordinary matrix-dispersed particles morphology without exception. Actually, the morphology of dispersed phase is a crucial factor that can affect the physical and mechanical properties of the blends. Verifiably, microfibrils dispersed in matrix could substantially improve the uniaxial strength of the blends.13 Consequently, it is of great importance to explore the morphological evolutions during processing, and to introduce the microfibrils in iPP/PLA blends so as to achieve our aims. Some methods have been carried out to perform in-situ deformation of the dispersed phases into fibers, even microfibrils. One typical example is the so-called in-situ composites, which refer to formation of in-situ microfibers of a thermotropic liquid crystalline polymer in a thermoplastic matrix.14, 15 However, thermotropic liquid crystalline polymers are mostly too expensive for general applications. Another example is the in-situ microfibrillar blends, which involves 2 thermoplastics with distinctly different processing temperatures.16-20 Nevertheless, the preparation process includes slit-die-extrusion, hot-stretching, quenching, and injection/compression process, which is complicated and time-consuming. Furthermore, the essential condition of the polymer pair with distinctly different processing temperatures has also restricted its widespread applications. For instance, the melting temperatures of iPP and PLA are almost identical, and this method cannot be used to fabricate the microfibril morphology in iPP/PLA blends.
Most synthetic polymers exhibit a substantial trade-off between rigidity (elastic modulus) and extensibility (strain at failure). Hard synthetic polymers such as composite resins have superb elastic moduli (E ≈ 1-10 GPa), but lack extensibility (εmax < 20%).1, 2 In contrast, soft synthetic polymers (elastomers) offer superior extensibility (up to 650%),3 but have much lower moduli (≈1-100 kPa).4 Because of the ubiquitous challenges in designing load-bearing materials, there is a great demand to improve-or at least maintain-high stiffness without significant detriment to elongation. Inspiration can be taken from nature, wherein several materials have this ability.5-8 The byssus of marine mussels, for example, is used as a holdfast that anchors to rocky surfaces in the hostile intertidal zone.6-8 The byssal thread (Figure 1A,B) is comprised of a soft, collagenous fiber-bundle core and a hard, 5-10 µm-thin protective cuticle. With this combination of stiffness (E ≈ 800 MPa) and extensibility (ε > 100%),6, 7 the thread allows for significant degree of tensile movement, preventing from being torn off under the high loads from waves and wind. The previous works have presented that this protective coating strategy can be endowed by (but not limited to) granular microstructure of the cuticle and catechol-iron coordination chemistry.6, 7 Inspired by this natural protective coating strategy, we here desire to mimic the mitigation of core-cuticle delamination to quantify its possible viability to increase overall material toughness through a simple gradient layering technique in a most common synthetic polymer (acrylate polymer). Synthetic polymers that utilize the similar heterogeneous structure to emulate such a unique stress-strain relationship have shown promise as a mechanism for improved load distribution such as traditional polymer composites containing organic/inorganic fillers. More recently, double-network architectures of synthetic polymers have been attained via interpenetrating one network to another to dissipate the strain energy by sacrificing one network upon tension.8-11 Dual physically cross-linked (DPC) hydrogels of acrylic polymers with primary cross-links of laponite nanoparticles and secondary cross-links of Fe3+ (ferric) ion coordination complexes were also introduced, which significantly improved both elastic modulus and extensibility of DPC hydrogels over non-DPC.11 However, these methods involve multi-step processes of network penetration, wherein a soft network is swollen in aqueous solution, followed by cross-linking with another polymer network.4, 6, 12 These approaches, therefore, are limited to hydrogels or polymers that swell in water such as polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based networks.6, 12 Additionally, high localization of stress in similar polymer matrices often causes failures in areas of localization and asymmetric cross-linkage, endowing high initial rigidity but resulting in premature fracture at only fractions of maximum strain.12, 13 Therefore, these moisture-sensitive materials cannot be applied for more general load-bearing applications which are mostly prepared from hydrophobic polymer networks.14 A heterogeneous bilayer or sandwich architecture of polymers can be a candidate to overcome these limitations, but since most bilayers laminate a rigid coating onto a flexible substrate, it results in trade-off between rigidity and elongation.15-17 The resulting extreme modulus mismatches can cause high interfacial stress localization, which intensifies until strain energy exceeds the critical strain energy release rate, causing the rigid coating to fracture or delaminate.16

ans_raw: The 'isostrain' condition in polymer blends assumes that fibers are continuously aligned longitudinally within the matrix, leading to uniform strain distribution across all constituents. This condition predicts the **upper boundary** of Young’s modulus and tensile strength in composite models, as it optimizes load transfer efficiency under ideal alignment [2]. However, experimental tensile strength often falls below isostrain predictions due to factors like imperfect fiber orientation, interfacial bonding defects, or fiber degradation during processing, which disrupt effective stress transfer [1]. For example, mixed fiber-reinforced composites showed reduced tensile strength compared to aligned configurations due to compromised longitudinal fiber integrity [1]. Additionally, models like Cox-Krenchel, which account for fiber orientation and interfacial effects, outperform isostrain assumptions in accuracy, as the latter’s deviation from experimental values can exceed 6000% when alignment or adhesion is suboptimal [2]. Thus, while isostrain provides a theoretical maximum, real-world mechanical performance is typically lower due to structural and interfacial imperfections.

There are several theoretical models that capture the interesting strain hardening response of semiflexible and flexible networks.[47] For flexible chains, classical rubber elasticity has been used to model polymer network mechanical behavior based on the entropy of the chains and cross-links of an isotropic network as a function of small strains.[1, 48, 49] Flory and Rehner extended this model to predict that the modulus of a gel would decrease as a function of swelling as the chains are stretched to accommodate the solvent.[50-52] To capture the effects of large strains, Yeoh and Fleming included finite extensibility of the network chains.[53] Mackintosh et al.[54] developed a model for cross-linked gels and entangled solutions of semiflexible biopolymers to explain the concentration dependence of the storage modulus and yield strain. This model assumes that chains are nearly straight and results in viscoelasticity having a dependence on the bending modulus. A later study also breaks the mechanical behaviors into two regimes, affine and nonaffine deformation, as a function of cross-link density and filament rigidity.[55] Dobrynin and Carrillo[20] took this theoretical analysis further and used molecular dynamics simulations to relate the strain-hardening behavior to the molecular parameters of the network chains. They found a universal relationship that captures the strain hardening response of flexible and semiflexible networks, by using an extension parameter, β, that relates the initial end to end vector of the network to the maximum stretch, . Carrillo et al.[56] expanded this model further to include the bending modulus of discrete chains and improve modeling of strain hardening segments of the gel network. These theoretical efforts capture the key parameters that can predict response of nonlinear networks, such as swelling, initial state of the chains, and maximum extension in the network. Control of the strain-hardening behavior in materials is important for both biological systems and synthetic materials. Matsumoto et al.[57] synthesized PLL hydrogels with large swelling ratios. These hydrogels were shown to undergo a structural change as a function of pH. A later study by Matsumoto et al.[58] uses this structural transition to functionalize the hydrogels as drug carriers of a model drug. Methylcellulose is a synthetically modified polysaccharide that forms fibrils spontaneously and gels with thermal treatment.[59] The moduli of the methylcellulose gels are an order of magnitude higher than would be expected for a flexible polymer gel at the same concentration because of this fibril structure.[60] Gkikas et al. synthesized poly-l-proline hydrogels that have higher shear modulus upon heating from 5 to 35 °C because of a change in chain conformation from a compact right-handed helix to a stretched left-handed helix.[61] Kouwer et al.[46] and Pochan and co-workers[62, 63] have created polyisocyanopeptide hydrogels formed from bundled chains and β-hairpin hydrogels formed from an exchangeable strand domain that transitions to a beta hairpin upon heating. These materials are being investigated as wound dressings[64] and injectable therapies.[65] To determine the onset of strain hardening of model polypeptide hydrogels, we have cross-linked PLL, a polypeptide which has a well-known random coil-helix transition as a function of the pH environment, as shown in Figure 1. We investigate the mechanical properties of the hydrogel network as a function of helicity and cross-link density with small and large amplitude oscillatory shear and dynamic light scattering. We compare the small amplitude and nonlinear response of these materials as a function of the percent helicity of the network. As the network chains form helical structure, a transition from strain softening to strain hardening occurs, which we are able to model with Dobrynin and Carrillo's[20] model at large strains. Using these model systems, we observe the transition to strain hardening as a function of chain structure, which occurs in various biological systems, and can possibly be used to store stresses and generate mechanical forces in the material.
Mechanical properties of acetylated hemicellulose/nanocellulose (AH/ACNC) films can be enhanced by manipulating the ACNC degree of acetylation and loading. It is critical to predict the mechanical performance of the ACNC reinforced AH films before their development for specific application. Therefore, this study investigated, both experimentally and theoretically, the effects of varying ACNC degree of substitution (DS) (0-2.34) and loading (10-50%) on the mechanical properties (Young’s modulus and tensile strength) of acetylated hemicellulose-based films (AH). Young’s modulus predictions were carried out using the Halpin-Tsai, isostrain, isostress, Tsai-Pagano, and Cox-Krenchel models. In addition, Bowyer-Bader, Modified Rule of mixtures, Hirsh, parallel and series models were used for predicting the tensile strength of the AH/ACNC biocomposite films. Increasing the nanocellulose’s DS from 0 to 2.34 enhanced the AH Young’s modulus by 59.2% and tensile strength by 101.2%. Similarly, increasing the ACNC loading from 10-50% improved the reinforcement efficiency of the ACNC in AH based films from 0.059 to 6.29. The Young’s modulus increased from 63.68 to 590.15 MPa and tensile strength from 2.28 MPa to 10.59 MPa. The tensile strength and Young’s modulus were best predicted (95% confidence level) with the Bowyer-Bader and the Cox-Krenchel models, respectively. The ACNC has shown potential to customise AH-based films’ mechanical properties. In addition, the mechanical performance of AH/ACNC films can be predicted by theoretically, which is a cost-effective strategy in film formulation, and allows for diversification of end application of the films (for example for food packaging applications). Understanding nanofibrous membranes’ mechanics is essential when evaluating their mechanical properties at various structural levels, both during processing and final applications. Computer modeling of electrospun nanofiber membranes is a difficult task because of the randomness of the mesostructure of the fiber web and its sophisticated mechanical response. These responses often involve large deformations and rotations, bonding and fiber fracture, fiber slippage, and the continuous recombination of the fiber network topology. The literature shows that the mechanical properties of an electrospun mat are tunable by changing the characteristics of the polymer,9 the diameter of the constituent fibers,10 fiber alignment,11 porosity,12 and bonding at the cross-points of the fibers.13 Wei et al.14 showed that the fusion between fibers affects the tensile strength of fiber membranes. More fusion points can increase the strength of the membrane, while over-fusing may decrease the fracture energy. However, this study was only at the nanoscale, not in a multi-stage medium. It could not explain why excessive fusion of fiber bonding points did not significantly affect the tensile strength of the membranes. The study of Chavoshnejad et al.15 shows that a large percentage of interfiber bonding at a predefined porosity of a mat does not increase the elastic modulus of the mat, nor does it have considerable effects on the failure behavior. Moreover, the effect of interfiber bonding increases with a mat’s porosity. Even after considering those parameters, it remains challenging to link the overall bulk material behavior to the small-scale constituent elements. In recent years, many researchers have investigated the uniaxial mechanics of polymer nanofibers and membranes.16-21 However, the force of nanofibrous membranes in practical applications is mainly a two-dimensional plane force. Uniaxial stress analysis cannot entirely reflect the actual stress state of the material. Therefore, double-axis mechanical tensile analysis must be conducted on the electrospun nanofibrous mats. Yin and Xiong22 established the biaxial tensile relationship between the fiber and fiber membrane according to the microstructure characteristics of the electrospinning nanofiber membrane, which was verified by the biaxial tensile experiment of the silk fibroin/polycaprolactone composite nanofiber membrane. The results of the study confirmed that the model developed for the biaxial tensile relationship could better explain the elastic-plastic tensile mechanical behavior of the polymer. Chavoshnejad and Razavi23 studied the tensile mechanical behavior of the membranes by considering the microstructure of the electrostatically spun fiber membranes and the percentage of intersections that were bonded, and they developed three finite element models with no interactions between fibers, half of the intersections acting, and all of the intersections acting, respectively, assuming that the distribution of fibers in the fiber membranes was uniform. The biaxial tensile mechanical properties of the fiber membranes showed that at a fiber membrane porosity of 0.25, inter-fiber fusion could increase the nanofiber membranes’ stiffness, independent of the tensile loading mode and the mechanical properties of the individual fibers. However, as the porosity of the fiber film increases, the inter-fiber bonding will be weakened. These studies, in some aspects, elucidated the relationship between the composition, structure, and properties of the electrostatically spun nanofiber membranes under external tension. However, these studies are more or less complicated with derivation calculations and high operating costs, which are not conducive to the microstructural design and practical application of electrostatically spun nanofiber membranes. In this study, an analytical model was developed to predict the biaxial behaviors of randomly oriented nanofibrous membranes. Stress-strain data from a single nanofiber were tested for use in the model. The model starts from the mechanical properties of single fibers and the membrane structure and studies the biaxial tensile mechanical properties of the membrane in tension by calculating the energy change in the membrane during deformation. Four control groups with different ratios of stretching speed during biaxial tension were investigated. The applicability of the analytical model was examined by a comparison between modeling prediction and experimental data. This model has the advantages of a simple calculation process and low calculation cost, and its derivation results have sure accuracy, which is very convenient for the design of the biaxial tensile mechanical properties of the electrospinning nanofiber membrane. It is envisaged that this work will provide insights to understand the biaxial mechanical characteristics of nanofibrous membranes in applications.

AI/ML has made a substantial contribution to predicting the mechanical properties of NFPCs. These models can accurately forecast a range of mechanical properties, including tensile strength, modulus of elasticity, and impact resistance, by analysing the composition and processing parameters of NFPCs. This reduces the need for extensive experimental testing, accelerating the development process and optimizing resource utilization. Understanding how and why materials fail under various loading conditions allows researchers and engineers to develop strategies to mitigate these failures, thereby enhancing the reliability and lifespan of composites. This insight is vital for designing NFPCs with improved toughness and durability. AI/ML also proves beneficial in sensitivity analysis. Machine learning models facilitate this analysis by identifying critical parameters influencing the mechanical properties of NFPCs. Sensitivity analysis involves examining the impact of each feature on the model's prediction. A significant change in the model's outcome due to a change in a feature value indicates that the feature has a substantial impact on the prediction. By identifying the most influential factors, researchers can concentrate their efforts on enhancing specific features of NFPCs, refining the manufacturing process, and optimizing the material composition for improved performance [25, 37, 38]. The Weibull distribution is a great way to model the tensile properties of natural fibres because it accurately shows how heterogeneities, size effects, brittle failures, and irregularities affect the mechanical behaviour of materials. This distribution is commonly used for both synthetic fiber [31] and natural fibers [32] as well as composite yarns [33]. This model is founded on the concept of chain failure, where the rupture is determined by the weakest link. It has been useful in describing tensile test results prediction at a certain gauge lengths. The Weibull distribution is categorised as linear law model (two- or three-parameter Weibull model) and power law model (modified Weibull). In two parameter (2P) Weibull model, the goal is to find the scale and shape parameters that best fit the experimental results, such as diameters, strength, Young modulus, and strain distribution. However, this model was shown to be insufficient for some fibers (ceramic fibers and other natural fibers), prompting to the development of three-parameter (3P) model which is described by three parameters: the shape parameter, the scale parameter and the location parameter. Considerable effort was undertaken in the various studies on Weibull distribution analysis for different natural fibers to predict their physical properties. Amroune et al. [34] utilized the 2P Weibull model to assess the variability in strength, failure strain, and Young modulus of flax fibers across different gauge lengths, demonstrating that it yielded results more consistent with experimental data than the 3P model. Naik and Fronk [35] reported that the 3P-Weibull model for Kenaf fiber showed a 26-46% error in parameter estimation. However, the anticipated average strength differed by 3-7% when compared to experimental data. Wang et al. [36, 37] proposed that the linear-law model is not necessarily accurate for describing variability in brittle fiber properties and their dependence on gauge length size. So, they investigated the effect of variation in bamboo fiber gauge length and diameter size on tensile strength using a modified Weibull model which was firstly introduced by Watson and Smith [38]. Some of the recent studies using different Weibull distribution on newly extracted various fibers can be found in literatures [39,40,41,42,43]. While the traditional Griffith and Weibull models are effective in predicting variability in fiber tensile properties, more advanced statistical models and machine learning techniques [44], such as generalized extreme value (GEV) distributions, neural networks [45], data-driven approaches, support vector machines, and decision trees, offer the potential for even more accurate and nuanced predictions. These sophisticated models have the capability to process large as well as small size datasets, uncovering complex patterns and insights that traditional models may miss [46]. Properly tested and precisely classified biodegradable polymers with complete biodegradation in a definite time matching to the application are surely an opportunity for stepping toward an MP-reduced environment. They can be especially of significant use in some specific scenarios. The first case is replacing nondegradable polyolefins with the appropriate biodegradable polymers for specific time-bound environmental applications, such as in agricultural fields as mulch film, slow release fertilizers, pesticides and water carriers, plantation pots and bags. The non-soil biodegradable polymers used for these applications stay in the environment and should be considered as intentional creation of MPs in the environment. Agricultural fields are gigantic, and the number of plastic products used for various agricultural applications are huge. It is not easy to recover plastics after use from such a huge area. Replacing polyolefins with agricultural soil-degradable, biodegradable polymers would eliminate the need to collect plastic fragments after use, and the plastic will not persist in the environment. There is a need to develop a series of agricultural soil-degradable biodegradable polymers with different physical properties and biodegradation profiles so that large number of applications can be covered. Furthermore, biodegradability in combination with managed, closed-loop disposal systems, such as composting and anaerobic digestion, is highly promising regarding environmentally responsible solutions to MP problem when used for specific applications. In this way, biodegradable waste is recycled into useful products and not dumped in landfills. There is a need to use proper i-compostable polymers, as discussed above. Presently, industrial composting plants are very often seen coping with plastic bags, packaging films, and bottle caps, because they come with the biowaste, and the fragments from the plastic articles are even seen in the finished compost. Whosoever uses this compost either in agricultural fields, or public or private gardens bring MPs unintentionally into the environment. The use of i-compostable polymers with fast biodegradability matching the speed of the composting cycle would be a very big step to stop the leakage of MP through compost into the environment. Additionally, this has the advantage of organic recycling of the plastic, in which the plastic C is being converted to CO2 and biomass and not landing in landfills. Regarding short-term use items, the best scenario, like any other plastic, would also be to reuse and recycle even if they are made up of biodegradable polymer articles. Biodegradability can offer additional advantage in case there is an unintentional leak into the environment: such polymers will not persist unlike polyolefins and PET if suitable environmentally biodegradable polymers are used. For this intention, a polymer biodegrading in different natural environments (soils and water bodies) is required, which is still not available. Also, there is a serious concern about complications for existing plastic recycling systems in case biodegradable polymers enter the plastic waste stream. One should be encouraged with the beneficial degradation property of biodegradable polymers in case of their leak to the environment and should weigh the benefits against arising concerns and problems. In future, for short-term use items, environmentally degradable polymers with either mechanical recyclability matching with that of conventional plastics or advanced measures for collection and sorting of plastic waste are needed.
