First published on 28th October 2022 Nanoplastics and microplastics (NMPs) in natural environments are an emerging global concern and understanding their formation processes from macro-plastic items during degradation/weathering is critical for predicting their quantities and impacts in different ecological systems. Here, we show the risk of enormous emissions of NMPs from polymer blends, a source that has not been specifically studied, by taking immiscible (most common case) partially biodegradable polymer blends as an example. The blends have the common “sea-island” morphology, where the minor non-biodegradable polymer phase (polyethylene and polypropylene) is dispersed as NMP particles in the major continuous biodegradable matrix (poly(ε-caprolactone)). The dispersed NMP particles with spherical and rod-like shapes are gradually liberated and released to the surrounding aquatic environment during the biodegradation of the matrix polymer. Strikingly, the number of released NMPs from the blend is very high. The blend film surface erosion process, induced by enzymatic hydrolysis of the matrix, involving fragmentation, hole formation, and hole wall detachment, was systematically investigated to reveal the NMP release process. Our findings present direct evidence and detailed insights into the high risk of emissions of NMPs from partially biodegradable immiscible polymer blends with a widespread “sea-island” morphology. Efforts from authorities, developers, manufacturers, and the public are needed to avoid the use of non-biodegradable polymers in blends with biodegradable polymers. Many countries, such as the USA, China, and Sweden, have banned microbead-added products to reduce the primary MP emissions.14,15 However, the emissions of secondary NMPs, the main origin of the MPs in marine environments,8 continue to grow rapidly because of continuously growing plastic production and largely uncontrolled waste.16,17 Besides, more than 5000 million tons of plastic waste are accumulated either in landfills or natural environments (mostly in the oceans)18 and they are continuously emitting numerous NMPs because of mechanical stress, heat, UV radiation, and biological degradation.9,16,19 In addition, an increasing number of studies show that the highly degraded secondary NMPs contain a greater content of hazardous substances than pristine NMPs due to the presence of degradation products such as monomers, oligomers and oxidative products.20-23 Therefore, it is particularly crucial to understand the degradation-induced formation process of NMPs in various environmental conditions for better prediction of NMP emissions.16,24-28 Most studies focus on pure plastics,24-27 and overlook an important source for NMPs: the degradation of polymer blends.
Biological waste treatments tailored for biodegradable plastics represent sophisticated end-of-life management strategies. These treatments can be implemented under aerobic conditions (with oxygen, such as composting) or anaerobic conditions (without oxygen, such as anaerobic digestion). Composting, which utilizes a diverse microbial community including fungi, bacteria, and actinomycetes, can occur at psychrophilic temperatures (below 35 °C for home composting) or thermophilic temperatures (50-60 °C for industrial composting) [11]. For example, kitchen scraps and garden waste are commonly composted in home settings, while large-scale operations might process municipal organic waste. This process reduces waste and produces valuable compost, rich in nutrients and beneficial for soil health. It can also be used in agriculture and landscaping. Similarly, anaerobic digestion, exclusively facilitated by bacteria, can be performed under mesophilic (below 35 °C) or thermophilic (50-60 °C) conditions. This method is often applied in wastewater treatment plants and livestock farms, where organic materials such as food waste, manure, and sewage sludge are digested [108]. The primary factor determining a bioplastic’s suitability for specific waste Management methods is its duration for complete degradation. International standards for biodegradability, such as those set by ISO and ASTM, define a Material as biodegradable if it fully decomposes within 56 days in aquatic environments or within two years in soil. However, these standards often rely on elevated temperatures that surpass typical conditions found in unmanaged natural environments, leading to a disparity between laboratory results and actual biodegradation in the real world. This highlights the importance of aligning biodegradation standards with actual environmental conditions when developing policies for managing plastic waste. Additionally, the design of plastic products must account for potential end-of-life scenarios, ensuring they align with the degradation timelines and processes of intended waste management systems. A cohesive strategy integrating policy, standards, and design is key to crafting practical and reliable solutions for bioplastic waste [101]. The study of biodegradation kinetics and carbon fate of bioplastics under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions offers valuable insights, but it also highlights critical limitations in their practical applications. While PHB and PHBV exhibit versatility by biodegrading under both conditions, PCL’s reliance on aerobic environments restricts its utility in anaerobic waste systems [99]. Integrating carbon balance analysis adds depth by tracking carbon sinks, such as gases, biomass, and soluble compounds; however, its complexity and resource demands may hinder scalability in industrial contexts. Additionally, the observed enhancement of mineralization rates with smaller particle sizes, though beneficial for assay duration, is impractical for real-world waste management, where uniform particle reduction is challenging and costly. Combining carbon balance with kinetic analysis provides a promising framework for testing and improving biodegradable materials, but the feasibility of implementing such rigorous methods at scale remains questionable. Addressing these challenges by focusing on scalable, realistic conditions and simplifying analytical methodologies will be critical to translating these findings into effective waste management solutions [99].
Polymer degradation is defined as the “chemical changes in a polymeric material that usually result in undesirable changes in the in-use properties of the material” [184]. In spite of such definition and within the framework here discussed, the term degradation is considered an enormous asset instead of an undesirable property as many polymers should be degradable to avoid their accumulation in the environment. Polymer degradation is an irreversible phenomenon that takes place through scission of the main chain or side chain of the macromolecules. Under natural conditions, polymer degradation may be induced by processes such as photolysis, oxidation, radiolysis, thermal activation, hydrolysis or biological activity [185]. It should be taken into account that degradable does not necessarily mean biodegradable. A wide number of polymers which undergo fragmentation into smaller pieces and even degrade into invisible residues to the naked eye are available. Although these materials are eroded (or degraded) into microscopic pieces and several synthetic approaches are available to accelerate this process, such microgranules may accumulate in the oceans or landfills as they are not completely degraded within a reasonable period of time [186]. Henceforth, this fragmentation does not mean biodegradation per se. Accordingly, the American Society of Testing and Materials (ASTM), in its standard D6813 defines the term biodegradability as “capable of undergoing decomposition into carbon dioxide, methane, water, inorganic compounds, or biomass in which the predominant mechanism is the enzymatic action of microorganisms, that can be measured by standardized tests in a specified period of time, reflecting available disposal conditions”. Similarly, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) defined a biodegradable polymer as a “polymer susceptible to degradation by biological activity, with the degradation accompanied by a lowering of its molar mass” [184]. Essentially, during biodegradation, long macromolecular chains are broken down in vitro or in vivo by enzymes (and other biologically active entities) into shorter chains, which are further metabolized by microorganisms. Among all the available degradation processes, hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation are of special interest as they allow closed‐loop recycling processes which are seen as the preferred choice to face current plastic waste issues [187]. Indeed, hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation are the most important degradation mechanisms in polyesters thanks to the high susceptibility of the ester linkages to chemical hydrolysis and microbial/enzymatic chain cleavage reactions. Polyester hydrolytic degradation is defined as the scission of ester bond linkages in the backbone via H2O uptake to yield first oligomers, and then monomers [188]. Enzymatic degradation occurs when the action of living organisms such as enzymes cut down the macromolecules into lower molar mass chains, which are then bio-assimilated and mineralized by such living organism to yield H2O and CO2 or CH4 depending if the process is aerobic or anaerobic respectively [188], [189], [190]. In some cases, the degradation could also undergo through combined mechanisms of microbial, enzymatic and chemical hydrolysis.
The big question is whether the biodegradation of biodegradable polymer blends and composites raises concerns regarding the degradation of by-products and their potential environmental impact. While biodegradation offers the advantage of reducing the accumulation of plastic waste in landfills and oceans, concerns have been raised about the potential of releasing harmful substances. Under controlled industrial or laboratory conditions, assessing biodegradation based on standard procedures is simpler than in real-life contexts including soils and oceans, which have varying microbial populations.301 According to Ali et al.,302 because biodegradation involves a mixture of identified and unidentified substances that may be hazardous to animals and soil health, it can both pose challenges and offer advantages in complex ecosystems. Unknown substances with roughly 32% cytotoxicity, 23% anti-androgenicity, 42% oxidative stress, and 67% baseline toxicity in bioassays have been shown to be present in bioplastics according to some studies. These compounds have the potential to negatively impact soil and animal health. Ecotoxicity assessments play a crucial role in evaluating the environmental implications of biodegradable polymer blends and composites. These assessments involve evaluating the potential toxicity resulting from the degradation of various organisms in aquatic and terrestrial environments. Such testing includes a focus on endpoints such as reproductive effects, acute and chronic toxicity, and bioaccumulation potential. To be deemed environmentally benign, these polymers, their blends, and composites must pass toxicity testing and break down into fragments within a given amount of time. However, one of the major setbacks in assessing the ecotoxicity of biodegradable polymers is the lack of standardized testing procedures and regulatory frameworks, unlike the biodegradation and compostability of plastics that have standardized and established testing procedures with clearly outlined regulatory requirements.303 Unlike biodegradation and controlled composting, there seems to be no specific standard for assessing the ecotoxicity of these materials in different environments. In fact, two ASTM standards, i.e., ASTM D5152-91; practice for water extraction of residual solids from degraded plastics for toxicity testing304 and ASTM D5951-96(2002); standard practice for preparing residual solids obtained after biodegradability standard methods for plastics in solid waste for toxicity and compost quality testing305 were withdrawn in 1998 and 2011, respectively, with no replacements. Hence the assessment of the ecotoxicity of biodegradable materials presents unique complexities as a result of their various compositions and degradation pathways. The multifaceted complexities in the assessment of the ecotoxicity of polymer blends and composites require ecotoxicity testing procedures suited for biodegradable polymers for understanding the possible environmental problems that may be associated with them. A study by Palsikowski et al.306 on ecotoxicological assessment of PLA, PBAT, and their compatibilized blend in soil found that the biodegradable materials and their blends did not exhibit phytotoxic (adverse effects on plant growth, physiology, or metabolism), cytotoxic (quality of being toxic to cells), genotoxic (damaging to DNA or genetic material), or mutagenic (causing genetic mutations) effects on the meristematic cells of Allium cepa, except for a chromosomal aberration index observed in one experiment with the blend 25/75. Sforzini et al.307 used biotests to evaluate the ecotoxicity impact of Mater-Bi, a biodegradable plastic, on soil organisms. The ecotoxicity tests on Mater-Bi biodegradable plastic showed no harmful effects on soil organisms, including autotrophic organisms, Daphnia magna, and Eisenia andrei. In their discussion of the environmental fate and ecotoxicity assessment of biodegradable polymers, Farachi et al.308 emphasized the importance of assessing the possible ecological dangers that may be connected to biodegradable materials. Carteny et al.309 hypothesized that in marine environments, biodegradable microplastics may accumulate more contaminants than conventional microplastics, despite emitting fewer additives. Life cycle analyses (LCAs) are the most complete tools to evaluate the entire lifecycle of recyclable polymers, blends and their composites, starting from the raw material stage to the final disposal stage or end of life. Through LCAs, factors such as greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, and ecotoxicity potential are evaluated. These analyses help identify challenges and opportunities to enhance the sustainability of biodegradable materials.
Widespread adoption of degradable biopolymers therefore faces challenges such as cost, performance and the need for appropriate waste management infrastructures. In addition, proper waste management is essential to ensure that biodegradable products are properly disposed of and processed to maximise their environmental benefits. The production of biodegradable biopolymers is less than 10 % of the global plastic market and the presence of biopolymers in plastic separates waste resulting in contamination of the polymer waste. According to the literature, if the biodegradable biopolymer waste are mixed with durable polymer waste, unfortunately, the mixes show very poor properties and performance and they could not be considered useful for materials recovery, improving the circularity [118,119]. Based on European statistical data, the polymers and biopolymers waste at their end-of-life are subject to materials recovery of one-third of the total waste amount, disposal of about one-third and incineration for energy recovery of about one-third [120]. Anaerobic digestion transforms organic material into three primary products: biogas, biosolids, and digestate liquor. Biogas, primarily composed of methane, can be harnessed as a renewable energy source. Biosolids, which consist of the microbial biomass that proliferates on the organic substrate and the digestate liquor, containing dissolved nutrients, are typically utilized as fertilizers, contributing to soil health and nutrient cycling [88]. On the contrary, if depolymerized products cannot be fully assimilated or mineralised, they may present ecotoxic hazard under specific conditions. Microorganisms in this stage may differ from those involved in depolymerisation.37 Clearly, disintegration of a polymer is only the beginning of this process and therefore not a good definition for biodegradability. Thus, we recommend the published scientific opinion of the European Union, where biodegradation of plastics is considered as “the microbial conversion of all its organic constituents to carbon dioxide (CO2) (or carbon dioxide and methane in conditions where oxygen is not present), new microbial biomass and mineral salts, within a timescale short enough not to lead to lasting harm or accumulation in the open environment”.52 This emphasises that the ‘results’ from biodegradation of (biodegradable) plastics should have relatively less environmental impact on nature. The “timescale short enough not to lead to lasting harm or accumulation” is powerful, as this will be very different for each material and for all local circumstances. “Lasting harm and accumulation” are criteria that can be objectively assessed. Consumers expect that the so-called biodegradable plastics can biodegrade fast in nature without resulting in any negative impact on the environment.53 However, some of those commercial plastics claimed to be biodegradable were tested under industrial composting conditions, as described in standard methods ISO 14855,54 ASTM D6400,55 EN 13432.56 The fact that industrial composting provides more favourable conditions (i.e. higher temperature, higher total concentration of microorganisms, a higher moisture content for soil) can easily explain that polylactic acid (PLA), a well-known bio-based biodegradable polyester, completely degrades within several months under these conditions, yet only very slow degradation has been observed at ambient temperature.57-60 Particularly, the temperature of industrial composting (55-60 °C) could be equal to or above the Tg of poly(lactic acid) (PLA) (55-62 °C), which leads to the glassy and crystalline polymer becoming softer. Combining carbon balance with kinetic analysis provides a promising framework for testing and improving biodegradable materials, but the feasibility of implementing such rigorous methods at scale remains questionable. Composting is a controlled biological aerobic process that transforms organic waste into carbon dioxide (CO2), water (H2O), heat, minerals, biomass, and humus, all of which are beneficial for plant growth [54]. This transformation is driven by microorganisms that decompose organic matter into stable, nutrient-rich soil amendments. Contextual caveats: biodegradability and land-use change While biodegradability is often promoted as a key sustainability advantage of bio-based polymers particularly for single-use disposable products, its environmental benefits are heavily conditional on proper disposal environments, such as industrial composting or anaerobic digestion facilities. In the absence of such controlled conditions, biodegradable plastics may persist, fragment into microplastics, and act as vectors for persistent organic pollutants and heavy metals through trophic transfer, thus posing substantive risks to both ecological systems and human health [120]. Anaerobic digestion transforms organic material into three primary products: biogas, biosolids, and digestate liquor. Biogas, primarily composed of methane, can be harnessed as a renewable energy source. Biosolids, which consist of the microbial biomass that proliferates on the organic substrate and the digestate liquor, containing dissolved nutrients, are typically utilized as fertilizers, contributing to soil health and nutrient cycling [88]. Anaerobic digestion for plastic waste, particularly biodegradable plastics, can break down plastics designed to be biodegradable under anaerobic conditions. However, the efficiency of this process varies, as does its chemical composition. For instance, plastics such as polylactic acid (PLA) may require specific pretreatment to facilitate breakdown in anaerobic digesters. The effectiveness of anaerobic digestion in treating biodegradable plastics is an area of ongoing research, focusing on optimizing conditions to enhance biodegradation rates and understanding the fate of plastic additives during digestion [59]. Recent advancements are exploring co-digestion techniques, where biodegradable plastics are processed alongside organic waste, potentially improving the degradation rates of the plastics and enhancing biogas yields. However, there are challenges in ensuring a complete breakdown and avoiding the formation of microplastics or other residuals that could impact the quality of the biosolids and digestate liquor. Therefore, integrating biodegradable plastics into anaerobic digestion systems must be carefully managed and monitored to maximize environmental benefits and ensure the safety and efficacy of the resulting bioproducts [169].
IntroductionIn recent years, production of biodegradable polymers has become ever more popular, these finding application mainly in medicine, packaging technology and agriculture. After reaching the end of their life, the materials are much more susceptible to external influences than conventional plastics. Biodegradable materials, along with other organic substances, such as organic residues, can then form suitable matter for activities like composting or the anaerobic treatment of waste (fermentation). While the biodegradability of such materials in an aerobic environment has been extensively explored, their anaerobic biodegradability has not been given sufficient attention.Polycaprolactone (PCL) is biodegradable synthetic polymer that is currently used in controlled drug release systems as well as in other medical applications [1]. For improving further the processing and mechanical properties, PCL is usually modified by blending with resins or filled with inorganic particles [2]. Biodegradability of PCL was tested in a variety of environments - river and lake water, sewage sludge, soil, sediment and compost [3], [4]. In the present study it was found that PCL biodegradability in anaerobic environments is significantly influenced by ambient temperature, molecular weight and the crystallinity of the polymer, with higher levels of degradation achieved at higher temperatures [5], [6] One reason for improved PCL degradation in the presence of thermophilic anaerobic sewage sludge (50-55 °C) is the fact that the representation of microorganisms found in this form of sludge is very diverse; the factors determining this include greater mobility of the PCL chains under thermophilic conditions within the biodegradation environment. This is closely related to the PCL melting temperature (58-65 °C) [7]. In contrast, the degradability of PCL under the mesophilic conditions of anaerobic aqueous environments is almost zero [6], [8], and temperatures in many natural anaerobic environments where biodegradation processes may be underway (e.g. river and sea sediments, anaerobic digested sludge and septic tanks) are lower. This makes it necessary to know PCL biodegradability under these conditions also.Although PCL belongs among biodegradable polymers, this does not mean that it is degradable under anaerobic conditions. The options for the improvement of PCL degradation under anaerobic conditions include the addition of easily degradable materials, particularly polysaccharides (starch), in addition to the example of polyesters - poly-β-hydroxy butyric acid. The anaerobic biodegradation of blends of PCL with other substances has been evaluated in a number of studies [6], [9], [10], [11]. It is noted that adding starch, other polyesters or co-polyesters blended with PCL significantly influences the resulting levels of anaerobic biodegradation.The type of starch used in the polymer blend significantly contributes to the blend's resulting properties. The production of biodegradable plastics can utilize starch from various crops, such as maize, rice or potatoes, no matter if it takes the native or a modified form of the starch. One option for modifying starch is to add glycerol, referred to as the plasticization of starch, since starch tends to prove difficult to integrate into the polymer matrix. The plasticization of starch using glycerol significantly improves processing, thus also positively influencing the mechanical properties of polymer blends [10], [12].Also, modifying certain starch properties can result in obtaining materials with other desired properties. For example, a greater proportion of amylase in starch causes an increase in the crystalline phase of a blend with PCL, in comparison with blends containing starch with a branched structure (amylopectin). This is then reflected in reduced tensile strength and increased elongation at break [10].This report assesses the effect of four different types of starch (native Meritena starch, Waxy starch from genetically modified maize, Gel Instant - pre-gelatinized maize starch, and Amaranth starch) on the degree of biodegradation of polymer blends containing poly(ɛ-caprolactone). In addition, assessment is made of the influence of the method for integration of the starch into the blend, i.e. starch plasticized with glycerol and a non-plasticized starch.This effect was also evaluated in terms of mechanical, thermal and morphological changes in the properties of polymer blends. Treatment of fibres with acids, alkalines, or silanes as per the literature found in this review caused no improvement in the water absorption and reduced the degradation in PHAs. The processes either removed the hemicellulose fraction, increasing crystallinity, or crosslinked the fibres, inhibiting the enzymatic functions. Grafting of the PHA with anhydrides did improve the extent of degradation - however, with the addition of fibres, the grafted PHAs performed poorly as crosslinked fibres inhibited enzymatic activity. Other forms of structural treatment such as cellulose regeneration (lyocell) gave no improvement, and the use of decaying organic matter improved the biodegradation of PHAs. PHAs are considered the most readily biodegradable polymer among many (i.e. PLA, PBS, PBAT etc.), supported by the literature, in aerobic environments (soil, compost and marine), and show promising biodegradable behaviour in anaerobic (sewage sludge, digesters and landfills) environments. PHAs benefit from biotic degradation by several types of bacterial and fungal enzymes. Furthermore, the surface area can be maximized and the crystallinity lowered based on different processing techniques or longer chain PHAs to optimize the biodegradation performance. The characteristics all improve the permeation of moisture and the enzyme interaction that accelerate the enzymatic catalysed hydrolysis. Furthermore, PHA degradation products are easily assimilated into usable products for microbial growth. However, the addition of certain additives (chain extenders) and other biodegradable/non-biodegradable polymers that are used to improve its properties can be detrimental to its biodegradable performance. The negative effects of Joncryl, antifouling agents and non-degradable or hydrophobic plasticizers inhibit the onset and/or extent of PHA biodegradation in aerobic and anaerobic environments. Although these attributes are beneficial for biodegradation modulation in the agricultural industry, it is not desirable for single use plastic consumer waste. Blending PHAs with PLA, PBAT etc. all inhibit the biodegradation of PHAs in most environments, except for compost, where PLA does outperform PHAs.
Bioplastics are synthesized from renewable sources-including plant-based feedstocks and microbial biomass-in contrast to conventional plastics, which rely on non-renewable fossil resources such as petroleum. The accelerated depletion of global natural reserves, notably coal and petroleum, poses a substantial risk to future generations due to their finite availability and eventual exhaustion [19, 155]. Biodegradable polymers derived from renewable feedstocks have garnered significant attention for their favorable environmental profiles, chiefly their ability to undergo decomposition more readily under natural conditions. “Smart” polymers are materials that react to environment changes. Such polymers can respond to environmental alterations for example temperature, pH, specific ions, pressure, light, CO2, reducing/oxidizing agents, salts and etc. [1,2,3]. The polymers with these properties are also known as stimuli-responsive polymers or “environmentally-sensitive” materials and the potential areas of application of these polymers include molecular sensors, drug-controlled release other fields [4,5,6]. One of the most attractive “smart” polymers is poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAAm), because this homopolymer is thermoresponsive. The phases separate from aqueous solutions when heated through a narrow temperature range. It is investigated that this synthetic polymer tend to exhibit a lower critical solution temperature (LCST) and its molecules undergo a sharp transition from coil-to-globule in water around 32 °C temperature, changing from a hydrophilic state below this temperature to a hydrophobic state above it [7]. Above this specific temperature PNIPAAm becomes a precipitate and could be dissolved again by lowering the solution temperature [8]. Due to this phenomenon, PNIPAAm is a promising thermosensitive material as its transition temperature can be adjusted near human body temperature [9]. Meanwhile, crosslinked PNIPAAm behaves differently than linear PNIPAAm due to the polymer network formed during crosslinking [10]. Due to its structure, crosslinked PNIPAAm forms a thermosensitive hydrogel in water exhibiting the volume phase transition at approximately 32 °C. Below this temperature, the hydrogel is swollen, hydrated and hydrophilic, whereas above the LCST, the hydrogel become dehydrated and shrinks [11]. In addition, the LCST of this homopolymer can be changed during the copolymerization with hydrophilic or hydrophobic polymers. Usually, the copolymerization reaction with a hydrophobic polymer could help to decrease the LCST, meanwhile the copolymerization with a hydrophilic polymer could help to increase this temperature [12, 13]. Due to thermoresponsive properties of PNIPAAm could be suitable for biomedical applications such as controlled wound dressings, tissue engineering, and drug delivery systems [14]. However, this polymer has some disadvantages, including limited biodegradability [15, 16], low mechanical strength [17], limited drug loading capacity [15], rapid release of active compounds [18] and etc. Regarding to low biodegradability of PNIPAAm, its use in clinical practice is limited. A variety of agents and biodegradable polymers, including poly(amino acids), polysaccharides, proteins and synthetic polymers such as poly(esters), poly(caprolactone), and poly(ethylene glycol) could be perspective materials to improve the properties of PNIPAAm. Biopolymers or synthetic biodegradable compounds can modify the chemical composition of PNIPAAm to effectively increase biodegradability and biocompatibility [11]. Beyond the latter advantages, the combination with some synthetic or natural biopolymers may provide additional responsivity properties, e.g., pH, magnetic, concentration, etc., and allow for the preparation of dual-responsive smart delivery materials. The backbone of the thermoresponsive graft copolymer should be composed of relatively high molecular weight polymer [19]. Biocompatible amphiphilic block and graft copolymers, in particular those comprising biodegradable sequences, have found over the last two decades great attention due to their potential applications as micellar drug delivery systems [1], [2], [3], [4]. Beside their biodegradability, an important feature for the biomedical applications is also represented by their responsiveness to different environmental stimuli, such as: temperature, pH, light, etc, which will trigger their colloidal properties and consequently the drug release [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. Among these smart copolymers, the temperature-sensitive polymeric systems are of practical interest as this feature is an important physiological factor in the human body. Moreover, some diseases are manifested by a local temperature change. Two types of thermo-sensitive polymers were reported up to now, ones which become molecularly dispersed in aqueous media only upon heating above a certain temperature, called the upper critical solution temperature (UCST), and others undertake a reversible coil-globule transition when they are heated above a critical temperature, so-called the lower critical solution temperature (LCST). Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) and the poly(N-vinylcaprolactam) (PNVCL) are among the most studied thermo-sensitive polymers having a LCST, near human body temperature [10], [11]. In comparison to PNIPAM, PNVCL is characterized by a higher biocompatibility as the hydrolysis of the amide group of the NVCL units does not produce toxic low molar mass amines [11]. In fact, PNVCL is a nonionic, water-soluble polymer, with low cytotoxicity and with LCST values in the range of 32-36 °C, as a function of the concentration and molar mass [10]. Thus, these features make PNVCL-based polymers very attractive for different applications in the biomedical field.
Nanoparticles as carriers can be targeted into tumors passively through enhanced permeation and retention effect (EPR) due to leaky vasculature and impaired lymphatic drainage in tumor tissues. In addition, their small size can avoid rapid clearance by phagocytes which lead to long systemic circulation of nanoparticles [1]. Thus, nano-carriers are far more effective, for anti-cancer drug delivery than conventional drug delivery systems. Even though commercially available controlled release systems are therapeutically advantageous over the conventional systems, they are insensitive to the changing metabolic states of the body [2]. In this context, smart or stimuli-responsive polymeric drug delivery systems in which drug is delivered directly to the target site in response to an internal (e.g. pH, glucose, redox potential, and lysosomal enzymes) or external stimulus (e.g. temperature, magnetic field, ultrasound, and light) have been actively developed. In cancer therapy, the knowledge of tumor micro-environment such as vascular abnormalities, oxygenation, perfusion, pH, temperature and metabolic states allows researchers to design new therapies [3]. Rapid growth rate of tumor cells can cause a temperature increase and pH decrease i.e. slightly acidic micro-environments in extracellular (pH 6-7), endosomes (pH 5.5-6.0) and lysosomes (pH 4.5-5.0) as compared to physiological pH of 7.4 in the blood and normal tissues [3, 4]. Therefore, with a site specific drug delivery feature, thermo and pH dual responsive polymeric nanoparticulate drug delivery systems have tremendous potential. Chitosan (CS) exhibits pH responsive property due to large number of amino groups on its chains and is useful polymeric biomaterial due to its biological properties such as biocompatibility, biodegradability and nontoxicity [5]. Poly (N- isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAAm) is most extensively studied thermo-sensitive polymer with lower critical solution temperature (LCST) of 32 °C, below which it is water soluble and above which it becomes water insoluble [6]. It shows abrupt and reversible thermo-sensitive behavior (at LCST) with biocompatibility, which makes it attractive for biomedical applications while CS shows reversible swelling collapse transition when the net charge decreases [7, 8]. Previous studies indicated that co-polymer composed of CS and PNIPAAm (CS-g-PNIPAAm) is utilized as pH- responsive [9,10,11] and thermo-responsive [12, 13] carrier for anticancer drug delivery. As, such co-polymers show pH dependent LCST considering both pH and temperature stimuli will be more potential to develop a targeted drug delivery system. Indeed, some efforts for the synthesis and application of CS-g-PNIPPAm co-polymer as a pH and thermo dual responsive drug (anticancer) carrier have been made. For instant, Wang Y and co-workers Investigated dual-sensitive nanogels based on chitosan and N-isopropylacrylamide (CTS-g-PNIPAAm) and its intelligent drug delivery of 10-hydroxycamptothecine (HCPT) and it was reported that, loading efficiency of drug encapsulated in to nanogels increased and the cumulative percent release of drug decreased with increase in chitosan molecular weight [14]. Rejinold NS et al. developed pH and thermo-responsive 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU)-loaded chitosan-graft-poly (N-isopropylacrylamide) copolymeric nanoparticles by ionic cross-linking method and found that the higher LCST (40 °C), protonation and swelling at acidic pH (4.5) could lead to enhanced release of 5-FU from nanoparticles at lower pH [15]. Jaiswal MK et al. synthesized nanohydrogels based on poly (N-isopropylacrylamide)-chitosan. Fe3O4 magnetic nanoparticles have been incorporated into hydrogels to achieve temperature optimized magnetic nanohydrogel (MNHG) for magnetic hyperthermia with LCST >42 °C. The released amount of Doxorubicine was found to be nearly 4 μg/mg above hyperthermia temperature (∼42 °C) as opposed to only 1.9 μg/mg of MNHG at physiological temperature (37 °C) under acidic environment (pH ∼ 4.6) [16]. Antoniraj MG et al., synthesized thermo-responsive graft copolymer PNIPAm (amine-terminated)-g-Ocarboxymethylchitosan (PNIPAm-g-OCMC) by graft-onto method and used to prepare doxorubicin-loaded nanoparticles. At 25 °C only about 38.2% drug release was found from nanoparticles and when the temperature was increased to 37 and 42 °C, the release of doxorubicin was enhanced to73.2 and 98.8%, respectively. In this study drug release at normal physiological condition was 73.2% thus, only sustained delivery of drug can be achieved but not targeted delivery [17]. Luo YL et al., prepared temperature and pH responsive multiwalled carbon nanotubes semi-interpenetrating hydrogels for Doxorubicin. The percent release of DOX from the gel-formulations was found to be 43, 48 and 53% at 37 °C and at 38 °C approximately 63, 68 and 87% drug was released after 21 h, this is in accordance with the corbon nanotubes contents of 1, 2 and 5 wt%, respectively. In this study, more than 40% of drug was released at physiological temperature [18]. Though, some light has been shed on the development of thermo and pH responsive CS-g-PNIPPAm nanocarrier for anti-cancer drug delivery, nanoparticulate system optimized for extracellular pH and temperature of tumor micro-environment with significant drug loading and effective controllability is the need of the hour for better targeting efficiency. Physicochemical properties remain the challenge in development of platinum based anticancer drug delivery systems. Oxaliplatin (OXA) is third generation platinum based antitumor drug currently used as a drug of choice for treatment of colorectal cancer [19]. Oxaliplatin contains a large carrier ligand 1,2-diaminocyclohexane in its structure and creates DNA adducts which are more cytotoxic than those of cisplatin and carboplatin and also, it has been found to be less toxic and more effective than that of cisplatin against cisplatin-resistant tumours. Though effective, its clinical efficacy is limited due to its adverse effects in the form of neurotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, gastrointestinal and hypersensitivity reactions etc. [20,21,22]. Most importantly, nonselective action of oxaliplatin on normal and tumoral cells is the limiting factor for effective treatment of cancer. To overcome its limitations different carriers like liposomes [23,24,25], nanostructured lipid carriers [26], carbon nano-tubes [27], micelles [28] and nanoparticles [19, 29] have been reported with sustained drug release mechanism. Chitosan based pH-responsive nanocarrier for oxaliplatin exhibited rapid drug release at pH 4.5 than at pH 7.4 [30], whereas oxaliplatin-loaded thermosensitive liposomes released >80% of the encapsulated drug within 2 min with mild hyperthermia at 40-42o C [31]. This necessitates the development of tumor microenvironment responsive novel “smart” drug delivery system for oxaliplatin, as the antitumor activity of OXA-loaded CS-g-PNIPAAm nanoparticles in a model has not yet been reported.

Hydrogels are crosslinked hydrophilic polymers that are able to absorb aqueous solutions to a high degree without dissolving. Hydrogels have been used in many fields such as bioengineering, biotechnology, agriculture, food industry, and pharmacy. Hydrogels have unique advantages in drug delivery when they are synthesized as environmentally responsive in which especially pH and temperature responsive hydrogels have been taking great attention because pH and temperature are two important factors affecting the release of active agents inside the human body. Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPA) is one of the most widely studied temperature sensitive polymer which has a phase transition temperature at around 32 °C. Based on its temperature sensitive property, PNIPA has been used in controlled drug delivery1, enzyme immobilization2 and tissue engineering.3 The PNIPA hydrogels are usually crosslinked by some chemical organic crosslinkers to form conventional hydrogels. These conventional hydrogels have some limitations such as weak mechanical properties, brittleness, and slow response rates. On the contrary, polymer-clay nanocomposite hydrogels exhibited remarkably improved mechanical and thermal properties, and improved release rates when compared with the conventional hydrogels.4, 5 Sodium alginate (NaAlg) is a naturally derived, nontoxic, water soluble, and biocompatible polysaccharide which forms pH responsive hydrogels in presence of divalent cations such as Ca2+, Mg2+, and Ba2+. The interaction between functional groups of alginate and divalent cations results in the formation of crosslinks according to the “egg-box” model.6 The crosslinked structure of alginate has been used to produce drug delivery systems to release various drugs, proteins, and active agents from the matrix.7 Conventional polymeric drug delivery systems release the drug immediately without having any control on the release rate.8 Controlling the drug release using a responsive polymer system with a known release profile is necessary to avoid large fluctuations in release rates and obtain effective delivery. The aim of a controlled drug release system is to transfer the drug molecules to the target at a specific rate to maintain a predetermined concentration of drug in the release medium for a predetermined period of time. Hydrogels with controlled release properties improve therapeutic effectiveness of the drugs and reduce their side effects.9 The swelling ability of hydrogels allows them to absorb and release high quantities of drugs.10 The release rate of the drug is directly associated with the swelling behavior of the hydrogel.11 Hydrogels that are able to trigger the drug release by changing external properties, like pH or temperature, are classified as smart hydrogels.12 The oral route is the most convenient and comfortable way of administering drugs but the main challenge in an oral drug delivery is to prevent the drug release in the acidic stomach environment.13, 14 In addition, the carrier should be resistant to the body temperature and pH changes during the gastrointestinal transit time from the mouth to the colon to keep the bioactivity of the drug.15 Therefore, a smart hydrogel system with resistance to acidic medium is necessary for a successful oral delivery.

MN systems are novel drug delivery systems consisting of micron-sized needles. By forming an array of MNs, these systems enable minimally invasive transdermal drug delivery with virtually no pain, bridging the gap between non-invasive and invasive therapies.5 MNs have been extensively studied in the fields of drug delivery, vaccination, and disease monitoring.6-8 Based on different fabrication methods and structures, MNs can be classified into solid, hollow, coated, soluble, and hydrogel types and these MNs have found widespread applications in transdermal drug delivery and other areas (Fig. 2).9 This review aims to provide an overview of the historical development and recent advancements of MN applications in the context of cell-based therapies, exosomes, and nucleic acids. It also discusses the current challenges and prospects, aiming to inspire new ideas and provide references for researchers in the field. Silicon, metal, and glass are common MN raw materials with excellent mechanical properties. However, their potential for fracturing after insertion into tissues can lead to complications, limiting the application of MN. As a result, sugar glass MNs and biodegradable polymers such as polylactic acid and polycaprolactone have emerged as new options for MN materials. The choice of biocompatible and biodegradable MN materials aligns more closely with the original design intention of minimally invasive procedures.13-17 Coated MNs are composite structures consisting of a solid MN core and a coating layer. The quality of the coating, process reproducibility, and delivery efficiency are crucial for their application. Unlike MN fabrication techniques such as etching, the dip coating method is the simplest way to fabricate coated MNs. In this method, the solid MN is immersed in a solution and the coated MN is obtained by drying and molding. However, this construction method faces challenges in precisely controlling the dose and is time-consuming. It is also difficult to achieve a uniform coating on the inner tip surface due to surface tension. Ideally, the coating should only cover the MN tip uniformly without unnecessarily wasting coating material.18 Several spraying-based coating methods, such as Gas Jet Drying, Spray Coating, electrohydrodynamic atomization, and Piezoelectric Inkjet Printing, have been developed to achieve uniform coating by replacing liquid immersion with droplet spraying (Fig. 3).19,20 The use of microforming further ensures precise dose control of the coating. Dynamic vulcanization is conducted during the intimate mixing of a thermoplastic with an elastomeric material susceptible to vulcanization. This process produces a highly resistant material that can be processed through fusion. It involves the simultaneous crosslinking of the elastomer, facilitated by a crosslinking agent, either with the conventional thermoplastic or exclusively within the elastomeric phase [1, 4-8]. PLA is a biodegradable and biocompatible biopolymer widely used in the polymeric materials industry, mainly for obtaining parts by 3D printing. It comes from renewable sources such as potato, corn, and sugarcane starch, with high rigidity and mechanical strength, being an alternative to conventional polymers such as polystyrene (PS) and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) [9-13]. On the other hand, EVA, a material widely used in the footwear industry due to its characteristics such as high flexibility and good processability, has properties that are directly related to the vinyl acetate content present in its structure, being widely used as an impact modifier of several polymers, including PLA [14-16]. Given the above, several studies have been conducted recently, aiming to obtain PLA/EVA blends with different properties and applications [3, 17-23]. Thus, this work aims to investigate the ductile-brittle transition and thermal, rheological, and morphological properties in dynamically vulcanized PLA and EVA polymer blends using dicumyl peroxide (DCP). The analysis of the ductile-brittle transitions will provide valuable information on the temperature range in which the blends present adequate mechanical behavior. Furthermore, the study of the ductile-brittle transition of dynamically vulcanized PLA/EVA compounds using DCP is considered a novelty in the specialized polymer literature, in addition to the morphological evolution related to its transition. The results of this study are a significant contribution to the literature and industry, contributing to the advancement of knowledge about dynamically vulcanized PLA/EVA polymer blends and providing essential data for developing these materials with properties tailored to specific applications.

PLA has a high tensile strength, but it is brittle. Thus, it is important to impart ductility to PLA. Ductility has been induced with plasticizers11, 12 or by blending with a rubbery elastomer.13-21 Among these methods, blending is known to be economical. The toughening mechanism of the polymer blend has been widely studied. The main toughening mechanisms are crazing (fine cracks and fibril formation) and shear-yielding (chain slippage).26, 30, 31 The dominant mechanism for dissipating energy varies depending on the nature of the main matrix polymer.24, 30-33 However, the critical dispersed phase size or the distance between dispersed phases for blend toughening exists under the assumption that the interfacial adhesion within the blend is constant. Therefore, when using a blend system composite in which a third phase (particles, polymers, etc.) is added to the blend, the properties of the polymers or the blend interface changes due to the additives dispersed within the blend.34 Therefore, it is not possible to determine the toughening mechanism by considering the morphological effect alone.

As a kind of linear aliphatic polyesters synthesized by the ring-opening polymerization of lactides, PLA is typically derived from corn starch fermentation,1 and has good mechanical properties, thermal plasticity, biocompatibility, and ease of fabrication.2 These characteristics enable PLA as a promising polymer for various applications.3 Another feature of PLA is the good safety upon exposure to heat. For example, it does not produce any toxic nitrogen oxide gases and only one third of the combustible heat of polyolefins is generated when it is burned, so it does not damage the incinerator and provides significant energy savings.4 However, the instable processability of PLA needs to be concerned, that is, thermo-oxidative, hydrolytic degradations, and so on. The instability of PLA usually leads to break the polymer chains, as a result to decrease its molecular weight.5 And it would further result in a deterioration of rheological properties, which should be avoided for a processing purpose, especially when high levels of melt viscosity and strength are required. Many researches have been carried out to improve the brittleness of PLA. These researches can be classified into 3 groups, which are small-molecule plasticizers, flexible co-polymers and elastomeric toughening agents. Examples of small-molecule plasticizers include citrate esters, triacetine and low molecular weight poly (ethylene glycol) (Mw = 300-400 g/mol) [[5], [6], [7], [8], [9]]. Poly (ethylene glycol) (PEG) was the most studied plasticizer for PLA, where low molecular weight PEG possessed better plasticizing effect and could accelerate the spherulite growth rate of PLA [5]. However, PEG and other small-molecule plasticizers were not suitable for long-term usage due to the blooming problem [[10], [11], [12]]. Flexible co-polymers used to blend with PLA were usually block- or graft- copolymers, such as random aliphatic copolyesters, ethylene/n-butyl acrylate/glycidyl methacrylate (EBAGMA) [13], and ring opening of δ-valerolactone (VL) and ε-caprolactone (CL) [14]. Some of these polymers could improve the toughness of PLA, but their synthesis methods were complicated leading to high cost. The last alternative was by blending with toughening agents such as commercial natural and synthetic rubbers, as well as thermoplastic elastomers. This method is interesting as it could avoid complicated synthesis processes without a blooming problem. Bitinis et al. (2011) found that the optimal NR content to improve the brittleness of PLA was 10 wt%, where the tensile tests of the samples showed a drastic increase in the average elongation at break from 5% to 200% [2]. Kowalczyk and Piorkowska researched on mechanisms of plastic deformation in biodegradable polylactide/poly(1,4-cis-isoprene) blends and found that incorporation of only 5 wt% of rubber could significantly increase the strain at break of compression molded film during uniaxial drawing, and could improve its tensile strength by 80% [15]. Petchwattana and Covavisaruch studied the toughness improvement of poly (lactic acid)/ rubber wood sawdust composite by using acrylic core-shell rubber (CSR). (2014) studied the improvement in toughness of polylactic acid by melt blending with bio-based polyurethane elastomer (TPU). They found that 15 wt% of TPU had the highest improvement in impact strength from 4 kJ/m2 to 9 kJ/m2 [17]. Sachiko et al. [18] studied toughening of PLA by melt blending with various rubbers, which were ethylene-propylene copolymer (EPDM), ethylene-acrylic rubber (ACM), acrylonitrile-butadiene rubber (NBR), and isoprene rubber (IR) in an effort to toughen PLA. They found that PLA/NBR (20%wt) possessed the highest impact strength (250 J/m); however, their impact strength of referenced PLA (150 J/m) was much higher than those reported in other literatures (25-35 J/m). PLA is biodegradable and biocompatible, and above all, it has great potential for industrial applications due to its excellent processability.1-10 However, PLA has a serious limit for use in industrial applications because it is brittle due to its slow crystallization.1-5 Thus, it is critical to overcome this limitation of PLA for its use in future applications. PLA has a high tensile strength, but it is brittle. Thus, it is important to impart ductility to PLA. Ductility has been induced with plasticizers11, 12 or by blending with a rubbery elastomer.13-21 Among these methods, blending is known to be economical. The toughening mechanism of the polymer blend has been widely studied. The chain-extended PEG was prepared with melt condensation of a low molecular weight PEG and 4,4′-methylenebis(phenylisocyanate) (MDI) for enhancement of the molecular weight of PEG. In the development of sustainable or eco-friendly materials, polylactic acid (PLA) stands out because of its good stiffness and strength, which have enabled it to compete with some commodity plastics.1, 2 However, the inherent brittleness of PLA is a bottleneck that limits its use in engineering applications.3, 4 Although the addition of plasticizers such as poly (ethylene glycol) (PEG) will overcome the brittleness of PLA, it comes with a loss of stiffness or decreased elasticity modulus, which is an important property for semi-structural applications.2, 4, 5 A typical goal of the blending of PLA with other polymers is to increase elongation at break and toughness without adversely affecting the tensile strength and tensile modulus of the resulting material. There are broadly two classes of polymer blends containing PLA: blends with other degradable or renewable resource polymers and blends with non-degradable polymers.6-8 Within the blends with other degradable or renewable resource polymers, PLA and thermoplastic starch (TS) bio-based polymer blends standout because they present good stress-strain properties and biodegradability, which make them suitable alternatives to replace non-degradable polymers in some applications.1, 9 Nonetheless, the hydrophobic nature of PLA and the hydrophilic nature of starch tend to form thermodynamically immiscible phases with phase separation.10-13 It is well known that for a successful blending of thermodynamically immiscible polymeric phases, it is crucial to obtain a good compatibilization. In principle, compatibilization enhances interfacial characteristics, which allows for the tailoring of the blends' mechanical properties. Compatibilization is represented by morphology and proper interfacial adhesion.14 An enhancement of the blend's mechanical properties is expected due to compatibilization. The typical morphologies obtained in immiscible blends are sea-island and co-continuous structures. Another candidate broadly investigated is the first homolog of a group of polyhydroxyalkanoates, namely polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) [2]. Both PLA and PHB alone have excellent strength parameters but low toughness and are relatively brittle at room temperature, which limits their applications. Various approaches were proposed to modify these unfavorable characteristics. Physical modification by various additives belongs to the most frequent ways; from this point of view, a formation of polymer blends was approved to be effective in many cases [3].The blends of PLA and PHB have been described in the literature from various points of view. Mixtures of PLA and PHB exhibit in general higher flexibility compared to both basic components alone, but in spite of this, the maximal strain at break values are relatively low [4,5]. Recently, chemical recycling through depolymerization was explored to break down PCL and other polyesters [29], [30], [31] into monomers and/or oligomers, allowing for the synthesis of new virgin grade PCL or production of other chemicals and polyesters. Lipases can catalyze the hydrolysis of ester bonds to break down PCL utilizing water or alcohol as the reaction medium [24]. The depolymerization products (e.g., monomer and/or oligomers) can then be repolymerized to new PCL and ideally the repolymerization could be catalyzed by the same lipase enzyme by changing the reaction conditions. Overall, commercially available enzymes such as lipases, esterases and chitinases are the preferred choice for the degradation of polyesters as they preferentially catalyze the cleavage of ester bonds in both pure aliphatic and aliphatic/aromatic polyesters [322], [323]. However, especial care should be taken when selecting the appropriate enzyme as each polyester presents its own peculiarities. For instance, lipases hydrolyze the ester bonds of polyesters having a relatively large number of methylene groups such as PCL, PESu, PBSu and PBSA, but cannot catalyze degradation reactions in polyesters having optically active carbons [324]. Such optically active polyesters with high melting temperature; i.e. PLLA, P3HB and P3HV, require the use of proteinase-like enzymes or PHB-depolymerases [315], [325]. Since the discovery of the conversion of starch into sugars by diastase in 1833, the role of enzymes as biocatalysts has been deeply investigated [326]. Given the vast range of opportunities to isolate and design new enzymes with enhanced activity, biological catalysis procedures for polymer chain scission is becoming a growing area of interest at both academic and industrial levels. Despite to the fact that pioneering biodegradability studies were limited to aliphatic polyesters [298], further research efforts have shown that different aliphatic/aromatic polyesters could also be enzymatically degraded under proper circumstances [178]. These recent results opened the path towards the design and synthesis of novel biodegradable polyesters with improved physico-mechanical performance. Moreover, pure aromatic polyesters such as PBT or PET have been traditionally considered as inert against biological attack due to steric hindrance of aromatic groups inside the enzyme catalytic site [302], [314], [327]. Enzymes are proteins formed by many different amino acids with a peculiar three-dimensional structure and become essential to support life as they are responsible of catalyzing in vivo metabolic reactions in living cells [329], [330], [331]. The specific region where the catalytic reactions takes place within enzymes is known as the active site, whose activity is determined by the spatial arrangement and the electrostatic properties of the amino acids that surround this site [332], [333]. A growing body of research has explored the enzymatic degradation of biodegradable polyesters using externally added lipases, typically under physiological conditions (∼37 °C, pH 7) [26]. Huang et al. reported that polycaprolactone (PCL) and polybutylene succinate-co-adipate (PBSA) films exhibited faster enzymatic degradation than PBS when treated with various lipases [27]. Lee et al. identified a surface erosion mechanism for PBS degradation by Pseudomonas cepacian lipase based on the detected hydrolysis products [28]. Enzymatic degradation efficiency depends on factors such as polymer crystallinity, molecular weight, and environmental conditions like pH and temperature [29], [30]. Semicrystalline polymers with low molecular weight tend to degrade more readily, especially at temperatures near their melting point. However, enzyme stability may be compromised under such thermal conditions [31]. Candida antarctica lipase B (CALB) is widely used for polyester hydrolysis due to its robust activity across a broad pH range (3.5-9.5) and thermal stability up to 150 °C in polar solvents. Shinozaki et al. observed 50.4 % degradation of PLA films within 72 h using CALB [32]; Kanwal et al. reported 15.7 % weight loss in PBAT films over 12 days [33]; and Hu et al. noted ∼30 % weight loss in PBS films after 35 days [34]. In recent years, enzyme embedding into polymer matrices has emerged as a promising strategy for promoting self-degradation, particularly in biopolyesters with limited environmental degradability [35]. For instance, CALB-loaded PCL films prepared via solvent casting degraded completely within 24 h at 6.5 wt% enzyme loading and within 17 days at 1.6 wt% [36]. Under dynamic flow, degradation rates were further accelerated. Jbilou et al. achieved > 90 % reduction in PBS molecular weight within 30 min by embedding CalB through melt extrusion at 120 °C [37]. Iwasaki et al. also reported moderate degradation of PLLA films embedded with Proteinase K using hot-pressing techniques [38]. In this study, we investigate the enzymatic degradation behavior of PVA-containing BioPBS, PLA, and PBAT composites by analyzing the structural and property changes before and after degradation. The samples were immersed in enzyme solutions and phosphate buffer solutions, with their degradation characteristics evaluated based on weight loss measurements. Changes in material properties were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD), differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Additionally, dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) and thermogravimetric analysis (TG) were conducted to examine the thermal and mechanical properties. This study aims to elucidate the role of PVA in regulating the enzymatic degradability of these composites, providing valuable insights into the development of biodegradable polymer composites with enhanced degradation performance, which could contribute to reducing plastic pollution in agricultural environments. Enzymes such as cutinase, lipases, and proteases, as well as specialized enzymes like PETase, play a crucial role in biodegradation by breaking down bioplastic polymers into simpler, eco-friendly monomers that microbes can metabolize. Microorganisms like Pseudomonas, Bacillus, Aspergillus, and Penicillium secrete these enzymes, driving the decomposition process, which typically takes three to six months to degrade substrates (Fig. 8). However entirely, challenges persist such as the enzyme instability under extreme conditions (temperature, pH), poor substrate binding affinity, and susceptibility to proteolytic degradation limit their efficiency in industrial settings [115]. Advancements in protein engineering and immobilization techniques have been pivotal. Protein engineering utilizes tools such as machine learning and artificial intelligence to optimize enzyme structures, thereby enhancing thermostability, substrate specificity, and catalytic efficiency. Complementary strategies include novel high-throughput screening methods to identify superior enzyme variants and reinforcement of enzyme surfaces to improve substrate binding (highlighted in the “Bioengineered proteins for bioplastic degradation” framework). Immobilization techniques further enable enzyme reuse and stability by anchoring enzymes to solid supports, mitigating degradation risks. Modern bioengineering methods, such as gene cloning and metagenomics (Fig. 8), have expanded the discovery of novel enzymes and microbial producers. For instance, microbial consortia exhibit synergistic effects by combining multiple species with complementary enzymatic activities, accelerating degradation kinetics. Species like Bacillus and Aspergillus are particularly promising due to their robust secretion of lipases and proteases, while Pseudomonas demonstrates versatility in degrading complex polymer blends. Despite progress, scaling up enzyme production while maintaining cost-effectiveness, ensuring long-term stability in industrial waste streams, and optimizing microbial co-cultures for consistent performance remain key hurdles. AbstractThe enzyme-catalysed cleavage of ester bonds of poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) has been monitored by an improved approach for the quantification of glycolic acid as indicator of copolymer hydrolysis. Glycolic acid released into the degradation medium was determined colorimetrically using chromotropic acid. The assay established is sensitive, as well as being both rapid and economical. The proposed method was applied to assess enzymatic degradation of a series of PLGA polyesters containing different proportions of monomers, end groups of PLGA chains and molecular weights. Among 22 commercially available hydrolytic enzymes (i.e. esterases, lipases and proteases) from different sources, the lipases from Candida antarctica, Candida cylindracea, Candida rugosa, Mucor miehei, Rhizopus arrhizus and porcine pancreas and the esterase from M. miehei all had a significant effect on PLGA degradation, often increasing the rate of ester bond cleavage by a factor of 25 compared to non-enzymatic hydrolysis. The most remarkable substrate specificity was observed for C. antarctica lipase with the rate of degradation being directly proportional to the glycolic acid content. In contrast, degradation by M. miehei esterase and R. arrhizus lipase were nearly independent of PLGA structure. IntroductionWithin the frame of sustainable development, aliphatic polyesters based on lactic or glycolic acid and their copolymers have been extensively investigated due to their biocompatibility and biodegradability [1]. In particular, poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) has received considerable attention for use in temporary biomedical applications (e.g. drug-delivery systems, bioabsorbable sutures, bone fixation devices and tissue engineering scaffolds), but also as an industrial product for environmentally friendly packaging systems and single-use disposable items [2]. It is generally accepted that PLGA demonstrates desirable mechanical properties, good toxicological safety and tuneable degradation rates which are affected by several physical and chemical parameters, such as initial pH, ionic strength and temperature of external medium, the molar ratio of monomers, enantiomeric form, initial molecular weight, crystallinity and specimen size [3], [4]. The abiotic degradation of a solid PLGA matrix in an aqueous environment can occur through bulk erosion involving hydration of amorphous polymer regions, passive ester bond hydrolysis, significant mass loss and solubilisation of oligomers with release of lactic and glycolic acid, both incorporated into cellular intermediate metabolism and assimilated in vivo [5].As far as biodegradability is concerned, it was reported that PLGA fragmentation could be significantly accelerated by different microbial species which assimilated the degradation products as sole carbon source [6]. This would suggest the involvement of either intracellular enzymes or enzymes secreted from bacteria, yeast or fungi [7]. The evaluation of the microbial degradation process and mechanism requires fundamental understanding of the enzymatic activities which take place through adsorption of the enzyme on the surface of the polymer substrate followed up by hydrolysis of the polyester main chain. In contrast to reports on poly(lactic acid) (PLA), little is known about specific enzymes (i.e. esterases, lipases, proteases) from microbial origin responsible for cleavage of ester bonds between lactic and glycolic acid monomers in the PLGA backbone. Enzymatic hydrolysis of the copolymer has been investigated by few researchers, especially in the presence of the mammalian protease trypsin and proteinase K, a proteolytic enzyme secreted from the fungus Tritirachium album [8], [9]. Additionally, two kinds of fungal lipases were reported to promote degradation of PLGA, i.e. Rhizopus arrhizus lipase [9], [10], and Rhizopus delemer lipase [11]. However, there is a clear difficulty in comparing and explaining the degradation rates of the enzymes used in these studies due to the lack of standardization of reaction conditions and assay systems.Studies on degradation of raw PLGA samples have employed a broad range of techniques including gravimetry, viscosimetry, total organic carbon analysis of water-soluble fraction, size-exclusion chromatography, liquid chromatography of hydrolysis products, differential scanning calorimetry, scanning electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction [12]. These procedures, however, either are not readily applicable to small-scale studies or lack the accuracy and specificity required for assessing subtle variations in hydrolytic reactivity towards PLGA copolymers with different monomer compositions. More precise and rapid colorimetric methods have been described for the quantitative analysis of lactic acid released in aqueous medium [13]. The main limitation of the latter technique is that only the L-monomer is determined in samples with D,L-stereoisomers of lactic acid. Furthermore, since several factors of the enzyme-catalysed PLGA hydrolysis, such as temperature and enzyme concentration, play an important role in the polymer degradation rate, it is important to establish a reproducible and easy-handling method free of steric constraints suitable for processing large series of samples from multiple point degradation tests.In this paper, we report on the enzymatic biodegradation of PLGA copolymers with different amounts of glycolic acid using 22 commercially available hydrolytic enzymes. The aim of this work was to identify enzymes, especially from microbial origin, that are capable of rapid and complete ester-linkage scission. In order to accurately monitor the enzymatic degradation of PLGA and to overcome the analytical limitations of classical techniques, an improved colorimetric method based on the quantitative assay of glycolic acid released in the incubation medium is reported. The low-cost method established is simple with high precision, which is promising for testing of PLGA biodegradation in research and industry. Plastic waste is a global issue because it causes overflowing landfills and pollution, leading to environmental concerns. To address this crisis, materials that can be decomposed in the natural environment are introduced to replace conventional plastics. Poly-ɛ-caprolactone (PCL) is a commonly used plastic that can degrade in natural environments. However, owing to its hydrophobicity, its natural decomposition rate is low. In this study, PCL is modified with maleic anhydride (MA) (PCL-g-MA) to increase hydrophilicity and amorphous region for faster decomposition. Morphological (FESEM and POM images), thermal (TGA and DSC), and structural (FTIR, XRD, and XPS) analyzes support the hydrolysis reaction. The mechanisms proposed in this study confirm that lipase hydrolysis starts in the amorphous regions and then transfers to the crystal regions. This hydrolysis progress is expected to facilitate the creation of eco-friendly low-cost PCL-g-MA composites with high-rate hydrolysis, such as bio-plastics and bio-fibers. Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were put forward in 2015 to act as a roadmap to create a peaceful, equal, green world, and address environmental issues.[10-12] The introduction of biodegradable materials is a solution to resolve this issue, as they can be digested by enzymes or by reaction with living things.[13, 14] Biodegradable materials can be obtained from renewable resources and are classified into two main sources: natural polymers (cellulose, starch, etc.) and synthetic polymers (aliphatic polyester, poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(glycolic acid), poly(ɛ-caprolactone) (PCL), etc.).[15] As an environmentally-friendly polymer, PCL is a commonly used semicrystalline aliphatic synthetic polymer with outstanding properties. It is synthesized via the ring-opening polymerization of ε-caprolactone or the polycondensation of 6-hydroxyhexanoic.[16, 17] PCL exhibits excellent biocompatibility, biodegradability, and processability, and has been approved by the FDA with a high biodegradation rate in the human body.[18] It has been adopted in widespread applications, such as biomaterials, biomedicine, ecological products, and packaging.[19-21] Despite its considerable degradability in various environments (such as soil, rivers, and oceans), PCL still requires specific conditions for decomposition to occur.[22] In addition, academic studies on enzyme hydrolysis in seawater, especially aliphatic polyesters in marine microorganisms, have not received sufficient attention from current researchers. In the matter of ocean decomposition, enzymes are one of the influencing factors, as they play a crucial role in the aliphatic polyester hydrolysis which is the primary mechanism of degradation of these polymers due to their easily cleavable ester linkages. The hydrolysis of polyesters begins with water absorption, followed by ester bond hydrolytic fractionation. As a result, molecular fragmentation and chain splitting occur. Surface erosion (heterogeneous) and volume erosion (homogeneous) are the two main mechanisms of hydrolytic decomposition.[23] Cutinase (E.C.3.1.1.74) and lipase (EC.3.1.1.3) are two common types of enzymes that belong to the α/β hydrolase family and are found in biological carbon cycles in marine environments. Lipase hydrolyzes triacylglycerols, whereas cutinase hydrolyzes carboxy ester bonds of cutins.[24, 25] According to Gan et al.,[26] PCL can be destroyed easily by lipases produced by bacteria, particularly Pseudomonas cepecia, or the so-called Burkholderia cepacia lipase (Lipase PS).[27, 28] The hydrolysis of PCL in nature involves two major processes. In the first instance, PCL degrades by random chain scission of the ester groups in the bulk material via hydrolysis. This occurs preferentially in polymer's amorphous regions due to the polymer's loose structural packing, resulting in ester formation. Water molecules attack bonds more readily and ester bonds are cleaved from the polymer backbone, shortening the chain lengths and resulting in the formation of capronic acid, 6-hydroxycaproic acid, or 6-hydroxyhexanoic acid.[29, 30] However, because of its extremely hydrophobic nature and high crystallinity, microorganisms slowly decompose PCL in their natural surroundings.[31, 32] PCL hydrolysis in the presence of microorganisms or enzymes depends on a variety of parameters, including molecular weight, crystalline morphology, and environmental decomposition.[33] According to previous studies,[34] enzymatic hydrolysis seems to initiate decomposition in the amorphous region, which then shifts to the crystalline region.
As one of the most important aliphatic polyesters, PCL has been used in several FDA approved products due to its facile accessibility, good solubility, low melting temperature and excellent blend-compatibility [5], [6], [7]. The enzymatic and hydrolytic degradation of PCL has been widely investigated [8], [9], [10], [11], [12]. Three kinds of lipase, i.e. Rhizopus delemer lipase, Rhizopus arrhizus lipase and Pseudomonas lipase, have been reported as capable of effectively accelerating the hydrolytic degradation of PCL [13], [14], [15], [16]. Highly crystalline PCL was reported to totally degrade in several days in the presence of Pseudomonas lipase [17], while hydrolytic degradation required several years at 37 °C [18]. Recently, further studies have been focused on the properties modification of PCL polymers, by introducing hydrophilic/hydrophobic segment by blend or copolymerization techniques. In the family of biodegradable synthetic polymers, aliphatic polycarbonates, such as poly(trimethylene carbonate) and poly(5,5-dimethyltrimethylene carbonate), have also attracted great interests because of their good biocompatibility, favorable mechanical properties, low toxicity and biodegradability [19], [20]. Furthermore, the properties of aliphatic polycarbonates can be conveniently modified and designed by introducing pendent functional groups, which can be used to not only adjust the properties of polycarbonates but also facilitate further modification [21], [22]. Aliphatic polycarbonates with pendent functional groups can be synthesized by ring-opening polymerization (ROP), while the synthesis of novel cyclic monomers containing a variety of functionalities has become an important method for the development of new biodegradable polymer materials with special properties for different applications [23], [24], [25], [26]. Compared with another aliphatic polycarbonates with allyl ester group, poly(5-methyl-5-allyloxycarbonyl-1,3-dioxan-2-one) (PMAC) [28], the relatively stable ether bond within PATMC would be good for avoiding the uncontrollable transesterification of the ester bond within PMAC during the polymerization. In this study, synthesis and characterization of novel biodegradable copolymers of 5-allyloxy-1,3-dioxan-2-one with ε-caprolactone (poly(ATMC-co-CL)) were reported with special emphasis on the enzymatic degradation of polymers. The ring-opening copolymerization was performed using Sn(Oct)2 as the catalyst at 140 °C. Biodegradable copolymers with different compositions were characterized by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), gel permeation chromatography (GPC), differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), X-ray diffraction (XRD) and static contact angle method. In vitro MTT assay of the copolymers was also evaluated. The resulting copolymers were processed to films by solution-cast method, and allowed to degrade at 37 °C in a 0.1 M pH 7.4 phosphate buffer solution containing Pseudomonas lipase (0.2 mg/mL). Physicochemical property changes of polymers during degradation were monitored by weighing to determine weight loss profiles, GPC for molecular weight changes, DSC and XRD for crystalline phase transitions and changes in crystalline status, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to examine surface morphology changes.
Mechanical recycling of PCL can be more challenging compared to conventional plastics due to the faster reduction of mechanical properties after successive processing cycles [26], [27], [28]. Recently, chemical recycling through depolymerization was explored to break down PCL and other polyesters [29], [30], [31] into monomers and/or oligomers, allowing for the synthesis of new virgin grade PCL or production of other chemicals and polyesters. This involved both a non-linear regression analysis of the carbon mineralization datasets and a linear analysis of the acceleration phase, to provide more comprehensive understanding of the biodegradation dynamics.
