The water contact angle analysis shows interactions between a solid and a liquid substance which is important for food packaging as it indicates surface wettability and hydrophobicity of the packaging material [54]. Surface morphology and free energy are often used to identify the hydrophobic or hydrophilic nature of the material. A higher contact angle suggests higher hydrophobicity and lesser interaction between solid and liquid [55]. The hydrophobic surfaces exhibit high contact angle values (> 90°), whereas the most wettable surfaces have minimal values (< 20°) [54]. The contact angle images and values of all the samples are illustrated in Figure 7 [(a-(g)]. BioPBSA films with 15 and 25 wt.% S-t-WS exhibited contact angle values of 76.92° and 71.38°, respectively, indicating that the films primarily exhibit hydrophobic-like behavior. Moreover, increasing the filler content hardly shows any significant change in contact angle. This suggests that S-t-WS does not significantly increase the hydrophilicity of the films at increased concentrations. However, after uniaxial stretching, the contact angle decreased significantly, with the lowest value observed at SR 3.5 [Figure 7 (g)]. This reduction is probably due to an increase in surface smoothness resulting from uniaxial orientation, which enhances the water contact angle of stretched films [56]. This work studies the impact of uniaxial stretching of BioPBSA and S-t-WS-based composite films on the mechanical, thermal, barrier, and morphological attributes. The composite films filled with 15 and 25 wt.% S-t-WS were stretched at SR of 2.5 and 3.5. The addition of S-t-WS increased Young's modulus and TS of the films while the EAB reduced. Uniaxial stretching was able to increase the TS and Young's modulus by a maximum of ~213% and ~25%, respectively, for BioPBSA/15S-t-WS films compared to unstretched films probably due to increased crystallinity. DSC and XRD studies also corroborated with this observation and exhibited higher %crystallinity with an increase in SR. This enhancement in film performance was primarily influenced by polymer chain alignment, crystallinity development, and molecular relaxation. The WVP performance of the stretched films improved at 15% S-t-WS in comparison to their unstretched counterparts. The improvement is due to the free volume reduction in the matrix and an increase in %crystallinity after stretching. The water contact angle was also measured, which shows a reduction in values upon uniaxial stretching. Overall, uniaxial stretching improves the mechanical performance, the barrier performance of BioPBSA/15S-t-WS films (at SR 3.5) and crystallinity of the composite blown films. Nevertheless, the valuable insights into the orientation technique with its effects on the performance of BioPBSA/S-t-WS films will be useful to the scientific community and industry partners alike. Therefore, these robust biodegradable blown film-based composite films can be used to substitute nonbiodegradable packaging material for packaging applications. The contact angle assists in the validation of the hydrophilicity and hydrophobicity of biopolymer films. Materials with a contact angle greater than 90° are defined as hydrophobic, while those less than 90° reflect a hydrophilic nature. (32) The results of the contact angles are shown in Figure 2A. The collagen-PVA films with glycerol exhibited a contact angle of 45.54 ± 3°, confirming their highly hydrophilic nature. Interestingly, the addition of drug and [Cho]Ac increases the contact angle up to 74.22 ± 2°, demonstrating the decrease in wettability of the films. Further, the films’ swelling was also assessed by determination of the water contact angle with time (Figure 2B). It has been noted that the contact angle was stable up to 2 min for films with [Cho]Ac. This further confirms the decreased solubility and swelling of the polymer matrix due to the better hydrogen bonding by [Cho]Ac IL among the film components. The delayed swelling and dissolution of the films’ matrix may be helpful in sustained drug release. The mechanical properties such as elongation at break, tensile strength, elastic modulus, and stress-strain of the prepared films are shown in Figure 3. From Figure 3, it is evident that the elongation capacity and tensile strength of the composite films were increased after the addition of CIP (Figure 3A,B). This may occur by the formation of an intermolecular hydrogen bond between the hydroxyl groups of CIP and PVA or the amino acids of collagen. More interestingly, [Cho]Ac further increased the elongation capacity and tensile strength of the collagen-PVA films (Figure 3A,B). Additionally, the elastic modulus was significantly decreased for [Cho]Ac-based films (Figure 3C). These findings can be ascribed to the better hydrogen bonding and enhanced plasticizing effect by [Cho]Ac in the matrix of films. The stress-strain curve showed a breaking point at around 30, 46, and 51% for films with 10, 25, and 50% [Cho]Ac as plasticizer, whereas it showed breaking point at 24 and 28% with glycerol as plasticizer due to the breaking of hydrogen bonds (Figure 3D). Numerous studies have been performed by using different cross-linking agents for the better mechanical properties of collagen-based materials. Collagen has widespread applications due to its extra strength and good film-forming ability. Recently, Chen et al. found that the mechanical properties of collagen films improved significantly when cross-linking with glutaraldehyde. (38) Further, Li He et al. also showed that the glutaraldehyde cross-linking increased the tensile strength and elongation capacity of pig skin collagen-based films. (39) Although glutaraldehyde improves the mechanical properties, some contradictory evidences regarding their cytotoxicity at higher concentrations are also present. (40,41) In addition to glutaraldehyde, several other cross-linking agents including sodium metaphosphate, epichlorohydrin, and carbodiimide have also been used. (40) Presently, attempts are being made to use [Cho]Ac IL as a cross-linking agent for development of biopolymer films. Recently, Mehta et al. used choline salicylate IL for gelatin-based films, which showed excellent applicability in food packaging. (42) Abednejad et al. also developed IL-based polyvinylidene fluoride-hyaluronic acid wound dressing for controlled drug delivery. (43) Hence, ILs open new opportunities in fields like fabrication of new biomaterials and controlled drug release. The FTIR spectra of CIP powder are shown in Supporting Information (Figure 3S). The CIP shows characteristics peak at 1717 cm-1 attributed to carbonyl stretching, 1613 and 1285 cm-1 attributed to C-F bond stretching vibration, 3044 cm-1 attributed to O-H stretching vibration, and 2846 cm-1 attributed to C-H stretching vibrations. (44) The FTIR spectra of collagen-PVA composite films are presented in Figure 4A. The CIP-incorporated films exhibited all of the major peaks for CIP, indicating their presence in the composite films. However, some peaks are shifted to the higher wavenumber indicates the formation of intermolecular hydrogen bonds. Further, the inclusion of IL in a film-forming composite signifies more shift of amide I and amide II peaks toward higher wavenumbers, indicating more H-bonding between the films matrix and ions of ILs. From these results, it is clear that [Cho]Ac IL act as a plasticizer making the films’ fabrication simpler with the avoidance of a synthetic plasticizer. Recently, Mehta et al. constructed gelatin-based films with the help of choline salicylate IL for food packaging applications. These films showed excellent antimicrobial, antioxidant, UV shielding, and mechanical properties. However, as essential oil is a hydrophobic substance that hinders the interaction of gelatin peptide chains, resulting in a loose Gel-CA film structure, water vapor migrates easily [44]. Aggregated cinnamaldehyde may push the polymer chains apart, increasing the free volume through which water vapor can more easily pass. Therefore, ZO affects the organization of the polymer chains and modifies the film's microstructure, resulting in a decrease in tensile strength and an increase in water vapor transport [22]. Static or dynamic contact angle essays are essential techniques when referring to the study of the hydrophobicity of the materials. In case of bare or monolayer films dynamic contact angle technique is usually selected.29 In this case, dynamic contact angle measurements (advancing and receding) with needle-in-drop technique were performed in order to analyze the effect of plasticizers nature and aging phenomena on the wettability of films. In all cases, ethylene glycol was used due to angle measurement problems associated with the high hydrophilic nature of the films. The results shown in Figure 4 indicate that the advancing contact angle value (θa) was higher than receding contact angle value (θr), as reported elsewhere.29 Furthermore, the influence of plasticizer's structure on surface properties of PLS was demonstrated. CSi35-fresh films presented the highest contact angle values, revealing the lowest wettability of the material. Lower contact angle values were observed for both CSg35-fresh and CSpd35-fresh samples. Both glycerol and 1,3-propanediol plasticized films showed similar angle values, although the measurements were sometimes erratic for the latter. On the other hand, significant differences were observed in terms of the evolution of the contact angle values due to the aging of the films. Indeed, the contact angle values of samples plasticized with glycerol and 1,3-propanediol increased significantly after storage time, mainly in CSg35-aged films. Besides, contact angle values for CSi35 decreased after aging. According to the results, the retrogradation of the plasticized starch, usually linked to the amylose chains alignment and the partial recrystallization of amylopectin, seemed to affect significantly the surface energy of the films. A remarkable influence of retrogradation could be concluded for the glycerol and 1,3-propanediol containing samples, whereas the use of D-isosorbide as plasticizer seemed to reduce the effect of this phenomena. Avérous and Pollet6 reported that the aging of starch-based materials is strongly influenced by the glass transition temperature.6 The higher molecular weight and the cyclic chemical structure of D-isosorbide, may reduce the mobility of the chains leading to high transition temperatures. In order to evaluate the value of the main relaxation temperature dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) measurements were performed (Figure 5). As it could be observed, the relaxation temperatures associated with the plasticizer-rich domains were highly dependent on the type of plasticizer. Temperatures of −70 °C, −60 °C, and −30 °C were measured for the maximum of tan δ for CSpd35, CSg35, and CSi35 samples, subsequently. At room temperature, above the Tg of the plasticizer-rich phase, retrogradation involves the rearrangement of the polysaccharide chains.6 Thus, the mobility of the starch chains located in the plasticizer rich domains was higher in samples plasticized with 1,3-propanediol and glycerol compared with CSi35 sample. As a consequence, the retrogradation may occur in a greater extent leading to significant variations of the contact angle measurements for CSpd35 and CSg35 materials. However, plasticizer migration effects have to be considered during the storage time of the films,30 especially in those containing glycerol. For this reason, the angle measurement could be affected by the accumulation of plasticizer molecules in the surface. Nevertheless, it was concluded that the use of D-isosorbide as plasticizer for PLS led to higher stability of the film surface properties. The interaction between biodegradable food packaging films and water is significant for food packaging to determine its application. Surface free energy and morphology can be used to determine whether the films are hydrophilic or hydrophobic. The contact angle is used to determine the wetting qualities of films made with and without CNCs. Using the sessile drop method and the Kruss scientific apparatus with a CCD camera and manual syringe control system, the contact angle was calculated. Using the Kruss advanced image analysis software tool, the angle formed between the film's surface in contact with the drop and the liquid drop's tangent at that point was measured. A drop with a dimension of 4 × 4 mm was injected into the film surface using a syringe filled with 3 mL of distilled water for the measurements. The mean values were calculated after at least ten measurements were taken in various areas of the film surface. At a relative humidity of 35% relative humidity and a temperature of 20°C, all measurements were carried out in the open air.36 The thickness of the biodegradable films was measured using a digital micrometer (Mitutoyo) before analyzing the tensile strength. The film must be examined for creases and cracks before testing. Both the control film (a film without CNC) and the film with CNC (1%) were measured. The tensile strength of the resultant films was determined using Tinius Olsen Ltd., UK (H5KS). The tensile strength and elongation at break were calculated using the QMAT test zone software.37 The surface of the air-dried CNC integrated film was examined initially with a conventional light microscope and subsequently with a Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) (ZEISS (EVO18)) for morphological structure analysis. Energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) analysis was also performed along with SEM analysis to analyze the elemental composition.38

The PU curve has exhibited two-step weight losses at 277-420°C and 420-536°C, which were associated with the thermal decompositions of hard segments (dominantly urethane groups) and soft segments (mainly PCL component) in PU backbones, respectively.33 In the case of silk film, three-step weight losses were detected at 100-250°C, 250-550°C, and 550-700°C. The first weight loss at 100-250°C was related to the volatilization of some free water and low boiling point compounds. The second weight loss at 250-550°C originated from the decomposition and that weight loss was caused by the destruction of the regenerated silk fibroin molecular side chain, while the final weight loss at 550-700°C belonged to the destruction of the regenerated silk fibroin molecular main chain.34 The combination of silk fibroin and PU has improved the thermal stability of the material, either the initial degradation temperature or the degradation end temperature. The 'contact angle' is a critical parameter for evaluating the surface wettability and hydrophobicity/hydrophilicity of biodegradable polymer films, which directly impacts their functional performance and biodegradation behavior. A higher contact angle (>90°) indicates hydrophobicity, reducing water interaction and potentially slowing biodegradation, while lower angles (<90°) suggest hydrophilicity, enhancing water absorption and microbial adhesion to accelerate biodegradation [1][2][7]. For instance, PBAT films with a contact angle of 93.22° degrade slower than hydrophilic thermoplastic starch (TPS) blends (4°–13°) due to reduced microbial accessibility [1][3]. Conversely, cellulose nanocrystals (CNC) increase hydrophobicity (contact angle from 34.44° to 71.72°), altering moisture resistance and mechanical properties [3][11].

The standard gamma-irradiation sterilization dose used in the industry for most combination devices that come in contact with skin or tissue is 25 kGy. This dose is considered sufficient for gaining a minimum of 10−6 sterility assurance level (6 log reduction). For this reason, cooling the product to 0°C or less during irradiation is advised. The balance between the selected gamma radiation doses and the process temperatures allowing minimal damage is referred to as optimum sterilization.19 In the current study, the effects of gamma radiation on the physical and mechanical properties of our new biodegradable drug-eluting wound dressing were investigated. It is important to note that our new hybrid wound dressing, which contains the synthetic polymer PDLGA with the natural polymer collagen, combines the desired properties of both materials and therefore it is superior compared to other types of wound dressings. In addition, it releases antibiotics and pain killers in a controlled desired manner to the wound. Another motivation of this study arises from the possibility that there are changes in material properties of the probe membranes after sterilization. While there have been some studies on effects of sterilization on microdialysis membranes, this is the first attempt to compare two popular chemical sterilants for probes made of regenerated cellulose, and for dialysing two different molecules. Previously, Takesawa et al.12 compared the effects of gamma irradiation, ethylene oxide gas, and autoclaving on cellulose microdialysis membranes. Pore shrinkage was observed in wet membranes under gamma irradiation, and pure water permeability increased. Pore shrinkage was also observed in dry membranes under autoclaving. Polymers with ether, carbonate, carboxylic acid, amide and ester functionalities are selected from a family of poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) containing tyrosine-derived polycarbonates (TyrPCs) to include slow, medium, fast, and ultra-fast degrading polymers. Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is used for comparison. Molecular weight (Mw) of all tested polymers decreases upon gamma and E-beam, and this effect becomes more pronounced at higher PEG content. Gamma sterilization increases the glass transition temperature of polymers with high PEG content. EO esterifies the carboxylic acid groups in desaminotyrosol-tyrosine (DT) and causes significant degradation. VHP causes hydroxylation of the phenyl ring, and hydrolytic degradation. This study signifies the importance of the chemical composition when selecting a sterilization method, and provides suggested conditions for each of the sterilization methods. The most widely used biodegradable polymers in medical applications are poly(hydroxy acid)s such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(d-lactic acid) (PDLA), poly(glycolic acid) (PGA), poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), and poly(caprolactone) (PCL). Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) containing polymers are also widely used.1, 2 Recently, several medical devices were commercialized that incorporate derivatives of the natural amino acid l-tyrosine.3-5 However, unlike devices made from metals and ceramics, devices made from polymers can undergo physicochemical changes during sterilization that could compromise their clinical performance. Materials and devices intended for in vivo applications are either aseptically processed or terminally sterilized before use to avoid any implant-related infection. Aseptic processing of medical devices is rarely practical or economical.6 Therefore, terminal sterilization, where a device is sterilized within its final sterile barrier package, is preferred for medical device sterilization.6 Clinical success of polymeric biomaterials thus depends on the ability of the polymers to be sterilized while retaining their essential physical and chemical characteristics.

Water annealed silk fibroin scaffolds did not degrade significantly in PBS over an 8 d period (Figure 4C), while scaffolds exposed to protease XIV degraded and thus were reduced in mass over time (Figure 4D). The other sterilized scaffolds all remained similar to non-sterile scaffolds in the extent of degradation over time. The changes in silk fibroin following autoclaving are likely a result of changes in the amorphous regions of silk fibroin. Similar observations were made by Gil et al. with porous silk fibroin scaffolds generated by leaching salt from aqueous or organic silk fibroin solutions.48 There, the authors demonstrated that autoclaving promoted greater restriction in the inter- and intra-molecular interactions in the amorphous regions of the silk fibroin chain network, thus affecting mechanical properties and degradation of silk fibroin scaffolds, independent of β-sheet content.48 The accelerated rate of degradation in γ-irradiated silk fibroin scaffolds is likely a result of protein damage caused by γ rays. γ rays ionise water molecules in their trajectory, rupturing chemical bonds and, thereby, releasing radiation products in the form of H+ and OH-. In the present study, the effect of gamma irradiation of PLA under different absorbed doses of a Cobalt-60 source on the mechanical, rheological, thermal and morphological properties of PLA/PBAT blends was investigated. It was found that the mechanical properties of the samples are highly dependent on the absorbed irradiation dose, and despite the reduction in tensile strength when applying irradiation, the absorbed dose of 150 kGy shows a tendency to recover the initial strength. TGA analysis shows that as the absorbed gamma irradiation dose increases, the thermal stability of the material reduces. A small increase of the crystalline fraction was evidenced by DSC and XRD analyses. Rheological measurements showed a decrease in the complex viscosity of irradiated PLA when increasing the absorbed dose, indicating that a decrease in molecular weight occurs due to chain scission when using irradiated PLA. Therefore, PLA irradiation induces chain scission, and this scission improves the compatibility when blended with PBAT. SEM analysis reveals that gamma irradiation of PLA promotes the homogeneity of PLA/PBAT blends, indicating greater compatibility for the blends subjected to higher absorbed doses of 100 and 120 kGy. Further study of radicals decay should be carried out to broaden the discussion of the reactions between PLA radicals and PBAT. Currently, there is a growing intention to obtain composites with nanocellulose for greater efficiency of mechanical properties and sustainability of using cellulosic fillers. Therefore, since the modifications obtained by radiation are favorable to interfacial adhesion, the properties should be improved.

A wound dressing should ideally provide an optimal healing environment which enables rapid healing. It should maintain a moist environment at the wound surface, allow gas exchange, act as a barrier to microorganisms, remove excess exudates and afford mechanical protection to the wound. A new bioresorbable hybrid wound dressing which combines a poly(DL-lactic-co-glycolic acid) porous top layer with a spongy collagen sublayer was developed and studied. The top layer contained the antibiotic drug gentamicin for controlled release to the wound site. It is of very high importance to use an appropriate sterilization process for this special new wound dressing, which will not have a deleterious effect on its function. Our investigation therefore focused on the effects of gamma-irradiation sterilization (10, 25, 35 and 50 kGy) on the structure properties of this wound dressing. The physical and mechanical properties were of the wound dressings were affected by the gamma irradiation because of a combination of chain scission and crosslinking of the collagen layer mainly. The weight loss and water vapor transmission rate were increased, while the water uptake was decreased with the increase in the irradiation dose. The changes were small when doses of 10 or 25 kGy were applied at room temperature. The gamma-irradiation resulted in stronger but more brittle wound dressings. These trends were smaller when the sterilization process was carried out in liquid nitrogen. A wide range of wound dressings has been developed over the years in order to cope with different kinds of wounds.1 Any wound dressing used in the clinic should be sterile according to appropriate standards. Gamma-irradiation is the most suitable sterilization method for dressings that contain natural and sensitive polymers. The current study describes the effect of gamma radiation doses and conditions on the physical and mechanical properties of a new wound dressing developed by us, in order to find an appropriate sterilization process for this wound dressing that will not have a deleterious effect on its function.
Our study shows that irradiation doses of 10 and 25 kGy, which are commonly used for sterilization of medical devices, practically do not change the structural features of the hybrid wound dressing's layers. If a higher dose of 35 kGy is needed, the sterilization process can be safely performed in a L.N. environment, which practically does not change the structure of the PDLGA layer and even that of the more sensitive collagen layer. Based on the results described above a schematic representation of a qualitative model can be presented, describing the effect of the irradiation dose (at room temperature) on the physical and on the mechanical properties of the dressing and its performance (Fig. 9). A sign of a wide arrow in a box represents a case when an increase in the irradiation dose results in a decrease in the specific property. In all other cases, an increase in irradiation dose increases the property. As shown in the schematic model, the weight loss and the WVTR are increased while the water uptake is decreased with the increase in the irradiation dose. As expected, higher weight loss of the collagen layer mainly, which results from degradation, enables higher WVTR and lower water uptake. An increase in the radiation dose also resulted in an increase in both, tensile strength and modulus and a decrease in the maximal strain. These changes probably occur because of crosslinking of the collagen layer and result in stronger but more brittle wound dressings. An exception is the case of irradiation dose of 50 kGy which results in a collapse of the microstructure of both, collagen and PDLGA layers, leading to very low WVTR, strength and strain. It is important to note that all described above changes are much smaller when the irradiation is performed in liquid nitrogen, because of smaller changes in degradation and chain scission of both polymers. This study enabled us to assess the effect of the sterilization using gamma irradiation on the physical and mechanical properties of our newly developed hybrid wound dressing. We showed that irradiation at R.T. affect the relevant properties and function of the wound dressing, but when a dose of 25 kGy is used, which is standard for medical devices, the changes are not so dramatic in most properties, and enable function similar to that of non-sterilized samples. In fact, some increase in WVTR, maximal stress and Young's modulus can even be beneficial, as long as the wound dressings do not become brittle. In cases where these are not desired, irradiation in L.N. is a good alternative. As shown, the changes in properties are much smaller.

The effects of ethylene oxide (EO), vaporized hydrogen peroxide (VHP), gamma (γ) radiation, and electron-beam (E-beam) on the physiochemical and morphological properties of medical device polymers are investigated. Polymers with ether, carbonate, carboxylic acid, amide and ester functionalities are selected from a family of poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) containing tyrosine-derived polycarbonates (TyrPCs) to include slow, medium, fast, and ultra-fast degrading polymers. Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is used for comparison. Molecular weight (Mw) of all tested polymers decreases upon gamma and E-beam, and this effect becomes more pronounced at higher PEG content. Gamma sterilization increases the glass transition temperature of polymers with high PEG content. EO esterifies the carboxylic acid groups in desaminotyrosol-tyrosine (DT) and causes significant degradation. VHP causes hydroxylation of the phenyl ring, and hydrolytic degradation. This study signifies the importance of the chemical composition when selecting a sterilization method, and provides suggested conditions for each of the sterilization methods. The most widely used biodegradable polymers in medical applications are poly(hydroxy acid)s such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(d-lactic acid) (PDLA), poly(glycolic acid) (PGA), poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), and poly(caprolactone) (PCL). Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) containing polymers are also widely used.1, 2 Recently, several medical devices were commercialized that incorporate derivatives of the natural amino acid l-tyrosine.3-5 However, unlike devices made from metals and ceramics, devices made from polymers can undergo physicochemical changes during sterilization that could compromise their clinical performance. Materials and devices intended for in vivo applications are either aseptically processed or terminally sterilized before use to avoid any implant-related infection. Aseptic processing of medical devices is rarely practical or economical.6 Therefore, terminal sterilization, where a device is sterilized within its final sterile barrier package, is preferred for medical device sterilization.6 Clinical success of polymeric biomaterials thus depends on the ability of the polymers to be sterilized while retaining their essential physical and chemical characteristics.

The standard gamma-irradiation sterilization dose used in the industry for most combination devices that come in contact with skin or tissue is 25 kGy. This dose is considered sufficient for gaining a minimum of 10−6 sterility assurance level (6 log reduction). Use of an irradiation dose lower than the standard 25 kGy is of special interest in sterilization of medical devices, because of the damaging effect that this dose might have on physical-mechanical properties. During gamma irradiation at room temperature, the product temperature is elevated as a result of gamma ray absorption. For the sterilization of bioresorbable polymers, temperatures must be kept below the temperature at which changes occur in the polymer's molecular weight, in order to prevent degradation. For this reason, cooling the product to 0°C or less during irradiation is advised. This requires the use of cooling agents in the irradiation container to prevent heating to the critical temperature where molecular weight is affected. Various combinations of doses and temperatures can be employed to achieve product sterility without adversely affecting the product. The balance between the selected gamma radiation doses and the process temperatures allowing minimal damage is referred to as optimum sterilization.19 In the current study, the effects of gamma radiation on the physical and mechanical properties of our new biodegradable drug-eluting wound dressing were investigated. It is important to note that our new hybrid wound dressing, which contains the synthetic polymer PDLGA with the natural polymer collagen, combines the desired properties of both materials and therefore it is superior compared to other types of wound dressings. In addition, it releases antibiotics and pain killers in a controlled desired manner to the wound. Therefore, performing an appropriate sterilization process for this new system will enable to use it in the clinic. Schematic reaction of PEG: PVA blends exposed by γ-radiation In recent years, there has been increasing interest in the synthesis of oral drugs in controlled-release pharmaceutical forms that allow once or twice-a-day dosage administration. Gamma irradiation has several advantages over conventional curing processes: I) no catalyst or additives are needed to initiate the reaction; II) the initiation is homogenous throughout the system; III) it can be performed at any temperature and be interrupted at a chosen reaction time; IV) the polymer can be analyzed at selected reaction stages; and V) the temperature during reaction initialization is maintained in contrast to highly exothermic curing without irradiation. In addition, the gamma irradiation applied to polymers causes three different processes: chain scission, crosslinking, or grafting. These processes are dependent on the nature of irradiation, the chemical nature of the polymer, and the applied dose [6, 14]. Many researchers have investigated the properties of PVA-based hydrogels for application in the biomedical field. In a study, Nouh et al. [15] prepared PVA/PEG copolymer irradiated with gamma irradiation at a low dose range (1.5 to 20Gy). Their results led to enhancements of the crosslinking mechanism that resulted in an increase in the average molecular mass. In another study, Park et al. [16] reported the effects of PEG addition on the PVA-based hydrogel by gamma ray. They concluded that the thermal and mechanical properties increased with PEG concentration. Machado et al. [17] prepared different hydrogels from two aqueous solutions of PVA (15 and 20 mass/mass %) by chemical reactions using citric acid as a cross-linking agent and by electron beam (EB) irradiation with doses from 25 to 100 kGy. Their main approach was to development a new material to be used as artificial articular cartilage. From their obtained experimental results, it can be summarized that the PVA hydrogels produced by the irradiation cross-linking process have lower water absorption capacity, better mechanical properties, and higher thermal stability. In this work, the gamma radiation technique was used to synthesize a hydrogel network by crosslinking polyvinyl alcohol and polyethylene glycol blends ratios. The swelling behavior of the produced hydrogel and the controlled release kinetics of the drug model were investigated and the thermal-mechanical properties of the PVA-based hydrogel were improved for applications in drug delivery.

Evidence [8] shows PLGA/collagen hybrids exhibit increased strength and modulus with irradiation doses of 10-35 kGy at room temperature.

1.  **Initial Zones (Starch/Plasticizer Introduction):** Approximately **80°C** is used to introduce starch and plasticizer without premature degradation [6].

Evidence [8] explicitly states that higher temperature, screw speed, or residence time induced TPS thermal degradation.

To address this, a substantial amount of plasticizer must be added to starch under high temperature and shear to facilitate plasticization, resulting in thermoplastic starch (TPS) with melt processability. Common plasticizers for TPS include glycerol,21 citric acid,22 glycerol triacetate,23 formamide, water and small molecules of poly(vinyl alcohol),24-27 with glycerol being the most commonly used and effective. However, the low mechanical strength of TPS and the issue of plasticizer migration and exudation contribute to a significant reduction in the mechanical strength of PBAT/TPS blend materials. Additionally, the strong hygroscopicity of glycerol leads to increased water absorption in PBAT/TPS blend materials. IntroductionThe replacement of conventional petroleum-based polymers by other more environmentally friendly polymers has been focused research in recent times. To this end, starch is one of the most promising biopolymers due to its natural origin from renewable sources, economically competitive and biodegradable. Native starch is not a thermoplastic polymer in a natural way, due to its degradation temperature is lower than the temperature required for plasticization. However, in the presence of a suitable plasticizer, under temperature and shear conditions, it is converted in a thermoplastic starch (TPS) able to be processed as the conventional thermoplastic polymers [1].Plasticizers for starches must be small molecules capable of diffusing between the starch molecules and they must own groups capable of forming hydrogen bonds with hydroxyl groups of starch molecules. Glycerol is, among the polyols, the most used plasticizer for starch due to its low cost, high boiling point and no toxicity. Saponification, or de-esterification, typically describes the hydration reaction (hydrolysis) that breaks the ester bonds by either free hydroxides or acids. Such side reactions may happen to some extent among the complex heterogenous mixture (slurry) of hemp fibers and pectin under highly acidic or basic conditions. Under highly acidic conditions, such side reactions may happen and yield free carboxylic acids on the pectin. The free carboxylic acids of pectin can reform ester bonds with the hydroxyl groups on the hemp fibers. However, under high basic conditions, any saponification (or de-esterification) will yield free carboxylates, but the basic conditions cannot catalyze the re-formation of ester bonds with hydroxyl groups because the byproducts, hydroxide ions, are not good leaving groups. Thus, for the methyl carboxylate groups of pectin to react with hydroxyl groups on the fiber surface to produce robust biocomposite as we observed in our experiment, transesterification, though slow, is expected to happen. In other words, most of these methyl carboxylate groups probably do not hydrolyze under the basic conditions evaluated in our experiments. It is important to note that when the pH of the crosslinking reaction was adjusted in the fabrication process to either 1-2 or 12-14, only a few milliliters of the aqueous pectin solution were used for a reaction with 4 grams of hemp fibers. The total numbers of moles of acids or bases were relatively small when compared to the amount of hemp fibers used in the fabrication process. Also, our heating process at 70°C for 2 h and then at 100°C for 10 h will deplete most of the water needed for saponification and hence promote the formation of ester bonds by shifting the equilibrium. Though the transesterification reaction is relatively slow, we believe that sufficient crosslinking can happen due to such reaction mechanisms. Otherwise, we would not observe the V-shape compressive strength trend in Figure 10. In addition, the common method to measure the degree of methylation of pectin is by de-esterification of pectin with a 3× to 10× strong base (such as aqueous NaOH solution (pH = 13-14) mixed 50/50 with isopropanol).85 Even under such harsh conditions, a minimum of 2 h is recommended for complete esterification. This indicates that the de-esterification process is not too fast compared to our reaction period. Hence, the reaction time used in our method is expected to be sufficient for significant crosslinking via transesterification to happen. In this paper, a one-step water-based process to valorize hemp fiber was reported to fabricate hemp fiber composites with pectin. In our composite fabrication methodology, we highlighted the valorization approach to efficiently use surplus hemp fibers by crosslinking them using pectin into green and sustainable biocomposites. Unlike other synthetic polymers such as polyurethane, epoxy, and other petroleum-based products used in conventional composite fabrication,6, 20 we used pectin for crosslinking the hemp fibers in our process because pectin was a plant-based biopolymer extracted from fruit peel. This allowed these hemp fiber composites fabricated using this approach to be sustainable and biodegradable. Based on the provided evidence, the mechanism of chain scission during hydrolysis of ester bonds involves the cleavage of ester linkages in polymer backbones via nucleophilic attack by water molecules. This process reduces molecular weight and generates carboxylic acid end groups, as confirmed by FTIR detection of broad absorbance bands at 3300-3000 cm⁻¹ [1], [3]. Key aspects include:  

1.  **Random vs. non-random scission**: Hydrolysis typically proceeds through **random cleavage** of ester bonds in linear aliphatic polyesters (e.g., PLLA, PLGA), breaking chains throughout the polymer matrix [4], [5]. In branched architectures (e.g., multi-arm PEG-PLGA), **non-random scission** occurs if ester bonds near the core are preferentially cleaved, releasing arms before further random degradation [4], [5].  

2.  **Autocatalysis**: Acidic degradation products (e.g., carboxylic acids) accelerate hydrolysis by catalyzing additional ester bond scission, particularly in bulk-eroding polymers like PLGA [4], [5], [7]. This leads to heterogeneous degradation, with faster erosion in the polymer interior [4], [5].  

3.  **pH dependence**:  
    -   **Acidic conditions**: Preferential cleavage at chain ends produces lactic acid directly (e.g., in PLA) [13].  
    -   **Basic conditions**: Carbonate esters undergo nucleophilic attack by alcoholate anions, leading to chain scission [2]. Alkaline environments also promote random ester hydrolysis [13].  

4.  **Steric and chemical influences**: Electron-withdrawing groups (e.g., azide) near ester bonds reduce scission susceptibility by increasing steric hindrance [1], [3]. Conversely, hydrophilic polymers (e.g., non-energetic elastomers) exhibit faster hydrolysis due to higher water absorption [1], [3].  

5.  **Degradation products**: Chain scission generates low-molecular-weight fragments that become water-soluble, enabling mass loss (erosion) and further microbial breakdown [4], [5], [7].  

Thus, ester hydrolysis is a nucleophilic substitution reaction where water attacks the carbonyl carbon, cleaving the C–O bond and fragmenting the polymer chain [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [7], [13], [15].

Hydrolytic degradation involves the fragmentation of polymer chains due to the uptake of water, resulting in the formation of products with lower molecular weights than the original material, such as oligomers and monomers.143 For polyesters, hydrolytic degradation occurs due to ester bond scission in the presence of water. The susceptibility of these ester bonds to scission is determined by the charge value of the reacting carbon atoms, with functional groups having charge values greater than 0.3 being highly susceptible to hydrolysis.144 The choice of polyol during polyester synthesis also considerably affects the degradation rate of the polymer, with hyperbranched polyols leading to faster degradation due to their enhanced spatial distribution and increased amorphousness.88 The biodegradation rate is significantly influenced by crystallinity, which is associated with the processing techniques and conditions employed to obtain the end product. Amorphous regions are known to be more prone to hydrolytic degradation than crystalline regions.145 Polyesters with a higher number of hydroxyl functionalities also degrade faster due to their increased hydrophilicity. Hydrolytic degradation typically proceeds through random scission, resulting in the degradation product of carboxylic acid and alcohol.146 This leads to a decrease in pH in the reaction medium and acid-catalyzed hydrolysis over time.147 Therefore, one notable aspect of polyester degradation is the production of acidic byproducts during the hydrolytic breakdown, which can cause an inflammatory response and tissue damage during the degradation of the implanted scaffolds. Herein, in addition to polyol-based biopolyesters, the degradation of other aliphatic bio-polyesters, such as PCL, PBS, and PLA is discussed in order to provide a comprehensive comparison. Special emphasis is placed on the material properties and processing factors that can affect their biodegradation behavior. While the primary focus of this discussion is on the hydrolytic degradation of polyesters, some attention is also given to enzymatic degradation, as it similarly involves polyester breakdown via hydrolysis. Currently, it is well known that hydrolytic degradation via chain scission and water diffusion into the bulk both affect the erosion rate. Understanding these kinetic processes is crucial in designing and developing biodegradable polymers that can maintain their structural integrity while degrading at a controlled rate. According to von Burkersroda et al.,149 the degradation behavior of polyesters is influenced by multiple interdependent material properties. Both intrinsic and extrinsic factors can affect the modes of hydrolysis. Intrinsic factors include the polymer architecture, molecular weight, crystallinity, hydrophilicity, polymer thickness, and porosity, while extrinsic factors include the temperature, pH, and flow conditions of the degradation medium.149 The researchers explained that if bond hydrolysis takes place faster than water diffusion, then surface erosion is likely to occur. Conversely, if the rate of water diffusion is higher than the rate of bond hydrolysis, bulk erosion would take place. Fig. 3b compares the surface of poly(glycerol sebacate urethane) bioelastomers containing curcumin and nano-hydroxyapatite before and after hydrolytic degradation (in lipase enzyme-containing phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) solution, pH = 7.4, 37 °C, 30 days) through surface erosion.48 Depending on the degradation rate, the signs of the surface erosion mechanism, which is characterized by rough surfaces and irregular pits are observable. Interestingly, the results of SEM clearly show the difference in the degradation rate of the samples. Moreover, the degradation mode of polyesters is markedly influenced by part geometry, which includes thickness, porosity and surface characteristics that are defined during polymer processing.150 These parameters are crucial in determining the interaction of H2O molecules with the polymer and their diffusion through polymer bulk. For example, surface erosion occurs when the surface area of a sample is high, such as in microparticles, leading to an increased degradation kinetic due to the availability of more polymer chains to undergo chain scission reactions.151 Conversely, when bulk degradation occurs, thicker samples degrade faster as the acidic by-products released during hydrolysis cause a decrease in local pH. Porosity also plays a critical role in hydrolytic degradation, with nonporous samples accumulating acidic by-products in their interior and accelerating degradation rates, leading to undesired hollow structures.152 On the other hand, when sample morphology allows for the release of acidic by-products through pores, hydrolytic degradation occurs slower. This mechanism leads to highly porous materials being more resistant to hydrolytic degradation than solid bulk materials, which may seem counterintuitive.153

Tissue engineering scaffolds should provide mechanical support and physicochemical cues for the growth of cells to replace tissue [1]. Materials for such scaffolds should possess appropriate mechanical properties, chemical and biological compatibility and ideally should degrade in an appropriate time frame [1], [2]. Due to its biocompatibility, processability, and consistent degradation profile, polycaprolactone (PCl) has frequently been used as a long-term degradable implantable scaffold material for tissue engineering [3], [4], [5], [6]. The primary degradation pathway of pristine PCl is the hydrolysis of ester bonds leading to chain scission resulting in formation of shorter chains, oligomers and caproic acid [7]. This takes place in the amorphous bulk of the material and is dependent on its crystallinity and water transport into the material to enable hydrolysis [4], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12]. However, due to its semi-crystalline and hydrophobic nature, the rate of hydration and subsequent hydrolytic cleavage is low and hence the rate of degradation via this pathway is relatively slow (up to 4 years) [7], [10], [13]. Enzymatic degradation, on the other hand, occurs at the surface of the polymer with lipases and esterases attaching to the polymer surface before hydrolysing surface ester bonds in a much shorter time frame forming shorter chain polymers and oligomers. Degradation, while dependent on the enzyme used and the polymer composition and crystallinity, is generally complete after approximately 12 days and yields, among other fragments, ɛ-hydroxy caproic acid which, without clearance, can alter the pH of the host [14], [15], [16], [17], [18]. Tissue engineering of electro-responsive cells has been shown to be improved by electrical stimulation [19], [20]. The introduction of conducting fillers to such a well-studied tissue engineering matrix as PCl has been shown to result in conducting biocompatible composites which can be used to proliferate cells under electrical stimulation [21], [22]. However, the filler used must be biocompatible and have an appropriately low percolation threshold for conductivity so as not to adversely affect the degradation profile of the polymer scaffold. Graphene has shown promise as a filler for this application, as recent reports suggest it can enhance cell proliferation [23] and can be cleared by renal excretion, phagocytosis and/or endocytosis [24], [25], [26], [27]. In addition, the use of chemically converted reduced graphene oxide (CCG) has been reported to improve conductivities by orders of magnitude even at very low concentrations in a polymer matrix [22]. However, it is unknown what effects the addition of graphene would have on the degradation rates and products of a polymeric tissue engineering material.

Exposure of polymers to high-energy irradiation initiates a process known as chain scission, in which the covalent bonds within the polymer backbone are broken. This results in the formation of shorter polymer chains, known as oligomers, leading to a significant decrease in molecular weight [16]. Oxidative degradation catalyzed by irradiation and oxygen proceeds via a free radical mechanism, forming unstable hydroperoxides that decompose into reactive species and introduce hydrophilic terminal groups such as carboxylic acids (-COOH), hydroxyl (-OH), or carbonyl (C═O) groups [17]. Meanwhile, hydrolysis involves the cleavage of PBS ester bonds upon contact with water, resulting in smaller molecular fragments. These chemical changes increase the polymer's polarity and create an environment conducive to microbial colonization. Low-molecular weight polymers are more accessible and easier for microorganisms to metabolize [18]. Additionally, the hydrophilic nature of the irradiated surface helps retain moisture, further facilitating microbial adhesion and enzymatic degradation. Notably, hydrolysis enhances oxidative vulnerability by increasing hydrophilicity, while oxidation promotes hydrolysis through the formation of polar functional groups. This interplay accelerates the polymer degradation in soil environments and reduces the accumulation of plastic waste. Figure 1 shows the schematic illustration of the synergistic degradation mechanisms of polymers via irradiation and soil burial conditions, where irradiation induces radical formation and oxidation, enhancing hydrolysis and microbial degradation during soil exposure. For bioplastic, the free radicals are formed in C-H aliphatic bonds on PBS molecules when subjected to irradiation. Radicals (i) and (ii) are likely formed through the abstraction of hydrogen atoms from methane groups in the polymer backbone, as shown in Figure 2a. Meanwhile, radicals (i), (ii), and (iii) are formed through the breaking of C-O-C and C-C main chain bonds as depicted in Figure 2b due to the exposure to high irradiation dose [19]. The breaking of C-O-C bonds in the polymer backbone is the dominant effect of biodegradable polymers when exposed to irradiation [20]. According to a previous study, the irradiated bioblend films of polylactic acid (PLA) and starch showed an enhancement in thermal and mechanical properties due to an increase in interfacial adhesion between components, subsequently having the potential to replace conventional plastics [21]. It is necessary to investigate the influence of EB irradiation on the properties of polymer blends to ensure that they can maintain their integrity and serve their utilization purpose with the application of irradiation. Results representing the effects of irradiation with different LDPE/PBS/PE-g-MA blend compositions on structural, mechanical, thermal, and degradation properties are analyzed and reported to conclude the irradiation doses to these effects. Based on a previously published article [22], the researchers focused on the development of LDPE/PBS blends (10-50 wt% PBS) enhanced with a PE-g-MA compatibilizer (3-5 phr) to improve mechanical, thermal, and morphological properties for sustainable packaging applications. In the current study, the researchers investigate the degradation behavior of LDPE/PBS/PE-g-MA blends (10-30 wt% PBS, 5 phr PE-g-MA) subjected to EB irradiation and soil burial, aiming to accelerate environmental breakdown through oxidative degradation and microbial attack. In general, the former study aimed to improve the durability and performance of partially biodegradable blends, while the latter focused on promoting their environmental degradability by using irradiation as a pretreatment. Particular attention is given to the synergistic effect of irradiation-induced chain scission and biodegradation during soil exposure. As packaging materials must be nontoxic, biodegradable, and exhibit properties comparable to conventional plastics, the irradiated LDPE/PBS/PE-g-MA blends demonstrate promising potential as eco-friendly alternatives for commercial packaging.

Kenley et al.28 decribed three major features of PLGA degradation curves: 1) Induction period where mass and molecular weight values are unchanged; 2) onset of molecular weight loss becoming exponential with time; and 3) erosion onset. Several factors contribute to the hydrolytic degradation (molecular weight loss) of aliphatic polyesters. Among these are molecular weight, composition (monomer selection, ratios for copolymers), initiator selection, and morphology. Hydrolytic degradation of biodegradable polyesters occurs by random or nonrandom chain scission. Hydrolysis of linear PLLA and PLGA is generally considered to proceed by random cleavage of ester bonds. However, nonrandom ester cleavage of PLGA arms from a PEG block has been observed in 2-arm PEG-PLGA.29, 30 The chain scission mechanism in multiarm PLLA and PLGA has been shown to be dependent on the backbone material.20, 29 Random chain scission of the PLLA and PLGA branches has been observed in polymers with a backbone of diethyaminoethyl dextran chloride20 and nonrandom chain scission when the backbone was dextran sulfate sodium,20 4-arm PEO, or 8-arm PEO.29 Cleavage of the branches from the core material was followed by the degradation of the resulting linear polyester fragments via the random scission mechanism until the molecular weight was low enough for the fragments to be water-soluble. When the polymer fragments are small enough to be water-soluble then erosion (mass loss) is observed. Polymer mass loss may occur via a surface or a bulk erosion mechanism. Polymers that undergo bulk erosion absorb water into the polymer matrix and undergo hydrolysis uniformly throughout the sample. Surface-eroding polymers do not absorb water into the matrix rather, erode from the outer layer in. Bulk erosion is considered to be the primary erosion mechanism for PLA and PLGA, however, it has been shown that PLA and PLGA erode in a nonuniform manner with faster degradation in the center of implants than at the surface.31 This heterogeneous bulk erosion is caused by autocatalysis, accelerated degradation inside the polymer matrix by trapped acidic degradation products. It is expected that the 2-arm PEG-polyesters and the multiarm PG-polyesters in this study demonstrate similar degradation behavior to the 2-arm, 4-arm, and 8-arm PEG/PEO polymers discussed above. Degradation and erosion behavior of linear and branched poly(L-lactide)s and poly(L-lactide-co-glycolide)s were investigated. Normalized molecular weight loss versus time is reported in Figure 4 and follows the order PLLA35 < PG4-PLLA2 < PEG-PLLA7 < PG2-PLGA2 < PEG-PLGA6 < PLGA20 ≈ PLGA12. Figure 5 shows the normalized erosion versus time for the polymers studied. Normalized erosion rates followed the order of PLLA35 < PEG-PLLA7 ≈ PG4-PLLA2 ≪ PEG-PLGA6 ≈ PLGA20 < PG2-PLGA2 < PLGA12. Erosion and MW loss for the semicrystalline polymers (PLLA35, PEG-PLLA7, and PG4-PLLA2) was significantly slower than that of the amorphous polymers (PLGA12, PLGA20, PEG-PLGA6, and PG2-PLGA2). This was expected as polymers containing PLLA are more hydrophobic than the polymers containing PLGA. Hydrophobicity of PLLA slows the diffusion rate of water into the sample and the crystallinity of PLLA reduces the amount of free volume in the sample therefore less water is absorbed affecting the amount of water available for hydrolysis. Erosion lags behind MW loss for all of the polymers tested. The lag implies that hydrolysis proceeds throughout the polymer bulk. Degradation by the surface erosion mechanism requires mass loss precede MW loss.

Up to now, some studies on the hydrolytic degradation of PPDO have been reported. Bai et al. investigated the degradation of PPDO in the phosphate buffer solution of pH 7.44 at 37°C. Only after 4 weeks, PPDO with intrinsic viscosity of 2.4 dL g−1 lost 73% of its initial tensile strength and 95% of its initial maximum breaking elongation.9 Sabino et al. studied the hydrolytic degradation of PPDO on the surface morphology under the same conditions. Some small cracks were observed on the surface of PPDO sutures by scanning electronic microscopy at the 4th week of degradation.10 Sabino et al. also found PPDO lost almost 50% of its weight after 10 weeks degradation at 37°C in distilled water in their later study.11 Lin et al. presented a mechanism for PPDO suture degradation in phosphate buffer solution of pH 7.4 at 37°C.12 The random hydrolysis process of PPDO via two distinct stages: random scission of chain segments located in the amorphous regions of microfibrils and intermicrofibrillar space, followed by stepwise scission of chain segments located in the crystalline regions of microfibrils. This scission of chain segments is ascribed to the break of unstable ester bonds. The produced low molecular weight acid species can further catalyze the scission of ester bonds, suggesting the acceleration for PPDO hydrolysis.11 Conversely, if the catalytic activity of acid species is suppressed, the hydrolytic stability of PPDO can be enhanced. To improve the hydrolytic stability of PPDO, some efforts have been made. Liu investigated the hydrolytic degradation of PPDO containing polycarbodiimide (PCD) in the phosphate buffer solution of pH 7.44 at 37°C.13 During the degradation, PPDO containing 1 wt % PCD of 10th week was not as fragile as neat PPDO of 7th week from the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) graphs. It can also be observed that the elongation of PPDO ranged from 270% at origin to 14% at first week, whereas that of PPDO containing 1 wt % PCD changed from 245% to about 100% in the same time span. These results indicated that PCD could dramatically enhance the hydrolytic stability of PPDO. The reason for enhancement is that PCD can react with terminal carboxyl groups to generate stable N-acylurea and reduce the autocatalytic activity of acid species originated from the break of ester bonds.14 However, PCD is a multigroup carbodiimide and may give rise to the crosslinking of PPDO, which is to the disadvantage of further processing of PPDO. Therefore, it is not a good choice for the enhancement of hydrolytic stability of PPDO by adding PCD. To avoid the disadvantage of PCD, it is necessary to investigate further the influences of the hydrolytic stability of PPDO by adding the monogroup carbodiimide. In recent years, a kind of monogroup aromatic carbodiimide compound, bis-(2,6-diisopropylphenyl) carbodiimide (commercial name: stabaxol®-1) with high stability and suitable melting point of 40-45°C, was payed more and more attention. It has also been employed to improve the hydrolysis resistance for some aliphatic polyesters. The chemical structure of stabaxol®-1 is shown in Scheme 1. Adding stabaxol®-1 can satisfy durability, impact resistance, and moldability of the molded article made of the polylactic acid resin composition.15 Kim et al. found polybutylene succinate added stabaxol®-1 exhibited increased resistance to hydrolysis on tensile strength of ∼30% under 90% relatively humidity and 50°C condition for 30 days.16 On the basis of these good effectiveness obtained, it may be expected that stabaxol®-1 can also improve the hydrolytic stability of PPDO. In this article, the influences on hydrolytic degradation of PPDO under different temperature and relatively humidity are investigated by adding stabaxol®-1. The changes of intrinsic viscosity, mechanical properties, crystallinity, and surface morphologies of PPDO and PPDO containing stabaxol®-1 are monitored by Ubbelohde viscosimeter, electro mechanical universal testing machine, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and SEM, respectively. As far as the authors know, no available data have been reported on hydrolysis resistance for PPDO by using stabaxol®-1 as a stabilizer. In addition, the degradation behaviors of PPDO under the different temperature and relatively humidity conditions are still investigated for the first time, while the degradation conditions for all of the early studies are almost in phosphate buffer solution.11, 13, 17, 18

Saponification, or de-esterification, typically describes the hydration reaction (hydrolysis) that breaks the ester bonds by either free hydroxides or acids. Such side reactions may happen to some extent among the complex heterogenous mixture (slurry) of hemp fibers and pectin under highly acidic or basic conditions. Under highly acidic conditions, such side reactions may happen and yield free carboxylic acids on the pectin. The free carboxylic acids of pectin can reform ester bonds with the hydroxyl groups on the hemp fibers. However, under high basic conditions, any saponification (or de-esterification) will yield free carboxylates, but the basic conditions cannot catalyze the re-formation of ester bonds with hydroxyl groups because the byproducts, hydroxide ions, are not good leaving groups. Thus, for the methyl carboxylate groups of pectin to react with hydroxyl groups on the fiber surface to produce robust biocomposite as we observed in our experiment, transesterification, though slow, is expected to happen. In other words, most of these methyl carboxylate groups probably do not hydrolyze under the basic conditions evaluated in our experiments. It is important to note that when the pH of the crosslinking reaction was adjusted in the fabrication process to either 1-2 or 12-14, only a few milliliters of the aqueous pectin solution were used for a reaction with 4 grams of hemp fibers. The total numbers of moles of acids or bases were relatively small when compared to the amount of hemp fibers used in the fabrication process. Also, our heating process at 70°C for 2 h and then at 100°C for 10 h will deplete most of the water needed for saponification and hence promote the formation of ester bonds by shifting the equilibrium. Though the transesterification reaction is relatively slow, we believe that sufficient crosslinking can happen due to such reaction mechanisms. Otherwise, we would not observe the V-shape compressive strength trend in Figure 10. In addition, the common method to measure the degree of methylation of pectin is by de-esterification of pectin with a 3× to 10× strong base (such as aqueous NaOH solution (pH = 13-14) mixed 50/50 with isopropanol).85 Even under such harsh conditions, a minimum of 2 h is recommended for complete esterification. This indicates that the de-esterification process is not too fast compared to our reaction period. Hence, the reaction time used in our method is expected to be sufficient for significant crosslinking via transesterification to happen. Based solely on the provided evidence, the mechanism of hydrolytic chain scission in ester bonds involves:

1.  **Water attack on ester bonds**: Hydrolysis occurs when water molecules cleave ester bonds in the polymer backbone. This fragmentation produces shorter polymer chains, oligomers, and monomers [2][4][5][6][13].
2.  **Predominantly random scission**: Ester bond cleavage typically occurs randomly along the polymer chain, especially within amorphous regions which are more accessible to water penetration [3][8][9][10][11]. This random cleavage leads to a progressive decrease in molecular weight [3][4][5][6][8][9][12].
3.  **Amorphous region susceptibility**: The loosely packed amorphous regions undergo hydrolytic scission first due to higher water absorption and easier diffusion compared to crystalline regions [3][10][11].
4.  **Acid generation and autocatalysis**: The hydrolysis of ester bonds produces carboxylic acid end groups. These acidic degradation products can lower the local pH, accelerating further ester bond cleavage in an autocatalytic manner [10][11][12][13]. This is particularly problematic in bulk erosion where acidic products are trapped [8][9][10][11].
5.  **Formation of shorter chains and oligomers**: The chain scission event fragments the polymer backbone, resulting in lower molecular weight chains and oligomers, eventually forming acidic monomers like caproic acid [4][5][6][10][11][12].

Thus, the development of biodegradable implants that can perform the human body’s required function and self-degrade timely is a promising approach that eliminates the need for secondary surgery and facilitates the healing process. Compared to polymeric materials, which are also widely used as biodegradable implants, metals have higher mechanical strength and release inert ions during biocorrosion, thereby are not capable of causing local pH reduction and introducing an allergic reaction [1, 9]. The idea of degradable metal usage has brought more attention to temporary implants’ materials. Thus, several key issues should be extensively explored, including the choice of alloying elements, adjusting microstructural and mechanical properties, biodegradation mechanisms, their influence on the human body, controlling the rate of decomposition and metabolism of the degradation products, and the biocompatibility of metals. The biodegradable metal implants should satisfy the following characteristics: biocompatibility of materials themselves and products of their degradation, ability to corrode with appropriate degradation rates, stability for several months before it is fully bioabsorbed [10, 11]. Among the most commonly used metals are iron (Fe), magnesium (Mg), zinc (Zn), and various alloy combinations [12]. Magnesium, one of the most studied biodegradable materials, is a light metal with a high corrosion rate, which requires mandatory alloying with biocompatible elements to increase mechanical strength. Also, magnesium tends to release hydrogen during degradation, which leads to an undesirable increase in pH value in tissues [13]. Compared to magnesium, zinc has a low corrosion rate and no hydrogen evolution, but at the same time, low mechanical strength and a tendency to age hardening. Iron is a fairly strong, ductile, and easily processed material but has a low degree of corrosion compared to Mg and Zn. For the first time, pure iron was used as a biodegradable implant for peripheral stent construction and showed a low degradation rate [14-16]. Alloying iron with other elements can accelerate the degradation process; for example, an implant consisting of Fe-Mn [17] and Fe-Mn-Si [18] alloys and doped with Co, W, S, or C showed a higher decomposition rate than pure iron. At the same time, Fe-Mn-Pd [19] and alloys with Al and B did not show significant changes in the degradation rate. Alloying iron with other elements not only affects the rate of degradation, but also modification of structure and morphology by the method of fabrication [20]. 3D printing technology can accelerate the degradation of iron due to the presence of pores, changing the grain size and properties of boundaries, or by adding additional alloying elements [21-23]. Moreover, additive manufacturing is actively used to create metal implants with complex geometric shapes, sizes, customizable designs, and a certain degree of porosity [4]. When processing biodegradable metals such as zinc and magnesium, significant losses of matter and porosity can be observed [24]; therefore, we turned our attention to iron. In this work, we investigated a porous scaffold based on an iron-silicon (Fe-Si) alloy fabricated by 3D printing technology. As an alloying additive, silicon is a biocompatible element that can increase the strength of iron and reduce its corrosion rate, which can lead to the creation of stronger framework structures required for solid implants for bone grafting. Meanwhile, by forming the porosity and grain structures [25] using additive technologies, it is possible to control the biodegradation rate by increasing the area of the implant’s inner surface, which contact with tissue and reducing the difference in mechanical properties between bones and metals. Printed FeSi scaffolds were analyzed for mechanical properties and biocompatibility using cytotoxicity, and immunotoxicity tests.

Biodegradable metals and their alloys have found numerous applications in orthopedic and cardiovascular fields, prompting extensive research to enhance their performance. Biodegradable alloys must be non-toxic, be biologically compatible, and exhibit low corrosion rates in the body.65,66 Materials classified as biodegradable implants interact with damaged tissues within the human body, directly impacting human life. Consequently, it is critical that these materials exhibit unquestionable biocompatibility and biosafety to prevent adverse reactions with host tissues and minimize the release of corrosive by-products. As previously noted, alloying is essential for utilizing zinc in load-bearing biomedical applications. Alloying elements should enhance mechanical properties while positively influencing biodegradation and biological behavior. Incubation of MG-63 bone cells with undiluted pure zinc extracts in indirect cellular assays revealed cytotoxic effects, with insufficient biocompatibility at high Zn2+ concentrations repeatedly documented.67 In recent years, research has shifted toward alloying zinc to improve its mechanical properties, enabling its use in bone tissue engineering scaffolds. Key alloying elements include zirconium,34 lithium,35 aluminum,45 titanium,37 magnesium and calcium,30 magnesium and strontium,31 and copper and iron,33 among others. The enhancement of mechanical properties and control of corrosion rates in zinc-based alloys depend primarily on the choice, quantity, and distribution of alloying elements within the zinc matrix. These elements can be categorized into three groups: those with negligible or no solubility (e.g., iron, magnesium, and calcium), those with low or limited solubility (e.g., copper, aluminum, and lithium), and those with high solubility (e.g., silver) in zinc. Alloys of the first two categories may exhibit poor ductility and premature failure, which could be unacceptable for stent applications. However, severe plastic deformation techniques can adjust the mechanical properties of these alloys for specific uses.64 For cardiovascular stents, an ultimate tensile strength of ∼300 MPa is required, whereas pure zinc exhibits a tensile strength of only 20-120 MPa.68,69 Thus, developing zinc alloys with adequate strength and biocompatibility remains an area requiring further exploration with diverse alloying elements beyond those currently reported.

After the healing and reorganization of the bone in the fracture gap, common implants made from stainless steel or titanium alloys have to be removed in a second surgery [2-4]. In addition, stress-shielding effects can lead to an implant-induced osteopenia and an increase in cortical porosity [5]. To avoid or reduce both negative aspects of conventional materials, the development of biodegradable implant materials based on magnesium alloys has been the focus of research in recent years [6, 7], as common degradable polymers are not suitable for load-bearing applications due to insufficient mechanical stability [8]. In contrast, magnesium alloys, with an elastic modulus closer to natural bone, exceed the stability and Young's modulus of polymers [9] and therefore are promising implant materials for this application [10-14]. The degradation rate of the implant has to be consistent with the bone healing processes. A first stable initial fixation under a functional load should be replaced by a predictable step-by-step degradation of the material and a substitution with bone in the cortical area. Magnesium as a co-factor for many biological functions [15] is considered to be relatively safe [10]. While high-purity magnesium shows the slowest degradation [16, 17], the degradation rate of Mg-alloys depends on the alloy composition [18, 19]. The most commonly used magnesium alloys include zinc (Zn) [13, 20-24] or rare earths (RE) [12, 19, 25, 26] as alloying elements, although their innocuousness is not definitively proven [27-29]. Within Mg-alloys, Zn and RE improve strength and, depending on the alloy's composition, reduce the corrosion rate [30, 31]. In recent studies, various RE- or Zn-containing alloys showed good biocompatibility [12, 19, 24, 25, 30, 32]. The magnesium alloy ZEK100 contains Zn and RE as alloying elements; ZEK100-plates have already been evaluated in a Hanks' balanced salt solution in vitro [33] and ZEK100-pins intramedullary in rabbit tibia in vivo [34, 35] as a potential biodegradable implant material for osteosynthesis due to their good mechanical characteristics. However, their biocompatibility was not finally approved, because an increased bone reactive capacity was observed in the implant surrounding of the ZEK100-pins after a 6 month implantation period [36]. Subsequent investigations by Dziuba et al did not recommend ZEK100 for biomedical use as these intramedullary implanted pins induced adverse host reactions after 9 and 12 month investigation periods [35]. However, these investigations consider intramedullary implantation [36, 35]. Their degradation properties, as well as host responses like inflammatory reactions or removal of degradation products, might be different in other locations. Relating to a surgical procedure, initiation, resolution and organization as first sign of the acute host response are normally followed by the immigration of immuno-inflammatory cells, which infiltrate the implant adjacencies. Furthermore, various cellular and tissue responses can be associated with an implanted degrading biomaterial [37, 38]. These reactions in the implant surrounding have to be examined to assess the implant's biocompatibility, and can differ depending on the implant location [36, 39].
