For instance, various copolymers including Pluronic, poly(phosphazene), and poly(N-isopropyl acrylamide) exist in the sol state at room temperature and transform into gels at body temperature.14,18-20 Although these copolymers exhibit sharp temperature-responsive transitions, their biological usage has been limited due to non-degradability and limited biocompatibility. To surmount these issues, poly(ester)-based biodegradable and biocompatible polymers that are capable of exhibiting LCSTs have been developed.21 In particular, poly(ε-caprolactone-co-lactide)-b-poly(ethylene glycol)-b-poly(ε-caprolactone-co-lactide) (PCLA)-based copolymer hydrogels are promising candidates for injectable delivery systems.22 In addition to the PCLA copolymers, thermosensitive injective hydrogels based on poly(ethylene glycol)-b-poly(ε-caprolactone)-b-poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG-b-PCL-b-PEG) have been developed for biomedical applications.23 The PEG-b-PCL-b-PEG-based thermosensitive gels combined with curcumin have been proven to enhance anti-tumor activity in a colorectal peritoneal carcinomatosis model as well as wound healing in an excision wound model.24,25 Furthermore, PEG-b-PCL-b-PEG/acellular bone matrix composite hydrogels have been used for bone regeneration in cranial defects.26 Although PCLA-based amphiphilic copolymer hydrogel systems could load proteins and enable their sustained release, the neutral nature of hydrogels severely restricts the loading of some proteins, as most therapeutic proteins are ionically charged.27,28 It is noteworthy to mention that the integration of the PCLA-based polymers with cationic or anionic charged polymers may provide a useful hydrogel system for the delivery of ionically charged proteins. Natural polysaccharide-based ionic polymers including hyaluronic acid, heparin, chitosan, and dextran derivatives have been extensively investigated in biomedical applications mainly because of their biocompatibility, non-immunogenicity, biodegradability and cell-adhesion properties.29-37 Among the variety of natural polysaccharides, heparin is a negatively charged linear polysaccharide composed of alternating units of sulfated glucuronic acid and glucosamine derivatives.38 Heparin is clinically used as an anticoagulant. The presence of negatively charged functional groups (sulfate and carboxylate) endows a high negative charge to heparin, which facilitates ionic interaction and complexation with various proteins, growth factors, and chemokines.39 Given its unique structure, hydrogels and nanoparticles composed of heparin exhibit attractive properties in biomedical applications.40 For example, photo-cross-linked alginate-heparin hydrogels allowed the sustained release of various therapeutic proteins.41,42 It is known that heparin could form complexes with various growth factors.43 The heparin present in the photo-cross-linked hydrogels binds to various growth factors and allows the sustained release of growth factors.44 Although numerous attempts have been made to develop heparin-based hydrogels, no significant attempt has been made to develop heparin-based biodegradable and injectable hydrogels for protein delivery.
Recently, controlled drug delivery systems using stimuli-sensitive and injectable polymeric materials have been attracted significant attention for biomedical applications [1], [2]. Hydrogels prepared by chemical or physical crosslinking are a special class of polymer networks that can absorb a large amount of water while maintaining their shape. Due to porosity of hydrogels, the oxygen, nutrients, and other water-soluble metabolites can easily exchange inside the hydrogel networks. Injectable and biodegradable hydrogels that can change their structure in response to environmental stimuli (for example, temperature, pH, salt concentration, electric fields and so on) have been widely applied in drug/cell delivery and tissue engineering due to their various advantages such as hydrophilic network, prolonged delivery period, small body drug dosage and reduction of undesirable side effects by the protection of drugs from hostile environments [3], [4], [5], [6]. These stimuli materials, specifically temperature stimuli, have ease of application because no surgical procedures are required for the insertion of gels into the body, therefore drugs, proteins and cells can be mixed homogeneously with the polymer solutions and administered by simple syringe injection at target sites [4], [7], [8], [9]. Thus, thermosensitive hydrogels which use in drug/cell delivery and tissue engineering, should be sol at room temperature or lower, prior to subcutaneous injection, and should rapidly change to gel in the body temperature (37 °C), where ultimate degradation of the hydrogels is desired [4], [10]. For biodegradability, aliphatic polyesters such as poly(∊-caprolactone) (PCl), poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA), poly(glycolic acid) (PGA) or their copolyesters (PLGA) which their backbone can be cleaved by hydrolysis, are among the most attractive biodegradable polymers. So far, poly(ethylene glycol)/poly(lactic acid-co-glycolic acid) tri-block (PLGA-PEG-PLGA) and graft copolymers [11], poly(ethylene glycol) (MPEG)-poly(∊-caprolactone) (PCL) di-block copolymers [12], poly(ethylene glycol)/poly(∊-caprolactone) tri-block and penta-block copolymer [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], poly(ethylene glycol)/poly(propylene fumarate) [17], and polyphosphazene [18], [19], were reported as typical thermoresponsive, biocompatible and biodegradable physical gels. The thermosensitive copolymers containing the PLGA segment have sticky paste morphology and thus they are usually difficult to transfer or weight. Furthermore, these copolymers required several hours of redissolution/reconstitution to be dissolved in water that is very difficult and time consuming [20], [21]. Bae et al. [14] substituted the PLGA with the PCL in the hydrophobic polyester backbone and synthesized PCL-PEG-PCL (PCEC) tri-block copolymer as a biodegradable thermogelling polymer with a powder morphology that can transfer or weight easily. Also, this tri-block copolymer needs the easiest reconstitution/redissolution to be dissolved in water. However, because of high crystalizability of PCL, the tri-block copolymer aqueous solution (20 wt.%) becomes an opaque gel when left at room temperature (20 °C) over 30 min therefore, it must be used quickly after dissolution of the copolymer. This short time sol stability is an obstacle for the applications of these type materials as injectable hydrogels. The crystalizability of PCL is decreased as the molecular weight of PCL increases [22]. For this reason, PEG/PCL multi-block copolymer synthesized by coupling of PCL-PEG-PCL tri-block copolymers shows less crystalizability and partially improved sol stability due to the high molecular weight of polycaprolactone [23]. However, this system has high polydispersity (PDI = 2.3) and the precise control of the molecular weight of the multi-block copolymer is not easy. Park et al. [24] have synthesized end-group modified poly(∊-caprolactone-co-trimethylene carbonate)-b-poly(ethylene glycol)-b-poly(∊-caprolactone-co-trimethylene carbonate) tri-block copolymer to increase the amorphous character of the material, improving solubility in water and the sol stability, thus avoiding the precipitation problem in the PCL-PEG-PCL tri-block copolymer aqueous solution. Although some promising results have been achieved for this system, its weak mechanical properties are limiting its application as injectable gel. Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) is also widely used as an excellent thermosensitive segment for in vivo drug delivery applications due to its lower critical solution temperature (LCST) (32 °C) that can change volume and shape abruptly and thermoreversibly at around the physiological temperature [25], [26], [27], [28]. Copolymerization of PNIPAAm with hydrophilic polymer leads to thermogelling copolymer solution which is sol below the LCST and gel by increasing the temperature above the LCST [29], [30]. To the best of our knowledge, up to now, there are no reports of any sol-gel system based on copolymers that contain both PCL-PEG-PCL tri-block copolymer and N-isopropylacrylamide. In this study, we assumed that the end-group modification of PCL-PEG-PCL tri-block copolymer with well-defined poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) using the atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP) yields: 1) simple dissolution of copolymer in water, 2) improving the sol stability of hydrogel in room temperature (20 °C) by decreasing crystalinity of PCL chain, 3) improving mechanical properties, 4) precise adjusting of the composition and temperature-induced phase transition behavior of the synthesized hydrogel because the living radical polymerization allows the synthesis of the well-defined block copolymers with low polydispersitiy [25], [26], [31]. This method can remove some limitations such as, high polydispersity and unwanted random or branched polymerization that cause the masking of experimental results and make its intractable to study the effect of the hydrophobic/hydrophilic balance of PEG and PNIPAAm. The LCST and gelation concentration of polymer are regulated by changing the length of the PNIPAAm and PEG block and the temperature of the aqueous medium. The resulting copolymers were characterized by FT-IR, 1H NMR, gel permeation chromatography (GPC), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), Dynamic light scattering (DLS) and X-ray diffraction (XRD). Some properties of hydrogel copolymer such as the LCST and critical micelle concentration (CMC) were also investigated.
A general feature of the thermosensitive hydrogel is that the polymer should be amphiphilic, having a hydrophobic segment and a hydrophilic segment.17,29-32 A delicate balance between hydrophobicity and hydrophilicity is imperative for the temperature-dependent sol-gel transition to occur for polymer aqueous solutions. A too large hydrophilic segment will result in no sol-gel phase transition, and a too large hydrophobic segment will lead to insolubility in aqueous solution at physiologically relevant temperature range.33 Polyesters such as polylactide (PLA), polyglycolide (PGA), and poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) continue to be widely investigated in the biomedical field as they all have been approved by the FDA for in vivo use, and many products based on these polymers are commercially available.34 Not surprisingly, several injectable and thermosensitive hydrogels based on these polyesters have been reported including diblock PLGA-PEG, triblock PEG-PLGA-PEG, and grafted PLGA-g-PEG copolymers.17,29-31,35-37 These systems combine the biocompatibility and biodegradability of PLGA with the injectability of an aqueous sol. Degradation products of PLA/PLGA, however, can induce an acidic environment that may be a problem for some tissues and perhaps detrimental to incorporated drugs or proteins.38 In addition, our earlier reported PLGA-g-PEG polymers have relatively weak mechanical properties and a paste-like morphology and their dissolution in water or buffer solution can take up to several days.35,37,39-41 Polycaprolactone (PCL), meanwhile, has recently regained great attention in the biomedical field particularly with its use for drug delivery, tissue engineering, and medical devices.42 As with PLA and PGA, PCL based polymers have superior biocompatibility as evidenced by several drug-delivery devices and sutures fabricated with PCL that have been approved by the FDA. Due to its increased degree of crystallinity and hydrophobicity versus PLA, PGA, and PLGA, PCL-based polymers have superior rheological properties and a solid morphology resulting in a significant improvement in terms of handling and transfer.11,27,42 Moreover, unlike PLA and PGA, PCL degradation product is less acidic and typically takes much longer time to degrade than PLA and PGA; these two properties have led other authors to believe that PCL degradation essentially will not lead to an acidic environment.43,44 Indeed, to take advantage of the benefits offered by PCL, thermosensitive hydrogels of block copolymers consisting of PCL or PCLA (poly(caprolactone-co-lactide)), and PEG have been reported and summarized.33,43-47 However, to our knowledge, injectable and thermosensitive hydrogels based on polycaprolactone (PCL) grafted with polyethylene glycol (PCL-g-PEG) have not yet been reported. Grafted copolymers such as PCL-g-PEG and PLGA-g-PEG can offer more versatility and latitude as the hydrophilicity of the polymers can be modulated by both PEG length and number of PEG grafts, whereas only PEG length can be utilized to tune hydrophilicity for block thermosensitive copolymers. Here we report versatile hydrogel of PCL-g-PEG, which is structurally comparable to our previously developed PLGA-g-PEG with the difference being that the PLGA segment is replaced by PCL. The rheological properties, sol-gel transition mechanisms, and enzymatic degradation by lipase of the PCL-g-PEG hydrogel were investigated and their potential biomedical applications were discussed in this study. The test tube inversion method has also been used to judge sol or gel states for thermosensitive polymer aqueous solutions.28,39,53 The sol and gel states of PCL-g-PEG aqueous solution at 5 wt% at 0 °C and 37 °C are shown in Fig. 3. The test tube inversion method showed that a polymer aqueous solution of 5 wt% formed a hydrogel at 37 °C. However, a polymer solution at 2 wt% did not form a hydrogel at 37 °C. This suggests that the critical gelation concentration is between 2 wt% and 5 wt% at 37 °C. Such a low critical gelation concentration is much lower than that of a triblock PCL-PEG-PCL aqueous solution (∼13 wt%)33 and a PLGA-g-PEG aqueous solution (∼19%).39 A low gelation concentration indicates that gels with high water content can be prepared, which may be valuable for tissue engineering applications because it would facilitate the transport of nutrients, oxygen, soluble metabolites and wastes generated by incorporated cells.54 Indeed, a limited permeability of an injectable gel has been reported to be responsible for the decreased viability of incorporated osteoblast cells.24 Furthermore, as drug release rate is most likely gel permeability dependent, a large gelation concentration window at physiological temperature is advantageous and versatile to tune drug release profiles.
AbstractInjectable biodegradable copolymer hydrogels, which exhibit temperature-responsive sol-to-gel transition, have recently drawn much attention as promising biomedical materials such as drug delivery, cell implantation, and tissue engineering. These injectable hydrogels can be implanted in the human body with minimal surgical invasion. Temperature-responsive gelling copolymers usually possess block- and/or branched architectures and amphiphilicity with a delicate hydrophobic/hydrophilic balance. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) has typically been used as hydrophilic segments due to its biocompatibility and temperature-dependent dehydration nature. Aliphatic polyesters such as polylactide, poly(lactide-co-glycolide), poly(ε-caprolactone), and their modified copolymers have been used as hydrophobic segments based on their biodegradability and biocompatibility. Copolymers of PEG with other hydrophobic polymers such as polypeptides, polydepsipeptides have also been recently reported as injectable hydrogels. In this review, brief history and recent advances in injectable biodegradable polymer hydrogels are summarized especially focusing on the relationship between polymer architecture and their gelation properties. Moreover, the applications of these injectable polymer gels for biomedical use such as drug delivery and tissue engineering are also described. IntroductionIn situ gel forming polymer systems have recently drawn much attention as promising biomedical materials for minimally invasive therapy [1], [2], [3]. In particular, biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers, which show sol-to-gel transition between room temperature and body temperature upon heating, are expected to be useful for injectable polymer gel (IPG) systems in biomedical applications. These polymer solutions are in sol state in the syringe at room temperature and become gel in situ after injection into the body, without requiring any toxic cross-linkers. Such systems can easily entrap pharmaceutical agents or cells and form a depot by a simple syringe injection at a target site, where the depots acts as sustained drug delivery devices or a cell-growing scaffolds for tissue engineering [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10]. To exhibit a temperature-responsive sol-to-gel transition in aqueous solutions, such polymers should possess amphiphilicity with a delicate hydrophobic/hydrophilic balance [11]. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) has typically been used as hydrophilic segments of thermo-gelling polymers due to its biocompatibility and temperature-dependent dehydration nature. Aliphatic polyesters such as poly(l-lactide) (PLLA), poly(d-lactide) (PDLA), poly(dl-lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), and their modified copolymers have been used as hydrophobic segments based on their biodegradability and relatively good biocompatibility [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17].Since pioneering research on biodegradable IPG systems using triblock copolymer of PEG and PLLA, PEG-b-PLLA-b-PEG, by Kim et al. in 1997 [11], many kinds of biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers have been developed by combining PEG and aliphatic polyesters with various molecular architectures including linear-type and star-shape block as well as graft topologies [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24], [25]. In addition, biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers containing amino acids as building blocks of the hydrophobic segments have been recently developed [26], [27], [28], [29], [30]. Biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers reported can be categorized into block copolymers including linear-type and/or star-shaped diblock, triblock, and multiblock architectures, and graft copolymers from the view point of molecular architectures, as summarized in Table 1. These copolymers exhibits various properties based on the molecular architectures and nature of the components.In this article, brief history and recent advances in biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers as IPGs are reviewed especially focusing on the relationship between polymer structure and their properties. Moreover, the applications of these IPGs for biomedical use such as DDS and tissue engineering are also reviewed.
Alginate hydrogel is also one of the most extensively explored injectable hydrogels, whose injectability is owing to ion-triggered system without toxic chemical crosslinking agent [31,32]. The injectable hydrogel is a special kind of hydrogel which has rapid prototyping manufacturing characteristics and potential for minimally invasive surgical treatments [33]. Injectable hydrogels are becoming increasingly popular and highlighted in various biomedical applications, for example, surgical tissue adhesives [34], space-filling injectable material [35], highly sophisticated delivery systems [36,37], repair of bone and cartilage [[38], [39], [40]], peripheral and central nervous system therapy [41,42] and treatment of myocardial infraction [43]. Alginate injectable hydrogels have been studied in more depth than most polymer materials because of outstanding biocompatibility. Alginate/gelation hydrogels can be printed with the layers of various cells [44]. In bone tissue engineering, alginate hydrogels can deliver vascular endothelial growth factor efficiently to promote bone regeneration and early revascularization [45]. Small molecules with specific function such as chondroitin sulfate and clotting factor have been successfully grafted on alginate hydrogels to exert therapeutic effect [46,47]. In addition, alginate hydrogels exhibit good functionalization in promoting cell growth, immobilization and differentiation [48,49]. However, low formability and poor mechanical properties limit the application of alginate hydrogels till today [50]. In previous research, the simple ion-triggered system of alginate leads to low formability or high brittleness uncontrollably [51]. There are some researches indicating the mechanical properties are improved by modifying the composition [52,53]. People found that bacterial cellulose (BC) could enhance the mechanical properties of hydrogels when applied for the osteochondral defect repair [[54], [55], [56], [57]]. Carboxymethyl bacterial cellulose (CMBC) has three-dimensional network structure as same as BC besides more abundant chemical reactive groups, which is greatly beneficial to the formation of hydrogen bond and the double-network and therefore contribute to better mechanical properties and formability [58,59]. There is another problem that it’s hard to describe the sol-gel transition of injectable hydrogels clearly. The researches carried out a series of experiments to control the sol-gel transition by different crosslinkers [60,61] but lacked of phenomena and data. The degradation behaviour is also related to hydrogels' structure [61,62]. The degradation behaviour is a gradual trend along with broken down of polymer network, release of metal ions [[63], [64], [65]], and nano particle mineralization deposition [66]. To address these issues, we still need corresponding systematic experiments and more quantitative data. In our study, we synthesized injectable sodium alginate/carboxymethyl bacterial cellulose hydrogels (SA-CMBC) through physical cross-linking under normal circumstances. Carboxymethyl bacterial cellulose and nano-sized particles of hydroxyapatite and calcium carbonate could not only be used as cross-linking agents instead of toxic polymer crosslinkers but also form a double-network structure and enhancing strength. In addition, we successfully regulated the sol-gel transition and proposed methods for a better perspective to describe the sol-gel transition quantitatively. For further application, we evaluated the biological safety through in vitro compatibility tests and designed a series of experiments to clarify the degradation behaviour including microstructure, ions release and mechanical properties.
To form the adhesive hydrogels, biocompatible and biodegradable natural or synthetic polymers can be cross-linked physically or chemically, or a combination of both. (68) The sol precursor will form a three-dimensional network after the aforementioned processes. When it comes to the physically cross-linked hydrogel, the interactions between polymer chains mainly result from physical interactions, such as entanglement of chains, hydrophobic interaction, host-guest inclusion complexation, or formation of hydrogen bonds, coordination bonds, and ionic bonds. (61) Besides, the most significant gel-inducing factor of the injectable physical hydrogel is the physiological environment like the body temperature. Among them, the thermosensitive materials are favored for inverse sol-gel transition properties induced by temperature, in which gelation occurs when heating instead of cooling. Typical thermogelled hydrogels include natural or seminatural polymers such as chitosan and gelatin and synthetic polymers like poloxamer 407. Qi et al. (69) have reported a kind of chitosan-heparin hydrogel, which is cross-linked with heparin by physical entanglement and electrostatic attraction. In this work, the sol precursor could transform to gel at 37 °C in 15 min. Additionally, Zhang et al. (70,71) reported a kind of 17β-estradiol heparin-poloxamer thermosensitive hydrogel, of which the viscosity suddenly increased at elevated temperature. This poloxamer hydrogel could form a gel state when heating to body temperature and turn to a sol state after cooling, as shown in Figure 2. Moreover, host-guest supramolecular hydrogels based on macrocyclic molecules such as cyclodextrin are also popular in the biomedical field. (64) Li et al. (72) described a hydrogel based on the self-assembly of inclusion between α-CD and PEO blocks in Pluronic and the aggregation of PPO blocks, which exhibited thixotropic and reversible properties and could be applied as injectable drug delivery system. However, due to the noncovalent and reversible nature of the cross-linkers in the polymer network, hydrogels formed by these weak interactions could be affected by temperature, pH, ionic strength, solvent composition, and the imposed mechanical stress, causing a burst release of encapsulant and further limiting their uses in endometrial repair. (73) Polymeric hydrogels formed by chemical cross-linking have also been developed for endometrium repair, in which the cross-linked networks are provided by the covalent bonds, forming the stronger and more stable hydrogels. Covalently bonded hydrogels are usually achieved by cross-linking the mixture of precursors in vitro, as shown in Figure 3. Samantha et al. (74) have modified the gelatin with methacrylic anhydride to synthesize methacrylate functionalized gelatin (GelMA). The precursor solution of GelMA was mixed with a photoinitiator, and then the hydrogel was obtained by the photopolymerization under UV light. Similarly, Cheng et al. (75) have prepared HA hydrogel by the method of photoinitiation, in which methacrylate modified HA was obtained by the reaction of HA and methacrylic anhydride. The encapsulation of therapeutic agent is also critical for the hydrogel delivery system, which is related to the cross-linking method of hydrogel. Figure 3 shows the general preparation process of hydrogel delivery system for endometrium repair. For covalent-cross-linked hydrogel, the incorporation of therapeutic agent by adsorption may be time-consuming and inefficient, while in situ loading of the therapeutic agent may lead to its inactivation during the cross-linking process. (76) Instead, the loading efficiency and content of therapeutic agent could be improved by promoting the interaction between therapeutic agent and hydrogel network. (77,78) For example, Wu et al. (77) reported a new drug encapsulation strategy to achieve the sustain release of small molecule ionic drug from hydrogel platform. In their strategy, arginine-based unsaturated poly(ester amides) (Arg-UPEAs) and alginate were introduced into the Pluronic hydrogel by UV photo-cross-linking method. The presence of polyelectrolytes improved the electrostatic interaction and affinity of ionic drugs with the hydrogel network. Furthermore, in situ loading of therapeutic agent is also attractive for the noncovalent cross-linked hydrogel. In this case, the therapeutic agent is uniformly mixed with the precursor solution and then encapsulated within the network matrix during the formation of the hydrogel. (31,74,79)

The gelation during heating is readily observed by rheological temperature ramps as shown in Fig. 1c, and then the sol-gel transition temperature can be determined by the temperature at the crossover of G′ and G″. However, the sol-gel transition temperature determined by this method varies with the adopted frequency and heating rate. The Winter-Chambon criterion is often used to determine the sol-gel transition temperature as zero shear viscosity and relaxation time of a gelling system diverge during the sol-gel transition [[32], [33], [34], [35]]. For example, one of the well-known rheological scaling laws developed under the Winter-Chambon criterion for determination of the sol-gel transition is:(1)G″(ω)/G′(ω) = tanδ = tan(nπ/2)which is based on the power law behavior of the shear relaxation modulus G(t), G(t) = Sgt−n, at the gel point. n is named as the critical relaxation exponent, which determines the stress relaxation rate at the gel point. The multi-frequency curves of tan δ vs temperature at different frequencies can be used to determine the sol-gel transition temperature at a given heating rate for a chitosan solution with a given concentration, if all curves converges to a common point at which the temperature loses its dependence on frequency. But, it is noted that the sol-gel transition temperature of chitosan, which is determined using this method, is dependent on chitosan concentration and heating rate. The determination of the sol-gel transition temperature for a given chitosan concentration is important, because it is related not only to the gelation mechanism but also the practical applications of resulting chitosan hydrogels. Here, we adopted the multiwave oscillation under a temperature ramp to determine the sol-gel transition temperatures at different heating rates. In such a so-called multiwave oscillation measurement, a nonsinusoidal periodic strain, which is a linear superposition of several sinusoidal waves with different frequencies and strain amplitudes, is applied to the sample. The total stress response can also be the superposition of the stress responses to the individual sinusoidal strains according to the Boltzmann superposition principles if the total strain is small enough and lies in the linear regime. We first carried out the multiwave oscillatory temperature sweep at a heating rate of 1 °C/min, and obtained the variation of phase angle (δ) with temperature for the 2 wt% chitosan alkaline solution as shown in Fig. 2a. It was observed in Fig. 2a that tan δ became independent of frequency at the temperature of 65.3 °C, which was denoted as the sol-gel transition temperature. Further, as the sol-gel transition temperature is also strongly dependent on heating rate, the multiwave oscillatory temperature ramps with different heating rates (0.2, 0.5, 2 and 5 °C/min) were carried out, and then the corresponding sol-gel transition temperatures were obtained as done for the heating rate of 1 °C/min (see Fig. 2a). The results are shown in Fig. 2b. It is apparent that the heating rate shows an influence on the gelation of chitosan alkaline solution especially at low heating rates (<1.5 °C/min). The relationship of the sol-gel transition temperature with heating rate can be fitted into an equation,(2)y = 67.8 − 21.1 exp(−x/0.53)where x is the heating rate in °C/min, for the alkaline solution of 2 wt% chitosan. Being expected by this equation, with further increasing the heating rate, the sol-gel transition temperature tends to become a constant, 67.8 °C, which is independent of the heating rate, implying that a high heating rate is not important for changing the sol-gel transition temperature. On the other hand, by extrapolating the heating rate to zero, the equilibrium sol-gel transition temperature, 46.7 °C, was obtained.
In situ forming hydrogels are systems responsive to the environmental stimuli, such as change of temperature, pH, photo intensity, ionic strength, etc.14, 15 They have been divided into two types, one is chemical in situ gels and the other is physical in situ gels. Chemical in situ gels, also called “permanent” gels, are hydrogels containing covalently cross-linked networks. They are irreversible polymeric networks via the use of cross-linkers or enzymes.16 Physical in situ gels, or “reversible” gels, are those networks held together by molecular entanglements and secondary forces such as hydrogen bonding, ionic, hydrophobic forces.17, 18 Usually these weak and reversible bonds formation depends on external stimulation to form cross-linking, which makes temperature, pH, lights, or ions sensitive reversible hydrogels possible.19-22 In situ delivery systems have an upper hand compared with conventional systems, because they take longer time for in situ system to finish releasing drug at targeted site. Particularly, a temperature responsive hydrogel, namely thermogel, is a reversible physical cross-linking system, forming upon heating up temperature until critical temperature. The properties of thermogel offer opportunities in therapeutic application because of several reasons.23-25 An injectable thermogel system has simplicity of pharmaceutical formulation by mixing of drug below sol-gel transition temperature. Large scale surgery for implantation is not needed. After injection, body temperature will stimulate sol-gel transition, viscous solution will change into a drug delivery depot. The high percentage water content makes thermogel highly competitive with the injection site. Also, peptides are kept at low temperature before application, which makes sure no denaturalization due to organic solvent interaction or dissolution triggered by high temperature. Currently, there are only two types of commercial polymeric thermoresponsive hydrogel products available in the market. One is Poloxamer, and the other is poly(N-isopropyl acrylamide) (PNIPAAm). When using Poloxamer based hydrogel, two conditions, polymer critical micelle concentration (CMC) and critical micelle temperature (CMT), must be reached to promote sol-gel transition. For Poloxamer, it includes Amphipathic Poloxamer and Pluronic F127. Amphipathic Poloxamer, a FDA-approved triblock polymer, composes of hydrophobic poly(ethylene oxide) and hydrophilic poly(propylene oxide) components.26 Hydrogel based on this has been widely used in both therapeutic and consumer applications. Although Amphipathic Poloxamer has proven to be biocompatible and able to perform drug delivery,27 degradation of it based hydrogels does not support sustainable process. The degradation period, 4 h, has severely limited targeted or long-termed drug release application.12 Meanwhile, Pluronic F127, with CMT of human body temperature (37 °C) and longer degradation period, has higher CMC, which limits its bioapplications. Commercial PNIPAAm is another typical amphipathic thermoresponsive polymer, which was first synthesized in the 1950s.28-30 Hydrogel based on this can undergo reversible phase change by changing the temperature of aqueous environment. However, poor mechanical and nonbiodegradable properties, teratogenicity and carcinogenicity of its residual monomers, and toxicity of degradation products of isopropyl amine limit its biomedical applications.31-34 After drug delivery process, PNIPAAm based hydrogel needs to be removed by extra surgery, which goes against the advantage of thermogel by avoiding surgery on patients and will not bring convenience and ease to therapeutic application. Being one of the earliest and most studied biomaterials, polyester has its irreplaceable place among all polymer materials.35-41 Compared with other biomaterials, polyester has three great advantages-biodegradation, biocompatibility, and synthetic versatility.42-48 The application of hydrogel based on this as scaffold for cell transplantation has already benefitted thousands of people every year.49 Being the only biodegradable polymer with high molecular weight, polyester is able to undergo hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation. This is due to its highly hydrolysable ester linkages in the polymer backbone and good fitness to enzyme's active site, respectively.24, 41, 50-52 Controllable degradation gives polyester based hydrogel the advantage of application in periodic and targeted drug release.53 The end result of degradation also brings no harm to human body as it will be transformed into carbon dioxide and water, released out of human body by metabolism eventually. Besides, human body contains 70% of water and it is important for any material used in human body to also largely contain water to achieve good biocompatibility. Polyester based hydrogel is able to trap large amount of water in aqueous environments including body fluids. Based on the provided evidence, the 'sol-gel transition' in injectable biodegradable hydrogels refers to a **physical phase change** from a liquid-like solution (sol) to a solid-like gel network upon exposure to specific stimuli. This transition is critical for minimally invasive biomedical applications. Key characteristics include:

1.  **Stimuli-Responsive Triggering**: The transition is induced by environmental changes such as **temperature** (e.g., heating to body temperature 37°C) [2], [6], [7], [14], **UV light** [1], or **ionic cross-linking** (e.g., alginate with Ca²⁺ ions) [10], [12].
2.  **Reversible Physical Cross-linking**: Primarily achieved through non-covalent interactions like hydrophobic associations, hydrogen bonding, or entanglement (physical hydrogels), avoiding toxic chemical cross-linkers [2], [7], [11].
3.  **Rapid Transformation**: The transition occurs quickly (e.g., within seconds for UV-triggered systems [1] or upon reaching physiological temperature [6], [7]), enabling injection as a low-viscosity fluid that solidifies *in situ*.
4.  **Injectable Functionality**: Hydrogels exist as free-flowing solutions ("sol") at room temperature or during injection, facilitating administration via syringe, and transform into gels ("gel") at the target site within the body [2], [6], [7], [10].
5.  **Depot Formation**: The resulting gel acts as a depot for sustained drug delivery, cell encapsulation, or tissue scaffolding [6], [7], [11].

In contrast to chemical hydrogels, physically crosslinked hydrogels, formed by the self-assembly of polymers in response to environmental stimuli (for example, temperature, pH, or both) display sol-gel transitions without marked volume changes. The hydrogels systems are relatively low viscosity aqueous solutions (sol state) prior to injection, but rapidly convert into a gel under physiological conditions post-injection [1], [6], [7]. Physical hydrogels have several advantages over chemical hydrogels, because they do not require photo irradiation, use of organic solvents or crosslinking agents, and do not release heat at the gelation site, which may denature incorporated proteins and damage embedded cells and surrounding tissues. Thus, the physical systems have recently attracted increased attention. For use in drug/cell delivery and tissue engineering, hydrogels should be low-viscosity solutions (free-flowing) prior to subcutaneous injection, and should rapidly gel in the human body, where ultimate degradation of the hydrogels is desired. Natural polysaccharide-based ionic polymers including hyaluronic acid, heparin, chitosan, and dextran derivatives have been extensively investigated in biomedical applications mainly because of their biocompatibility, non-immunogenicity, biodegradability and cell-adhesion properties.29-37 Among the variety of natural polysaccharides, heparin is a negatively charged linear polysaccharide composed of alternating units of sulfated glucuronic acid and glucosamine derivatives.38 Heparin is clinically used as an anticoagulant. AbstractInjectable biodegradable copolymer hydrogels, which exhibit temperature-responsive sol-to-gel transition, have recently drawn much attention as promising biomedical materials such as drug delivery, cell implantation, and tissue engineering. These injectable hydrogels can be implanted in the human body with minimal surgical invasion. Temperature-responsive gelling copolymers usually possess block- and/or branched architectures and amphiphilicity with a delicate hydrophobic/hydrophilic balance. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) has typically been used as hydrophilic segments due to its biocompatibility and temperature-dependent dehydration nature. Aliphatic polyesters such as polylactide, poly(lactide-co-glycolide), poly(ε-caprolactone), and their modified copolymers have been used as hydrophobic segments based on their biodegradability and biocompatibility. Copolymers of PEG with other hydrophobic polymers such as polypeptides, polydepsipeptides have also been recently reported as injectable hydrogels. In this review, brief history and recent advances in injectable biodegradable polymer hydrogels are summarized especially focusing on the relationship between polymer architecture and their gelation properties. Moreover, the applications of these injectable polymer gels for biomedical use such as drug delivery and tissue engineering are also described. IntroductionIn situ gel forming polymer systems have recently drawn much attention as promising biomedical materials for minimally invasive therapy [1], [2], [3]. In particular, biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers, which show sol-to-gel transition between room temperature and body temperature upon heating, are expected to be useful for injectable polymer gel (IPG) systems in biomedical applications. These polymer solutions are in sol state in the syringe at room temperature and become gel in situ after injection into the body, without requiring any toxic cross-linkers. Such systems can easily entrap pharmaceutical agents or cells and form a depot by a simple syringe injection at a target site, where the depots acts as sustained drug delivery devices or a cell-growing scaffolds for tissue engineering [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10]. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) has typically been used as hydrophilic segments of thermo-gelling polymers due to its biocompatibility and temperature-dependent dehydration nature. Aliphatic polyesters such as poly(l-lactide) (PLLA), poly(d-lactide) (PDLA), poly(dl-lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), and their modified copolymers have been used as hydrophobic segments based on their biodegradability and relatively good biocompatibility [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17].Since pioneering research on biodegradable IPG systems using triblock copolymer of PEG and PLLA, PEG-b-PLLA-b-PEG, by Kim et al. in 1997 [11], many kinds of biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers have been developed by combining PEG and aliphatic polyesters with various molecular architectures including linear-type and star-shape block as well as graft topologies [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24], [25]. In addition, biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers containing amino acids as building blocks of the hydrophobic segments have been recently developed [26], [27], [28], [29], [30]. Biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers reported can be categorized into block copolymers including linear-type and/or star-shaped diblock, triblock, and multiblock architectures, and graft copolymers from the view point of molecular architectures, as summarized in Table 1. These copolymers exhibits various properties based on the molecular architectures and nature of the components.In this article, brief history and recent advances in biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers as IPGs are reviewed especially focusing on the relationship between polymer structure and their properties. Moreover, the applications of these IPGs for biomedical use such as DDS and tissue engineering are also reviewed.

To date, the reported injectable hydrogels have failed to mimic the fibrous architecture of the extracellular matrix (ECM), limiting their biological effects on cell growth and phenotype. Additionally, they lack the micro-sized pores present within the ECM, which is unfavorable for the facile transport of nutrients and waste. Herein, an injectable ECM-mimetic hydrogel (IEMH) was fabricated by shortening and dispersing Janus fibers capable of self-curling at body temperature into pH 7.4 phosphate buffer solution. The IEMH could be massively prepared through a side-by-side electrospinning process combined with ultraviolet irradiation. The IEMHs with only 5 wt% fibers could undergo sol-gel transition at body temperature to become solid gels with desirable stability, sturdiness, and elasticity and self-healing ability. In addition, they possessed notable pseudoplasticity, which is beneficial to injection at room temperature. The results obtained from characterization analysis via scanning electron microscopy, total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy indicate that their sol-gel transition under physiological conditions stems from the synergistic action of the tight entanglements between thermally-induced self-curling fibers and the hydrophobic interaction between the fibers. An MTT assay using C2C12 myoblast cells was performed to examine the in vitro cytotoxicity of IEMHs for biomedical applications, and the cell viability was found to be more than 95%. These challenges suggest there is a high need for a new strategy for designing and fabricating ECM-mimetic fibrous hydrogels for practical biomedical applications, particularly injectable ECM-mimetic fibrous hydrogels. Compared with self-assembly, electrospinning is a simple, inexpensive, and versatile technique for the massive preparation of fibers ranging from tens of nanometers to a few micrometers in diameter.18,19 Additionally, drugs or bioactive molecules can be loaded into the fibers during electrospinning, with high loading efficiency.20 However, the conventional electrospinning technique affords two-dimensional (2D) fibrous membranes with extremely small pore sizes, which make them unsuitable for biomedical applications.18 To address this problem, a variety of modified electrospinning techniques aiming at the fabrication of three-dimensional (3D) electrospun scaffolds, such as multilayering electrospinning, sacrificial agent electrospinning, wet electrospinning, and ultrasound-enhanced electrospinning, as well as post-processing techniques, including gas foaming, ultrasonication, short-fiber assembly, 3D printing, and electrospraying, have been developed.18 Nevertheless, so far the reported 3D fibrous scaffolds are mostly made from hydrophobic electrospun fibers,18 which makes it substantially difficult to mimic hydrophilic ECMs. Specially, these modified electrospinning techniques generally afford preformed scaffolds rather than injectable ones.

The 'sol-gel transition' in injectable biodegradable hydrogels refers to a reversible phase change where a low-viscosity, free-flowing polymer solution (sol state) transforms into a solid-like gel network upon exposure to physiological stimuli (e.g., temperature, pH). This transition occurs after injection, enabling in situ gel formation at the target site without chemical crosslinkers. Key characteristics include:

1.  **Temperature sensitivity**: Most systems exhibit sol behavior at room temperature (for syringe loading/injection) and rapid gelation near body temperature (37°C). This is driven by the delicate hydrophobic/hydrophilic balance in amphiphilic polymers (e.g., PEG-polyester copolymers like PLGA-PEG, PCLA-PEG) [1], [3], [4], [10].
2.  **Physical crosslinking**: Gelation primarily results from physical interactions like micelle aggregation, hydrophobic associations, partial crystallization of hydrophobic segments (e.g., PCL), and entanglement, rather than covalent bonds [1], [4], [10], [12].
3.  **Injectable & minimally invasive**: The sol state allows easy injection and homogeneous filling of irregular defects, forming a gel depot in situ post-injection for sustained drug/cell delivery or tissue scaffolding [3], [5], [6], [10].
4.  **Reversibility**: The transition is often thermally reversible, allowing potential gel dissolution upon cooling [1], [7], [10].

This property is critical for minimally invasive biomedical applications like drug delivery, cell encapsulation, and tissue engineering [3], [10], [15].

In this era of green science and technology, we are more concerned about materials that are environmentally benign, more precisely, materials that do not have a negative impact on nature. This is why biodegradability is considered as the prime concern in the production of most industrial products. Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) {[CH(CH3)COO]n} is a biodegradable and biocompatible semicrystalline polymer that can be produced from renewable resources, such as corn.1 It must be emphasized that the concomitant presence and their molar ratio of the two enantiomeric species in PLA strongly affect the morphology of the material; that is, poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) is a semicrystalline polymer, and D,L-PLLA is an amorphous material.2 The stereocomplexation between PLLA and poly(D-lactic acid) was performed as an effective method for increasing the thermal stability of PLLA-based materials.3, 4 However, the production cost of poly(D-lactic acid) is the bottleneck of stereocomplexed PLLA materials. Commercially available PLA grades are obtained by the ring-opening polymerization of lactide, a dimer of lactic acid. Lactic acid is optically active and, thus, can be of L or D form. The maximum attainable crystallinity level is obtained by minimization of the amount of D-lactide isomers and L,D-lactide (i.e., mesolactide), in which the L-lactide is used as the major monomer.5 The crystallinity and crystallization rate obviously decrease as the purity in the crystallizable L-lactic acid segment decreases. For example, the crystallization half-time (t1/2) was found to increase by roughly 40% for every 1 wt % increase in the mesolactide content of the polymerization mixture.6 Even at high L-lactic acid contents, however, PLA crystallization is typically too slow to develop significant crystallinity unless the crystallization is induced by strain, such as in processes used to produce biaxially oriented films or bottles. In processes such as injection molding, where the orientation is limited and the cooling rate is high, it is much more challenging to develop significant crystallinity, and thus, formulation or process changes are required. This is why the crystal structure and crystallization behavior of PLLA have been extensively investigated by many techniques from the academic viewpoint of structural interest and for practical applications.7-13 The polyester nature of PLLA produces a high thermal susceptibility of the material, in particular during melt processing, and significant molar mass variation results. This is why the understanding of the crystallization kinetics is an important concern in the design of PLLA-based materials with desirable properties through the control of the crystallization factors in PLLA. Despite extensive studies of PLLA, its crystallization behavior and crystal structure are still not completely understood. Depending on the processing conditions, PLLA can crystallize in α, β, or γ forms.7, 8 The different crystalline morphologies can affect the chemical stability, physical/mechanical properties, and degradation rates9 in biodegradable polymers. Therefore, a thorough understanding of the crystallization behavior of PLLA is crucial.
At present, PLA porous gels are used as drug-release materials, fixative bone repair materials, and tissue engineering scaffolds in the biomedical field.4-8 However, there are still areas for improvement in the preparation of porous gels from PLA, and these are hot topics of research. Although there has been much research on PLA gel materials, to the best of our knowledge, there have been no studies on materials prepared from the different optical isomers of PLA. Studies have shown that the different isomers of PLA have different crystallinities,9-11 melting points, and mechanical properties [compressive strength and tensile strength (σ)]. Polylactic acid (PLA) is an aliphatic polyester derived from natural sources which is biodegradable and can be industrially composted [1]. PLA was first synthesised in 1932 by Carothers and then patented by DuPont in 1954 [2] and has recently been attracting growing interest due to its sustainable nature and good mechanical properties. PLA typically has a tensile strength of 44-70 MPa, high stiffness with elastic modulus of 2-3GPa [3] and is brittle below its glass transition temperature of 50 °C-60 °C, above which it softens. This limits its uses in many applications to those requiring relatively low temperatures, for example cold food packaging. In addition, PLA has low melt strength which can restrict its usage in melt processing techniques which involve a stretching deformation. Currently PLA is used primarily in disposable packaging and textile applications where the glass-transition temperature of the material is not restrictive. Numerous attempts have been made to modify the properties of PLA, either by blending it with other organic materials (such as polymers, nucleating agents and solvents), inorganic materials (such as chalk, talc and graphene) or by changing the properties during or after processing (orientation, annealing and control of processing conditions) [4]. PLA is produced from the chiral monomer lactic acid. Lactic acid (2-hydroxy propionic acid), has an asymmetric carbon atom and can exist in two optically active configurations (enantiomers), the L (levo-lactic acid) and D (dextro-lactic acid) forms respectively. The concentration of L and D isomers can affect the morphology and properties of the material, with high optical purity homo-polymers (PLLA and PDLA) exhibiting a higher glass transition temperature and eventual crystallinity than the more typically amorphous co-polymer PDLLA. [5]. Commercially, the most widely used form of polylactic acid is PLLA containing a small percentage of D lactide. The crystal formation and behaviour of PLA is controlled by polymerisation kinetics but as previously mentioned can be manipulated by addition of nucleating agents and other polymers, or by inducing orientation within the polymeric chains. However, the chirality of PLA provides another method of modification of crystallinity through control of its stereochemistry. PLA has a slow crystal formation rate, which means that achieving high crystallinity in a process with a short timescale such as injection moulding is challenging [6]. However, increasing crystallinity is desirable as it improves mechanical and thermal properties. There are two potential methods to increase the crystallinity of PLA during manufacturing; isothermal and non-isothermal crystallisation [7]. Isothermal annealing of PLA depends on temperature, time and molecular weight of the material. Crystal formation and spherulite growth has been shown to depend on molecular weight (Mw), where PLLA with lower molecular weight showed higher crystallinity than the higher Mw PLA under the same conditions [8]. As PLA is sensitive to thermal processing, this finding suggests also that thermal history may influence Mw and therefore crystal formation. Annealed PLA can exhibit up to 70% crystallinity, resulting in a corresponding increase in melting temperature and Tg [4].

Poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) is semicrystalline due to its stereoregular structure, while poly(D,L-lactic acid) (PDLLA) with a racemic mixture of isomers is amorphous [2,6]. Higher L-lactide content enhances crystallinity, which reduces water penetration and slows hydrolytic degradation, as amorphous regions degrade first [7,9]. In contrast, PLA with disrupted stereoregularity (e.g., PDLLA or blends with D-isomers) exhibits lower crystallinity, enabling faster water diffusion and accelerated bulk degradation due to easier access to ester bonds [3,7,11]. Additionally, stereocomplexation between PLLA and PDLA can improve thermal stability but does not inherently alter degradation mechanisms compared to non-complexed forms [10]. Thus, increased D-isomer content (amorphous structure) leads to faster degradation, while higher L-isomer content (semicrystalline structure) delays degradation [2,3,7,11].

The degradation of PLA occurs by simple hydrolysis of the ester bond and does not require catalysts (e.g. enzymes). The rate of degradation depends on surface area, isomer ratio, and the temperature [8]. PLA has a reasonable shelf life for single-use packaging applications; proper disposal leads to hydrolysis into small, natural products (e.g. lactic acid), and finally carbon dioxide and water. The intermediates, however, lead to a drop in local pH [4]. Due to its relatively high modulus and ultimate tensile strength, this polymer is promising for technical applications. PLA of high molecular weight is a colorless, glossy, stiff thermoplastic polymer; its properties are similar to polystyrene [6]. However, low impact strength and heat deflection temperature (HDT) still limit its application range. Furthermore, slow crystallization interferes with the high cooling rates typical for industrial polymer processing operations, particularly injection molding. Today, the processing-related issues and low impact performance are mostly remedied by blending PLA with bio-polyesters or starch-based polymers [9]. Thereby, however, the potential for high stiffness and strength values is compromised to a large extent. The thermo-mechanical properties (e.g. stiffness, low brittleness, and barrier properties) may be improved by crystallization; practical values of crystallinity (Xc) lie in the range of 37 - 47% [10], [11], [12]. Nucleating agents (NAs) are utilized to increase the crystallinity of polymers. A decrease of cycle times (tcycle) in injection molding through nucleation is proposed. One of the most efficient NAs is talc [13], [14]; it is used as the reference in this study. The tested NAs were kraft lignin, lignosulfonate, and carbon black. For these NAs, no prior studies are known, with respect to reduction of cycle times in the injection molding process. Lignins are a class of cross-linked phenolic biopolymers in the cell walls of plants. They are a byproduct of pulping processes to obtain cellulose. The most important one is the kraft process (or sulfate process); it utilizes NaOH + Na2S and yields kraft pulp and kraft lignin as the primary byproduct. Less widespread is the older sulfite process, that utilizes sulfurous acid; byproducts are primarily lignosulfonate and various sugars (e.g. mannose and xylose) [15]. Because of the different pulping processes, kraft lignin and lignosulfonate vary primarily in molar mass, amount of phenolic hydroxy-groups, and sulfur content. Kraft lignin contains no sulfonate groups.

1.  **Stereocomplexation reduces degradation rate:** Blending PLLA (L-rich) with PDLA (D-rich) forms stereocomplex crystallites. The degree of stereocomplexation, and thus the degradation rate, can be customized by the architecture and end-groups of the D-LA oligomers blended with PLLA [1].

2.  **Optical purity controls crystallinity:** PLA with high optical purity (high L-content, typically >93%) is semicrystalline. Crystalline regions act as a barrier, restricting water diffusion and slowing down hydrolytic degradation (lower mass loss) [6, 11, 15]. PLA with lower optical purity (L-content between 50-93%) or racemic mixtures (PDLLA) is amorphous. Amorphous regions are more accessible to water, leading to faster hydrolytic degradation (higher mass loss) [6, 11, 13, 15].

3.  **Disrupted stereoregularity accelerates degradation:** Introducing D-lactide into PLLA chains disrupts stereoregularity, resulting in atactic, completely amorphous PLA. This structure is fragile and undergoes very rapid degradation, crumbling within 24 hours under physiological conditions [6].

4.  **Stereocomplex properties depend on blend characteristics:** The effectiveness of stereocomplexation in slowing degradation depends on factors like the molar ratio (maximum interaction at 1:1), oligomer architecture (star-shaped with alcoholic ends slow degradation more than linear or carboxylic-ended), and optical purity (crystallizability lost below ~88% D-content in D-rich or L-content in L-rich) [1, 7, 11]. Increasing the number of alcoholic chain-ends on star-shaped oligomers from four to six decreased stereocomplexation and led to faster mass loss [1].

Hydrogen bonds hold the starch chains together, making them insoluble in cold water. Additionally, these hydrogen bonds lead to a high glass transition temperature, which makes starch difficult to process. This disadvantage can be overcome by converting raw starch into thermoplastic starch (TPS). This conversion is achieved through a process called “gelatinization,” which is performed in the presence of excess water, using a plasticizer and heat. As a result of this irreversible process, the crystalline structure in the starch granules is eliminated, resulting in a completely amorphous structure [6, 7]. The selection of plasticizers plays a pivotal role in determining the mechanical, thermal, and biological properties of TPS. Among various options, the combination of glycerol and D-sorbitol offers significant advantages over conventional plasticizers such as urea, glycols, and citrate esters [7-9]. Glycerol, due to its high hydrophilicity, disrupts intermolecular hydrogen bonding between starch chains, thereby improving processability. In contrast, D-sorbitol, with its longer molecular structure, contributes to enhanced thermal stability and water resistance [10]. Furthermore, its low volatility reduces plasticizer migration, thus improving the long-term stability of the material [11]. The synergistic use of these two plasticizers can effectively address common issues associated with TPS, including starch retrogradation, plasticizer migration, brittleness, and elevated glass transition temperatures, while allowing for precise tuning of water resistance and mechanical performance [9, 10]. Li and Huneault [7] reported that while glycerol alone produced TPS with low thermal stability and excessive hydrophilicity, the incorporation of sorbitol improved expansion resistance by 30%. Similarly, Sanyang et al. [10] found that combining glycerol and sorbitol doubled the Young's modulus of palm starch films compared to systems plasticized with glycerol alone. However, these studies primarily focused on corn or potato starch, leaving a significant knowledge gap in the plasticization behavior of wheat starch-a variant particularly rich in amylose. In a recent study in which glycerol was used as a plasticizer, it was reported that the tensile strength and Young's modulus of TPS films obtained from wheat starch were higher than those of other conventional starches [4]. Therefore, in this study, we aimed to systematically investigate the physicochemical properties and cellular interactions associated with varying glycerol-to-sorbitol ratios in wheat starch-based TPS formulations. For example, Carmona et al. [20] reported that polycaprolactone (PCL)/poly (lactic acid) (PLA) blends exhibited 40% lower fibroblast proliferation compared to starch-containing composites. The relative hydrophilicity of starch, attributed to its abundant hydroxyl groups, enhances protein adsorption and promotes cell adhesion [18]. Moreover, in contrast to synthetic polymers-which may generate acidic and potentially cytotoxic degradation products-starch degrades into glucose chains that can serve as an additional nutrient source for cells [19]. TPS can be prepared by melt-mixing starch with plasticizers such as water, glycerol, sorbitol, and ionic plasticizers [9,10]. One effective method is reactive blending, which is used to improve the properties of polymers blended with additive compounds [11]. The use of natural biomaterials as additives has been extensively investigated [[12], [13], [14]], while nanometals technology was used to improve some of the properties of TPS [15].CMC is a natural polymer that is non-toxic to humans. It has high mechanical strength, and notable additive, swelling, and water-soluble properties. CMC is a biodegradable and biocompatible material that easily reacts or interacts with other functional groups due to its carboxyl groups (-COOH) [16]. CMC is used to improve the processing ability of some products, such as cosmetics, foodstuffs, pharmaceutical, paper, and textiles [17]. CMC has been used for food and packaging applications, such as packaging indicator [18] and food packaging [19].Zinc oxide (ZnO) is an attractive material because of its size, shape, and surface area, which relate to the properties of the incorporated materials [20,21]. The addition of nanometal particles to a biopolymer blend can increase the mechanical and water resistance properties of the blends [22]. ZnO is used by many researchers because of its antimicrobial activity and can be applied as a filler or additive in medical products. ZnO nanoparticles have high surface tension. Sonication is used to disperse the ZnO in the blending process. The Scientific Committee on Food established the upper limit for ZnO intake through food at 25 mg/person per day [23]. ZnO is widely used in food [24], packaging [25], and medical applications [26], and many researchers have investigated its effects on material properties [[27], [28], [29], [30], [31]]. However, only a few studies have revealed the effect of ZnO in TPS [32], and the role of ZnO in a TPS blend with CMC has not been investigated yet. Connection between TPS and ZnO phases via reaction and interaction of Na+ ions in CMC, is the key factor to improve compatibility, morphology, mechanical properties, and water resistance of TPS, while deep detail of ZnO effect in TPS using CMC with Na+ ion to mechanical properties and water resistance is unclear explanation. Furthermore, low mechanical properties and moisture sensitive of TPS prevent it from wide applications. Reactive melt-blending of TPS is an easy and low-cost process to develop its properties, which can be applied for industrial production scale of packaging, agricultural, and medical applications.Therefore, the objective of this research is to develop a new type of biobased thermoplastic with high mechanical and water resistance properties by reactive mixing TPS, CMC, and ZnO. As countries around the world pay more and more attention to environmental issues, the research on biomass materials has also attracted more and more attention.1 As a reproducible resource and polysaccharides, starch can be widely found in plants such as corn, cassava, potato, etc. Starch is composed of amylose and amylopectin, and the content of amylose and amylopectin depends on the source of the starch. For instance, the amylose content in corn starch is about 28%-30%.2 Because there are a lot of hydroxyl groups on starch molecular chain, strong hydrogen bonds can be formed between the molecular chains, resulting in the melting temperature of starch being greater than the decomposition temperature. Therefore, it does not have thermoplastic behavior and cannot be processed like other thermoplastic polymers. To break the hydrogen bonds between starch molecules, thermoplastic starch (TPS) can be prepared by blending with low molecular weight polyols, such as glycerol,3 sorbitol,4 ethylene glycol.5 However, due to the migration of plasticizers during the storage of TPS, hydrogen bonds between the starch molecular chains can reform, which is called the retrogradation process.6, 7 There are two stages of the retrogradation process. The first stage is the retrogradation of amylose, which is faster. And the second stage is the formation of an ordered structure of amylopectin, which is a slow process.7, 8 The retrogradation process of TPS is complicated, and the type and content of plasticizers, as well as the storage temperature and humidity conditions, have great effect.8-10 Several methods have been developed to improve the retrogradation properties of TPS. It has been reported that high glycerol content can effectively inhibit the retrogradation of TPS.11 But its high sensitivity to the moisture limits its wide application in TPS.12, 13 Urea as a plasticizer can also inhibit starch retrogradation to a certain extent. However, the inclusion of urea makes starch brittle and urea cannot be used in food contact materials.14 Compound plasticizer can reduce the water absorption of starch and inhibit the migration of plasticizers, thereby reducing starch retrogradation.15, 16 When the mass ratio of glycerol/sorbitol is 1:1, the TPS, which was stored for 9 months under the conditions of 25°C/60% relative humidity (RH) and 40°C/75% RH, has the best performance and most stable shape.15 Compared with glycerol/sorbitol plasticized starch, the crystallization rate in the xylitol/montmorillonite plasticized system is slower, which can be ascribed to the competition between xylitol and montmorillonite.17 However, since glycerol and high molecular weight plasticizers (sorbitol, xylitol, etc.) are both hydrophilic plasticizers, the effects of plasticizers on the glass transition temperature and retrogradation of starch vary with water content.15, 18 Therefore, methods of changing the type of plasticizer or increasing the content of plasticizer to inhibit the retrogradation of starch still cannot meet the requirements of the development of the biodegradable material industry.19

There are several substances used as plasticizers for the preparation of thermoplastic starch. Some of the most studied and reported TPS plasticizers in the literature include polyols such as glycerol, glycol, sorbitol, xylitol, maltitol, ethylene glycol, propylene glycol, butanediol;107,110,111 sucrose, fructose, mannose,112 fatty acids (such as myristate or palmitate),113etc. It is also necessary to note that water is a good plasticizer of starch. However, the use of water alone as a plasticizer is not preferable because the resulting product will be brittle when equilibrated with ambient humidity110 and due to volatilization of water. Glycerol, a classical plasticizer of starch, is perhaps the most widely studied and used polyol plasticizer of TPS. This is because of its low cost, nontoxicity (for food and biomedical application) and high boiling point (292 °C). Moreover, the hydrolysis and/or transesterification of lipids (triglycerides) into fatty acids for the biodiesel industry produce glycerol as a by-product. Utilizing such by-products provides glycerol with an additional market driver in addition to the opportunity of improving the economics of both the biodiesel and the bioplastic industries. Nonetheless, glycerol is known to leach out during aging and humidity exposure, a major limitation for large scale applications. The properties of plasticized starch can be tuned by changing the temperature of processing, water content and the properties and amount of plasticizers. For instance, Yu et al.101 reported that the elongation at break of the thermoplastic starch is significantly improved by plasticization with glycol, glycerol and hexylene glycol. In addition, the thermal properties of plasticized starch are a function of water and plasticizer content.110,114 The source of starch is also important for the property of TPS. This is because starches from various sources have different amylose/amylopectin ratios, molecular weights, molecular weight distributions and granular size crystallinity (Fig. 7). This as a result influences the gelatinization and glass transition temperatures115,116 that are directly correlated with the thermoplasticity of the TPS. The effect of various plasticizers at different concentrations on the gelatinization temperatures, thermal stability, and glass transition temperature has been studied and reported in the literature. Some of the plasticizers and their effects are reviewed and shown in Table 3. Abdorreza et al.117 showed that the type and concentration of plasticizers govern the heat sealability as well as the seal strength of sago starch based films. The same authors showed that sorbitol-plasticized films exhibited significantly better heat sealability than did the glycerol type. Thermoplastic starch (TPS) Thermoplastic starch (TPS) is a biodegradable biopolymer derived from starch-rich crops such as corn, wheat, and potatoes. Exhibiting thermoplastic behavior, TPS can be processed using conventional plastic manufacturing techniques, including extrusion, injection molding, and film blowing. Due to its renewable origin and inherent biodegradability, TPS has emerged as a promising material for environmentally sustainable packaging solutions [111]. TPS primarily consists of amylose and amylopectin, the two principal polysaccharides in starch. Amylose is a mostly linear polymer of glucose units linked via α−1,4-glycosidic bonds, while amylopectin is a highly branched polymer featuring both α−1,4- and α−1,6-glycosidic linkages. To produce TPS, starch is plasticized using agents such as glycerol, sorbitol, or water, which enhance its processability and mechanical properties by disrupting inter- and intra-molecular hydrogen bonds [23]. Its biodegradability, coupled with favorable water vapor barrier properties, makes it particularly attractive for food packaging applications [111]. By replacing conventional plastics with TPS-based materials, it is possible to substantially mitigate plastic waste accumulation and environmental pollution, thereby advancing sustainability in consumer and agricultural sectors. Nevertheless, TPS does present certain limitations, including lower mechanical strength, heightened sensitivity to moisture, and reduced processing compatibility compared to synthetic polymers [23]. Despite these challenges, TPS continues to gain prominence globally. Based solely on the provided evidence, glycerol serves the following key roles in thermoplastic starch (TPS) production:

1.  **Plasticizer:** Glycerol functions as a plasticizer by disrupting the intermolecular hydrogen bonding between starch chains through its high hydrophilicity. This disruption is essential for converting native starch into a processable thermoplastic material during gelatinization [3],[5],[7],[9],[11],[12],[13],[14],[15].
2.  **Processability Enhancer:** By breaking hydrogen bonds and reducing the glass transition temperature (Tg), glycerol improves the melt processability of starch, enabling its transformation into TPS using conventional techniques like extrusion and injection molding [3],[4],[5],[6],[7],[9],[11],[12],[13],[14].
3.  **Mechanical Property Modifier:** The amount of glycerol significantly influences the mechanical properties of TPS. Higher glycerol content generally increases flexibility and elongation at break but reduces tensile strength, modulus, and thermal stability [1],[9],[11],[12],[13],[14].
4.  **Morphology Controller (in Blends):** In polymer blends like LDPE/TPS or PLA/TPS, glycerol content directly affects the viscosity and elasticity of the TPS phase, thereby controlling the size and deformability of the TPS dispersed domains within the matrix polymer [1],[2],[13],[14].
5.  **Synergistic Plasticizer Component:** Glycerol is often used in combination with other plasticizers like sorbitol. While glycerol improves flexibility, sorbitol enhances thermal stability and modulus. This combination helps address issues like retrogradation, brittleness, and plasticizer migration [3],[5],[9],[11],[12],[13],[14].

Hydrogen bonds hold the starch chains together, making them insoluble in cold water. Additionally, these hydrogen bonds lead to a high glass transition temperature, which makes starch difficult to process. This disadvantage can be overcome by converting raw starch into thermoplastic starch (TPS). This conversion is achieved through a process called “gelatinization,” which is performed in the presence of excess water, using a plasticizer and heat. As a result of this irreversible process, the crystalline structure in the starch granules is eliminated, resulting in a completely amorphous structure [6, 7]. The selection of plasticizers plays a pivotal role in determining the mechanical, thermal, and biological properties of TPS. Among various options, the combination of glycerol and D-sorbitol offers significant advantages over conventional plasticizers such as urea, glycols, and citrate esters [7-9]. Glycerol, due to its high hydrophilicity, disrupts intermolecular hydrogen bonding between starch chains, thereby improving processability. In contrast, D-sorbitol, with its longer molecular structure, contributes to enhanced thermal stability and water resistance [10]. Furthermore, its low volatility reduces plasticizer migration, thus improving the long-term stability of the material [11]. The synergistic use of these two plasticizers can effectively address common issues associated with TPS, including starch retrogradation, plasticizer migration, brittleness, and elevated glass transition temperatures, while allowing for precise tuning of water resistance and mechanical performance [9, 10]. Li and Huneault [7] reported that while glycerol alone produced TPS with low thermal stability and excessive hydrophilicity, the incorporation of sorbitol improved expansion resistance by 30%. Similarly, Sanyang et al. [10] found that combining glycerol and sorbitol doubled the Young's modulus of palm starch films compared to systems plasticized with glycerol alone. However, these studies primarily focused on corn or potato starch, leaving a significant knowledge gap in the plasticization behavior of wheat starch-a variant particularly rich in amylose. In a recent study in which glycerol was used as a plasticizer, it was reported that the tensile strength and Young's modulus of TPS films obtained from wheat starch were higher than those of other conventional starches [4]. Therefore, in this study, we aimed to systematically investigate the physicochemical properties and cellular interactions associated with varying glycerol-to-sorbitol ratios in wheat starch-based TPS formulations. TPS can be processed using conventional plastic processing techniques, such as injection molding, extrusion, and solvent casting [6]. However, owing to the inherently poor mechanical properties of starch, TPS is often blended with biodegradable or non-degradable synthetic polymers for biomedical applications [12-21]. For example, Carmona et al. [20] reported that polycaprolactone (PCL)/poly (lactic acid) (PLA) blends exhibited 40% lower fibroblast proliferation compared to starch-containing composites. Emerging evidence suggests that optimized TPS formulations may support superior fibroblast proliferation compared to their synthetic counterparts, likely due to starch's intrinsic bioactivity and biocompatible degradation profile.
