The replacement of conventional petroleum-based polymers by other more environmentally friendly polymers has been focused research in recent times. To this end, starch is one of the most promising biopolymers due to its natural origin from renewable sources, economically competitive and biodegradable. Native starch is not a thermoplastic polymer in a natural way, due to its degradation temperature is lower than the temperature required for plasticization. However, in the presence of a suitable plasticizer, under temperature and shear conditions, it is converted in a thermoplastic starch (TPS) able to be processed as the conventional thermoplastic polymers [1]. Plasticizers for starches must be small molecules capable of diffusing between the starch molecules and they must own groups capable of forming hydrogen bonds with hydroxyl groups of starch molecules. Glycerol is, among the polyols, the most used plasticizer for starch due to its low cost, high boiling point and no toxicity. However, the interaction between glycerol and starch is not strong enough, so the starch often recrystallizes after being stored for a period of time. This undesirable process, very frequent in the TPS, is known as retrogradation [2,3]. Isosorbide is a bicyclic compound obtained from the glucose dehydration, characterized by having two OH groups and two oxygen atoms intercalated in the double carbon ring. Recently, isosorbide has been tested as a novel, effective and green plasticizer for starch due to its biodegradability and no toxicity, which prevents the starch retrogradation [4,5]. Although the studies about the use of isosorbide as a plasticizer for starches are scarce at the moment, its use is revealed as an interesting strategy to obtain more durable materials that do not present the disadvantages generated by retrogradation processes. The TPS have two main disadvantages compared to the common thermoplastic polymers including poor mechanical properties and a low moisture resistance. A strategy widely used in recent years to overcoming the TPS drawbacks consists of the incorporation of biodegradable micro or nanoparticles used as a filler in the TPS matrix. The disrupted amylose and amylopectin chains can gently recrystallize to different ordered structures when starch is cooled following heating in the presence of water in a phenomenon named retrogradation.16 The retrogradation rate of glycerol plasticized starch (GPS) limited the application of this plasticizer for longer periods of time and storing.17 In order to decrease the retrogradation rate and limit the structural changes, use of plasticizers which contain amide groups such as formamide, acetamide and urea has been suggested.13, 18 However, because of the toxicity of these kinds of plasticizer, their use cannot be allowed in some hygienic applications: food packaging, disposable food containers, pharmacy and biomedical applications. Starch plasticized using sorbitol which slows the recrystallization rate, enhances tensile strength and modulus and improves thermal stability should be more effective than other plasticizers when toxicity is important, while sorbitol plasticized thermoplastic starch (SPS) shows brittle fracture along with low elongation and toughness of the final product. At first glance, TPS production with two or more plasticizers may show advantages of each one and eliminate their drawbacks for the final optimized TPS. According to this viewpoint, some researchers have worked on the co-plasticization of starch.9,11,13,18−22 Citric acid and glycerol co-plasticized starch shows partial esterification as well as crosslinking due to the chemical reaction between starch chains and citric acid resulting in a strong covalent interaction between citric acid and starch. Starch, characterized by its abundant source, low cost, renewability and complete biodegradability,20 is considered one of the most promising fillers for PBAT. However, due to the strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding in starch molecules, the melting temperature of starch is higher than its decomposition temperature, rendering it unsuitable for melt processing. To address this, a substantial amount of plasticizer must be added to starch under high temperature and shear to facilitate plasticization, resulting in thermoplastic starch (TPS) with melt processability. Common plasticizers for TPS include glycerol,21 citric acid,22 glycerol triacetate,23 formamide, water and small molecules of poly(vinyl alcohol),24-27 with glycerol being the most commonly used and effective. However, the low mechanical strength of TPS and the issue of plasticizer migration and exudation contribute to a significant reduction in the mechanical strength of PBAT/TPS blend materials. Additionally, the strong hygroscopicity of glycerol leads to increased water absorption in PBAT/TPS blend materials. Therefore, improving the mechanical strength of TPS and addressing plasticizer migration and exudation are essential to effectively produce low-cost PBAT/TPS blend films with high starch content. Sorbitol, a commonly used sweetener in daily life, is obtained through glucose-catalyzed hydrogenation. Esmaeili et al. reported in 2017 that using sorbitol as a plasticizer for starch resulted in TPS with higher tensile strength and elastic modulus than when glycerol was used as the plasticizer.21 Sorbitol melts under TPS processing conditions, plasticizing starch by disrupting intramolecular and intermolecular hydrogen bonds. Excess sorbitol solidifies after processing, preventing plasticizer exudation and migration. However, using sorbitol alone as a plasticizer for starch requires a longer plasticization time and higher processing temperature, potentially causing starch coking issues during processing. Furthermore, ordinary starch can be modified to obtain hydroxypropyl starch by grafting epoxy propane, weakening the hydrogen bonds within starch molecules.28 This modification allows plasticizers to enter and plasticize the starch more effectively. Typically, after plasticization, the disrupted linear and branched starch chains can recrystallize into different ordered structures in a process known as regeneration.29 The regenerative capacity of hydroxypropyl starch decreases due to steric hindrance from hydroxypropyl groups,28 stabilizing the performance of plasticized starch and increasing the transparency of the resulting blend films.30 Therefore, the use of hydroxypropyl starch can not only reduce the amount of plasticizer used, increase plasticization efficiency and effectively avoid the transfer and precipitation of small-molecule plasticizers, but also reduce the impact of recrystallization of TPS on film properties.
Like any common thermoplastic polymer, starch can be processed via melt compounding techniques in presence of suitable plasticizers.2, 9, 14 Various plasticizers have been tried to convert starch into TPS but the most widely used ones are water, polyols (e.g., glycerol), vegetable oils, and sorbitol.9, 15-17 Being a by-product of biodiesel production glycerol is low priced and thus especially suited for mass production of TPS even if the mechanical properties of sorbitol plasticized TPS have been found to be slightly better.16 The amount of plasticizer used can be varied in certain limits to adjust the stiffness and strength of TPS to our needs. However, one has to bear in mind that if the plasticizer content in the mixture is not optimal, processing issues are often encountered,4, 18 also leading to the presence of residual granules (referred to “ghost granules” in the literature.1, 4). The presence of these ghost granules decreases the mechanical properties and gives a hazy appearance of the originally transparent material. This should be avoided in many cases, especially for selected packaging applications. Among the main disadvantages of TPS its hydrophilic character and poor mechanical properties should be mentioned. From this reason many studies have addressed the improvement of the properties of TPS.3, 9, 10, 12, 17, 19 Trials, done so far, include chemical modifications, grafting, blending with other biopolymers, and also the incorporation of a reinforcing particles.3, 5, 9, 11-13, 17, 20-24 Main goal of these studies was to improve the properties, while still preserving the biodegradability of the related TPS-based systems. As far as particulate fillers and reinforcements is concerned, the most promising ones for TPS are cellulose and layered silicates. These additives can improve the mechanical and barrier properties which are of great relevance for packaging. The dispersion of these particles and its effect on the properties of TPS were already topics of some publications.5, 9, 10, 13, 15, 17, 19, 25 Extensive kneading associated with melt shearing during extrusion support the disintegration of the entangled cellulose micro- and nanofibers when introduced in dry form. As countries around the world pay more and more attention to environmental issues, the research on biomass materials has also attracted more and more attention.1 As a reproducible resource and polysaccharides, starch can be widely found in plants such as corn, cassava, potato, etc. Starch is composed of amylose and amylopectin, and the content of amylose and amylopectin depends on the source of the starch. For instance, the amylose content in corn starch is about 28%-30%.2 Because there are a lot of hydroxyl groups on starch molecular chain, strong hydrogen bonds can be formed between the molecular chains, resulting in the melting temperature of starch being greater than the decomposition temperature. Therefore, it does not have thermoplastic behavior and cannot be processed like other thermoplastic polymers. To break the hydrogen bonds between starch molecules, thermoplastic starch (TPS) can be prepared by blending with low molecular weight polyols, such as glycerol,3 sorbitol,4 ethylene glycol.5 However, due to the migration of plasticizers during the storage of TPS, hydrogen bonds between the starch molecular chains can reform, which is called the retrogradation process.6, 7 There are two stages of the retrogradation process. The first stage is the retrogradation of amylose, which is faster. And the second stage is the formation of an ordered structure of amylopectin, which is a slow process.7, 8 The retrogradation process of TPS is complicated, and the type and content of plasticizers, as well as the storage temperature and humidity conditions, have great effect.8-10 Several methods have been developed to improve the retrogradation properties of TPS. It has been reported that high glycerol content can effectively inhibit the retrogradation of TPS.11 But its high sensitivity to the moisture limits its wide application in TPS.12, 13 Urea as a plasticizer can also inhibit starch retrogradation to a certain extent. However, the inclusion of urea makes starch brittle and urea cannot be used in food contact materials.14 Compound plasticizer can reduce the water absorption of starch and inhibit the migration of plasticizers, thereby reducing starch retrogradation.15, 16 When the mass ratio of glycerol/sorbitol is 1:1, the TPS, which was stored for 9 months under the conditions of 25°C/60% relative humidity (RH) and 40°C/75% RH, has the best performance and most stable shape.15 Compared with glycerol/sorbitol plasticized starch, the crystallization rate in the xylitol/montmorillonite plasticized system is slower, which can be ascribed to the competition between xylitol and montmorillonite.17 However, since glycerol and high molecular weight plasticizers (sorbitol, xylitol, etc.) are both hydrophilic plasticizers, the effects of plasticizers on the glass transition temperature and retrogradation of starch vary with water content.15, 18 Therefore, methods of changing the type of plasticizer or increasing the content of plasticizer to inhibit the retrogradation of starch still cannot meet the requirements of the development of the biodegradable material industry.19
Thermoplastic starch (TPS) Thermoplastic starch (TPS) is a biodegradable biopolymer derived from starch-rich crops such as corn, wheat, and potatoes. Exhibiting thermoplastic behavior, TPS can be processed using conventional plastic manufacturing techniques, including extrusion, injection molding, and film blowing. Due to its renewable origin and inherent biodegradability, TPS has emerged as a promising material for environmentally sustainable packaging solutions [111]. TPS primarily consists of amylose and amylopectin, the two principal polysaccharides in starch. Amylose is a mostly linear polymer of glucose units linked via α−1,4-glycosidic bonds, while amylopectin is a highly branched polymer featuring both α−1,4- and α−1,6-glycosidic linkages. To produce TPS, starch is plasticized using agents such as glycerol, sorbitol, or water, which enhance its processability and mechanical properties by disrupting inter- and intra-molecular hydrogen bonds [23]. The typical manufacturing process involves starch extraction through wet milling or enzymatic hydrolysis, followed by compounding with plasticizers under controlled heat and pressure to yield TPS in the form of films, sheets, or molded items [132]. TPS is widely utilized in producing biodegradable products such as bags, trays, containers, and agricultural mulch films. Its biodegradability, coupled with favorable water vapor barrier properties, makes it particularly attractive for food packaging applications [111]. By replacing conventional plastics with TPS-based materials, it is possible to substantially mitigate plastic waste accumulation and environmental pollution, thereby advancing sustainability in consumer and agricultural sectors. Nevertheless, TPS does present certain limitations, including lower mechanical strength, heightened sensitivity to moisture, and reduced processing compatibility compared to synthetic polymers [23]. Despite these challenges, TPS continues to gain prominence globally. According to Mordor Intelligence (2024), the thermoplastic starch market was valued at approximately 219.20 kilotons in 2024 and is projected to Reach 333.92 kilotons by 2029, reflecting a robust compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8.79% over the forecast period.
Among natural polymers, starch has stood out due to its abundant availability, biodegradability, and lower cost than other biodegradable polymers [6]. Starch has garnered significant interest from researchers and industry, with applications extending beyond the food sector [7], including controlled drug release [8], tissue engineering [9], and packaging [10]. However, starch-based polymers face limitations compared to conventional fossil-based plastics. Their fragility and high affinity for water significantly affect their use in packaging and other applications exposed to moisture [11, 12]. Thermoplastic starch (TPS) is a biodegradable material obtained by adding plasticizers, such as glycerol, to starch. Structural modifications of starch using natural organic acids or those derived from metabolic pathways have been studied to improve its physical, chemical, and mechanical properties [13, 14]. These modifications aim to enhance the performance of polymers, making them more suitable for a broader range of sustainable and biodegradable applications. However, despite research involving carboxylic acids and TPS, the interactions between starch and additives still require further elucidation to understand their behavior and effects on material properties fully. As a plasticizer, glycerol interacts with the hydroxyl groups of starch, breaking interactions between polymer chains and integrating into the system. However, when glycerol exudes from the material, it can lead to drying and cracking, compromising the structure over time [15]. The chemical modification of starch, involving cross-linking reactions, consists of forming networks between amylopectin and amylose chains with functionalizing agents such as carboxylic acids and aldehydes [6, 13]. These modifications aim to increase the hydrophobicity of starch, replacing single bonds with cross-links, which prevents the swelling of granules and results in greater thermal and mechanical stability [16]. Starch cross-linking is promoted by bi- or polyfunctional reagents that react with the hydroxyl groups in polymer chains, forming covalent bonds. This process enhances TPS properties, such as increased resistance to extreme temperature and mechanical agitation, as well as greater stability in the presence of moisture.
Common TPS plasticizers include water, polyols such as glycerol and sorbitol and amide functionalized chemicals such as urea, formamide, and ethylene-bisformamide. Recently, the combination of different plasticizers was investigated as a means of overcoming or reducing problems such as the starch retrogradation, long-term plasticizer migration, and TPS embrittlement. Investigated combinations include formamide/urea,13 ethylene-bisformamide/sorbitol,14, 15 sorbitol/glycerol,16 and glycerol/maltose.17 The use of plasticizer mixtures may also open the possibility of tuning the water resistance and tensile properties of the material. In this study, we will concentrate on sorbitol and glycerol as plasticizers for TPS. Glycerol and sorbitol are both FDA-approved as food additives, and are plasticizers known to strongly interact with starch at the molecular scale by forming hydrogen bonds with the starch (i.e., amylose) macromolecules. The effect of glycerol and sorbitol on the glass transition temperature (Tg) of starch was thoroughly investigated by Lourdin et al.18 using DSC analysis. It was shown that both plasticizers can decrease the Tg of the TPS and that they are therefore effective plasticizers for starch. For example, the Tg of starch with 15% moisture and 30% plasticizer was decreased from around 87 to 25°C for glycerol and to 35°C for sorbitol. Similar observations were also reported by Yang et al.14 On the basis of DMA analysis, they reported that the Tg for the sorbitol-plasticized TPS was decreased to around 60°C, comparing with the value of 38°C for the glycerol plasticized TPS at the same weight content of 30%. One advantage of sorbitol during blend preparation is that it has a lower volatility; sorbitol has a melting point of 95°C compared to 18°C for glycerol. Figure 1 compares the reported vapor pressure of sorbitol19 and glycerol20 as a function of temperature. Above 200°C, the vapor pressure of glycerol increases dramatically following an exponential growth while the vapor pressure of sorbitol remains almost negligible. This is an advantage in terms of limiting plasticizer losses and improving the thermal stability of the material. The use of sorbitol is also expected to improve water resistance as well as tensile properties. Yang et al.14 reported that the equilibrium moisture content of sorbitol plasticized TPS was much lower than that of glycerol plasticized ones. The sorbitol plasticized TPS also exhibited a higher decomposition temperature. The stronger starch-sorbitol interaction was also believed to reduce water absorption and thus increase the TPS's water resistance. Vapor pressure of sorbitol and glycerol. Biodegradable bio-sourced plastics minimize environmental impact and increase plastic sustainability. Starch-based thermoplastic polymers are relatively cheap and are manufactured using an annually renewable source as raw material. Unfortunately, starch degrades before melting because it has a high number of intermolecular and intramolecular hydrogen bonds of hydroxyl groups. Thus it is not truly a thermoplastic polymer.1 This problem is partially overcome by the use of plasticizers (such as water, glycerol, sorbitol etc.). In the presence of plasticizers at high temperature (90-180 °C) and under shear, the starch crystalline structure dissolves and becomes suitable for use as an injection, extrusion or blow moulding material, similarly to most conventional synthetic thermoplastic polymers. This is the so-called thermoplastic starch (TPS).1, 2 Polyols such as glycerol,3-6 glycol,5, 6 sorbitol and sugars,7, 8 amide9, 10 and isosorbide11 are usually used as plasticizers. Unfortunately, TPS properties do not fulfil the requirements for applications such as packaging, because of great moisture sensitivity and rather weak mechanical properties despite a lot of effort on the study of the fittest plasticizer agent.12-14 To overcome these weaknesses, during the last decades, different strategies have been elaborated: (i) chemical starch modification has been carried out from the first half of the twentieth century15 until nowadays,16, 17 but it generally implies the use of solvents and processes that are not environmental friendly; (ii) the association of TPS with other biodegradable compounds to obtain compostable multiphase materials of starch/polymer blends,18-24 but the mechanical properties of the blends remain far below those of the main polymer matrix and the advantage of low cost is partially lost; (iii) addition of reinforcement fillers to the TPS matrix to make a composite with different types of fibres or microfibrils25-31 or silicates.32-36 In the last few years a lot of effort has been dedicated to studying filler addition, with a corresponding increase in research papers. Some examples of the bio-based reinforcements used in these composites are cellulose and nano cellulose.37, 38 However, most nanocomposites were obtained by the casting method limiting a possible industrial exploitation.39 On the other hand, when conventional melt processing methods were used, only a low amount of fillers were added, reaching in some cases great improvement in the mechanical properties.40 Generally, results show that incorporation of bio-based nano or micro reinforcements in TPS improves mechanical properties41 and the improvements are proportional to the filler loading.

ans_rerank: Glycerol acts as a plasticizer in the production of thermoplastic starch (TPS) by disrupting intermolecular hydrogen bonds between starch chains, which lowers the glass transition temperature (T<sub>g</sub>) and improves processability [1,2,5,6,12]. Its high hydrophilicity enables effective hydrogen bonding with starch hydroxyl groups, replacing starch-starch interactions and facilitating the gelatinization process to create an amorphous structure [1,2,4,5]. However, glycerol alone may lead to excessive hydrophilicity, low thermal stability, and plasticizer migration over time [1,7,9]. When combined with sorbitol, glycerol synergistically enhances mechanical properties (e.g., Young’s modulus) and reduces retrogradation while maintaining biocompatibility for biomedical applications [1,5,6,12]. Despite its limitations, glycerol remains widely used due to its low cost, non-toxicity, and high boiling point [3,7,8,14].

question: What is the 'lag phase' in the biodegradation of plastics in compost?
ground_truth: The lag phase is the initial period where no significant mineralization (CO2 evolution) occurs. During this time, microorganisms colonize the surface and secrete extracellular enzymes to begin fragmenting the polymer chain. Only after the molecular weight drops sufficiently to produce water-soluble intermediates does rapid assimilation and mineralization begin.

It should be also obvious that the environment is not a dumping ground for plastic waste, and no environmentally biodegradable polymer will be developed with the aim of throwing and dumping into the environment after use. However, the property of biodegradability can be beneficially used for managing plastic waste originating especially from specific sectors such as food packaging as a managed end-of-life cycle option in controlled industrial compost (i-compost) plants. Packaging is one of the biggest sectors both using plastics and generating waste. Lot of plastic food packaging based on polyolefins and PET lands up in composting plants when food items are discarded together with packaging. New i-compostable biodegradable polymers with fast biodegradation and suitable mechanical and gas-barrier properties as a substitute for polyolefins used presently would be a promising solution for MPs generated from packaging. This will also be advantageous for disposable items used for only a short period of time. This is in accord with the E.U. strategy for circular economy utilizing organic recycling of such polymers in compost plants. At present, ASTM D-6400 (Standard Specification for Labeling of Plastics Designed to be Aerobically Composted in Municipal or Industrial Facilities) and the test procedure described in ASTM 5338 is used for testing the composting capability of plastics. According to the method, the sample is labeled positive (compostable in industrial facilities) in the case it fulfills the combined requirements: 1) after 12 weeks, not more than 10% of fragments more than 2 mm in size should be left; and 2) 90% of the organic carbon must be converted to CO2 in 180 days (24 weeks). The problem is that real composting times in industrial compost plants are much shorter than the procedure allows. Most of these plants already distribute compost after 8-12 weeks. In some other compost plants, the time of composting is still shorter. This implies that the plastic with slow biodegradation in compost (biodegradation in compost not completed till the compost is ready in plants say in 8-12 weeks but which might be completed in 24 weeks) will also have the label of i-compostable biodegradation but will certainly be a source of MP as it will contain plastic fragments at the time of distribution. This is the present situation regarding several of the classified biodegradable polymers, one of which is PLA that is compostable but takes several weeks. The PBAT showed >90% conversion to CO2 after 80 days in mature compost at about 58 °C in a laboratory test in a batch process.[16] The biodegradation profile of PBAT in controlled compost is highly attractive, with a caution that the compost in which PBAT was mineralized should not go onto the fields after only 8 weeks. If compost is distributed after 12 weeks, then PBAT is one of the promising compostable polymers available today. Similar to those mentioned above, real field tests are always required to confirm the biodegradability and degradability profile. In general, in case the time of biodegradation of plastics in compost plants matches the duration of a compost cycle in such facilities, replacing polyolefins and PET in packaging and disposable items with i-compostable biodegradable polymers would be one of the significant steps forward. Therefore, there is a need to invest more research efforts in making i-compostable biodegradable polymers that work fast. Properly tested and precisely classified biodegradable polymers with complete biodegradation in a definite time matching to the application are surely an opportunity for stepping toward an MP-reduced environment. They can be especially of significant use in some specific scenarios. The first case is replacing nondegradable polyolefins with the appropriate biodegradable polymers for specific time-bound environmental applications, such as in agricultural fields as mulch film, slow release fertilizers, pesticides and water carriers, plantation pots and bags. The non-soil biodegradable polymers used for these applications stay in the environment and should be considered as intentional creation of MPs in the environment. Agricultural fields are gigantic, and the number of plastic products used for various agricultural applications are huge. It is not easy to recover plastics after use from such a huge area. Replacing polyolefins with agricultural soil-degradable, biodegradable polymers would eliminate the need to collect plastic fragments after use, and the plastic will not persist in the environment. There is a need to develop a series of agricultural soil-degradable biodegradable polymers with different physical properties and biodegradation profiles so that large number of applications can be covered.

Plastics represent 12.9% of the 258 million tons of municipal solid waste (MSW) generated in 2014 in the USA, from which only 9.5% was recovered (i.e., recycling and composting), the recycled plastics were mostly polyethylene and polyethylene terephthalate. Hence, most plastic waste (25.1 million tons) ended up accumulating in landfills, which is a major environmental concern [1]. Compostable polymers, like poly (lactic acid) (PLA), represent a promising way to divert plastic waste from landfills, replacing conventional polymers for some applications, especially for non-durable goods and single-use products like packaging, disposable plates and cutlery, and contaminated plastic waste (e.g., food packaging and agricultural mulch films) [2]. However, such benefit is only accomplished if PLA-based products reach the desired disposal system at their end of life. The ideal scenario is one in which these products/packaging would be collected and sent along with the organic wastes to commercial composting facilities. However, one of the main current challenges for PLA-based materials to be widely accepted in composting facilities at their end of life is that their biodegradation in composting is usually slower than that for other organic wastes [3]. In our previous work, we studied the impact of different nanoclays (e.g., organo-modified montmorillonite, OMMT, and its organo-modifier, methyl, tallow, bis-2-hydroxyethyl, quaternary ammonium, QAC) on the biodegradation rate of PLA bio-nanocomposites (BNCs) in different solid environments (i.e., compost and vermiculite), and on microbial attachment using a “mixed culture” extracted from the compost. It was found that the presence of OMMT seems to accelerate the initial phase of biodegradation, but not the final mineralization phase, and to promote microbial attachment in comparison to the pristine PLA under certain conditions [3]. Therefore, there is interest in knowing which specific microbial strains present in the compost can bind to PLA and preferentially biodegrade PLA and its BNCs, and whether they can be purposely used to accelerate the biodegradation mechanism. Some researchers have identified the microbial consortia present in the compost environment [[4], [5], [6], [7]], and others have reported the isolation and identification of several species capable of biodegrading PLA [[8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]], and other polymers [[16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24]] by 16 S rRNA sequence analysis. In this context, bioaugmentation (i.e., the addition of specific microbial strains) is a promising technique that can be studied and used to accelerate the biodegradation of compostable plastics, so that they biodegrade in comparable time frames with other organic wastes. Increasing the biodegradation rate of PLA should facilitate its disposal through composting since PLA-based products and organic materials could biodegrade in a similar period of time.

Composting is a controlled biological aerobic process that transforms organic waste into carbon dioxide (CO2), water (H2O), heat, minerals, biomass, and humus, all of which are beneficial for plant growth [54]. This transformation is driven by microorganisms that decompose organic matter into stable, nutrient-rich soil amendments. It is crucial to distinguish between compostable plastics and other biodegradable plastics, as this distinction has a significant impact on waste management and environmental impact. Compostable plastics, such as polylactic acid (PLA) and thermoplastic starch (TPS), are engineered to decompose under industrial composting conditions, typically within a few weeks to months. These conditions include specific temperature, humidity, and microbial activity levels that facilitate the rapid breakdown of these materials into carbon dioxide, water, and biomass without leaving toxic residues [98]. Biodegradable plastics refer to a broader category that includes materials capable of breaking down through natural processes into water, carbon dioxide, and biomass [121]. However, the rate and conditions under which this degradation occurs can vary widely. Some biodegradable plastics may require specific environments, such as high-temperature industrial composting facilities, to degrade effectively. Others may take years to break down in natural environments and may not fully degrade in landfill conditions, where oxygen levels are low. Compostable polymers, such as polylactic acid (PLA) and thermoplastic starch (TPS), are engineered with ester or glycosidic bonds that hydrolyze under industrial composting conditions (58-65 °C, high humidity, and microbial consortia). PLA, a polyester derived from corn starch, undergoes microbial enzymatic degradation (proteinases and lipases) to produce CO₂, water, and biomass. However, incomplete degradation leaves behind oligomers (lactic acid dimers), which exhibit persistence and toxicity in soil ecosystems, as evidenced by genotoxic effects on earthworms (Eisenia fetida) at concentrations > 5%. This aligns with findings that weathering of biodegradable plastics releases oligomers resembling persistent organic pollutants (POPs), raising concerns about bioaccumulation and ecosystem disruption [64]. The distinction between compostable and biodegradable plastics has significant implications for waste management and environmental sustainability. Compostable plastics, when disposed of correctly in composting facilities, can contribute to the production of nutrient-rich compost, enhancing soil quality and reducing reliance on chemical fertilizers. However, suppose compostable plastics are not separated correctly from non-compostable waste. In that case, they can contaminate recycling streams or fail to decompose properly in landfills, where conditions are not conducive to composting [146]. Moreover, not all biodegradable plastics can be treated in industrial composting facilities due to the potential release of harmful substances or the requirement for prolonged degradation times. This necessitates clear labeling and consumer education to ensure proper disposal and treatment of these materials. Mismanagement can lead to increased pollution and undermine the environmental benefits that these materials are intended to provide [31].

Biological waste treatments tailored for biodegradable plastics represent sophisticated end-of-life management strategies. These treatments can be implemented under aerobic conditions (with oxygen, such as composting) or anaerobic conditions (without oxygen, such as anaerobic digestion). Composting, which utilizes a diverse microbial community including fungi, bacteria, and actinomycetes, can occur at psychrophilic temperatures (below 35 °C for home composting) or thermophilic temperatures (50-60 °C for industrial composting) [11]. For example, kitchen scraps and garden waste are commonly composted in home settings, while large-scale operations might process municipal organic waste. This process reduces waste and produces valuable compost, rich in nutrients and beneficial for soil health. It can also be used in agriculture and landscaping. Similarly, anaerobic digestion, exclusively facilitated by bacteria, can be performed under mesophilic (below 35 °C) or thermophilic (50-60 °C) conditions. This method is often applied in wastewater treatment plants and livestock farms, where organic materials such as food waste, manure, and sewage sludge are digested [108]. The primary factor determining a bioplastic’s suitability for specific waste Management methods is its duration for complete degradation. International standards for biodegradability, such as those set by ISO and ASTM, define a Material as biodegradable if it fully decomposes within 56 days in aquatic environments or within two years in soil. However, these standards often rely on elevated temperatures that surpass typical conditions found in unmanaged natural environments, leading to a disparity between laboratory results and actual biodegradation in the real world. This highlights the importance of aligning biodegradation standards with actual environmental conditions when developing policies for managing plastic waste. Additionally, the design of plastic products must account for potential end-of-life scenarios, ensuring they align with the degradation timelines and processes of intended waste management systems. A cohesive strategy integrating policy, standards, and design is key to crafting practical and reliable solutions for bioplastic waste [101]. The study of biodegradation kinetics and carbon fate of bioplastics under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions offers valuable insights, but it also highlights critical limitations in their practical applications. While PHB and PHBV exhibit versatility by biodegrading under both conditions, PCL’s reliance on aerobic environments restricts its utility in anaerobic waste systems [99]. Integrating carbon balance analysis adds depth by tracking carbon sinks, such as gases, biomass, and soluble compounds; however, its complexity and resource demands may hinder scalability in industrial contexts. Additionally, the observed enhancement of mineralization rates with smaller particle sizes, though beneficial for assay duration, is impractical for real-world waste management, where uniform particle reduction is challenging and costly. Combining carbon balance with kinetic analysis provides a promising framework for testing and improving biodegradable materials, but the feasibility of implementing such rigorous methods at scale remains questionable. Addressing these challenges by focusing on scalable, realistic conditions and simplifying analytical methodologies will be critical to translating these findings into effective waste management solutions [99].

Based on the provided evidence, the 'lag phase' in plastic biodegradation within compost refers to the initial period where minimal biodegradation occurs, characterized by:  

1.  **Delayed onset of significant degradation**: It is the time before the active biodegradation phase begins, during which little to no mineralization (conversion to CO₂) is observed [5][6][10].  
2.  **Preparation period for degradation**: This phase involves the time required for water to penetrate the polymer matrix and for microorganisms to secrete enzymes that begin cleaving the polymer chains [8].  
3.  **Material-dependent duration**: The length of the lag phase varies significantly depending on the plastic material. For example:  
    *   Cellulose (a positive reference) exhibits a lag phase of about 10 days [5][6].  
    *   Natural fiber-polypropylene composites (PALF, banana, bamboo-PP) show a lag phase of about 30 days [5][6].  
    *   Neat PLA typically has a lag phase of around 20 days in compost [10][13].  
    *   PLA with additives like graphene (GRH) or nanoclays (OMMT) can exhibit altered lag phases, sometimes shorter due to factors like reduced initial molecular weight [10][13].  

This initial period is a critical part of the biodegradation curve (often sigmoidal), preceding the active "degradation phase" where the rate of mineralization increases significantly [5][6][8].

The main and combined abiotic and biotic mechanisms associated with polyesters degradation are chemical hydrolysis and enzymatic degradation. For natural polymers, like cellulose and starch, the biodegradation phase starts almost immediately, and the rate of biodegradation is high since depolymerization by extracellular enzymes and bioassimilation occurs quickly with no requirement for a conditioning lag phase. The lag phase, where the abiotic degradation (mainly chemical hydrolysis) mechanism is dominant over the biotic mechanism (enzymatic depolymerization), is assumed to occur due to the acclimatization of the microbial population to the environment and to the presence of an exogenous material such as synthetic polymers that are not readily assimilable by microorganisms. A significant drawback of using PLA as a biodegradable material is the slow rate of degradation when compared to other biodegradable materials. The biodegradation of PLA in a composting environment has two steps. In the first step, the high-molecular-weight PLA chains hydrolyze into low-molecular-weight oligomers. This step is catalyzed by temperature and moisture. The second step is the conversion of the oligomeric components into CO2, water, and humus by means of the action of microorganisms. Therefore, any factors that increase the hydrolysis tendency can promote the degradation of PLA. Other factors affecting the biodegradation of polymers are the molecular weight and the degree of crystallinity. Lower molecular weight PLA materials do show higher rates of enzymatic degradation due to the higher concentration of accessible chain-end groups. It is also known that the amorphous phase is easier to biodegrade compared to the crystalline phase.31, 32 Figure 3 shows the degradation patterns of a polycaprolactone (PCL) film. Waste breakdown and management methods Degradation and disposal methods diverge from recycling strategies, with their primary focus being the elimination of waste rather than the recovery of polymers or monomers for reintegration into the plastics production cycle. Conventional disposal techniques, including quaternary recycling with energy recovery and landfilling, are utilized for traditional plastics and non-biodegradable bioplastics [107]. However, biodegradable bioplastics present an alternative pathway: biodegradation. This process, sometimes referred to as organic recovery or organic recycling, encompasses methods such as industrial and home composting, anaerobic digestion, or biodegradation in agricultural contexts, with industrial composting being the most prevalent approach. The rate and extent of biodegradation are contingent upon various factors beyond the bioplastic’s chemical and microstructural properties. Key influences include the chosen end-of-life treatment method and a combination of biotic and abiotic factors [109]. Biotic factors refer to the composition and activity of the microbial community, whereas abiotic factors encompass environmental conditions such as temperature, oxygen levels, moisture content, and pH. The design and operation of composting or anaerobic digestion facilities, including parameters like aeration, mixing, and retention time, also play critical roles in determining biodegradation efficiency. Furthermore, regulatory frameworks and standards for compostability, such as those set by organizations like ASTM, ISO, or EN, guide the development and certification of biodegradable plastics, ensuring they meet specific criteria for degradation rates and environmental safety.
Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) has garnered interest due to its low environmental footprint and ability to replace conventional polymers and be disposed of in industrial composting environments. Although PLA is compostable when subjected to a suitable set of conditions, its broader acceptance in industrial composting facilities has been affected adversely due to longer degradation timeframes than the readily biodegradable organic waste fraction. PLA must be fully exposed to thermophilic conditions for prolonged periods to biodegrade, which has restricted its adoption and hindered its acceptance in industrial composting facilities, negating its home composting potential. Thus, enhancing PLA biodegradation is crucial to expand its acceptance. PLA's biodegradability is investigated in a compost matrix under mesophilic conditions at 37 °C for 180 days by biostimulating the compost environment with skim milk, gelatin, and ethyl lactate to enhance the different stages of PLA biodegradation. The evolved CO2, number average molecular weight (Mn), and crystallinity evolution are tracked. To achieve a Mn ≲ 10 kDa for PLA, the biodegradation rate is accelerated by 15% by adding skim milk, 25% by adding gelatin, and 22% by adding ethyl lactate. This work shows potential techniques to help biodegrade PLA in home composting setting by adding biostimulants. Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is a well-known biodegradable thermoplastic polymer and has garnered a lot of interest due to its ability to exhibit reasonable properties as compared to fossil-based conventional polymers.[1] In addition, PLA has turned out to be a key player leading the global bioplastic segment as per the market research conducted by nova-Institute, which estimates an increase in bioplastic production from 2.18 million tonnes in 2023 to 7.43 million tonnes in 2028.[2] Due to its biodegradable nature, PLA can be rerouted to composting facilities instead of contributing to plastic waste in landfills.[3] PLA is known to undergo chemical hydrolytic degradation during composting, significantly reducing its molecular weight.[4] This reduction in molecular weight precedes the assimilation by microorganisms and final mineralization to CO2. However, it is difficult to degrade PLA at lower temperatures (e.g., backyard or home composting environments - mostly mesophilic conditions) because of its dependence on higher temperatures (≳60 °C) to undergo chemical hydrolysis. Additionally, PLA degradation in natural environments (usually associated with lower temperatures) is slow due to the sparse distribution of PLA-degrading microbes compared with other more aggressive thermophilic degradable environments such as industrial composting.[5, 6] A detailed discussion about the compostability and biodegradation of PLA can be found elsewhere.[7, 8]

Based **only** on the provided context evidence, the 'lag phase' in the biodegradation of plastics in compost is:

1.  **A period at the start of biodegradation** where little to no significant mineralization (e.g., CO₂ evolution) occurs. It is often observed as the initial flat part of a sigmoid-shaped biodegradation curve before the main biodegradation phase begins [1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11].

2.  **It corresponds to the time required** for abiotic and biotic preparatory processes. These include:
    *   Water penetration into the polymer matrix [1, 2].
    *   Abiotic chemical hydrolysis (dominant mechanism for synthetic polyesters like PLA), which cleaves polymer chains into shorter, more accessible fragments [2, 12, 13].
    *   Microbial acclimatization to the environment and the presence of the exogenous polymer material [2].
    *   The build-up and action of microbial biofilms secreting extracellular enzymes capable of depolymerizing the polymer chains [1, 2].

3.  **Its duration varies significantly depending on the polymer material:**
    *   Readily biodegradable natural polymers like cellulose, starch, and skim milk typically show **no** or a **very short/negligible lag phase** (<10 days for cellulose) because enzymatic depolymerization and bioassimilation start almost immediately [2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 11].
    *   Synthetic biodegradable polymers like PLA exhibit a **distinct lag phase** (≈20 days cited for PLA in compost [7]; longer under mesophilic conditions [15]). This is due to the time needed for hydrolytic chain scission to reduce molecular weight sufficiently for enzymatic attack [2, 7, 12, 13, 15].
    *   Natural fiber composites with non-biodegradable matrices (e.g., natural fiber-PP composites) also show a **longer lag phase** (30 days cited) compared to the cellulose reference (10 days) [5, 6].

4.  **Factors influencing the lag phase duration** include polymer type, molecular weight (lower Mₙ can shorten the lag phase for PLA [7]), crystallinity (hydrolysis slower in crystalline regions [2]), and the presence of additives or blends (e.g., GRH can shorten the PLA lag phase at 1% loading but delay it at 0.1% [7]; compatibilization can alter lag phase compared to physical blends [7, 8]).

First, PHAs are very difficult to convert into packages with conventional plastic processing techniques. In addition to their low viscosity and melt strength, PHA thermal degradation occurs upon melting;5 this depresses the final structural and mechanical properties of the plastic part or package. In this respect, polyhydroxy(butyrate-co-valerate) (PHBV) is a microbial copolyester showing lower melting temperatures (Tm's) than polyhydroxybutyrate. Slow crystallization is a strong drawback in applications such as injection molding, as it significantly extends the cycle time. IntroductionPoly (hydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) is one type of polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) that can be produced by bacteria from agricultural raw materials. The chemical structures of several PHAs are shown in Fig. 1. The biobased PHBV can be processed to form a variety of useful products and has attracted the attention of academia and industry due to its good biodegradability, biocompatibility and thermoplasticity. Compared with poly (hydroxybutyrate) (PHB), PHBV has good toughness and ease of processing. However, its poor thermal stability, low elongation at break, slow crystallization rate and high degree of crystallinity still remain problematic. Therefore, it has been subject to chemical and physical modifications.In the chemical modifications, the HV content of PHBV can be adjusted by controlling the amount of propanoic acid during the biosynthesis process [1], [2], [3]. Other chemical methods, such as grafting and reactive blending have also been used to modify its properties [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10]. It was found that the melting temperature of PHBV decreased with increase of HV content when the total molar content of HV was less than 28%, but increased when the molar content of HV was more than 28% [11]. The toughness of PHBV was also affected by the HV content in the molecular chains. It could vary from rigid to flexible with change of HV content, for example, it could behave like polyethylene, polypropylene and polyvinylchloride when the HV content is high, medium and low, respectively [12].Obviously, the modification of PHBV should not destroy its biodegradability, which is its most important advantage, regardless of the aims of modification. The massive use of petroleum-based polymers has resulted in environmental concerns derived not only from waste management issues, but also from their low degradation rates. As a result, there is a growing interest in the development of renewable and biodegradable materials to partially replace the oil-based ones. Alternatives such as polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) have sparked great interest due to their biodegradable, biocompatible and renewable features. PHAs can be produced in different ways, i.e., chemically or biologically through fermentation from feedstock. This family comprises mainly the homopolymer, polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), which has been extensively studied since it presents mechanical properties similar to those of conventional petroleum-based polymers, relatively good thermal properties and high stiffness due to its high crystallinity degree.1 However, although high crystallinity is useful for some applications, the high stiffness limits its usage in other commercial applications. Moreover, another drawback of this polymer is its low thermal stability, making it unstable during melt processing and also limiting its applicability.2 Several strategies have been developed to overcome these drawbacks, including blending with other polymers, such as poly (vinyl alcohol) (PVA),3 polypropylene glycol (PPG),4 and poly-ε-caprolactone (PCL)5 or modification of the homopolymer by incorporation of different monomer types during the fermentation process. Copolymerization with hydroxyvalerate (HV) results in poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) which has improved mechanical and thermal properties, since incorporation of HV reduces the crystallinity, thus decreasing stiffness and brittleness, and also reducing the melting point without decreasing the thermal stability of the material, although greater improvements in this parameter are still needed.1, 6 However, reduction in crystallinity is widely known to affect the barrier properties of materials to low molecular weight substances, which is a key property of materials intended to be used in packaging applications.7, 8 Because of that, PHBV copolymers still present several drawbacks including high cost, relative brittleness and thermal instability, which had hampered the widespread usage of this family of polymers. As a strategy to improve biopolymer performance, many studies have focussed on the development of composites and, especially, nanocomposites using a variety of fillers. Natural fibres such as kenaf fibres have been incorporated into PHBV matrix achieving significant improvements in mechanical properties.9 Furthermore, the addition of cellulose nanowhiskers resulted in significant improvements in thermal, mechanical and barrier properties, as well as in thermal stability.1 Apart from natural organic fillers, lamellar inorganic reinforcing fillers, including nanoclays or double layered hydroxides, among others, have been widely studied, giving rise to materials with improved mechanical, barrier and thermal stability properties.10-13 It is noteworthy that the improved performance of nanocomposites is achieved, not only by using the inherent properties of the nanofiller, but more importantly by optimizing the dispersion, interface chemistry and nanoscale morphology.14 Great interest has recently arisen about carbonaceous nanofillers such as carbon nanotubes and carbon nanosheets due to their excellent mechanical, thermal, and electrical properties. Several works have been published about the effect of carbon nanotubes in polymer matrices,15-19 and more specifically in PHBV matrix.20-24 Graphene, another carbon-filler material which is the elementary structure of graphite, composed of one atomic thick layer of sp2-bonded carbon atoms arranged in a honey comb structure, has emerged in last years. The interest in this specific nanofiller derives not only from its excellent mechanical strength, electrical and thermal conductivity, but also from its high surface area and, thus, high barrier effect on polymer matrices.25, 26 Therefore, its inherent physical properties along with its lamellar structure have made it excellent reinforcing nanofiller for polymer and biopolymer nanocomposites.27 It has been, for instance used as filler in many polymer matrices such as poly (lactic acid) (PLA),26, 28 PVA,29 polyethylene (PE)30 and polystyrene (PS)31 among others, improving their barrier, mechanical and electrical properties. Recent works have also incorporated low contents of graphene sheets in PHBV matrices through solution casting methods improving, in the same way, the final properties of the obtained materials.6, 32 The ball milling technique is an alternative and efficient method to produce novel composites with high performances since during the milling “intimate mixing” is promoted.17, 33 It is considered a novel compounding method and it is based in a high-energy grinding technique, able to induce several mechano-chemical changes in the materials. This technique has been previously used in the development of clay-based and carbon nanotubes-based nanocomposites.17, 34-36 Moreover, graphene-based nanocomposites have also been synthesized by ball milling since the high energy milling induces graphite delamination, thus improving the final properties of the obtained materials.37 An effective grafting of PS matrix onto the surface of graphene sheets using ball milling was reported. With this aim, graphite nanoplatelets were used as initial material, corroborating the effectiveness of its mechano-chemical characteristic of this technique.38 To the best of our knowledge, the high-energy ball milling technique has not been used up to date to develop PHBV-graphene nanocomposites. Because of that, the aim of this work was to evaluate the ball milling technique capacity for the production of PHBV-graphene nanocomposites and the study of the final properties of the so-obtained materials. It has been previously reported that when graphene is functionalized, single-sheet graphene is expected to serve as nanofiller in nanocomposites applications, as functional sites will favor interactions with the matrix.39 Because of that, a derivative graphene material such as functionalized graphene sheets (FGS) was used attempting to optimize the filler-matrix compatibilization. This paper is the first part of a wide work in which we aimed to prepare novel PHVB-graphene nanocomposites using mechanical energy. We analysed morphological organization, through SEM and TEM analysis. We conducted a detailed study of behavior in the molten state of PHVB as function of filler content, either in isothermal or in non-isothermal conditions. We also analyzed the degradation behavior of PHVB, either in inert atmosphere or in air, depending on graphene content.
Poly(hydroxybutyrate-co-valerate) (PHBV) is a biodegradable, biocompostable polyester along with poly(lactic acid) and polyglycolide. This polymer is used in biomedical applications, but has not been widely used in the packaging industry. This is because it has a few shortcomings, of which low thermal stability and brittleness are the most disturbing. The brittleness is caused by its high degree of crystallinity [1], and this property limits its use in most packaging applications. To overcome these shortcomings, PHBV can be blended with other rubbery biodegradable polymers to improve its toughness without compromising its biodegradability [2]. The usual objective for preparing a blend of two or more polymers is not to significantly change the properties of the components, but to capitalize on the maximum possible performance of the blend. In this case, the choice of polymer to blend with PHBV should only be to overcome the brittleness and improve the thermal stability. One such a polymer is poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) [3]. PCL belongs to the category of biocompatible, biodegradable and nontoxic polyesters with excellent mechanical strength. It is a synthetic semicrystalline polyester, also considered as an interesting blend component due to its good ductility, thermal resistance and moderate degree of crystallinity [4-6]. It has a low glass transition temperature of about −60 °C, existing always in a rubbery state at room temperature, and a melting temperature of 60 °C. It has a very good toughness and thermal stability. The only limiting factor for using this polymer individually for many applications is its low melting temperature [4, 7]. To overcome this, it may be blended with another biopolymer which has a higher melting temperature. A blend of PHBV and PCL should produce a balanced final product with the toughness and thermal stability of PHBV being improved by the presence of PCL, and the disadvantage of PCL’s low melting temperature being improved. Although the melting temperature of PCL is significantly lower than that of PHBV, PCL does not degrade at lower temperatures and it can therefore be processed at temperatures well above its melting temperature [8, 9].

Chitosan PHB blend acts as an ideal matrix in drug delivery applications. The controlled drug delivery is possible as PHB/chitosan blend possesses a porous texture due to cross-linking [116]. The mix of PHA/PHB is used in food packing and medical implantation as it has better mechanical properties [117]. On blending of PHB with PEG (polyethylene glycol), the increase in the hydrophilic property of PHB is reported [118]. For the safety from bacterial infections post-operations, the micro- and nanospheres of PHB with PEG loaded with antibiotics are used. PEG/PHB blends promoted the growth of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs). The presence of different-sized pores leads to MSCs growth with a slow rate of differentiation [119]. FDA has approved the use of PHB/PEG films for tissue engineering. Polyhydroxybutyrate and poly-ε-caprolactone (PHB/PCL) are used to manufacture fibrous membranes by the electrospinning method. Load-bearing biodegradable biocompatible materials are always needed for medical applications to serve mainly as osteoconductive implants [[1], [2], [3], [4]]. In many cases, the bone fracture healing is currently supported by fixations using plates, nails, wires and screws to join the broken bone parts together to reach a mechanically suitable situation. These metallurgical implants are usually non-degradable with high modulus materials made from titanium, stainless steel or cobalt chromium, which remain in the human body and must be removed in an additional surgery after healing. They may cause stress shielding accompanied by bone resorption and implant loosening due to high modulus implants. Therefore, the goal is to develop new materials dissolving within the body and in the same time supporting the healing process in a reliable and sustainable way. Magnesium (Mg)-based implants are appropriate for such applications where short or medium period for bone healing is necessary [2,[5], [6], [7]]. Mg-based screws can be used with equal operative techniques and handling as conventional metal screws made of titanium, although magnesium alloys are generally less stiff than titanium [8,9]. Mg implants were tested for orthopedic applications [3,10, 11]. In vivo, pure Mg [[12], [13], [14], [15]] and its alloys up to approximately 10 % (Ca) [16,17], (Al) [18,19], (Zn) [20], (Li) [21], and rare earth elements or zirconium [15,21,22] have already been tested. Complete degradation of MgYREZr (Mg-Yitrium-Rare Earth-Zirconium) implants in rabbits took about one year [9]. Another MgYREZr alloy (trade name MAGNEZIX®) compression screws are the world’s first approved/CE-certified magnesium-based implants designed for biodegradable osteosyntheses applications in humans which have already been on the market for two years and used in surgery [23]. The processing route of Mg alloys for orthopedic implants have been the subject of several works. Implants based on extrusion of high strength Mg-alloy powders are introduced to the market [[5],6]. In addition, more cost-effective powder metallurgy methods such as Metal Injection Molding and Additive Manufacturing in combination with sintering are proposed [24]. Recently, powder injection molding of Mg-Ca alloys was tested for mass production of near net shape parts of small size and with complex shapes. An ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of up to 141 MPa with an elongation to rupture (El) of 7% and a Young’s modulus of 38 GPa were achieved [6]. The processing route of compression screws MAGNEZIX includes powder metallurgy and extrusion processes. After the final extrusion process, a yield strength YS > 260 MPa, UTS > 290 MPa and El >8% with a Modulus of elasticity (E) of 45 GPa were achieved [23]. Sintered Mg-Nd-Gd-Zr-Zn-alloy powder (EZK400) materials indicated a higher degradation rate than the as- cast ones [24]. High-purity magnesium (HP Mg) screws were fabricated by rolling and implanted in vivo in fixations of rabbit femoral intracondylar fracture. They showed a uniform degradation morphology, a sufficient bending force and an enhanced fracture healing with good osseointegration in the area surrounding the screws [25].

Stress corrosion cracking (SCC) can also occur due to the combined effect of corrosion in SBF and the applied tensile load and result in sudden catastrophic failure of the implant at loads well below the yield strength [[26], [27], [28], [29], [30]]. Conventional metallic implants such as Ti or stainless steel are reported to fail prematurely by catastrophic SCC fracture in spite of their good corrosion resistance in the body [31,32]. Hence, it can be expected that Mg alloys with rapid corrosion and predisposition to pitting in chloride rich environments [20] would be highly susceptible to SCC with the roots of corrosion pits acting as initiation spots for crack growth [20,26,27]. Hence, there is an imminent danger of implant failure before bone union that results in inflammation, pain and revision surgery in case of Mg based biodegradable implant materials.
Biodegradable polymers are becoming more popular as implant materials in orthopedics. One of these popular orthopedic implants is biodegradable fixation screws which have been utilized for the fixation of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) grafts to secure the graft in the femur and tibia [1]. To overcome some of the potential problems attributed to metallic interference screws, the biodegradable screws were generated. Some of these problems include the necessity of a secondary surgery as well as distorting the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Moreover, the metal screws can lacerate the graft and it can also hinder future reconstructions [2]. On the other hand, the biodegradable screws may possess some adverse features too. For instance, they may be broken during the insertion or may induce some inflammatory reactions. Most importantly, the current biodegradable screws suffer this feature to promote the bone ingrowth and subsequently leaving voids in the tissue once the screws have been fully degraded. Although these polymers do not have sufficient mechanical characteristics for ACL fixation screw applications on their own [3], a vast variety of these biodegradable polymers such as polylacticacid (PLA), polyglycolicacid (PGA) and polycaprolactone (PCL) have been vastly used in the medical device field including ACL reconstruction screws. Polylacticacid (PLA) is a well-known linear aliphatic polyester with a glass transition temperature of 45-55 °C. It is produced from l-lactide and d-lactide enantiomers in which the ratio of l to d-enantiomers determines the crystallinity of polymer structure [4]. The PLA has proper mechanical and biological properties, making it desirable for biodegradable bone fixation uses, such as ACL fixation, artificial cartilage and pharmaceutical devices [5], [6]. However, PLA suffers a low toughness, leading to a highly brittle material at ambient condition. It possesses a high strength and stiffness. For instance, the ACL screws comprised of biodegradable polymers not only should have a good initial strength and stiffness, but also should have a suitable ductility to avoid brittle fracture during application. In this regard, a feasible strategy to decrease the brittleness of PLA is blending it with polycaprolactone (PCL), without using a commercially adverse copolymerization method [7]. PCL is also a biodegradable semicrystalline polyester with melting point and glass transition temperature of 55-65 °C and − 60 °C, respectively. PCL possesses high toughness because of its chain flexibility. Thus, it can give a toughness feature when blended with PLA matrix. Therefore, blending these polymers can produce a new biodegradable material with well-balanced properties. In our previous study [8], the PDLLA/PCL blends and its morphological and mechanical characteristics were evaluated.

Comparing to the conventional metal interference screw, the bioabsorbable interference screw avoids the screw removal and replaces the bone after degradation [15]. Previously, many researches were conducted to investigate the degradation process of bioabsorbable interference screw with different materials including PGA, PLA, composite of PGA/PLA, Poly-l-lactide acid (PLLA), etc. [[11], [12], [13],[16], [17], [18], [19]] and it was noted that the degradation rate of screw results from the design, dimension of the screw, the material used and the environment of implantation [20]. Walton [11] conducted a long-term in vivo degradation in sheep's bone to investigate the interference screw made of PLLA. However, the research reported that although PLLA was a satisfactory bioabsorbable material in clinical field, the poor ability of replacement of the bone made this material not an ideal implant in bone reconstruction. Barber [12] evaluated the in vivo degradation of bioabsorbable interference screw made of poly-elevo (96%)/dextro (4%)- elactide/β-tricalcium phosphate with the use of computed tomography (CT) scanning. It was found that the interference screw with this kind of material could be degraded completely in 4 years after implantation and foundβ-tricalcium phosphate has a good ability in osteoconduction. Alex [2] compared the degradation process over a period of 180 days of two bioabsorbable interference screws with different composite polymer (PLDL poly(L,DLLactic acid) v.s. composite PLDL + 30 wt%β-TCP) . The composite material (PLDL +TCP) showed higher degradation rate which indicated that the bioactive ceramic TCP enhanced the performance of screw in the degradation process. Landes [21] compare the degradation rate of poly(70L-lactide-co-30DL-lactide) (P(L/DL)LA) and poly(85L-lactide-co-15-glycolide) (PLGA) copolymer. The results showed the latter material had a faster degradation rate than the former one. However, rare literature introduced the in vitro degradation kinetics of interference screw made of composite PLGA/β-TCP. Although bioabsorbable interference screws show superiority to the metal interference screw in repairing the bone, the weakness in strength made bioabsorbable material has a risk of screw fracture during insertion [22]. The study on the mechanical property is also essential to evaluate the performance of bioabsorbable interference screws apart from degradation rate. When the screws are inserted into the bone tunnel, the interference between the bone tunnel and the wrench may lead to large shear and bending forces acting on the implant core, which causing the failure to the screw. The factors affecting the resistance of screw to breakage included the materials used and the screw design. Wendell [23] evaluated the mechanical property of four commercial interference screws with different designs but found no significant difference in terms of in yield load, stiffness, or maximum failure load. Weiler [24] tested on six different biodegradable interference screws by measuring the pull-out force and torque at failure. The results indicated that the fixation rigidity of the screw had relationship between the design and the torque at failure depended on the drive design. Alex [2] investigated the mechanical strength of the biodegradable screws with different composites and geometries. They also conducted Finite Element Analysis (FEA) to optimal the geometry of the screw. The results presented that the PLDL with 9 holes and PLDL+TCP models had better mechanical strength and degradation time. The main purpose of this research was to evaluate the effects of thread design on the mechanical properties of interference screw and conduct an in vitro degradation for the interference screw composited of PLGA and β-TCP. In the first stage, the mechanical properties of three interference screws with different screw thread designs were evaluated via the maximum insertion torque and pullout force by the virtue of FEM. Then, the interference screw with the best mechanical performance was used as the sample to be tested in an in vitro degradation experiment.

In terms of biodegradable materials for temporary implants, PLA/Mg composites have been developed in the last few years as new bioabsorbable biomaterials for several biomedical applications. These applications include dental [1], vascular stent [2], skin regeneration [3], bone repair [4], orthopedic [5] and tissue engineering [6]. Magnesium (Mg) is the fourth most abundant element in the human body, is essential in metabolism and is necessary in more than 300 biochemical reactions in the body [7]. Despite these benefits, before proposing Mg as a suitable temporary implant material, its degradation rate should be properly controlled, as Mg is one of the most reactive structural materials [8]. Several alloys and composites have been developed to control the degradation rate of Mg since uncontrolled degradation could result in loss of mechanical integrity, metal contamination in the body and intolerable hydrogen evolution by tissue [9]. A composite that combines Mg particles in a biopolymeric matrix, such as polylactic acid (PLA), could present similar properties to Mg but with a controlled degradation ratio. Additionally, PLA is a biocompatible and biodegradable polymeric biomaterial, approved by the FDA [10]. Nowadays, there are certain types of PLA polymer implants on the market, such as spinal implants, intramedullary plugs, artificial cartilage frames, screws, plates, meshes, tissue anchors, etc., offered by several companies [11]. PLA/Mg composites have been widely reported in the literature [12]. With regards to the neat polymer, Mg enhances its mechanical properties, particularly the compressive strength, and stiffness with a 15-30 vol% Mg loading [4]. The degradation of these composites in vitro has also been studied by several authors in several simulated media [13]. In PBS PLA/Mg experienced significantly higher weight loss compared to PLA scaffolds, and this weight loss increased proportionally with the addition of Mg. However, this degradation increase is also correlated with a trend towards higher alkalinity [14]. Conversely, in Simulated Body Fluid (SBF), it is revealed that PLA/Mg composites could effectively degrade in the medium, and the incorporation of Mg does not compromise the pH for 28 days [15]. The biological behaviour of PLA/Mg composites has been tested in vitro with several cellular lines such as pre-osteoblast cells [16], fibroblasts [3], [5], epithelial cells [14] and osteoblasts [17]. Additionally, PLA/Mg has been tested in vivo [18] showing that composites with a 10 % Mg loading exhibited optimal osteogenic properties, whereas a 20 % Mg composite group showed angiogenic effects and promising osteoinduction properties.

PLA is a hydrophobic aliphatic polyester derived from renewable resources (e.g., corns and rice), thus the production of which can well match the concept of “low-carbon economy” unlike those petroleum-based polymers. Depending on different isomers used for polymerization, four types of materials can be obtained - poly (D-lactic acid) (PDLA), poly (L-lactic acid) (PLLA), poly (D,L-lactic acid) (PDLLA) and meso-PLA, among which PDLA and PLLA are the most widely used ones. Either PLA or its degradation products is nontoxic and biocompatible, thus making it a promising candidate for biomedical applications including orthopedic regenerative engineering. Furthermore, the ease of processing makes PLA capable of well adapting to various clinical cases via different techniques, like film-casting, electrospinning, thermal forming, phase separation, and so forth.42, 43 In the past few decades, the incorporation of PLA membranes on biodegradable Mg implant surfaces have been intensively studied to slow down the dissolution of Mg substrates at early stage, in order to meet the balance of bone regeneration and implant resorption.
