Bone is a part of the body that functions as a body frame that provides attachment to muscles and organs in a person’s body. There are to methods for restoring broken bones, external bone fixation and internal bone fixation. External bone fixation is a method with a device placed outside the skin to stabilize bone fragments using pins that are connected to one another with an outer frame or rigid bars. Internal bone fixation is a method that aims to improve stability and encourage bone healing in a functional position. In the process of connecting the bones, there is stress shielding which causes pain to the patient. Stress shielding analysis carried out in the process of connecting bones using stainless steel and titanium as a comparison material of the use of magnesium for screws and plates in the process of bone fixation. Magnesium is also known as a biodegradable material. The analysis of static loading shows that bones with stainless steel plate and screws have a greater maximum von mises stress value than bone with titanium plate and screws, whereas bones with titanium plate and screws have a greater maximum von mises stress value than bone with magnesium plate and screws. The stress shielding calculation results show that the bone with titanium plate and screws have a value of 1.98, the bone with stainless steel plate and screws have a value of 3.82, the bone with Magnesium plate and screws have a value of 1.52. The Magnesium is a potential material for replacing Titanium and Stainless Steel as raw material of plate and screw in a internal bone fixation due to the low stress shielding.
Surgeons often focus on residual volume ratio of magnesium-based alloy after implantation at specific time points due to concerns about the reliability of early fixation. For the same magnesium-based material for different applications, previous literature-based analyses have suggested that the implant location has little impact on its degradation rate in the field of orthopedics,15 thus the surface area to volume ratio are rightly considered a determinant of the residual volume at specific time points. However, considering the dynamic changes in volume and surface area during the degradation process in vivo, as well as the active regulation and transportation of tissues around the implants, when applied to different devices, residual volume cannot be accurately predicted solely by considering the differences in surface area and volume parameters before implantation based on previous degradation data of the same material.15 How and to what degree the surface-area-to volume ratio differences in various implants can affect the degradation behavior in vivo remains incompletely clear so far. Recent evidence suggested that the therapeutic effect of Mg2+ shows a significant concentration- and stage-dependent behavior.19 For example, Mg2+ in the culture medium with concentration higher than 0.5 × 10−3M could act as a Ca2+ antagonist and inhibit the production of collagen and other raw materials so that impaired the bone biomineralization degree.20 In another report, Qiao et al.21 found that continued exposure of Mg2+ lead to the excessive osteoclastogenesis and bone destruction due to the overactivation of NF-κB signaling in macrophages. However, due to limitations such as difficulty in real-time tracking of degradation rate in vivo,22 it is difficult to quantify the relationship between the in vivo degradation performance and the osteogenic effect of Mg. Based on this, this experiment further aims to examine whether the difference in degradation rate of HP magnesium with gradient of surface area-to-volume ratio is sufficient to cause changes in the osteogenic effect of HP magnesium rods, then quantify the differences. This current study directly compares the performance of four different designs of HP magnesium bone defect implants in vitro and in rat femoral condylar defects, with the intention of identifying the effect of surface area-to-volume ratio on the degradation behavior and in vivo biological effects. The use of different number of grooves to set the group is to simulate the effect of different number of threads of bone screws in clinical application. Ultimately, the aim of this work is to facilitate the clinical promotion of well-established magnesium-based materials and the screening and improvement of newly developed materials and processing techniques for future investigators.
Biodegradable materials based on magnesium alloys have a huge potential for bone fracture fixation devices due to their adequate mechanical properties and biocompatibility. However, their fast degradation and the consequent liberation of hydrogen gas at the initial stages of implantation is the major limitation for their use. In this study, the AZ91D magnesium alloy was surface treated by an environment-friendly, nontoxic, and low-cost anodizing process and the early in vivo response was studied in a rat transcortical model. Adequate maturation of woven bone around implants-detected at day 7 post implantation-to lamellar bone was observed from day 15. Lamellar bone after 15 and 30 days of implantation presented similar volume, mineralization pattern, mineral to protein content, and estimated bone maturity between anodized AZ91D and polylactic acid (control) implants. Thus, anodizing of AZ91D in the conditions stated here induced an adequate short-term in vivo response, which postulates their use as potential biodegradable fracture fixation devices for bone healing. Bone fractures are commonly treated by the use of metallic devices, such as screws and plates, to stabilize the bone and allow their correct healing. Bone is a highly dynamic and diverse living tissue. In our bodies, bone tissue exists in compact (cortical bone) or trabecular (cancellous bone) arrangements, varying in mechanical strength and modulus. While cortical bone presents a compressive strength of 130-225 MPa and a Young's modulus of 17-20 GPa, trabecular bone has a strength of 5-10 MPa and a modulus of 50-100 MPa [1, 2]. Bone extracellular matrix is comprised of approximately 30 wt% non-mineralized organic component (collagen) and 60 wt% mineralized inorganic component (apatite mineralites) [1]. These two components are organized as a nanocomposite, where the hydroxyapatite (HA) crystals are embedded into the collagen fibers, increasing its compressive strength and toughness. Despite its high strength, bone is susceptible to fractures caused by traumas; the risk of which increases in elderly people, who are more susceptible to developing osteoporosis [3]. Risk factors for fractures in younger people include cancer, obesity, and sedentary lifestyles [4-6]. To treat these fractures, metal plates and screws are widely used clinically [7], as they provide strong stability to the healing bone. However, they also present some disadvantages. Metal implants are not biodegradable, which may necessitate the removal of the implant in a second surgery after bone healing, not only increasing the recovery time of the patient but also the possibility of surgical site infections and complications [8, 9]. Moreover, as these implants are usually made of stainless steel, titanium, or its alloys, there is a mismatch in the mechanical properties of metal implants and human bone. This mismatch can result in stress shielding, which can promote bone resorption and implant loosening [10, 11]. Due to these disadvantages, alternatives to metal plates such as degradable alloys and composites are attracting attention due to their high versatility. Some of these materials can be tailored to mimic bone composition and/or mechanical properties, increasing their compatibility and reducing the risks of stress shielding. Magnesium and magnesium alloy based implants have been used in tissue engineering [12]. Thanks to their similar mechanical properties to bone and good biocompatibility and biodegradability, these alloys have been studied for applications in orthopedic surgery [13-15]. Such implants degrade via surface erosion, and a slow erosion rate of between 0.2 and 0.5 mm/year has been suggested as the ideal rate for matching bone healing [16]. Another advantage is that the release of Mg2+ can be beneficial for regulating inflammatory reactions and improving angiogenesis [17]. However, pure magnesium is rarely used as the rapid corrosion can generate an accumulation of hydrogen, lowering the pH in the local environment, which can be harmful for the surrounding tissues. Moreover, the hydrogen accumulation can affect the mechanical properties of the implant, requiring that implants be made with alloys of magnesium and rare-earth elements or other metals [18-20].

Traditionally, permanent metallic materials have been used in orthopaedic applications due to their high strength and inert nature. However, problems, such as stress shielding, implant migration or loosening and the risks associated with revision surgery have led to the development of implants based on bioresorbable polymers [1]. Upon in vivo implantation these polymers degrade via hydrolytic chain scission, as injured tissue regenerates, and are excreted from the body via metabolic pathways. Members of the poly (α-hydroxy acid) family, such as polyglycolide (PGA), polylactide (PLA) and their related copolymers have been used in various biomedical applications including internal sutures, orthopaedic screws and scaffolds, drug delivery and tissue engineering [2]. PLA exists in two enantiomeric forms, D and L. For biomedical applications, the most commonly used forms are Poly(l-lactide) (PLLA) and Poly(d,l-lactide) PDLLA. PLLA is a semi-crystalline polymer with high mechanical strength, rendering it a suitable material for load bearing applications. However, its degradation time is slow with total resorption time in excess of 5 years [[2], [3], [4], [5], [6]]. PDLLA is more suited to non-load bearing applications, such as drug delivery, due to its amorphous nature and fast degradation time [[2], [3], [4], [5], [6]]. PGA, on the other hand, is highly crystalline with high mechanical strength, however, due to its hydrophilic nature its degradation is rapid, being reported as losing strength after one or two months and complete resorption after 6-12 months [2,3,6]. The ability to tailor polymers to meet required mechanical and/or degradation properties has made them an attractive alternative to their metallic counterparts. The ideal bioresorbable polymer would maintain sufficient mechanical strength during tissue healing (approximately 8-12 weeks depending on the application) [5], then begin to lose mass to allow new tissue to grow, eventually replacing the implanted polymer. One of the most significant challenges in the research of bioresorbable polymers is the development of this type of degradation profile. Copolymerisation of PLA and PGA, forming Poly(l-lactide-co-glycolide) (PLLGA) and Poly(d,l-lactide-co-glycolide) (PDLLGA), has become increasingly popular for preparation of bone substitute constructs since the use of different copolymer ratios allows greater control of mechanical and physicochemical properties, and degradation rates.

Magnesium (Mg) and its alloys are representative materials in the fields of engineering and biomedical applications owing to their low density and superior biocompatibility [1-4]. For a few years, Mg-based products have been offered in the market owing to the tireless work of researchers [5-7]. Specially, many implants, such as vascular stents and screws, have been successfully fabricated from Mg alloys [8-11]. Numerous in vitro and in vivo trials promote Mg implants conduct or is going to conduct clinical studies. At present, Mg alloys are mainly produced by casting and plastic deformation process. The forming processes play a key role in mechanical properties of Mg alloys [12]. As for biodegradable metals, mechanical requirements should be met: tensile strength >300 MPa, and elongation >15% [13]. According to previous researches, the tensile strength of cast and deformed Mg alloys is lower than 300 MPa [14]. This low strength indicates that it is difficult to apply biodegradable Mg alloys to load-bearing parts. Moreover, strength of biodegradable Mg alloys is related to the final size of biomedical products [15]. High-strength Mg alloys are more conducive for the preparation of stents and screws with smaller diameters [16]. This is beneficial for healing damaged tissues and organic matter. In addition to their mechanical properties, the rapid degradation of Mg alloys is a big concern because of their low standard electron potential. Mg is susceptible to form Mg(OH)2 via combining with hydroxide ion in an aqueous solution. The formation of corrosion products is unable to prevent Mg substrate because their structure is not dense. The mechanical integrity of biodegradable Mg alloys is lost when they undergo rapid biodegradation. High-purity pure Mg has very good corrosion resistance, but its mechanical properties are poor [17, 18]. Therefore, it is vital to design and construct Mg-based implants with a good balance between mechanical properties and corrosion resistance.
Besides performance limitations, another drawback of PLA is its slow biodegradation rate [t1/2 > 45 days; Figure 1(a)] as compared to other biodegradable polymers such as PHB, polycaprolactone (PCL), and polybutylene succinate (PBS), which have been reported to undergo near-complete biodegradation within two weeks10 implying half-lives of a week or less.11 The formation of microplastics during PLA degradation, particularly in aquatic environments where biodegradation is slow, remains a viable concern.12 When degradation does occur, it generally proceeds through acid-catalyzed hydrolysis or photo-degradation of the ester backbone, resulting in a decrease of molecular weight.12, 13 Theses oligomers can then be consumed by microorganisms, and several microbial enzymes capable of PLA degradation have been reported.14-16 The rates of hydrolysis in PLA and its composites increases with increasing water content temperature17, 18 and are enhanced by the unrestricted carboxyl groups of the hydrolyzed PLA ends. Degradation of PLA is faster at a temperature above its glass transition temperature coupled with high moisture content. Fillers have been used to improve the overall mechanical and biodegradation properties of PLA. Starch, an attractive biodegradable filler due to its low cost and processing ease is used with PLA to tailor mechanical properties. Starch undergoes complete degradation in a natural environment by enzymatic hydrolysis. Degradation of PLA is enhanced in composites with starch, as starch acts as a biological fuel that provides glucose for growth of microorganisms.19, 20 The incorporation of nanoclays into a PLA matrix also represents a promising approach for enhancing polymer performance and increasing its biodegradation rate in composting conditions.21-27 It has been proposed that nanoclays facilitate degradation by encouraging the permeation of water into the PLA matrix, thereby accelerating hydrolysis.28 The results found in the literature indicate that, in general, nanoclay-PLA composites biodegrade faster than their respective pristine polymers. In most of these studies, organo-modified montmorillonite (OMMT) were used to prepare the nanocomposites. However, the effect of different nanoclays on the biotic degradation of PLA is still unclear and needs further investigation. The purpose of this study was to determine the effect of adding a mixed mineral product derived from coal-mining waste streams to PLA and comparing the biodegradation and mechanical properties of the resulting inorganic-organic composite material against neat PLA. The specific mixed mineral product, termed NTM, is being tested as a soil amendment because of its high levels of calcium and magnesium, which promote plant growth. It was hypothesized that the incorporation of this mineral into PLA would increase biodegradation in soil composting conditions, which should facilitate and broaden the disposal of PLA and other biodegradable polymers through composting facilities by degrading composites in a reasonable time frame under standard conditions.

In this manner, biodegradable materials would eliminate the need of the second surgery, diminishing time of patient recovery, health care costs, and risks associated with a surgical intervention. Magnesium (Mg) based alloys are promising candidates for fracture fixation devices mainly due to their mechanical properties-density, elastic modulus, and yield strength-, which are similar to that of bone. (1) In addition, Mg is an element naturally present in the body, involved in several physiological processes, (2) and thus the degradation of a Mg based implant in the body is biocompatible. (3,4) The major limitation for the use of Mg based materials as implants is their fast degradation and the consequent liberation of hydrogen gas, a product of their corrosion in aqueous media. (5) Strategies of alloying with other elements such as aluminum, zinc, or rare earth elements, (6) and the surface protection with coatings (7) have been successful in retarding the corrosion rate of Mg. In some cases, promising uncoated or coated Mg alloys were studied in small (mice, rat, and rabbit) or large (guinea pig, goat, mini pig, and sheep) animal models (see Sekar et al. (8) for a review), which provide information regarding material safety, biodegradability, bone formation stimulation, and inflammatory response, among others. For example, fluoride, (9) calcium phosphate, (9,10) hydroxyapatite-MgO coatings, (11,12) aluminum, (13) and silicate oxides (14) coatings were demonstrated to increase corrosion resistance of Mg alloys in vivo and/or to favor bone formation. In spite of these favorable results, the use of Mg based materials in the orthopedic field is still scarce. Only one company is commercializing Mg based (Mg-Zn-Ca alloys) screws named MAGNEZIX since 2013, with good results in restoring motor function (15,16) and similar therapeutic efficiency than titanium screws. (17) On the basis of all this evidence, it is clear that Mg based implants have huge potential to replace inert permanent materials (e.g., titanium, stainless steel) for bone fracture fixation devices. Besides, when compared with other biodegradable materials as polymers (e.g., polylactic acid; PLA) Mg alloys present better and “close to bone” mechanical properties. However, although there is a profuse literature about the in vitro performance of the alloys, additional research is required to continue elucidating the in vivo corrosion process and to find surface treatments that could mitigate the hydrogen liberation during the first stage of implantation, which is still evidenced even in patients implanted with the new commercial Mg screws. Besides performance limitations, another drawback of PLA is its slow biodegradation rate [t1/2 > 45 days; Figure 1(a)] as compared to other biodegradable polymers such as PHB, polycaprolactone (PCL), and polybutylene succinate (PBS), which have been reported to undergo near-complete biodegradation within two weeks10 implying half-lives of a week or less.11 The formation of microplastics during PLA degradation, particularly in aquatic environments where biodegradation is slow, remains a viable concern.12 When degradation does occur, it generally proceeds through acid-catalyzed hydrolysis or photo-degradation of the ester backbone, resulting in a decrease of molecular weight.12, 13 Theses oligomers can then be consumed by microorganisms, and several microbial enzymes capable of PLA degradation have been reported.14-16 The rates of hydrolysis in PLA and its composites increases with increasing water content temperature17, 18 and are enhanced by the unrestricted carboxyl groups of the hydrolyzed PLA ends. Degradation of PLA is faster at a temperature above its glass transition temperature coupled with high moisture content. Fillers have been used to improve the overall mechanical and biodegradation properties of PLA. Starch, an attractive biodegradable filler due to its low cost and processing ease is used with PLA to tailor mechanical properties. Starch undergoes complete degradation in a natural environment by enzymatic hydrolysis. Degradation of PLA is enhanced in composites with starch, as starch acts as a biological fuel that provides glucose for growth of microorganisms.19, 20 The incorporation of nanoclays into a PLA matrix also represents a promising approach for enhancing polymer performance and increasing its biodegradation rate in composting conditions.21-27 It has been proposed that nanoclays facilitate degradation by encouraging the permeation of water into the PLA matrix, thereby accelerating hydrolysis.28 The results found in the literature indicate that, in general, nanoclay-PLA composites biodegrade faster than their respective pristine polymers. In most of these studies, organo-modified montmorillonite (OMMT) were used to prepare the nanocomposites. However, the effect of different nanoclays on the biotic degradation of PLA is still unclear and needs further investigation. The purpose of this study was to determine the effect of adding a mixed mineral product derived from coal-mining waste streams to PLA and comparing the biodegradation and mechanical properties of the resulting inorganic-organic composite material against neat PLA. The specific mixed mineral product, termed NTM, is being tested as a soil amendment because of its high levels of calcium and magnesium, which promote plant growth. It was hypothesized that the incorporation of this mineral into PLA would increase biodegradation in soil composting conditions, which should facilitate and broaden the disposal of PLA and other biodegradable polymers through composting facilities by degrading composites in a reasonable time frame under standard conditions.

Magnesium possesses a modulus of elasticity similar to bone, and hence has been widely explored for orthopedic applications to avoid stress shielding. Challenges of utilizing magnesium alloys as an implant material are: (i) the substantial corrosion rate, which rapidly raises the local pH that harms the local tissue, (ii) the tendency for magnesium corrosion to produce hydrogen gas139 and form gas cavities next to the magnesium implant, which has induced mortality in rats,140 and (iii) the rapid decrease of mechanical strength due to the substantial corrosion.141 All these challenges could lead to premature failure of a magnesium implant. The substantial corrosion rate (and concomitant high pH values) can be obviated by the use of magnesium alloys with good corrosion performance, such as WE43, which has been used for applications such as bone screws47 and stents.142 Zinc has recently become of interest as a biodegradable metal. Zinc contributes to biological functions such as signal transduction and gene expression.143 The challenges for utilizing zinc for medical applications are the large creep strains, susceptibility to natural aging, and static recrystallization.137 Iron possesses the best mechanical properties and the slowest corrosion rate, slower than magnesium and zinc.144 Iron plays an essential role in red blood cells.145 However, iron can be lost through skin renewal, and especially by menstruation in pre-menopausal women.145 Therefore, a balanced iron diet is necessary to ensure adequate iron in the body (i.e. by eating plenty of green vegetables, particularly spinach). Thus, iron is indeed one of the essential elements, and this guarantees its safety when implanted in the body. However, the main challenges to utilizing iron for medical applications are: (i) the bulky non-soluble corrosion products (particularly those containing the oxidized ferric form Fe3+),32 which could disrupt the local tissue and (ii) the low corrosion rate, which may be too low for practical applications.146
Load-bearing biodegradable biocompatible materials are always needed for medical applications to serve mainly as osteoconductive implants [[1], [2], [3], [4]]. In many cases, the bone fracture healing is currently supported by fixations using plates, nails, wires and screws to join the broken bone parts together to reach a mechanically suitable situation. These metallurgical implants are usually non-degradable with high modulus materials made from titanium, stainless steel or cobalt chromium, which remain in the human body and must be removed in an additional surgery after healing. They may cause stress shielding accompanied by bone resorption and implant loosening due to high modulus implants. Therefore, the goal is to develop new materials dissolving within the body and in the same time supporting the healing process in a reliable and sustainable way. Magnesium (Mg)-based implants are appropriate for such applications where short or medium period for bone healing is necessary [2,[5], [6], [7]]. Mg-based screws can be used with equal operative techniques and handling as conventional metal screws made of titanium, although magnesium alloys are generally less stiff than titanium [8,9]. Mg implants were tested for orthopedic applications [3,10, 11]. In vivo, pure Mg [[12], [13], [14], [15]] and its alloys up to approximately 10 % (Ca) [16,17], (Al) [18,19], (Zn) [20], (Li) [21], and rare earth elements or zirconium [15,21,22] have already been tested. Complete degradation of MgYREZr (Mg-Yitrium-Rare Earth-Zirconium) implants in rabbits took about one year [9]. Another MgYREZr alloy (trade name MAGNEZIX®) compression screws are the world’s first approved/CE-certified magnesium-based implants designed for biodegradable osteosyntheses applications in humans which have already been on the market for two years and used in surgery [23]. The processing route of Mg alloys for orthopedic implants have been the subject of several works. Implants based on extrusion of high strength Mg-alloy powders are introduced to the market [[5],6]. In addition, more cost-effective powder metallurgy methods such as Metal Injection Molding and Additive Manufacturing in combination with sintering are proposed [24]. Recently, powder injection molding of Mg-Ca alloys was tested for mass production of near net shape parts of small size and with complex shapes. An ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of up to 141 MPa with an elongation to rupture (El) of 7% and a Young’s modulus of 38 GPa were achieved [6]. The processing route of compression screws MAGNEZIX includes powder metallurgy and extrusion processes. After the final extrusion process, a yield strength YS > 260 MPa, UTS > 290 MPa and El >8% with a Modulus of elasticity (E) of 45 GPa were achieved [23]. Sintered Mg-Nd-Gd-Zr-Zn-alloy powder (EZK400) materials indicated a higher degradation rate than the as- cast ones [24]. High-purity magnesium (HP Mg) screws were fabricated by rolling and implanted in vivo in fixations of rabbit femoral intracondylar fracture. They showed a uniform degradation morphology, a sufficient bending force and an enhanced fracture healing with good osseointegration in the area surrounding the screws [25].

Temporary implants based on Mg alloys exploit the corrodible property of Mg in the human body to avoid revision surgery after healing of the fractured bone [1,2]. With a density of 1.74-2.0 g cm−3 and Young's modulus of E = 40-45 GPa, Mg can be used as a light weight metallic implant that offers minimal stress shielding effect compared to conventional metallic implant materials such as Ti (E = 100-110 GPa) [3,4]. Moreover, Mg is the fourth major cation in the human body with a daily dietary allowance of 700 mg/day and plays a crucial role in metabolism, tissue repair and cell adhesion [2,5]. Thus Mg finds applications in small orthopedic fixtures such as plates, ligatures, wires, stents, pins and screws where slow and controlled degradation over the span of fracture repair will ensure that the material gets absorbed in the body and eliminated in the metabolic pathway with no toxicity [[6], [7], [8], [9], [10]]. In addition, biomechanical characterization of magnesium based screws [11] indicated better pull out strengths compared to commercially existing polymer screws for orthopedic functions. Clinical trials on MgYREZr alloys prepared by powder metallurgy route and used in fixation during chevron osteotomy in patients with mild hallux valgus demonstrated no toxicity or gas bubble formation, and good bony healing with no foreign body reaction [12]. The MAGNEZIX® compression screw based on the MgYREZr alloy is the first biodegradable Mg based orthopedic fixture to receive the CE certification and is commercialized after the clinical trials [10]. In addition, the latest research also focuses on other degradable materials for bone healing, such as biopolymers, bioceramics, and biomedical metals [[13], [14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19]]. The major challenges to the incubation of Mg based alloys as implants lie in their limitations such as high corrosion rates, associated pH change and rapid hydrogen gas evolution in the physiological environment [1,[20], [21], [22], [23], [24]]. In addition, as the material degrades within the human body, there is a change in the shape of implant [25] and loss of mechanical integrity with degradation time. Stress corrosion cracking (SCC) can also occur due to the combined effect of corrosion in SBF and the applied tensile load and result in sudden catastrophic failure of the implant at loads well below the yield strength [[26], [27], [28], [29], [30]]. Conventional metallic implants such as Ti or stainless steel are reported to fail prematurely by catastrophic SCC fracture in spite of their good corrosion resistance in the body [31,32]. Hence, it can be expected that Mg alloys with rapid corrosion and predisposition to pitting in chloride rich environments [20] would be highly susceptible to SCC with the roots of corrosion pits acting as initiation spots for crack growth [20,26,27]. Hence, there is an imminent danger of implant failure before bone union that results in inflammation, pain and revision surgery in case of Mg based biodegradable implant materials.

In terms of biodegradable materials for temporary implants, PLA/Mg composites have been developed in the last few years as new bioabsorbable biomaterials for several biomedical applications. These applications include dental [1], vascular stent [2], skin regeneration [3], bone repair [4], orthopedic [5] and tissue engineering [6]. Magnesium (Mg) is the fourth most abundant element in the human body, is essential in metabolism and is necessary in more than 300 biochemical reactions in the body [7]. Despite these benefits, before proposing Mg as a suitable temporary implant material, its degradation rate should be properly controlled, as Mg is one of the most reactive structural materials [8]. Several alloys and composites have been developed to control the degradation rate of Mg since uncontrolled degradation could result in loss of mechanical integrity, metal contamination in the body and intolerable hydrogen evolution by tissue [9]. A composite that combines Mg particles in a biopolymeric matrix, such as polylactic acid (PLA), could present similar properties to Mg but with a controlled degradation ratio. Additionally, PLA is a biocompatible and biodegradable polymeric biomaterial, approved by the FDA [10]. Nowadays, there are certain types of PLA polymer implants on the market, such as spinal implants, intramedullary plugs, artificial cartilage frames, screws, plates, meshes, tissue anchors, etc., offered by several companies [11]. PLA/Mg composites have been widely reported in the literature [12]. With regards to the neat polymer, Mg enhances its mechanical properties, particularly the compressive strength, and stiffness with a 15-30 vol% Mg loading [4]. The degradation of these composites in vitro has also been studied by several authors in several simulated media [13]. In PBS PLA/Mg experienced significantly higher weight loss compared to PLA scaffolds, and this weight loss increased proportionally with the addition of Mg. However, this degradation increase is also correlated with a trend towards higher alkalinity [14]. Conversely, in Simulated Body Fluid (SBF), it is revealed that PLA/Mg composites could effectively degrade in the medium, and the incorporation of Mg does not compromise the pH for 28 days [15]. The biological behaviour of PLA/Mg composites has been tested in vitro with several cellular lines such as pre-osteoblast cells [16], fibroblasts [3], [5], epithelial cells [14] and osteoblasts [17]. Additionally, PLA/Mg has been tested in vivo [18] showing that composites with a 10 % Mg loading exhibited optimal osteogenic properties, whereas a 20 % Mg composite group showed angiogenic effects and promising osteoinduction properties.

Traditionally, permanent metallic materials have been used in orthopaedic applications due to their high strength and inert nature. However, problems, such as stress shielding, implant migration or loosening and the risks associated with revision surgery have led to the development of implants based on bioresorbable polymers [1]. Upon in vivo implantation these polymers degrade via hydrolytic chain scission, as injured tissue regenerates, and are excreted from the body via metabolic pathways. Members of the poly (α-hydroxy acid) family, such as polyglycolide (PGA), polylactide (PLA) and their related copolymers have been used in various biomedical applications including internal sutures, orthopaedic screws and scaffolds, drug delivery and tissue engineering [2]. PLA exists in two enantiomeric forms, D and L. For biomedical applications, the most commonly used forms are Poly(l-lactide) (PLLA) and Poly(d,l-lactide) PDLLA. PLLA is a semi-crystalline polymer with high mechanical strength, rendering it a suitable material for load bearing applications. However, its degradation time is slow with total resorption time in excess of 5 years [[2], [3], [4], [5], [6]]. PDLLA is more suited to non-load bearing applications, such as drug delivery, due to its amorphous nature and fast degradation time [[2], [3], [4], [5], [6]]. PGA, on the other hand, is highly crystalline with high mechanical strength, however, due to its hydrophilic nature its degradation is rapid, being reported as losing strength after one or two months and complete resorption after 6-12 months [2,3,6]. The ability to tailor polymers to meet required mechanical and/or degradation properties has made them an attractive alternative to their metallic counterparts. The ideal bioresorbable polymer would maintain sufficient mechanical strength during tissue healing (approximately 8-12 weeks depending on the application) [5], then begin to lose mass to allow new tissue to grow, eventually replacing the implanted polymer. One of the most significant challenges in the research of bioresorbable polymers is the development of this type of degradation profile. Copolymerisation of PLA and PGA, forming Poly(l-lactide-co-glycolide) (PLLGA) and Poly(d,l-lactide-co-glycolide) (PDLLGA), has become increasingly popular for preparation of bone substitute constructs since the use of different copolymer ratios allows greater control of mechanical and physicochemical properties, and degradation rates.
Magnesium (Mg) and its alloys are representative materials in the fields of engineering and biomedical applications owing to their low density and superior biocompatibility [1-4]. For a few years, Mg-based products have been offered in the market owing to the tireless work of researchers [5-7]. Specially, many implants, such as vascular stents and screws, have been successfully fabricated from Mg alloys [8-11]. Numerous in vitro and in vivo trials promote Mg implants conduct or is going to conduct clinical studies. At present, Mg alloys are mainly produced by casting and plastic deformation process. The forming processes play a key role in mechanical properties of Mg alloys [12]. As for biodegradable metals, mechanical requirements should be met: tensile strength >300 MPa, and elongation >15% [13]. According to previous researches, the tensile strength of cast and deformed Mg alloys is lower than 300 MPa [14]. This low strength indicates that it is difficult to apply biodegradable Mg alloys to load-bearing parts. Moreover, strength of biodegradable Mg alloys is related to the final size of biomedical products [15]. High-strength Mg alloys are more conducive for the preparation of stents and screws with smaller diameters [16]. This is beneficial for healing damaged tissues and organic matter. In addition to their mechanical properties, the rapid degradation of Mg alloys is a big concern because of their low standard electron potential. Mg is susceptible to form Mg(OH)2 via combining with hydroxide ion in an aqueous solution. The formation of corrosion products is unable to prevent Mg substrate because their structure is not dense. The mechanical integrity of biodegradable Mg alloys is lost when they undergo rapid biodegradation. High-purity pure Mg has very good corrosion resistance, but its mechanical properties are poor [17, 18]. Therefore, it is vital to design and construct Mg-based implants with a good balance between mechanical properties and corrosion resistance.

Export citation and abstractBibTeXRIS In orthopaedic surgery, bone screws, often in combination with plates, are routinely used implants for fracture fixation in weight-bearing bones [1]. After the healing and reorganization of the bone in the fracture gap, common implants made from stainless steel or titanium alloys have to be removed in a second surgery [2-4]. In addition, stress-shielding effects can lead to an implant-induced osteopenia and an increase in cortical porosity [5]. To avoid or reduce both negative aspects of conventional materials, the development of biodegradable implant materials based on magnesium alloys has been the focus of research in recent years [6, 7], as common degradable polymers are not suitable for load-bearing applications due to insufficient mechanical stability [8]. In contrast, magnesium alloys, with an elastic modulus closer to natural bone, exceed the stability and Young's modulus of polymers [9] and therefore are promising implant materials for this application [10-14]. The degradation rate of the implant has to be consistent with the bone healing processes. A first stable initial fixation under a functional load should be replaced by a predictable step-by-step degradation of the material and a substitution with bone in the cortical area. Magnesium as a co-factor for many biological functions [15] is considered to be relatively safe [10]. While high-purity magnesium shows the slowest degradation [16, 17], the degradation rate of Mg-alloys depends on the alloy composition [18, 19]. The most commonly used magnesium alloys include zinc (Zn) [13, 20-24] or rare earths (RE) [12, 19, 25, 26] as alloying elements, although their innocuousness is not definitively proven [27-29]. Within Mg-alloys, Zn and RE improve strength and, depending on the alloy's composition, reduce the corrosion rate [30, 31]. In recent studies, various RE- or Zn-containing alloys showed good biocompatibility [12, 19, 24, 25, 30, 32]. The magnesium alloy ZEK100 contains Zn and RE as alloying elements; ZEK100-plates have already been evaluated in a Hanks' balanced salt solution in vitro [33] and ZEK100-pins intramedullary in rabbit tibia in vivo [34, 35] as a potential biodegradable implant material for osteosynthesis due to their good mechanical characteristics. However, their biocompatibility was not finally approved, because an increased bone reactive capacity was observed in the implant surrounding of the ZEK100-pins after a 6 month implantation period [36]. Subsequent investigations by Dziuba et al did not recommend ZEK100 for biomedical use as these intramedullary implanted pins induced adverse host reactions after 9 and 12 month investigation periods [35]. However, these investigations consider intramedullary implantation [36, 35]. Their degradation properties, as well as host responses like inflammatory reactions or removal of degradation products, might be different in other locations. Relating to a surgical procedure, initiation, resolution and organization as first sign of the acute host response are normally followed by the immigration of immuno-inflammatory cells, which infiltrate the implant adjacencies. Furthermore, various cellular and tissue responses can be associated with an implanted degrading biomaterial [37, 38]. These reactions in the implant surrounding have to be examined to assess the implant's biocompatibility, and can differ depending on the implant location [36, 39].
Nowadays, the study of innovative degradable biomaterials is one of the most interesting research topics in biomaterials. Degradable biomaterials have been proposed from polymers, ceramics, and metals. Metals are more mechanically interesting compared to polymers for load-bearing implants, such as internal bone fixation screws/pins and plates and for coronary stents, which require high strength to bulk ratio [7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 17,18,19,20,21]. The most promising candidates for designing biodegradable metallic implants are magnesium, zinc, and iron alloys. Among these, Mg-based alloys and Fe-based alloys are the most widely explored [3, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 19, 22]. Magnesium and its alloys have already been successfully tested in vivo and in clinical studies (Fig. 1) [15, 23, 24]. Most of the studies on Mg-based implants reported a rapid degradation rate in physiological environments accompanied by the evolution of considerable amounts of hydrogen [14, 15, 25]. Excessive rate of degradation can lead to undesired loss of mechanical integrity of the implant; therefore, various methods have been used to control it [26]. An alloying with other elements (Al, Zn, Ca, Ag, Ce, Th) and the preparation of composites were used to improve mechanical properties of Mg-based biomaterials [27]. The main challenge for both Mg and Fe materials is the successful implementation of long-term in vivo experiments. A look at the status of Mg-based metals shows that it is very complicated to develop the material that would be load-bearing, biodegradable, and biocompatible. Magnesium (Mg) and its alloys have been considered a potential material for fabricating biodegradable metallic stents and several orthopaedic applications in recent years [1]. Magnesium possesses low density and high specific strength, and has an elastic modulus closer to that of natural bones when compared with other implant metallic materials such as stainless steel, titanium alloys and cobalt chromium alloys [2], [3], [4]. However, the use of magnesium is hindered by its poor corrosion resistance, which causes the mechanical properties of the implant to decrease significantly, resulting in the inability of tissue to heal [5], [6], [7]. Furthermore, the Mg corrosion process involves evolution of hydrogen gas, which accumulates in vivo adjacent to the implant. The H2 gas and subsequent formation of hydrogen bubbles can noticeably impair the clinical applications of Mg [5], [8]. Apart from alloying, surface modifications such as plasma electrolytic oxidation (PEO), ion implantation, pulsed laser deposition, Ca-P coatings and polymer coatings have been widely applied in order to reduce the initial degradation rate of Mg alloys [9], [10], [11], [12]. Polymer-based biodegradable materials such as poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA), poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) and polycaprolactone (PCL) have been widely used in clinics to help with the repair of human tissues, for example as absorbable bone screws, plates and pins [13], [14]. Among these, PCL, (−[(CH2)5COO]n-) is a promising polymer because of its significant toughness and good biocompatibility as well as remarkable mechanical properties, such as 80% elongation at break point [15], [16]. PCL is a semicrystalline aliphatic polymer that has a slower degradation rate and higher fracture energy than most biocompatible polymers [15], [16], [17]. In addition, PCL is hydrophobic, which is desirable for a coating applied on magnesium because magnesium shows a high corrosion rate when exposed to physiological media containing Cl− [1], [16]. However, PCL has several disadvantages when used alone because of insufficient strength and a lack of the desired bioactivity [13]. To address this problem, fluorine-doped hydroxyapatite (FHA; Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2-xFx, where 0 < x < 2) films beneath organic coatings appear to have excellent potential to obtain both corrosion protection and surface stability without adversely affecting mechanical properties [18], [19]. FHA was reported to be a promising candidate for replacement of hydroxyapatite (HA) because of its low solubility and similar biocompatibility compared with HA [18], [20]. FHA coatings could provide lower dissolution, better apatite-like layer deposition, better protein adsorption and improved alkaline phosphatase activity in cell cultures [21]. Hence, it is reasonable to deduce that a composite material of polymer and calcium phosphate may combine the advantages of the two materials for the enhancement of corrosion resistance of Mg alloys [14]. In this study, a combination of two methods was used for the synthesis of fluorine-doped HA and PCL on the surface of Mg alloys. An initial electrodeposition (ED) was carried out to deposit a fluorine-doped HA layer on the surface of the Mg substrate. Subsequently, dip coating was performed to deposit a PCL film on the surface of the Mg substrate. These techniques have been selected because of their simple operation, ease of particle-size control, compact coating, low temperature processing and low cost [22], [23]. Various studies have reported that polymer and ceramic-polymer coatings can increase the corrosion resistance of Mg alloys in SBF [16], [24], [25], [26]. Abdal-hay et al. Balancing biodegradation and stability is challenging and requires precise control over hydrogel composition, crosslinking density, and degradation kinetics. Rapid degradation may lead to premature loss of mechanical support, while slow degradation can impede tissue remodeling and integration. Organic-inorganic hybrid biomaterials stand as a promise for combining bone bonding and bone mineral-forming ability, stimulation of osteogenic cells, and adequate mechanical properties. Bioactive glass (BG)-polycaprolactone (PCL) hybrids are of special interest as they gather the ability of BG to enhance osteoblast-mediated bone formation with the slow degradation rate and the toughness of PCL. BG can be synthesized into macroporous structures required for guiding the bone regeneration in the case of major trauma and large bone defects, but the resulting BG scaffolds suffer from brittleness and may collapse under physiological cyclic loading due to their poor resistance to crack propagation. (7) In order to improve the toughness and resilience of the material, BG particles can be dispersed in a bioresorbable polymer matrix to produce osteogenic BG-polymer composites. However, it is very difficult to control the exposure of BG particles to the external environment at the surface of the polymer and thereby to control the bioactive and osteogenic properties of the composite. (8) To address those limitations, organic-inorganic hybrids associating BG and polymers have been developed. Plastics are synthetic polymer compounds made substantially from petrochemical materials extracted from coal, oil, and natural gas.[1] In general, fossil fuel plastics achieve high mechanical and fluid barrier properties by packing their chains into specific crystalline and amorphous regions. However, its hydrophobic and long-chain structural features make it lack bio-accessible organic chemical groups, limiting the ability of microorganisms to break them down.[2] The accumulation of fossil fuel plastics in the environment has severely affected soil quality, the aquatic environment, flora, and fauna.[3] The depletion of fossil fuels and environmental pollution have prompted researchers to develop eco-friendly biodegradable polymers to replace petrochemical-based polymers. In this context, bioplastics appear as a promising alternative. A bioplastic is often considered bio-based and/or biodegradable material[4, 5] such as polyvinyl alcohol, polylactic acid, polybutylene succinate, as well as carbohydrate derivatives and blends based on protein, starch, chitin, and cellulose. The global market size for bioplastics is considered to burgeon every day. The global production capacity of bioplastics in 2023 was ≈2.18 million tonnes, which is projected to expand to 7.43 million tonnes by 2028.[6] This shows that bioplastics have great application value and development prospects in various fields of modern society. Currently, PLA is the most important among the biobased biodegradable plastics because of its zero toxicity, biodegradability, and good mechanical attributes.[7] PLA is produced by the polymerization of lactides or lactic acid monomers fermented from starch, mainly used in 3D printing, food packaging, transport, agriculture, and textile industries.[8] Upon biodegradation, PLA releases CO2, water, and decomposed organic matter without leaving any visible and toxic residues.[7] These substances are absorbed by plants, thus imparting less carbon footprint. Although, compared to fossil fuel plastics, neat PLA has some disadvantages such as brittleness and low crystallization rate, which restricts commercial usage.[9] The mechanical performance of PLA is greatly affected by the crystallinity degree, which depends on the source and processing conditions.[10, 11] For example, the oriented samples of PLA were prepared by being heated and mechanically drawn, the tensile strength and crystallinity increased significantly with the increase in draw ratio.[12] In addition, there is also a study on increasing the crystallinity of PLA by adding nucleating agents (Zinc PhenylPhosphonate, Ecopromote, and EcopromoteHD) to improve its mechanical properties.[13] Heterogeneous nucleation is a frequently encountered phenomenon in the crystallization of composite systems.[14] By adding inorganic compounds,[15] polysaccharide polymers,[16] carbon-based materials,[17] and other substances[18] as nucleation sites, the heterogeneous nucleation rate of the matrix can be effectively promoted.[19] For instance, lignin was used as a heterogeneous nucleating agent to increase the crystallinity of PLA, which also results in the enhancements of PLA tensile strength and gas barrier properties.[20] However, the heterogeneous nucleation effect of proteins as nucleating agents is rarely reported. Blending the protein with biodegradable synthetic polymers has been shown to be an effective strategy to improve performances,[21-23] but whether this is related to nucleation effects still remains unclear. Proteins are commonly used for biocomposite materials owing to their abundance, biodegradability, low price, and better film development capability. In 2023, worldwide protein meal production reached 369.79 million metric tons, of which ≈4% were cottonseed meal.[24] Cottonseed meal is one of the most important sources of plant protein, but little research has been carried out on its high value-added value, especially cottonseed protein bioplastics. According to the report, cottonseed proteins (CP) have almost the same primary amino acid components as soy protein.[25] The excellent processing properties and plasticizer efficiency make CP a smart choice for bioplastic production.[26] Nevertheless, hydrophobic PLA is incompatible with amphiphilic CP, so interfacial compatibility between PLA and CP needs to be improved by adding compatibilizers. MA is typically used as a compatibilizer agent.[27] MA is highly reactive with a variety of polymer chains and biomacromolecules such as proteins, lipids, and glucose, increasing the polarity of the thermoplastic polymer for better adhesion with biofillers that have polar groups on their surfaces.[28]

Delgove et al. investigated LCA by comparing chemical and biochemical synthesis of lactones and found no significant difference in climate change impact between the two routes.[73] Bio-based CFs, particularly those derived from lignin, offer significant environmental benefits over traditional PAN-based fibers. LCA of lignin-based CFs reported a 30% reduction in life cycle energy use compared to PAN-based fibers.[74] The GHG emissions of lignin-based CFs are 5-15 kgCO2eq/kg CF whereas PAN-based CF is observed as 20-30 kgCO2eq/kg CF. Addressing these issues through green pretreatment methods and renewable energy integration in carbonization is vital for enhancing the overall sustainability of bio-based CF production.

The depletion of fossil resources, as well as environmental issues, are serious problems and are the basis for the shift towards renewable sources for the production of materials. Plastics made from non-fossil sources such as polylactide (PLA) are an important part of ecological waste management, Circular Economy and carbon footprint reduction. PLA, as a biodegradable polymer made from renewable sources, has similar properties to polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and polystyrene (PS). It can be processed in many ways to create a full range of products such as films, fibres, injection molded details and preforms. Unfortunately, this material also has disadvantages. The main ones include the high cost of the material and some limitation in mechanical properties, which discourages manufacturers from using it [1]. One of the ways to reduce the cost of the material is to create a biocomposite with the addition of lignocellulosic filler. According to Mohanty et al. [2], adding a biodegradable filler to a biodegradable polymer matrix should allow for obtaining a biodegradable composite. Lignocellulose filler from agri-food waste allows the recycling of residue. All of this is in line with the EU Strategy for Plastics and Bioeconomy in the Circular Economy, encouraging sustainable waste management and the idea of „zero waste” [3]. Using agri-food waste as a plastic filler is a method used by scientists. Leszczyńska et al., used chokeberry pomace, raspberry seeds, hazelnut and walnut shells as a natural filler and natural blowing agent in rigid polyurethane foam composites [4]. Scafarro et al. used Posidonia oceanica dead leaves and as well as Botta et al., used artichoke stem as a PLA filler [5,6].
Green biocomposites are environmentally friendly composites made from natural fibers and biopolymers. These biocomposites can be made from either renewable materials derived from agricultural or forestry waste, providing alternative environmentally friendly options. Green biocomposites therefore appear to have huge potential in a wide range of industries such as healthcare, automotive, and packaging, helping to reduce the carbon footprint left by fossil fuel-based materials. In addition, the high tensile strength of natural fibers and the flexibility of the biopolymer matrix make these composites lightweight, durable, and affordable. As a result, biopolymers and those formed by blending the above components are among the most important topics in sustainable materials research today. Biopolymers are natural structures and have the unique ability to degrade without leaving harmful residues in the ecosystem [1-5]. For a variety of applications and biodegradability as well as eco-friendliness, polylactic acid (PLA) is above all other types of polymers. Different from the traditional petroleum-based polymers, PLA is made from renewable resources, mainly cornstarch or sugarcane, and thus becomes less harmful to the environment. It entirely and completely dissolves under appropriate conditions, which reduces the long-term environmental impact. Most especially, it has a huge potential for packaging and agriculture. Whereby, this quality increases its area of application: for instance, composites with very good mechanical strength, heat stability, and biocompatibility can be produced easily because PLA is compatible with natural fibers and other additives. All of these factors combine to make PLA an ideal alternative to conventional products for industries seeking to reduce their carbon footprint while maintaining acceptable performance standards. PLA outperforms any other synthetic or partially biodegradable polymer in terms of performance or sustainability [6-8]. PLA-based biocomposites have emerged as a trending topic in the last few years because of their prospective applications in several fields, most notably in biomedicine and environmental sustainability. PLA-based biocomposites can also be reinforced with natural fibers, such as jute, hemp, and flax, which have been studied mostly for mechanical characteristics and biodegradability [9, 10]. Other types of composites that incorporate PLA are the addition of nano-fillers such as graphene for enhanced thermal and mechanical properties of the polymer [11]. Furthermore, PLA composites mixed with natural rubber were analyzed for better elasticity and flexibility [12]. PLA with chitosan has demonstrated antibacterial and biocompatible properties, making it suitable for applications in medicine [13]. Recently, there has been an increasing interest in natural resources such as agricultural food by-products for the production of films worldwide. One of these natural resources is the olive leaf, a residue produced in large quantities by the olive tree pruning and olive harvesting by the olive oil industry [14]. The leaves of the olive are a cheap raw material that can be used as an advantageous source of products with a high added value [15-17]. Research on the important trends in developing olive leaf extracts into PLA matrixes has demonstrated relevant antioxidant properties, rendering this bio-additive inestimable. Olive leaves are known to be rich in polyphenols like oleuropein, flavones, flavonols, catechin, and hydroxytyrosol, providing them with powerful antioxidant and anti-inflammatory benefits [14, 17-20]. Such properties may significantly enhance the biocompatibility and functional longevity of PLA-based biocomposites in medical applications. However, more research is to be carried out to develop the manufacturing and functional attributes of such composites to benefit from their applications in biological and environmental settings to the fullest degree.

Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is one of the most important bioplastics on the global market and accounts for 20.5% of the total amount of bioplastics produced annually.1 Despite good mechanical properties and high availability, the use is inhibited by the high price compared to polyolefins. One way to solve this problem is to add low-cost fillers such as native starch.2 The use of starch is accompanied by a change in the mechanical, thermal, and structural properties, but also leads to an improvement in the carbon footprint.3 By saving PLA, not only costs can be reduced, but also the energy that must be expended for the synthesis. Starch, on the other hand, already binds CO2 during the plant growth phase.2, 4 Composites of starch types from different origins have already been produced. In addition to potato starch, rice, tapioca and corn starch were also used.5-18 The addition of native starch to a PLA matrix leads to an embrittlement and thus a decrease in tensile strength and elongation at break, with an increasing effect with rising starch content.3, 13 Due to their properties, PLA starch composites are suitable for a wide range of applications, which are currently mainly limited to plastic trays, loose-fills, cutlery, and writing instruments.2, 19 During use, components are exposed to numerous environmental influences such as temperature, humidity, and UV radiation. These influences, in turn, cause complex aging phenomena, which become noticeable in the properties of the composites. In particular, starch can increase the causes of aging such as water absorption, and therefore promote aging processes.20 This is based on the polar groups of the starch, which lead to hydrogen bondings and thus form the strongly hydrophilic character of starch.2 For PLA, which is known to be a material prone to hydrolysis, the increased water absorption is accompanied by a change in properties.21-25 In 2003, Wang et al.26 investigated the physical aging of composites of PLA and starch and observed a deterioration of the mechanical properties as a result of storage at 25°C and 50% humidity. In addition, the microstructure of the composites also changed and showed an increasing ductility of the matrix with continued physical aging and a simultaneous deterioration of the bond between the starch and the matrix, which in turn caused a decrease in tensile strength. Yew et al.27 and Gáspár et al.28 also showed a reduction in mechanical properties as a result of humid storage. Yew et al.27 showed a clearly stronger and accelerated water absorption of PLA through the addition of hygroscopic starch, whereby the samples with 20% starch absorbed 5 times as much water as pure PLA samples. It is assumed that the absorbed water leads on the one hand to hydrolysis of the PLA and on the other hand to a deterioration of the adhesion between PLA and starch and thus to a reduction in the mechanical properties. Similarly, artificial weathering of PLA starch composites led to a reduction in tensile strength, although the reduction was less for starch-containing samples than for pure PLA. The reason for this is the UV-shielding effect of the starch particles, which slows down the UV-induced chain degradation.6 In addition to starch-filled PLA, there are also numerous studies on LDPE that have been filled with starch: Danjaji et al.29 showed a decrease in the tensile strength of starch-filled LLDPE as a result of significantly increased water absorption. Furthermore, the thermal degradation of LDPE can be inhibited by the addition of starch.30
There are various origins for natural polymers, where as far as the biomaterials field is concerned, natural polymers are sourced from microorganisms, plants, and animals. Due to the benefits, natural polymers offer, especially environmentally, they are a considered good substitute for fiber production, especially for biomedical-related applications. Some of the major benefits of utilizing natural polymers are the fast integration onto wounded sites and resemblance to the host tissue, along with its biocompatibility and biodegradation. It also has the potential to degrade by enzymes and the capacity to react with biological structures in a controlled method.[94] At present, there are a large number of natural polymers that are compatible with current polymer fiber manufacturing methods, which have been extensively researched in the recent past.[37] In general, biopolymers are thought to be ecofriendlier than traditional polymers. However, a 2010 study by the University of Pittsburgh concluded that this is not particularly factual when the entire material life cycle was analyzed.[95] The research contrasted seven traditional plastics, along with four bioplastics and a single plastic produced from both fossil fuels and renewable resources. The investigators discovered that bioplastics manufacture produced a larger quantity of pollutants when fertilizers and pesticides were taken into account. These chemicals are utilized in growing crops and chemical processing which are required to convert organic material into bioplastic. It was also found that bioplastics promote ozone depletion more than regular plastics and also require large-scale land use. However, bioplastics do emit a remarkably lower amount of greenhouse gas emissions in comparison to traditional plastics. There is no resulting increase in carbon dioxide when bioplastics break down as they are produced from the same quantity of carbon dioxide. A 2017 report concluded that substituting traditional plastics with corn-based PLA would reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 25% in the USA.[92] The report also determined that the production of traditional plastics from only renewable energy sources can reduce emissions by 50-75%. Although the biodegradability of biopolymers is beneficial, most of these biopolymers require high-temperature industrial compositing provisions, which is uncommon and only a few cities seem to possess such provisions. Subsequently, these biopolymers culminate in landfills, where there is risk of methane being released from them, a greenhouse gas known to be 23 times more potent than carbon dioxide. Solar UV radiation is necessary to trigger the photo-oxidation degradation process of most polymers, which occurs through a radical chain mechanism that results in bond cleavage and a reduction in molecular weight.[4] Polymers discarded in landfills are unlikely to have enough access to UV radiation. Bioplastics (and biodegradable) when discarded incorrectly can contaminate recycled plastics and can impair recycling infrastructure. For instance, if PET (polyethylene terephthalate) which is common plastic utilized to produce bottles, is exposed to bioplastics, the whole lot may be declined and end up in a landfill. Therefore, there is need for separate streams to appropriately discard both biodegradable plastics and bioplastics. Bioplastics are produced from natural materials and hence, composting of bioplastic components can make soil fertile, due to the absence of artificial chemicals.[96] The land need for the production of bioplastics may hinder food production, as the crops that are used to manufacture these plastics can be utilized for food which is known to be in a shortage. In 2017, a joint report of European environmental organizations, estimated that the area of land required to keep up with global demand would equate to more than 1.3 million acres of land by 2019.[97] This is an area larger than Denmark, the Netherlands and Belgium put together. It can also be noted that the petroleum required to maneuver farming machinery will also emit greenhouse gases. Bioplastics can also be relatively costly. For instance, PLA can be up to 50% more expensive in comparison to similar traditional plastics due to the intricate method utilized to convert corn or sugarcane into the building blocks for PLA.[93] Regardless, the costs of bioplastics have slowly reduced as businesses and researchers evolve more greener and efficient techniques for manufacturing bioplastics. The production of bioplastics such as PLA, commonly used to make nanofibers for various applications, does not require the process of discovery, acquisition, and transportation of hydrocarbons. This results in the use of fewer fossil fuels and produces up to 67% less greenhouse gases during manufacture.[98] The manufacture of biodegradable plastics can be costly. However, considering the clean-up costs along with the lower negative environmental effects, biodegradable polymers are the better option. They also require less energy for production in comparison to regular plastics. Crude oil (petroleum) is a major element in the production of traditional plastics. The extraction and refinement of crude oil significantly affect the environment. According to the British Plastic Federation, it is believed that 4-6% of oil is used in the manufacture of plastics in Europe alone.[99] Biodegradable plastics use up to 20% renewable materials in its production when compared to traditional plastics. Current research is being undertaken on biodegradable plastics, where in the future, these plastics will only release the same quantity of energy used in manufactur.[100] Nonpetroleum-based plastics such as PLA, that are made from plants such as corn and sugarcane also curtail carbon dioxide as they do not emit an excess amount of CO2 during decomposition.[101] The use of plant oil as renewable feedstock for the synthesis of polymers has also been recently researched for development.[102]

Biobased polymers have become a valuable alternative to fossil-based polymers to prepare materials with a reduced carbon footprint and that are not dependent on petrochemicals. In this context, Polylactic acid, also known as polylactide or PLA, has been one of the most successful bioplastic in the last decade. It boasts a high tensile modulus and strength, it has a high transparency, it is fully biodegradable once hydrolyzed and it can be processed with the same equipment as other polyesters. Commodity PLA grades have mainly been serving the packaging markets where its biobased origin is valued by consumers and where its biodegradability offers the possibility of composting as an end-of-life option [1]. The life cycle of PLA packaging is relatively short since it is typically aimed at the protection of fresh food products. Therefore, taking advantage of its good mechanical properties in longer life cycle engineering applications would be interesting. Additionally, increased use of PLA would give environmental benefits over current engineering materials since PLA production requires less fossil fuel and generates less greenhouse gases compared to most fossil-based engineering resins. Nevertheless, for longer-term applications, PLA has two major deficiencies. First, it suffers from a relatively low temperature resistance when used in its amorphous form due to its glass transition temperature occurring at around 60 °C. Secondly, PLA can suffer from hydrolysis in a hot and humid environment which is a serious issue when contemplating durable material applications. There is a whole window of opportunity in longer-term engineering applications that is nearly untouched for the moment greatly due to these deficiencies. Polymer blending represents a practical and economical route to modify physical properties of polymeric materials, sometimes obtaining attractive novel properties which each individual material does not possess. Several polymers have been blended with PLA, typically with PLA as the major phase. Basic thermodynamics teaches us that two substances will be miscible if the Gibbs free energy of the solution is smaller than the sum of the components free Energy. In terms of change in free energy, ΔG m , this condition can be expressed from the enthalpy and entropy of mixing by the well-known Gibbs equation [2]. For polymer mixtures, the entropy of mixing is greatly reduced compared to small molecules due to the much lower number of conformations that can be taken by macromolecules. Since the enthalpy of mixing is generally small or positive, the vast majority of polymer pairs are immiscible. PLA based blends are no exception and PLA was shown to form immiscible blends with polyethylene [3], polypropylene [4], polystyrene [5], polyvinyl acetate [6], thermoplastic starch [7] as well as with other polyesters such as polybutylene succinate [8], polyhydroxybutyrate [9] and polyethylene terephthalate [10, 11]. PLA, however, can form partially miscible blends with polycaprolactone [12, 13], and with polyols such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) [14, 15]. The latter has a low glass transition and can be used to plasticize PLA.
Cappiello et al. mentioned in their LCA (cradle-to-grave) on milk packages based on fossil PET and HDPE, glass, multilayer cartoon, and PLA-based bioplastic bottle, PLA performs best in terms of CC, OD, HT, acidification but unsatisfactory in POF, TEU and FEU, while considering the recycling scenario, PLA’s FEU impact also performed better alongside CC, OD, HT [35]. O’Loughlin et al. showed that there is a considerable CF reduction with PLA-based containers compared to PP (PLA 1.8-3.7 kg CO2 eqv./kg PLA and PP 3.7-5.2 kg CO2 eqv./kg); however, PLA suffers due to its brittleness, poor thermal response, and water resistance which otherwise needs modification to improve its properties as composite form to replace PP [36]. Moreover, the study did not mention on the effect of other environmental parameters. Moretti et al. made LCA (cradle-to-grave) study on single-use cups made of PLA, PET, and PP materials, considering 50% recycle and 50% composting for PLA and 100% recycle for PET and PP as EOL, where PLA cups showed better performance in on CC, FD but performed poor in POF, acidification, TEU compared to both PP and PET. The environmental impacts are attributed to the cultivation stage, using fertilizers, and the production of PLA causes a substantial burden, as mentioned below, countering the biogenic CO2’s benefit (Table 4) [37]. PLA can be modified with nanocellulose fiber to enhance its dynamic mechanical properties with improved storage modulus and water barrier properties, which increases PLA’s performance in packaging applications [42]. PLA modified with micro- and nanocrystalline cellulose has application in fused filament fabrication as an insulator in the electrical field which can replace expensive ceramic-based material [43]. PLA composite reinforced with natural fiber (Cordenka rayon fiber) and flax fiber, produces a very high tensile and impact strength-based biodegradable composite for engineering applications, which can partially replace fossil-based polymers [44]. PLA is focused on the application of smart (active and intelligent) food packaging. PLA film infused with β-cyclodextrin and allyl isothiocyanate inclusion complexes (AITC) as active packaging shows mitigation of microbial attack for a longer period [45]. PLA with chitosan has demonstrated antibacterial and biocompatible properties, making it suitable for applications in medicine [13]. Recently, there has been an increasing interest in natural resources such as agricultural food by-products for the production of films worldwide. One of these natural resources is the olive leaf, a residue produced in large quantities by the olive tree pruning and olive harvesting by the olive oil industry [14]. The leaves of the olive are a cheap raw material that can be used as an advantageous source of products with a high added value [15-17]. Research on the important trends in developing olive leaf extracts into PLA matrixes has demonstrated relevant antioxidant properties, rendering this bio-additive inestimable. Olive leaves are known to be rich in polyphenols like oleuropein, flavones, flavonols, catechin, and hydroxytyrosol, providing them with powerful antioxidant and anti-inflammatory benefits [14, 17-20]. Such properties may significantly enhance the biocompatibility and functional longevity of PLA-based biocomposites in medical applications. However, more research is to be carried out to develop the manufacturing and functional attributes of such composites to benefit from their applications in biological and environmental settings to the fullest degree.

Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is one of the most important bioplastics on the global market and accounts for 20.5% of the total amount of bioplastics produced annually.1 Despite good mechanical properties and high availability, the use is inhibited by the high price compared to polyolefins. One way to solve this problem is to add low-cost fillers such as native starch.2 The use of starch is accompanied by a change in the mechanical, thermal, and structural properties, but also leads to an improvement in the carbon footprint.3 By saving PLA, not only costs can be reduced, but also the energy that must be expended for the synthesis. Starch, on the other hand, already binds CO2 during the plant growth phase.2, 4 Composites of starch types from different origins have already been produced. In addition to potato starch, rice, tapioca and corn starch were also used.5-18 The addition of native starch to a PLA matrix leads to an embrittlement and thus a decrease in tensile strength and elongation at break, with an increasing effect with rising starch content.3, 13 Due to their properties, PLA starch composites are suitable for a wide range of applications, which are currently mainly limited to plastic trays, loose-fills, cutlery, and writing instruments.2, 19 During use, components are exposed to numerous environmental influences such as temperature, humidity, and UV radiation. These influences, in turn, cause complex aging phenomena, which become noticeable in the properties of the composites. In particular, starch can increase the causes of aging such as water absorption, and therefore promote aging processes.20 This is based on the polar groups of the starch, which lead to hydrogen bondings and thus form the strongly hydrophilic character of starch.2 For PLA, which is known to be a material prone to hydrolysis, the increased water absorption is accompanied by a change in properties.21-25 In 2003, Wang et al.26 investigated the physical aging of composites of PLA and starch and observed a deterioration of the mechanical properties as a result of storage at 25°C and 50% humidity. In addition, the microstructure of the composites also changed and showed an increasing ductility of the matrix with continued physical aging and a simultaneous deterioration of the bond between the starch and the matrix, which in turn caused a decrease in tensile strength. Yew et al.27 and Gáspár et al.28 also showed a reduction in mechanical properties as a result of humid storage. Yew et al.27 showed a clearly stronger and accelerated water absorption of PLA through the addition of hygroscopic starch, whereby the samples with 20% starch absorbed 5 times as much water as pure PLA samples. It is assumed that the absorbed water leads on the one hand to hydrolysis of the PLA and on the other hand to a deterioration of the adhesion between PLA and starch and thus to a reduction in the mechanical properties. Similarly, artificial weathering of PLA starch composites led to a reduction in tensile strength, although the reduction was less for starch-containing samples than for pure PLA. The reason for this is the UV-shielding effect of the starch particles, which slows down the UV-induced chain degradation.6 In addition to starch-filled PLA, there are also numerous studies on LDPE that have been filled with starch: Danjaji et al.29 showed a decrease in the tensile strength of starch-filled LLDPE as a result of significantly increased water absorption. question: What is the 'enzymatic mechanism' of degradation for natural polymers like starch?
ground_truth: Starch is degraded by amylases (alpha and beta). Alpha-amylase acts as an endo-enzyme, randomly cleaving alpha-1,4-glycosidic bonds in the interior of the chain. Beta-amylase acts as an exo-enzyme, removing maltose units from the non-reducing end. This synergistic action rapidly reduces molecular weight and produces metabolizable sugars.
