Among the biopolymers that can be used to produce biocomposite materials, starch is highly promising because it has many advantages, such as renewable and biodegradable properties in addition to being relatively inexpensive [129]. Starch is made up of amylose, a linear polymeric unit of glucose attached by α-1-4 link, and amylopectin, a branched polymer of α-1-4 linked chains attached by α-1-6 links [130], [131]. Since starch can be made into thermoplastic starch (TPS) through disruption and plasticization of starch granules, the development of biocomposites has continued to grow widely [132]. Due to its biodegradability, it has been vastly blended with several non-biodegradable polymers and composites to increase their overall degradation rate. The effect of nanoparticles on such blends and nanocomposites of starch has been analysed. The effect of α-Amylase on enzymatic degradation of Poly (vinyl alcohol)/starch nanocomposites containing montmorillonite was carried out by incorporating montmorillonite silicate nanoparticles (Nanocore I28, Bentonite, Peruvian clay) into polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)/starch. According to this study, the amount of water uptake influenced the enzymatic degradation. Higher water sorption resulted in more degradation. Nanocomposites containing nanocore absorbed more water hence it had the most significant mass loss while nanocomposites containing peruvian clay did not absorbed more water content which is why its degradation was lesser. Thus, it was established that dissolution/erosion is the main driving mechanism for a pronounced degradation[133]. On the other hand, some nanoparticles can also act as a barrier and reduce the moisture absorbing capacity [134] i.e. Adding processed carbon nanotubes (CNTs) to polylactic acid (PLA) nanocomposites was discovered to decrease water absorption and weight loss, ultimately slowing down the rate of biodegradation [135]. A recent study reported that the nanocomposite of Bent-CS nano clays and agricultural mulch films produced from oxidized starch showed no increment in the rate of nanocomposite degradation [136]. A study on enzymatic degradation of Polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)/Starch nanocomposite in the presence of naturally occurring sodium montmorillonite clay along with α-amylase enzyme was reported [137]. The enzymatic hydrolysis is complementary with glucose release and hence the release of glucose was considered as a measurement of starch hydrolysis. It was found that Na-MMT displays stabilizing effect in odds with enzymatic attacks due to which the glucose production in case of Starch/PVA-Na MMT nanocomposites were lower than the neat Starch/PVA films. This led to the conclusion of low water uptake in nanocomposites. The addition of Na-MMT in Starch/PVA blends decreased their enzymatic degradation rates. An experiment to study the effect of nano-SiO2 and PVA in thermoplastic starch (TPS) blends was carried out and identical results were concluded that the nanoparticles impede the enzymatic degradation of starch-based nanocomposite [138]. Nano-SiO2 reinforced starch/PVOH nanocomposite films were studied by Tang and his team for biodegradability [139]. In the presence of 5 % nano- SiO2, the weight loss could reach 60 %, which was very similar to the weight loss without nano- SiO2 in starch-PVOH. There is little evidence that nanoparticles influenced the biodegradability of starch/PVOH blend films. The addition of graphene to the PVA/starch matrix has significantly increased the rate of crystallinity change of the PVA/starch matrix. When graphene was incorporated into PVA/starch blends, the nanocomposite became less susceptible to environmental degradation due to the ability of graphene to weaken molecule-to-molecule interactions and speeding up the dissolution of the amorphous portion of PVA/starch blends [140]. As the dissolution of amorphous region proceeded, the percentage of crystallinity went increasing with the time which can be observed from Fig. 11. It has been observed that the incorporation of nanoparticles in the starch-based nanocomposites reduces the biodegradability like in the case of Bentonite nanofillers in the Thermoplastic starch (TPS)/Ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) increased the interfacial adhesion and reduced the coalescence between EVA matrix and TPS phase and hence the biodegradation was delayed [141]. Also, TPS may undergo aging process resulting in accelerated long-chain amylose recrystallization, especially in the presence of glycerol and high levels of water. Recrystallization makes the starch less accessible for enzymatic breakdown, ultimately reducing the rate at which the starch disintegrates. Furthermore, a greater concentration of EVA in TPS/EVA blends can enhance the encapsulation capability of starch domains, thus impeding their breakdown. The degradation rate in compost environment was slowed, when the intermolecular hydrogen bonding was increased by the incorporation of Sugar palm starch nano fibrillated cellulose (SPNFCs) into sugar palm starch (SPS) biopolymer, and the biodegradation was retarded [142]. For nanoclays according to Chuayjulet al., they have a capability to act as a barrier and prevent moisture absorption which retards the biodegradation process [143]. Even organic nanomaterials like graphene were found to weaken the molecule-molecule interaction and carry out dissolution of amorphous regions in a biopolymer. Due to this, crystallinity increases and its biodegradation becomes more difficult. It can be concluded from the above studies that most of the nanocomposites of starch have a reduced rate of overall degradation but still a border line conclusion about this is difficult to make because, very less studies have gone into the direct degradation of starch nanocomposites.

IntroductionBiodegradation is a biochemical transformation in the mineralization of compounds by microorganisms. Mineralization of organic compounds under aerobic conditions produces carbon dioxide and water, and under anaerobic conditions, methane and carbon dioxide. The tracking of the enzymatic action of microorganisms, the predominant mechanism in this process, is measured over a specific period of time under standard conditions (ASTM/D-5488-94d). Biodegradability is also defined as the propensity of a material to break down its constituent molecules by natural processes (often microbial digestion). The metabolites released by degradation, if not toxic to the environment, are expected to be redistributed through the carbon, nitrogen and sulphur cycles. The main and combined abiotic and biotic mechanisms associated with polyesters degradation are chemical hydrolysis and enzymatic degradation. For natural polymers, like cellulose and starch, the biodegradation phase starts almost immediately, and the rate of biodegradation is high since depolymerization by extracellular enzymes and bioassimilation occurs quickly with no requirement for a conditioning lag phase. Degradation by chemical hydrolysis is considered the most relevant abiotic mechanism for biodegradable polymers such as polyesters, where a common example is PLA. The opposite can be said for readily biodegradable polymers such as cellulose and starch. Starch is the second-most abundant natural polymer after cellulose. It is produced as a storage polymer in several granular plants such as corn, cassava, cereal, rice and potato. It is an odorless and tasteless white powder, and insoluble in cold water or alcohol. Starch is a semi-crystalline polymer, with a crystallinity varying from 15 % to 45 % depending on the plant species from which it originates (Vall zabala, 2020). Morphologically, starch is composed of mostly microscopic spherical granules with diameters ranging from 2 to 100 μm, depending on the botanical origin. Chemically, starch molecules are composed of two main macromolecular components: amylose and amylopectin. Amylose has a linear or slightly branched structure consisting of 2 × 105-106 glucose units per molecule, which are joined together by ∼99 % α-D (1 → 4) glucosidic bonds and ∼1% α-D (1 → 6) glucosidic linkages. Amylopectin has a highly branched structure with approximately 106 glucose units per molecule, which are connected with α-D (1 → 4) linkages and 5-6% of α-D (1 → 6) glucosidic side chains (Wu et al., 2018). Generally, amylose and amylopectin constitute ∼20-25 % and ∼75-80 % of a starch granule, respectively. There are three reactive hydroxyl groups on the glucose unit of the starch chain: one primary and two secondary hydroxyl groups. These hydroxyl groups serve as anchoring platforms for surface modifications or cross-linking reactions (Ojogbo, Ogunsona, & Mekonnen, 2020). Starch molecules have two critical features that make them a unique and promising material for the production of composites. First, starch is naturally biodegradable in soil and water and can be easily degraded into sugars and organic acids, which is of utmost importance from an environmental viewpoint. Second, owing to its unique chemical characteristics, starch is amenable to a variety of chemical and enzymatic modifications that provide many opportunities to confer new functionalities on starch polymers. To meet the necessary requirements of green chemistry, renewable resources are increasingly in demand to enable the manufacture of sustainable composites. Starch, which seems to meet these expectations, can be employed as a green polyol component for the synthesis of PU-based materials. Thermoplastic starch (TPS) has also attracted considerable attention during the past two decades as an interesting alternative to synthetic polymers (Gironès et al., 2012). PUs are a diverse class of polymeric materials that possess urethane linkages within their backbone. PUs are generally composed of hard and soft segments. The soft segment consists of a polyol, such as a polyester or polyether, which renders flexibility to the PU’s structure; the hard segment is composed of a wide variety of isocyanate-based components that impart mechanical strength to the PU network. The use of a varying range of hard and soft segments with different chemistries gives rise to the development of PUs with a broad range of physical and mechanical properties (Costa et al., 2015; Sáenz-Pérez, Laza, García-Barrasa, Vilas, & León, 2017). For example, PUs can be either thermoplastic or irreversibly thermoset depending on the ratio of hard and soft segments in their structure. The versatile PU chemistry and its ability to form different types of molecular architectures enable PUs to meet the highly diversified demands of modern technologies, including coatings, adhesives, foams and thermoplastic elastomers (Dandeniyage et al., 2018; Kausar, 2018). It is worth mentioning that almost all traditional PUs are non-degradable; however, they can be specifically designed to show some degrees of degradation. Biodegradable PUs have recently gained great interest because of their sustainable features and potential for use in different biomedical applications. Biodegradable PUs can be devised with a simple manipulation of PU structure and/or its composition, particularly modification of the soft segment (Dou et al., 2019). Soft segments, which are composed of polyester or polyether polyols with a hydrolysable backbone, are more susceptible to microbial attack. Thus, the incorporation of a biodegradable unit (particularly an ester group) into the PU backbone is a pragmatic approach to impart higher susceptibility to microbial action under natural environmental conditions. The potential to introduce biodegradability and tailor a multitude of structures and mechanical properties makes PUs versatile polymers for developing starch-PU composites or hybrids (Mahajan & Gupta, 2015). Conventional PUs are synthesized through a step-growth polymerization reaction between isocyanate and polyol molecules in the presence of either a catalyst or UV light irradiation (Fig. 1a). Polyols that are commonly used for PU synthesis often have two or more OH groups. Isocyanates are another essential component for PU synthesis. They are often di-functional in nature, containing two NCO groups per molecule. They can be classified as aliphatic or aromatic isocyanates. Aromatic isocyanates, such as toluene diisocyanate (TDI) and diphenylmethane diisocyanate (MDI), tend to be more reactive towards polyols than their aliphatic counterparts, such as isophorone diisocyanate (IPDI) and hexamethylene diisocyanate (HDI) (Akindoyo et al., 2016). Isocyanates can react with OH groups to produce PUs at room temperature (and up to 50 °C), while, they generate allophanate, biuret, and isocyanate linkages at higher temperatures above 100 °C. If linear PUs are desired, the use of the low temperature is required. If high cross-linked PUs are desired, higher temperatures (100-150 °C) are indeed required (Engels et al., 2013). Synthesis of PUs can be carried out as one- or two-step reactions. In one-step synthesis, all required ingredients are mixed at the beginning; in two-step synthesis, the polyols are first reacted in excess with a diisocyanate component to prepare NCO-terminated PU prepolymers, after which a chain extender is added to produce a final long-chain PU (Janik, Sienkiewicz, & Kucinska-Lipka, 2013). The two-step reaction method is generally preferred because it allows more control over the reaction, and yields PUs with well-defined structural and physical properties (Akindoyo et al., 2016). Even though these PU materials are highly durable and safe, the main drawback of classic PU synthesis is the use of isocyanates, which are classified as carcinogenic and mutagenic. Prolonged exposure to isocyanate substances in the workplace can have dramatic impacts on health, such as asthma, dermatitis and acute poisoning. Therefore, despite the continuous efforts of the PU industry to improve the quality of PU raw materials (e.g., using bio-based diisocyanates derived from natural resources), the need for more environmentally friendly processes that address both the renewability of the starting material and the sustainability of the synthesis is urgent (Llevot & Meier, 2019). NIPUs, which are mainly synthesized through a ring-opening reaction between poly(cyclic carbonates) and polyamines, have been shown to have substantial green credentials (Fig. 1b). The phosgene-free and isocyanate-free reactions represent a suitable greener alternative for PU synthesis, with structures comparable to those produced by the polyaddition of diisocyanates and polyols (Ghasemlou, Daver, Ivanova, & Adhikari, 2019). The isocyanate-free reactions can be carried out at ambient temperatures although a moderately high temperature (ca. 60-80 °C) can achieve high conversion rate of NIPU (Cornille et al., 2016). More importantly, due to their hydrophilic nature, NIPUs tend to be more compatible with hydrophilic native starch in composites. We have recently reviewed the various green routes that have been used to synthesize NIPUs and their precursors to pave the way for their application in the PU industry (Ghasemlou et al., 2019a).

One of the most convenient way to reduce the usage of synthetic plastics is to blend them with renewable ones. Using a proportion of biopolymers in synthetic polymers would not only reduce the dependence on petroleum products but also reduce the amount of plastic waste. Here, the most critical question is: What happens to the degradation mechanism of synthetic polymers after the addition of biopolymer? Previous studies have shown that when biopolymer is mixed with synthetic one, the degradation rate of the synthetic polymer increases.19-23 It was suggested that microbes first create pores by consumption of biopolymer and thereby increase the surface area of the composite. Increased surface area enhances oxygen-based reactions, which could increase synthetic polymer chain oxidation. Because this is the slowest step in the degradation mechanism of synthetic polymers, any factor which increases the oxidation tendency of polymers also controls the degradation process of plastics. Hence, creating oxidized polymer chain ends in a degraded composite will make a synthetic polymer susceptible to biotic reactions. In the family of renewable based polymeric materials, starch has been considered as one of the most promising materials for the future because it is readily available and may form cost effective end products. As a synthetic counterpart, LDPE is a good candidate, as it is the most commonly used packaging material. There are many studies in the literature related to the addition of starch into polyethylene.24-36 However, in most of them, it was reported that the properties of polyethylene has begun to deteriorate with the incorporation of biopolymer. The deterioration is most commonly seen in gloss, transparency, tensile elongation, tensile strength, tear strength, and gas barrier properties.24-29 The main problem associated with the use of biopolymer as a filler is its hydrophilic nature and consequent incompatibility with the hydrophobic polymers. Recently, increased interest has focused on the use of biopolymers together with polymers containing reactive groups (e.g., maleic anhydride, glycidyl methacrylate, and hydroxyl) as compatibilizers due to the better dispersion of biopolymers in the polymer blends containing functional groups.30-36 However, the problem in poor mechanical properties in the blends could not be completely solved by the addition of these compatibilizers. The main purpose of this study is to prepare starch-containing LDPE films with good physical and mechanical properties. For this purpose, the effects of using compatibilizer, reinforcing filler, and plasticizer on these properties were investigated. Na+-montmorillonite (Na+mmt) type of clay was used as a reinforcing filler. To provide compatibility between LDPE and starch, MAgPE was first prepared and then incorporated into the formula. The resultant nanocomposite film having intercalated clay layers, plasticized starch phase and compatibilizer exhibited superior physico-mechanical properties.

The enzymatic degradation mechanism for natural polymers like starch primarily involves glycoside hydrolases. α-Amylase initiates the process by cleaving long starch polymers into shorter fragments [1][2][4][8]. These fragments are further hydrolyzed by enzymes specialized in breaking α-glycosidic bonds, including β-amylase, glucoamylase, and α-glucosidase [1][2][4]. Additionally, lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases (LPMOs) contribute by catalyzing oxidative cleavage of glucose linkages [1][2].  

The degradation rate and pattern depend on starch characteristics:  
- Botanical origin affects granule surface area and accessibility, influencing enzyme-substrate encounter probability [4][6].  
- Molecular size impacts kinetics, with larger molecules degrading slower [5].  
- Crystalline regions (e.g., retrograded starch) resist enzymatic attack more than amorphous regions [5][8].  
- Bond types (α-1,4 vs. α-1,6 linkages in amylose and amylopectin) affect susceptibility [4].  

Enzymatic hydrolysis occurs without a lag phase, as microbial enzymes readily depolymerize starch into assimilable sugars [9][10].

Fused deposition modelling (FDM) Fused Deposition modelling is another extrusion-based 3D printing technology, firstly presented by crump [94]. In FDM, melted thermoplastic materials are utilized and extruded through a nozzle with certain pressure in FDM. These melted thermoplastics change to a solid state when they are deposited on the fabrication platform of the printer. For fabricating the 3D structure, a layer-by-layer deposition of this melted thermoplastic is done in [95]. Most common thermoplastic materials for FDM contact of Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) filaments. Besides, polylactic acid (PLA) and polycarbonate (PC) function as filament for FDM printers. The schematic diagram of FDM printers is presented in Fig. 9 and FDM printers setup used in the literature for TENG development is demonstrated in Fig. 10. The fabrication process of FDM consists of several stages. Initially, thermoplastic filaments are feed to the printer’s head and then the nozzle temperature of FDM is adjusted to the desired temperature. Once the required temperature of the nozzle head is reached filaments are then fed to the extrusion head and nozzle, where they melt. These melted materials are then deposited in predetermined locations. Depositions of these materials are extruded from the nozzle in the form of thin strands and are deposited on the fabrication platform in a layer-by-layer manner. The extrusion head of FDM is also attached to the 3 axis system, which allows a printer head to move in the X, Y and Z axes. Most FDM printers can adjust several processing parameters, including the temperature adjustment of both nozzle and fabricating platform, speed of nozzle movement, speed of cooling fan and adjustment of layer height. Most commonly, the built platform for FDM printers are 200 × 200 × 200 mm and the normal layer height in FDM varies from 50 to 400 microns. Smaller layer height helps to improve the quality of printed material. There are some challenges associated with FDM, which includes the warping of melted materials extruded from the nozzle. During the solidification process, the size of the material shrinks down as different levels of printed materials cool down at different rates. The dimension of layers is also shrunk with different speeds. To overcome this challenge, precise monitoring of temperature for FDM systems are required which include the platform temperature adjustment and chamber temperature adjustment. Another challenge of FDM printing is to maintain the proper adhesion among the deposited layers. As deposition of material is done by layer-to-layer deposition, the previous layer is pressed, when melted filaments are extruded from the nozzle head. This means higher temperature builds the pressure on the previous layer, and the surface of this layer is re-melted which is responsible for the binding of the new layer and previously printed one. To avoid this problem, bond strength among different layers is always set lower than the base strength of filaments. Adding support structure is also required while creating some complex geometries as melted thermoplastics will not deposit directly on thin air. Fused deposition modeling (FDM) is considered one of the 3D printing techniques that can directly translate a computer-aided design into a 3D physical model of the required material through a layer-by-layer deposition process [6]. The main advantage of the FDM technique is the ability to accurately and rapidly fabricate 3D-designed scaffolds with complex porosity and pores interconnectivity [7]. Hence, the 3D-printed scaffolds by using the FDM technique show a 3D architecture that closely mimics the native cell environment. However, the FDM technique is restricted only to thermoplastic polymers [8]. Poly--caprolactone (PCL) is a thermoplastic, semi-crystalline, and biodegradable polyester polymer that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration for biomedical applications [9]. It has good biocompatibility, appropriate mechanical properties, and unique viscoelastic properties; therefore, it is frequently used in the field of bone TE [10]. Also, the PCL has a low melting point at 60 °C and high thermal stability, which makes it an ideal thermoplastic polymer for 3D printing applications [11]. However, the PCL has a hydrophobic surface that impairs its cellular activity and makes its surface modification necessary to improve its surface properties and subsequent cellular behavior [12, 13]. Different surface modification techniques have been introduced to enhance the surface properties of biomaterials [14]. Of these methods, a plasma surface deposition can be effective in tailoring the surface properties, and subsequently improving and enhancing its interaction with cells [15, 16]. Plasma treatment shows a convenient method for modifying polymer surface properties in terms of hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity, surface roughness, surface energy, and surface charge [15]. In addition to surface functionalization required for cell adhesion which could be tailored by the choice of the plasma gas [17, 18]. The plasma surface deposition can be performed using a non-thermal plasma focus (PF) device, where the ions and radicals have a temperature near room temperature which enables the use of plasma deposition for thermally sensitive polymers and reduces the risk of their thermal degradation [19, 20]. Also, the PF device can be used for the deposition of the nanoparticles on a substrate surface, which allows surface topography modification in addition to chemical modifications [18, 21].

The expansion of global markets for additive manufacturing (AM), also referred to as 3D printing, is expected to grow at a very large and rapid pace over the next few years [1]. The ability to produce complex and customizable designs at a low production cost has become the main attraction of this technology [2]. From aerospace to biomedical as well as electronic packaging and household products, everything can be fabricated through computer-aided design (CAD) before being “printed” into 3D objects without the need to manufacture the mold first, reducing production time, cost, and material expenses [3, 4]. Among the various 3D printing techniques, fused deposition modeling (FDM) is widely used because it is conceptually basic, easy to handle, and economically affordable [5, 6]. The FDM manufacturing technique is effortless because the thermoplastic filament, acting as the “ink,” is continuously fed into the extrusion chamber at a predefined temperature. The material melts to form a highly viscous fluid and is deposited on the printing bed, solidifying after printing [7, 8]. Therefore, the development of the filament with excellent mechanical properties is crucial, in order to improve and broaden the functionality of 3D printing applications6. Previously, polylactic acid (PLA) has been used as filaments in 3D printing due to the material's sustainability, biocompatibility, and nontoxic properties, which make it a suitable candidate for many applications [9, 10]. The printability of PLA is undeniable since it possesses a low melting temperature, good adhesion to the printing bed, and a low degree of warpage and delamination [11, 12]. However, PLA has some serious drawbacks that limit its application, such as its inherent brittleness, low deformation at breaking, poor impact resistance, and slow degradability [13, 14]. Several approaches have been studied to overcome these disadvantages, particularly to improve the toughness and degradability of PLA. The addition of additives, copolymerization, and blending are among the methods which have been proposed by researchers [15, 16]. The melt blending technique is the most preferred method, as it is more economical and easier to implement, requiring only an instrument similar to an industrial plastic mixer. Blending PLA with elastomeric materials, such as rubber, is a promising approach for improving the ductility and rate of degradation of PLA [14, 17]. Rubber toughening is a viable method to enhance the mechanical properties of PLA by incorporating rubber particles into the polymer matrix. The rubber particles that disperse in the polymer matrix act as stress concentration spots, which initiate crazes or shear bands in the matrix and this prevents premature cracking. A large amount of energy is dissipated during the deformation process; thus, the toughness of the materials is enhanced [18, 19]. One of the toughening mechanisms involved when rubber particles are present in the polymer matrix is known as “interfacial adhesion.” Strong bonds between the rubber particles and the polymer matrix ensure the efficient load transfer when stress is applied, improving the toughness of the materials. In addition, the distribution of rubber particles is important, to make certain that the optimum toughening effect takes place, thus liquid natural rubber (LNR) is regarded as an ideal elastomer due to its liquid form, which improves the polymer mixing and processing.

Additive manufacturing (AM) is an advanced mode of production that is characterized by rapid prototype fabrication, low energy consumption, and personalized design customization. AM technology is always dependent on computer-aided design data, including 3D models, to build the prototypes. Slicing software divides such 3D models into many layers that contain printing nozzle position coordinates, printing temperature, and printing speed, which can be used to build a sample layer-by-layer.1-3 As a kind of AM, fused deposition modelling (FDM) is a rapid prototype technology characterized by a facile approach, easy operation, low cost, and low production time that is capable of manufacturing functional structural parts with complex geometries.4-8 Currently, the need for FDM has grown substantially because FDM has attractive advantages, which include the ability to easily make molds; therefore, FDM is used for many applications, such as automobiles, aerospace vehicles, medical implants, and household appliances.9, 10 In the forming process, the printing feedstock is generally plastic and made into a filament bundle, which is partially melted and then extruded from a printing nozzle controlled by an xyz motor system (the main components of the printing nozzle are shown in Figure 1). Afterward, the semi-liquid polymer is fused onto the building plate and then stacked layer-by-layer to form a physical entity.11 Normally, ABS and PLA are used as feedstocks. Unfortunately, PLA and ABS still do not yet fully meet realistic requirements, since PLA is an eco-friendly polymer that has a high printing temperature and ABS exhibits great mechanical properties but has biodegradability issues; these flaws are the main factors that restrict the application of PLA and ABS in many fields. Recently, some newly developed plastics have been applied to FDM, such as high-impact polystyrene (HIPS), polycarbonate, polyamide, polyether ether ketone, ethylene vinyl acetate, polypropylene, and their blends,12-19 but the low applicability, nondegradable nature, and high printing temperature of these plastics still suppress their printability. Therefore, the preparation of new printing materials with biodegradability, wide applicability, and low printing temperature has become a popular topic. Currently, resource crises associated with oil-based energy have triggered investigations into biodegradable polymers. PBS, a biocompatible polyester, is a superiorly biodegradable plastic that provides solutions for “white pollution.”20 PBS is from the condensation polymerization of succinic acid and 1,4-butanediol and is a potential candidate for manufacturing environmentally friendly products,21 such as agricultural films, biomedical materials, packing, fibers, and injection-molded products.22 The application of PBS in the FDM process is possible because of the ductility, relatively low melting point, good processing performance, and eco-friendly nature of PBS.23, 24 Unfortunately, the melt strength of synthesized PBS is too low to meet the demands of FDM; a printed object is made by stacking the fuse extruded from printer nozzles, and if the melt strength is insufficient, the fuse stacking could collapse. Hence, it is extremely important to enhance the melt strength of PBS, and the application of adding inorganic fillers into polymer matrixes is an effective method to promote composite mechanical properties.25 Talc is an efficient filler that has a low price, good dispersion, and a unique layer structure; talc is formed by magnesium silicate and has the following chemical formula: Mg3Si4O10(OH)2.26, 27 Likewise, polymer composites containing talc represent a new direction of research due to their unexpected properties, including apparent improvement in mechanical performance, thermal stability, barrier properties, and biodegradability. In this work, PBS/talc composite printing filaments with various talc concentrations were prepared to test their formabilities by using a commercial 3D printer. Afterward, the thermal, rheological, and morphological properties were investigated. Finally, the differences in mechanical properties were analyzed by comparing the injection-molded and 3D-printed specimens.

Fused deposition modeling (FDM), is a highly regarded extrusion-based 3D printing technology. It is the most widely adopted technique because of its simple fabrication process, dimensional stability, inexpensiveness, and minimal material wastage.1, 2 During FDM process, a heated nozzle is supplied with a continuous polymeric filament, causing the polymer to melt. Subsequently, it is meticulously deposited layer by layer onto a printing surface, leading to the formation of three-dimensional objects.3-5 The characteristics and properties of the FDM printed product primarily depend on the selection of the appropriate polymer for the filament. Initially, the available materials were limited to polymers. Yet, within a short period, scientists have rapidly advanced in the development of tailor-made filaments such as polymer composites. Polymer composites enhance the properties of the printing material by reinforcing fillers of micro or nano size into a polymer matrix. Essentially, the development of bio-based polymer nanocomposite materials could be a promising advancement in the fabrication of filaments for FDM. The term “bio-based polymer nanocomposites” refers to composite materials where either filler, polymer matrices or both are derived from biological sources.6 The most commonly used biopolymers in 3D printing are polylactic acid (PLA), poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), poly(caprolactone) (PCL), and poly(hydroxyalkanoates) (PHAs). PLA is an extensively used bio-based aliphatic polymer in FDM process. It is derived from lactic acid, which is extracted from organic and renewable resources such as potato starch, sugar cane, and cassava.7 PLA exhibits exceptional properties such as high strength and hardness, renewability, and low toxicity. Nevertheless, the industrial application of this material is limited due to its brittleness, low heat deflection temperature, poor crystallization, low elongation at break, and restricted drawability. To enrich the functionality of PLA, researchers have incorporated reinforcements such as cellulose, metals, carbon, and continuous fibers. This has led to improvements in properties such as thermal conductivity, electrical conductivity, mechanical strength, and degradation time. In recent years, bio-carbon, also known as biochar has emerged as the most enthralling reinforcement filler in the preparation of biobased polymer composites. Bio-carbon has garnered significant attention as a substitute filler for other non-environmentally and non-economically viable carbon fillers like carbon nanotubes, carbon black, and graphene. Biochar possesses a high specific surface area in addition to high thermal stability.8 This environment- friendly biocarbon is produced from biomass,9 includes various solid wastes, such as industrial and agro-base wastes, which have a high ligno-cellulosic content and are highly suitable for the production of carbon. Among all biomass sources, agro-waste is an intriguing source of biomass as it is inexpensive and plentiful in nations such as India that practice agriculture. Bio-carbon is synthesized by thermochemical pyrolysis of biomass under an inert atmosphere. Several forms of biocarbon, such as carbon nanotubes, carbon dots, carbon black, carbon nanoparticles, and graphene are obtained through the pyrolysis of biomass. The nanosized carbon materials yield superior physio-chemical, biological, thermal, electrical, and mechanical properties compared to conventional materials.10 Nanofillers made of carbon nanoparticles are widely employed in various polymer matrices as they can form strong connections with lighter materials and with themselves, carbon nanomaterials are well suited for the synthesis of materials with a high strength-to-weight ratio. As a result, carbon nanoparticles produced from biowaste have proven to be beneficial in a multitude of cutting-edge industries, including biomedicine, energy storage, material science, and numerous modern technologies. The production of carbon nanomaterials uses a variety of biomass materials as precursors, such as spent coffee grounds, banana peel, walnut shell, wheat straw, sugarcane bagasse, rice husk, coconut shell, and corn cob.11-16
Additive manufacturing (AM), also known as 3D printing, is one of the most promising and revolutionary technologies for manufacturing three-dimensional parts with unique structures and various properties.1-3 This technology has aroused great interest in both industry and academia as it can create complex shaped objects and reduce the use of harmful chemicals4-6 Among AM techniques, fused deposition modeling (FDM) is highly regarded for its cost-effectiveness, rapid prototyping capability, and ease of use. A typical FDM process involves melting filament at a heated point, and then the molten material is extruded and systematically deposited layer by layer onto the construction platform using a printing nozzle. These layers, following deposition, undergo a cooling process to ultimately form a solidified final product.7-9 Thermoplastic polymers such as polylactic acid (PLA), acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), polycarbonate (PC), polyetherimide (PEI), polyether ether ketone (PEEK), and polyamide (PA) are currently common materials for FDM 3D printing. Among these, PLA is the most widely used FDM 3D printing polymer due to its superior biocompatibility, biodegradability, and mechanical properties.10-12 Nonetheless, PLA still faces several limitations, including insufficient strength, low toughness, and long crystallization process.13-17 Extensive research and development have been devoted to overcoming these drawbacks.18-22 The research results have shown that inorganic filler modification,23-25 especially one-dimensional (1D) inorganic nanomaterials such as carbon nanotubes, whiskers, and so on, is an effective way to improve the comprehensive mechanical properties of PLA. Only a small amount of addition can significantly enhance the strength of composite materials. However, this enhancement is often accompanied by a decrease in elongation at break.26-28 In addition, the fabrications of artificial synthetic nanofibers such as carbon nanotubes and whiskers are generally relatively harsh, requiring specific conditions and complex processes, resulting in high preparation costs and limited applications. Hence, the use of natural inorganic nanofibers in polymer composites to replace synthetic nanofibers receives an increasing attention because of their advantages such as abundance, extreme hardness, high thermal stability, and low-cost.
The main goal of this study is to develop PVA for 3-dimensional printing (3D printing). 3D printing is a rapidly developing technology that is quick inexpensive and can produce complex parts without geometry limitations.14 Fused deposition modeling (FDM), an important type of 3D printing that uses layer-by-layer deposition of extruded filament to build up a part, has been widely studied because it is fast, safe, inexpensive, and simple to operate.15 FDM has been utilized for tissue engineering such as fabricating scaffolds with controllable pore shapes and sizes.16-19 However, the multi-hydroxyl groups lead to strong inter and intra-molecular hydrogen bonding in PVA, narrowing the gap between the melting point of PVA and its decomposition temperature; thus, products fabricated from this material cannot be prepared by melt processing. Therefore, FDM of PVA scaffold remains a significant challenge. Previous studies have shown that intermolecular complexion and plasticization are effective to realize melt-processing of PVA.20-22 To meet the requirements for use with thermal processing equipment or improving the thermal processability and mechanical properties of PVA, complex plasticizers were chosen. Chen23 used an amide containing group(Ac) combined with water to realize the PVA melt spinning. Wang24 used glycerol/caprolactam/water as a plasticizer for PVA to retard water evaporation, which is beneficial to the melt-processing of PVA. Jiang25 examined using urea/ethanolamine as a high-efficiency plasticizer to produce PVA products with excellent mechanical properties. Zhou26 used glycerol/urea to improve the rheological and mechanical properties of PVA/starch products. In this research, glycerol is chosen as a blend plasticizer for PVA, as it is product of metabolism and is nontoxic. Water is the key plasticizer as it enhances the plasticization effect and inhibits the precipitation of the other components in the plasticizer. Our earlier research proved that, to achieve smooth FDM processing without buckling, the feedstock material should possess an appropriate compressive modulus and viscosity.27 By adjusting the composition of the plasticizers, different mechanical and rheological properties can be obtained for PVA. Thus, PVA filament feedstock with appropriate properties and suitable for FDM processing can be successfully prepared. It is believed that this work will not only provide an effective strategy for thermally processing PVA but also a novel FDM-compatible material for use in the biomedical field.

In FDM, melted thermoplastic materials are utilized and extruded through a nozzle with certain pressure in FDM. The fabrication process of FDM consists of several stages. Initially, thermoplastic filaments are feed to the printer’s head and then the nozzle temperature of FDM is adjusted to the desired temperature. Once the required temperature of the nozzle head is reached filaments are then fed to the extrusion head and nozzle, where they melt. These melted materials are then deposited in predetermined locations. Depositions of these materials are extruded from the nozzle in the form of thin strands and are deposited on the fabrication platform in a layer-by-layer manner. The extrusion head of FDM is also attached to the 3 axis system, which allows a printer head to move in the X, Y and Z axes. Most FDM printers can adjust several processing parameters, including the temperature adjustment of both nozzle and fabricating platform, speed of nozzle movement, speed of cooling fan and adjustment of layer height. Most commonly, the built platform for FDM printers are 200 × 200 × 200 mm and the normal layer height in FDM varies from 50 to 400 microns. Smaller layer height helps to improve the quality of printed material. There are some challenges associated with FDM, which includes the warping of melted materials extruded from the nozzle. During the solidification process, the size of the material shrinks down as different levels of printed materials cool down at different rates. The dimension of layers is also shrunk with different speeds. To overcome this challenge, precise monitoring of temperature for FDM systems are required which include the platform temperature adjustment and chamber temperature adjustment. Another challenge of FDM printing is to maintain the proper adhesion among the deposited layers. As deposition of material is done by layer-to-layer deposition, the previous layer is pressed, when melted filaments are extruded from the nozzle head. This means higher temperature builds the pressure on the previous layer, and the surface of this layer is re-melted which is responsible for the binding of the new layer and previously printed one. To avoid this problem, bond strength among different layers is always set lower than the base strength of filaments. Adding support structure is also required while creating some complex geometries as melted thermoplastics will not deposit directly on thin air. Export citation and abstractBibTeXRIS Using biodegradable polymers as biomaterials has contributed to significant advancements in the fields of regenerative medicine and tissue engineering [1]. In particular, polycaprolactone (PCL) has received considerable attention due to its excellent mechanical and structural properties, and tuneable degradation kinetics. Moreover, the non-immunogenicity of PCL, combined with the possibility of using it as an interporous scaffold material, has resulted in better tissue ingrowth [2-4]. The above-mentioned benefits, in addition to the inexpensive production routes of PCL, have encouraged many research groups to investigate its potential applications in numerous fields of tissue engineering [2, 5]. However, the bioactivity of the tissue-engineered constructs is threatened by the hydrophobic nature of PCL [4, 6-8]. In general, it is known that a moderate surface hydrophilicity allows for an increased adsorption of proteins without modifying their natural conformation. In turn, this increases the cell affinity towards the surface, leading to stimulated cell adhesion and cell proliferation [9, 10]. As a consequence, PCL hydrophobicity negatively impacts cell-material interactions [1]. In order to overcome this issue, surface modification is required. Several approaches have previously been investigated, including wet-chemical treatments, and ion beam, x-ray and gamma radiation. However, the wet-chemical treatment route generates large amounts of hazardous chemical waste and often impacts on bulk properties such as structural strength and elasticity, while most radiation methods can cause severe degradation of the polymer [11]. As an alternative, non-thermal plasma treatment has shown to be a promising method because it is highly versatile, only modifying the top few nanometer layers of the polymer without altering the bulk properties [4, 6, 12, 13]. By choosing an appropriate working gas, this treatment incorporates oxygen-containing functional groups, either directly or via post-oxidation [14]. These polar groups increase the surface energy and wettability and thus improve protein adsorption and cytocompatibility [7, 12]. Many studies have shown that plasma treatment of PCL performed at low pressure enhances the adhesion and proliferation of a wide variety of cell types [4, 8, 12, 15, 16]. As an alternative to low-pressure plasma treatments using expensive vacuum equipment, a few authors have reported that atmospheric pressure plasma treatment is also effective, giving rise to high cellular adhesion and proliferation [7, 17, 18]. Medium pressure plasma is rarely used to treat PCL, despite its potential to easily acquire a larger volume of plasma compared to atmospheric pressure plasma treatments, with relatively cost-effective pumping systems [19]. Therefore, our research group has previously used a dielectric barrier discharge (DBD), operating in different gases at medium pressure, in order to modify PCL surface properties. Both air and argon plasmas introduce oxygen-containing functionalities onto the PCL surface and thus increase its wettability, positively influencing the adhesion and the proliferation of human foreskin fibroblasts and mouse calvaria pre-osteoblasts [3, 20]. Once an efficient surface modification is accomplished, a crucial and final prerequisite for the use of PCL in vitro and in vivo is required: the material sterility [21, 22]. Consequently, after sterilization, PCL should maintain the introduced surface properties that determine to a large extent the success of the implant. Despite the importance of the material properties, the impact of sterilization on the PCL structure and surface is largely overlooked in the literature, as the majority of studies solely focus on the microbial activity to check for the sterilization efficacy [23].
Integrin binding domains, incorporated inside aECMs are involved in bidirectional transmembrane signalling between cells and their environment and play an important role in cell growth.31 Integrins are involved in the regulation of physiological processes such as migration, proliferation, survival, and apoptosis. The focal adhesion mechanisms between the ECM ligand and the integrin receptor heterodimers, consisting of α and β integrin subunits, have been extensively studied.32,33 Linear RGD peptides, cyclic RGD peptides, and peptidomimetic ligands have evolved progressively for binding integrin subunits.34 Flanking linear RGD peptides with amino acids, such as glycine (G) at the N terminus and serine (S) at the C terminus, results in a decrease in half-maximum inhibitory concentration (IC50) values by 3 and 4 folds for αvβ3 and α5β1 integrin subunits, respectively.35 Lower IC50 values indicate a higher affinity to integrin subunits and the lowest IC50 value is observed for heptapeptide GRGDSPK, which is 7 folds lower than for tripeptide RGD in the case of αvβ3.35 Similarly, the cyclization of linear RGD peptides (RGDfK) and incorporation of one D-amino acid residue between Asp (D) and Lys (K) improves affinity to integrin subunits and increases stability towards enzymatic degradation.35,36 Monocyclic RGD peptides show moderate to low IC50 values towards multiple integrin subunits, such as αvβ3, αvβ5, αvβ6, and α5β1. The lowest IC50 values are observed for αvβ3 subunits and cyclization improves integrin αvβ3 binding affinity in the range of 1.5-6.0 nM and integrin α5β1 binding affinity in the range of 141-236 nM.35 Similar to flanking in linear RGD, flanking in cyclic RGD peptides with linear polyproline improves cell spreading and focal adhesions in rat embryo fibroblasts in comparison to other spacers like PEG.37 Another class of high affinity and selective integrin-binding ligands are the peptidomimetics, which can distinguish between different integrin subtypes in vitro and in vivo.38,39 It is important to understand the role of integrin-mediated adhesion to its corresponding ligands in the ECM for achieving directed cell fate in tissue engineering applications. For example, the ability of cells to sense the mechanical properties of its fibronectin based ECM is mediated by the synergy between the α5β1 and αv-class integrin subunits.40 Similarly, the inter-dependence of integrins (α5β1, αvβ3) employed during focal adhesions is explored on 2D platforms with integrin specific RGD-coupled gold nanoparticles on PEG gels. The study revealed that during focal adhesion, the recruitment of αvβ3 integrins occurs on patterned substrates that are exclusive for α5β1, but the vice versa is not true.41 In addition, 3D hyaluronic acid hydrogels with specific integrin activation (α3/α5β1) induced sprouting in an endothelial cell angiogenic model in vitro and enabled the formation of non-leaky blood vessels in stroke models.8 Such examples show the importance of integrin-mediated cell adhesion and migration, which in turn determines cell fate. In this report, a new class of integrin selective engineered bicyclic peptides with one loop containing the integrin-binding RGD peptide is employed to study neuronal growth in 3D PEG-based hydrogels and Anisogels. These peptides have demonstrated greater conformational rigidity, metabolic stability, and most importantly, high integrin selectivity. The primary loop consists of an RGD peptide flanked with cysteine residues that bind to a tri-covalent scaffold (1,3,5-tris(bromomethyl)benzene). The secondary loop consists of a tri amino-acid sequence, which is screened using a ‘random approach’ and imparts the potential to affect the RGD selectivity towards different integrin subunits (αvβ3 or α5β1).42,43 Elastin-like recombinamers (ELR), produced with recombinant proteins and coupled with bicyclic RGD peptides selective for α5β1 show an increase in HUVEC proliferation at early periods of culture.44 Here, we describe for the first time the effect of bicyclic RGD peptides for nerve growth in synthetic 3D PEG hydrogels to study the affinity towards selective integrin sites. Soft, synthetic, degradable multi-arm PEG hydrogels are enzymatically crosslinked using transglutaminase and conjugated with different bicyclic RGD peptides. Domains cleavable by MMP 1, MMP 2, and plasmin are incorporated in the PEG precursors to enable on cell-demand degradation at the crosslinking arms. The MMP 1 and MMP 2 sensitive domains enable extensive cell growth inside the hydrogel. Expansion of both mouse fibroblasts and primary nerve cells from chick DRGs is investigated and compared with linear and monocyclic RGD and a specific fibronectin fragment FNIII9*-10/12-1429 (FN*). Bicyclic RGD conjugated gels show superior nerve and fibroblast growth. Also, cell growth and innervation in PEG gels are dependent on the type of proteolytic cleavable MMP-sensitive peptide present in the crosslinker. Finally, fully synthetic Anisogels are prepared by mixing and orienting short, magneto-responsive polycaprolactone (PCL) fibers (diameter ∼5 μm, length ∼50 μm, 1 vol%) before crosslinking of the surrounding PEG hydrogels, modified with the bicyclic peptides and optimal degradation domain VPMS↓MRGG (K2). Embedded DRGs inside Anisogels, tethered with bicyclic RGD peptides (K-P2 RGD), linear RGD (K-RGD) and fibronectin fragment (FN*) demonstrate unidirectional nerve growth.
Biodegradable polymers play a crucial role in the development of materials for biomedical applications. This study investigates the enzymatic biodegradation, bioactivity, and cytotoxicity of poly(butylene succinate-dilinoleic succinate) (PBS-DLS) copolymers modified with poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG). Two copolymer variations with different segmental compositions (70 wt.% and 60 wt.% of hard segments) are synthesized. After modifying the copolymers with PEG, the presence of a lipase catalyst accelerated degradation after 20 days, evidenced by reduced residual content. Gel permeation chromatography analysis showed up to 40% decrease in molecular weight, while gravimetric analysis indicated a mass loss of up to 10%. Morphological examination revealed that the enzymatic breakdown, facilitated by hydrolase activity (boosted by the presence of PEG), resulted in surface erosion, holes, and changes in spherulitic morphology. Bioactivity studies demonstrated the formation of biomimetic calcium/phosphate (Ca/P) crystals. Copolymers with higher crystallinity (70 wt.% hard segments) favored tricalcium phosphate-like crystal formation, while those with lower crystallinity (60 wt.% hard segments) are more susceptible to hydroxyapatite precipitation. In vitro cytotoxicity tests exhibited excellent cell viability and attachment for all copolymers. The ability to control degradation through PEG modification, along with their bioactivity and cell compatibility, positions them as promising candidates for diverse biomedical applications. Biodegradable polymers are defined as natural or synthetic polymers that can be broken down by biological processes, typically into harmless natural compounds, over time.[1] These polymers have a wide range of biomedical applications, including drug delivery systems, tissue engineering scaffolds, sutures, and various implantable devices. They are designed to degrade gradually within the body, which can be advantageous for controlled release of drugs or supporting tissue regeneration.[2] Aliphatic polyesters have emerged as leading candidates due to their high susceptibility to enzymatic hydrolysis and degradation by microorganisms.[3] Commercially available biodegradable polyesters such as poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA), poly(caprolactone) (PCL), poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(propylene carbonate) (PPC), and poly(hydroxyalkanoates) (PHAs) have shown great potential.[4] Besides biodegradability, for successful medical applications, other material properties such as biocompatibility, bioactivity, carefully considered mechanical properties, and processability needs to be considered during the design and fabrication process. By addressing these properties diligently, it becomes possible to develop medical devices that not only exhibit sustainability and biodegradability but also fulfill the functional requirements for effective medical applications.[5, 6]
Alginate, a biocompatible polymer naturally derived from algae, is widely used as a synthetic analogue of the extracellular matrix in tissue engineering. Integrin-binding peptide motifs, including RGD, a derivative of fibronectin, are typically grafted to the alginate polymer through carbodiimide reactions between peptide amines and alginate uronic acids. However, lack of chemo-selectivity of carbodiimide reactions can lead to side reactions that lower peptide bioactivity. To overcome these limitations, we developed an approach for copper-free, strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC)-mediated conjugation of azide-modified adhesive peptides (azido-cyclo-RGD, Az-cRGD) onto alginate. Successful conjugation of azide-reactive cyclooctynes onto alginates using a heterobifunctional crosslinker was confirmed by azido-coumarin fluorescent assay, NMR, and through click reactions with azide-modified fluorescent probes. Compared to cyclo-RGD peptides directly conjugated to alginate polymers with standard carbodiimide chemistry, Az-cyclo-RGD peptides exhibited higher bioactivity, as demonstrated by cell adhesion and proliferation assays. Finally, Az-cRGD peptides enhanced the effects of recombinant bone morphogenetic proteins on inducing osteogenesis of osteoblasts and bone marrow stromal stem cells in 3D alginate gels. SPAAC-mediated click approaches for peptide-alginate bioconjugation overcome the limitations of previous alginate bioconjugation approaches and potentially expand the range of ligands that can be grafted to alginate polymers for tissue engineering applications. Since the early 2000s, there has been an increasing interest in biodegradable polymers and materials based on them in regenerative medicine [1]. Unlike biologically inert implants, these biomaterials are designed for controlled degradation and promote the growth of new tissues or support the growth of the body’s own cells [2,3,4,5,6,7]. In addition to biodegradability, materials for tissue engineering should have biocompatibility, i.e., they should be incorporated into the body without causing adverse clinical implications [4, 8], and biological potency, such as antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and antitumor potency [9, 10]. Two classes of biodegradable polymers should be distinguished: synthetic and natural. The former are produced from raw materials obtained from oil resources (non-renewable), and the latter are produced from biological resources (renewable). As a rule, natural polymers are inferior in physical and mechanical properties to synthetic ones [11]. However, the properties that make synthetic polymers more preferable for many practical applications lead to difficulties in their utilization, prolonged biodegradation, and, consequently, environmental accumulation [11, 12].
Developing multifunctional nanoparticles (NPs) to improve therapeutic efficacy is highly desirable in cancer therapy. In an attempt to respond to such a challenge, a novel copolymer, D-α-tocopherol polyethylene glycol succinate-SS-poly(lactide) (TPGS-SS-PLA) with a disulfide linkage between the TPGS and PLA units, was synthesized for paclitaxel (PTX) delivery. PTX-loaded NPs were fabricated using a nanoprecipitation method to form a particle size of ∼130 nm with good in vitro stability, which can be disassociated under intracellular reductive conditions to release PTX rapidly. The detached TPGS can further promote the drug retention and cytotoxicity through its P-glycoprotein inhibiting property. Integrin-specific targeting peptide, cyclic RGD (cRGD), was further conjugated to the surface of the NPs for targeting the drug delivery. The RGD-decorated NPs exhibited enhanced cellular uptake, PTX accumulation and cell cytotoxicity as compared to non-targeted NPs on murine melanoma B16F10 cells, PTX-sensitive human ovarian A2780 cells and PTX-resistant A2780/T cells. In vivo evaluation of the targeted NPs further showed an extended half-life, increased AUC (area under the concentration-time curve), and significant tumor growth inhibition in mouse sarcoma S180- and B16F10-tumor bearing mice, with reduced side effects as compared to Taxol® and non-targeted NPs. These results indicate that the RGD decorated redox-sensitive NPs could deliver chemotherapies specifically inside the cell via receptor-mediated endocytosis with enhanced efficacy, especially in integrin αvβ3/αvβ5-rich tumor cells. Such a targeted nanocarrier against receptor clustering prepared from a non-cytotoxic and biodegradable copolymer might have great potential in cancer treatment. Among them, biodegradable polymeric NPs have attracted considerable attention for drug delivery due to their good drug encapsulation capability and stability, and ease of surface modification for site-specific drug delivery in passive and active targeting. Passive targeting indicates that NPs can penetrate the tumor vasculature through the leaky endothelium and accumulate in certain solid tumors by an enhanced permeation and retention (EPR) effect. Active targeting involves drug delivery to a specific site in light of molecular recognition with a suitable targeting ligand which can bind to its receptor on the tumor cells and endothelium.10,11 One common methodology for successful active targeting is to conjugate specific ligands, such as small molecules, antibodies and peptides, to the NP surface through chemical modification.12-15 Among these ligands, as one of the most popular ligands in drug delivery systems, synthetic peptides containing the arginine-glycine-aspartate (RGD) motif has been identified as an attractive candidate. The RGD peptide exhibits a high binding affinity and selectivity for αvβ3 and αvβ5 integrin receptors, which serve as markers of angiogenesis, tumor development, and metastasis.16 The linear peptide for specific accumulation in tumors is limited because of a low affinity and high biodegradability. Compared with the linear RGD peptide, cyclic RGD (cRGD) has already been proven to improve tumor targeting efficacy due to a high resistance to proteolysis and conformational restriction.17 Therefore, when polymeric NPs are decorated or co-administrated with RGD, the tissue penetrating and targeting abilities of drug-loaded NPs may be improved.18,19 Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is the best known polymer of aliphatic polyesters.20 Its high biocompatibility and biodegradability, renewable origins, good mechanical properties and the ability to be dissolved in common solvents for processing make PLA widely used as a drug delivery carrier.21 Despite its well-established importance, PLA still has some drawbacks in particular applications, such as the autocatalytic effect, acidic degradation products and slow degradation rate.22 Increased investigations have reported that the introduction of D-α-tocopherol polyethylene glycol 1000 succinate (vitamin E TPGS or simply TPGS) into the hydrophobic PLA backbone may overcome these drawbacks. TPGS, which has been approved as a safe pharmaceutical adjuvant in drug formulation by the FDA, is a water-soluble derivative of the natural vitamin E, formed by the esterification of vitamin E succinate with polyethylene glycol 1000.23-25 TPGS can act as a P-glycoprotein (P-gp) inhibitor and has served as an excipient for overcoming multidrug resistance (MDR) and for increasing the oral bioavailability of many anticancer drugs.25,26 Our previous studies confirmed that PLA-TPGS NPs have exhibited enhanced drug encapsulation efficiency and strengthened the overall treatment efficacy in tumors.27
In recent years, regeneration of damaged or lost tissue by tissue engineering is of intense interest to biomedical materials science researchers [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]. Guided tissue regeneration (GTR) is an approach whereby cells are cultivated on temporary scaffolds at the site of damaged or lost tissue for regeneration of the tissue [6], [7]. For this purpose, biodegradable polymers exhibiting controllable degradation behavior, good cell attachment, and excellent biocompatibility are desirable materials for scaffolds. Such scaffolds are used to supply cells to a desired location in the body and to provide a space for cell growth and tissue formation. It is well known that some growth factors improve the early healing process and regeneration of damaged tissue [8], [9], [10], [11], [12]. Growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), insulin-like growth factor (IGF), transforming growth factor (TGF) and fibroblast growth factor (FGF) are known to exhibit functions such as regulation of proliferation, chemotaxis and differentiation of various pluripotent cells [12], [13]. Aliphatic polyesters such as polyglycolide (PGA), poly-l-lactide (PLLA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) and their copolymers have been frequently applied as implantable carriers for drug delivery systems and for surgical repair due to their good biodegradation properties, relatively high biocompatibility, high mechanical strength, and excellent shaping and molding properties [14], [15], [16], [17], [18]. Polydepsipeptides are copolymers consisting of amino acids and hydroxy acids that possess biodegradability similar to that of aliphatic polyesters and functionality as polypeptides. We previously synthesized biodegradable copolymers of depsipeptide and lactide, poly(depsipeptide-co-lactide)s, by ring-opening copolymerization of l-lactide (LA) with cyclodepsipeptides consisting of glycolic acid (Glc) and aspartic acid (Asp) or lysine (Lys) to give poly[(Glc-alt-Asp)-co-lactide] (PGDLA) and poly[(Glc-alt-Lys)-co-lactide] (PGKLA) (Fig. 1) with reactive (hydrophilic and ionic) side-chain groups [19], [20], [21], [22]. The poly(depsipeptide-co-lactide)s obtained exhibited higher non-enzymatic degradability compared to PLLA depending on the depsipeptide unit content of the copolymers [20]. We investigated the cell attachment and growth on films and porous sponges composed of PGDLA and PGKLA and reported the potential utility of these copolymers as scaffolds for tissue regeneration [23], [24]. Other works on tissue engineering using biodegradable matrices containing amino acids or proteins have also been reported [25], [26], [27], [28], [29], [30]. To achieve efficient cell growth and cell differentiation, sustained release of growth factors from depots or matrices is effective [31], [32], [33], [34], [35]. In this study, to evaluate the utility of PGDLA and PGKLA as biodegradable scaffolds exhibiting the sustained release of growth factors, the entrapment and release of proteins into and from the matrices were investigated. We employed three types of growth factors, basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), epidermal growth factor (EGF) and nerve growth factor (NGF), which stimulate the proliferation of mesenchymal-derived cells, including fibroblasts and ligament cells. Three typical proteins (lysozyme, insulin and lactoferrin) with similar physicochemical characteristics to these growth factors (molecular weights and isoelectric points) were additionally chosen as model proteins for the growth factors. We then prepared biodegradable matrices (films and sponges) entrapping these model proteins or growth factors by a water in oil (w/o) emulsion method and investigated the release behavior of the proteins and the cell growth on the matrices.

Furthermore, a synthetic negatively charged peptide containing arginine-glycine-aspartic acid (RGD) sequence was coated on the complexes to improve the stability and provide targeting through interactions with integrins. Particularly, the preserved highly positive charge density in this ternary system would induce minimal cytotoxicity, substantially different from the long-held view that high charge density usually leads to high cytotoxicity.12,17 This multifunctional oligomer incorporation strategy would endow natural polycations with high flexibility as well as broad applicability to enhance the transfection efficiency without compromising their inherent cationic advantages. Another significant challenge in developing non-viral gene delivery vectors is to correlate how molecular structures influence the transfection activity, which is in general, through meticulous cell transfection experiments. Obviously, this is a time and resource consuming process, especially when a large number of materials are needed to be evaluated, and sensitive or passage limited cells (such as primary cells) need to be used. However, so far there is no alternative option to identify, at least partially, efficient vectors without massive gene transfection. Therefore, to develop a new method to screen vectors prior to tedious cell transfection is highly desired. After grafting the electrode, efficient vectors can be screened out through quantitatively comparing the interaction strength between the gene vectors and cells, circumventing the tedious and massive screening process of cell transfection.
First published on 25th February 2016 Phosphorylated polymers are promising for bone regeneration because they may recapitulate the essence of the phosphorylated bone extracellular matrix (ECM) to build an instructive environment for bone formation. However, most of the existing synthetic phosphorylated polymers are not fully biodegradable; thus, they are not ideal for tissue engineering. Here, we designed and synthesized a new phosphorylated polymer, poly(sebacoyl diglyceride) phosphate (PSeD-P), based on the biodegradable osteoconductive backbone PSeD. To our knowledge, PSeD-P is the first polymer to integrate the osteoinductive moiety β-glycerol phosphate (β-GP). PSeD-P shows good biodegradability and can be readily fabricated on 3D porous scaffolds. It has a porous structure with interconnected macropores (75-150 μm) and extensive micropores (several microns). PSeD-P promotes the adhesion, proliferation, and maturation of osteoblasts more effectively than poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA). Furthermore, PSeD-P induces a significantly higher expression of osteogenic biomarkers and ALP activity in mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) compared to its non-phosphorylated precursor, PSeD. The level of improvement is comparable to free β-GP in culture medium. More importantly, without using β-GP, the typical mineralization promoter in osteogenic culture media, PSeD-P substantially induces the mineralization of the ECM in MSCs, which is totally absent using PSeD under identical culture conditions. PSeD-P provides a new strategy to integrate bioactive phosphates via β-GP into biomaterial, and has promise for bone regeneration applications. In addition, the synthetic method is versatile; both the backbone and the side phosphate groups could be readily tailored to generate a family of phosphorylated polymers for a wide range of biomedical applications. Herein, we report a new phosphorylated polymer, poly(sebacoyl diglyceride) phosphate (PSeD-P), for bone regeneration (Fig. 1). This polymer is designed according to the following considerations: (I) osteocompatible backbone: the backbone is based on an osteocompatible polymer - PSeD, which was recently developed by our group.14 PSeD has been shown to promote the mineralization of osteoblasts and the human mesenchymal stem cell extracellular matrix, and it exhibits excellent in vitro and in vivo biocompatibility and biodegradability.15 In addition, PSeD is a refined version of another widely used polymeric biomaterial, poly(glycerol sebacate) (PGS). PGS has been shown to support the osteogenic phenotype of osteo-precursor cells in vitro and could fully regenerate a rabbit ulna critical size defect in vivo.16,17 (II) Biomimetic pendant phosphate groups: free dihydrogen phosphate (-PO4H2) groups are attached to the main chain via a phosphoester bond, which can be readily cleaved via hydrolytic degradation and biodegradation by alkaline phosphatase (ALP). The chemical nature of the phosphorus-containing moiety of materials plays a key role in mineralization.8 For example, poly(phosphazene), one of the most extensively investigated phosphorus-containing polymers, shows little effect on mineralization, possibly due to the unfavorable nature of the backbone phosphorus.8 Dihydrogen phosphate has been shown to be one of the most efficient inducers of mineralization, among various organic functional groups.8 In PSeD-P, the pendant phosphate groups mimic the native structure of the phosphorus-containing moiety and retain the corresponding bioactivity. (III) Bioactive degradation products: different from previously reported phosphorylated polymers, PSeD-P integrates an osteoinductive moiety, β-GP, by biodegradable ester bonds. It is expected to release β-GP upon degradation. β-GP has been widely used in osteogenic media to provide phosphate for the mineralization of osteoblasts and stem cells.18,19 β-GP serves as the substrate for ALP producing inorganic phosphate by hydrolysis, which could effectively induce calcium deposition in the culture medium.19

This composite material can be obtained by compression molding. The thermogravimetric degradation profile, the FTIR spectra, values of the water contact angle (WCA), water and phosphate-buffered saline uptake values, and the results of a cytotoxicity assessment are presented herein. Based solely on the provided context evidence, surface modification with RGD peptides improves synthetic biodegradable polymers by:

1.  **Enhancing Cell Adhesion:** RGD peptides specifically bind to integrin receptors on cell surfaces, significantly improving cell attachment to the otherwise hydrophobic polymer surfaces. This direct targeting mediates stronger adhesion than unmodified surfaces [6], [8], [12].
2.  **Promoting Cell Spreading and Proliferation:** Binding to integrins via RGD facilitates the formation of focal adhesions, leading to better cell spreading [14], cytoskeleton organization [14], and ultimately increased cell proliferation [2], [4], [6], [8].
3.  **Improving Bioactivity and Cellular Response:** RGD conjugation makes the polymer surface more bioactive, mimicking natural extracellular matrix (ECM) components. This improves cellular interactions, including adhesion, spreading, and proliferation, compared to polymers modified with standard conjugation techniques like carbodiimide chemistry [4]. Specific RGD sequences (like cyclic or bicyclic forms) show higher affinity and stability, further enhancing these effects [2], [8].
4.  **Overcoming Hydrophobicity Limitations:** Synthetic biodegradable polymers like polycaprolactone (PCL) are inherently hydrophobic, which limits cell attachment and wettability. Coating the surface with hydrophilic RGD peptides is a strategy used to overcome this limitation and improve biocompatibility [6], [12]. This improved interaction facilitates diffusion of biological media and promotes tissue integration [12].
5.  **Enabling Targeted Delivery:** When conjugated onto nanoparticles made from biodegradable polymers (e.g., PLA derivatives), RGD peptides act as targeting ligands. They bind specifically to integrins (e.g., αvβ3, αvβ5) overexpressed on certain tumor cells, enhancing cellular uptake and accumulation of therapeutic agents [8].
6.  **Facilitating Specific Cellular Functions:** RGD peptides, particularly engineered variants like bicyclic RGD, can promote specific tissue regeneration outcomes. For example, they enable superior nerve growth and fibroblast proliferation within synthetic hydrogels compared to linear RGD or fibronectin fragments [2]. They also support endothelial cell adhesion and morphology under shear stress [14].

A considerable problem related to the biomaterials is how hydrophobicity and lack of biological recognition sites on the surface of the material provide an unfriendly environment for cell adhesion.[12] To improve cell adhesion, previous functionalization studies focalized on modifying biomaterial surfaces have been developed. Further, surface modifications play a role in cell migration, proliferation, and differentiation of stem cells.[13] Therefore, cell adhesion enhancement would improve cell-biomaterial interaction.[14] Several functionalization methods were used based on the interaction of different components with cell membrane proteins. For example, the surface can be functionalized with the peptide RGD (Arg-Gly-Asp),[15] with 1-pyrene butyric acid (PBA),[16] or with different components present in the extracellular matrix (ECM) like fibronectin or collagen.[17] Synthetic polyesters, like 1,4 butanediol thermoplastic polyurethane (b-TPUe), have received considerable attention for cartilage TE, due to their appropriate mechanical properties such as the highly elastic recovery capacity.[18] However, its hydrophobicity does not provide the desired environment for cell adhesion and proliferation. Hence, the aim of this study was the set-up of two different functionalization methods, based on the biomaterial coating with collagen type I and PBA, probing how it is possible to reduce the hydrophobicity of b-TPUe improving cell-biomaterial interaction. Two methods were selected due following the objective of comparing a traditional coating method (Collagen type I) adapted from literature[17] with a new methodology (PBA) with reduced costs and good results obtained from making graphene biosensors.[16] Both methodologies are compared by evaluating the efficacy of functionalization by atomic force microscope (AFM) and ninhydrin reagent. Then, the biological efficacy of both functionalization methods was analyzed by seeding mesenchymal stem cells obtained from Hoffa's fat pad (infrapatellar mesenchymal stem cells (IPFP-MSCs) and performing the subsequent metabolic activity and viability studies. Together with cellular studies, extracellular matrix (ECM) secretion was analyzed through PCR, Glucosamine Glycans (GAG) quantification, and, finally, by SEM, to verify the chondrogenic potential of both functionalized methods.

Synthetic and functional grafts are a great alternative to conventional grafts. They can provide a physical support and the precise signaling for cells to heal damaged tissues. Despite several advantages of alginate hydrogels, the lack of cellular interaction is considered one of the critical limitations to using this material for tissue engineering applications. It is known that alginate usually discourages protein adsorption due to its hydrophilic character and that it is unable to specifically interact with mammalian cells. (2) For this reason, alginate has been engineered with cell adhesion peptides such as Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD) to promote cell adhesion. These modified alginate hydrogels could facilitate adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation of primary cells. (38, 39) Considering the capability of catechols to covalently conjugate nucleophiles (amine, thiol, and imidazole groups), diverse types of peptides, proteins, and molecules with these functional groups may be easily immobilized to the alginate-catechol hydrogel. (31, 35, 40) Therefore, simply mixing alginate-catechol with peptides or proteins would create biologically functional hydrogel scaffolds conjugated with bioactive molecules for improved therapeutic efficacy of cell transplantation. In this study, alginate hydrogels engineered by mussel-inspired adhesive chemistry were created by calcium-free cross-linking.
