The amount of composite waste from decommissioned wind turbine blades grows rapidly and recycling solutions should be generated to overcome this environmental challenge. This research aims to further develop a recycling method to recover components of dismantled turbine blades by reusing them as reinforcement for new composites. Recycled short glass fibers from shredded blade composites are incorporated into polylactic acid (PLA) to fabricate a composite (15 wt% fiber) that could be used for 3D filament fabrication. To improve the mechanical properties of the composite, a coupling agent was employed to refine the interactions between PLA and recycled glass fibers at the interface of the two components and enhance the adhesion. Due to the inherent brittleness of PLA, which is aggravated with the addition of recycled glass fibers, a toughening agent involving chain-end modification was incorporated into the composite to improve the toughness of the system. The concurrent outcome of the coupling agent and the toughener on the morphology, mechanical properties and thermal behavior of the composite was evaluated. The incorporation of 1,2,3,4-butane tetracarboxylic acid and silane-treating of the recycled fibers improved the strength by 30% and elongation at break and impact strength of the composite 3 and 2 times, respectively. Wind energy is a fast-growing industry with the aim to replace fossil fuels as a green and renewable source of energy. Although wind industry provides power with far less CO2 emission compared to fossil fuels, they produce a large amount of non-recyclable waste. This problem emphasizes the importance of discovering recycling solutions. The most common type of wind turbine blade is glass fiber reinforced plastics (GFRP).[1] Many studies focused on methods for separating fibers from resin in composites and then reuse the recovered fibers in new composites.[2-5] Mechanical recycling is one of the most straightforward methods to deal with decomposed blades. By grinding the composite, a mixture of single fibers, chunks of resin and fiber mats embedded in resin are obtained. The recycled materials can reinforce new materials such as cement and asphalt that are used in the construction industry. Beauson et al.,[6] studied the reuse of shredded composite materials as reinforcement for new polymer-based composites and observed a reduction in the mechanical properties compared to virgin reinforcement, by increasing the shredded composite percentage. In another work by Beauson et al.,[7] the shredded composites obtained from a blade were incorporated into polyester resin. The decomposed blade first were ground using a miller and the obtained materials went through sifters. Composites with different concentrations of shredded materials from 10 to 30 wt% were manufactured via vacuum resin infusion. The stiffness of the final composites increased significantly compared to the pristine polyester resin. However, the ultimate tensile strength and the elongation at break of the composites showed a decrease compared to the neat polyester. Most of the studies on the reincorporation of the shredded composites suggest that using the recyclates can deteriorate the final mechanical properties of the new composites.[8] Mamanpush et al.,[9] hammer milled the scrap blades and incorporated them into methyl-diisocyanate to produce a new composite in the form of panels. They suggested that these panels can be developed and used in form of floor tiles and plastic road barriers. They also used recycled wind turbine blades to produce reinforced thermoplastic composite using high-density polyethylene (HDPE). They also investigated the effect of coupling agents (Silane and Maleic anhydride) on the composite properties. The addition of modifiers significantly increased the flexural strength and young's modulus compared to non-modified composites.[10]
Fiber reinforced thermoplastic composites is a big category of thermoplastic composite materials, which has been developing for half a century so far this year. The fiber reinforcements can be glass fiber, carbon fiber and metal fiber, and so forth, and they vary from short fiber, long fiber to continuous fibers in composite materials.17-21 The earlier studies found that the mechanical properties of fiber reinforced thermoplastic composite materials are highly depends on the fiber length, and generally the longer length of the fiber, the higher mechanical properties of the thermoplastic composites.22, 23 Therefore, researchers normally prefer the longest length of fiber in the thermoplastic composites, especially for those thermoplastic composites used as structural materials requiring high mechanical properties. Continuous fibers act as a kind of unbroken long reinforcement, which have been used in thermoplastic composites to further enhance their mechanical properties.24, 25 And they really do have much higher mechanical performance than those thermoplastic composite materials with short or long fiber reinforcements. However, it should be noted that the impregnation and molding preparation of continuous fiber reinforcements with thermoplastic polymer matrix is a challenge due to the high melt viscosity of thermoplastic polymer matrix and inhomogeneous distribution of continuous fiber in thermoplastic polymer matrix.2, 26 In recent years, the use of continuous fibers as reinforcing materials for thermoplastic composites and their combination with 3D printing technology has become a new research hotspot.27, 28 However, 3D printing continuous fiber reinforced thermoplastic composites involves many factors and process parameters such as equipment process principle, material type, printing temperature, speed, fiber orientation, and so forth. The process is complex and not conducive to mass production. In addition, there are a lot of conventional molding methods for thermoplastic composites, such as injection-molding, rotational-molding, vacuum forming and compression-molding. However, these molding processes have disadvantages such as high cost, long molding cycle and low efficiency. The pultrusion process is a resin-impregnated continuous fiber or its fabric heated through a die under the action of a stretching device to cure the resin, which has the advantages of controlled fiber content, high raw material utilization, and high production efficiency. Howald et al first proposed the use of fibers impregnated with liquid polymers to make fishing rods.29 In the 1960s, the industrial demand for pultruded products grew the pultrusion process technology and production equipment improved, and the variety of pultrusion resin systems and reinforcing materials expanded. Pultrusion method for preparing continuous fiber reinforced thermoplastic composites is promising and very suitable for the fabrication of continuous fiber reinforced thermoplastic composites. Through reasonable design of impregnating agent and adjustment of pultrusion parameters, the impregnation effect can be effectively improved and the continuous fiber reinforcement can be induced to mix uniformly with the thermoplastic polymer matrix. Polylactic acid (PLA) is a kind of thermoplastic polymer produced from lactic acid, which has been successfully utilized in biodegradable material and as a composite matrix material.30-34 In addition, PLA is a promising and prominent biomaterial that has been widely used to replace the traditional petrochemical-based polymers in various applications because of the environmental concerns and relatively good mechanical properties.35 Especially green thermoplastic composites have gained greater attention as ecological consciousness has grown to be more appealing than conventional toxic and nonbiodegradable petroleum-based composites.36 Nevertheless, it is necessary to chemically modify PLA or mechanically reinforce it to broaden its applications because of its weak thermal stability and brittleness compared with the traditional petrochemical-based polymers, such as polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), polycarbonate (PC) and acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) resins, and so forth.37, 38 At present, glass fiber was widely used to prepare glass fiber reinforced composites for its excellent properties, such as light weight, high strength, high modulus and high temperature resistance. The incorporation of glass fiber into PLA thermoplastic polymer had been proved to improve the mechanical and thermal properties of the PLA-based composites, and which have been extensively utilized in a variety of applications, from packaging to medical apparatus and instruments due to their biodegradable, recyclable, high mechanical strength, low toxicity, good barrier properties, friendly processing and excellent characteristics.36, 39, 40 However, it should be noted that most glass fiber reinforced PLA thermoplastic composites use short or long glass fibers, there are only a small number of researchers has yet currently used continuous glass fiber reinforced PLA thermoplastic composites with not very good mechanical properties because of the impregnation and molding challenges.39, 41, 42 Regarding those above issues, it would be desirable to solve these challenges and successfully fabricate continuous glass fiber reinforced PLA thermoplastic composites with higher mechanical properties through the pultrusion method. This would offer technological advantages for further wide applications in structural materials and therefore, open up new possibilities with great significance for future scientific research. In this work, continuous glass fiber (CGF) reinforced polylactic acid thermoplastic composites (CGF/PLA) were fabricated through the pultrusion process. Key parameters involved in the pultrusion process (e.g., processing temperature, tension, traction speed and CGF content) were systematically optimized, and their effects on the tensile strength of CGF/PLA were carefully investigated. In addition, the morphology of tensile fractured surfaces of CGF/PLA and interface between CGF and PLA matrix were also examined. All of those above characterizations were to finally demonstrate that this pultrusion fabrication strategy of CGF/PLA could promote a low-cost and high-strength method for the industrial application of CGF/PLA with desired properties, and thus open possibilities for the rational design and pultrusion preparation of CGF/PLA for specific applications.

As the climate change in global generates a major problem to human society, more countries have elevated “carbon neutrality” as a national strategy and proposed a vision for a carbon-free future [1], which restricts the use of natural resources such as oil and coal [2]. It has been understood that the petroleum-based plastics are widely used in various industries due to their high quality and low price [3]. With the development of society, the usage in plastics was grown quickly and caused a serious environmental pollution [4,5,6]. Significant attention has been focused on the application of transportation, aviation, and construction of the biodegradable composite [7, 8]. Polylactic acid (PLA), which is the most commonly used biodegradable thermoplastic aliphatic polyester, produces from glucose derived from renewable corn, sugar cane and sugar beets [9]. It has the characteristics of recyclability and composability widely used for 3D printing applications primarily, and it is one of the most hopefully replaced petroleum-based polymers [10,11,12,13,14]. The tensile strength and Young's modulus of PLA are equivalent to polypropylene (PP), polyethylene (PE) and polystyrene (PS), but low strength, poor heat resistance and high-cost limits its application [9, 15]. Many methods are developed to improve the performance of PLA, which has a research hotspot utilized fiber reinforcement [16,17,18,19,20]. PLA is reinforced by two types of fiber that is natural fiber and artificial fiber [21,22,23]. Natural fibers are more environmentally friendly, while artificial fibers have stronger mechanical and thermal performance [24, 25]. Natural fibers have the characteristics of natural growth, light weight and recyclability that can reduce the health problems caused to operators such as skin irritation, etc. [26,27,28,29,30,31,32]. As a kind of natural fiber, rice residue (RR), including rice straw (RS) and rice husk (RH), a remaining biomass resources after rice harvest, has the advantage of abundant content, cheap cost, and completely degradable [33, 34]. The incineration of RR usually exhausts a large amount of greenhouse gas, which will have a great negative impact for the environment [35]. According to research, the RS and RH cellulose content keeps 41-57% and 35-45%, respectively, suggests that they have the function in enhancing PLA [36,37,38]. Comprehensive literature shows that the tensile strength of RR/PLA composites is mostly around 50 MPa and the bending strength of RR/PLA composites is mostly around 80 MPa [39,40,41]. The performance can meet the less demanding decorative parts such as the interior decorative parts of automobiles or airplanes [22, 42, 43]. For secondary load-bearing parts and load-bearing parts that require higher mechanical properties, they are usually reinforced by artificial fibers [44, 45]. Carbon fiber (CF) reinforced composites are the mainstream of research and development in high-performance composites, and it have been widely applied in the primary and secondary bearing structures of aircraft [46, 47]. However, fiber reinforced composites have been used a few in load-bearing parts and secondary load-bearing parts of automobiles due to the limitations of cost and performance. Glass fiber (GF), which often manufactured high-performance composites, is cheaper than carbon fiber and has the characteristics that natural fiber does not possess (high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, strong mechanical properties, etc.) [48,49,50]. The tensile strength and bending strength of GF/PLA composites can reach 120 MPa and 170 MPa, respectively. The value greatly exceeded the properties of modified polypropylene widely used in automobiles and met the performance requirements in some main and secondary load-bearing components in transportation and aviation [51, 52]. In conclusion, the industrial application of RR/PLA and GF/PLA composites has great potential and it is very necessary to summarize the factors that affect the mechanical properties to obtain better properties [53, 54]. In addition, the fiber composites need heat resistance adequately, as it would inevitably contact with the environment in application. The degradation of fiber composite is also considered after the service cycle [55, 56]. It is beneficial to summarize the thermal properties and biodegradation properties of fiber composites [57, 58].

As discussed in the previous section, the fiber stiffness depends strongly on the final size of the cross-section, whereas the fiber strength is a function of the fiber length. Both fiber diameter and length are affected during compounding. In the end, the composite properties are related to the initial fiber performance and the processing history of the composite. A detailed discussion regarding the influence of processing on the fiber-size distribution and resulting mechanical behavior of composites was published elsewhere.25 Man-made cellulose provides much higher strengths and significantly improved impact behavior.4-6, 24 Unfortunately, the stiffness may be insufficient for several applications. The solution could be a hybrid composites made of both, man-made cellulose and native natural fibers (e.g., see Figure 3). At temperatures above 60°C (glass transition of PLA), the storage modulus of PLA decreases rapidly. The typical drop for amorphous thermoplastics is due to amorphous phase, which dominates the storage modulus at higher temperatures. Below their softening temperature amorphous polymers are rigid. During heating they soften in the region of glass transition temperature and, in consequence, the viscosity above Tg decreases without any distinct melting point. This behavior indicates that PLA was solidified into an amorphous state by quenching during injection molding. Pothan et al.16 consider that the banana fibers in unsaturated polyester have larger effect on the storage modulus above Tg than below it. They observed that the difference in storage modulus of unreinforced polyester compared to its composites is noticeably higher at temperatures exceeding Tg. It is, however, taking into account unsaturated resins only, and not like in the present study, where the polyester is an aliphatic thermoplastic. In PLA, no crosslinkages occur and the decrease in modulus continues even though reinforced with fibers.

PLA/natural fiber composites have been investigated by numerous researchers. Du et al.7 studied the properties of PLA/cellulosic natural fiber composites produced by film stacking method. The natural fibers were hardwood high yield pulp, softwood high yield pulp, and bleached kraft softwood pulp fibers. They investigated the mechanical and thermal properties of the composites. They showed that the incorporation of pulp fibers increased the composite storage modulus significantly, and improved the tensile modulus and the tensile strength. They reported that the highest composite tensile strength achieved was nearly onefold higher than that of the neat PLA. Huda and coworkers8 investigated the effect of fiber surface treatments on the properties of laminated biocomposites from PLA and kenaf fibers. Kenaf fiber reinforced PLA laminated composites were prepared by compression molding using the film stacking method. The kenaf fibers were alkaline treated and silanized prior to composite preparation. They reported that both silane-treated fiber (FIBSI) reinforced composite and alkali-treated fiber (FIBNA) reinforced composite offered superior mechanical properties compared to untreated fiber-reinforced composite. The heat deflection temperature (HDT) of the PLA laminated composites was found to be significantly higher than that of neat PLA resin. They concluded that standard PLA resins were suitable for the manufacture of kenaf fiber reinforced laminated biocomposites with useful engineering properties. In other study, a commercial PLA was converted to film and then used in combination with jute fiber mats to generate composites by a film stacking technique.9 It was highlighted that the tensile properties of composites produced at temperatures in the 180-220 °C range were significantly higher than those of PLA alone. They observed that the composites fractured in a brittle nature under tensile load. Size exclusion chromatography revealed that only minor changes in the molecular weight distribution of the PLA occurred during the process. In a recent study, Porras and Maranon10 focused on the development and characterization of a laminate composite material from PLA and woven bamboo fabric. Film stacking method was used to prepare the samples. The performance of laminate composites was investigated and compared with bamboo fabric and neat PLA. The results showed that the strength of the plain-woven bamboo fabric in the weft direction was greater than in the warp direction. The mechanical properties of composites were better when weft direction bamboo fabric reinforcement was used. In other study, aligned discontinuous harakeke and hemp fiber mats reinforced PLA composites were prepared by produced using a dynamic sheet former and hot pressing to obtain of 5-40 wt % fiber. It was found that the fiber orientation factors for both harakeke and hemp fiber composites were higher those of reported in the literature. The highest orientation factor values for harakeke and hemp fibers in this work were found to be 0.58 and 0.44, respectively. It was shown that the orientation factor decreased with increasing fiber content due to the agglomeration and the higher pressure required during the processing.11 Georgiopoulos and coworkers12 addressed the fiber-matrix interface. In their study, unidirectional flax fiber reinforced PLA composites were fabricated through film stacking method. Prior to preparation of the composites, flax fibers were treated using amino silane at different silane content values. They showed that silane treatment over a specific level resulted in the deterioration of the composites mechanical properties. Among the other natural fibers, jute, a 100% biodegradable, environmentally friendly and recyclable natural fiber, serves as a potential candidate for the production of natural fiber reinforced composites since it has relatively high tensile strength and tensile modulus. In this study, jute is used as the reinforcing fiber. There are some studies in the literature regarding to the PLA/jute composites. For example, Boccardi and coworkers13 focused on monitoring with infrared thermography on the impact damage of a biobased thermoplastic composite based on PLA and jute. They stated that the visualization of thermal signatures that develop under impact supplies information useful to understanding the material impact damage mechanisms, such as formation of cracks and their propagation and the overall extension of damage. Rajesh et al.14 investigated the water uptake behavior of surface treated PLA/jute composites. It was found that the increasing fiber content increased the water uptake, but the composites with surface-treated fibers exhibited lower values. The authors stated that Fickian behavior was observed in plain PLA and its composite with untreated and alkali treated jute fiber at 5 and 10% concentrations of NaOH in the treatment, but at higher concentrations, a deviation was observed. Ding et al.15 investigated the biodegradation of jute/PLA composites in fungi environment. They showed that the top PLA layer on the surface of composites slowly degraded under the fungi environment. Then, fibers at the surface were exposed to air, the interface gap between fiber and matrix enlarged, and as a result, a decrease in the mechanical properties was observed. Yu and coworkers16 investigated the mechanical and properties of the PLA/jute composites. Results indicated that the mechanical properties of PLA-based composites increased with the addition of the fiber firstly, and then decreased when the content of fibers is over 30%. Moreover, thermomechanical properties of PLA increased the in the presence of jute fiber. “Organic hybrid composites,” recently developed thermoplastic composite technology, lead to obtain lightweight composite components for structural parts. In this process, a thermoplastic carbon or glass continuous fiber composite reinforcing sheet, named as “organo-sheet” is overmolded using a thermoplastic polymer in an injection molding process. The obtained composites sheets are stiff, high strength and at the same time, still detailed in shape. By inspiring from that new technology, in the current work, it was demonstrated the overmolded PLA/jute-woven fabric (JWF) composite production at the laboratory scale. The composites were called “ecosheets,” composed of a PLA/jute-mat composites overmolded by PLA. The mechanical, thermomechanical, and morphological properties of PLA/JWF and overmolded PLA/JWF composites were investigated.

This dose is considered sufficient for gaining a minimum of 10−6 sterility assurance level (6 log reduction). Use of an irradiation dose lower than the standard 25 kGy is of special interest in sterilization of medical devices, because of the damaging effect that this dose might have on physical-mechanical properties. Cellulose in the nano-size domain (nanocellulose) has attracted much attention due to its high strength, dimensional anisotropy, high aspect ratio, and high surface area. Therefore, nanocellulose is a material with suitable properties for producing aerogels [11], [12]. Cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) are a form of nanocellulose used to manufacture aerogels due to their high crystallinity, high porosity, and large number of -OH groups that allow for a variety of modifications [13], [14], [15]. Although CNCs are less brittle than silica, it is challenging to employ CNCs alone in the production of aerogels. Furthermore, CNC aerogels are inherently hydrophilic [14]; as a result, they require surface modification to promote hydrophobicity and specific oil or gas absorption [13], [16]. There exist two methods to improve the physical and chemical properties of CNC aerogel: (i) constructing a network of CNCs via chemical cross-linking and (ii) physical cross-linking with other biopolymer binders [17]. Methyltrimethoxysilane (MTMS) has been widely used to produce hydrophobic materials that can be applied as oil adsorbents [18], [19]. It has been used to modify the surface of cellulose [20], nanofibrillated cellulose [21], and CNCs [22] by substituting the -OH group in cellulose with the HO-Si-CH3- group of MTMS. Recently, a study has shown that MTMS can improve the hydrophobicity and compressive strength of CNC aerogels [13]. However, silica was employed in their investigation, which may affect the characteristics of the produced aerogels [13]. Both strategies for improving the physical and chemical properties of CNC aerogels were explored in this work. In the physical cross-linking method, gelatin is a biopolymer widely used as a binder in the production of aerogels [23], [24]. Nonetheless, due to a lack of data from related studies, gelatin as a binder for CNCs is still considered a novel approach. Our research is believed to be the first to investigate gelatin as a possible binder in CNC aerogels. In contrast, previous studies have only reported using CNC as a reinforcing agent for gelatin [25], [26], [27]. However, gelatin can form a thermally reversible gel at low temperatures due to its abundance of hydroxyl, carbonyl, and amino groups in its chain. An irreversible cross-linked gelatin gel can be realized by introducing a chemical or physical crosslinker into the gelatin matrix [28], [29], [30]. Chemical crosslinkers for gelatin include glyceraldehyde, glyoxal, isocyanates, epoxides, carbodiimides and formaldehyde, tannin, ferulic acid, and enzymes. These chemical crosslinkers can form a toxic or complex molecule residue. In contrast, the physical cross-linking method includes dehydrothermal treatment, ultraviolet, and γ-irradiation [31]. Of these methods, gamma irradiation has become a subject of interest due to its simple preparation process and the fact that it does not leave behind residual chemical reagents such as toxic cross-linkers [27], [32]. [33] found that gamma irradiation improved mechanical characteristics in gelatin/poly (γ-glutamic acid) hydrogels. The adoption of fiber-reinforced composite materials is steadily increasing due to its remarkable mechanical strength, resistance to corrosion, and capacity to withstand wear. A wide range of high-performance sectors, such as aerospace, automotive, and construction industries, extensively utilize these materials. In contrast to traditional materials such as iron, steel, and aluminum alloys, composites have notable benefits including their lightweight characteristics, improved resilience to fatigue, more design freedom, and reduced costs associated with maintenance and processing throughout their lifespan [1]. Composite materials are essential in various industries, offering a combination of desirable characteristics such as strong durability, lightweight nature, and corrosion resistance. However, the application of irradiation can cause significant modifications in composites, therefore affecting their efficacy and durability. One can classify irradiation into two main categories: ionizing radiation and non-ionizing radiation. Ionizing radiation, which includes components such as gamma rays and X-rays, is characterized by its tremendous energy and ability to cause significant harm to composite materials. In contrast, non-ionizing radiation, such as ultraviolet light, has lower energy levels but can still cause structural deterioration in composites [2]. Irradiation exposure elicits both physical and chemical modifications in composite materials. Polymer chains undergo degradation when exposed to irradiation, leading to a reduction in the strength, stiffness, and ductility of the composite material. In addition, irradiation can induce cross-linking and oxidation, hence exacerbating the damage to material characteristics. The radiation resilience of composites is dependent on various aspects, including the choice of matrix and reinforcement components. Certain polymers and fibers exhibit enhanced resistance to radiation. Critical areas such as aerospace, nuclear power, and space exploration heavily rely on the utilization of irradiation-resistant composite materials. In applications where components are exposed to radiation, the preservation of structural integrity is of utmost importance. question: What is the 'barrier property' trade-off in biodegradable packaging films?
ground_truth: Most biodegradable polymers (PLA, starch, PBAT) have relatively poor gas and water vapor barrier properties compared to conventional laminates. Multilayer films have gained relevance in many industrial applications, especially in the fresh food packaging industry, for extending shelf-life [1]. Lamination is widely used to improve polymeric films performance by combining the properties of several types of layers into one film or sheet [2], [3], [4], [5]. However, while the combination of various layers is required for good food preservation, the recyclability or biodegradability of the multilayer packaging could become compromised. The impact of packaging waste on the environment can be minimized by prudently selecting materials and reviewing packaging expectations in terms of environmental impact [6], [7], [8]. Polymers derived from natural products, such as carbohydrates and proteins, offer the greatest opportunities as components of multilayer structures since their biodegradability and environmental compatibility are assured. Protein films are excellent oxygen and aroma barriers at low relative humidity with potential to replace synthetic oxygen-barrier components in multilayer formulations. Nevertheless, such property fails in high moisture environments due to the hydrophilic character of most proteins [4], [9]. In an attempt to overcome this issue, numerous studies have focused on the use of bio-polyesters as protective layers of protein films, including three-layer films from a soybean protein isolate (SPI) laminated with poly(lactic acid) (PLA) by means of a solvent-casting procedure [3], [10]; bi-layer PLA-SPI films obtained by casting [7], polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs)- ultrathin zein fibers [5] and bi-layer Bioflex™-isolate whey protein films (IWP) [8]. Most of these materials have proven to be biodegraded under the stimulus of an environmental trigger after use [7], [8]. In a previous work [4], the authors described the design and performance of a biodegradable, high barrier, self-adhesive, three-layer sheet based on glycerol plasticized bovine gelatin layer acting as the oxygen barrier component and PLA as the outer layers produced by compression molding, as a potential thermoforming packaging solution. The favorable combination into a multilayer material enhanced the oxygen barrier of the pure PLA component (a limiting factor for PLA packaging applications), improved moisture resistance, and enhanced the mechanical and impact properties of its plasticized gelatin counterpart [4]. To consider such a multilayer sheet as a viable packaging material, it must retain the physical properties during the in-use period and ensure that lamination does not compromise the inherent biodegradability of the individual components under specific conditions, such as in indoor soil burial experiments.

Biopolymers including proteins and polysaccharides are the main natural resources utilized in development of biodegradable packaging material [1]. Proteins films are mechanically more strong than polysaccharide one [2] and show appropriate gas barrier properties [3]. Denaturation followed by association through new intermolecular interactions is the main mechanism for proteins to form film [4]. Gelatin, the product of collagen splitting and depolymerization [5], has excellent film forming and barrier (against oxygen and aroma compounds) properties at low and intermediate relative humidity (RH). Gelatin films suffer from high water vapor permeability (WVP) and poor mechanical and thermal properties [6]. Polysaccharides are usually cost-effective and available raw materials for biodegradable films [4] and different types of them (starches, gums and cellulose derivatives) have been used as packaging and coating materials [7]. It has been used in a number of edible film formulations. CMC films are transparent, flexible, soluble in water, resistant to oil/fat and of moderate strength, moisture and oxygen barrier properties [9]. Interactions of different origins between proteins and polysaccharides result in tailor-made functional properties [10]. Depending on the molecular charge and concentration, different phenomena including co-solubility, thermodynamic incompatibility, depletion flocculation and thermodynamic compatibility take place in a mixture of protein and polysaccharide [2]. When two partners are oppositely charged, soluble complexes are developed at the first stage, followed by formation of inter-polymeric (insoluble) complexes [6]. Different factors including composition, concentration and ratio of reagents, order of mixing, pH, charge distribution, molecular weight, and conformation, ionic strength and ion type affect the complexation phenomenon [10]. The 'barrier property' trade-off in biodegradable packaging films primarily involves a compromise between **oxygen barrier performance** and **water vapor barrier capability**. Biodegradable polymers typically excel in one property but underperform in the other due to their inherent material characteristics. For example:  

- **Protein-based films** (e.g., gelatin, soy protein) exhibit excellent oxygen and aroma barrier properties at low humidity but become ineffective in high-moisture environments due to their hydrophilic nature, leading to poor water vapor resistance [1], [4], [12].  
- **Polysaccharide-based films** (e.g., cellulose derivatives, starch) are similarly limited by hydrophilicity, resulting in high water vapor permeability despite moderate oxygen barrier performance [6], [12].  

This trade-off arises because materials with polar groups (e.g., proteins, polysaccharides) inherently resist oxygen diffusion but absorb water, weakening their moisture barrier [1], [4], [6]. Modifications to improve one barrier often exacerbate the other—e.g., hydrophobic additives like fatty acid cellulose esters (FACEs) enhance water resistance but may disrupt structural cohesion, reducing oxygen barrier efficacy [9], [11]. Additionally, strategies to enhance barrier properties (e.g., nanocomposite coatings) risk compromising biodegradability or mechanical integrity [5], [7], [14]. For instance, nanoclay dispersion in PLA blends improves gas barriers but may reduce biocompatibility [7], while PLA-PBS composites achieve oxygen barrier enhancement at the cost of tensile strength [13].  

Thus, the core challenge lies in balancing these opposing barrier requirements while maintaining biodegradability, mechanical performance, and scalability [4], [5], [14].

Degradable bio-based polyesters, such as commercially available poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), poly(butylene adipate terephthalate) (PBAT), and poly(lactic acid) (PLA), provide important ecological benefits by breaking down into carbon dioxide (CO2) and water under natural conditions within a short period (<5 years).10-12 However, these materials are structurally limited, with their aliphatic-rich backbones resulting in insufficient mechanical strength (tensile strength ∼30-40 MPa) and thermal stability (melting temperature ∼130 °C). This renders them unsuitable for high-load industrial applications such as high-grade packaging, electronic casings, or durable textiles.13,14 The trade-off between performance and degradability has significantly hindered the widespread replacement of PET and PBT with bio-based alternatives. Bio-based polymeric materials derived from renewable lignocellulosic biomass and waste feedstock, such as agricultural and plant decay residues, offer a transformative solution for bio-sourced monomeric compounds. For example, lignin, an abundant byproduct of the pulp and paper industry, contains aromatic moieties that can structurally mimic the rigidity of terephthalate (PET and PBT) while reducing reliance on fossil resources, an important step toward a circular bioeconomy.6,10,11 By leveraging lignin's aromatic character, it is possible to enhance the mechanical performance of polyesters while simultaneously incorporating aliphatic segments to promote degradability.15,16 However, many researchers have encountered challenges related to the rigid-flexible property trade-off, hindering the development of high-performance bio-based polyesters. Recently, there has been growing interest from both academia and industry in harnessing lignin-derived aromatics to create high-value functional products, possibly through lignin depolymerization, which produces various hydroxyaldehydes, such as p-hydroxybenzaldehyde, vanillin, and syringaldehyde, that can be easily extracted with their corresponding hydroxyacids.17-19 Notably, syringaldehyde, derived by the depolymerization of syringyl-rich hardwood lignin, undergoes a two-step transformation to yield methylparaben, a bio-based aromatic compound.17,20 Meanwhile, guaiacol, a guaiacyl lignin monomer abundant in softwood lignin, can be easily converted to hydroquinone bis(2-hydroxyethyl) ether (HQEE), a polymer chain extender widely used in the preparation of polyesters, polyurethanes, polyamides, thermosetting epoxy resins, and thermally reversible self-healing materials.19,21 The flexible-rigid HQEE phenyl ring significantly enhances the thermomechanical properties of polymers. Although co-segments (methylparaben and HQEE) share rigidity similarities with terephthalate (TPA) structures, differences in the ring size, polarity, and geometry often result in distinct characteristics within the overall polyester matrix.22-24 Specifically, the interatomic distance between the hydroxyl oxygen atoms in methylparaben is approximately 4.45 Å, whereas in HQEE, this distance extends to approximately 6.10 Å, indicating significant differences in molecular geometry that could influence their respective hydrophilicity and structural conformation in solution. Similarly, Mialon et al.27 and Fodor et al.28 incorporated aliphatic diols (C4-C8) into polydihydroferulic acid-based polyesters, resulting in a balanced rigid-flexibility structural matrix akin to poly(butylene succinate-co-terephthalate) (PBST), achieving higher thermal stability (Tg: 20-60 °C), and confirming the advantages of aliphatic spacers within the polyester matrix. Jiang et al.29 and Wang et al.30 synthesized biobased copolyesters based on 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid and 2,5-thiophenedicarboxylic acid, which feature five-membered rings and varying heteroatoms, combined with different aliphatic diols (C4-C10), resulting in polyesters with good thermal stability (Tg: 45-71 °C). This work emphasizes understanding the structure-property relationships of aromatic polyesters by varying the aliphatic diacid spacers under mild condensation conditions. Methylparaben and HQEE were derived from green industrial lignin depolymerization processes. Molecular dynamics simulations were employed to calculate the energy barrier of the chain segments in solutions. The findings offer new insights into the design of high-performance biodegradable copolyesters with potential applications in sustainable plastic packaging materials.

With the demand for flexible packaging growing at an average rate of 3.5% each year, flexible materials need to meet and exceed the high expectations of consumers and the stressors of the supply chain.1 Increased competition between suppliers, along with government regulations, have resulted in innovations in films that enhance product and package performance, as well as address worldwide concerns with packaging waste.1 Concerns over the persistence of plastics in the environment, shortage of landfill space, emissions during incineration, and a negative impact on wildlife through ingestion and entrapment in the marine environment have increased research and development efforts on green bio-based alternatives and/or biodegradable polymers. The use of biodegradable polymers that are disposed of through composting can reduce the amount of solid waste generated in most areas of the world. This alone is a significant reason to use biodegradable polymers; however, there needs to be a balance with price, performance, properties, and manufacturing methods used to create these polymers.3 Among biodegradable materials, three families are usually considered.4 The first being polymers directly extracted from biomass such as polysaccharides, starch, chitosan, and cellulose as well as proteins such as gluten, soy protein, and zein. A second family comprises petroleum-based monomers or biomass-derived monomers, but uses classical chemical synthetic routes to obtain the final biodegradable material; this is the case for poly(e-caprolactones) (PCL), polyvinyl alcohol (PVOH), and polylactic acid (PLA). The third family comprises polymers produced by natural or genetically modified microorganisms instead of plants. Examples of these include polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) and polypeptides.5 PVOH is considered to be inherently biodegradable and has been the subject of extensive technological advances over the past few years.6 It has been demonstrated that PVOH can be efficiently degraded only in the presence of selected microorganisms whose occurrence in natural environments may be relatively uncommon. This information is in keeping with the limited biodegradation of many PVOH-based items in natural solid matrices such as soil and compost, as well as in aqueous media lacking specific PVOH-degrading microorganisms.7 It was first synthesized in 1924 by Herman and Haehnel by the hydrolysis of polyvinyl acetate and its major initial use was for textile sizing.8, 9 PVOH has traditionally been useable or processable only in the form of aqueous solutions or films cast from these, rather than as a thermoplastic. These PVOH-based materials represent a viable biodegradable and compostable alternative to present nondegradable materials for many applications.10 Recently developed, proprietary formulating and processing technologies represent a highly significant technological advance in allowing PVOH grades from partially to fully hydrolyzed, and including the highest commercially available molecular weights, to be processed as thermoplastics while still retaining a wide range of desirable property combinations.11-13 In regards to gas barrier properties, PVOH-based materials have very low permeability (i.e., high barrier characteristics) toward oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen, often lower than ethylene co-vinyl alcohol (EVOH) co-polymers, and much lower permeability as compared with other traditional polyolefins. Multilayer films have gained relevance in many industrial applications, especially in the fresh food packaging industry, for extending shelf-life [1]. Lamination is widely used to improve polymeric films performance by combining the properties of several types of layers into one film or sheet [2], [3], [4], [5]. However, while the combination of various layers is required for good food preservation, the recyclability or biodegradability of the multilayer packaging could become compromised. The impact of packaging waste on the environment can be minimized by prudently selecting materials and reviewing packaging expectations in terms of environmental impact [6], [7], [8]. Polymers derived from natural products, such as carbohydrates and proteins, offer the greatest opportunities as components of multilayer structures since their biodegradability and environmental compatibility are assured. Protein films are excellent oxygen and aroma barriers at low relative humidity with potential to replace synthetic oxygen-barrier components in multilayer formulations. Nevertheless, such property fails in high moisture environments due to the hydrophilic character of most proteins [4], [9]. In an attempt to overcome this issue, numerous studies have focused on the use of bio-polyesters as protective layers of protein films, including three-layer films from a soybean protein isolate (SPI) laminated with poly(lactic acid) (PLA) by means of a solvent-casting procedure [3], [10]; bi-layer PLA-SPI films obtained by casting [7], polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs)- ultrathin zein fibers [5] and bi-layer Bioflex™-isolate whey protein films (IWP) [8]. The favorable combination into a multilayer material enhanced the oxygen barrier of the pure PLA component (a limiting factor for PLA packaging applications), improved moisture resistance, and enhanced the mechanical and impact properties of its plasticized gelatin counterpart [4]. To consider such a multilayer sheet as a viable packaging material, it must retain the physical properties during the in-use period and ensure that lamination does not compromise the inherent biodegradability of the individual components under specific conditions, such as in indoor soil burial experiments.
First published on 5th April 2024 This review article provides a thorough overview of barrier coating materials that have been used in food packaging with a focus on biodegradable (bio-based or petroleum-based) materials, such as lipids, proteins, polysaccharides, agriculture waste and polyesters. The goal is to provide an opportunity to acknowledge progress made in this field, focusing on modifications made to coatings. These modifications aim to address the shortcomings of biodegradable substrates (either plastic or paper) and improve their performance, enabling them to compete with traditional petroleum-based food packaging materials. This includes their barrier against water vapor and oxygen, mechanical and surface characteristics (sealability and adhesion), as well as antimicrobial properties. The barrier of most biodegradable polymers underperforms in comparison with petroleum-based non-biodegradable polymers, which possess either high water vapor barrier or high oxygen barrier. Coating technology is a promising solution particularly in barrier improvement of biodegradable polymers. Currently, there are only metallized, or inorganic nanosheet coatings available for biodegradable films that meet food packaging requirements. There are some challenges in this field, for example, being able to retain the coating's biodegradability despite applied modifications to improve it's performance, the large-scale fabrication of biodegradable coatings, the coating's delamination and heat-sealability during service time, and the migration of the coating into the packaged food. Moreover, green chemistry and its sustainability needs in biodegradable polymeric coatings are also discussed regarding new ideas and possible directions for widespread application of coatings in food packaging. This is the first review that specifically summarizes biodegradable coatings on plastic and paper substrates with a focus on coating modifications to improve the performance of the base substrate to meet the required properties for food packaging applications.

ans_rerank: The 'barrier property' trade-off in biodegradable packaging films refers to the challenge of balancing high oxygen barrier performance with effective water vapor resistance. Biodegradable polymers often exhibit either strong oxygen barrier properties but poor moisture resistance or vice versa due to their inherent chemical structures. For example, polyvinyl alcohol (PVOH) offers excellent oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen barrier properties but is highly permeable to water vapor, which plasticizes and compromises its gas barrier performance [2][13]. Conversely, hydrophobic modifications to improve water vapor barrier properties can reduce oxygen permeability to levels unsuitable for fresh produce packaging, where high gas permeability is required to prevent spoilage [10]. Similarly, natural polymers like proteins and polysaccharides typically show good oxygen barrier properties at low humidity but poor water vapor resistance due to their hydrophilic nature [3][8][12]. Advanced strategies, such as multilayer laminates (e.g., PPC/PVA/PPC films) or clay nanocomposite coatings, aim to mitigate this trade-off by combining complementary materials [12][13][14]. However, achieving simultaneous optimization of both properties without compromising biodegradability remains a key challenge [5][7].

Ring opening polymerization (ROP) of strained lactones is the method of choice for the synthesis of poly(hydroxyalkanoate)s whereas poly(alkylene alkanedioate)s are preferably produced by polycondensation of alkanediols with dicarboxylic acids or their esters [5], [6]. ROP usually takes place at milder conditions than polycondensation with less generation of undesirable by-products [7], [8]. Furthermore, the ROP reaction is efficiently catalysed by enzymes making feasible the preparation of metal-free polymers [9], [10], [11]. Additional advantages of ROP are the low viscosity of the reaction medium and the absence of volatiles therein produced. These features are largely appreciated when polymerization has to be performed in situ as it is the case of nanocomposite manufacture and reactive injection moulding. In 2004, the US Department of Energy declared bio-based succinic acid (SA) as a high-potential chemical platform for the synthesis of compounds able to replace those currently in use but coming from fossil resources [12]. This is one of the main reasons explaining why poly(alkylene succinate)s, and in particular poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) and poly(ethylene succinate (PES), are ahead of bio-based polyesters of AA-BB type [13]. The industrial synthesis of PBS is currently performed by polycondensation of SA (or its dimethyl ester, DMS) with 1,4-butanediol (BDO) assisted by tin or titanium organometallic catalysts. In 2006 Matsamura et al. [14], [15] reported the synthesis of PBS by enzymatically catalysed ROP (e-ROP) of cyclic di(butylene succinate). This dilactone may be isolated in large amounts as a subproduct of the polycondensation process industrially used for the manufacture of PBS [16]. PES is also commercially accessible although it has not achieved production at the ton-scale yet. The synthesis of PES is carried out by reaction of succinic acid either with ethylene glycol or ethylene oxide. PES is more biodegradable than PBS, melts slightly above 100 °C, and displays fair mechanical properties [17], [18], [19]. This polyester is currently under vigorous investigation addressed to create PES-copolyesters suitable for new demanding biomaterial applications [20], [21], [22]. IntroductionAn increasing number of studies have focused on the development of biodegradable polymers in order to replace petrochemical-based polymers. There is an increasing interest in using renewable resources to develop biodegradable materials-based packaging in order to facilitate integrated waste management approaches [1]. In recent years, a majority of studies has focused on starch as a biodegradable polymer. However, plasticised starch cannot be used to replace conventional plastics because of its poor mechanical properties and high water sensitivity [2]. To overcome this problem it is necessary to improve the physicochemical properties of starch by chemical modification or by the incorporation of other polymers [3]. However, for many applications, the proposed strategy must preserve the inherent biodegradability of these bio-based materials. The use of materials prepared from polymer blends derived from agricultural resources has grown strongly in recent years, with an increasing interest in polyester/starch mixtures [4]. Several polyesters such as polycaprolactone, polyesteramide, polylactic acid and aliphatic copolyester were mixed in different ratios with thermoplastic starch [5]. These studies have mainly shown an improvement in mechanical properties and a decrease of water sensitivity.Poly(butylene succinate-co-butylene adipate) (PBSA) is one of the promising aliphatic thermoplastic polyesters with a range of desirable properties including biodegradability, melt processability, good mechanical properties and both thermal and chemical resistance [6]. PBSA is a random copolymer synthesized by polycondensation of 1,4-butanediol in the presence of succinic and adipic acids. Recent developments in fermentation technology have made it possible to produce new bio-based monomers. Succinic acid is one of the top twelve bio-based chemicals that are produced from sugars [7] and have a potential market. This compound appears particularly interesting for the production of PBS. Moreover, 1,4-butanediol, the other monomer used in PBS synthesis, could be easily obtained by reduction of succinic acid [7], thus giving access to a fully bio-based PBS. Aliphatic polyesters can be naturally degraded into the natural environment by bacteria and fungi [8]. PBSA, compared with PBS, is more susceptible to biodegradation both because of its lower crystallinity and the greater flexibility of its polymer chains [9].This study focused on plasticised corn flour/PBSA blends because of the semi-polarity of PBSA allowing a decrease in water sensitivity, and its interesting mechanical and thermal properties compared to the well-known packaging polymers such as polyethylene and polypropylene. A previous study has shown that corn flour-based materials have high hygroscopicity and less interesting mechanical properties [10]. In the present work, the possibility to combine thermoplastic corn flour with PBSA instead of thermoplastic corn starch was considered for both economic and environmental reasons: corn flour is cheaper than corn starch and is obtained with less processing steps (and thus less water and energy consumption). Starch from glycerol plasticised corn flour was in the gelatinised (or destructurized) state in blends and not in its natural granular form (as filler). Kim et al. [11] have shown that the addition of PBS to rice husk flour led to an increase in elongation and tensile strength of corresponding materials. Therefore, PBSA was added to plasticised corn flour in order to obtain materials with improved mechanical properties, which would be more adapted to possible applications as food contact materials. Corn flour materials are completely and rapidly biodegradable by microorganisms [12]. Kim et al. [4] observed that materials prepared with rice husk flour (from 10 to 40% (w/w))/PBS blends were still biodegradable. However, high PBSA ratios may prevent the materials meeting criteria such as a biodegradation rate (determined following ISO 14851) exceeding 90% in less than 6 months, which is one of the criteria listed in EN 13432 regarding the biodegradability of a material.The objective of this work is to study (i) the effect of the addition of PBSA (at different ratios) to glycerol plasticised corn flour on the physicochemical properties (hydrophobicity, crystallinity, mechanical properties and morphology) and (ii) to study their biodegradation kinetics (aerobic and anerobic biodegradation following ISO 14851 and ISO 14853, respectively, and enzymatic hydrolysis of corn flour starch and PBSA by amylolytic enzymes and lipase, respectively).This characterisation of materials containing from 30% (w/w) to 100% (w/w) PBSA blended with plasticised corn flour will thus allow (i) to identify the formulations with improved mechanical and water sorption properties when compared with corn flour-based materials, while still being considered as biodegradable and (ii) to get insight into the factors controlling both physico-chemical characteristics and biodegradability of these materials. The most common strategy for the synthesis of PSI as precursor for PASP is through the thermal condensation of l-aspartic acid at high temperature, usually exceeding 160 °C. The l-aspartic acid starting material is industrially produced via enzymatic conversion of fumaric acid in the presence of ammonia with l-aspartate ammonia-lyase (l-aspartase) [37]. Mainly E. Coli and Cornybacterium Glutamacium are used as producers of l-aspartic acid [38,39]. Fumaric acid in turn is produced through fermentation of glucose by Rhizopus arrhizus, a type of saprophytic fungi [40]. When exploiting this method, a polymer with both D- and L-succinimide units is obtained. Water formed as a by-product during the reaction should be removed to drive the equilibrium of the polycondensation reaction towards the condensation products. Examples of this synthetic pathway carried out both in bulk [41,42] and in solution [34,43,44] and in the absence or presence of a catalyst have already been reported. The use of a catalyst is not required for the polycondensation, but it typically results in PSI with higher molecular weight (Mw > 5000 g mol−1) [[45], [46], [47]]. Several acid catalysts have been reported [44,48], but phosphoric acid (H3PO4) is the most commonly used [30]. The presence of a catalyst also has an influence on the biodegradability of the resulting polymer. A structure-biodegradability relationship study of sodium polyaspartate showed that employing a H3PO4 catalyst in the thermal polycondensation reaction resulted in polymers that were linear and completely biodegradable while polycondensation in the absence of a catalyst resulted in more branched structures with limited biodegradability (about 70 %) [49,50]. Although high Mw PSI can be obtained in bulk using an acid catalyst, this method is characterized by an inefficient heat transfer and the formation of semi-solid materials which are difficult to be heated uniformly. Therefore, the synthesis is also frequently carried out in solvent. The use of solvents improves the heat transfer and promotes dispersion and mixing of the reactants maintaining homogeneous conditions during the reaction. Usually sulfur-containing solvents, more specifically thioether solvents, are used because they are inactive towards aspartic acid and they have high boiling points up to 350 °C [44]. Tomida et al. evaluated the influence of a range of solvents on the yield and molecular weight of PSI and concluded that the highest molecular weight and yield could be obtained when a mesitylene/sulfolane (7/3) mixture was used as solvent in combination with 85 % H3PO4 as catalyst [43,51]. This solvent mixture has been reported in several other studies to obtain high Mw (64,300 g mol−1) PSI with high yields [[52], [53], [54]].
Conventionally, PBS is synthesized from polycondensation of succinic acid with butane diol, followed by chain extension to attain high molecular weight [11], [13]. Substitution of either the dicarboxylic acid or the diol is an option for copolymer formation. One of the interesting diols is 1,6-hexanediol which is also obtainable from renewable resources and can directly polymerize with succinic acid to form poly(hexamethylene succinate) (PHS) [27], [28]. Like PBS, PHS has also received increasing attention because of its many interesting properties, including biodegradability and compostability. The synthesis, thermal and mechanical properties, and flammability of both neat PHS and PHS-based copolymers have also recently been reported [29], [30], [31]. Compared with PBS, neat PHS has two more methylene moieties (CH2CH2) between the ester groups, and these additional methylene moieties induce a significant difference in thermal and mechanical properties as well as crystalline behavior. Considering the contrasting properties of neat PBS and PHS, the structure and properties of poly(butylene succinate-co-hexamethylene succinate) (P(BS-co-HS)), have the potential to offer properties complementary to those of PBS or PHS. So far, only Wang and Gan have investigated the crystallization kinetics of P(BS-co-HS) with hexamethylene succinate (HS) content up to 35 mol% [32], [33], [34], [35]. Systematic reports on structure, thermal and mechanical properties, and crystallization behavior of P(BS-co-HS) copolyesters are limited. In this work, P(BS-co-HS) copolyesters with varied butylene succinate (BS)/hexamethylene succinate (HS) molar ratios over the entire compositional range were synthesized using direct melt polycondensation. Thorough spectroscopic characterization was performed and the effects of composition on structure, thermal properties, crystallization behavior and mechanical properties were investigated. The solubility of these polymers in a range of greener solvents is also described. This novel family of bio-based polyesters has tunable properties that render it suitable for melt or solution coating. The results from this work provide guidance for polymer selection in the diverse applications of sustainable PBS-based biodegradable copolyesters. Poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) has emerged as a promising bio-based material for packaging applications. However, linear PBS can form branched chain structures during continuous processing, as we have previously shown for commercial samples (see J. Hallstein, et al., J. Appl. Polym. Sci. 2021; 138:e50669). Fumaric acid moieties were identified as “olefinic defects” and thought to lend PBS the susceptibility for branching. This postulate is challenged by new findings we describe in this article: “self-synthesized” PBS without fumaric acid moieties can also form branched polymer chains, as rheological measurements prove. A mechanism is hypothesized which relates the branching susceptibility of the as-prepared PBS to butenyl-terminated PBS chains, as suggested by the correlation between varying reaction conditions, namely PBS synthesis under mixing conditions with different shear stresses, and results from extrusion studies. 1H NMR clearly shows that PBS prepared under mixing with negligible shear stress contains virtually no butenyl-terminated PBS chains, leading to PBS samples not prone to branching. In contrast, PBS prepared under forced conditions bears butenyl end groups and is prone to branching. This work demonstrates the importance of inspecting the origins of non-intended side effects carefully, as polyester syntheses are typically conducted under shearing. The investigations presented are aimed at providing new insights on the causes of processing instabilities of poly(butylene succinate)s (PBS), which we observed repeatedly in the past [1]. It is our second contribution on this topic and is driven by the firm belief that an in-depth understanding is essential to guarantee the continuous production of plastics with a reproducible and well-balanced property profile. It is common to stabilize polymers by additives that inhibit or retard degradation induced during processing and usage [2]. Not surprisingly, PBS can also be treated by similar means [3, 4]. However, it is certainly worth knowing the prime effect triggering the degradation, as this simplifies the selection of suitable stabilizers and limits its excessive use, which bears a risk potential [4, 5].
SA is an intermediate of the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and naturally present producers of SA are regarded as promising candidates for industrial SA.16 A variety of microorganisms, including Actinobacillus succinogenes, Anaerobiospirillum succiniciproducens, Basfia succiniciproducens, etc., have been reported to produce SA naturally.17 However, the industrial applications of these bacterial hosts are limited due to their potential pathogenicity, poor cell growth, and stress tolerance. In particular, the above-mentioned bacteria isolated from bovine rumen have multiple auxotrophies, and complex component media must be set up to promote their growth.18 An alternative strategy is to use genetically modified industrial microorganisms that do not naturally produce large amounts of SA, such as Escherichia coli, Corynebacterium glutamicum, etc. Through combined mutagenesis and subsequent optimization, Gao et al. constructed an engineered E. coli strain, FMME-N-30, which could obtain 119.0 g L−1 succinate from glucose.19 Li et al. introduced the isomerase pathway and the Weimberg pathway into C. glutamicum to obtain a recombinant strain that could simultaneously use glucose and xylose to produce succinate.20 However, due to the toxicity of various inhibitors in the hydrolysates, the utilization of lignocellulosic hydrolysates by bacteria requires the adoption of high-density fermentation strategies or diluting the hydrolysates with the medium before inoculation. Additionally, the pH during bacterial fermentation needs to be maintained at neutral, which greatly increases the production and downstream purification costs. In contrast to using bacteria, numerous studies have shown that yeast could produce more than 100 g L−1 of organic acids, including succinic acid and malic acid, without requiring neutral pH maintenance owing to its acid-tolerance property.21,22 For lignocellulosic biorefinery, the yeast Y. lipolytica Hi-SA2-YlGsh2 was reported to achieve a high SA titer of 45.34 g L−1 from lignocellulosic hydrolysate without pH control.23 Hence, yeast is considered a preferred candidate for industrial production due to its safety and robustness, especially when considering the intricate features of lignocellulosic biorefinery.10 Yarrowia lipolytica, an unconventional yeast generally recognized as safe, has attracted increasing interest due to its unique characteristics, including ease of genetic manipulation, broad substrate adaptability, and potential applications in the biosynthesis of different bio-chemicals.24,25 In recent years, various carbon sources have been used in genetically modified Y. lipolytica to enhance SA production.22,26,27 Among them, Y. lipolytica PGC01003 achieved the highest ever SA titer of 209.7 g L−1 using crude glycerol as the sole carbon source with an in situ fibrous bed bioreactor derived from sugarcane bagasse. In addition, the genetic pathway-optimized Y. lipolytica strain PGC62-SYF-Mae could obtain an SA titer exceeding 100 g L−1 with glucose as the sole carbon source.28 When considering xylose as the carbon source, even though it has been reported that the engineered Y. lipolytica without xylose metabolic pathway could also utilize a small amount of xylose in the presence of glucose, it remained unclear whether xylose could be successfully converted into SA.23,29 Researchers have also introduced xylose metabolism pathways in Y. lipolytica to generate recombinant strains PSA02004PP, which can only produce SA at a maximum titer of 22.3 g L−1 with a low yield of 0.15 g g−1 using xylose as the sole carbon resource. Besides, a low SA titer of 5.6 g L−1 was detected when sugarcane bagasse-derived hydrolysate was employed.30 Until now, despite many efforts that have been made to produce SA from xylose, these engineered Y. lipolytica yeasts are still unable to produce sufficient bio-SA to meet industrial demands employing lignocellulose as a carbon source. Herein, an engineered Y. lipolytica yeast capable of biosynthesizing SA using xylose as the sole carbon source was first constructed (Fig. 1). Afterward, tailored strategies were developed for simulating the proportion of glucose and xylose components contained in lignocellulosic hydrolysate, which allowed the engineered strain to completely co-ferment high-concentration mixed sugars. Finally, an efficient fermentation process was developed for SA production from undetoxified corn stover (CS) hydrolysate. In general, this study demonstrated that glucose and xylose in actual lignocellulosic hydrolysate could be completely consumed by engineered Y. lipolytica to produce SA, and the developed process proposed based on this robust strain could reduce the overall production cost, offering a green and sustainable alternative for large-scale industrial production of bio-SA.

ester bonds.[22, 23] PGS is cost-effective for industrial-scale production, with simple processes that do not require solvents or catalysts.[22] The Ts of PGS ranges from 0.4 to 0.7 MPa, and its Eb is Based solely on the provided evidence, succinic acid acts as a **core monomer** in the synthesis of poly(butylene succinate) (PBS). Its specific roles are:

1.  **Dicarboxylic Acid Monomer:** Succinic acid provides the dicarboxylic acid component that reacts with the diol monomer, 1,4-butanediol (BDO), via a **polycondensation reaction**. During this reaction, the carboxylic acid groups (-COOH) of succinic acid react with the hydroxyl groups (-OH) of BDO to form ester linkages (-COO-), releasing water as a by-product. This forms the repeating unit (C8H12O4) of the PBS polymer backbone [1, 3, 4, 6, 10, 13, 15].
2.  **Structural Backbone Contributor:** The succinate units derived from succinic acid are integral structural components of the PBS chain, determining key properties like crystallinity and biodegradability [3, 13, 15].
3.  **Source for Renewable PBS:** Succinic acid can be produced from renewable resources (e.g., via fermentation of sugars from biomass like lignocellulose or corn stover), enabling the synthesis of bio-based PBS [1, 3, 7, 12, 13, 15].
4.  **Precursor for Copolymers:** Succinic acid is also a key monomer in the synthesis of PBS copolymers, such as poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA) or poly(butylene succinate-co-hexamethylene succinate) (P(BS-co-HS)), where it is copolymerized with other diacids (e.g., adipic acid) or diols (e.g., 1,6-hexanediol) [7, 8, 10].

Poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) is a commercially available biodegradable thermoplastic polyester synthesized via the polycondensation reaction of 1,4-butanediol and succinic acid [13]. The biotechnological breakthrough in commercial production of the succinic acid from biomass resources makes PBS more eco-friendly [14]. Besides the outstanding biodegradability, PBS also possesses the superior flexibility and excellent thermoplastic processability [15, 16]. Therefore, among the degradable polymers developed so far, PBS is expected to be the ideal candidate for blending with CAB in term of decreasing its melt viscosity as well as increasing its flexibility. In general, it is of great significance to study the crystallization and miscibility of crystalline/amorphous polymer blends because these factors could greatly affect the material performances. Tatsushima et al. [17] obtained CAB/PBS blend films through solution casting from chloroform solutions. The composition dependences of miscibility and phase structure of the blend films at solid state were determined. The blends were considered to be highly miscible in an amorphous state when PBS content ranging from 0 to 30 wt.%. Interestingly, the mechanical performances of PBS can be drastically changed through thermal compounding with 10 wt.% CAB due to the change in crystalline state of PBS [18]. However, the crystallization behaviors when crystallized form melt, the miscibility in the molten state, melt viscosity, thermal stability and the mechanical properties of the specific CAB/PBS blends are not well known based on previous studies. To further understand this promising biodegradable CAB/PBS blend material, the current work affords a detailed investigation on the crystallization behaviors and miscibility of CAB/PBS blends with the entire composition. Meanwhile, rheological properties, thermal stability and mechanical properties of the blends were also examined in view of actual applications.
PBS is a biodegradable synthetic aliphatic polyester synthesized by the polycondensation of 1,4-butanediol and succinic acid and was invented in the early 1990s by Showa Highpolymer in Japan. It exhibits superior mechanical and thermal properties, high chemical resistance, great availability, and lower material cost over other biodegradable polymers.3-5 However, the production of PBS involves poly(alkylene succinate), which is synthesized from petrochemical precursors. Manufacturers are developing the production of PBS with biobased succinic acid for the synthesis of PBS, but synthetic PBS is still more common in the market. Therefore, blending synthetic PBS with other biobased materials is another option for replacing a fraction of PBS with a more environmentally friendly material, and it offers us the possibility of modifying or tuning its properties. The objective of this research was to investigate the microstructure and thermomechanical properties of blends between PBS and another biobased polymer, that is, poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV). PHBV is a family of polyhydroxyalkanoates, which are fully biobased and biodegradable polymers.6, 7 PHBV is a brittle plastic with a high modulus value, low elongation at break, and poor thermal resistance.8 On the other hand, PBS is a softer material with a relatively low modulus and a higher elongation at break and thermal stability.9 Therefore, the blending of PBS and PHBV offers us the possibility of combining the advantages of these polymers while simultaneously mitigating their less desirable properties. To the best of our knowledge, research on biodegradable blends based on PBS and PHBV has not been extensively reported in the open scientific literature.10-15 The miscibility and crystallization behavior of PBS/PHBV blends at different compositions in the range from 80 : 20 to 20 : 80 was investigated by Qiu et al.12 on PHBV with a 3-hydroxyvalerate content of 14 mol %. According to their findings, PBS was immiscible with PHBV, which was inferred from the independence of the glass-transition temperature (Tg) and the phase-separated melt. Ma et al.11 reported on the toughening of PHBV/PBS and blends via in situ compatibilization with dicumyl peroxide as a free-radical grafting initiator. In the aforementioned research, a PHBV with a 3-hydroxyvalerate content of 1 mol % was used. In this study, we selected a PHBV with 5 mol % 3-hydroxyvalerate as an attempt to study the effects of the PHBV composition on the properties of the PBS/PHBV blends. Previous work on PBS/PHBV blends has mainly focused on investigating the miscibility and crystallization behavior of the blends. However, little attention has been paid to the study of the mechanical and thermomechanical properties of the blends. Therefore, in this study, we focused our attention on the mechanical and thermal properties of PBS/PHBV blends with various compositions and with PBS as the dominant phase.

Recent developments in fermentation technology have made possible new bio-based monomer production. Succinic acid is one of the top twelve bio-based chemicals produced from sugars [7] which have an actual potential market. This compound appears particularly interesting for the production of PBS. Moreover, 1,4-butanediol, the other monomer used in PBS synthesis, could be easily obtained by the reduction of succinic acid [2], thus giving access to a fully bio-based PBS. In the literature, the majority of enzymatic depolymerizations of polyesters has been performed by lipase in water, organic solvents, or supercritical carbon dioxide [8], [9]. In the case of organic solvents, toluene, acetonitrile and volatile dichloromethane have been used; however their release in the environment could cause serious pollution problems. Therefore, the objective of the present study was to perform PBS degradation by a lipase during a continuous process like reactive extrusion. Only a few studies using the enzymatic hydrolysis during extrusion process have been published because of the low thermal stability of the majority of the enzymes. De Messa-Stonestreet et al. [10] developed a novel method for concentrating proteins from sorghum flour utilizing a combination of extrusion and thermostable α-amylase (optimal activity at 86 °C) treatment for starch liquefaction: they reported a higher starch liquefaction following extrusion in the presence of this enzyme than following action of this enzyme during a traditional batch process. In comparison to traditional batch liquefaction, extrusion is a high throughput process. In our case the PBS hydrolysis by lipase in an extruder requires a thermal stability of this enzyme at temperatures higher than the polymer melting one (i.e. >110 °C). For this reason the thermostable lipase B of Candida antarctica (CALB) recombinant from Aspergillus niger was selected. Pfeffer et al. [11] reported that the optimal temperature for its activity in water was 70 °C. According to the literature, CALB is a thermostable enzyme which can be used at temperatures up to 120 °C [12], in polar organic solvents such as acetonitrile and dimethyl sulfoxide, in ionic liquids [13], in solid/gas systems [14], and in supercritical carbon dioxide [12]. Indeed, the water activity (aw) of the solvent is a very important parameter for both the activity and the stability of the enzyme [15]. Rhizomucor miehei lipase was shown to be active even at a less than 0.0001 aw value [16]. Moreover, the thermal stability of numerous enzymes was shown to increase when aw decreases [17]. Taken together, these observations are in favor of a good preservation of both the stability and the activity of enzymes during processes such as extrusion if the enzymatic reaction occurs in a medium with a low aw value. The objective of this work was to investigate the possibility of PBS depolymerization by lipase during an extrusion process. The PBS extrusion was performed at 120 °C using both single screw and twin screw extruders to study the effect of shear stress and residence time on PBS hydrolysis by lipase. The degradation products were analyzed to check up the molecular weight change of PBS and the oligomer or monomer (succinic acid) formation. PBS pellets with a melting temperature of 115 °C and a density of 1.26 g cm−3 were purchased from NaturePlast (PBE003, Natureplast, Ifs, France).
