Poly(butylene succinate-co-butylene adipate) (PBSA) is one of the promising aliphatic thermoplastic polyesters with a range of desirable properties including biodegradability, melt processability, good mechanical properties and both thermal and chemical resistance [6]. PBSA is a random copolymer synthesized by polycondensation of 1,4-butanediol in the presence of succinic and adipic acids. Recent developments in fermentation technology have made it possible to produce new bio-based monomers. Succinic acid is one of the top twelve bio-based chemicals that are produced from sugars [7] and have a potential market. This compound appears particularly interesting for the production of PBS. Moreover, 1,4-butanediol, the other monomer used in PBS synthesis, could be easily obtained by reduction of succinic acid [7], thus giving access to a fully bio-based PBS. Aliphatic polyesters can be naturally degraded into the natural environment by bacteria and fungi [8]. PBSA, compared with PBS, is more susceptible to biodegradation both because of its lower crystallinity and the greater flexibility of its polymer chains [9]. This study focused on plasticised corn flour/PBSA blends because of the semi-polarity of PBSA allowing a decrease in water sensitivity, and its interesting mechanical and thermal properties compared to the well-known packaging polymers such as polyethylene and polypropylene. In the present work, the possibility to combine thermoplastic corn flour with PBSA instead of thermoplastic corn starch was considered for both economic and environmental reasons: corn flour is cheaper than corn starch and is obtained with less processing steps (and thus less water and energy consumption). [11] have shown that the addition of PBS to rice husk flour led to an increase in elongation and tensile strength of corresponding materials. [4] observed that materials prepared with rice husk flour (from 10 to 40% (w/w))/PBS blends were still biodegradable. The objective of this work is to study (i) the effect of the addition of PBSA (at different ratios) to glycerol plasticised corn flour on the physicochemical properties (hydrophobicity, crystallinity, mechanical properties and morphology) and (ii) to study their biodegradation kinetics (aerobic and anerobic biodegradation following ISO 14851 and ISO 14853, respectively, and enzymatic hydrolysis of corn flour starch and PBSA by amylolytic enzymes and lipase, respectively).
Poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) is a biodegradable polyester synthesized from succinic acid and 1,4-butanediol. PBS is recognized for its excellent balance of mechanical properties, processability, and biodegradability, making it versatile for various applications. Structurally, PBS consists of repeating units of butylene and succinate, linked by ester bonds (Fig. 2). This structure imparts flexibility and strength, enabling PBS to exhibit good tensile strength and elongation at break [116]. The polymer’s molecular Weight and crystallinity can be tailored through the synthesis conditions, which in turn influence its mechanical properties and degradation rate. PBS has a relatively low melting point of around 115-120 °C, facilitating easy processing using conventional plastic manufacturing techniques such as injection molding, extrusion, and thermoforming. Its thermal stability allows it to maintain integrity during processing while degrading into water and carbon dioxide under composting conditions. The biodegradability of PBS is a significant advantage, especially in applications where environmental impact is a concern. When exposed to microbial activity in composting environments, the ester bonds in PBS undergo hydrolysis, breaking down the polymer into non-toxic byproducts [170]. Polycaprolactone (PCL) is a biodegradable polyester that melts at about 60 °C and has a glass transition temperature of approximately − 60 °C. It is synthesized through ring-opening polymerization of ε-caprolactone (Fig. 2), typically using a catalyst such as stannous octoate. PCL’s high compatibility with various materials and ability to biodegrade in biological environments make it ideal for biomedical applications. Its biodegradability supports environmental sustainability, as it decomposes into non-toxic substances that natural processes can quickly assimilate [66]. Additionally, PCL is utilized to fabricate specialty polyurethanes and in polymer blends to enhance processing characteristics and mechanical properties [15]. In the class of synthetic polymers, polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) is counted, which is soluble in water and is particularly known for its excellent film-forming, emulsifying, and adhesive properties. It is fabricated by the polymerization of vinyl acetate, followed by hydrolysis to remove the acetate groups [38]. PVA is widely used in various industrial applications, including textile sizing, paper coatings, adhesives, and as a protective film. Its biocompatibility and non-toxicity also make it suitable for medical and pharmaceutical uses, such as contact lenses, drug delivery systems, and wound dressings. PVA’s water solubility and biodegradability further enhance its appeal for environmentally friendly applications, as it can break down into harmless products in aquatic environments [140]. However, PVA does have limitations. While beneficial in specific contexts, its water solubility can also be a drawback as it may dissolve or weaken in a moist environment, reducing its applicability in environments where water resistance is crucial [83]. Additionally, PVA can be sensitive to microbial degradation, which might affect its stability and performance in specific applications.

Compared with PBS, neat PHS has two more methylene moieties (CH2CH2) between the ester groups, and these additional methylene moieties induce a significant difference in thermal and mechanical properties as well as crystalline behavior. However, linear PBS can form branched chain structures during continuous processing, as we have previously shown for commercial samples (see J. Hallstein, et al., J. Appl. Polym. Sci. 2021; 138:e50669). Fumaric acid moieties were identified as “olefinic defects” and thought to lend PBS the susceptibility for branching. This postulate is challenged by new findings we describe in this article: “self-synthesized” PBS without fumaric acid moieties can also form branched polymer chains, as rheological measurements prove. A mechanism is hypothesized which relates the branching susceptibility of the as-prepared PBS to butenyl-terminated PBS chains, as suggested by the correlation between varying reaction conditions, namely PBS synthesis under mixing conditions with different shear stresses, and results from extrusion studies. 1H NMR clearly shows that PBS prepared under mixing with negligible shear stress contains virtually no butenyl-terminated PBS chains, leading to PBS samples not prone to branching. In contrast, PBS prepared under forced conditions bears butenyl end groups and is prone to branching. This work demonstrates the importance of inspecting the origins of non-intended side effects carefully, as polyester syntheses are typically conducted under shearing. The investigations presented are aimed at providing new insights on the causes of processing instabilities of poly(butylene succinate)s (PBS), which we observed repeatedly in the past [1]. It is our second contribution on this topic and is driven by the firm belief that an in-depth understanding is essential to guarantee the continuous production of plastics with a reproducible and well-balanced property profile. It is common to stabilize polymers by additives that inhibit or retard degradation induced during processing and usage [2]. Not surprisingly, PBS can also be treated by similar means [3, 4]. However, it is certainly worth knowing the prime effect triggering the degradation, as this simplifies the selection of suitable stabilizers and limits its excessive use, which bears a risk potential [4, 5].

question: How does 'electrospinning' create scaffolds that mimic the Extracellular Matrix (ECM)?

These nanofibers physically mimic the scale and arrangement of natural collagen fibrils in the ECM, providing a high surface area and porosity that supports cell attachment and nutrient transport.

Electrospinning is a high-performance and simple process for producing continuous fibers in nano and micro sizes for application in various fields, for example, drug delivery, catalyst structure, sensor design and fabrication, textiles, and especially in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine (TERM) [1-6]. TERM introduces functional substitutes to the repair and regeneration of damaged tissues and organs. It employs various sciences, including biology, chemistry, and engineering, to arrive at these goals. TERM needs three integral components: scaffold, cells, and biological signals, to facilitate cell growth, differentiation, and angiogenesis [4, 7]. Nanofibrous structures exhibit multiple advantages, such as a range of fiber diameters similar to the fibrillary ECM, high porosity, and large surface-to-volume area [8]. Fabricated scaffolds should mimic the 3D extracellular matrix (ECM) and provide a biocompatible environment for cell homing, proliferation, and differentiation toward tissue repair and regeneration. Along with biodegradability and sufficient mechanical strength, the porous structure of scaffolds facilitates the transportation of nutrients and oxygen while must be nontoxic, capable of being sterilized, and simple to manufacture and handle [9-12]. The nanofibers fabricated with electrospinning can recapitulate the nanofibrous structure of natural ECM. However, the structures prepared by traditional electrospinning are two-dimensional and cannot simulate a three-dimensional structure of native ECM. The porosity and fibrous structure of the native ECM could be simulated using nanofiber-based scaffolds with networking structures mimicking collagen fibrils [13]. 2D scaffolds have limitations such as insufficient porosity, low cell infiltration, and restriction of cell-cell and cell-ECM interaction. These limitations led to the emergence of 3D scaffolds that overcome 2D-associated limitations. 3D scaffolds create a microenvironment mimicking the in vivo tissue interconnectivity where cells create molecular gradients within the implanted scaffolds [14]. Moreover, 3D scaffolds provide a three-dimensional environment for cell transfer and infiltration, cell-cell interactions, and nutrient and waste exchange, which is essential for cell-cycle regulation and tissue function. To date, several electrospinning methods (e.g., cold-plate electrospinning, multilayering, wet electrospinning, postprocessing, template-assisted electrospinning, and self-assembly) have been developed for the 3D nanofibrous structures preparation. 3D nanofibrous structures fabricated via these electrospinning methods are time-consuming and require other processing or instruments along with these methods. On the other hand, most of these electrospinning techniques produce large diameter fibers resulting in significantly decreasing the pore sizes and porosity of prepared 3D scaffolds [15, 16]. Reducing the pore size as well as the porosity of the fabricated scaffold can hinder the infiltration and migration of the cells seeded on these scaffolds. Therefore, there are still challenges to the fabrication of a 3D nanofibrous scaffold by electrospinning with acceptable properties for application in TERM.
The physiological structure of extracellular matrix (ECM) is a natural network of intricate nanofibers, which provides an instructive background to guide cell behavior [4]. With the ability to form nanofibrous structures, a drive to mimic the native ECM has begun. Among the various approaches available, electrostatic spinning (popularly known as electrospinning) has gained reputation for its capability to make native ECM-mimicking (in terms of geometry, morphology or topography) scaffolds [5]. Electrospinning is capable of fabricating nanometer-scale fibers that yield very high specific surface area. It is otherwise difficult to produce such fibers by conventional non-woven fiber fabrication techniques [6]. Electrospun (e-spun) nanofibers are therefore very useful for developing a variety of structures whose functional efficiency is surface area dependent. With the advent of electrospinning, mimicking the physical dimensions of native ECM has become easier. However, conferring bioactivity to e-spun scaffold will decide its ultimate utility in the creation of functional tissue. In addition to the architectural features, a scaffold should also mimic the biological/biochemical features of the native ECM which is regarded as a complex organization of fibrous structural proteins such as collagens and a wide variety of proteoglycans [7, 8]. With respect to the biochemical attributes of materials used in tissue engineering, several synthetic biodegradable polymers have been tested previously. However, lack of cell recognition sites, aggravated hydrophobicity and acidic degradation products are few major issues which limit their use [9]. Hence, the attention has shifted toward natural biodegradable polymers. The most ideal candidate material should be collagen itself-the major component of native ECM. However, the major shortcomings for collagen are its inadequate mechanical properties and anti-genecity [10]. An alternative and intriguing biopolymer which has features similar to collagen is silk fibroin. Produced by several Lepidoptera larvae, including silkworms, fibroin is famous for its biocompatibility, slow degradability and excellent mechanical properties, and has been exploited for various biomedical applications including liver tissue engineering [11, 12]. Besides protein factors, native ECM also has variety of proteoglycans. Therefore, modification of artificial scaffold with such ligands is often necessary for optimization of ECM for hepatic tissue engineering. Given the fact that the hepatocytes have asialoglycoprotein (ASGP) receptors that recognize and bind to molecules with exposed galactose, N-acetyl galactosamine or glucose residues, many have demonstrated the use of galactosylated materials for use in liver tissue engineering [13]. Owing to biocompatibility, biodegradability, antibacterial activity and resemblance with native ECM glycans, chitosan has been widely used in tissue engineering applications [14]. Recently, galactosylation of chitosan has gained importance to increase its aqueous solubility and to improve hepatocyte attachment [13]. Hence, galactosylated chitosan (GalCS) is another appropriate material of choice which can be used along with regenerated silk fibroin (RSF) for hepatic tissue engineering.
The extracellular matrix (ECM), the noncellular component within all tissues, is a 3D construct primarily composed of water, proteins, and polysaccharides that provides cells with physical scaffolding as well as biochemical and physical cues necessary for cell differentiation and tissue morphogenesis. (1) In tissues, the composition and structure of the ECM secreted by cells impacts their morphology and physiological function, binds biomolecules (e.g., growth factors), and maintains homeostasis. (1) Abnormalities in the ECM are at the root of a variety of diseases, such as osteogenesis imperfecta, Marfan’s syndrome, and other congenital disorders. (2) Changes in the ECM also lead to more common disorders such as coronary heart disease (2) and can play a crucial role in the progression and metastasis of tumors due to defects in the normal wound repair process, (3,4) the increased deposition of ECM proteins, (3,5) and the increase in vascular permeability. (6) The importance of the structural, mechanical, and biochemical properties of the ECM in biology and medicine has prompted the development of scaffolds that can mimic some of these properties to isolate and study their effect on cell behavior in vitro. A number of approaches have been used to mimic the ECM in vitro to better understand how its biochemical and physical properties govern cell behavior. (1) Matrigel, for example, is a basal membrane extract derived from mouse carcinoma that is commonly used as a scaffold to study cell differentiation, angiogenesis, and tumor growth. (7,8) While Matrigel has the advantage of being naturally derived, its composition is complex and poorly defined, and batch-to-batch differences can lead to a high variability in experimental results. (7) Other natural materials, such as collagen, hyaluronan, or gelatin, can be used to mimic some aspects of the ECM. (1,9,10) However, the use of natural proteins, peptides, or polysaccharides as sole materials for the construction of biomimetic scaffolds limits their interfacial chemistry and mechanical properties. Scaffolds made from synthetic polymers, with well-defined chemical (e.g., reactivity and degradability) and physical (e.g., elastic modulus) properties or mixtures of synthetic polymers and biopolymers have been proposed as solutions to eliminate the batch-to-batch variability of natural matrices, such as Matrigel, and provide tunable materials properties. Synthetic polymer hydrogels can be functionalized chemically or through enzymatic reactions to tune their surface chemistry and promote cell adhesion. (11−13) The mechanical properties of synthetic scaffolds can also be controlled by tuning the degree of cross-linking between the polymer components (11) or by introducing dopants, such as nanoparticles. (12) Thus, synthetic polymers are attractive for the fabrication of scaffolds with precise chemical functionalities and tunable mechanical properties that can be more effectively used in vitro to study the impact of biochemical and physical cues on cell behavior. Over the last few decades, we have learned that the micro- and nanoscale structure of the ECM also plays a central role in dictating cell behavior within tissues. Because two-dimensional films or bulk hydrogel scaffolds fail to mimic the organization and structural motifs of the ECM, the most recent developments in tissue engineering and cell mobility assays involve scaffolds whose properties can be precisely controlled in 3D, including their feature size, stiffness, and surface chemistry. (13) For example, electrospinning has been extensively used to produce fibrous scaffolds from a wide variety of hydrophilic polymers, including hyaluronan, poly(ester urethane)urea, poly(lactide-co-glycolide), poly(ε-caprolactone), and poly(olygoethylene glycol-methacrylate), among many others. (14−19) In these applications, cell adhesion and proliferation were promoted by the polymeric components (e.g., hyaluronan) themselves or through the addition of ECM proteins such as collagen, elastin, or gelatin. Recently, 3D printing has also been used to produce hydrogel scaffolds with features in the micron to millimeter size functionalized with laminin, fibrin, collagen, and gelatin. (20−22) Similarly, nanofibrillated cellulose hydrogels and aerogels with a tunable macro- and mesoporosity and surface functionalities have been used to evaluate the effect of the mechanical modulus and surface charge on the adhesion, proliferation, and penetration of tumor cells on the scaffolds. (23) Yet, one of the recurrent challenges facing techniques used to fabricate 3D scaffolds is the ability to tune the critical feature sizes in the nanometer to micrometer range, a scale that is commensurate with cellular processes and thus highly relevant to cell behavior, while maintaining the flexibility to tune their mechanical properties and (bio)chemical functionality. In this sense, micro/nanostructured polymer films could represent interesting alternatives for the fabrication of 3D scaffolds. Our group has recently developed a simple and inexpensive benchtop technique, based on the thermal shrinking of a shape-memory polymer, to fabricate micro/nanostructured surfaces from a variety of rigid thin films. (24−28) Here, we propose that this simple technique can be extended to structure polymeric films, resulting in new types of 3D scaffolds that offer tunable feature sizes and chemical functionalities.

In contrast to conventional transplantation methods, the technique of tissue engineering (or regenerate medicine) provided new medical therapy, which used biomaterials with or without living precursor.1 The ultimate purpose of tissue engineering is to reestablish the destroyed human tissues or organs by provide scaffolds for functional tissue regeneration. In human tissue, extracellular matrix (ECM) is a chemically and physically cross-linked complex network with structural fibers such as collagen fibers and elastin fibers having diameters ranging from several ten to several hundred nanometers.2 These protein fibers entangle with each other to form a nonwoven mesh which provides tensile strength and elasticity for cells. In addition to providing a physical support, they also create a substrate with for cell adhesion, migration, and regulate cellular proliferation. Electrospinning technology is a simple and versatile method to prepare ultrathin fibers from polymer solutions or melts. The obtained fibers usually have a diameter from several nanometers to a few micrometers, and mostly in hundreds of nanometers. Therefore, the scaffolds generated from electrospun nanofibers could be capable to mimic the natural ECM.3 The ultrathin diameters of electrospun nanofibers make them possess large specific surface areas. Additionally, the nonwoven fabrics (mats) from electrospun polymer nanofibers offer a unique capability to control the pore sizes among nanofibers.4 Unlike nanorods, nanotubes, and nanowires that are produced mostly by synthetic, bottom-up methods, electrospun nanofibers are produced through a top-down nanomanufacturing process, which results in continuous and low-cost nanofibers that are also relatively easy to be aligned, assembled, and processed into applications. Many synthetic and/or natural polymers including, but not limited to, polylactide (PLA),5 poly(ε-caprolactone),6 poly(L-lactide-co-caprolactone),7, 8 proteins (e.g., collagen),9 and polysaccharides (e.g., chitosan)10 have been electrospun into nanofibrous mats as tissue engineering scaffolds.
Soft-tissue organs have unique ECM compositions that enable tightly regulated biochemical and mechanical properties for specific lineage commitment and differentiation during organ development and maintenance of cellular function in adult organs. Healthy soft-tissue stromal ECM is composed of an insoluble backbone of ECM proteins and soluble hydrogel-forming glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) of varying concentrations, depending on the organ. The mechanical and biochemical cues from the ECM (e.g. composition, topography, pore size, porosity, viscoelasticity) modulate cell viability, growth, homeostasis, migration, and differentiation. For example, the topography, pore size, and porosity modulate the amount of ECM backbone material interacting with the cell and thereby affect cell viability and growth [11, 12]. The matrix viscoelastic properties and the extent of cell attachment to the matrix regulate the cell-generated traction forces and the substrate resistance that the cells experience in response, which impact cell phenotype and differentiation [13-18]. As matrix mechanics drive cell health and disease progression, artificial matrices for in vivo implantation and in vitro culture must closely emulate the native, healthy ECM to maintain cellular function as expected in a healthy organ. Synthetic scaffolds of various types, including nanofiber (NF) mats, sponges, hydrogels, and NF-hydrogel composites, have been engineered to simulate various aspects of ECM. NF mats have fibrous topography, impenetrable pores, and high stiffness, typically in the MPa range or higher [19, 20], which make them good candidates for basement membrane mimetics for monolayer epithelial or endothelial growth [21-24]. However, they fail to mimic both the 3D topography and the stiffness of soft-tissue stromal ECM within the connective tissue compartment. Sponges fabricated by freeze-drying, particulate- or salt-leaching, gas foaming, or phase separation have excessive ECM backbone and excessively large pore sizes (>100 µm) when stiffness is in the sub-kPa range; hence, cells attach flush against the backbone, similar to 2D culture [13]. Hydrogels allow tunable stiffness in the kPa range for soft tissue scaffolds. However, bulk hydrogels, e.g. alginate, poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), lack an insoluble fibrous backbone that mechanically supports cells. Their extremely small pore sizes, in the submicron range, support molecular movement but, without cell attachment sites, impede cellular movement crucial for cell migration and organization. While existing hybrid NF-hydrogel scaffolds reinforce hydrogels with a fibrous backbone, they may have a non-homogenous distribution of cell anchorage points [25]. Hence, a new fabrication strategy is necessary to produce scaffolds that concurrently mimic these essential properties of soft-tissue stromal ECM, including porous topography with 10-50 μm pores [26-29], minimal insoluble fibrous backbone, soluble hydrogel cushion, and sub-kPa range stiffness (∼100-600 Pa) [30-34]. Cryoelectrospinning, also known as cryogenic electrospinning, low temperature electrospinning, and cold plate electrospinning, is an emerging technique to fabricate 3D nanofibrous scaffolds with high porosity and low bulk stiffness. The cryoelectrospinning process includes a cold collector plate, maintained at a temperature less than 0 °C [35-37] (figure S1 available online at stacks.iop.org/BF/14/035010/mmedia), to collect deposited electrospun scaffolds, which are then lyophilized, a major difference from traditional electrospinning techniques. The cryogenically cooled collector plate promotes deposition of atmospheric water vapor as ice crystals on the collector plate and between deposited fibers. Upon contacting the collector plate at sub-zero temperature, the aqueous electrospun solution freezes to form ice crystals as well. When homogenous solutions with multiple components freeze, the solutes and solvent undergo phase separation, and the frozen water can subsequently be lyophilized to produce porous scaffolds. The nucleation of ice crystals allows scalable 3D growth, increased porosity, and consequentially, reduced scaffold density and kPa-range bulk stiffness [38]. The remainder of the cryoelectrospinning process is similar to traditional electrospinning, in which a viscous, long-chain polymer solution becomes electrically charged when passed through a needle tip at high voltage (5-20 kV), and the electrostatic repulsion in the charged fluid exceeds the forces of surface tension, thereby pulling the charged droplet at the needle tip to the nearest electrical ground. The chain-chain interactions of the polymer molecules in the charged droplet prevent the droplet from falling to the electrically grounded collector plate as a drop and instead pull the droplet as a fiber with micro/nanometer diameter to the electrical ground. While the fibers deposit to form a 2.5D NF mat in traditional electrospinning, when cryoelectrospun, they form a 3D fibrous scaffold following lyophilization. As shown in table S1, cryoelectrospinning has primarily been explored with synthetic polymers (e.g. poly(lactic acid) (PLA) [35, 39-42], poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) [37, 43], polycaprolactone (PCL) [38, 41, 44, 45], polyester-urethane (PEU) [43], pyridinium formate (PF) [41]) dissolved in toxic organic solvents or glacial acetic acid, but natural polymers, such as silk fibronin [36, 44, 46], have also been used. While synthetic polymers are easier to manipulate, they do not provide biochemical cues that can be recognized by cells and non-biodegradable polymers require further chemical modification to be biodegradable [47, 48]. Additionally, organic solvents, even at low residual amounts, can have toxic effects on cells [49] and when used in combination with natural proteins, may alter the conformation of the proteins. We hypothesized that cryoelectrospinning of natural biomaterials, comprising ECM proteins and hydrogel materials with water as the solvent could yield biocompatible scaffolds that mimic the topography and viscoelasticity of soft-tissue stromal ECM.

Tissue engineering has emerged as an effective method for the repair and regeneration of damaged tissue. A large variety of tissue-engineered skin substitutes were used to improve the wound healing and restore normal skin architecture.1-3 Biological tissues are built of cells integrated in an extracellular matrix (ECM), which not only provides dynamic biochemical and structural support for cells but also acts as a reservoir for soluble cell signaling molecules.4 Therefore, ECM contributes enormously to tissue morphogenesis, homeostasis, and regeneration. One main challenge in tissue engineering is the design of three-dimensional (3D) scaffolds that can mimic the structure and biological functions of the ECM, for facilitating cell attachment, proliferation, migration, and new tissue formation.5, 6 The ECM of skin is mostly composed of collagen fibers with other proteins and polysaccharides (such as proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans) in smaller quantities.7 However, the application of collagen is limited due to lack of cost-effective production and risk of disease transmission from bovine sources currently utilized.8 Silk fibroin (SF) is a natural protein derived from Bombyx mori and exhibits similar structure to collagen.9, 10 Due to its biocompatibility, ease of chemical modifications, controllable biodegradability and tunable mechanical properties, SF is widely utilized to develop tissue engineering scaffolds.11, 12 SF is proved to support the human keratinocytes and fibroblasts well.13 However, the complex structure of native tissue requires composite materials.14 Therefore, bio-mimicking approaches with other natural polymers are proposed. Hereof, incorporation of sodium alginate (SA), a glycosaminoglycan-like linear copolymer, into SF-based scaffolds closely mimic the chemical composition of ECM of skin. Researchers found that SA/SF composite scaffolds showed higher adhesion to cells as compared with pure SF and SA scaffolds.15 The SA/SF composite scaffolds have been reported by many researchers. However, the studies about fabricating scaffolds with nanofibrous and interconnected porous structures to mimic the structure of nature ECM are seldom. Most studies employ the freeze-drying method and electrospinning to fabricate the SA/SF composite scaffolds.15-20 The interconnected macropores could be observed in the lyophilized scaffolds. However, the freeze-drying method is hard to obtain nanofibrous structures. Electrospinning is commonly performed to fabricate nanofibrous scaffolds in tissue engineering.21 However, electrospinning results in limited thickness of 3D porous structures without macropores, which is insufficient for cell seeding and infiltration.22, 23 Therefore, there is a strong need to develop the SA/SF scaffolds with ECM-like nanofibrous structures and macropores simultaneously for guiding cell activities and tissue growth .
Electrospinning is one of the most common methods to produce fibrous substrates for tissue engineering applications by use of natural and synthetic polymers. It is known that morphology, architecture and surface properties have strong influence on cells growth, spreading, activity and functions [2]. Thereby, scaffolds formed by electrospinning are gaining increasing interest due to their tunable properties to provide ideal microenvironments for various kinds of cell types. Naturally occurring polymers such as collagen (Col) and gelatine (Ge) do not cause foreign body response [3], [4]. PCL does elicit such a response, though minimal. As major drawbacks the poor mechanical properties and their variable physical properties have been identified [5]. In contrast, synthetic biopolymers have predictable and reproducible mechanical and physical properties (e.g. tensile strength, elastic moduli and degradation rate) and they can be synthesised with high reproducibility. Most synthetic polymers incorporate strong hydrophobic surface properties which present poor cell adhesion sites and thus promote a low level of cell attachment. Thereby, different approaches have been realised to adjust surface wettability properties e.g. by chemical and coating routes. A timely fashioned way is the use of hydrophilic and water soluble native extracellular matrix materials such as Col or Ge to form a hybrid of natural and synthetic polymers. In that way, scaffolds are generated which combine the advantages of both types of material and mainly alter materials surface properties. Up to now, various research works describe influencing parameters such as morphology and architecture of electrospun patches with respect to cell growth and proliferation (e.g. [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13]). Focusing on blend nanofibers, Col/elastin [14], [15], polyurethane/polycaprolactone (PCL) [16], and PCL/Ge [17], PCL/Col [18], [19] have been described. However most of them concentrate on morphological topics, chemical structure and biological investigations (cell morphology, cytotoxicity and proliferation). For instance, Chong et al. showed reasonable growth of human dermal fibroblast on polyurethane - PCL/Ge sandwiched structures being promising candidates for wound healing applications [19]. Zhang et al. prepared PCL/Ge 1:1 electrospun nanofibers and found improved bone marrow stromal cell attachment compared to pure synthetic PCL nanofiber scaffolds. Cellular infiltration was demonstrated on the blend fibres of up to 114 μm in-depth [20]. PCL/Col electrospun fibres were investigated by Lee et al. [18]. Compared to pure PCL, the Col-added nanofibers showed better cell responses (adhesion and growth) in vitro and penetration in vivo.
Through these biochemical and biomechanical features, the ECM orchestrates individual organ's biochemical and mechanical characteristics, encompassing aspects such as tensile and compressive strength and elasticity, and also facilitates a protective mechanism through a buffering action, helping to maintain extracellular homeostasis and water retention. Also, the ECM plays a crucial role in supervisory structural organization and physiological functions through binding growth factors and networking with cell-surface receptors, thereby facilitating signal transduction and modulating gene transcription.6 Conversely, enzymes like matrix metalloproteinases and certain glycosidases, such as hyaluronidases and heparanase, play a significant role in ECM remodeling.7 The ECM is composed of fibrous proteins (such as collagen, fibrillin, and elastin), glycoproteins (e.g., laminin, fibronectin, and tenascin), proteoglycans (e.g., glycosaminoglycans), and enzymes like matrix metalloproteinases.8 Natural extracellular matrix (ECM) components are sourced from native tissues and organs. Various decellularization methods are utilized to derive this ECM matrix.9 Decellularization is a vital tissue engineering process involving removing cellular components from donor tissues while preserving the extracellular matrix. The ECM is essential as it provides structural and biochemical signals necessary for tissue regeneration. Several decellularization methods have been developed to achieve this objective, including mechanical, enzymatic, and chemical approaches. Among these methods, chemical decellularization has gained popularity due to its effectiveness in completely removing cells while maintaining the integrity and functionality of the ECM. Chemical decellularization typically uses detergents, such as sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), Triton X-100, or ionic detergents, in combination with other chemical agents like acids or alcohols. This process disrupts cell membranes and facilitates the removal of cellular contents. One of the main advantages of chemical decellularization is its ability to thoroughly eliminate cellular debris while minimizing damage to the ECM structure. By carefully controlling the concentration and exposure time of the chemical agents, researchers can effectively preserve the mechanical properties and biochemical composition of the ECM, which are crucial for supporting cell adhesion, migration, and differentiation.10 Furthermore, chemical decellularization can be easily standardized and scaled, making it a versatile and reproducible method for producing ECM scaffolds. This scalability is significant when producing large quantities of ECM-based scaffolds for tissue engineering applications, such as organ regeneration or wound healing. Subsequent techniques like cross-linking (either chemical or physical cross-linking) can further enhance the structural stability and functional performance of decellularized extracellular matrix (dECM) scaffolds, offering promising outcomes in tissue regeneration and developing bioengineered organs.11 dECM retains the chemical properties of native tendons, including collagen fibre orientation, allowing tendon cells to grow and regenerate. Decellularized tendons can also encourage macrophages to remodel tissue, reducing inflammation and promoting healing. Biomimetic scaffolds made from dECM replicate native tissue, promoting integration and regeneration. Unlike other cross-linking techniques, photo-crosslinking provides unmatched precision in controlling the degree and location of cross-linking, which allows for better preservation of the biological properties of the scaffold while significantly enhancing its mechanical strength. Photo-crosslinking has become vital in various research fields, mainly biomaterials and tissue engineering. This technique employs light to create covalent bonds between polymer chains and some proteins in biological samples, leading to stable three-dimensional structures.12 In tissue engineering, photo-crosslinking provides significant advantages due to its precise control over the spatial and temporal aspects of gelation that help to maintain the matrix stiffness of the biomaterial.13 dECM retains the chemical properties of native tendons, including collagen fibre orientation, allowing tendon cells to grow and regenerate. Decellularized tendons can also encourage macrophages to remodel tissue, reducing inflammation and promoting healing. Biomimetic scaffolds made from dECM replicate native tissue, promoting integration and regeneration. By utilizing photoinitiators and photo-reactive polymers, researchers can manipulate the gelation process by adjusting the intensity of light, exposure time, and wavelength. This ability is crucial for creating hydrogels that closely mimic the native ECM, which is vital for supporting cell growth and proliferation and promoting tissue regeneration.14 Gelatin methacrylate (GelMA), a photo-cross-linkable polymer, undergoes free-radical crosslinking and forms covalent bonds between methacrylate groups, when exposed to ultraviolet (UV) light.15 This process is valuable for developing hydrogels with desirable mechanical properties and degradation profiles, making them suitable for various biomedical applications. The field of 3D bioprinting has dramatically benefited from photo-crosslinking methods. These techniques allow the fabrication of complex tissue constructs that mimic natural tissues' architecture and functionality. Various bioprinting strategies, including stereolithography and digital light processing, employ photo-cross-linkable bioinks to build structures layer by layer. In this technique, Ru2+ is photolytically oxidized in the presence of visible light and the electron acceptor SPS, forming crosslinks within the ECM. This allows for real-time manipulation of scaffold stiffness, providing a powerful tool for studying the impact of ECM rigidity on cellular responses and disease development. Our group has been actively engaged in optimizing decellularization strategies and characterizing ECM-derived scaffolds with the dual aim of advancing tissue engineering and developing physiologically relevant disease models.18,19 We focus on engineering biomimetic platforms that closely replicate the native tissue microenvironment in terms of biochemical composition, mechanical properties, and cellular interactions. These scaffolds are designed for diverse applications, ranging from regenerative medicine to the modeling of complex disease states. By integrating structural, biochemical, and immunological evaluations, we strive to design bioactive ECM scaffolds that can support cellular functions and mimic disease pathophysiology.20,21
The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a complex microenvironment that provides structural, mechanical, and biochemical cues to cells, which ultimately dictate their fate.1, 2 The ECM is composed of a variety of polymeric biomacromolecules, varying between different tissues. In general, ECM components include: proteins, glycoproteins, proteoglycans, and polysaccharides.3, 4 Collagen is one of the main components of the ECM of all connective tissues.5 In tissues, collagen is presented as fibers, but its morphological features such as fiber diameter and organization vary between different types of tissues. For instance, collagen forms highly aligned fibers in cardiac tissues, while in some regions of cartilage collagen forms a random structure with a diameter range between 10 and 100 nm.6 Collagen provides strength and structure to the ECM by directly interacting with cells and other ECM molecules.7 Cell-matrix interactions imply cells interact with collagen, indicating that cells contain receptors for specific collagen peptide sequences.5 Collagen is considered a family of closely related but genetically distinct molecules. There are 28 different types recognized, but 80-90% of collagens in the body belong to types I, II, and III.8 Type I collagen is found abundantly in the skin, bone, tendon, ligaments, and cornea.9 Type II collagen is present in the eye vitreous humor, in the nucleus pulposus of the vertebral discs, and is the main component of cartilage.9 Type III collagen is abundant in the loose connective tissue on the walls of blood vessels, the skin dermis, and the stroma of various glands.9 Due to its abundance in nature, collagen has become an attractive biopolymer for the engineering of ECM mimetic scaffolds to be used in tissue regeneration. Toward fabricating a scaffold that would mimic the physical, chemical, and mechanical properties of tissues in the human body, researchers have focused their studies in manufacturing collagen-based scaffolds, including sponges,10 hydrogels,11 membranes,12 and nanofibers.13 Nanofibrous collagen scaffolds are of particular interest due to its resemblance to native ECM in composition, scale, orientation, and geometry.11 One of the most popular techniques to produce collagen nanofibers is electrospinning. Electrospinning is a technique where a polymeric solution is exposed to a high voltage by pumping the solution through a needle attached to a high voltage power supply (Figure 1). The applied voltage generates an electric field between the needle and a metallic collector in which a thin polymer fiber travels until collected. The polymer solution flows through the needle forming in the tip a cone-like structure (i.e., Taylor cone) produced by action of the electric field. Once the repulsive electrical force overcomes the force of surface tension, a jet of electrically charged solution is expelled from the tip of the Taylor cone. This jet travels to the metallic collector and as it moves in the air the solvent evaporates, yielding polymeric nanosized fibers.14 The electrospinning process is controlled by several parameters, which in turn control fiber structure. It has been shown-using synthetic polymers-that fiber diameter depends on solution viscosity, applied voltage, flow rate, temperature, humidity, and tip-to-collector distance, among others.15 Moreover, fibers may be aligned by electrospinning onto a rotating collector.16 Electrospun nanofibrous mats have been shown to be ideal ECM mimetic scaffolds for the culture of mesenchymal stem cells,17 and cells derived from different tissues such as neural,18 cardiac,19 and musculoskeletal.20 Electrospinning of collagen is challenging due to its limited solubility. Several reports successfully present electrospun collagen nanofibers from fluorinated solvents such as trifluoroacetic acid,21 trifluoroethanol,22 and 1,1,1,3,3,3,-hexafluoro-2-propanol (HFIP).23-26 However, fluorinated solvents disrupt collagen's secondary structure,27, 28 effectively converting the electrospun collagen into gelatin.29 In fact, one group reported a decrease of 45% of collagen's triple helical structure after electrospinning from HFIP.30 Several efforts to electrospun collagen from benign solvents have been proposed including blends with other synthetic polymers,31, 32 and a phosphate buffer and ethanol mixture.27 Recently, weak acids-such as acetic acid-have been proposed as an attractive solvent for the production of collagen nanofibers because they are able to generate stable fibers with uniform morphology that preserve collagen's secondary structure.28, 32-36

Scaffolds used for tissue engineering are made to mimic natural surroundings of tissues, the extracellular matrix (ECM). The ECM plays a large part in maintaining the structural integrity of the connective tissue. When producing a tissue in the laboratory, structural integrity of the cells is ensured only when a biomimetic ECM is present. Nanofibrous polymer fibers have been chosen for their resemblance to natural fibers of the ECM and their capability to provide the support necessary for cells to grow and differentiate into tissue. Polycaprolactone based nanofibrous scaffolds for tissue engineering have been fabricated through the electrospinning process. Electrospinning is a simple and cost-effective method for producing nanofibers which involves applying a high voltage to a falling polymer solution to form a fluid jet producing nanofibers. Magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) have been incorporated within the nanofibers by addition of MNPs to the polymer solution to increase the rate of bone cell growth, proliferation, and differentiation. Studies by Nomura and Takano-Yamamoto, [Matrix Biol. 19, 91 (2000)] demonstrated an increase in the expression levels of multiple genes in bone tissue including growth factors when shear stress was applied at the cellular level. MNPs are around 1-100 nm and exhibit superparamagnetism. These properties of MNPs allow for high noninvasive control over them using an external magnetic field. While under an ac (15 Hz, 1-6 Gauss) or pulsed magnetic fields, MNPs will induce low level mechanical stresses within the scaffold causing shear stresses at the cellular level of the preosteoblast MC3T3-E1 cells to stimulate their growth, proliferation, and differentiation. Engineering living tissue for the purpose of healing or replacing tissues and organs requires attention to both the biological and structural properties of tissues. Langer and Vacanti1 describe this area of research as “an interdisciplinary field that applies the principles of engineering and life sciences toward the development of biological substitutes that restore, maintain, or improve tissue function or a whole organ.” In order to produce an in vitro tissue that can be implanted in vivo, three important components are necessary: a biocompatible/biodegradable scaffold, a cell source, and growth/differentiation conducing cell culture conditions.2

Based solely on the provided evidence, electrospinning creates scaffolds that mimic the Extracellular Matrix (ECM) through the following mechanisms:

1.  **Structural Mimicry (Fiber Scale and Morphology):** Electrospinning produces microfibers and nanofibers with diameters ranging from nanometers to micrometers, closely resembling the fibrillary structure (e.g., collagen fibers) of the native ECM. This similarity in scale and fibrous topography allows the scaffold to physically emulate the non-cellular component of tissues. [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 13, 14]
2.  **Architectural Mimicry (Network Formation):** The electrospinning process results in the formation of non-woven meshes or mats of randomly deposited, entangled fibers. This creates a 3D network structure with interconnected pores that mimics the intricate fibrous network found in natural ECM, facilitating cell attachment and infiltration. [1, 2, 4, 6, 13]
3.  **High Surface Area and Porosity:** Electrospun nanofibers possess a very high specific surface area and high porosity relative to their volume. This large surface area enhances interactions with cells and biomolecules, while the porosity facilitates the transportation of nutrients, oxygen, and waste – key functions supported by the native ECM. [3, 4, 6]
4.  **Material Versatility for Biochemical Mimicry:** Electrospinning can utilize a wide range of materials, including natural polymers (like collagen, silk fibroin, chitosan), synthetic polymers (like PCL, PLA, PLGA), and their blends/composites. Using natural polymers incorporates inherent biochemical cues (e.g., cell recognition sites) found in the ECM. Synthetic polymers offer tunable properties and stability, often blended or coated with natural components like decellularized ECM (dECM) to combine structural integrity with bioactivity. Blending allows the scaffold to mimic both the chemical and fibrillar properties of target tissues. [1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14]
5.  **Facilitation of Cell Functions:** Due to their structural and biochemical resemblance, electrospun nanofibrous scaffolds provide an instructive microenvironment that promotes essential cellular functions mediated by the ECM *in vivo*, including cell attachment, adhesion, proliferation, migration, and differentiation. The nanotopographical cues significantly influence cell morphology and behavior. [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11, 13]

PCL is widely employed in tissue engineering applications, often in combination with other compositions, to form nanofiber scaffolds.[27, 28] In recent times, there has been a growing interest among researchers in utilizing graphene oxide (GO) as a biomaterial for tissue regeneration and drug delivery, owing to its unique properties such as bio-adaptability, mechanical stability, and electroconductivity.[29] Nanoparticles have emerged as promising candidates for enhancing the characteristics of polymer scaffolds due to their antibacterial properties and high mechanical strength.[30] Moreover, GO offers an intriguing structure for modulating the behavior of stem cells. It facilitates the release of active biological factors, including pro-survival and anti-inflammatory molecules, from delivery systems containing stem cells. Additionally, GO enables the intracellular delivery of growth factors, DNA, synthetic proteins, and other molecules, thereby regulating stem cell differentiation and proliferation.[31, 32]

The physiological structure of extracellular matrix (ECM) is a natural network of intricate nanofibers, which provides an instructive background to guide cell behavior [4]. With the ability to form nanofibrous structures, a drive to mimic the native ECM has begun. Among the various approaches available, electrostatic spinning (popularly known as electrospinning) has gained reputation for its capability to make native ECM-mimicking (in terms of geometry, morphology or topography) scaffolds [5]. Electrospinning is capable of fabricating nanometer-scale fibers that yield very high specific surface area. It is otherwise difficult to produce such fibers by conventional non-woven fiber fabrication techniques [6]. Electrospun (e-spun) nanofibers are therefore very useful for developing a variety of structures whose functional efficiency is surface area dependent. With the advent of electrospinning, mimicking the physical dimensions of native ECM has become easier. However, conferring bioactivity to e-spun scaffold will decide its ultimate utility in the creation of functional tissue. In addition to the architectural features, a scaffold should also mimic the biological/biochemical features of the native ECM which is regarded as a complex organization of fibrous structural proteins such as collagens and a wide variety of proteoglycans [7, 8]. With respect to the biochemical attributes of materials used in tissue engineering, several synthetic biodegradable polymers have been tested previously. However, lack of cell recognition sites, aggravated hydrophobicity and acidic degradation products are few major issues which limit their use [9]. Hence, the attention has shifted toward natural biodegradable polymers. The most ideal candidate material should be collagen itself-the major component of native ECM. However, the major shortcomings for collagen are its inadequate mechanical properties and anti-genecity [10]. An alternative and intriguing biopolymer which has features similar to collagen is silk fibroin. Produced by several Lepidoptera larvae, including silkworms, fibroin is famous for its biocompatibility, slow degradability and excellent mechanical properties, and has been exploited for various biomedical applications including liver tissue engineering [11, 12]. Besides protein factors, native ECM also has variety of proteoglycans. Therefore, modification of artificial scaffold with such ligands is often necessary for optimization of ECM for hepatic tissue engineering. Given the fact that the hepatocytes have asialoglycoprotein (ASGP) receptors that recognize and bind to molecules with exposed galactose, N-acetyl galactosamine or glucose residues, many have demonstrated the use of galactosylated materials for use in liver tissue engineering [13]. Owing to biocompatibility, biodegradability, antibacterial activity and resemblance with native ECM glycans, chitosan has been widely used in tissue engineering applications [14]. Recently, galactosylation of chitosan has gained importance to increase its aqueous solubility and to improve hepatocyte attachment [13]. Hence, galactosylated chitosan (GalCS) is another appropriate material of choice which can be used along with regenerated silk fibroin (RSF) for hepatic tissue engineering.
Electrospinning is a primary method for producing low-cost, multifunctional scaffolds for tissue engineering, affording microsized and nanosized scaffolds that imitate the extracellular matrix (ECM).7 The size and structural resemblance of electrospun nanofibers to ECM makes them ideal for tissue regeneration.8,9 Significantly, the nanotopographical characteristics exhibited by electrospun nanofibers influence the morphology, migration, and differentiation. The short diameter, adequate contact surface area, and high porosity of electrospun nanofibers have established electrospinning as a frequently employed fabrication method for tissue engineering scaffolds, particularly in wound healing and cartilage, tendon, and nerve tissue regeneration.10 However, conventional electrospinning does not replicate the organization found in tendon fibers. To address this limitation, gap electrospinning, which can produce uniaxially parallel fibers by manipulating the electric field across the electrode poles, has been developed. Another technique for obtaining aligned nanofibers involves the use of the rapidly rotating-mandrel technique, which is energy- and time-consuming. Moreover, transferring fibers fabricated via this method is difficult because they stick to the collecting surface. In contrast, uniaxially aligned nanofibers prepared by gap electrospinning rest on an air gap between the poles, which facilitates the fiber collection procedure.11 Polycaprolactone (PCL) is a biodegradable, nontoxic polymer with good mechanical properties.12,13 However, its poor hydrophilicity and cytocompatibility are unfavorable for creating a cell-friendly scaffold. Accordingly, the surface modification of the PCL fibers without altering their bulk properties is essential.14 We immobilize collagen on PCL fibers by aminolysis to enhance its cytocompatibility. Collagen is the main component of the ECM and contributes to 65%-80% of the dry weight of tendon tissue.15 By adding collagen to the fibers, we further mimic the natural chemistry of the tendon tissue. The cell-imprinting method has been extensively studied to physically mimic the natural topography of cells and induce stable and efficient differentiation signals in stem cells. Several studies have shown the significance of cultural platform elements, ranging from topography, stiffness, and surface nanopatterns in cell differentiation.16-23 The ECM maintains the physical, chemical, and mechanical functions of a cell, determining the differentiation path for stem cells.22,24,25 Previously published reports have revealed that a tenocyte-imprinted substrate stimulates tenogenic signals in rat adipose-derived stem cells in vitro.26,27 In other studies, chondrogenic, osteogenic, myogenic, neurogenic, keratinogenic, and Schwann cell differentiation signals were successfully transmitted to stem cells by the imprinting technique.27-35 The main advantages of the cell-imprinting method for regulating the cell fate are safety, stability, and time and concentration independence. It is a potential replacement for standard polystyrene tissue culture plates as an effective and safe differentiation mechanism.27
Electrospinning is one of the most common methods to produce fibrous substrates for tissue engineering applications by use of natural and synthetic polymers. Ideally, a substrate should mimic both the form and functionality of the native extracellular matrix (ECM) [1]. It is known that morphology, architecture and surface properties have strong influence on cells growth, spreading, activity and functions [2]. Thereby, scaffolds formed by electrospinning are gaining increasing interest due to their tunable properties to provide ideal microenvironments for various kinds of cell types. Naturally occurring polymers such as collagen (Col) and gelatine (Ge) do not cause foreign body response [3], [4]. PCL does elicit such a response, though minimal. As major drawbacks the poor mechanical properties and their variable physical properties have been identified [5]. In contrast, synthetic biopolymers have predictable and reproducible mechanical and physical properties (e.g. tensile strength, elastic moduli and degradation rate) and they can be synthesised with high reproducibility. Most synthetic polymers incorporate strong hydrophobic surface properties which present poor cell adhesion sites and thus promote a low level of cell attachment. Thereby, different approaches have been realised to adjust surface wettability properties e.g. by chemical and coating routes. A timely fashioned way is the use of hydrophilic and water soluble native extracellular matrix materials such as Col or Ge to form a hybrid of natural and synthetic polymers. In that way, scaffolds are generated which combine the advantages of both types of material and mainly alter materials surface properties. Up to now, various research works describe influencing parameters such as morphology and architecture of electrospun patches with respect to cell growth and proliferation (e.g. [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13]). Focusing on blend nanofibers, Col/elastin [14], [15], polyurethane/polycaprolactone (PCL) [16], and PCL/Ge [17], PCL/Col [18], [19] have been described. However most of them concentrate on morphological topics, chemical structure and biological investigations (cell morphology, cytotoxicity and proliferation). For instance, Chong et al. showed reasonable growth of human dermal fibroblast on polyurethane - PCL/Ge sandwiched structures being promising candidates for wound healing applications [19]. Zhang et al. prepared PCL/Ge 1:1 electrospun nanofibers and found improved bone marrow stromal cell attachment compared to pure synthetic PCL nanofiber scaffolds. Cellular infiltration was demonstrated on the blend fibres of up to 114 μm in-depth [20]. PCL/Col electrospun fibres were investigated by Lee et al. [18]. Compared to pure PCL, the Col-added nanofibers showed better cell responses (adhesion and growth) in vitro and penetration in vivo.
Scaffolds used for tissue engineering are made to mimic natural surroundings of tissues, the extracellular matrix (ECM). The ECM plays a large part in maintaining the structural integrity of the connective tissue. When producing a tissue in the laboratory, structural integrity of the cells is ensured only when a biomimetic ECM is present. Nanofibrous polymer fibers have been chosen for their resemblance to natural fibers of the ECM and their capability to provide the support necessary for cells to grow and differentiate into tissue. Polycaprolactone based nanofibrous scaffolds for tissue engineering have been fabricated through the electrospinning process. Electrospinning is a simple and cost-effective method for producing nanofibers which involves applying a high voltage to a falling polymer solution to form a fluid jet producing nanofibers. Magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) have been incorporated within the nanofibers by addition of MNPs to the polymer solution to increase the rate of bone cell growth, proliferation, and differentiation. Studies by Nomura and Takano-Yamamoto, [Matrix Biol. 19, 91 (2000)] demonstrated an increase in the expression levels of multiple genes in bone tissue including growth factors when shear stress was applied at the cellular level. MNPs are around 1-100 nm and exhibit superparamagnetism. These properties of MNPs allow for high noninvasive control over them using an external magnetic field. While under an ac (15 Hz, 1-6 Gauss) or pulsed magnetic fields, MNPs will induce low level mechanical stresses within the scaffold causing shear stresses at the cellular level of the preosteoblast MC3T3-E1 cells to stimulate their growth, proliferation, and differentiation. Engineering living tissue for the purpose of healing or replacing tissues and organs requires attention to both the biological and structural properties of tissues. Langer and Vacanti1 describe this area of research as “an interdisciplinary field that applies the principles of engineering and life sciences toward the development of biological substitutes that restore, maintain, or improve tissue function or a whole organ.” In order to produce an in vitro tissue that can be implanted in vivo, three important components are necessary: a biocompatible/biodegradable scaffold, a cell source, and growth/differentiation conducing cell culture conditions.2
Recent advances in biomaterial science have highlighted the promise of combining synthetic polymers like polycaprolactone (PCL), poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA), or poly(glycolic acid) with natural polymers such as collagen or chitosan derivatives to generate scaffolds that closely mimic the extracellular matrix (ECM), enhancing biocompatibility, mechanical robustness, and controlled biodegradation [1-5]. Such hybrid constructs, which are often electrospun or self-assembled, offer high surface area and tunable porosity, thereby facilitating cell attachment, proliferation, and differentiation toward diverse regenerative therapies, including cardiac repair, neural regeneration, and bone tissue engineering [1, 3, 6-10]. These strategies highlight the promise of advanced biomaterials in promoting safe, effective, and applicable solutions for tissue engineering and individualized regenerative medicine [7, 8]. Hence, within the range of emerging strategies, biocompatible electrospun nanofibers have become increasingly significant in biomedical applications, as they effectively mimic the ECM, enhance cell-material interactions, and offer crucial structural support for successful tissue engineering results [11, 12]. These nanofibers exhibit potential for use in wound dressings, scaffolds, and drug delivery systems due to their antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral properties [13]. The electrospinning technique is employed to create these textures, enabling the fabrication of fibrous scaffolds with specific properties designed to meet diverse medical requirements [14]. Biocompatible electrospun nanofibers fill a significant void in existing biomedical materials that do not possess the surface characteristics required for effective cellular interactions and tissue integration. For instance, nanofibers could mimic the structure of the ECM, offering a scaffold that facilitates cell attachment, proliferation, and differentiation, essential for advancements in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine [15, 16]. Electrospun nanofibers characterized by high porosity and interconnected structures, particularly those composed of poly-L-lactic acid (PLA) and chitosan, facilitate increased cell density and promote cell growth compared to dense films [11]. Also, incorporating cell-adhesion domains in nanofibers enhances cell proliferation and adhesion, which is essential for applications such as wound healing [17].
Tissue engineering involves the fabrication of three-dimensional scaffolds to support cellular in-growth and proliferation. Ideally, the scaffolds should be similar to the native extracellular matrix (ECM). Electrospun polymer nanofibrous scaffolds are appropriate candidates for ECM mimetic materials since they mimic the nanoscale properties of ECM. Electrospun polymer nanocomposites based on poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA)/poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) and organically modified montmorillonite (OMMT) were prepared by a solution intercalation technique followed by electrospinning. The morphology of fibrous scaffolds based on these nanocomposites was investigated using scanning electron microscopy. The scaffolds showed highly porous structure within the nanofibres of diameters ranging from 400 to 700 nm. X-ray diffractometry gave evidence of good dispersion of the OMMT in the blends with exfoliated morphology. Measurements of the water uptake and water contact angle of the fibrous scaffolds indicated significant improvement in the hydrophilicity of the scaffolds. Evaluations of the mechanical properties and unrestricted somatic stem cell culture of the electrospun fibrous nanocomposite scaffolds revealed that the PLGA90/PVA10/1.5% OMMT and PLGA90/PVA10/3% OMMT samples are the most useful from the tissue engineering application viewpoint. There are currently a variety of strategies for the treatment of vascular disease (a subset of CVD focusing on the vessels), including extracellular matrix (ECM) mimicking structures, the use of native ECM components, and functionalized protein laden scaffolds.2-5 Combining ECM with polymers to manufacture electrospun bioscaffolds has previously been utilized to harness the repeatable mechanical properties of the polymer with the biochemical and mechanical properties of the ECM.5-8 Electrospinning polymers produces a network of fibers that can be heavily tailored depending on the properties desired.9 They can be designed to have isotropic or anisotropic mechanical properties, along with three-dimensional architectural properties that favor cell survival and growth.10 It is possible through electrospinning to include bioactive cues into a repeatable polymer structure and alter its mechanical and physical properties.5-7, 11 This has huge implications in tissue engineering where mimicking the physical and biological properties of the native ECM are major research focusses, especially when the final aim is generation of new functional tissue. Previous studies have shown that including ECM or ECM proteins into an electrospun polymer scaffold alters its mechanical properties and positively affects seeded cells.5-7, 12 Therefore, in this study, we propose electrospinning a combination of aortic ECM with polycaprolactone (PCL) at two different ECM concentrations and biomechanically evaluating the resulting fibrous scaffolds along with a conventional PCL-only scaffold. Aortic ECM has been chosen as we are looking at a novel solution for the treatment of vascular disease, and therefore have decided to use a type of native ECM directly from a vascular source. Bovine aorta was harvested from a 2 year old female cow. Samples were frozen within 4 h of harvesting at −80 °C and stored until required. A 40 mm diameter sample from the aortic arch was cut out, and all connective tissue was removed after cleaning with ethanol and bathing in water for 30 min to remove blood. A 2 mm punch was used to punch out pieces of aorta for decellularization. The pieces were placed in a decellularizing device and perfusion decellularized with 0.5% w/v sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) in diH2O for 36 h as previously described.13 Aorta samples were then perfused with 20 L of diH2O at 170 mL/min to remove remnant SDS. Samples were frozen and lyophilized in a FreeZone 4.5 freeze-drier (Labconco). Dry ECM was then milled in a plenary ball mill PM 100 (Retsch). ECM powder was then collected and stored at 4 °C for use in electrospinning.

One of the important components in this method is a scaffold, which is a three-dimensional structure that supports the growth and regeneration of bone cells. On a nanometer scale, bone tissue has a structure called the extracellular matrix (ECM). The ECM consists of nano- to micro-scale collagen fibers inserted with bone minerals measuring tens of nanometers [2, 3]. Therefore, a good scaffold must be able to mimic the structure and function of the ECM. One method that is widely used to produce nano-fiber scaffolds is electrospinning [2]. This method is able to produce fine fibers that resemble the ECM. In addition, electrospinning allows the combination of organic and inorganic materials in one composite system [4]. However, the success of a scaffold is not only determined by its structure. The selection of the constituent materials also greatly affects the biological and mechanical performance of the scaffold [5]. Polycaprolactone (PCL) is a synthetic polymer that is often used in this application [6-8]. PCL is biocompatible, biodegradable, and has good mechanical strength. However, PCL also has disadvantages. Among them are low hydrophilic properties, slow degradation rates, and less than optimal cell adhesion capabilities [9-11]. To overcome this, PCL can be combined with natural polymers such as starch. One type that is easily available is potato starch. Starch is hydrophilic, biocompatible, and easily decomposed in the body [12-14]. In addition, starch is abundant in nature and relatively cheap. However, starch also has disadvantages, such as low thermal stability and poor mechanical strength [15]. In addition to organic components, the inorganic phase is also important to increase the bioactivity of the scaffold [16]. Carbonate-hydroxyapatite (CHA) is a modified form of hydroxyapatite (HA) [17]. This modification is carried out by adding carbonate ions to mimic the composition of natural bone minerals. CHA has a large particle size and surface area [18, 19]. This makes CHA have better bioactivity, biocompatibility, and the ability to form bonds with hard tissue compared to conventional HA [20-22].

In this study, alternating field electrospinning (AFES) fabricates cold water fish skin gelatin nanofibrous materials (FGel NFM) with up to 10 wt.% Dextran (DEX) or acetyl glucosamine (AGA) from pure aqueous solutions at process productivity of 7.92-8.90 g∙h−1. With the growing need for sustainable biomedical platforms for various applications in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine, nanofibrous materials (NFM) have gained much attraction due to their high surface-area to pore volume ratio combined with good mechanical integrity for a porous, low-density material which promotes cell growth and proliferation. An ideal tissue engineered biomedical platform should mimic the body's natural tissue structure that is created during the regeneration process, the extracellular matrix (ECM). As the first layer of tissue regeneration, the ECM consists of fibers with diameters in the range from 50 to 500 nm[1] composed mainly of collagen, elastin, and other macromolecules.[2, 3] The ECM's ideal mechanical integrity varies depending on the intended tissue it replaces, but mechanical property mimic is necessary to detour a stressful environment for cells during the regeneration process.[4] To further promote healthy cell structure formation across the ECM, the ECM must contain nutrients for the growing cells to minimize scarring[4, 5] while causing a low immunogenic response.[6] This ideal engineered ECM would additionally need to demonstrate scale-up production capability as a sustainable material.

Electrospinning is a high-performance and simple process for producing continuous fibers in nano and micro sizes for application in various fields, for example, drug delivery, catalyst structure, sensor design and fabrication, textiles, and especially in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine (TERM) [1-6]. TERM introduces functional substitutes to the repair and regeneration of damaged tissues and organs. It employs various sciences, including biology, chemistry, and engineering, to arrive at these goals. TERM needs three integral components: scaffold, cells, and biological signals, to facilitate cell growth, differentiation, and angiogenesis [4, 7]. Nanofibrous structures exhibit multiple advantages, such as a range of fiber diameters similar to the fibrillary ECM, high porosity, and large surface-to-volume area [8]. Fabricated scaffolds should mimic the 3D extracellular matrix (ECM) and provide a biocompatible environment for cell homing, proliferation, and differentiation toward tissue repair and regeneration. Along with biodegradability and sufficient mechanical strength, the porous structure of scaffolds facilitates the transportation of nutrients and oxygen while must be nontoxic, capable of being sterilized, and simple to manufacture and handle [9-12]. The nanofibers fabricated with electrospinning can recapitulate the nanofibrous structure of natural ECM. However, the structures prepared by traditional electrospinning are two-dimensional and cannot simulate a three-dimensional structure of native ECM. The porosity and fibrous structure of the native ECM could be simulated using nanofiber-based scaffolds with networking structures mimicking collagen fibrils [13]. 2D scaffolds have limitations such as insufficient porosity, low cell infiltration, and restriction of cell-cell and cell-ECM interaction. These limitations led to the emergence of 3D scaffolds that overcome 2D-associated limitations. 3D scaffolds create a microenvironment mimicking the in vivo tissue interconnectivity where cells create molecular gradients within the implanted scaffolds [14]. Moreover, 3D scaffolds provide a three-dimensional environment for cell transfer and infiltration, cell-cell interactions, and nutrient and waste exchange, which is essential for cell-cycle regulation and tissue function. To date, several electrospinning methods (e.g., cold-plate electrospinning, multilayering, wet electrospinning, postprocessing, template-assisted electrospinning, and self-assembly) have been developed for the 3D nanofibrous structures preparation. 3D nanofibrous structures fabricated via these electrospinning methods are time-consuming and require other processing or instruments along with these methods. On the other hand, most of these electrospinning techniques produce large diameter fibers resulting in significantly decreasing the pore sizes and porosity of prepared 3D scaffolds [15, 16]. Reducing the pore size as well as the porosity of the fabricated scaffold can hinder the infiltration and migration of the cells seeded on these scaffolds. Therefore, there are still challenges to the fabrication of a 3D nanofibrous scaffold by electrospinning with acceptable properties for application in TERM.

In contrast to conventional transplantation methods, the technique of tissue engineering (or regenerate medicine) provided new medical therapy, which used biomaterials with or without living precursor.1 The ultimate purpose of tissue engineering is to reestablish the destroyed human tissues or organs by provide scaffolds for functional tissue regeneration. In human tissue, extracellular matrix (ECM) is a chemically and physically cross-linked complex network with structural fibers such as collagen fibers and elastin fibers having diameters ranging from several ten to several hundred nanometers.2 These protein fibers entangle with each other to form a nonwoven mesh which provides tensile strength and elasticity for cells. In addition to providing a physical support, they also create a substrate with for cell adhesion, migration, and regulate cellular proliferation. Electrospinning technology is a simple and versatile method to prepare ultrathin fibers from polymer solutions or melts. The obtained fibers usually have a diameter from several nanometers to a few micrometers, and mostly in hundreds of nanometers. Therefore, the scaffolds generated from electrospun nanofibers could be capable to mimic the natural ECM.3 The ultrathin diameters of electrospun nanofibers make them possess large specific surface areas. Additionally, the nonwoven fabrics (mats) from electrospun polymer nanofibers offer a unique capability to control the pore sizes among nanofibers.4 Unlike nanorods, nanotubes, and nanowires that are produced mostly by synthetic, bottom-up methods, electrospun nanofibers are produced through a top-down nanomanufacturing process, which results in continuous and low-cost nanofibers that are also relatively easy to be aligned, assembled, and processed into applications. Many synthetic and/or natural polymers including, but not limited to, polylactide (PLA),5 poly(ε-caprolactone),6 poly(L-lactide-co-caprolactone),7, 8 proteins (e.g., collagen),9 and polysaccharides (e.g., chitosan)10 have been electrospun into nanofibrous mats as tissue engineering scaffolds.

ground_truth: In block copolymers (e.g., PEG-PLA), the ratio of the hydrophilic block (PEG) to the hydrophobic block (PLA) dictates the self-assembly into micelles or vesicles. A balance is crucial: too much hydrophobicity leads to precipitation; too much hydrophilicity prevents stable micelle formation. The core serves as a reservoir for hydrophobic drugs.
