These copolymers have been investigated for their ability to self-assemble in supramolecular aggregates of different sizes and shapes, which can be employed as drug nanostructured delivery systems [8,9]. In addition, some of them display a thermogelling behaviour, undergoing to a sol-gel transition as a function of temperature [10,11]. These amphiphilic thermogelling copolymers can be employed for the design of thermogelling systems, also called thermogels, which are a class of stimuli-responsive hydrogels able to form spontaneously upon heating [[12], [13], [14]]. The thermogelling hydrogels displaying a sol-to-gel transition close to body temperature (37 °C) have gained a great attention since they can be used for a wide range of applications in the biomedical and pharmaceutical fields, such as injectable formulations for drug or gene delivery and scaffolds for tissue engineering [[15], [16], [17]]. The driving force leading to the formation of the hydrogel is a further dehydration of the polymeric chain at the micellar state, triggered, in the case of thermogels, by an increase of temperature [18]. Among the different classes of amphiphilic copolymers displaying a thermogelling ability (e.g. poloxamer and its analogs), those characterized by biodegradability and biocompatibility offer considerable advantages, especially since they do not need removal or surgical interventions after they have fulfilled their function [12,[19], [20], [21]]. Polyesters are the most common biodegradable thermogelling copolymers investigated, constituted by polyethylene glycol (PEG) as hydrophilic block and poly (lactide) (PLA), poly (lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) or polycaprolactone (PCL) as hydrophobic moieties. These materials, after administration are hydrolysed in their initial components, lactic acid, glycolic acid, caprolactone and PEG, which are generally recognised as safe (GRAS) by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) [22]. One of the most studied class of biodegradable thermogelling copolymers is the A-B-A arranged triblock PLGA-PEG-PLGA or the B-A-B arranged triblock PEG-PLGA-PEG [23]. Their thermogelling behaviour was firstly described by Jeong and colleagues in 1999 for PEG-PLGA-PEG [24] and by Zentner and colleagues in 2001 for PLGA-PEG-PLGA [25]. Since then, these copolymers were employed in a plethora of studies, mainly intended to the development of drug delivery systems or materials for biomedical applications [[26], [27], [28]]. Despite a large number of experimental studies focusing on the drug delivery properties of these copolymers has been conducted [[29], [30], [31], [32]], some aspects of their behaviour have still to be clarified. Indeed, the thermogelling behaviour is well documented and their sol-gel transitions have been evaluated both by the “tube immersion method” and rheological tests. However, these works have focused on a single or a very limited number of selected copolymers for drug delivery or scaffolding applications [33] and only few studies have provided a general overview about the rheological properties of these copolymers and how the structural characteristics (e.g. MW, ratio between the hydrophobic and hydrophilic block) affect their temperature-dependent behaviour [34,35]. The aim of the present study is to provide an overall characterization of PLGA-PEG-PLGA triblock copolymers both at solid state and as aqueous dispersions. As such, fifteen tri-block copolymers, differing from MW and hydrophobicity (PEG/PLGA ratio) were synthesized and analysed. Thermal solid state properties were investigated through differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), while the behaviour as aqueous dispersions at three concentrations (15%, 20% and 25% w/w) were studied by rheological analysis, highlighting the effect of concentration as well as the chemical characteristics of the copolymer (MW and PEG/PLGA ratio) on the temperature-dependent behaviour. Bacterial infection is a serious clinical threat. The misuse of antibiotics has already resulted in the emergence of antibiotic-resistant strains of pathogenic bacteria. Efficient membrane-destructive antibacterial agents are considered as an alternative, promising solution against bacterial infection. Herein, we prepared a new type of comb-like cationic, polyethylene glycol (PEG) block polycarbonates with polyquaternium arms (G-CgQAs). The amphiphilic G-CgQAs could self-assemble into about 60 nm sized nanoparticles (NPs) with positive charges (20~30 mV). G-CgQA-3 NPs with an appropriate hydrophobic-hydrophilic balance in the polyquaternium arms showed antibacterial activity against Gram-negative, Gram-positive, and drug-resistant strains at low concentrations (MIC 64-128 μg mL−1) and low hemolysis (HC50 > 2000 μg mL−1). In vivo anti-infection tests indicated G-CgQA-3 NPs could highly inhibit the growth of vancomycin-resistant bacteria by spraying on wounds. Collectively, G-CgQA NPs hold great promise for the prevention of infection, serving as new antibacterial agents. This study also highlights the significance of a hydrophobic block in positive polyquaternium arms to facilitate the antibacterial activity of cationic, quaternized polymers. The design of comb-like amphiphilic cationic polycarbonates provides a new method for manufacturing antibacterial nano-agents. Due to the good biocompatibility and biodegradation, quaternized polycarbonates have attracted lots of attention because they can interact with bacterial outer membranes, thereby inhibiting bacterial growth.17-24 Besides the various types of quaternary ammonium groups, different hydrophobic moieties (dimethyl, benzene, and ether, etc.) have been adopted to modify the adjacent structure of amine groups to modulate the hydrophilic-hydrophobic balance.23-26 Yang's group revealed that highly dynamic random cationic polycarbonates showed a wider spectrum of antimicrobial activities than block copolymers.22 And cationic polycarbonates with a graft structure have stronger antibacterial and fungicidal effects than the linear homopolymers,27 which was attributed to the hydrophilic-hydrophobic balance, facilitating rapid membrane permeation and disruption. Furthermore, the density of positive charges is key to improving antibacterial activity, which has been demonstrated by the self-assembled nanostructures of amphiphilic AMP.28-30 Our previous study indicated that grafted architectures of PEGylated polycaprolactone with cationic arms could offer a higher density of surface positive charges on the self-assembled nanoparticles than the block copolymers, evidently facilitating membrane disruption.31 Therefore, cationic polycarbonates with synergistic functions including grafted cationic species, hydrophobic structure, and balanced hydrophobic-hydrophilic ratio, could be promising for boosting the antibacterial activity of quaternized cationic polymers. A strategy with precise structure control and flexible adjustability is required to develop such cationic polycarbonates. Herein, comb-like amphiphilic cationic polycarbonates for curbing drug-resistant bacterial infection were prepared via side chain atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP) with good control over the length of hydrophobic segments and the hydrophilic-hydrophobic balance of grafted polycationic blocks. As shown in Scheme 1, poly(ethylene glycol)-block-polycarbonate grafted with poly-(N-2-(methacryloyloxy)ethyl-N,N,N trimethylammonium iodide and n-butyl methyl acrylate) (PEG-b-(PMTC-g-PQA), G-CgQA) were synthesized by PEG initiated ring-opening polymerization of a cyclic carbonate monomer with an ATRP initiation site (MTC-Br), followed by side-chain ATRP of N-2-(methacryloyloxy)ethyl-N,N,N trimethylammonium iodide (MTAI) and n-butyl methyl acrylate (n-BMA). To optimize the balance of hydrophobicity and hydrophilicity and promote antibacterial efficiency, three comb-like polycarbonates with discrepant lengths of hydrophobic and cationic segments were synthesized, in which poly(n-butyl methyl acrylate) (PBMA) was used as the hydrophobic block to tune the hydrophobicity of the graft. Amphiphilic G-CgQA could spontaneously self-assemble into nanoparticles (NPs) with dense positive charges in water. G-CgQA NPs were expected to bind to bacterial membrane through electrostatic interaction and the hydrophobic segment, PBMA, could disturb the membrane. G-CgQA NPs demonstrated broad antibacterial activity against Gram-negative/positive and drug-resistant bacteria. The value of minimum inhibitory concentration was as low as 64 μg mL−1 and HC50 for hemolysis was more than 2000 μg mL−1. Furthermore, G-CgQA-3 NPs could efficiently restrict the growth of vancomycin-resistant bacteria in skin wounds established in mice. Therefore, the design of comb-like amphiphilic cationic polycarbonates could be utilized as a distinct approach for fabricating antibacterial nano-agents.
There has been great interest in colloid microcarriers as effective drug delivery systems, for example, liposomes, and polymeric spherical particles/micelles. It is well known that when amphiphilic block copolymers are dissolved in a selective solvent, they usually form nanoscale core-shell structures in an aqueous solution and can be used as a vehicle of drug delivery [1-5]. Polymeric micelles have received special attention due to their potential application and academic interest in many interdisciplinary field [6-10]. These core-shell type micelles may be used as drug delivery vehicles for poorly water-soluble drugs, especially when the micelles are made with suitable biodegradable polymers Recent trends in drug delivery technology have focused on biodegradable polymers requiring no surgical removal once the drug supply is depleted. PCL is a kind of biodegradable materials with low toxicity, excellent biocompatibility and bioabsorbability in vivo. It has been widely used in biomedical applications, such as sustained drug delivery systems, implants for orthopedic devices and absorbable fibers. However, the low hydrophilicity and high crystallimity of PCL reduce its degradation rate, which results in poorer soft tissue compatibility [11-13]. The most widely studied amphiphilic polymers for drug delivery include diblock copolymers and triblock copolymers [14]. However, these conventional micelle drug delivery systems are based on the linear amphiphilic copolymers with insufficient reactive groups at molecular chains, low encapsulation efficiency and fast initial release rate, which limit further modification, ligand coupling, and thus their application in drug delivery [15, 16]. In contrast, dendrimers and hyperbranched polymers, with good hydrophilicity and biocompatibility, seem to be attractive alternatives to PEG hydrophilic segments for designing amphiphilic graft copolymers. Since the molecular architecture of amphiphilic copolymers is the most important factor in determining micellar structure and property, research efforts have thus focused on the design of molecular structures of amphiphilic copolymers. Recently, amphiphilic copolymers with nonlinear structure exhibited improved property as drug carriers in many researches [17]. Polymeric micelles compositing of branched copolymers may have special application for drug delivery due to their abundant terminal groups.
Amphiphilic block copolymers have attracted a lot of interest in recent years due to their spontaneous self-assembling ability in aqueous solutions leading to the formation of micelles.[1 ] In this case, the hydrophilic block is in contact with the aqueous surrounding solvent and a hydrophobic core is formed, enabling hydrophobic compounds to be encapsulated in the structure. Kinetically frozen micelles consisting of biocompatible and/or biodegradable diblock copolymers are particularly interesting for the development of long circulating drug delivery nanoparticles. The incorporation of functional biomolecules (biotin, folic acid, etc.) on the micelle corona assists in the delivery of the encapsulated drug to a specific target cell.[2 ] Nanomaterials used in drug delivery include liposomes, polymersomes, drug-conjugated polymers, polymer-DNA complexes, polyplexes, and polymeric micelles.[3 ] Polymeric micelles have exhibited a large number of features and advantages over other drug carriers, such as increased thermodynamic and kinetic stability.[4 ] More recently, biodegradable polymers are increasingly used in biomedical applications due to their unique properties, such as the controlled release of pharmaceuticals using polymeric micelles. Hydrophobic linear aliphatic polylactides are particularly attractive biodegradable polymers. The biodegradation (hydrolysis) of these materials in physiological medium produces the nontoxic lactic acid, which participates in the Krebs cycle and is eliminated by the human body as water and carbon dioxide eventually.[5 ] Ring opening polymerization (ROP) of lactides using specific metal complexes[6 ] or organic catalysts[7 ] with (macro)initiators leads to the preparation of well-defined (co)polymers. One of the most studied systems by our team[8-12 ] and others[13-17 ] is stannous octoate Sn(oct)2/alcohol, which was also employed in this study. Poly[oligo(ethylene glycol) methyl ether methacrylate)] (POEGMA) and poly[oligo(ethylene glycol) methyl ether acrylate)] (POEGA) are hydrophilic polymers due to the oligo(ethylene glycol) (OEG) fragment of the side groups. They have been used for the formation of micelles from amphiphilic copolymers.[18-20 ] Apart from the hydrophilicity, the OEG fragment would provide the “stealth” feature, which is required for all drug carrier vessels. That is, the ability to circulate in the blood without triggering the immune system. A diblock copolymer (PDLLA-b-POEGMA) similar to those in this study has been synthesized by Armes and his group, exploiting a hydroxyl-functionalized trithiocarbonate-based chain transfer agent for reversible addition fragmentation chain transfer process (RAFT) polymerization of OEGMA and ROP of lactide.[21 ] Simultaneous ROP and RAFT provided the desired amphiphilic diblock copolymer with well-defined molecular characteristics. This synthetic approach is quite different from the one described in the present study. Furthermore, the adhesion of human mesenchymal progenitor cells on electrospun fibers of this amphiphilic block copolymer (and others) was studied, and the ability to fine-tune the local adhesive properties of electrospun amphiphilic copolymers was examined in order to provide a means of designing scaffolds with the potential for applications in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine.[22 ]

There has been great interest in the use of micelles based on amphiphilic block copolymers as drug delivery systems for anticancer therapeutics [3, 4]. In aqueous solution, amphiphilic block copolymers with the concentration higher than critical micelle concentration (CMC) self-assemble themselves forming core-shell structure with the hydrophobic core for the encapsulation of hydrophobic compounds [5]. Another attraction of block copolymers in the drug delivery application is that their chemical compositions can be easily controlled to obtain the appropriate properties in the formulated drug delivery systems [6-8]. A biocompatible water-soluble polymer, PEG, has widely been utilized as a hydrophilic block because of its excellent water solubility, chain mobility, nontoxic, and non-immunogenicity [9]. The hydrophobic blocks have been tailor-made corresponding to the physical/chemical properties required for functional drug carriers [10]. The hydrophobic blocks with their different natures, molecular weights (MWs), and structures can enable the micellar drug carriers to be more effective for some drugs by changing the drug-polymer compatibility, formation of a rigid core, and controlled drug release. Poly(lactide) (PLA) is a biocompatible, biodegradable polymer with low immunogenicity and good mechanical properties that facilitate its use in pharmaceutical and biomedical applications, such as sutures, implants for bone fixation, drug delivery vehicles, and tissue engineering scaffolds [11-13]. Amphiphilic block copolymers composed of PLA and PEG, including diblock copolymer and triblock copolymer (ABA and BAB with PLA as A and PEG as B), have been extensively investigated as materials for drug delivery systems [14-17]. Among them, the micelles composed of BAB triblock copolymers seem to be the ideal drug delivery platforms, because they have a high PEG density on the surface, small sizes, and an enhanced stability [17-20]. We developed a BAB type, PEG-PLA-PEG triblock copolymer using Steglich esterification as a new synthesis method, which showed favorable properties, such as high stability, high drug loading efficiency, greater reconstitution property, etc., compared to PEG-PLA diblock copolymer in the previous reports [21]. This method could prepare the triblock copolymer without toxic linkers but with the functional groups at the end of polymer which could be decorated by imaging probes or targeting moieties [21]. To date, most of studies on nano-sized drug delivery systems have not focused on the long-term stability as well as on the formulation optimization for the best efficacy. The relationship between polymeric materials and drug delivery system properties as well final efficacy has not been seriously taken into account. Since formulation optimization from the early steps can result in more opportunities to acquire the success in clinical trial and the huge financial saving, this investigation should be conducted carefully before any further studies. The purpose of this study is to investigate the impact of PLA composition on the physicochemical characterizations of PEG-PLA-PEG triblock copolymers, micelles, and the in vitro anticancer efficacy of doxorubicin (DOX)-loaded micelles. A series of PEG-PLA-PEG triblock copolymers with the same PEG MW and different PLA MWs were synthesized and characterized as the platform for micellar systems for DOX, a typical anticancer drug. The relationships between the copolymer composition and micelle properties, including sizes, stability, and morphology, were investigated. DOX release profiles from micelles depending on the PLA block length were also evaluated. The toxicity of block copolymers themselves as well as DOX-loaded micelles against cancer cells was also investigated. The optimized formulation will be selected for further studies.
Polymeric micelles can encapsulate hydrophobic drug molecules and transport them stealthily through the bloodstream.5-7 These micelles tend to accumulate in tumor tissues by the enhanced permeation and retention (EPR) effect, and can be designed to release their drug cargoes upon thermal or other stimulus.2,5 Diblock copolymers intended for polymeric micelles consist of a hydrophobic block and a hydrophilic block, which drive the self-assembly in aqueous solution above their critical micelle concentration (CMC).6,8,9 Typically, the hydrophobic core is comprised of a biodegradable polyester while the shell is the highly hydrophilic poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG).2,5 While the PEG block's good biocompatibility and hydrophilicity help prolong the micelle circulation time in the body, its inability to biodegrade has spurred the development of alternatives. With respect to the controlled release of encapsulated drugs, diblock copolymers with thermoresponsive behavior, i.e. those that exhibit a lower critical solution temperature (LCST) above which they are insoluble in water, are of particular interest. One of the most widely studied thermoresponsive polymers for biomedical applications is poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAAM), which exhibits an LCST of 32 °C.10,11 Although PNIPAAM has shown promise in hydrogel-based materials for drug delivery, its low LCST and non-biodegradable backbone largely preclude its use as an internal drug carrier.6,12 As evidenced by numerous reports and reviews, aliphatic polyesters are common components in drug delivery applications largely due to their biocompatibility and biodegradability by ester hydrolysis.1,5 More specifically, ε-caprolactones have garnered much interest due to the ease with which they can be functionalized, polymerized, and tailored to specific applications.4,13-15 While numerous copolymers have been investigated and have shown promising potential for drug delivery applications, few amphiphilic diblock copolymers combine a fully biodegradable backbone with physiologically relevant and highly tunable thermoresponsive behavior.12,16 We report here the synthesis and characterization of new micelle-forming amphiphilic, biodegradable, and thermosensitive diblock copolymers from γ-substituted caprolactone monomers. As first reported by the Stefan group, the substituted ε-caprolactone monomer γ-2-[2-(2-methoxyethoxy)ethoxy]ethoxy-ε-caprolactone (MEEECL) may be polymerized by ring opening polymerization (ROP) to generate poly{γ-2-[2-(2-methoxyethoxy)ethoxy]ethoxy-ε-caprolactone} (PMEEECL), which displays a LCST of about 48 °C, or even lower if coupled with a hydrophobic block as in a diblock copolymer.16 Previous studies with MEEECL-based polymers have demonstrated the great potential of MEEECL as a thermoresponsive, biodegradable hydrophilic block in micellar assemblies, as opposed to the typical PEG block in most micelles for biomedical applications. Alkoxy- and benzyloxy-substituted caprolactones have been combined with MEEECL to form thermosensitive diblock copolymers capable of self-assembling into micelles.16,17 While these polymers have demonstrated acceptable preliminary results, other γ-substituted caprolactones are being investigated to further enhance biocompatibility, micelle stability, and drug loading capacities while maintaining desirable thermosensitive attributes.18
In this regard, amphiphilic polymers have been extensively exploited for constructing hydrogels with desired properties for biomedical applications. In particular, triblock copolymers with an ABA-architecture containing hydrophobic A-blocks and hydrophilic B-blocks have been most commonly employed for hydrogel constructs preparation [11]. In contrast, poloxamer 407, a well-known triblock copolymer system has a hydrophilic polyethylene glycol (PEG) as the A-blocks of the ABA-architecture, which can also form a hydrogel network [12]. However, such hydrogel matrices with hydrophilic end blocks are reported to exhibit poor homogeneity and limited drug carrying capacity and stability to sustain drug release for longer periods [1]. Herein, we synthesized various triblock co-polymers based on the ABA-architecture with an aim to develop a thermosensitive hydrogel-based drug delivery system. Polyethylene glycol (PEG) and polycaprolactone (PCL) polymers of differing molecular weights (Mw) were employed in varying ratios to design triblock co-polymer sequences for the evaluation of thermosensitive hydrogelling properties. PEG and PCL are US Food and Drug Administration (USFDA) approved polymers [13]. PEG is a widely used non-ionic hydrophilic polymer and considered as a stealth polymer, with improved aqueous solubility and biocompatibility [14]. It prevents particle aggregation by steric stabilization, thereby producing constructs with higher storage stability in pharmaceutical applications [13]. PCL is also one of the most commonly used building blocks for constructing biomaterials for drug delivery and other pharmaceutical applications [15]. Additionally, the labile aliphatic ester linkages in PCL may undergo hydrolysis to generate a non-toxic metabolic product, 6-hydroxyhexanoic acid. However, the degradation rate of PCL is moderate due to its semi-crystalline structure and hydrophobicity. To improve degradation and physical properties of polymeric constructs, inclusion of ester and ether soft segments may be a feasible strategy in the preparation of copolymers [16, 17]. Thus, the modification of PCL has been performed with hydrophilic PEG to prepare triblock copolymers. PEG has been included in the center as well as two end terminals to generate different triblock sequences of PEG-PCL-PEG and PCL-PEG-PCL copolymers. Such arrangements of the amphiphilic block co-polymers are anticipated to improve the stability and interaction of the individual polymers, leading to formation of a stable micellar structure/hydrogel network based drug delivery system [18]. Consequently, hydrophilicity, mechanical properties and biodegradability of the individual polymers can be further improved or optimized for wider applications. These polymers with long PCL sequences bear the same crystalline structure as homo polymer, PCL. Moreover, these modified polymers are anticipated to exhibit improved degradation in comparison to other homo polymers [19]. Furthermore, in order to evaluate the sustained release properties of the newly developed hydrogel-based drug delivery system, we have utilized diclofenac sodium, a commonly used nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). Amphiphilic polymers (i.e., block or graft copolymers) possess distinct hydrophilic and hydrophobic domains, enabling the spontaneous formation of nanosized micellar structures in the aqueous environment. These polymers have attracted significant interest as potent drug delivery platforms due to their peculiar characteristics. Notably, they feature a hydrophobic core that facilitates the solubilization of poorly soluble therapeutics, coupled with a hydrophilic shell that ensures compatibility and stability of micelles in an aqueous surrounding environment. Additionally, their tunable size allows preferential accumulation at compromised tissue sites, such as tumors, leveraging the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect [1], [2], [3]. Over the past recent decades, in order to advance nanomedicines for humans, an array of functional block copolymers have been proposed to develop micelle-based delivery systems tailored for clinical use [4]. Biodegradability and biocompatibility are two critical factors in designing polymeric micelles for safe and efficient drug delivery. The incorporation of biodegradable materials as drug nanocarriers offer a number of advantages, including prolonged circulation time, sustained release, improved therapeutic efficacy, reduced toxicity, and in vivo degradability [3]. Lipids, as naturally occurring biomolecules, have broad applications in the pharmaceutical industry [5], [6]. Most drug delivery systems approved by FDA rely on liposome or lipid-based formulations, in particular, lipid nanoparticles have been successfully utilized for transporting mRNA-based vaccines against SARS-CoV-2. Conjugates of phospholipids with hydrophilic polymers (PEG or PVP) have also been reported for their capacity to load sparingly soluble drugs [7], [8]. However, their efficiency to encapsulate drugs is restricted by the limited space within the hydrophobic core due to the two relatively short fatty acid acyls. In the meantime, with the growing concern of environmental and health-related issues, the scientific community has put forth various polymers such as polyesters and polyurethanes that are developed from vegetable oils through step growth polymerization or oxypolymerization for different industrial applications [9], [10], [11]. The primary constituents of vegetable oils are fatty acids which are mostly saturated and perform as chain terminators in the polymerization process. Only a few attempts have been made on fatty acid-based polymers through radical polymerization by modifying carboxylic acid functional groups on the fatty acid structure [12]. Lately, the advancement of controlled radical polymerization (CRP) techniques has enabled the preparation of various well-defined fatty acid-based (meth)acrylate block copolymers via reversible addition-fragmentation chain transfer (RAFT) or atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP) [13], [14], [15], [16]. Despite these developments, the majority of studies on fatty acid-based polymers have been directed toward their applications as coating, elastomer, or adhesives, [17], [18], [19] with little attention given to their potential biomedical applications as amphiphilic block copolymers for drug delivery. Fatty acid residues are anticipated to offer a robust capability for drug encapsulation as hydrophobic core-forming materials for the fabrication of controlled block copolymer micelles, along with favorable attributes such as biocompatibility and biodegradability. Furthermore, the use of monomers derived from renewable feedstocks to substitute fossil-based monomers holds the potential to advance green and sustainable approaches within drug delivery systems.
Chemotheraphy is one of the common ways for cancer therapy. Although the current chemotherapy drugs (such as doxorubicin, paclitaxel, and curcumin) are all effective in killing cancer cells, most of them are hydrophobic and have low solubility in water medium [1]. To address these issues, the chemotherapy drugs should be conducted some modification to increase the solubility or delivered to the cancerous cells by attaching to a hydrophilic compartment. In recent years, amphiphilic copolymers are of increasing interest due to their applications in biomaterials, biomedicine and biosensing [2]. As a promising biomedicine, amphiphilic copolymers are broadly used in target drug delivery system [3]. The amphiphile could self-assemble into spherical micelles in aqueous solution, and then these micelles could incorporate a hydrophobic drug to form a smart drug delivery vehicle. It is noticeable that the assembled-micelles could respond to specific triggers in the physiological environment, leading to the disassembly of the micellar assemblies and the stimuli-responsive or controlled drug release [4], [5]. In drug delivery, the pH/enzyme dual-responsive amphiphilic polymer systems have gained tremendous attention, because such systems could be stable in the circulatory system, however, it could release more drugs in the target cells owing to a combined stimulation of low pH and a higher level of enzyme compared with that in normal cells. For example, Pan and coworkers designed a pH/enzyme responsive polymeric prodrug nanoparticles by conjugating 10-Hydroxycamptothecin 10-HCPT to carboxymethylchitosan via pH/enzyme sensitive succinyl linkage [6]. Furthermore, Wu et al. also prepared a pH/enzyme dual-responsive polymer nanoparticles through assembling in aqueous solution of an amphiphilic polymeric prodrug [7]. Alginates are unbranched polysaccharides which are found mainly in marine brown seaweed and soil bacteria and have been widely used in variety of biomedical applications [8]. As a well-known supra-amphiphile, alginate is a popular choice for the design of drug delivery carriers due to its good biocompatibility, low toxicity and relatively less expensive. In particularly, they have other excellent properties such as mechanical stiffness, cell attachment ability and binding or releasing the bioactive molecules upon modifications [9]. In order to increase drug efficacy and reduce side effects, alginate-based materials that are responsive to external stimuli, such as temperature [10], pH [9], [11], [12], light [13], enzyme [14], [15], and magnetic field [16], have been extensively investigated for drug delivery systems. In our previous work, an amphiphilic polymer composed of hydrophilic alginate and hydrophobic dodecyl glycidyl ether was synthesized and its micelle properties were discussed. We found that the hydrophobic modified alginate (HMA) show a remarkable tendency to self-assemble into micelle above the critical micelle concentration (CMC) [17], [18]. With the aim of designing a potential pH/enzyme dual-responsive drug delivery system, the present study has been focused to demonstrate the potential ability to carry and release drug of the amphiphilic polymer. Doxorubicin (DOX), the most frequently used anti-cancer drugs for clinical treatment of major organ carcinoma and soft tissue sarcoma, was chosen as a model anti-cancer drug and incorporated into the polymeric micelles [19]. The HMA was further self-assembled into micelles to load DOX. The solubilization, drug release behavior, and anticancer cytotoxicity of the formed micelles were investigated. The present study shows that the HMA are promising assembled-micelles to achieve a highly efficient anticancer therapy without obvious systemic toxicity.
The amphiphilic block copolymer micelles are currently considered as an ideal drug delivery carrier due to their self-assembled core-shell structure, particle size, and surface properties [2-4]. The unique characteristics make them be able to solubilize unstable and insoluble drugs and avoid nonselective absorption by reticuloendothelial systems. Therefore, the passive targeting can be implemented through enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect [5]. The polymeric micelles have shown the abilities to improve drug delivery to target sites, to weaken nonspecific toxicities and to improve the therapeutic efficacy in the end [6-10]. For therapy of colorectal cancer, the copolymer micelle drug carriers should keep a sufficient stability in the stomach (pH 1.0-2.5) while they rapidly deliver the drug entrapped in the core of the copolymer micelles in the intestine environment of pH 5.1-7.8 [11]. Significant efforts have been devoted to develop biodegradable copolymer micelle drug release carriers with drug targeting and improved bioavailability. pH-Sensitive copolymer micelles containing poly(meth)acrylic acid (P(M)AA) are favorable for encapsulation and oral release of hydrophobic drugs [11-13]. On the other hand, poly(d,l-lactide) (PLA), as the most frequently employed structural motif for the hydrophobic components of block copolymers, has high biocompatibility and biodegradability [14]. Based on the provided evidence, the thermal stability limit of PHA during processing is constrained by its degradation onset temperature, which occurs very close to its melting point (Tm). This narrow processing window poses significant challenges:

1.  **PHA degrades upon melting**, with thermal degradation occurring at temperatures near or slightly above its Tm. Conventional processing techniques (e.g., melt extrusion, injection molding) are problematic due to this low thermal stability and the resulting chain scission, which leads to molecular weight reduction and inferior mechanical properties in the final product [3][5][7][15].
2.  The **melting temperature (Tm) of PHA** produced from glucose is reported to be in the range of **174-184 °C** [2][4]. Degradation begins close to these temperatures, severely limiting the usable processing temperature range above Tm [2][3][4][5][7][15].
3.  **PHB**, the most common PHA, has a **degradation onset temperature (Tonset) around 200 °C**, but its Tm is also high, creating a **very narrow processing window**. This necessitates precise temperature control during melt processing [8][10][15].
4.  **PHBV**, a copolymer (poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-*co*-3-hydroxyvalerate)), exhibits **improved processability** compared to PHB homopolymer because its **Tm is lower** (though specific values are not given in the evidence), resulting in reduced thermal degradation during melt processing [3][5]. Adjusting the hydroxyvalerate (HV) content in PHBV is a strategy to lower Tm and widen the processing window [3][5][6].
5.  **Recovered PHA residues** from purification processes can further **lower the temperature for the onset of thermal degradation**, exacerbating the processing instability [3][5]. The effects of these residues are poorly documented [3][5].
6.  **Strategies to mitigate thermal instability** include:
    *   Copolymerization (e.g., incorporating HV units into PHB to form PHBV) [3][5][6]
    *   Blending with other biodegradable polymers or additives [6][7][9]
    *   Forming nanocomposites (e.g., with modified graphene oxide or cellulose nanocrystals) [7][15]
    *   Improving purification to minimize residues that lower degradation onset [3][5]

Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are biological polyesters synthesized by many microbial species as intracellular carbon and energy reserve.1-3 The biopolyesters can be melted and molded like conventional petroleum-based plastics and, after use, completely degraded into benign products via microbial activities.4-7 The thermal properties of PHAs are of great interest to polymer processors. Polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) is the most extensively studied member of the PHA family [24,25] and is classified as a homopolymer within the group of biodegradable intracellular polyesters synthesized by various bacterial species. It is considered a promising alternative to petroleum-based plastics [26]. PHB exhibits properties comparable to those of polypropylene; however, its higher production cost remains a major drawback. Its inherent stiffness and brittleness, along with thermal instability during processing, significantly limit its practical applications [[27], [28], [29], [30]]. The high cost of PHB production is primarily attributed to the expense of raw materials and downstream processing. To reduce production costs, the use of low-cost substrates, optimized cultivation strategies, and simplified downstream processes is essential [31,32]. For instance, Jung et al. [33] successfully produced PHB using a novel strain, Priestia sp. YH4, cultivated on sugarcane molasses and tap water without the need for sterilization or supplemental nitrogen sources, demonstrating a cost-effective and simplified approach to biopolymer synthesis. Similarly, Bhatia et al. [34] explored the potential of Halomonas sp. YLGW01 for PHA production using macroalgal biomass-derived sugars and detoxifier biochar under non-sterile conditions, highlighting a sustainable and low-cost strategy. In a separate study, Bhatia et al. [35] also reported the coproduction of exopolysaccharides and PHAs by Sphingobium yanoikuyae BBL01 when cultivated on biochar-pretreated plant biomass hydrolysate, demonstrating the strain's capacity to valorize lignocellulosic feedstocks into multiple biopolymers under optimized conditions. This biopolymer can be molded into various shapes and utilized for film production. Additionally, it can form heteropolymers with synthetic polymers that exhibit similar mechanical properties [36]. Owing to its biodegradability, favorable light transmittance, and successful migration test results, this material presents a promising alternative for food packaging applications [37]. However, a fundamental challenge in the use of bioplastics for food packaging lies in ensuring that the durability of the packaging aligns with the shelf-life requirements of the product [38,39]. The narrow gap between the thermal degradation temperature and melting point of PHB results in a limited processing window, posing a significant challenge for its practical application [40]. Despite its drawbacks, such as low thermal stability with degradation onset at 200 °C, limited elongation at break, and pronounced brittleness due to its high crystallinity, this biopolymer has garnered considerable attention owing to its excellent gas barrier properties and physical characteristics comparable to conventional polymers [41]. The high cost of PHA synthesis, coupled with the availability of inexpensive petrochemical alternatives, has rendered its production economically unjustifiable. A significant portion of this expense arises from the cost of carbon substrates and the limited efficiency of biopolymer yield. To enable cost-effective and commercially viable production, the use of low-cost substrates should be prioritized [42,43]. The cost of the substrate and the recovery process is approximately ten times higher than that of conventional polymers [44]. Despite their biodegradability, the use of bioplastics remains limited due to economic constraints. Raw material costs account for more than half of the total production expenses, with approximately 70-80 % of these costs attributed to the carbon substrates required for biopolymer synthesis [44]. Accordingly, this study explores the use of a novel carbon source for PHB production. Utilizing low-cost, renewable agricultural and industrial by-products as feedstock, under conditions that promote high productivity, offers a promising strategy for economically viable biopolymer synthesis [45]. Oil-based substrates have gained attention due to their high theoretical yield of 1 g of PHA per 1 g of substrate, compared to a yield of 0.3-0.4 g of PHA per gram of glucose [46,47]. Chicken skin, a by-product of the poultry industry, is typically discarded during carcass processing and considered waste. Fat waste from the food industry, estimated at 29 million tons annually, imposes significant disposal costs. Chicken skin accounts for approximately 15 % of the carcass and contains around 30 % fat, with a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids compared to other animal fats. Given the substantial volume of this by-product, its high nutritional value, and the environmental and economic burden of disposal, optimal utilization is both practical and beneficial [12,[51], [52], [53]]. As previously noted, the application of PHB is limited due to its pronounced brittleness, which stems from a slow crystallization rate and the resulting low nucleation density [58]. Incorporating nanoscale reinforcements into environmentally friendly green nanocomposites, alongside biodegradable polymers, can enhance the mechanical, physical, and barrier properties of the PHB matrix by accelerating crystallization and increasing nucleation density [59]. CNCs can be incorporated into various biodegradable polymer matrices as heterogeneous nucleating agents and reinforcing fillers, contributing to improved crystallization behavior, mechanical properties, hydrophilicity, and biodegradability [[60], [61], [62]]. The reinforcing effect of CNCs depends on their intrinsic properties, concentration, dispersion within the polymer matrix, and the intermolecular interactions between the components [63]. Notably, the addition of nucleating agents is a well-established strategy for enhancing the crystallization rate of polymers [64]. Ensuring the quality and safety of food during transportation and storage, along with extending its shelf life, is highly dependent on effective packaging. Achieving this requires minimizing exposure to oxygen and moisture, and controlling light transmission to prevent chemical and microbial contamination. To meet these demands, packaging materials must offer both physical protection and appropriate physicochemical conditions. In this context, nanobiocomposites with enhanced barrier, mechanical, and thermal properties have emerged as a promising approach for improving biopolymer-based packaging systems [65]. The primary objective of incorporating CNCs as reinforcing agents is to accelerate crystallization and enhance mechanical properties, including Young's modulus and tensile strength [54,66]. In this study, the solvent casting method was employed to prepare the nanobiocomposite. Solvent casting is a widely used technique for producing thermoplastic nanobiocomposites by dissolving a polymer or a blend of polymers in a common solvent [54,67].

Chain extender is a substance that can react with the functional groups on the linear polymer chain to expand the molecular chain and increase the molecular weight.17 It greatly affects rheological properties and thermal behavior. First published on 7th January 2011 Spider silk shows great potential as a biomaterial: in addition to biocompatibility and biodegradability, its strength and toughness are greater than native biological fibres (e.g.collagen), with toughness exceeding that of synthetic fibres (e.g.nylon). Although the ultimate tensile strength and toughness at failure are unlikely to be limiting factors, its yield strain of 2% is insufficient, particularly for biomedical application because of the inability to mimic the complex ultrastructure of natural tissues with current tissue engineering approaches. To harness the full potential of spider silk as a biomaterial, it is therefore necessary to increase its yield strain. In this paper, we discuss the means by which the mechanical properties of spider silk, particularly the yield strain, can be optimized through structural modifications.
Spider silk has garnered attention as a structural material and a medical resource for next generation because it is tough, lightweight, and biodegradable. Nonwoven silk fabrics are emerging in research and industries owing to advanced electrospinning techniques. Several studies have reported nonwoven fabrics made of spider silk-like proteins, which are originated from recombinant expression systems, with lower molecular weights than the natural counterpart. The lower molecular weight causes a lack of mechanical strength and durability, preventing the evaluation of industrial potential of the spider silk-based nonwoven fabric to use as a structural and medical material. In this study, an electrospun nonwoven fabric is produced using native spider silk fibers forcibly reeled from live spiders. The spider silk-based nonwoven fabrics demonstrate cell compatibility, and the mechanical properties are superior to the silkworm silk-based nonwoven fabrics. The availability of spider silk-based nonwoven fabrics introduces an unexplored set of potential uses, along with the context of sustainable development goals. Silk is a natural structural material used in the outer shell of silkworm cocoons and as a lifeline by spiders.1 Biodegradable proteinous fibers can replace petroleum-based manmade fibers and be used as a promising bio-based material to meet sustainable development goals (SDGs).2 Furthermore, silk displays excellent mechanical features with high strength and ductility.3 The silkworm silk fiber is the most abundantly produced and studied silk worldwide.4 It is a traditionally expensive clothing textile owing to its lightness, drapability, softness, and lustrous appearance.5 Silkworm silk is not limited to textile use: they have also been utilized as surgical sutures for decades because of the excellent knot strength and biocompatibility of silk.6
Spider silk is a polymer with potential shape and mechanical behavior memory. Spiders, as one of the oldest species on the Earth's mainland, constitute a vast family with a great variety of species and a wide range of distribution. These phylogenetic and ecological varieties has led to the appearance of specific adaptations to the most diverse various environmental conditions over nearly 400 million years [1,2]. Among these adaptations, the complex and diverse family of spiders evolved to span up to different different silk-derived materials with specific compositions, structures, and properties [[3], [4], [5]]. The most extensively studied of all these silk types is the silk spun from the major ampullate gland, commonly referred to as dragline silk or MAS, which exhibits exceptional mechanical properties, boasting a mechanical behavior that greatly exceeds that of Kevlar in terms of work to fracture [6,7]. In addition, MAS possesses not only excellent mechanical properties, but is also biocompatible and biodegradable, making it suitable for a wide range of applications in biomedicine, as well as in the chemical, aerospace and defense industries, among other fields [[8], [9], [10], [11], [12]]. However, due to the limited availability of natural spider silk (from now on, unless otherwise indicated, spider silk will be used as a synonym for MAS), mimicking natural silk to produce bionic materials with specific properties has become the focus of many researchers [13]. In this regard, the composition of spider silk proteins and the spinning process have evolved to form an inseparable and unique natural spinning system, whose complexity has posed a significant challenge in efforts to understand the effects of each component on spider silk [14]. Basic spider silk spinning mechanisms have been established, however, the findings primarily focus on fundamental theoretical principles [[15], [16], [17]]. In particular, the existing knowledge about the natural spinning process of spiders provides limited practical assistance for the artificial bioimitation of spider silk in production applications [18]. However, we can still benefit from the rich interplay between protein composition, unique structure and singular properties function, to continue optimizing the production and properties of biomimetic materials. All types of silk proteins, known as spidroins, exist in an aqueous solution within the abdominal glands of spiders in which the various silk types for different applications are produced [19,20]. MAS is mainly made up of two groups of proteins termed major ampullate spidroin 1 (MaSp 1) and major ampullate spidroin 2 (MaSp 2). Both types comprise large proteins with a molecular weight in the range 250-350 kDa, and show a characteristic structure with a highly repetitive core region, and two non repetitive N- and C-termini [[21], [22], [23]]. Members of the MaSp1 type generally exhibit the motifs GGX, (GA)n, and (A)n, while spidroins of the MaSp2 exhibit the (A)n and, most significantly, the GPGXX motif. A third type, termed major ampullate spidroin 3 (MaSp3), whose role in the formation of the fiber is less clear than that of MaSp1 and MaSp2 has been described and is characterized by the presence of the SSX motif, and the absence of the G(A)n motifs [24,25]. However, the reported spider silk protein sequences (primary structure) are mostly fragmented due to the large size of these proteins, and the extensive repetition of the motifs indicated previously [26,27]. With the development of Next Generation Sequencing technologies, overall diversity and complexity of the repetitive structures in the existing studies were found to be higher than expected when compared to the previously sequenced fragments. Needless to say, the usage of fragmented sequences presented obvious limitations in the study of the secondary structure, tertiary structure and in function of spider silk protein [24,[28], [29], [30], [31]]. The impressive mechanical properties of silk fibers and the efficiency of silk spinning in nature have allowed insight into the nature of silk processing from biosynthesis to silk spinning into fibers. However, many aspects and mechanisms of this process remain to be revealed. Silk fibers are fine, lustrous and consist of β-sheet crystals with a high degree of molecular orientation. These fibers are formed under ambient temperature and pressure,3 spun from an aqueous solution, and the resulting fiber is insoluble in water due to an irreversible phase transition during the spinning process. An oriented liquid crystalline state of silk with highly ordered precrystalline molecules can help explain the natural process, which transforms random coils in aqueous solution to an insoluble oriented fiber.4, 5 Artificial variants of silk would be desirable in order to gain insight into these mechanisms while also tuning physical properties, diameter, cross-section, as well as morphology and structure. Silk is used as a structural material in nature such as a lifeline and framework of spiders and the silkworm cocoon to protect larvae from predators [1]. The silk fibers are lightweight and show excellent mechanical toughness, thus being a candidate of bio-based materials for next generation [2]. Although the silkworm silk is used as surgical sutures for decades, the bulk-scale production of the natural silk is still limited especially in the case of spider silk [3]. Hence the artificial silk production has been reported using recombinant protein expression and chemical synthesis [4,5]. Furthermore, the artificial spinning of regenerated silk fibroin solution has been used to modify the diameter and physical properties of resultant silk fibers by varying the reeling speed and coagulation bath [6]. However, the mechanical strength of the resultant silk fiber is often inferior compared with that of the natural counterpart [6]. One of the causes of the inferior strength is the lower molecular weight of the synthesized silk [7]. In addition, the lack of knowledge on the mechanism of structural transition from random coil/helix to β-sheet retards the development of the artificial silk production [8]. Spiders and silkworms are thought to precisely and simultaneously adjust physiological conditions such as water contents and internal pressure in their glands to secret silk fibers with excellent mechanical properties [9]. In order to understand the mechanism of silk fiber formation in detail, it is important to investigate effects of each factor on structural transition of silk fibroin. Water molecules inhibit the intermolecular hydrogen bonds between silk molecular chains and cause the plasticization of silk fibroin, inducing the β-sheet structures of silkworm silk [10,11]. Dynamic mechanical thermal analysis demonstrated that water molecules interacted with the disordered structure of the silk fibroin and lowered the glass transition temperature [12]. Spider silk fibers are known to shrink when immersed in water, which is known as supercontraction [13]. The supercontraction of spider silk is triggered by an entropic relaxation mainly occurred in an amorphous region of the spider silk [14]. Accordingly, the mechanical properties of spider and silkworm silk are largely dependent on the environmental humidity [15].
Force-spinning at a controlled drawing rate. When silkworms are being immobilized, the silk can be artificially drawn by external force (i.e., force-spinning) to achieve superior mechanical properties, including strength, toughness and extensibility. Such force-spinning extrudes the silk at a constant speed and in a single direction, thereby eliminating any inconsistencies associated with the natural spinning (i.e., ‘Figure of eight’ spinning motion). Different force-spinning speeds were applied to obtain silk with greatly enhanced mechanical properties as compared to naturally spun counterpart (Fig. 11A) [54]. It was reported that slow force-spinning (e.g., 4 mm s−1) produced highly extensible silk with breaking strain comparable to that of Nephila spider silk, whereas fast force-spinning (e.g., 13 mm s−1) resulted in stronger and tougher silk with breaking stress and toughness approaching that of Nephila spider dragline silk. Modulated spinning in electric field. When silkworms spin in alternating electric field, the silk produced are stronger, tougher and more extensible than naturally spun silk, as shown in Fig. 11B. The enhanced silk fibers have β-sheet crystallites more oriented along the fiber axis, while the crystallinity and crystallite sizes are similar to that of naturally spun silk [73]. This strategy for enhancing the mechanical properties is based on the use of electric field to align the liquid-crystals (i.e., the water-soluble liquid crystalline state) of silk fibroin in the silk gland. Electric field has been shown to be able to align protein dipoles along the direction of the field [84]. The better oriented β-sheet crystallites are thus able to withstand the higher load applied along the fiber axis upon stretching during tensile test. The gene sequence of spider silk (e.g., Nephila clavata or Nephila clavipes) has been successfully transfected into silkworms via piggyBac vector, and this has enabled its co-expression in silk glands of the transgenic silkworms [85], [86]. Even at low expression level, the genetically-modified silk has an overall improved mechanical performance (Fig. 11C). It is noted that the favorable effect could also be observed through subsequent silkworm lineages, occasionally with highly enhanced effect. Successful incorporation of the guest proteins into the silk requires that their expression occurs in spatial and temporal proximity to the endogenous silk proteins [85], [86]. Besides, successful gene transfection relies greatly on environmental and genetic factors and thus explains the low rate of attaining the desired phenotypic expression [86].
The strength and stiffness of silk are dictated mainly by β-sheet crystallites (Table 1: experimental and simulation results of β-sheet crystallites of silkworm silk). In β-sheet crystallites, there are hydrogen bonds, together with intersheet van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions, that contribute significantly to the stability of the structure [58], [68]. On the other hand, the extensibility and toughness of silk are governed mainly by the semi-amorphous matrix [17], [64], [69]. Respectively, the semi-amorphous matrix and β-sheet crystallites of silk govern its mechanical behavior at small and large deformation during tensile loading. Upon tensile loading, the material undergoes homogeneous stretching until the onset of yielding, when the material ceases to behave elastically and starts to deform plastically. This is when the semi-amorphous components start to unravel, after which the load is transferred to the β-sheet crystallites, that subsequently handle the load up to the point of fracture [64]. Fundamentally, silk fibroin can form intramolecular/intermolecular β-sheet crystallites [67], [70], parallel/antiparallel β-sheet crystallites, as well as β-sheet crystallites of different sizes and orientations along fiber axis. Below, we discuss these structural aspects of the β-sheet crystallites pertaining to the mechanical properties of silk. Essentially, the splitting of intermolecular β-sheet crystallites leads to weakening of the overall molecular network in silk, and thus results in failure of the material. On the contrary, the splitting of intramolecular β-sheet crystallites leads to lengthening of silk as they split (i.e., unfold) [56], [65]. The content of intramolecular β-sheet crystallites significantly influences the mechanical properties of silk. Evidently, the superb mechanical strength and toughness of spider silk (Nephila pilipes) have been attributed to its high content of intramolecular β-sheet crystallites [56]. Spider silk has a content of about 57% of intramolecular β-sheet crystallites (of total β-sheet crystallites content), significantly above that of silkworm silk (18%). A possible explanation for the lower content in silkworm silk is that the H-chain has comparatively larger crystal-forming domains [55], that increase their likelihood of interactions with those from neighboring H-chains to form intermolecular β-sheet crystallites when the domains are well-aligned during spinning [71]. With this understanding, the mechanical properties of silkworm silk may be further enhanced if there is a way to increase the amount of the intramolecular β-sheet crystallites in silk fibroin. Different arrangements of β-strands in β-sheet crystallites have been proposed, i.e., parallel vs. antiparallel. When arranged in a parallel sense, adjacent β-strands form lengthier and non-linear hydrogen bonds, whereas antiparallel adjacent strands are able to form shorter and linear hydrogen bonds [42]. The arrangement of the β-strands thus influences the mechanical properties owing to the geometrical and energetic differences in the hydrogen bonding. Mechanical behavior of poly(GA) crystalline units, in both parallel and antiparallel arrangements, have been simulated to compare any difference in mechanical properties (Fig. 8A). It was found that antiparallel β-sheet crystallites outperform the parallel counterparts, in terms of rupture strength and stiffness, as shown in Fig. 8B. Experimental stress-strain data of silk fiber are also presented (green curve), presenting a lower strength and stiffness than the simulation data (i.e., antiparallel crystalline unit). This is because the experimental result was calculated using cross-sectional area of fiber, that includes also the area contribution from semi-amorphous region, in addition to the β-sheet crystallites. Meanwhile, it was also reported that the hydrogen bonds are stronger in the antiparallel arrangement [68].
Liquid-liquid phase separation, also known as coacervation, is a well-known phenomenon for many polyelectrolytes [1]. Liquid-liquid phase separation has been reported to play an important role for biological processes ranging from the formation of proteinaceous membrane-less organelles (PMLOs) [2], [3], [4], [5] and spindle assembly [6], to the assembly of underwater adhesives [7], [8], amyloid formation [9], and the assembly of biopolymeric materials [10], [11], [12], [13], [14]. Coacervation of biopolymers, such as elastin [12] and squid beak proteins [10], [11] is reported to have a role in assembling molecules as an intermediate step prior to the final transition from liquid to solid. Spider silk is an extraordinary example of the properties that a natural fiber can possess. It has high tensile strength yet it is very elastic, both properties leading to extreme toughness that one has so far escaped attempts at synthetic reproduction [15]. In addition, spider silk is biodegradable and causes low immunogenic response which makes it attractive for biomedical applications [16]. On a molecular level, spider silk consists of proteins with long highly repetitive regions capped by globular terminal domains [14], [17], [18]. Typical to biological materials, the properties of spider silk stem from weak inter- and intramolecular interactions and a precise molecular alignment of the constituent spider silk proteins [19]. Synthetic approaches to producing spider silk-mimicking fibers are attractive, but both the recombinant production of full-length spider silk and the assembly of the fibers have proven challenging [14]. Progress in recombinant DNA technologies allow the production of shorter spider silk-mimicking proteins in bacteria, but the molecular assembly of soluble proteins remains challenging and the biologically relevant mechanisms are at the moment not fully understood. In a previous study, we described that a silk-like triblock fusion protein self-coacervates in high protein concentration in water, yielding droplets that coalesce spontaneously, relax back to spherical structures after fusing together, and easily wet surfaces. Importantly, coacervation seems to be an important part of the early steps of assembly to various fibrous structures [20]. The coacervation occurred in solutions containing only the triblock fusion protein, and hence the system is classified as a self-coacervating one, as opposed to systems where polymers of at least two types form complexes, leading to complex coacervates [11], [21]. The triblock architecture was essential for achieving high solubility and functionality of the coacervates. Native terminal domains were not required, but could be replaced with for example unrelated folded domains such as cellulose-binding modules (CBMs) [22]. The exact nature of the terminal domains was not crucial for function but CBMs proved to function well for high solubility, good production levels, and coacervate formation [20], [23].

The crystal region of spider silk consists of polyalanine, whereas that of silkworm silk is composed predominantly of glycine and alanine, which yield specific structural features and the corresponding mechanical properties.3 The evolutionary correlations between the molecular composition and mechanical features of a number of spider silks are influenced by the highly repetitive amino acid sequences of the component proteins.18 The biomimicry of spider silk fibers has been developed using recombinant expression systems, such as Escherichia coli,19 yeast,20 goat milk,21 and plant vectors22 as well as chemical synthesis.23 However, synthetic spider silks have a lower molecular weight than their native counterparts and lack the natural spinning mechanism of spiders, limiting its use as bulk-scale structural material.24 Spiders have a territorial nature and cannibal tendencies, making them difficult to domesticate, unlike silkworms.25 Furthermore, the amount of spider silk per individual is less than that of a silkworm.26 Hence, the potential of naturally spun spider silk, which has a higher molecular weight than the synthetic spider silk, is largely unexplored owing to its scarcity. This study presented a promising direction for the development of high-performance hydrogels with diverse biomedical applications. All types of silk proteins, known as spidroins, exist in an aqueous solution within the abdominal glands of spiders in which the various silk types for different applications are produced [19,20]. Members of the MaSp1 type generally exhibit the motifs GGX, (GA)n, and (A)n, while spidroins of the MaSp2 exhibit the (A)n and, most significantly, the GPGXX motif. A third type, termed major ampullate spidroin 3 (MaSp3), whose role in the formation of the fiber is less clear than that of MaSp1 and MaSp2 has been described and is characterized by the presence of the SSX motif, and the absence of the G(A)n motifs [24,25]. The impressive mechanical properties of silk fibers and the efficiency of silk spinning in nature have allowed insight into the nature of silk processing from biosynthesis to silk spinning into fibers. An oriented liquid crystalline state of silk with highly ordered precrystalline molecules can help explain the natural process, which transforms random coils in aqueous solution to an insoluble oriented fiber.4, 5 Artificial variants of silk would be desirable in order to gain insight into these mechanisms while also tuning physical properties, diameter, cross-section, as well as morphology and structure. Understanding processing conditions that induce hierarchical self-assembly of spider silk leading to the excellent physical properties would also help in materials-related applications for these proteins. Controlling how a protein interacts with itself, other proteins or the environmental milieu, is important in order to understand self-assembly. Methods to reprocess silk proteins into new morphologies including films, foams, meshes,6 nanoscale diameter fibers,7 fiber bundles8 and tissue engineering scaffolds9, 10 have been reported. For instance, 3D porous scaffolds were derived from regenerated Bombyx mori silk fibroin solution using either an all aqueous process or an organic solvent (hexafluoroisopropanol) (HFIP) with salt leaching, gas foaming, and freeze-drying modes to generate inter-connected pore structures in 3D matrices.9, 11 A number of recent studies have explored a tissue-engineering approach using silk fibroin scaffolds in various formats to repair bone with diverse morphologies.11-13 Silk fibroin hydrogels, membranes or nets without preseeded cells have been used for bone regeneration. The highly porous scaffold prepared by salt leaching possesses a useful combination of compressive strength and uniform, interconnected pores with controllable size distribution.9, 11, 12 The morphological structural features of the scaffolds depend on number of variables including silk concentration, salt particle size, and the use of aqueous- or HFIP- driven process. A phase diagram for the formation of the aqueous and HFIP-derived 3D porous scaffolds has been generated based on these approaches.11 Silk fibroin scaffolds, regardless of their processing, undergo a structural transition from random coil to β-sheets.11 The mechanism of silk processing, including formation of globular micelles as a key step in formation of silk fibers has been reported.14 The pattern of hydrophobic and hydrophilic domains in the silk fibroin includes larger hydrophilic domains at the termini, smaller internal hydrophilic domains, and larger hydrophobic domains.15 Based on thermodynamics, silk fibroin acts as a tri-block copolymer, with the formation of micellar structures in water in which the larger hydrophilic termini define the outer edges, while the hydrophobic blocks are present inside the micelles.14 However, the structural and conformational changes in the assembly process remain challenging to control in order to regulate nanostructure formation. The hydrophobic blocks are assumed to form more regular structures, while the hydrophilic blocks move to the surface of micelles to interact with water by chain folding, reducing the free energy of the silk fibroin-water system. With these goals in mind, we investigated how pH, salt, and water interacted with the spider silk-like block copolymer, HBA6 (H, B, and A are hexahistidine tag, hydrophilic, and hydrophobic blocks, respectively) to produce different morphologies.
Liquid-liquid phase separation, also known as coacervation, is a well-known phenomenon for many polyelectrolytes [1]. Liquid-liquid phase separation has been reported to play an important role for biological processes ranging from the formation of proteinaceous membrane-less organelles (PMLOs) [2], [3], [4], [5] and spindle assembly [6], to the assembly of underwater adhesives [7], [8], amyloid formation [9], and the assembly of biopolymeric materials [10], [11], [12], [13], [14]. Coacervation of biopolymers, such as elastin [12] and squid beak proteins [10], [11] is reported to have a role in assembling molecules as an intermediate step prior to the final transition from liquid to solid. Spider silk is an extraordinary example of the properties that a natural fiber can possess. It has high tensile strength yet it is very elastic, both properties leading to extreme toughness that one has so far escaped attempts at synthetic reproduction [15]. In addition, spider silk is biodegradable and causes low immunogenic response which makes it attractive for biomedical applications [16]. On a molecular level, spider silk consists of proteins with long highly repetitive regions capped by globular terminal domains [14], [17], [18]. Typical to biological materials, the properties of spider silk stem from weak inter- and intramolecular interactions and a precise molecular alignment of the constituent spider silk proteins [19]. Synthetic approaches to producing spider silk-mimicking fibers are attractive, but both the recombinant production of full-length spider silk and the assembly of the fibers have proven challenging [14]. Progress in recombinant DNA technologies allow the production of shorter spider silk-mimicking proteins in bacteria, but the molecular assembly of soluble proteins remains challenging and the biologically relevant mechanisms are at the moment not fully understood. In a previous study, we described that a silk-like triblock fusion protein self-coacervates in high protein concentration in water, yielding droplets that coalesce spontaneously, relax back to spherical structures after fusing together, and easily wet surfaces. Importantly, coacervation seems to be an important part of the early steps of assembly to various fibrous structures [20]. The coacervation occurred in solutions containing only the triblock fusion protein, and hence the system is classified as a self-coacervating one, as opposed to systems where polymers of at least two types form complexes, leading to complex coacervates [11], [21]. The triblock architecture was essential for achieving high solubility and functionality of the coacervates. Native terminal domains were not required, but could be replaced with for example unrelated folded domains such as cellulose-binding modules (CBMs) [22]. The exact nature of the terminal domains was not crucial for function but CBMs proved to function well for high solubility, good production levels, and coacervate formation [20], [23].
Recent advancements in biomimetic materials have brought spider silk to the forefront of scientific attention. Its exceptional combination of Young′s modulus, tensile strength, and toughness makes it a highly versatile material with extensive potential applications.8 This remarkable performance originates from the unique molecular architecture of spider silk, characterized by stacked β-pleated crystallites surrounded by a disordered (amorphous) matrix rich in glycine.9 The amorphous polypeptide chains in silk are interconnected through β-sheet crystallites, which enhance the structural integrity of the protein strands under high strains as reinforcing elements. The presence of the amorphous region enhances the exceptional stretchiness of silk through the provision of entropic elasticity.10 Regenerated silk fibroin, mimicking this structure with anti-parallel β-sheet nanocrystals and an amorphous matrix composed of α-helices and random coils, offers a promising route for replicating the properties of spider silk in artificial materials.11 In this study, we presented a biomimetic approach through hydrogen bonding-induced self-assembly to enhance both the mechanical characteristics and self-repairing effectiveness of hyaluronic acid-based hydrogels, inspired by the heterogeneous structure of spider silk (Figure 1a). Specifically, the β-sheet crystallite domain of spider silk was simulated by the addition of tannic acid (TA) to induce the formation of a β-folded structure of silk fibroin (SF) through hydrogen bonds. Concurrently, the dynamic hydrogen-bonded amorphous domain of spider silk was emulated through acylhydrazone bond cross-linking between aldehyde hyaluronic acid (AHA) and a synthesized cross-linking agent 3,3′-dithiobis (propionohydrazide) (DTP), which contains hydrazide groups and disulfide bonds (Figure 1b). Additionally, the incorporation of TA provided the hydrogel with antibacterial and antioxidant properties. We comprehensively investigated the rheological properties, swelling kinetics, and morphology of the resulting hydrogel. Mechanical testing was used to quantitatively analyze the hydrogel′s mechanical properties, adhesion, and self-healing ability. This study presented a promising direction for the development of high-performance hydrogels with diverse biomedical applications.
