Natural polymer materials mainly include hyaluronic acid, collagen, polylactic acid [18, 19], etc., which have good biocompatibility and degradable absorption. However, they exhibit limited mechanical strength, rapid degradation [20], and the potential to produce acidic degradation products that can disrupt the local acid-base environment. Silk, as a natural protein fiber, has excellent mechanical properties comparable to synthetic polymers. Meanwhile, it displays high biocompatibility [21-23], does not elicit significant inflammatory responses [24]. Besides, it can be fully degraded and absorbed, and can regulate the degradation rate [25]. It has been employed as a novel biomaterial for tissue regeneration, including in tendon and rotator cuff repair [26-29]. There are two main categories of silk fibroin materials: natural silk fibroin materials (derived from raw silk degumming) and regenerated silk fibroin materials [30]. In terms of mechanical properties, the β-sheet structure plays an important role in the mechanical properties of silk [31], which is the main factor that endows silk fibroin with high strength and high elastic modulus [32]. However, the protein secondary structure of regenerated silk fibroin has been changed after dissolution, dialysis, and freeze-drying. The mechanical properties of regenerated silk fibroin are weak and brittle [33, 34]. The tensile strength of regenerated silk fibroin films is about 0.02 GPa, and the elongation at break is < 2% [35, 36]. Furthermore, the random coil and α-helix structures can be transformed into β-sheet structures through the application of specific external factors, including temperature, pH value, organic solvent, and shear stretching [37, 38]. This process can enhance the mechanical properties. Compared with the tensile strength of natural fibers about 0.5-0.6 GPa and the elongation at break of 10%-40%, there is still a huge gap. In terms of degradation rate, the degradation rate of regenerated silk fibroin materials is significantly faster than that of natural silk fibroin materials [39], which cannot match the tissue growth rate. Nevertheless, while natural silk protein materials exhibit superior mechanical properties and degradation rates compared to regenerated silk fibroin materials, natural silk fibroin materials have some limitations in processing and molding. The majority of studies currently concentrate on the utilization of electrospinning [40], freeze-drying, 3D printing [41, 42], self-assembly [43] and other technologies for the preparation of regenerated silk fibroin materials, which exhibit inadequate mechanical strength and are unsuitable for the repair of extensive soft tissue defects. Although the mechanical properties can be improved by producing composite materials with a multi-layer structure [44], this also increases the thickness and weight of the material. Concurrently, the cost is greater, and the capacity for large-scale production is limited.
In the past decades, growing emphasis on environmental concerns and exhausting depletion of petroleum sources have triggered the exploration of natural fibers as a “green” alternative for synthetic polymer fibers in composites. Because of their advantages such as low cost, low density, renewability, biodegradability and acceptable specific strength etc., a bulk of natural fibers have been utilized for structural/semi-structural materials in various fields including aerospace, automotive, building, furniture, packaging and sports articles. However, most of them are originated from lignocellulosic fibers [1], [2], [3]. Bombyx mori silkworm silk, a representative animal fiber of luster and fineness, has been used in the textile industry for centuries. It structurally consists of a fibrous core protein named fibroin, and a family of glue-like proteins named sericin that surround the fibroin threads to cement them together. The high crystallinity of β-sheets (ca. 50%) as well as the well orientation of these nanocrystallites in the core filament [4] gives silkworm silk the remarkable mechanical properties, especially strength (0.4 GPa) and extensibility (20%) [5], [6]. In addition, the homogeneous physicochemical properties of silkworm silk as a continuous fiber allow for the fabrication facilities via filament winding and pultrusion processes. Recently, silkworm silk has received great interest as a filling material in composites. For example, chopped silk and commercial silk fabric have been used to reinforce biodegradable or synthetic polymers such as poly(butylene succinate) [7], [8], poly(ɛ-caprolactone) [9], poly(lactic acid) [10], or even polychloroprene rubber [11]. However, chopped silk loses the mechanical merits as a continuous fiber, and commercial silk fabric suffers from the wetting problem of twisted fibroin threads in the matrix, both of which may result in the uncompetitive mechanical performance of the reported silk composites. It is well known that the adhesion between components (e.g. the fiber phase and the matrix phase) is crucial for the mechanical performance of a composite. On one hand, Jin et al. [8] modified silk fabric with carbon nanotubes to improve its compatibility with poly[(butylene succinate)-co-(butylene adipate)], and obtained a composite with fairly increased mechanical properties. On the other hand, Li et al. [12] directly composed silk fabric with regenerated silk fibroin (RSF); however, the overall mechanical properties of the composite were still unsatisfactory. This was likely caused by the immiscibility between the different fine structures of silk fibroin, i.e., the well-ordered β-sheet in silk fiber [13] and either the amorphous state [14] or the randomly-aligned β-sheet [15] in RSF matrix. Furthermore, due to the highly-repeating GAGAGS (G = glycine, A = alanine and S = serine) motifs and the highly-ordered structure, silk fiber presents a water-resistant feature [16] that indicates its inadequate wettability with RSF solution. Since partial fiber dissolution (either by solvent or by thermal melting) seems a straightforward approach to prepare fiber composites with good interface adhesion [3], [17], [18], [19], [20], a moderate concentration of LiBr aqueous solution (i.e. 6 mol L−1) was applied on silk fiber to improve its adhesion with RSF matrix in this work. Therefore, a robust and tough all-silk composite was successfully produced by embedding the LiBr-pretreated silk fibers in alignment to the high concentration of RSF aqueous solution and through an eco-friendly solution casting process.

HA, a calcium phosphate mineral embedded in fish scale's collagen matrix provides hardness to the scales. Plasma treatment serves to modify the surface of materials to achieve effective surface modification techniques to alter the surface properties of various materials without damaging the bulk material. Based solely on the provided evidence, oxygen plasma treatment enhances PCL surfaces through the following mechanisms:

1.  **Increasing Hydrophilicity:** It introduces oxygen-containing functional groups (such as carboxyl (-COOH) and hydroxyl (-OH)) onto the PCL surface, significantly reducing the water contact angle and improving wettability [1, 3, 6, 13]. This increased hydrophilicity promotes better interactions with biological components like cells and water [1, 3].

2.  **Improving Cell Interaction:** The enhanced hydrophilicity and chemical activation of the PCL surface lead to increased cell adhesion and proliferation [1, 13]. The modified surface provides a more biocompatible and cell-receptive interface [1, 13].

3.  **Enabling Biomolecule Immobilization/Grafting:** The reactive surface created by oxygen plasma (e.g., creating carboxyl groups) provides strong binding sites for immobilizing bioactive molecules. This is crucial for grafting materials like gelatin onto the PCL surface, which further enhances cell attachment, spreading, and proliferation due to integrin-binding sites [1, 13]. The grafting efficiency is significantly improved due to the plasma-induced activation [1].

4.  **Minimal Impact on Bulk Properties:** While modifying the surface chemistry and roughness, oxygen plasma treatment has a low impact on the tensile strength and mechanical properties of the bulk PCL material. This is because the treatment primarily affects the surface layer, which constitutes a very small fraction of the total mass [3, 9, 13]. Evidence [13] specifically notes that 60s exposure achieves significant functionalization (-COOH density of 40 nM/cm² and reduced contact angle) while preserving mechanical properties suitable for applications like blood vessel scaffolds [13].

5.  **Surface Activation for Further Modification:** Plasma treatment activates the PCL surface, making it more receptive to subsequent chemical modifications or coatings, such as collagen grafting [1, 8].

Among the synthetic bioplastics, poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) is a widely used polymer for its excellent biocompatibility, bioresorbability, nontoxicity, and processability. PCL also exhibits good thermal stability and mechanical properties and is used in high-pressure water treatment applications such as microfiltration and nanofiltration [26, 27]. However, PCL is hydrophobic (water contact angle [WCA] ~110° [28]) and exhibits slow hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation [29]. However, these limitations of PCL can be circumvented by suitable modifications. For instance, Rouba et al. modified the electrospun PCL membrane surface by plasma treatment which significantly enhanced water wettability due to the attachment of oxygen-containing functional groups on the surface and improved adhesion with adipose-derived stem cells [30]. Arbade et al. found improved hydrophilicity, biodegradability, and biocompatibility of PCL by adding poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and poly(L-lactide-co-ε-caprolactone-co-glycolide) (PLCG) [31]. Also, they reported that the addition of chloramphenicol drug [32] and Emblica officinalis [28] improved the hydrophilicity of PCL. PCL-based membranes and nanofiber mats for capturing water contaminants have been studied extensively in the literature. For example, Tu et al. prepared electrospun PCL membranes by incorporating 10% TiO2 and 1% rectorite, achieving over 98% efficiency in breaking down rhodamine B dye through photocatalysis [33]. Nivedita et al. prepared PCL membranes with 10% unmodified (UMMT) and organically modified montmorillonite (OMMT) clay by phase-inversion method. They reported Congo red dye rejection rates of 37% and 45% for UMMT- and OMMT-filled membranes, respectively. The pure water flux (PWF) increased from 200 Lm−2 h−1 for the UMMT-filled to 1600 Lm−2 h−1 for the OMMT-filled membranes [27]. Hinestroza et al. prepared a composite membrane combining PCL and cellulose nanofibers (CNF) via electrospinning and showed that PCL:CNF blend in a 50:50 ratio removed 75% and 99% of Fe2+ and Cr3+ ions, respectively, from their aqueous solutions [20]. A biodegradable electrospun nanofiber of PCL, gelatin, and chitosan in the weight ratio of 40:40:20 showed 96% MB dye removal, stable flux, and tensile strength of 12 MPa [21]. However, they did not compare the results with the pristine PCL membrane. Sadeghi et al. prepared a PCL/poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) blend membrane via the NIPS technique. PCL/30 wt% PBS blend membrane exhibited 106%, 26%, and 37% higher PWF, fouling recovery rate (FRR), and permeate flux than the pristine PCL membrane [34]. Wen et al. fabricated electrospun PCL membranes embedded with Fe3O4 nanoparticles and used as catalysts in Fenton reactions with H2O2 and UV light to degrade MB dye. They achieved 99% efficiency of MB degradation and retained high efficiency (~96%) after six cycles of adsorption-desorption [35]. The rate of biodegradation of PCL by hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation is slow, which has spurred considerable research to enhance its biodegradability. Various fillers and additives were incorporated into PCL to accelerate its degradation under composting conditions [29, 36-39]. For instance, Singh et al. found ~89% weight loss for PCL/Cloisite 30B (4 wt%) composite compared to only ~42% for pristine PCL, both after 75 days [36]. A PCL/Cloisite C20A (40 wt%) composite, made via melt mixing, exhibited a 51% weight loss after 180 days, while PCL alone lost only 22% weight [37]. A PCL/rice husk (50 wt%) composite, also prepared by melt mixing, showed a 78.4% weight loss after 57 days [38]. PCL/4 wt% MXene membranes increased in weight loss from ~6% for pure PCL to ~32% after 28 days in compost [39]. Cesur et al. reported ~45% weight loss after 150 days for PCL composites with 1 wt% OMMT and 1 wt% oleic acid, while neat PCL degrades in 8 months [40]. Singh et al. observed ~78% weight loss after 20 days for PCL/starch blends and PCL-grafted dextran amphiphilic copolymer (5 wt%) composites, prepared by melt mixing and only 45% weight loss for neat PCL [41]. However, there is a lack of literature on the use of oligomeric PCL and laponite (Lap) as additives to the PCL to prepare mixed matrix membranes. Oligomeric PCL is expected to provide higher hydroxyl groups to the PCL membrane, facilitating its biodegradation by hydroenzymatic reaction. Lap, on the other hand, is synthetic magnesium aluminosilicate clay and belongs to the 2:1 smectite family. Lap is widely used as a filler in agricultural products, paints, cosmetics, and polymers [42]. It provides functional groups and stiffness to the polymers and has been suitably modified for a large number of applications including water treatment [43], proton exchange membrane [44], and drug delivery [45]. Lap is highly hydrophilic and contains negatively charged edges due to cation deficiency owing to isomorphous substitution. These groups provide functionality and hydrophilicity. Therefore, Lap is envisaged to bind with positively charged organic dyes and heavy metal ions in water, provide mechanical stiffness, and improve the biodegradability of PCL as well.

In general, to improve various synthetic scaffolds and make them more conducive to cellular responses, a protein-based surface-coating has been used to obtain highly bioactive interfaces that allow for efficient cell adhesion and sustain differentiated phenotypes.20,21 Thus, a variety of protein components from the extracellular matrix (ECM) (collagen, gelatin, and fibronectin etc.) have been conjugated on plasma-modified surfaces to increase cellular responses, such as cell attachment and proliferation.22,23 In general, PCL has several advantages, including flexible mechanical and degradation properties and biocompatibility, and it can alter the surface by modifying hydrophobicity using various surface modification methods with preferred functional groups.24 Collagen has been extensively used to increase interactions between cells and materials because it provides both mechanical support to tissues and cell-binding sites (Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD) and GFOGER).25-27 In this study, we propose a newly modified surface for electrospun PCL/collagen fibers, which was obtained by an electrospinning/coating/selective-plasma-treatment process. We applied oxygen plasma treatment on the collagen-coated fibrous PCL to achieve a highly bioactive surface. We used plasma-etching supplemented with a nanosized AAO template (hole size = 800 nm) to obtain controlled roughness of the collagen region on the fibrous PCL surface. Various in vitro cellular activities of the fabricated PCL biomedical substitutes with micro-scale fibers and a nanoscale pattern were examined using osteoblast-like-cells (MG63) to assess its feasibility for use in a tissue regenerative scaffold. Plasma, the fourth state of matter, is a quasi-neutral gas in which protons and neutrons are ionized. Plasma is generated by the collision of electrons and photons with neutral gas. Gases that generate plasma include oxygen, nitrogen, argon, and helium, and their effects may vary depending on the gas injected [16,17]. Plasma is a simple and well-known method of surface modification and can be used to modify polymer surfaces by generating it. Surface plasma-modifying strategies for polymers include plasma treatment, plasma polymerization, plasma syn-irradiation, and plasma post-irradiation grafting. Plasma treatment implants hydroxyl (O-H), carbonyl (C=O), and carboxyl (COOH) groups on the polymer surfaces [18,19]. In addition, hydrophobic surfaces become hydrophilic through changes in wettability, surface energy, and roughness of the polymer surfaces. Therefore, several studies have been conducted to improve the degradation rate of biodegradable polymers via plasma treatment. Although many studies have investigated the use of plasma treatment to accelerate the degradation of electrospun biodegradable polymers [9,20,21], few have systemically examined the effect of plasma treatment time on the degradation rate of electrospun biodegradable polymer membranes. In this study, atmospheric-pressure non-thermal argon plasma, which is clinically applicable, was applied to electrospun biodegradable polymer membranes. By varying the plasma treatment time, we evaluated the differences in degradation after 1, 4, and 12 weeks. The aim of this study is to regulate the degradation rate of electrospun biodegradable polymer membranes for GBR by controlling the plasma treatment time. Electrospun biodegradable polymer membranes were fabricated using biodegradable polymers: PCL (Mn: 80,000, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), PLA (Mw: 193,300, GoodFellow, Seoul, Korea), and PLGA (lactide:glycolide = 75:25, Mw: 66,000-107,000, Sigma-Aldrich, U.K.). These polymers have been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and are biocompatible and biodegradable. The solvents used were Chloroform (CF, Sigma-Aldrich, U.K.), N,N-Dimethylformamide(DMF, Tokyo Chemical Industry, Chuo-ku, Japan), and Acetone(AC, DUKSAN, Korea); PCL and PLA used a mixture of DMF and CF, and PLA used a mixture of DMF and AC. Each Polymer was dispersed within proper solvents and stirred magnetically at 60 ℃ and 600 rpm overnight. The prepared solution was loaded into a 5 mL syringe (KOVAX, Seoul, Korea) with a 23 G metal nozzle (NanoNC, Seoul, Korea). The membranes were fabricated using an electrospinning machine (ESR200RD, NanoNC, Seoul, Korea). As shown in Table 1, the flow rate of all polymer solutions was maintained at 2 mL/h, the voltages of PCL and PLA were 15 kV and PLGA was 9.5 kV; the distance between syringe and collector was 14 cm for PCL, and that between syringe and collector was 12 cm for PLA and PLGA. The fabricated membrane was dried overnight in a vacuum dryer (ilShinBioBase Lab Co. Ltd., Dongducheon, Korea) to remove any residual solvent.

question: What is the 'degradation product' of Poly(ortho esters) and why is it beneficial?
ground_truth: Poly(ortho esters) degrade into acidic byproducts, but they are often designed to degrade via surface erosion. Importantly, some formulations include basic excipients to neutralize the acidic degradation products, or they degrade into neutral products, preventing the acidic autocatalysis seen in polyesters and reducing inflammation in surrounding tissue.

Poly(ortho esters) (POEs) are a group of biodegradable polyesters that were firstly synthesized in the 1970s by the ALZA Corporation in order to develop materials that may potentially undergo surface erosion degradation process, which is not commonly found in biodegradable polyesters [138], [139]. The high hydrophobicity provided by the orthoesther linkages ensures that the degradation proceeds faster than the H2O diffusion into the material. POEs are synthesized by using diols having different chain flexibility. Till the date, four types of these surface eroding materials have been reported [140], [141]. 1st generation POEs (or POE I) are obtained upon transesterification of a diol together with diethoxytetrahydrofuran. POE II (2nd generation) were developed to avoid the release of acidic by-products during its degradation (as occurring in POE I). Such materials are obtained by reacting diols with diketene acetal 3,9-bis(ethylidene 2,4,8,10-tetraoxaspiro[5,5]undecane). POE III (3rd generation) could be obtained upon direct polymerization of a triol together with an orthoester, yielding a highly mechanically flexible gel-like material. Finally, 4th generation POEs (POE IV, Fig. 2) were developed to solve the up-scaling difficulties of POE III and, similarly to POE II, they can be obtained by incorporating soft segments based on LA and GA into the chain backbone. Although generally speaking POE IV show weak mechanical properties, their good biodegradability has boosted their use in tissue engineering and drug delivery applications [142]. This last group of POE presents a scalable synthetic procedure and has the highest versatility as their properties could be tuned by properly selecting the nature of diols and the amount of LA or GA in the main chain [141], [143], [144]. Thus, depending on the flexibility of the diol chain, a wide variety of thermo-mechanical properties can be achieved; from hard, glassy materials showing a high glass transition temperature to semi-solid polymers showing low glass transition temperature. As polyesters usually display rather brittle mechanical behaviour which is not adequate for some biomedical applications, novel elastomeric biodegradable polyesters such as poly(diol citrates) and poly(glycerol sebacate) (PGS) have been synthesized for soft tissue engineering applications (Fig. 2) [145], [146]. Poly(diol citrates) can be synthesized via polycondensation reactions using non-toxic and inexpensive monomers, such as citric acid. Besides, considering the availability of various diols with different chain flexibility, biodegradable elastomers with tuneable mechanical properties can be obtained through relatively simple synthesis procedures. In this sense, a series of poly(diol citrates) were synthesized by reacting citric acid with various diols: poly(1,6-hexanediol-co-citrate) (PHC), poly(1,8-octanediol-co-citrate) (POC), poly(1,10-decanediol-co-citrate) (PDC) and poly(1,12-dodecanediol-co-citrate) (PDDC) [147]. All the synthesized polymers were totally amorphous and displayed low Tg ranging from −5 to 10 °C. Regarding the mechanical properties, which are summarized in Table 5, all the poly(diol citrates) displayed an elastomeric behaviour with no permanent deformation. Moreover, these mechanical properties were finely adjusted, not only by the selected diol, but also through cross-link density, by adjusting the post-polymerization temperature and time [148]. Similar to the poly(alkylene dicarboxylate)s based on dicarboxylic acids and dihydroxy compounds analysed in the previous section, polymers based on glycerol can also be synthesized, being PGS the most studied one within this category. The first polymerization of PGS was reported in 2002 through polycondensation reaction of equimolar ratios of glycerol and sebacic acid reacted at 120 °C in the absence of a catalyst under inert conditions [145]. Owing to its physico-mechanical properties and easy of synthesis, these non-toxic polyesters show a huge potential for developing inexpensive and biodegradable elastomeric materials for tissue engineering applications [146]. The thermo-mechanical properties of PGS, which have been recently reviewed by Rai et al. [149], can be adjusted by varying the glycerol to sebacic acid ratio, curing temperature and time. In general, this thermoset polymer shows a Tg at around −37 °C. Regarding its mechanical properties, it shows elastomeric behaviour with elastic modulus ranging from 0.025 to 1.2 MPa, ultimate tensile strength >0.5 MPa and elongation at break >330%. Poly(propylene fumarate) (PPF), depicted in Fig. 2, is another type of linear polyester. It has an unsaturated linear structure and could be obtained via a transesterification reaction of fumaric diester [150]. Thanks to the presence of fumarate double groups in its main backbone, PPF shows a unique property to form crosslinked structures [151], resulting in higher mechanical strength material that can be employed as an injectable material as bone cement [152]. Overall, the physico-mechanical properties of PPF are mainly dependant on the molecular weight and crosslinking. For example, the compressive strengths and modulus of PPF samples crosslinked with biocompatible poly(ethylene glycol)-dimethacrylate (PEG-DMA) increased from 5.9 to 11.2 MPa and from 30.2 to 58.4 MPa, respectively, when the double-bond ratio of PEG-DMA/PPF increased from 0.38 to 1.88 [153]. In a different study [154], where PPF-diacrylate was employed as a crosslinking agent, compressive modulus up to 1.7 GPa were reported.
Branched PEI (bPEI), often regarded as the ''gold standard'' for polymeric gene carriers, is known to achieve reasonably high transfection in many cell types [8]. This is mainly attributed to the ''proton sponge'' effect and the high positive charge density of bPEI, owing to its numerous amino groups and highly branched structure. At the same time, bPEI can be quite toxic to cells with typical IC50 values in the range of μg/mL [8]. To improve the performance of bPEI, various studies have focused on chemical modification of the amine groups [13], [14], [15], reduction of molecular weight [16], [17], [18], and incorporation of degradable linkages [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24]. While these approaches are quite promising, they focus on optimizing single parameters (such as chemical composition, molecular weights and degradability). Rational design that integrates multiple design principles simultaneously is challenging to accomplish but may produce more effective polymeric gene carriers. Here we report a new family of rationally designed cationic polymer gene carriers with superior gene transfection efficiency and low cytotoxicity. These are acid-labile branched poly(ortho ester amino alcohol)s (bPOEAAs) with a molecular blueprint analogous to bPEI that embody three design principles about degradability of backbone, chain architecture, and chemistry of functional groups, described as follows.(1)''Acid-labile backbone''. A biodegradable polymer backbone is highly desirable, for it facilitates release of cargo [25], [26] and ensures low cytotoxicity [27]. Various acid-labile bonds (such as acetal and ketal) have been used to construct cationic polymer backbones that degrade in response to the mildly acidic environment of the endosome [28]. Ortho esters are highly sensitive to acidification and hydrolyzes more rapidly than acetal and ketal [29]. Previously, we have reported linear poly(ortho esters) that degrade rapidly at endosomal pH to release plasmid DNA [30], [31]. Here, ortho ester linkages are used to construct bPOEAAs, hoping that acid-triggered backbone degradation would result in high transfection efficiency and low cytotoxicity.(2)''Proper degree of branching''. The degree of branching is known to impact the performance of polymeric gene carriers [32], [33]. Compared with linear PEI, hyper-branched PEI has higher positive charge density and is more effective in condensing DNA into small nanoparticles [34]. However, bPEI is also more toxic than its linear form [35]. Here, a simple epoxide-amine reaction is used to synthesize bPOEAAs with proper degree of branching that would strike an optimal balance between transfection and cytotoxicity.(3)''Proper type of amine''. bPEI contains protonated primary amines that bind DNA strongly, ensuring protection and stability of the polyplexes under physiological conditions [36]. However, secondary and tertiary amines are also necessary, because they serve as ''proton sponges'' with buffering capacity to facilitate endosomal escape and are less toxic than primary amine [37]. Therefore, bPOEAAs are designed to contain optimal fractions of secondary and tertiary amines in the backbone, aiming to maximize the benefit of the ''proton sponge'' effect while minimizing cytotoxicity ''Acid-labile backbone''. A biodegradable polymer backbone is highly desirable, for it facilitates release of cargo [25], [26] and ensures low cytotoxicity [27]. Various acid-labile bonds (such as acetal and ketal) have been used to construct cationic polymer backbones that degrade in response to the mildly acidic environment of the endosome [28]. Ortho esters are highly sensitive to acidification and hydrolyzes more rapidly than acetal and ketal [29]. Previously, we have reported linear poly(ortho esters) that degrade rapidly at endosomal pH to release plasmid DNA [30], [31]. Here, ortho ester linkages are used to construct bPOEAAs, hoping that acid-triggered backbone degradation would result in high transfection efficiency and low cytotoxicity.

Over the past few decades, polymeric nanoparticles (NPs) have been widely explored for the delivery of therapeutic agents because of their favorable advantages including prolonged drug circulation duration, enhanced solubility of poorly soluble drugs, and ability to offer protection against pharmaceutical activity and reduce side effect [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. A large variety of synthetic biopolymers have been developed to form polymeric NPs for drug delivery applications [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]. Among these biopolymers, biodegradable polyurethanes are considered as one of the most promising platforms for various biomedical applications including drug delivery and tissue engineering because of their excellent biocompatibility and outstanding physical properties [14], [15], [16], [17]. Generally, biodegradable polyurethanes are prepared by embedded degradable polyesters or polycarbonates into polymer backbones [14], [15], [18], [19], [20]. However, these biodegradable polyurethanes usually display a slow degradation rate. It is worth noting that the drug released from such biodegradable polymeric NPs is blocked and generally incomplete, which often results in compromised potency of drugs in vitro and in vivo [14], [15], [21]. Recently, several groups' research have shown that pH-sensitive polyurethanes display enormous potential in drug delivery applications because of the existence of pH gradient in inflamed tissues, tumor microenvironment and endo/lysosome of cells [22], [23], [24], [25], [26]. In addition, the researchers have demonstrated that the polymeric NPs with accelerated degradation kinetic are beneficial for many drug delivery applications that need different time frames for the release of therapeutic drugs [24], [27]. So far, very little focus has been paid on the preparation of pH-sensitive polyurethanes with a controlled degradation kinetic [24]. Paramonov et al. used to report a library of polyurethanes containing acid-labile dimethyl ketal moiety in the polymer backbone. These polyurethanes-based NPs degraded significantly faster at pH 5.0 than at pH 7.4 with degradation kinetic closely relate to the hydrophobicity of starting polymers. As a result, these polyurethanes display great potential for the delivery of several bioactive agents [24]. As well-known, ortho ester bond is prone to acid cleavage [28]. Poly(ortho ester) (POE) is a family of hydrophobic, biocompatible and bio-erodible materials [34], [35]. Researchers have found that the degradation kinetic of POE can be controlled by several factors such as their molecular weight, hydrophobicity, and flexibility of polymer chains [32], [36], [37], [38] Generally, more flexible or hydrophilic POE has easier water penetration and loaded drug release, which is resulted from the accelerated hydrolysis of ortho esters [35], [38]. Thus, we postulate that the introduction of acid-labile ortho ester linkage into polymer main-chains can endow polyurethanes with controlled degradation kinetic and improved drug delivery.

Since their first application as suture materials, almost 50 years ago, these materials are used for various reconstruction procedures as scaffolding for three-dimensional cell cultures and transplantation of articular, auricular, nasal, cartilage,1 and intervertebral disk,2 in bone surgery such as fixation devices, for bone regeneration,3-5 tissue engineering,6-8 carriers for delivery of bioactive molecules as well as for drug delivery devices.9-11 As opposed to the initial simple processing procedures of these materials, current studies are extended to knitted stents,12 biodegradable polymer / bioceramic composites scaffold,13-15 nanocomposites,16 nanofibres,17 etc. Largely, this is because of the availability, biocompatibility, biodegradability, and processability of these materials. Initial detailed studies of artifacts made out of poly-α-hydroxyacids, PGA, and PLA, or other biodegradable materials such as polydioxanone, poly(trimethylene carbonate), poly(ethylene glycol), and poly (ε-caprolactone), homopolymers and copolymers, have witnessed their biodegradability18-26 and the absence of significant side effects such as inflammatory reactions, apart from a local pH reduction that results from cleavage of ester bonds and could cause a mild inflammatory influence on tissue.26-32 This implies that the realm of materials' properties can be widened by modification via copolymerization, which provides a number of advantages because the architecture and composition of the biomaterials can be tailored to control their properties.24, 33, 34 The functions of the scaffold in tissue engineering include providing mechanical integrity to the construct to impart dimensional stability, resist deformation because of body forces, and impart impulse to cells growing on the material. Copolymers of glycolide (GA) and lactide [poly(lactide-co-glycolide), PLGA] are amorphous where altering the ratio of PLA to PGA results in significant differences in the compression moduli and degradation times of the scaffolds. One of the limitations of scaffolds fabricated from PGA fibers is the small range of mechanical properties of these meshes. The compression modulus of scaffolds increases linearly with the incorporation of LA units, ranging from less than 1 kPa for PGA to approximately 20 kPa for scaffolds with 68% LA content. Hence, increasing the content of LA increases the compression modulus of the scaffolds by more than 20 folds.14 Furthermore, altering the ratio of LA to GA results in significant changes in adhesion, shape, and proliferation rates of cells seeded onto these scaffolds, since PLA and PGA differ significantly in hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity.35-38 Since one possible use of these materials is as a substrate for growing a layer of living cells, the material can be customized as a hydrogel, that will allow the proper nourishment and proliferation of the layer of living cells, after their attachment and spreading on the surface of the film, owing to the right hydrophobicity.39 Therefore, it is reasonable to hypothesize that combining of hydrophilic poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) with PLA (PLGA) that add dimensional stability and rigidity to scaffolds, may facilitate cell adhesion and additionally alter the process of hydrolysis to these materials. According to everything previously noted, the objective of this study is to examine PLA/PLGA-PVA hydrogels, regarding formulation, hydrophilic/hydrophobic ratio, and consistency against mechanical load, whereas the cell adhesion pliability is tested as well.

Thermosensitive PCL‐PEG‐PCL hydrogels: Synthesis, characterization, and delivery of proteins Accelerated in vivo degradation of polymers provides a unique strategy in applications of various biomedical polymers. Enzymes, biochemicals, and other biosignals including pH variations can be used as a triggering mechanism for polymer degradation. In particular, reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), super oxide anion (O2•−), hydroxyl radicals (HO•−), and singlet oxygen are common biochemicals in the human body. The ROS level is reported to increase around sites of inflammation, cancers, and several other diseases.1-5 Even a biocompatible polymer such as poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) induces mild inflammation upon implantation in the subcutaneous layer.6, 7 Therefore, incorporation of ROS-sensitive moieties along a polymer backbone can provide accelerated polymer biodegradation kinetics. Several ROS-sensitive polymers have been reported including poly(propylene sulfide), polythioketal, boronic ester polymers, and oxalate-based polymers.8-15 In particular, the oxalate functional groups are degraded into carbon dioxide by H2O2, where the cyclic dioxetanedione was suggested as a reactive intermediate (Figure 1).16 Oxalate-based polymers were also used for ultrasound imaging by taking advantage of enhanced ultrasound signal intensity by the degradation products of carbon dioxide.14 A cancer prodrug conjugated with oxalate was designed to take advantage of the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) as well as oxalate cleavage through increased ROS levels around cancer tissues.17 Recently, we reported fast degradable polycaprolactone (PCL) microspheres by incorporating oxalate groups along the polymers. The PCL microsphere degrades over 2 years. However, oxalate group-incorporated PCL microspheres completely degraded over 2 months in the subcutaneous layer of rats.18

Because of its special qualities, elastomers-a type of polymer with a low modulus and high elasticity-can rapidly return to their initial form following the removal of an external force. Because of these qualities, they are indispensable in both daily life and the economy [1,2,3,4]. Elastomers have been the subject of ongoing research and development to improve their strength, stability, aging resistance, and wear resistance in order to fulfill the ever-increasing performance requirements. However, these advantages make it harder to dispose of the waste products made from conventional elastomers, which pollutes the environment over time [5, 6]. However, the majority of elastomers are derived from poorly sustainable non-renewable fossil fuels. The creation of novel elastomers that are not dependent on fossil fuels has become highly demanded in recent times due to the immense strain imposed by carbon emissions. Bio-based elastomers are a great way to reduce carbon emissions and conserve resources in the elastomer sector since they may be made from natural plants directly or by synthesizing them from bio-based monomers produced from biomass resources. Due to excellent biodegradability, aliphatic polyester became a prominent area of research for environmentally-friendly products. Linear polyesters, such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA), polyglycolide acid (PGA), polycaprolactone (PCL), and their copolymers, have been extensively studied in the field of plastic for many years. And their industrial production is seeing tremendous growth [7,8,9]. Polyesters having a three-dimensional network have gained increasing interest, motivated by these linear polymers [10, 11]. Like vulcanized rubber, the cross-linked network is formed by the incorporation of "star" monomers to create multi-branched chains, enabling the material to rapidly regain its shape when subjected to substantial deformation. Poly (glycerol sebacate) (PGS), polyoctyl citrate (POC), and their copolymers are the primary biodegradable polyester elastomers that have undergone substantial research. The pioneering work is the synthesis of PGS, an in-situ cross-linked polyester elastomer with a three-dimensional network structure and exceptional robustness, conducted by Langer et al. successfully synthesized in 2002 [10, 12]. In 2011, Zhang et al. firstly introduced chemically crosslinked polyester elastomer [13]. Subsequently, many other bio-based elastomers have been created [14, 15]. It is well known that monomers of longer chain are easier to be synthesized to be polyester with higher stability, due to the lower density of ester linkage. For example, PCL and PBS are commercially mature materials, which employ 4- or 6- carbon chain monomer [16], while polyglycolide acid (PGA) with 2-carbon monomer is unstable to hydrolysis and its commercial application is very limited [17]. However, on the other hand, when the goal of our research is to obtain elastomers, the high crystallinity and rigidity due to longer chains becomes a disadvantage. Hereby a technical difficulty arises, how to construct biodegradable polyester with decent stability, cross-linkage network, and sufficient elasticity? That is, we probably need longer chain monomers, multi-functional “star” monomer, and some component to lower the crystallinity.

POE represent a versatile class of biodegradable polymers that have been explored for various biomedical applications, particularly in DDSs for cancer treatment. The effectiveness of POEs is largely attributed to their unique chemical structure, which consists of ortho ester linkages that confer hydrolytic stability while promoting biodegradability. These properties allow for tailored drug release profiles, enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of encapsulated chemotherapeutic agents. For instance, POE can be designed to exhibit pH-sensitive drug release, ensuring that therapeutic agents are released at specific sites, such as the acidic microenvironments of tumours [67]. The copolymerisation of ortho esters with primary amines allows for the synthesis of POEA and poly(ortho ester amidines), offering a broad range of functionalities for targeting efficiency and bioactivity [68]. This adaptability is significant, as it enables the formulation of multifunctional carriers that can encapsulate various anticancer drugs, thus providing a mechanism to overcome challenges such as drug resistance. For example, Khodabandehloo et al reported that such nanocarriers can enhance the bioavailability of drugs while mitigating systemic toxicity, illustrating their potential for improving therapeutic outcomes in preclinical models [68]. Furthermore, these POE-based nanocarriers can potentially facilitate the simultaneous delivery of multiple drugs, addressing the complex polypharmacy often necessary for effective cancer treatment [69]. Existing studies underline the important role of optimising POE formulations to enhance drug loading and release behaviours, potentially advancing personalised cancer therapies. Synthetic polymers, i.e., plastics and rubbers, have been providing us benefits, such as hygiene, safety, functions, and convenience. Thus, we cannot imagine our lives without them. However, we have minimal knowledge regarding what to do after their lifecycle.1,2 Currently, plastics are not only contaminating our food sources but also threatening the whole ecosystem.3 The COVID-19 pandemic has clearly shown that we cannot live without plastics,4,5 especially disposable ones. It is scandalous that approximately half the production of plastics is used for single-use applications.6 We are now consuming these more than ever before,7 and the environmental issues will become even more drastic. Unfortunately, we are not ready to deal with all the polymer wastes that are disposed intentionally or accidentally. All those issues arise from the non-biodegradability of plastics. Plastics can be fragmented but not completely decomposed into simpler molecules.8 Today, biodegradable plastics provide a possible solution to prevent those issues.9,10 However, biodegradable plastics are not recycled in most countries, including New Zealand, since those are designed to degrade, i.e., break down, compromising mechanical strength, and thus those should be disposed of in regular garbage bins. This is practiced by applying materials with a recycling code number of 7 (OTHER). For example, cutlery made of biodegradable plastics eventually end up in either landfill or energy recovery. One of the main reasons why biodegradability has been introduced to the plastic industry is to minimize adverse impacts on the environment due to disposals. It is an irony that the end of life of those is either landfill or burning rather than recycling, which is a much better treatment. Thus, it would be more constructive to develop methods to recycle biodegradable plastics or develop recyclable biodegradable plastics. If recyclable plastics degrade during physical recycling, that should be more expected for biodegradable plastics during physical recycling. For example, it does not seem to be a practical or favorable approach to recycle biodegradable cutlery back into cutlery due to lowered strength after recycling. Hence, it is reasonable to only consider recycling biodegradable cutlery in the applications where its mechanical strength is less significant. It is challenging to recycle one plastic product to another application because each product is made of a grade specifically suitable for each application. We have chosen cutlery made of poly(lactic acid) or polylactide (PLA) to study the possibility of recycling it to make foams, as mechanical strength is not crucial, and defining the process windows. PLA is a thermoplastic aliphatic polyester which can be obtained by polymerizing derivatives from biomasses, such as cornstarch, sugarcane, and other wastes. PLA is the most successfully adopted synthetic bio-based plastic in the industry and research for applications, including three-dimensional (3D) printing, fabrics, packaging/bottles, films, automotive, electronics, and tissue engineering.11 Moreover, its properties are similar to various non-degradable plastics. Approximately more than 200 000 patents have currently been published,12 and this polymer is still actively studied. The number of relevant publications increases exponentially, such as for phase and stereocomplex behavior,13-16 rheology,17-20 foaming,21-25 and recycling.26-28 In addition, there are a significant number of reviews and monographs11,12,29-42 that are available.
The rapid development of polymer materials has greatly enhanced our daily lives. However, the widespread use of these products has led to significant environmental pollution due to discarded polymers. Biodegradable polymers are a specific type of polymer that can be broken down and decomposed by microorganisms or their secretions under suitable and demonstrable natural environmental conditions.[1, 2] This degradation process results in a decrease in molecular weight, as well as changes in physical and chemical properties, ultimately leading to the formation of small molecules such as carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O). Biodegradable elastomers, in particular, offer notable advantages in clinical applications and have been extensively used in biomedical fields, including drug delivery systems,[3, 4] repair materials,[5, 6] surgical sutures,[7] tissue scaffolds,[8, 9] and implantable devices.[10, 11] Since many tissues and organs in the human body are elastic, these elastomers must provide excellent flexibility and compatibility with the corresponding tissues.[12, 13] Additionally, biodegradable elastomers need to endure repeated tensile recovery without losing mechanical properties or causing irritation to the surrounding tissues.[2, 14] Poly(1,8-octanediol-co-citrate) (POC) is a notable biodegradable elastomer that has gained significant attention in materials science and biomedical engineering in recent years.[15-18] It offers a combination of excellent properties, including good elasticity, biodegradability, and biocompatibility.[16, 19] These characteristics provide new opportunities to overcome the limitations of traditional materials, especially in sustainable development and biomedical applications.[15, 20] POC elastomer is a copolymer synthesized through the condensation reaction of 1,8-octanediol and citric acid.[19] The 1,8-octanediol is a water-soluble and nontoxic aliphatic diol that contributes a flexible, long-chain structure, giving the material its flexibility and elasticity.[21] Meanwhile, citric acid introduces multiple carboxyl and hydroxyl groups, which not only participate in the polymerization process but also significantly influence the material's hydrophilicity, biodegradability, and interaction with biomolecules.[22] POC elastomers exhibit excellent elastic recovery due to the chemical cross-linking network, allowing them to quickly return to their original shape after being stretched by external forces. By optimizing the synthesis process and adjusting the monomer ratio, their tensile strength can be enhanced to meet the basic strength requirements for various practical applications.[19] Furthermore, POC can be prepared under mild conditions without the addition of toxic catalysts and cross-linkers, which offers significant advantages over other biodegradable bioelastomers.[19] Numerous cell experiments have demonstrated that POC elastomers exhibit good compatibility with various cell lines and show minimal cytotoxicity.[15, 17] When designing scaffolds for cartilage tissue engineering, POC elastomers effectively mimic the mechanical properties of natural cartilage, creating an optimal microenvironment for the growth and proliferation of chondrocytes. As a result, POC elastomers have emerged as one of the ideal materials for tissue engineering scaffolds, thanks for their outstanding elasticity, biodegradability, and biocompatibility.[23] Delara et al. investigated the use of POC as a material for artificial blood vessel for transplanting human arterial endothelial cells.[24] They found that POC exhibits excellent compatibility with blood, indicating its potential to serve as a replacement for blood vessels in the human body. In the treating cardiovascular diseases, POC elastomers can be utilized to create biodegradable materials for cardiovascular interventions, such as vascular stents. These stents provide support to the walls of blood vessels and help restore vascular patency after implantation. Additionally, POC elastomers can serve as versatile substrate materials for flexible sensors and wearable electronic devices.[12, 25] Their high elasticity and remarkable flexibility ensure that these devices perform optimally, even when subjected to bending or stretching. For example, encapsulating devices with POC elastomers can enhance their mechanical and electrochemical stability, making them more resilient to the deformations caused by repeated stretching.[26] Although POC has several advantages, including ease of processing, excellent biocompatibility, and non-toxicity, it is limited by poor mechanical properties, particularly low elongation at break due to dense chemical cross-linking. To address these challenges, numerous studies have focused on improving its mechanical and chemical properties through copolymerization or physical blending.[27-33] Notably, the copolymerization strategy offers the benefits of adjustable molecular chain structures and enhanced compatibility. For instance, silica-based monomers or sols have been incorporated into POC to improve tensile strength, modulus, and elongation at break. One example is the addition of polysilsesquioxane sols to the POC prepolymer, which are cross-linked during a thermal curing process. This addition improves the thermomechanical properties and chemical resistance of the POC elastomer.[34] In another study, Yang et al. developed a biodegradable elastomer known as poly(octamethylene maleate (anhydride) citrate) (POMaC) using citric acid, maleic anhydride, and 1,8-octanediol. POMaC possesses dual networks of carbon-carbon cross-linking and ester bond cross-linking. It demonstrates excellent biocompatibility with cells and tissues, as well as mechanical properties that are comparable to those of soft biological tissues.[35]
ans_raw: The degradation products of Poly(ortho esters) (POEs) are primarily small molecules such as **diols, lactic acid (LA), and glycolic acid (GA)**, depending on the generation and composition of the POE [1], [4], [12]. For example, POE IV incorporates LA and GA into its backbone, leading to their release during hydrolysis [1]. These degradation products are **beneficial due to their biocompatibility and reduced cytotoxicity**. Earlier POE generations (e.g., POE I) released acidic by-products, which were addressed in later generations (POE II and IV) to avoid adverse effects [1]. The acid-labile ortho ester linkages in POEs enable controlled, pH-sensitive degradation, particularly in acidic environments like tumor microenvironments or endosomes, ensuring timely drug release while minimizing systemic toxicity [2], [4], [12]. Additionally, the hydrolytic breakdown into non-toxic, metabolizable compounds (e.g., diols, LA, GA) supports their use in biomedical applications such as tissue engineering and drug delivery [1], [12].

Polydioxanone (PDO, PDS) undergoes hydrolytic degradation through a combination of both surface and bulk erosion mechanisms. When degraded in aqueous buffer solution (pH:7.4) at 37 °C, PDO films show a mass loss of ~50% after 270 days [293], which can be accelerated to yield a mass loss of ~50% after 50 days by increasing the surface area of the material [261]. A pH drop from 7.40 to 5.64 after 10 weeks was observed, suggesting the release of acidic by-products to the degrading medium (the resulting glyoxylic acid (pKa = 3.3) can be excreted in the urine or converted into glycine and then into CO2 and H2O by the human body) [261]. Poly(ortho ester)s are hydrophobic polyesters having hydrolytically labile linkages that undergo through surface erosion degradation. POEs display a degradation profile that could be easily tuned by controlling the pH of the degrading medium by using acidic or basic excipients [141]. The hydrolytic degradation of POE I yields the initial diol and γ-butyrolactone as a by-product, which is further hydrolyzed to 4-hydroxybutanoic acid. To avoid the autocatalytic behaviour during the degradation of POE I, POE II was developed, which yields neutral products as a by-product (which include pentaerythritol dipropionate and the diol) [5]. The degradation rate of this polymer can be modulated by adding acid excipient such as itaconic and adipic acids. POE III yields 5-flurouracil, acetic acid and 1,2,6-hexanetriol. POE IV yields LA or GA which further autocatalize the degradation, which can be tuned by the proportion of glycolic or lactic acid in the sequence to last from days to months [197]. Overall, as a segment having a carboxylic acid end-group initially catalyzed the ortho ester hydrolysis to generate a diol (or a mixture of them), the hydrolytic degradation profile of POEs can be tuned upon controlling the ratio of the diol to the latent acid in the backbone [141]. Segmented poly(ester amide)s (PEAs) consisting on amide blocks linked to amorphous polyester matrix display tuneable mechanical, thermal and degradation properties depending on their hard-to-soft ratio [133]. The scission of ester bonds result in the formation of water-soluble and non-toxic bisamide-diol monomers/oligomers which can be excreted by the kidneys [262]. In this line, Lips et al. thoroughly studied the in vitro and in vivo degradation of aliphatic poly(ester amide)s comprising 1,4‐butanediol/dimethyl adipate and dimethyl adipate/ε‐caprolactone/1,4‐diaminobutane or 1,2‐diaminoethane [133]. Degradation tests carried out in PBS at 37 °C (0.03 wt% sodium azide as antibacterial agent) showed a weight loss of ~ 3% (depending on the composition) after 7 months. Results suggested that the degradation takes place via ester bond cleavage with a bulk degradation process. The degradation of polyesters containing below 50% amide content showed no cytotoxic response, while the sample having 50% of amide content resulted in mild undesired body reactions. Other PEAs based on L-alanine showed a weight loss of 7.5% after 150 days at 37 °C in PBS medium, suggesting that the α-amino acid contributes to speed-up the degradation rate of PEAs [263]. Due to these inherent characteristics, PEAs emerge as perfect candidates for long-term biomedical implants as they offer tuneable degradation rate (the degradation is favoured with the ester content) with lower pH drop in comparison with more widely used polyesters [264]. As poly(propylene fumarate) (PPF) is usually crosslinked to obtain polymer networks, it is difficult to find the time required for the hydrolytic degradation of neat PPF. A slow degradation rate with a mass loss of 22% after 70 days in PBS solution at 37 °C was found (bulk degradation process) [265], yielding fumaric acid (pKa = 4.4) and propylene glycol (pKa = 14.9) as a by-product [266]. As a combination of these two by-products, medium pH remains unchanged (±0.1) upon degradation [267], which is in contrast with the pH decrease suffered by the medium degrading other polyesters. Poly(glycerol sebacate) (PGS) is other interesting biodegradable polyester which shows a surface erosion mechanism [268]. Agitation for 60 days in PBS solution at 37 °C yields a weight loss of 17%, while the in vivo degradation is much faster in comparison with in vitro conditions [145]. The degradation rate of PGS could be varied by modifying processing parameters; i.e., when PGS is synthesized at 110 °C it shows a fast degradation, while a negligible degradation was observed when synthesized at 130 °C [146]. Degradation products are non-toxic as sebacic acid is the natural metabolic intermediate in ω-oxidation of medium- to long-chain fatty acids and glycerol has been approved by the FDA to be used as humectant in foods [149]. Poly(diol citrate)s are an interesting family of biodegradable and elastomeric polyesters with potential for tissue engineering applications. Poly(1,8-octanediol-co-citrate) (POC) is the most prominent type of poly(diol citrate). POC is degraded by hydrolysis of its ester linkages [148], with a weight loss of 8% after being immersed for 3 weeks in PBS at 37 °C [269]. Such degradation time is expected to fall within the appropriate time-scales required for most tissue engineering applications [148]. Jeon et al. suggested a concomitant effect of bulk (with autocatalysis) and surface degradation for POC scaffolds degraded in PBS (pH:7.4) and 0.1 M NaOH solutions at 37 °C (scaffolds showed a pore collapse after 3 week degradation in PBS and after 24 h in 0.1 NaOH) [269]. Yang et al. synthesized a series of poly(diol citrate)s including poly(1,6-hexanediol-co-citrate) (PHC), poly(1,8-octanediol-co-citrate) (POC), poly(1,10-decanediol-co-citrate) (PDC), poly(1,12-dodecanediol-co-citrate) (PDDC) and observed that the degradation rate could be increased with decreasing number of methylene units in the diol monomer [147]. When tested in vivo, a mild acute inflammatory response was observed at 1 week after implantation, suggesting that non-toxic degradation products were expelled. Indeed, produced citric acid during degradation may be metabolized in the body via Krebs or citric acid cycles. A fast degrading poly(diol citrate) was obtained by Lei et al. [270], who showed that when degraded in PBS at 37 °C, poly((1,2-propanediol-sebacate)-citrate) (PPSC) suffers a weight loss of nearly 90% after 14 days (PGS and POC need 2 and 6 months respectively for a complete degradation). Fast degradation was ascribed to a higher density of ester bonds and an increased number of methyl side groups which decrease the regularity of the chain and increase diffusion coefficients. Till the date, most of the works dealing with biodegradable polyesters have been focused on pure aliphatic polyesters as ester linkages in the main chain could be relatively easily cleaved. In comparison, traditional aromatic polymers show a much larger resistance to hydrolytic degradation (they even tend to be non-biodegradable). However, recent advances in polymer chemistry have expanded the range of biodegradable polymers, including those known as aliphatic/aromatic polyesters through the introduction of aromaticity into either the backbone or pendant to the main chain. Furanic-based polyesters based on the renewable 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA) represent an interesting group of novel aliphatic aromatic polyesters, from which poly(ethylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate) (PEF) is the best known one. Despite to its relatively slow hydrolytic degradation rate, where only 2% of weight loss is achieved after 84 days in PBS at 37 °C (for comparison PLLA displays a weight loss of 7% under the same conditions), PEF shows an improved degradability in comparison with fossil-based PET and it degrades to yield non-toxic 2,5- furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA) and ethylene glycol as by-products [162], [271]. As the furan ring makes the attack of water molecules more difficult because it results in a rigid macromolecule due to the rig-flipping hindering by the nonlinear axis of furan ring rotation coupled with the ring polarity [168], Matos et al. copolymerized FDCA with other easily degradable aliphatic precursor to obtain potentially biodegradable aliphatic/aromatic polyesters [162]. Degradation studies performed in PBS (pH 6.9) at 37 °C reveal that the incorporation of lactyl units accelerated the degradation rate of the resulting PEF-co-PLA up to a 60% of weight loss after 84 days (in comparison with 2% for neat PEF). Interestingly, the degradation could be finely tuned upon the variation of the relative amount of 2,5-furandicarboxylate, allowing FDCA-based polyesters to hydrolyze on a reasonable timescale. Similarly, Terzopoulou et al. synthesized further FDCA-based polyesters upon the incorporation of succinic acid to obtain biodegradability [168]. The hydrolytic degradation in PBS (pH:7) at 25 °C of poly(butylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate-co-butylene adipate) (PBF-co-PBAd) and poly(butylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate-co-butylene succinate) (PBF-co-PBSu) was studied by the group of Prof. Dubois [272]. A reduced weight loss of 1-2% was found to occur after 150 days, although marked changes on the molecular weight were observed. Indeed, it was concluded that the hydrolysis proceeds through a random chain scission mechanism, where the hydrolytic degradation rate of both PBF-co-PBAd and PBF-co-PBSu decreased with increasing butylene furandicarboxylate content. They also found that, although PBF-co-PBSu has more hydrophilic chains than PBF-co-PBAd, for a given composition PBF-co-PBAd degraded slightly faster than PBF-co-PBSu, which suggests that crystallinity plays a significant role in influencing the hydrolytic degradability of these copolyesters. Although till the date several works have highlighted the potential of furan-based aliphatic/aromatic polyesters to develop novel materials such as poly(propylene 2,5-furan dicarboxylate) (PPF) [273], poly(butylene 2,5-furan dicarboxylate) (PBF) [274], poly(trimethylene furandicarboxylate) (PTF) [275], their hydrolytic degradation behaviour remains barely investigated. This fact emphasizes the need of comprehensive works aimed at determining the end-of-life of furanic aliphatic/aromatic polyesters.
Poly(ortho esters) (POEs) are a group of biodegradable polyesters that were firstly synthesized in the 1970s by the ALZA Corporation in order to develop materials that may potentially undergo surface erosion degradation process, which is not commonly found in biodegradable polyesters [138], [139]. The high hydrophobicity provided by the orthoesther linkages ensures that the degradation proceeds faster than the H2O diffusion into the material. POEs are synthesized by using diols having different chain flexibility. Till the date, four types of these surface eroding materials have been reported [140], [141]. 1st generation POEs (or POE I) are obtained upon transesterification of a diol together with diethoxytetrahydrofuran. POE II (2nd generation) were developed to avoid the release of acidic by-products during its degradation (as occurring in POE I). Such materials are obtained by reacting diols with diketene acetal 3,9-bis(ethylidene 2,4,8,10-tetraoxaspiro[5,5]undecane). POE III (3rd generation) could be obtained upon direct polymerization of a triol together with an orthoester, yielding a highly mechanically flexible gel-like material. Finally, 4th generation POEs (POE IV, Fig. 2) were developed to solve the up-scaling difficulties of POE III and, similarly to POE II, they can be obtained by incorporating soft segments based on LA and GA into the chain backbone. Although generally speaking POE IV show weak mechanical properties, their good biodegradability has boosted their use in tissue engineering and drug delivery applications [142]. This last group of POE presents a scalable synthetic procedure and has the highest versatility as their properties could be tuned by properly selecting the nature of diols and the amount of LA or GA in the main chain [141], [143], [144]. Thus, depending on the flexibility of the diol chain, a wide variety of thermo-mechanical properties can be achieved; from hard, glassy materials showing a high glass transition temperature to semi-solid polymers showing low glass transition temperature. As polyesters usually display rather brittle mechanical behaviour which is not adequate for some biomedical applications, novel elastomeric biodegradable polyesters such as poly(diol citrates) and poly(glycerol sebacate) (PGS) have been synthesized for soft tissue engineering applications (Fig. 2) [145], [146]. Poly(diol citrates) can be synthesized via polycondensation reactions using non-toxic and inexpensive monomers, such as citric acid. Besides, considering the availability of various diols with different chain flexibility, biodegradable elastomers with tuneable mechanical properties can be obtained through relatively simple synthesis procedures. In this sense, a series of poly(diol citrates) were synthesized by reacting citric acid with various diols: poly(1,6-hexanediol-co-citrate) (PHC), poly(1,8-octanediol-co-citrate) (POC), poly(1,10-decanediol-co-citrate) (PDC) and poly(1,12-dodecanediol-co-citrate) (PDDC) [147]. All the synthesized polymers were totally amorphous and displayed low Tg ranging from −5 to 10 °C. Regarding the mechanical properties, which are summarized in Table 5, all the poly(diol citrates) displayed an elastomeric behaviour with no permanent deformation. Moreover, these mechanical properties were finely adjusted, not only by the selected diol, but also through cross-link density, by adjusting the post-polymerization temperature and time [148]. Similar to the poly(alkylene dicarboxylate)s based on dicarboxylic acids and dihydroxy compounds analysed in the previous section, polymers based on glycerol can also be synthesized, being PGS the most studied one within this category. The first polymerization of PGS was reported in 2002 through polycondensation reaction of equimolar ratios of glycerol and sebacic acid reacted at 120 °C in the absence of a catalyst under inert conditions [145]. Owing to its physico-mechanical properties and easy of synthesis, these non-toxic polyesters show a huge potential for developing inexpensive and biodegradable elastomeric materials for tissue engineering applications [146]. The thermo-mechanical properties of PGS, which have been recently reviewed by Rai et al. [149], can be adjusted by varying the glycerol to sebacic acid ratio, curing temperature and time. In general, this thermoset polymer shows a Tg at around −37 °C. Regarding its mechanical properties, it shows elastomeric behaviour with elastic modulus ranging from 0.025 to 1.2 MPa, ultimate tensile strength >0.5 MPa and elongation at break >330%. Poly(propylene fumarate) (PPF), depicted in Fig. 2, is another type of linear polyester. It has an unsaturated linear structure and could be obtained via a transesterification reaction of fumaric diester [150]. Thanks to the presence of fumarate double groups in its main backbone, PPF shows a unique property to form crosslinked structures [151], resulting in higher mechanical strength material that can be employed as an injectable material as bone cement [152]. Overall, the physico-mechanical properties of PPF are mainly dependant on the molecular weight and crosslinking. For example, the compressive strengths and modulus of PPF samples crosslinked with biocompatible poly(ethylene glycol)-dimethacrylate (PEG-DMA) increased from 5.9 to 11.2 MPa and from 30.2 to 58.4 MPa, respectively, when the double-bond ratio of PEG-DMA/PPF increased from 0.38 to 1.88 [153]. In a different study [154], where PPF-diacrylate was employed as a crosslinking agent, compressive modulus up to 1.7 GPa were reported.
Branched PEI (bPEI), often regarded as the ''gold standard'' for polymeric gene carriers, is known to achieve reasonably high transfection in many cell types [8]. This is mainly attributed to the ''proton sponge'' effect and the high positive charge density of bPEI, owing to its numerous amino groups and highly branched structure. At the same time, bPEI can be quite toxic to cells with typical IC50 values in the range of μg/mL [8]. To improve the performance of bPEI, various studies have focused on chemical modification of the amine groups [13], [14], [15], reduction of molecular weight [16], [17], [18], and incorporation of degradable linkages [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24]. While these approaches are quite promising, they focus on optimizing single parameters (such as chemical composition, molecular weights and degradability). Rational design that integrates multiple design principles simultaneously is challenging to accomplish but may produce more effective polymeric gene carriers. Here we report a new family of rationally designed cationic polymer gene carriers with superior gene transfection efficiency and low cytotoxicity. These are acid-labile branched poly(ortho ester amino alcohol)s (bPOEAAs) with a molecular blueprint analogous to bPEI that embody three design principles about degradability of backbone, chain architecture, and chemistry of functional groups, described as follows.(1)''Acid-labile backbone''. A biodegradable polymer backbone is highly desirable, for it facilitates release of cargo [25], [26] and ensures low cytotoxicity [27]. Various acid-labile bonds (such as acetal and ketal) have been used to construct cationic polymer backbones that degrade in response to the mildly acidic environment of the endosome [28]. Ortho esters are highly sensitive to acidification and hydrolyzes more rapidly than acetal and ketal [29]. Previously, we have reported linear poly(ortho esters) that degrade rapidly at endosomal pH to release plasmid DNA [30], [31]. Here, ortho ester linkages are used to construct bPOEAAs, hoping that acid-triggered backbone degradation would result in high transfection efficiency and low cytotoxicity.(2)''Proper degree of branching''. The degree of branching is known to impact the performance of polymeric gene carriers [32], [33]. Compared with linear PEI, hyper-branched PEI has higher positive charge density and is more effective in condensing DNA into small nanoparticles [34]. However, bPEI is also more toxic than its linear form [35]. Here, a simple epoxide-amine reaction is used to synthesize bPOEAAs with proper degree of branching that would strike an optimal balance between transfection and cytotoxicity.(3)''Proper type of amine''. bPEI contains protonated primary amines that bind DNA strongly, ensuring protection and stability of the polyplexes under physiological conditions [36]. However, secondary and tertiary amines are also necessary, because they serve as ''proton sponges'' with buffering capacity to facilitate endosomal escape and are less toxic than primary amine [37]. Therefore, bPOEAAs are designed to contain optimal fractions of secondary and tertiary amines in the backbone, aiming to maximize the benefit of the ''proton sponge'' effect while minimizing cytotoxicity ''Acid-labile backbone''. A biodegradable polymer backbone is highly desirable, for it facilitates release of cargo [25], [26] and ensures low cytotoxicity [27]. Various acid-labile bonds (such as acetal and ketal) have been used to construct cationic polymer backbones that degrade in response to the mildly acidic environment of the endosome [28]. Ortho esters are highly sensitive to acidification and hydrolyzes more rapidly than acetal and ketal [29]. Previously, we have reported linear poly(ortho esters) that degrade rapidly at endosomal pH to release plasmid DNA [30], [31]. Here, ortho ester linkages are used to construct bPOEAAs, hoping that acid-triggered backbone degradation would result in high transfection efficiency and low cytotoxicity.

DOX-loaded POEUs nanoparticles show greatly improved antitumor efficiency. Over the past few decades, polymeric nanoparticles (NPs) have been widely explored for the delivery of therapeutic agents because of their favorable advantages including prolonged drug circulation duration, enhanced solubility of poorly soluble drugs, and ability to offer protection against pharmaceutical activity and reduce side effect [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. A large variety of synthetic biopolymers have been developed to form polymeric NPs for drug delivery applications [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]. Among these biopolymers, biodegradable polyurethanes are considered as one of the most promising platforms for various biomedical applications including drug delivery and tissue engineering because of their excellent biocompatibility and outstanding physical properties [14], [15], [16], [17]. Generally, biodegradable polyurethanes are prepared by embedded degradable polyesters or polycarbonates into polymer backbones [14], [15], [18], [19], [20]. However, these biodegradable polyurethanes usually display a slow degradation rate. It is worth noting that the drug released from such biodegradable polymeric NPs is blocked and generally incomplete, which often results in compromised potency of drugs in vitro and in vivo [14], [15], [21]. Recently, several groups' research have shown that pH-sensitive polyurethanes display enormous potential in drug delivery applications because of the existence of pH gradient in inflamed tissues, tumor microenvironment and endo/lysosome of cells [22], [23], [24], [25], [26]. In addition, the researchers have demonstrated that the polymeric NPs with accelerated degradation kinetic are beneficial for many drug delivery applications that need different time frames for the release of therapeutic drugs [24], [27]. So far, very little focus has been paid on the preparation of pH-sensitive polyurethanes with a controlled degradation kinetic [24]. Paramonov et al. used to report a library of polyurethanes containing acid-labile dimethyl ketal moiety in the polymer backbone. These polyurethanes-based NPs degraded significantly faster at pH 5.0 than at pH 7.4 with degradation kinetic closely relate to the hydrophobicity of starting polymers. As a result, these polyurethanes display great potential for the delivery of several bioactive agents [24]. As well-known, ortho ester bond is prone to acid cleavage [28]. Several groups have developed a series of ortho ester-based polymeric NPs for the delivery of antitumor drugs, DNA and other bioactive agents [13], [29], [30], [31], [32], [33]. Poly(ortho ester) (POE) is a family of hydrophobic, biocompatible and bio-erodible materials [34], [35]. Researchers have found that the degradation kinetic of POE can be controlled by several factors such as their molecular weight, hydrophobicity, and flexibility of polymer chains [32], [36], [37], [38] Generally, more flexible or hydrophilic POE has easier water penetration and loaded drug release, which is resulted from the accelerated hydrolysis of ortho esters [35], [38]. Thus, we postulate that the introduction of acid-labile ortho ester linkage into polymer main-chains can endow polyurethanes with controlled degradation kinetic and improved drug delivery.
