The families of poly(hydroxyortho esters) such as polyglycolide (PGA), polylactide (PLA), and their copolymers (PLGAs), all biodegradable, are among the most intensively studied synthetic polymers that have found significant use in medical and pharmaceutical fields. Since their first application as suture materials, almost 50 years ago, these materials are used for various reconstruction procedures as scaffolding for three-dimensional cell cultures and transplantation of articular, auricular, nasal, cartilage,1 and intervertebral disk,2 in bone surgery such as fixation devices, for bone regeneration,3-5 tissue engineering,6-8 carriers for delivery of bioactive molecules as well as for drug delivery devices.9-11 As opposed to the initial simple processing procedures of these materials, current studies are extended to knitted stents,12 biodegradable polymer / bioceramic composites scaffold,13-15 nanocomposites,16 nanofibres,17 etc. Largely, this is because of the availability, biocompatibility, biodegradability, and processability of these materials. Initial detailed studies of artifacts made out of poly-α-hydroxyacids, PGA, and PLA, or other biodegradable materials such as polydioxanone, poly(trimethylene carbonate), poly(ethylene glycol), and poly (ε-caprolactone), homopolymers and copolymers, have witnessed their biodegradability18-26 and the absence of significant side effects such as inflammatory reactions, apart from a local pH reduction that results from cleavage of ester bonds and could cause a mild inflammatory influence on tissue.26-32 This implies that the realm of materials' properties can be widened by modification via copolymerization, which provides a number of advantages because the architecture and composition of the biomaterials can be tailored to control their properties.24, 33, 34 The functions of the scaffold in tissue engineering include providing mechanical integrity to the construct to impart dimensional stability, resist deformation because of body forces, and impart impulse to cells growing on the material. Copolymers of glycolide (GA) and lactide [poly(lactide-co-glycolide), PLGA] are amorphous where altering the ratio of PLA to PGA results in significant differences in the compression moduli and degradation times of the scaffolds. One of the limitations of scaffolds fabricated from PGA fibers is the small range of mechanical properties of these meshes. The compression modulus of scaffolds increases linearly with the incorporation of LA units, ranging from less than 1 kPa for PGA to approximately 20 kPa for scaffolds with 68% LA content. Hence, increasing the content of LA increases the compression modulus of the scaffolds by more than 20 folds.14 Furthermore, altering the ratio of LA to GA results in significant changes in adhesion, shape, and proliferation rates of cells seeded onto these scaffolds, since PLA and PGA differ significantly in hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity.35-38 Since one possible use of these materials is as a substrate for growing a layer of living cells, the material can be customized as a hydrogel, that will allow the proper nourishment and proliferation of the layer of living cells, after their attachment and spreading on the surface of the film, owing to the right hydrophobicity.39 Therefore, it is reasonable to hypothesize that combining of hydrophilic poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) with PLA (PLGA) that add dimensional stability and rigidity to scaffolds, may facilitate cell adhesion and additionally alter the process of hydrolysis to these materials. According to everything previously noted, the objective of this study is to examine PLA/PLGA-PVA hydrogels, regarding formulation, hydrophilic/hydrophobic ratio, and consistency against mechanical load, whereas the cell adhesion pliability is tested as well.
Acetylation allowed IS to introduce acetic ester groups while maintaining good fluidity. Acetic ester group interfered with the association of starch hydroxyl groups, improved the flexibility and elasticity of the starch bonding layer, reduced the internal stress at the rubber layer-fibers interface, and improved the adhesion in effect. The introduction of ester groups also increased the interfacial force between the starch and the polyester fibers since the structure of the ester group and the polyester fiber is similar, the affinity with the polyester is high.54, 55 According to the 'similarity and intermiscibility' principle of diffusion theory, the adhesion between polymers of the same polarity is higher. The ester group introduced on the starch macromolecule enhanced the Van der Waals' forces interaction between the IS and the polyester fiber macromolecule, improved the interfacial force between the size rubber layer and the polyester fiber interface for reducing the possibility of interfacial failure, thus the adhesion between starch and polyester fiber was remarkably improved (158.2 to 172.9 N). HEA branches also have the same type of effect, and the ester chain is longer, moreover, it is hydrophilic which increased the flexibility of the glue layer. This was why ISA-g-PHEA (185.6 N) was superior to ISA-g-PAA (178.5 N) and ISA-g-P(AA-co-HEA) (183 N) in the bonding forces to polyester fibers under a similar grafting ratio (3.86% to 4.28%), despite its acceptable advantage, the inferior grafting ratio limits its application. And the relatively high C.V. (10.2%) shows that the stability of adhesive force is worse than that of grafted starch with PAA branches product. What is more, the grafting ratio of 7.37% ISA-g-P(AA-co-HEA) shows excellent adhesion, stability and tensile properties. With the increased grafting ratio (from 4.15% to 8.90%) of ISA-g-P(AA-co-HEA), the bonding forces and percentage of elongation at break gradually increased due to the length of grafted branches and the number of end-group added. It evinced that extending branches can raise the adhesion of starch to polyester fibers. This is because the P (AA-co-HEA) branches grafted to the starch main chain prevent starch hydroxyl groups from binding and hinder the regular placement of amylose in cooked starch aqueous paste due to steric hindrance, and interfere with the phenomenon of starch retrogradation. The steric hindrance also caused the starch molecules to pile up loosely, which provides interior plasticization for the starch adhesive layer to minimize concentrative internal stress near unsaturated areas, the possibility of interface damage was reduced, and the overall bonding fastness was improved, gained better toughness and flexibility. It was beneficial to the cement layer against external friction. Better elongation can intuitively certify that P(AA-co-HEA) branches made the fibers bond more tightly and the bonding layer is more plastic. When a layer consists of a brittle material such as starch, membrane integrity is usually poor and is rather fragile.53 ISA-g-P(AA-co-HEA) possessed oil-water amphiphilic nature due to having both hydrophobic and hydrophilic group, thus has a certain surface activity which was conducive to the spreading and uniform adsorption of the size between the fiber to boost film completeness.
Thermosensitive PCL‐PEG‐PCL hydrogels: Synthesis, characterization, and delivery of proteins Accelerated in vivo degradation of polymers provides a unique strategy in applications of various biomedical polymers. Enzymes, biochemicals, and other biosignals including pH variations can be used as a triggering mechanism for polymer degradation. In particular, reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), super oxide anion (O2•−), hydroxyl radicals (HO•−), and singlet oxygen are common biochemicals in the human body. The ROS level is reported to increase around sites of inflammation, cancers, and several other diseases.1-5 Even a biocompatible polymer such as poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) induces mild inflammation upon implantation in the subcutaneous layer.6, 7 Therefore, incorporation of ROS-sensitive moieties along a polymer backbone can provide accelerated polymer biodegradation kinetics. Several ROS-sensitive polymers have been reported including poly(propylene sulfide), polythioketal, boronic ester polymers, and oxalate-based polymers.8-15 In particular, the oxalate functional groups are degraded into carbon dioxide by H2O2, where the cyclic dioxetanedione was suggested as a reactive intermediate (Figure 1).16 Oxalate-based polymers were also used for ultrasound imaging by taking advantage of enhanced ultrasound signal intensity by the degradation products of carbon dioxide.14 A cancer prodrug conjugated with oxalate was designed to take advantage of the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) as well as oxalate cleavage through increased ROS levels around cancer tissues.17 Recently, we reported fast degradable polycaprolactone (PCL) microspheres by incorporating oxalate groups along the polymers. The PCL microsphere degrades over 2 years. However, oxalate group-incorporated PCL microspheres completely degraded over 2 months in the subcutaneous layer of rats.18

Because of its special qualities, elastomers-a type of polymer with a low modulus and high elasticity-can rapidly return to their initial form following the removal of an external force. Because of these qualities, they are indispensable in both daily life and the economy [1,2,3,4]. Elastomers have been the subject of ongoing research and development to improve their strength, stability, aging resistance, and wear resistance in order to fulfill the ever-increasing performance requirements. However, these advantages make it harder to dispose of the waste products made from conventional elastomers, which pollutes the environment over time [5, 6]. However, the majority of elastomers are derived from poorly sustainable non-renewable fossil fuels. The creation of novel elastomers that are not dependent on fossil fuels has become highly demanded in recent times due to the immense strain imposed by carbon emissions. Bio-based elastomers are a great way to reduce carbon emissions and conserve resources in the elastomer sector since they may be made from natural plants directly or by synthesizing them from bio-based monomers produced from biomass resources. Due to excellent biodegradability, aliphatic polyester became a prominent area of research for environmentally-friendly products. Linear polyesters, such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA), polyglycolide acid (PGA), polycaprolactone (PCL), and their copolymers, have been extensively studied in the field of plastic for many years. And their industrial production is seeing tremendous growth [7,8,9]. Polyesters having a three-dimensional network have gained increasing interest, motivated by these linear polymers [10, 11]. Like vulcanized rubber, the cross-linked network is formed by the incorporation of "star" monomers to create multi-branched chains, enabling the material to rapidly regain its shape when subjected to substantial deformation. Poly (glycerol sebacate) (PGS), polyoctyl citrate (POC), and their copolymers are the primary biodegradable polyester elastomers that have undergone substantial research. The pioneering work is the synthesis of PGS, an in-situ cross-linked polyester elastomer with a three-dimensional network structure and exceptional robustness, conducted by Langer et al. successfully synthesized in 2002 [10, 12]. In 2011, Zhang et al. firstly introduced chemically crosslinked polyester elastomer [13]. Subsequently, many other bio-based elastomers have been created [14, 15]. It is well known that monomers of longer chain are easier to be synthesized to be polyester with higher stability, due to the lower density of ester linkage. For example, PCL and PBS are commercially mature materials, which employ 4- or 6- carbon chain monomer [16], while polyglycolide acid (PGA) with 2-carbon monomer is unstable to hydrolysis and its commercial application is very limited [17]. However, on the other hand, when the goal of our research is to obtain elastomers, the high crystallinity and rigidity due to longer chains becomes a disadvantage. In the cell culture area, not only does the physicochemical properties of the microsphere affect cell growth, but the morphology and porous structure of the microspheres affect cell growth and attachment [6]. Particularly, porous microspheres can be used as dermal fillers. Porous microspheres are low-density, so they will not deposit in the skin. Moreover, the surface topographic properties can lead to differential adhesion, proliferation, growth, and differentiation of inflammatory cells [9]. The role of the surface morphology and internal structure of microspheres in applications has been attracting strong interest. Therefore, the morphology is precisely controlled during the preparation of the microspheres. In recent years, great progress has been made in the preparation of porous and hollow microspheres, including the emulsion solvent evaporation method [10], microfluidic method [11], electrospray method [12], and membrane emulsification method [13]. For the latter three methods, they can well control the thickness and size of the monodispersity of the microspheres. However, the equipment for preparing microspheres by these methods is expensive, and the preparation of microspheres takes a long time. The emulsion solvent evaporation method is a common way to prepare microspheres, which is easy to operate and inexpensive [14]. First, various emulsification methods are used to prepare different types of emulsions (w/o, o/w, w/o/w, o/w/o type emulsions), and then the dispersed phase is solidified by solvent evaporation to remove the solvent [15]. It has been successfully used for designing drug delivery systems such as scaffolds, microspheres, nanospheres, and implants [1, 2]. Along the last two decades, special efforts have been done in the development of in situ forming devices (implants and microspheres) as alternative delivery systems. These systems are injected into the body and once in contact with the physiological fluids, solidify to form a semi-solid depot able to entrap a drug. Some of their advantages are: ease of fabrication, less invasive administration, and less stressful manufacturing conditions for sensitive bioactive molecules [3, 4]. The release profile of the entrapped drug depends on its diffusion through the polymer matrix and/or on the matrix degradation/erosion processes [2, 5]. For this reason, the degradation of PLGA is an important issue to be considered in controlled drug release systems [6]. The erosion of degradable polymers starts with degradation, i.e., the process of chain scission. For biodegradable polymers, chain scission occurs by hydrolysis of the functional groups in an aqueous environment. Then, degradation products such as oligomers and monomers are released from the polymer matrix to the surrounding medium leading to the characteristic mass loss of the erosion process. Hydrolysis starts with the penetration of water into the polymer matrix. When hydrolysis is slow compared to diffusion of water inside the matrix, then the whole polymer matrix is simultaneously eroded. This behavior is known as bulk erosion. In contrast, when hydrolysis is faster than the water uptake, then erosion mainly occurs at the matrix surface. This degradation process is termed as surface erosion. Nevertheless, these two erosion mechanisms are ideal limiting cases that cannot be unambiguously assigned to most polymer degradation processes [7].

Degradable polyester microspheres, recognized for their excellent biocompatibility, controlled drug release capabilities, tunable degradation rates, and ease of fabrication, have become a focal point in bone tissue engineering (BTE) research. (2) PLGA has been used in biomaterials research since the 1970s, and there are now more than 20 PLGA-based biodegradable microspheres on the market, many of which are still in the R&D or clinical trial phase. Poly(d,l-lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) is one of the few biocompatible and biodegradable polymers approved by U.S. Food and Drug Administration for its use in pharmaceutical products or biomedical devices. It has been successfully used for designing drug delivery systems such as scaffolds, microspheres, nanospheres, and implants [1, 2]. Along the last two decades, special efforts have been done in the development of in situ forming devices (implants and microspheres) as alternative delivery systems. These systems are injected into the body and once in contact with the physiological fluids, solidify to form a semi-solid depot able to entrap a drug. Some of their advantages are: ease of fabrication, less invasive administration, and less stressful manufacturing conditions for sensitive bioactive molecules [3, 4]. The release profile of the entrapped drug depends on its diffusion through the polymer matrix and/or on the matrix degradation/erosion processes [2, 5]. For this reason, the degradation of PLGA is an important issue to be considered in controlled drug release systems [6]. The erosion of degradable polymers starts with degradation, i.e., the process of chain scission. For biodegradable polymers, chain scission occurs by hydrolysis of the functional groups in an aqueous environment. Then, degradation products such as oligomers and monomers are released from the polymer matrix to the surrounding medium leading to the characteristic mass loss of the erosion process. Hydrolysis starts with the penetration of water into the polymer matrix. When hydrolysis is slow compared to diffusion of water inside the matrix, then the whole polymer matrix is simultaneously eroded. This behavior is known as bulk erosion. In contrast, when hydrolysis is faster than the water uptake, then erosion mainly occurs at the matrix surface. This degradation process is termed as surface erosion. Nevertheless, these two erosion mechanisms are ideal limiting cases that cannot be unambiguously assigned to most polymer degradation processes [7].

In particular, poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), the biodegradable synthetic aliphatic polyester, has gained extensive attention owing to its excellent biocompatibility, controllable biodegradability, structural stability, and easy processability.7-11 Recently, water-in-oil-in-water (W/O/W) double-emulsion solvent evaporation method involving porogen has been considered as one of the most common methods for fabricating porous PLGA microspheres.12-15 In this method, the W/O/W double emulsions are typically prepared in a two-step emulsification process of first making water-in-oil (W/O) emulsions and then emulsifying of the W/O emulsions in water-containing surfactants. And the porogen added into the double-emulsion template is used as pore-forming agent to achieve porous structures in PLGA microspheres. Although the porous PLGA microspheres can be effectively obtained using W/O/W double-emulsion solvent evaporation method involving porogen, the approach is a relatively complex and time-consuming technique requiring multistep procedures to produce double emulsions and an additional processing step to remove the porogen, which limit the practical, large-scale production of porous PLGA microspheres. Furthermore, the surfactants used to stabilize emulsions often remain in the obtained microspheres, which may result in allergy-like reactions and carcinogenicity.16 Therefore, the facile and large-scale fabrication of porous PLGA microspheres by solvent evaporation from W/O/W double emulsions that would not involve any porogens and surfactants and could be obtained using a one-step emulsification method is highly desired for the biomedical applications.

Based on the provided evidence, citric acid acts as a crosslinking agent in starch-based films through the following mechanisms:

1.  **Forms covalent ester bonds**: Citric acid's carboxylic groups react with hydroxyl groups on starch chains under heat or catalytic conditions, forming intermolecular covalent ester bonds. This crosslinks starch molecules, acting as a chemical bridge between polymer chains [3][9][11][13]. This process reduces hydrophilic groups and introduces hydrophobic ester bonds [9][11][13].

2.  **Restricts chain mobility**: The crosslinks formed by citric acid limit the mobility of starch molecules, decreasing hydrogen bonding between hydroxyl groups in the amorphous regions of starch [5][7][9][13].

3.  **Improves mechanical properties**: At moderate concentrations (e.g., 1-5 wt%), crosslinking enhances tensile strength, modulus (stiffness), and thermal stability by increasing intermolecular interactions and reducing chain mobility [4][9][10][13]. Evidence shows a 5% citric acid concentration is often optimal for improving these properties in starch/PLA/PVA blends [4].

4.  **Concentration-dependent effects**: Low citric acid content (1-3 wt%) primarily promotes crosslinking, increasing stiffness and strength [10][13]. However, higher concentrations (>5 wt%) lead to competing effects:
    *   **Plasticization**: Unreacted citric acid or its degradation products can plasticize the starch, increasing elongation but decreasing tensile strength and stiffness [10].
    *   **Starch degradation**: Excessive citric acid degrades starch chains under processing conditions (e.g., high shear stress during extrusion), producing lower molecular weight fragments and significantly reducing mechanical properties and water resistance [10][13].

5.  **Enhances water resistance**: Crosslinking reduces the number of hydrophilic hydroxyl groups and creates a more restricted network, decreasing water solubility and slowing the deterioration of mechanical properties in water [9][11][13]. However, excessive citric acid counteracts this by promoting degradation [13].

Based on the provided evidence, citric acid acts as a crosslinking agent in starch-based films by forming covalent ester bonds between hydroxyl groups on different starch molecules. This occurs through a reaction mechanism where citric acid, when heated, initially forms a five-membered cyclic anhydride intermediate. This anhydride reacts with starch to form a monoester. Subsequently, a second cyclic anhydride forms and reacts with a hydroxyl group on another starch chain, creating intermolecular crosslinks [1][2].

This crosslinking process:
1.  **Connects starch molecules:** Citric acid acts as a "chemical bridge," forming stable covalent intermolecular ester bonds between hydroxyl groups of starch chains, linking multiple molecules together [4][5][6][7][12].
2.  **Alters material properties:**
    *   **Improves mechanical properties:** Crosslinking increases tensile strength and stiffness/modulus (at optimal concentrations) by enhancing inter-chain interactions and cohesion within the starch matrix [1][2][6][7][9][12][13].
    *   **Reduces hydrophilicity:** Formation of hydrophobic ester bonds replaces hydrophilic hydroxyl groups, decreasing water sensitivity (water absorption and solubility) and improving water resistance [4][5][6][7][9][12][13].
    *   **Enhances thermal stability:** Crosslinking contributes to improved thermal stability of the starch material [8][11][13].
3.  **Has concentration dependency:** Moderate amounts of citric acid effectively crosslink starch, improving mechanical properties and water resistance. However, excessive amounts can lead to starch degradation under processing conditions (especially high-shear extrusion), breaking chains and forming lower molecular weight fragments, which weakens the crosslinked network and degrades mechanical properties while increasing solubility [6][7][9][13].
4.  **Requires thermal activation:** Crosslinking reactions are induced by heat treatment (typically between 90-180 °C) applied either during film formation or as a post-treatment [8][11]. A catalyst like sodium dihydrogen phosphate is sometimes used [11].

CVDs have the highest mortality rate among humans. The result is that research to find an effective treatment for heart disease is needed. Therefore, there is a need to continuously improve in vitro cellular models that will adequately mimic the complex working of cardiac tissue. A conventional 2D culture model using a polystyrene plate does not correspond to cardiac tissue’s complex, oriented, and 3D structure. In the current research, most in vitro models use immature cardiac cells with different morphology and physiology than adult CMs. Therefore, they do not appropriately mimic the cardiac tissue’s in vivo conditions. To imitate in vivo conditions, more and more studies are being conducted on a 3D model using nanofibers, which structural and mechanical are, like heart ECM. Additionally, based on previous studies, nanofibers affect cell arrangement, morphology, proliferation, and maturation [23-35, 43]. Nanofibers are widely used in cardiac in vitro models. However, it is still unknown how nanofibers’ physicochemical properties should be selected, such as the size of diameter, porosity, elasticity, conductivity, and type of biomaterial, to mimic the structure of heart tissue. Nowadays, it is studied how the structure, materials composite, and modification of nanofibers influence cardiac cells adhesion, viability, orientation, and morphology [19-23, 44]. However, few studies compare nanofibers’ effect with different physicochemical properties on cardiac cell functioning [19, 20, 34, 35]. We used alignment nanofibers made of biodegradable synthetic polyester such as PCL and biocompatible with heart tissue synthetic polymer such as PU fabricated using the SBS method. The SBS method was chosen because it is more efficient, cheaper, and safer than the commonly used ES technique. In addition, SBS allows to obtain nanofibers with structural and mechanical properties similar to the native ECM than the properties of nanofibers obtained after production by the ES method [14-19]. We have determined how different nanofibers ‘properties influenced heart cells’ orientation, morphology, viability, and maturation. In addition, it was investigated whether these properties had a different effect on different heart cell types taken from the heart ventricle or atrium. Scaffolds used in the TE of cardiac cells should have adequate elasticity because it impacts the morphology and contraction of myocardial cells. The value of Young’s modulus of the myocardium is in the range of 70-160 kPa (elasticity depends on the part of the heart) [45, 46]. The exact values vary with the location of the heart tissue, as well as the patient’s age and state of health. Literature sources indicate that materials with Young’s modulus ranging from 20 kPa to 92 MPa were used [45-47], and nanofibers whose elasticity was in this range were biocompatible with cardiac cells. However, which elasticity is the most appropriate for the TE of cardiac cells is still unknown. In this research, nanofibrous mats have four different elasticities (PCL (1) > PCL (2) ∼ PU (1) > PU (2)) (figure 2). However, significant differences were not observed in the phenotype of cardiac cells depending on the elasticity of these nanofibers. Such differences were observed in the case of the size of nanofibers. The structure of the ECM in the human cardiac tissue is built by fibers whose diameter is up to 300 nm [48, 49], and the most common range of diameter of nanofibers used in TE for cardiac cells is 200−700 nm [50, 51]. For comparison, the PCL and PU nanofibers were produced in two diameters similar to the diameter of fibers building the ECM heart in vivo. The PCL (1) and PU (1) nanofibers had a c.a. 250 nm diameter. On the other hand, PCL (2) and PU (2) nanofibers were around 500 nm. For all types of nanofibers, the increase in proliferation varied depending on the cell line. For H9c2 cells, the greatest increase in proliferation was observed on PCL (1) nanofibrous mats, for HL-1 on PCL (2), and for HCM on PU (2) nanofibers. Based on this, it is difficult to conclude which of the tested nanofibrous materials is the most universal for culturing different types of cell lines. It is worth mentioning that H9c2 are embryonic cells, HL-1 are immortalized cells that can proliferate indefinitely. At the same time, HCM are primary cells whose proliferation stops after a limited number of cell divisions, which may affect the results we obtained. Based on the results, it was concluded that PCL and PU nanofiber mats have no negative effect on the culture of cardiac cells, can stimulate their proliferation, and can be used to culture various types of cardiac cells [19, 27].

Effect of biodegradation on PHAs-based blends and composites In general, stable composites are developed by shaping PHB polymers with suitable plasticizers, compatibilizers, stabilizers, fillers, and matrixes. In comparison to the original polymer, the composite may therefore have altered physicochemical properties and a faster rate of degradation [163]. PHB's functional group, crystallinity, hydrophobicity, and morphological characteristics all have an impact on how quickly it degrades in biological systems. Therefore, mcl-PHAs that has low crystallinity and low Tm degrades more rapidly than scl-PHAs that has higher crystallinity and Tm. The factors that affect the biodegradation of polymer blends include the blend's composition, surface roughness of the blend, miscibility between components, and phase structure (i.e., crystalline or amorphous) [89]. The entire biodegradability of the composite materials can be ensured by selecting a biodegradable polymer to be included with PHB in the blends. However, the second polymer's effects on the morphostructural, thermal, and mechanical characteristics of the PHB blends could potentially affect the degree of biodegradability [188]. The majority of biodegradable polymers break down into components that are safe for the environment, like biomass, CO2, CH4, and water. Nevertheless, this is only possible in controlled industrial composting environments or physiological settings [189]. In natural environments, a variety of chemical-physical (oxygen availability, temperature, pH, light, humidity), and biological (microbial population and enzyme types) factors influence the biodegradation of biodegradable polymers. Because of this, the rate of biodegradation and the profile of degradation might also differ greatly, possibly lasting a long time in the environment. As a result, biopolymers and their composites may weather and eventually generate biodegradable microplastics [190]. Few biopolymers such as PHAs and TPS degrade in a wide spectrum of controlled and uncontrolled environmental circumstances, but the majority (PLA, PCL, and PBS) degrade in a more limited range of environmental conditions [191]. There are very few biodegradation investigations of PHA blends and composites in natural environments (marine and soil), mostly due to the scarcity of alternative bio-based polymers that exhibit biodegradation, for instance, PLA. Blends of PHA and PLA ought to improve the biodegradation of PHA components by reducing their crystallinity. However, because of the unfavourable temperatures, virgin PLA is not easily biodegradable in soil or marine water. As per ASTM D5988-12, a PHA/PLA blend was observed to deteriorate to 99% within 176 days; however, the composition and existence of additives were not determined [192]. PHB absorbs more water than PLA does, and the incorporation of PHB enhanced this absorption. After the first three weeks, the weight change value of PLA is practically constant, suggesting that the PLA samples might not decompose at ambient temperature. Pure PHB exhibits a rapid drop in weight over the course of 8 weeks as a result of biodegradation. The induction period for the PLA/PHB 50/50 and 25/75 blends lasts for approximately 14 weeks, with more weight reduction occurring with the blend containing more PHB. The weight of the PLA/PHB 75/25 blend gradually dropped after week 23 due to slow biodegradation. Additionally, it is seen that PHB and PLA have different mechanisms for degradation: PHB is degraded from the sample surface, whereas PLA degradation occurs throughout the entire sample. PHB is mostly broken down by surface-attacked enzymes, whereas PLA is primarily broken down by a non-enzymatic hydrolysis that is substantially temperature-dependent [125]. In one study conducted earlier by Kumagai and Doi [193] showed the ability of PHB/PCL, PHB/PBA, and PHB/PVA blends to biodegrade. An extracellular PHB from Alcaligenes faecalis T1 that has been depolymerized underwent enzymatic film breakdown at 37°C and a pH of 7.4. The polymer blended with PHB affected the mixtures' enzyme degradation patterns. In the case of PHB/PCL, a quick weight loss was seen, however with increasing weight fractions of PBA or PVA, the weight loss of PHB/PBA or PHB/PVA reduced. A biodegradation study was conducted on PHB/PCL composite, in accordance with the laboratory-scale composting test method. After 21 days of composting, the composite sample degraded completely. Furthermore, it has been noted that as blends' PCL content rises, biodegradation rates rise quickly. This acceleration could be triggered by surface alteration or a decrease in the samples' overall crystallinity [194].
The rapid advancement of technology and growing industries has resulted in many advancements in the human standard of living throughout the world; however, this has also fed the growing problem of industrial waste. Many sources of this waste exist, from manufacturing industries, electrical device production, construction, and other sectors, while treatments and sustainability efforts are often lagging. Throughout the world, more than 80% of this waste is dumped or stored instead of recycled, increasing pollution levels and threatening ecosystems and human health. A very large percentage of this waste are various thermoplastics [Hapuwatte et al 2016, Marks et al 2020, Neo et al 2021]. This is one of the most important and urgent thrusts toward more sustainable manufacturing and production methods to minimize the negative impact of production while maintaining and increasing technological innovation and advancement [Jambeck et al 2017, Mohammed et al 2018, Ghimire et al 2021, Lee et al 2021, Taghavi et al 2021]. This issue is becoming even more urgent due to the growing scarcity of resources in the past few years because of natural resource depletion, rapid lifestyle changes, growing demand, and growing socioeconomic problems throughout the world. The development and refinement of 3D printing processes in recent years offers much toward more sustainable production, as it is a fundamentally low-waste manufacturing approach also easily handles recycled materials, unlike many traditional thermoplastic manufacturing processes [Gebler et al 2014, Neumüller et al 2014, Faludi et al 2015, Al-Meslemi et al 2018, Ntousia & Fudos 2019, Shahrubudin et al 2019, Hossain & Liao 2020, Khalid & Peng 2021, Ruckstuhl et al 2020, Dharnidharka et al 2021, Chadha et al 2022]. Many materials which would otherwise not be cost-effective to recycle can be easily used with these processes in the form of plastic powder (using a basic chopper or grinder) and extruded filament [McAlister & Wood 2014, Ford & Despeisse 2016, Lundbäck, Lindgren 2017, Yang et al 2017, Colorado et al 2020, Shuaib et al 2021]. The most commonly used (and by far lowest cost) 3D printing technology is based on material extrusion and is often known as fused filament fabrication (FFF) (or, alternatively, fused deposition modeling (FDM)). For this process, waste thermoplastic materials can be chopped up and extruded as filaments and used directly. In many cases, especially if the resulting part does not need to be made from a specific material, the waste plastics can be mixed, reducing the cost and labor involved in recycling the waste. Additives such as dyes, powder, chopped fibers, and other things can also easily be added, increasing the usefulness or value of recycled plastic. One of the most useful and promising materials commonly processed using FFF is polylactic acid (PLA), a biodegadable thermoplastic with excellent mechanical properties made from biomass such as corn and sugar cane. However, PLA does have one major disadvantage: It has been observed to degrade quickly for some applications [Nampoothiri et al 2010, Elsawy et al 2017, Kakanuru & Pochiraju 2020, Kumar and Kumar 2021]. The question of how much and in what ways it degrades is still open and how severe the effect is is not known. If it can be successfully recycled with little or no degradation in the needed properties, it would expand its usefulness as a standard industrial engineering plastic that can be used within an effective circular production economy [Jambeck et al 2018, Burkhart & Aurich 2015, Freitas et al 2016, Tang et al 2016, Liu et al 2016, Jiang et al 2019, Niaki et al 2019,Wang et al 2020, Pasricha & Greeninger 2018] (figure 1). PCL is a semicrystalline aliphatic polyester,13 which is biodegradable and nontoxic.14 It is synthesized from ring-opening polymerization of caprolactone and is generally decomposed through the enzyme activity.13 Also, the solubility of PCL in a wide range of organic solvents was reported previously.15 The polymer also has some unusual properties which have not been observed in other aliphatic polyesters: Its glass transition temperature is low, which makes it be in the rubbery state at room temperature, and its thermal stability is higher than that of other tested aliphatic polyesters.16 Despite its outstanding properties, limited studies have been conducted on the application of PCL in membrane filtration. For instance, Aslan et al.17 fabricated poly(d,l-lactic acid) (PDLLA)/PCL blend and membrane and observed a lower elastic modulus for the blend in comparison with that for PDLLA. They investigated neither the biodegradation nor performance of the membrane. In another research, Temtem et al.18 fabricated a membrane by blending PCL and polysulfone (PSU). They observed a higher water flux with increasing PCL content because of increased porosity.18 In contrast to the advantageous properties of PCL, the reasons for the limited survey on PCL application in membrane processes are its poor processability19 and high price.20 Moreover, previous studies reported a low biodegradability for PCL due to its high crystalline property,14 as well as the relative hydrophobicity of this polymer.21 The mentioned drawbacks can be addressed if it is blended with a proper biodegradable polymer.

As the amount of cellulose added to the PCL matrix is increased, small decreases in Tonset values are observed. However, the temperature at which 10% NC/PCL composite film starts to degrade is the same as that of pure PCL with 333 °C and higher than other composites. The reason for this is thought to be that a homogenous distribution of nanocellulose in the prepared films is obtained. In contrast, the decline of Tonset after inclusion of MCC may be due to the the reduced formation of thermally stable interface between MCC and polymer matrix under the agglomeration of high amount MCC. Looking at the point at which the ISO-NC-added PCL films begin to degrade, there is a decline compared to other films. The imperfect purification during preparation of modified nanocellulose may lead to ISO-NC particles containing certain amount of thermally unstable noncellulosic material that weaken the inherent thermal resistance of NC [23]. Although for other composite systems containing cellulose fillers it has been observed an improved thermal stability of the cellulose fraction in compatibilized composites, Visakh et al. More importantly, the ester group (-COO-) in PCL allows it to be completely degraded under the action of microorganisms. For example, PCL can be used as a surgical suture, fracture fixation device, and missing repair of the chest wall in medical treatment [2, 3]. Polycaprolactone has crystalline properties, it takes some time to degrade and has good drug permeability. It can be used as a drug carrier to achieve a sustained release effect. Extrusion based methods such as Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF) and Fused Granular Fabrication (FGF) are widely adopted for their simplicity, material efficiency, and low operating costs. Both use a heated nozzle to deposit thermoplastic material layer by layer [3]. While FFF uses filament, FGF processes polymer granules, enabling faster deposition. Studies show that FGF can match FFF’s mechanical performance, especially when using recycled PLA [4]. Recent studies have also demonstrated that FGF systems operating with PLA granules can achieve consistent tensile strength across a wide range of infill levels, with improved eco-efficiency at lower infill densities and higher printing speeds [5]. Polylactic acid (PLA) is one of the most widely used thermoplastics in extrusion-based 3D printing due to its low processing temperature, biodegradability, and availability [2]. Its mechanical behavior is highly sensitive to process parameters, making it suitable for evaluating the effects of process parameters and post-processing. Although studied in FGF systems, PLA remains less explored than filament-based processes, especially regarding parameter interactions and thermal post-processing. However, extrusion-based methods such as FFF and FGF face limitations including weak interlayer bonding, internal porosity, and pronounced anisotropy. These issues make parameter optimization critical for improving strength and structural performance [6]. Thermal conditioning is a widely used thermal post-processing method for improving the mechanical performance of FFF-printed PLA parts. By relieving internal stress and increasing crystallinity, it enhances tensile strength and interlayer adhesion, key factors in reducing anisotropic effects. For PLA, optimal thermal conditioning, typically occurs between the glass transition temperature and the cold crystallization temperature (Tcc ≈ 110 °C), with tensile strength improvements reported up to 42% and crystallinity increases up to 34% [7,8,9,10]. However, overexposure to heat or improper temperature control can result in warping, dimensional shrinkage, or loss of structural enhancements. Infill geometry also influences the response to thermal conditioning, with honeycomb structures showing the most consistent improvement [11].
Fused filament fabrication (FFF), one of the most versatile additive manufacturing (AM) technologies, can prepare complicated, functional and personalized polymer products based on three-dimensional digital models in a layer-by-layer way. It possesses advantages over other polymer-based AM techniques, including simplicity of the working principle and good compatibility with more kinds of feedstock materials [1,2]. However, most FFF-printed parts exhibit weak and anisotropic mechanical properties, compared with their counterparts fabricated with traditional processing methods [3,4]. Specifically, polymer parts along the build direction often possess weaker strength than that perpendicular to the build direction. This is mainly a result of poor weld interface between adjacent deposited strands in FFF-printed parts, induced by the highly non-isothermal profile intrinsic to the FFF process [5]. Especially for semicrystalline polymer materials, the interfacial welding is accompanied with the occurrence of crystallization, leading to complicated inter-filament microstructure and therefore unexpected mechanical properties for the FFF-printed parts [[6], [7], [8], [9]]. At present, FFF is used as a rapid prototyping method, rather than a manufacture technique to prepare final parts for industrial application. Recently, extensive efforts have been devoted to producing mechanically robust FFF-printed parts. One option is to optimize printing parameters including nozzle temperature and platform temperature [[10], [11], [12], [13]], by governing the thermal history of the deposited strands [13,14]. For example, raising nozzle temperature increased the interfacial tensile strength of acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS) and poly (lactic acid) (PLA) parts by 10 MPa and 12 MPa, respectively [15,16]. Correspondingly, the mechanical anisotropy for these FFF-printed parts was reduced essentially [13]. Another route is post- or in-process heat treatments to facilitate molecular interdiffusion across the weld interface and/or enhance the degree of crystallinity, thus improving the mechanical properties of FFF-printed parts [[17], [18], [19], [20], [21]]. Besides those printing-related methods, some researchers have employed polymer modification, i.e. preparing polymer/polymer blends or polymer/filler composites, to improve the mechanical properties of FFF-printed parts. Blending plasticizer or low-molecular-weight polymer with the printing materials is found to significantly enhance the interfacial weld strength of FFF-printed samples, by balancing the plasticizing effect and the entanglement with the additives at the interface [[22], [23], [24], [25]]. Gao et al. utilized polyethylene glycol (PEG) with three distinct molecular weights (4k, 8k and 20k) to improve the interfacial weld strength of PLA parts. PEG-8k showed the best enhancement effect on the weld strength among these additives, resulting in an increase of 22% than that of neat PLA [23]. Levenhagen et al. developed the bimodal blend of PLA as the feedstock material and found that the tensile strength of the weld interface in the FFF-printed specimens was increased by 100%, since the low-molecular-weight PLA enhanced both molecular diffusion and entanglement across adjacent strands [24,26]. Notably, these low-molecular-weight additives tended to result in 13%-32% reduction in the mechanical strength for the FFF parts along the deposited filament, owing to their plasticization effect on the printing materials [23,24].
Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF), also known as Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM), is a popular AM technology valued for its simplicity, low costs, and ability to produce complex geometries efficiently and affordably [[8], [9], [10]]. The flexibility and minimal material waste of FFF makes it an excellent choice for prototyping and small-scale production [11,12]. Nevertheless, the layer-by-layer structure of FFF-printed parts can lead to anisotropic mechanical properties, where the strength differs across various loading directions. Optimizing printing parameters and post-processing techniques is crucial to enhancing the mechanical properties of FFF-produced parts [[13], [14], [15]]. Adjusting parameters such as layer thickness, nozzle temperature, infill density, and raster angle play a significant role in boosting the durability and performance of the printed parts [[16], [17], [18]]. Additionally, FFF process parameters not only impact mechanical performance but also affect production time, weight, and bonding quality. For instance, higher printing speeds reduce manufacturing time but may compromise interlayer adhesion and surface quality. Similarly, increasing infill density enhances mechanical strength but results in longer print times and increased material usage, while adjusting nozzle temperature optimizes bonding between layers by controlling material flow and adhesion [[19], [20], [21]]. Furthermore, studies have shown that post-processing methods like annealing can further improve these properties [[22], [23], [24]], as this process enhances crystallinity and strengthens interlayer adhesion, leading to superior mechanical performance in the final product [25]. Poly Lactic Acid (PLA) is a biodegradable plastic widely used in biomedical applications, food packaging, and textiles. Despite its versatility, PLA's low glass transition temperature (Tgl) and slow crystallization kinetics limit its mechanical and thermal properties. These characteristics result in poor heat resistance and limited load-bearing capacity under stress, restricting PLA's use in certain engineering applications [26,27]. Thermal annealing can enhance PLA's crystallization to address these limitations. By carefully controlling the annealing time and temperature, the crystal structure of PLA can be improved, leading to increased mechanical strength [28,29]. The final performance of PLA depends on crystal phase transitions and the degree of crystallization, as appropriate annealing conditions can transform PLA into a semi-crystalline polymer with higher strength [30,31]. For instance, annealing at 80 °C can significantly enhance PLA's crystal structure, while temperatures between 100 °C and 120 °C can optimize its mechanical properties by inducing the α′-α phase transition [32]. During annealing, PLA's amorphous regions are reorganized into more stable crystalline structures, which can significantly improve mechanical properties such as tensile and flexural strength, hardness, and impact resistance. This paragraph summarizes the studies in the literature on the thermal annealing and crystallization properties of PLA. Kartal and Kaptan [33] demonstrated that annealing PLA at 85 °C for 90 min resulted in a 48 % increase in tensile strength and a 78 % increase in elastic modulus. Pazhamannil et al. [34] reported that annealing PLA at 95 °C for 60 min improved the ultimate tensile strength by 25.26 % and compressive strength by 21.87 %. Chen et al. [35] analyzed the crystal phase transitions of PLA after annealing and found a 25 % increase in crystallinity. Jayanth et al. [24] stated that annealing at 80 °C increased the tensile strength of PLA by 20 % and fracture toughness by 15 % but resulted in a 10 % decrease in elasticity. Windheim et al. [36] investigated the effects of annealing on the crystallization and porosity of PLA, showing that the crystallization rate increased from 4.1 % to 11.7 % at 80 °C and reached 43.6 % at 95 °C. However, despite this increase in crystallinity, no significant improvement in mechanical strength was observed. This was attributed to insufficient co-crystallization between filament layers, indicating that enhanced crystallinity was limited by weak interlayer bonding. Zisopol et al. [37] demonstrated that annealing at 75 °C for 3 h increased the tensile strength of PLA by 30 % and flexural strength by 15 %. Luna et al. [39] reported that annealing at 80 °C and 90 °C increased the crystallinity index to 33 % and improved the elastic modulus by 26-51 %. Stojkovic et al. [40] examined the effects of layer thickness and annealing parameters on PLA's tensile strength and dimensional accuracy, finding that a layer thickness of 0.1 mm and annealing at 90 °C for 60 min yielded the best results. Wach et al. [41] indicated that annealing at 85 °C and 95 °C increased the flexural strength of PLA by 17 % and 11 %, respectively, and raised the degree of crystallinity. Behzadnasab et al. [42] emphasized that annealing can negatively affect the mechanical properties of PLA; thus, careful selection of parameters is necessary.
Polylactic acid (PLA) is widely used in fused filament fabrication (FFF) due to its biocompatibility and low cost, but its inherent brittleness and limited mechanical strength restrict its application in load-bearing and structural components. Reinforcing PLA with nanofillers such as carbon fiber (CF), graphene (Gr), and multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) offers a promising route to overcome these limitations, yet the combined influence of build parameters and reinforcement type remains underexplored. In this study, PLA composites were fabricated via FFF with systematic variation of raster orientation (RO), layer height (LH), and print speed (PS), and their tensile, compressive, and flexural properties were evaluated. Among the reinforcements, PLA-MWCNT composites demonstrated the highest compressive strength (121.25 MPa at 0° RO, 0.1 mm LH, 30 mm/s PS), while PLA-CF composites exhibited superior tensile performance, and PLA-Gr composites offered balanced mechanical behavior. To predict and optimize these outcomes, machine learning (ML) models-Linear Regression, Random Forest Regression, and Extreme Gradient Boosting Regression-were employed, with XGBR achieving the highest accuracy (R2 up to 0.99). This integrated experimental-computational framework identifies reinforcement-parameter combinations most suitable for real-world applications such as lightweight automotive components while also highlighting the need for larger datasets to further strengthen ML-driven predictions. Additive manufacturing (AM), commonly referred to as 3D printing, has transformed modern manufacturing by enabling the precise creation of complex, customized, and lightweight components [1, 2]. This layer-by-layer process begins with a digital model, which is sliced into layers and converted into machine instructions [3]. Among various AM techniques, fused filament fabrication (FFF) has gained prominence due to its simplicity [4, 5], cost-effectiveness [6], and adaptability [7]. In FFF, thermoplastic filament is heated to a semi-liquid state and extruded through a nozzle onto a build platform [8, 9]. The extruder moves along predefined paths, depositing material layer by layer until the object is fully formed.
Additive manufacturing (AM), widely known as 3D printing, has emerged as a transformative technology in the manufacturing sector due to its ability to produce complex geometries, reduced material wastage, and cost-effective small-batch production [1]. Among the various AM techniques, Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF) has gained significant attention for fabricating thermoplastic-based components, particularly due to its simplicity, affordability, and adaptability for a wide range of materials [2]. Despite these advantages, the mechanical properties of FFF-produced components often lag behind those manufactured using conventional methods, primarily due to issues such as weak interlayer adhesion and void formation [3]. Addressing these limitations has become a focal point for researchers, with one promising avenue being the incorporation of reinforcing fibers to enhance mechanical performance [4]. Continuous carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) have demonstrated exceptional potential in overcoming the mechanical limitations of FFF-printed parts [5]. These composites leverage the high strength-to-weight ratio and stiffness of continuous carbon fibers, which, when embedded into a thermoplastic matrix such as polylactic acid (PLA), yield components suitable for applications in aerospace, automotive, and structural engineering [6, 7]. PLA, a biodegradable and environmentally friendly thermoplastic, further enhances the appeal of these composites by aligning with global sustainability goals [8]. The integration of continuous fibers has shown to significantly improve tensile strength and modulus, making it a preferred choice for advanced composite fabrication [9]. Process parameters, such as line width and layer thickness, play a crucial role in determining the mechanical properties of FFF-printed CFRP components [3]. Variations in these parameters influence fiber alignment, interlayer bonding, and overall part density, directly impacting tensile properties. For instance, optimizing line width can enhance the fiber-matrix interface, while layer thickness adjustments affect the interlaminar strength and porosity [10]. Previous studies have emphasized the need for systematic exploration of these parameters to achieve composites with tailored mechanical properties [6]. One effective approach to achieve such optimization is the application of the Taguchi method, which provides a robust statistical framework for analyzing and optimizing process parameters. It becomes possible to systematically identify the optimal combination of line width and layer thickness by employing this method, minimizing variability and enhancing the mechanical performance of the composites. Optimization plays a crucial role in additive manufacturing, where small changes in process parameters can lead to significant variations in mechanical properties and production quality [11]. Effective optimization not only improves part performance but also reduces material waste, production time, and costs, making it an integral aspect of advancing additive manufacturing technologies [9, 12].
The incorporation of FFF-printed components within industries has encountered limited acceptance thus far. This hesitancy arises primarily from a notable discrepancy in the mechanical attributes of these parts when compared to conventionally manufactured injection moulded counterparts [5]. The suboptimal performance of FFF-printed components frequently arises from the selection of polymeric base materials primarily chosen based on their rheological properties to facilitate the extrusion process, rather than choosing materials that possess superior mechanical properties [6]. Furthermore, the fundamental nature of the FFF process, characterized by the sequential deposition of layers, significantly influences the final mechanical properties of the printed parts [7]. The inherent layer-by-layer deposition in FFF, generally fails to achieve complete interlayer diffusion, resulting in pores and leading to poor mechanical performance and pronounced anisotropy [8]. The phenomenon of interlayer diffusion is predominantly influenced by two key factors: the properties of the filament material and a range of processing parameters inherent to the fabrication process. These parameters include layer thickness, nozzle diameter, extrusion temperature, build orientation, infill pattern and infill density, raster angle and speed of deposition [9,10,11]. Several experimental studies have been done previously with an aim to improve the mechanical properties of the FFF-printed parts by optimizing these mentioned parameters. Rezaeian et al. [12] investigated the influence of printing speed on the tensile as well as fracture strength of FFF-printed ABS, concluding highest level of printing speed of 70 mm/s responsible for maximum elongation and fracture resistance. A study by Gopi Mohan et al. [13] examined the effect of raster angle on flexural, impact and compressive specimens of FFF-printed PLA material. While Shergill et al. [14] explored the influence of layer thickness on both ABS and PLA material and came to the conclusion that mechanical properties decreased with increasing layer thickness. This layer thickness parameter has been extensively studied by various researchers to investigate its impact on both mechanical and geometrical characteristics [15, 16]. Layer thickness, defined as the thickness of the deposited layer during fabrication, significantly influences fabrication time, the thermal cycles the specimen undergoes, and the residual stress within the specimen [17]. Consequently, numerous parametric optimization studies have been undertaken, utilizing various experimental designs (DoE) such as Central Composite Design (CCD), Box-Behnken Design (BBD), and Taguchi methods. These approaches facilitate systematic experimentation while reducing the number of experimental runs required [18]. Layer thickness has been consistently employed as a key variable in these studies, underscoring its significant impact on enhancing mechanical properties. Beyond layer thickness, other process parameters have also been extensively studied. Kafshgar et al. Additive manufacturing, a key driver of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, has redefined production processes by introducing unparalleled design and fabrication flexibility [1], [2]. Additive manufacturing, also commonly known as 3D printing, enables the creation of intricate structures while significantly minimizing material waste [3]. According to the ISO/ASTM 52900 standard, additive manufacturing encompasses seven distinct techniques [4]. Among these, Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF) is the most widely used materials extrusion-based method for processing thermoplastic polymers [5]. FFF operates by heating and extruding polymer filaments, which are systematically deposited in layers to build the desired structure [6]. Various thermoplastics, including acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) [7], [8], polycarbonate [9], and polylactic acid (PLA) [10], [11], are commonly employed in this process. Among these thermoplastic polymers, PLA is the most widely adopted polymer in extrusion-based AM due to its low cost [12], ease of processing [13], and biodegradability [14], [15]. Derived from renewable feedstocks such as corn starch or sugarcane, PLA represents a sustainable alternative to petroleum-based polymers such as ABS [11]. Its widespread use in research and industry makes it a benchmark material for evaluating the performance of AM process models. However, PLA also presents unique challenges, such as sensitivity to processing conditions, thermal degradation at high extrusion temperatures, and variable mechanical performance depending on print settings, which underscore the importance of predictive modeling. Furthermore, PLA is particularly favored for its versatility, making it a preferred material across multiple industries such as biomedicine [16], aerospace [17], [18], agriculture [13], [19], and automotive manufacturing [20]. Due to the widespread applications of PLA in various industries, its Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS) is a critical performance factor. Manufacturers can precisely regulate and enhance PLA’s UTS by systematically analyzing and adjusting process parameters, ensuring tailored mechanical properties for specific applications. A wide range of studies has investigated the effect of various process parameters on the strength of additively manufactured PLA. Lanzotti et al. [21] explored the impact of raster angle on the UTS of PLA fabricated via the FFF method. Their results illustrated that increasing the raster angle leads to a reduction in UTS. Lokesh et al. [22] investigated how the layer thickness impacts the UTS of additively manufactured parts. Their findings indicated that the higher the layer thickness, the lower the UTS. Tang et al. [23] examined the influences of printing speed and nozzle temperature, observing that while faster printing speeds enhance strength, nozzle temperature follows a nonlinear trend, initially increasing strength but decreasing it at higher temperatures. Rajpurohit and Dave [24] assessed how layer thickness, nozzle diameter, and raster angle affect UTS, concluding that larger nozzle diameters increase UTS, while thicker layers and greater raster angles reduce it. Khatwani and Srivastava [25] analyzed the effects of bed temperature, layer thickness, and nozzle diameter on UTS, finding that higher bed temperatures and larger nozzle diameters improve UTS, but thicker layers lower it. Chacón et al. [26] investigated feed rate, layer thickness, and building orientation, with results indicating that the lowest value of UTS is obtained in upright orientations and improves with slower feed rates and thicker layers. Chokshi et al. [27] examined how the perimeter number and infill geometry impact UTS, identifying these two process parameters as both effective. Maguluri et al. [28] demonstrated that higher nozzle temperatures and increased infill density improve UTS, while faster printing speeds result in lower UTS. Hanon et al. [29] focused on layer thickness and building orientation, showing that the highest value of UTS is obtained in on-edge orientations, with thinner layers enhancing these properties. Gonabadi et al. [30] and Yu et al. [31] evaluated the effects of infill density and infill pattern on the UTS of PLA components. Their results illustrated that the infill pattern has a lesser effect on the UTS compared to the effect of infill density. Murugan et al. [32] and Huynh et al. [33] reinforced these findings and provided further insight into the influence of printing temperature. Naveed [34] found the best raster orientation for achieving strong PLA components via FFF. Behzadnasab et al. [35] found that while higher nozzle temperatures improve UTS, annealing has an adverse effect. These studies collectively highlight the critical role of process parameters in determining the tensile strength of PLA, emphasizing the importance of efficient and cost-effective methods for accurately predicting UTS while minimizing material waste.

Fused filament fabrication (FFF), one of the most versatile additive manufacturing (AM) technologies, can prepare complicated, functional and personalized polymer products based on three-dimensional digital models in a layer-by-layer way. It possesses advantages over other polymer-based AM techniques, including simplicity of the working principle and good compatibility with more kinds of feedstock materials [1,2]. However, most FFF-printed parts exhibit weak and anisotropic mechanical properties, compared with their counterparts fabricated with traditional processing methods [3,4]. Specifically, polymer parts along the build direction often possess weaker strength than that perpendicular to the build direction. This is mainly a result of poor weld interface between adjacent deposited strands in FFF-printed parts, induced by the highly non-isothermal profile intrinsic to the FFF process [5]. Especially for semicrystalline polymer materials, the interfacial welding is accompanied with the occurrence of crystallization, leading to complicated inter-filament microstructure and therefore unexpected mechanical properties for the FFF-printed parts [[6], [7], [8], [9]]. At present, FFF is used as a rapid prototyping method, rather than a manufacture technique to prepare final parts for industrial application. Recently, extensive efforts have been devoted to producing mechanically robust FFF-printed parts. One option is to optimize printing parameters including nozzle temperature and platform temperature [[10], [11], [12], [13]], by governing the thermal history of the deposited strands [13,14]. For example, raising nozzle temperature increased the interfacial tensile strength of acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS) and poly (lactic acid) (PLA) parts by 10 MPa and 12 MPa, respectively [15,16]. Correspondingly, the mechanical anisotropy for these FFF-printed parts was reduced essentially [13]. Another route is post- or in-process heat treatments to facilitate molecular interdiffusion across the weld interface and/or enhance the degree of crystallinity, thus improving the mechanical properties of FFF-printed parts [[17], [18], [19], [20], [21]]. Besides those printing-related methods, some researchers have employed polymer modification, i.e. preparing polymer/polymer blends or polymer/filler composites, to improve the mechanical properties of FFF-printed parts. Blending plasticizer or low-molecular-weight polymer with the printing materials is found to significantly enhance the interfacial weld strength of FFF-printed samples, by balancing the plasticizing effect and the entanglement with the additives at the interface [[22], [23], [24], [25]]. Gao et al. utilized polyethylene glycol (PEG) with three distinct molecular weights (4k, 8k and 20k) to improve the interfacial weld strength of PLA parts. PEG-8k showed the best enhancement effect on the weld strength among these additives, resulting in an increase of 22% than that of neat PLA [23]. Levenhagen et al. developed the bimodal blend of PLA as the feedstock material and found that the tensile strength of the weld interface in the FFF-printed specimens was increased by 100%, since the low-molecular-weight PLA enhanced both molecular diffusion and entanglement across adjacent strands [24,26]. Notably, these low-molecular-weight additives tended to result in 13%-32% reduction in the mechanical strength for the FFF parts along the deposited filament, owing to their plasticization effect on the printing materials [23,24].

Historically, the high cost of PLA production limited its use to the specialty biomedical niches such as sutures and drug delivery devices due to its biodegradability and biocompatibility.6 Presently technological innovations have slightly decreased PLA production cost while the recent increasing crude oil and natural gas prices has conversely increased the cost of traditional petroleum derived plastics, enhancing PLA economic competitiveness.6 More recently, PLA has been used as packaging materials for food and consumer goods (transparent bottles, meat trays, bags, films, etc.), with the polymer typically discarded after use. These applications benefit from their ability to decompose relatively quickly in landfill or compost environments. Unfortunately, PLA has not been used extensively beyond these areas due to its brittleness and lower impact resistance at room temperature,1, 2 resulting in splitting and other handling problems during sheet manufacture.8, 10-12 The necessity for improvement in its impact strength and toughness, which would eliminate the processing and handling deficiencies, precedes the possibility for widespread utilization and substitution for commodity plastics. The toughening of PLA includes blending with other polymers,5-7, 9-12 an exceptional method that is industrially relevant.13 Blending of PLA with rubbery polymers, as previously mentioned, has predominantly emphasized biomedical applications, resulting in the use of biodegradable and biocompatible polymers such as poly(vinyl alcohol), poly(ε-caprolactone), poly(ethylene glycol), polyhydroxyalkanoate, and poly(butylene succinate) as second-phase polymers.7, 12 These impact modifying additives are relatively exorbitant rendering their PLA blends expensive. Improving the impact strength of PLA by direct mechanical blending with inexpensive non-degradable polymers such as poly(ethylene oxide), poly(vinyl acetate), polyisoprene, acrylonitrile/butadiene/styrene copolymer, and polyethylene has successfully reduced cost and expanded its commercial applications.7, 10 However, the majority of these blends require compatibilizers to improve the miscibility between the impact modifier and the PLA. Therefore, using a commercially cost-effective impact modifier which is compatible with PLA would produce greater advantages. In response to this challenge, DuPont Packaging and Industrial Polymers has introduced Biomax strong 100®. This is a petroleum-based ethylene/acrylate copolymer (EAC) for commercial applications, noted as compatible with PLA and maintains its biodegradability at low concentrations.14 The feasibility of using this EAC as an impact modifier has been explored in a few studies and reported in literature. One study produced and analyzed not only PLA blend films with either Sukano PLA im S550 or EAC as additives for tensile properties and clarity but also correlated these properties to their micro-structures. EAC at a loading rate of 12% resulted in elongation at break of 255%, a significant improvement over that of neat PLA with about 90%.15 Another study reported the use of EAC as an impact modifier for neat PLA and highly filled PLA/calcium sulfate composites.16 Addition of 5-10% EAC into highly filled composites (30-40% of filler) led to a threefold increase of impact strength as compared to the compositions without the modifier.16 However, these studies failed to extensively account for the more subtle considerations of this impact modifier on different grades of PLA (effectiveness) and concentrations of impact modifier (efficiency)17 as well as providing detailed fracture mechanisms of impact modified PLA samples tested under various environmental conditions.

IntroductionPlastics like polyethylene, polypropylene and PET find their biggest application in the packaging industry, whose global market size was almost 143 million metric tons in volume and 265 billion USD by value in 2021 [1]. Due to high resistance to degradation, conventional plastics choke the ecosystem, raising serious environmental concerns [2]. Environmentalists often demand a blanket ban on plastics, which is not a feasible proposition from the perspective of the global economy [3]. Sustainable plastics, broadly termed biodegradable plastics, are relatively easier to degrade and hence identified as a potential alternative to conventional plastics. The global market of sustainable plastic packaging is expected to grow to about 126 billion USD by 2026[1]. Poly-lactic acid (PLA) is a popular sustainable plastic with a global market size of USD 624.97 million in 2022. It is expected to grow at a Compounded Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 21.4 % between 2023 and 2030[4].The PLA is a widely used biodegradable thermoelastic polyester manufactured from renewable feedstock[5,6]. Its backbone repeat unit is (C3H4O2)n and is synthesised through the ring-opening polymerization of lactide [7,8]. Over the past decade, there has been immense research on improving the material properties of PLA by forming composites and processing the material into utilisable products [[9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16]]. PLA is classified as a compostable polymer because 90 % of the polymer mass assimilates into carbon dioxide at simulated thermophilic composting conditions of 58 ± 2 °C as recommended by ASTM D5338 standard. [17]. Incorporation of binders, plasticisers and fillers contributes towards the properties of PLA. [18]. The material becomes less susceptible to physicochemical degradation and does not disintegrate easily, which is required for better shelf life of products made from such plastics. Subsequently, it resists enzymatic degradation through microbial attack and requires tailored strategies for enzymatic degradation.[19,20]. Moreover, being hydrophobic, PLA doesn't allow easy formation of biofilms on the surface[21]. Hence it limits significant degradation in the geoenvironment.PLA degradation can be witnessed through oxidative, hydrolytic, thermal, chemical, photodegradation, microbial and enzymatic pathways. The initial disintegration of long PLA chains into shorter chains is ester hydrolysis. It [22] is influenced by several factors like physical dimensions of the PLA, molecular weight, isomer ratio, crystallinity, pH of the medium, time of exposure, oxygen content in the medium, ambient temperature and humidity[23,24]. Polymer processing methods also influence degradation kinetics[25,26]. A significant number of studies have reported trends of PLA degradation in different environments and methods of increasing the rate of PLA degradation [[27], [28], [29], [30], [31], [32]]. Different microbes involved in PLA degradation have also been identified and validated at the laboratory scale [[33], [34], [35]].Irrespective of such progress, readily implementable technology for large-scale application of PLA in the field scale has been limited. To understand the roadblock and mitigate the same, there needs to be a systematically catalogued knowledge base generated from studies performed to date, which would enable the development of a clear understanding of the complex interplay of abiotic and biotic factors influencing PLA degradation. There is also a need to understand methods available for accelerated degradation and value addition of PLA at its end of life to ensure the safe management of such waste in the geoenvironment.Therefore, the objective of this systematic review is to find answers to the following questions:•What are the abiotic and biotic factors influencing PLA degradation through hydrolysis in the geoenvironment?•What are the micro-organisms influencing PLA degradation through hydrolysis in the geoenvironment?•What micro-organisms influence the assimilation of short disintegrated chains of PLA into Carbon Dioxide in the geoenvironment?•Have the enzymes been identified that catalyse the hydrolysis and assimilation of PLA?•Whether the enzymes have been isolated, structure modelled and kinetics studied either in-silico or in-vitro?•What is the scope of studies, in terms of scale and time, which has reported the findings pertaining to PLA degradation?•What are the future research needs in terms of accelerated PLA degradation?To find answers to the above questions, the PRISMA framework (Moher et al., 2009) was used to conduct the systematic literature review. The Web of Science (WOS) and Scopus databases were used for the literature search. All studies till January 2024 were taken into account.Primarily keywords and keyword combinations like ‘Polylactic Acid’, ‘PLA’, ‘Polylactide’, ‘Degradation’, ‘Bio-assimilation’, ‘Abiotic Hydrolysis’, and ‘Composting’. ‘Soil Degradation’ and ‘Enzymatic Hydrolysis’ were used in the search command prompt of both databases.
