The use of polymers in biomedical applications is continuously increasing [1], [2], [3]. In spite of the recent development, poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) is still one of the most preferable candidate [4], [5]. Properties, such as the hydrophyilicity, biocompatibility and its low interaction with the blood components, make PEG one of the best option for bio-applications [6]. In addition, PEG has been already approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) which facilitates the commercialization of PEG based products. PEG is the most employed polymer when we referred to the stealth polymers and it has been widely used to transport drugs, gene or a protein through the blood due to its excellent circulation time and biocompatibility. Moreover, PEG is capable to transport the compound before being recognized by the immunologic system. It has been reported that high molar mass polymers is the best scenario for biomedical applications [6], as in these conditions the renal clearance is diminished and the long term stability is augmented [1], [2], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11]. Consequently, high molar mass PEG leads to increase the capability of targeting the desired properties owing to longer residence time in vivo. Moreover, several studies have demonstrated that the toxicity of PEG is inversely proportional to the molar mass, decreasing the in vivo cytotoxicity increasing the molar mass [12], [13]. Although there are many advantages about using PEG, there are also drawbacks. The most apparent disadvantage of PEG is the lack of degradability and can be accumulated in vivo after finishing its function. Therefore, there are different solutions to overcome the problem. Recently, it has been demonstrated the possibility of a slow biodegradation of PEG by oxidative degradation under biologically significant conditions [14]. However, when faster degradability of the polymer is desired the design of new polymers is required. As a partial solution, block copolymers can be synthesized, having PEG as non-degradable block, and polylactic acid [15] or polycaprolactone [16] as degradable block. On the other hand, high molar mass PEG with hydrolysable linkages within the polymer structure will also facilitate its clearance from the body [17]. The generation with degradable linkages has given several alternatives on the design of PEG based degradable polymers. For instance, esters [18], [19], urethanes [20], [21], [22], disulfides [23] and thiols [24], [25] are some of the functional groups that have been incorporated so far to induce degradability to PEG based polymers. Thus, the polymer will possess high molar mass favouring the targeting and at the same time will have the potential to degrade in vivo after completing the function. Depending on the moiety introduced to PEG, the degradation mechanism and time will be different. Moreover, the incorporated degradable linkages can generate some side products upon degradation, conditioning the application and the effectiveness of the polymer.
Of the polymers that can be incorporated into chitosan-crosslinked networks to yield semi-IPNs, poly(ethylene) glycol (PEG) (Figure 1) attracted our attention. PEG is a synthetic and FDA-approved polymer for use inside the human body.28 It is considered to be biologically inert, biocompatible, and safe to use in drug formulations. Its hydrophilic nature with an incredible thirst for water finds use in a broad range of applications such as laxatives for whole bowel irrigation,29 PEGylated interferon for injectable treatment of hepatitis C infections30 and PEG-coated virus vectors for gene therapy.31 Recently, PEG showed promise in treating spinal-cord damage due to its ability to fuse cells, repair cell membranes, and restore the motor function.32 Based on a broad range of diverse studies employing PEG, it is possible to envisage that incorporation of PEG into a genipin-crosslinked chitosan network could yield a semi-IPN hydrogel with an improved reproducibility, enhanced physiological efficiency, good biocompatibility, improved mechanical performance, and tunable porosity (as a function of concentration of constituents and conditions used during synthesis). Tunable porosity is of importance when the ability to alter responsiveness to pH changes is of interest. Furthermore, being able to alter porosity would offer an additional degree of freedom when aiming to use such hydrogels as a delivery vehicle for bioactive molecules. However, a literature search revealed only a handful of studies involving genipin-crosslinked chitosan-PEG hydrogels. Jin and colleagues21 developed a hydrogel film containing chitosan, PEG, and genipin using a solution casting technique. The tensile strength and elongation were confirmed by tensometer and swelling behavior was determined in different pH buffer solutions at 23°C and 38°C. They found that by crosslinking chitosan with genipin, the tensile strength increased to more than twice (compared to uncrosslinked film). For the fixed amount of genipin, the highest tensile strength was found in the film with 20% of PEG while the highest elongation at break was observed in the film with 65% of PEG. For the fixed PEG amount, the film with a genipin content of 0.1% showed the greatest increase in elongation at break compared to film with 0.5% or 0.8% of genipin. The swelling behavior was dependent on genipin and PEG content, as well as pH and temperature of the medium. Liu et al. investigated the swelling behavior and release kinetics of genipin-crosslinked chitosan-PEG hydrogels by varying PEG and genipin content and the molecular weight of PEG.33 The swelling ratio of the crosslinked gel was higher in acidic medium, proportional to PEG content, and inversely proportional to genipin content. The morphological study was carried out with swollen gels in various pH media with smaller pores seen in gels in pH 7 medium and larger pores seen in gels in pH 2 medium. Currently, little is known about the gelation kinetics of this semi-IPN network. Understanding the gelation kinetics would unveil the dynamics at which the network is formed which is important to understand for further development of these hydrogels and translation to medical applications, in particular as injectable forms. Furthermore, the effect of PEG addition on the morphological characteristics and mechanical stability of hydrogel samples is not sufficiently understood. Mechanical properties are important as they indicate the material's feasibility for a specific medical purpose. At the same time, to fully understand role of each constituent, we would benefit from understanding chemical changes induced by the crosslinking reaction between chitosan and genipin, and interactions with PEG. Until these studies are conducted, these promising materials will remain experimental. Therefore, work presented in this article offers important insights into the key physico-chemical properties of smart hydrogels formed from chitosan, PEG, and genipin. Biodegradable and biocompatible polyurethane (PU)-based thermoresponsive hydrogels have recently received increasing attention.6,7 PUs offer attractive mechanical properties and have been studied in regenerative medicine applications.8 They are synthesized from a variety of polyols, diisocyanates, and chain extenders or crosslinkers, offering the flexibility of tailoring their properties to match specific requirements. The thermoresponsive properties of PU-based hydrogels are dependent on the balance of hydrophilic/hydrophobic groups and their interactions with water molecules via hydrogen bonding, in which the polymer chain network collapses or swells in response to the change in temperature of the aqueous medium.1,9 Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) is one of the most used polyols for designing PU-based hydrogels and it has been approved for use in medical applications by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).10,11 PEG presents attractive physicochemical and biological properties, including hydrophilicity, solubility in water and polar organic solvents, non-toxicity and non-immunogenicity.2,12 Hence, the modulation of PU-based hydrogels with PEG improves the biocompatibility, and enables the adjustment of degradability and mechanical properties by varying the molecular mass or concentration of the PEG.7,13 The ability to design PU-based hydrogels using a biodegradable and biocompatible polymer building block, either natural2,12,14 or synthetic,2,12,15,16 is an essential feature in tailoring their biodegradability and biocompatibility. Natural polymers are generally biocompatible, however their poor mechanical properties, fast degradation rates, poor reproducibility and potential immunogenicity restrict their use.2 In contrast, synthetic polymers have more predictable and reproducible physical and biological properties.2 Poly(glycerol sebacate) (PGS) is a synthetic biodegradable and biocompatible elastomer, specifically designed for soft tissue applications.17,18 It is synthesized via a polycondensation reaction of glycerol and sebacic acid, forming a meltable and soluble pre-polymer (pre-PGS) which subsequently cures to create a covalently crosslinked PGS network.17,18 PGS can sustain and recover from deformations in mechanically dynamic environments, which is attributed to its 3D molecular structure and elastomeric nature.19 PGS is bioresorbable and both of its monomers haven been approved by the FDA for the utilization in medical applications.17 Previous in vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated good cell compatibility with minimal inflammatory response to PGS implants,17,20-22 as well as relatively linear degradation kinetics and good retention of mechanical strength during degradation due to its surface erosion patterns.17,20-22 While PGS itself exhibits tunable properties,18 the functional hydroxyl groups of PGS also allow one to incorporate different functionalities by reacting with the hydroxyls and hence tailoring its physiochemical properties, as shown by recently developed PGS-based copolymers, blends and composites.18,23-26 For instance, hydrophilic segments such as citric acid or PEG were successfully incorporated into the PGS backbone, resulting in PGS-based copolymers with improved and tunable hydrophilic properties,24,26,27 and the use of isocyanate-based crosslinkers allowed researchers to design mechanically highly tunable PU-based elastomers under mild reaction conditions.23 However, most of these studies aimed to either improve the processability of PGS, or modify the mechanical properties, degradation behaviour or hydration properties of PGS.18 While pristine PGS has been recently investigated for basic one-way shape-memory effects,28 the development of reversibly stimuli-responsive PGS-related hydrogels has not been reported. In this work, we report novel thermoresponsive, stretchable and biodegradable polyester-based polyurethane (PEU) hydrogels, synthesized from pre-PGS and PEGs of different molecular masses (MWts), both containing hydroxyl groups, with aliphatic hexamethylene diisocyanate (HDI). HDI was selected due to its extensive use in synthesizing biocompatible polyurethanes.23,29 We hypothesized that the synthesis of the PEU using (I) biodegradable pre-PGS as the main macromolecular crosslinker, (II) hydrophilic PEG as the main polyol component, and (III) hydrophobic HDI as the diisocyanate component, could create a chemically crosslinked thermoresponsive hydrogel with the combined advantages of PGS, PEG and PU. By varying the MWt of PEG, the chemical and physical characteristics of the PEU hydrogels could be tailored. The structure and properties of these thermoresponsive materials were investigated, and their potential applications for tissue engineering, drug delivery and thermal actuation were evaluated. The structure of the PEUs was characterized by spectroscopic and calorimetric measurements, the mechanical properties were analyzed via quasi-static and cyclic tensile and compression tests, and the hydration kinetics and swelling behavior were studied under various medium temperatures. In vitro degradation tests were carried out in media with and without lipase, and cell proliferation response was examined in vitro with human adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs) and dermal fibroblasts (FIBs). Drug encapsulation and release as well as temperature-induced actuation behaviour were studied. The potential of fabricating the PEU material into different forms such as microspheres and large 3D porous scaffolds was also demonstrated.
Among PEG-based systems, self-assembled nanoparticles (NPs) based on block copolymers of PEG and poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PEG-PLGA) have been demonstrated to be effective drug delivery systems to promote mucoadhesion or mucopenetration depending on the length and surface density of the PEG block.7,8 In terms of molecular weight, lower molecular weight PEG (<2 kDa) minimizes mucosal adhesion based on the inherent hydrophilic and electrostatically neutral properties of PEG while higher molecular weight PEG (>10 kDa) promotes mucosal adhesion based on physical interpenetration between the highly flexible PEG chains and the mucosal membrane and/or enhanced hydrogen bonding between the ether groups in the PEG backbone and sugars on glycosylated mucins.9 In terms of density, NPs with low coating densities cannot shield the NP from interactions with mucus and thus promote immobilization and entrapment within the mucin layer, while NPs with high PEG densities (particularly those achievable using low molecular weight PEG) can effectively shield the NP core from mucin interactions to promote mucopenetration.7 While linear PEG coatings have been primarily investigated in this context, changing the morphology of the PEG coating may also offer benefits for tuning NP mucoadhesion and mucopenetration. Brush, comb, or bottle-brush structures based on PEG are particularly promising given (1) their capacity to increase local PEG densities, (2) their potential to tune both the length of the polymer backbone and the length of the brushes independently, (3) their potential to mediate PEG flexibility based on the controllable steric crowding of the PEG chains, and (4) their reduced immunogenicity to counteract emerging concerns over PEG antibodies.10-12 Such benefits have been demonstrated in other materials; for example, enhanced mucoadhesion can be achieved by creating bottle-brush polymers composed of poly(acrylic acid) grafted onto cellulose nanocrystals relative to poly(acrylic acid) alone.13 The use of poly(oligoethylene glycol methacrylate) (POEGMA), which is characterized by a poly(methacrylate) backbone with regular PEG side-chains, is particularly attractive in this context given that oligo(ethylene glycol) methacrylate monomers with varying PEG side chain lengths are commercially available, allowing for the production of brush-length (co)-polymers with tunable brush lengths/brush length distributions via a single-step conventional or controlled free radical polymerization.14,15 For example, micelles containing a poly(cholesteryl methacrylate) hydrophobic block and poly(oligo(ethylene glycol)methacrylate) (n = 5-6 average side chain length) as the hydrophilic block exhibited enhanced penetration through reconstituted porcine mucus compared to those prepared with linear PEG (MW ∼5000 g mol−1).16 Similarly, wormlike nanocarriers composed of bottle-brush PEG (n = 20 average side chain length) have been shown to translocate through all barriers of the airway including the mucosal membrane and become internalized within epithelial cells.17 However, the ability to rationally tune the mucoadhesion and mucopenetration of POEGMA-coated nanoparticles by manipulating the brush length has not to the best of our knowledge previously been demonstrated. Herein, we report the mucoadhesion and mucopenetration properties of nanoparticles prepared via the self-assembly of amphiphilic block copolymers of poly(lactic acid) (PLA) and poly(oligo(ethylene glycol) methacrylate) (POEGMA) with various side chain lengths fabricated via atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP).18 We demonstrate that by tuning the length of the side chain we can optimize either mucoadhesion or mucopenetration of the self-assembled nanoparticles while also enabling easier preparation, modification, and/or functionalization of the nanoparticles based on the free radical synthesis approach in comparison to the ring opening synthetic method used for the fabrication of linear PEG-based blocks. We also demonstrate the biosafety and tissue tolerability of the self-assembled nanoparticles for ocular applications, in which optimal tuning of mucoadhesion/mucopenetration is essential to enhance nanoparticle retention in the eye while also ensuring drug transport to the cornea (Scheme 1).
Biofouling is an extremely problematic issue for a wide variety of applications,47-49 and thus has generated rigorous interest in the literature for trying to mitigate its prevalence.50 For example, polyethylene glycols (PEGs) have long been used as an antibiofouling coating because it resists the adsorption of free proteins in serum.51, 52 Similarly, PEG can be used to create so-called “stealth” particles, which evade uptake by cells (especially macrophages) and thus have prolonged circulation.53 However, while there have been some studies that address the effect of PEGylation on the properties of responsive structures,54-56 there has been less focus on how PEG copolymers affect the performance of polyelectrolyte multilayers as responsive devices. In particular, the impact of PEGylation on the organization of the multilayers and the subsequent effect on mechanical strength and toughness is largely unexamined. This approach, however, comes with the downside of increased complexity and often introduces nonbiocompatible elements to achieve these effects. Clearly, changing the properties of a final microcapsule without relying on extensive chemical modification is desirable to tuning a final product. Despite this need, few studies involving microcapsule synthesis (and particularly with those involving complex macromolecules) explore how processing conditions alter transport and mechanical behavior. In this report, we focus on one class of biopolymers derived from silk fibroin as materials for thin shell microcapsules. Silk fibroin has long been recognized as an excellent biomaterial, due to its negligible cytotoxicity, easy processability, high robustness, and low immunogenicity.57, 58 In addition, silk fibroin has been shown to have exceptional mechanical properties as a thin film, though stable, robust films often require treatment with methanol to crystalize the silk proteins.59, 60 This requirement can be avoided by grafting silk fibroin with short oligomeric chains consisting of a repeat unit of an amino acid with either an amine or carboxyl group as its side group (Figure 1A). These silk derivatives are referred to as silk ionomers, as they consist of weak polybases or polyacids (depending on the species), covalently bonded to the silk fibroin backbone as pendant group moieties.61 The addition of charged groups allows for the use of LbL processing techniques, which we use to construct both planar films and hollow, 3D microspheres and microcapsules. These molecules have been previously shown to have a high degree of biocompatibility when used to encapsulate cells.62 Silk fibroins exploited here are silk grafted with poly-l-lysine (SF-Plys) and silk fibroin grafted with poly-l-glutamic acid (SF-Pglu), which form positively and negatively charged molecules, respectively (Figure 1). In addition, we use a variant of the positively charged silk ionomer species that consists of silk fibroin grafted to poly-l-lysine-block-polyethylene glycol (SF-Plys-PEG), which we have previously shown to significantly alter the intermolecular properties of the silk ionomers.63 In this work, all of the grafted poly-l-lysine and poly-l-glutamic acid groups are made from 20 repeat units of their component amino acids, and are all grafted to the serine and glutamic acid residues of the silk fibroin backbone. This report demonstrates the results of PEGylation and contrasts it to variations due to changes in processing parameters using low grafting silk ionomers as a model system. This length and grafting density is significantly shorter than silk ionomer species that have previously been utilized in making microcapsules, and thus have a lower charge density per molecule. These molecules have been shown to be more cytocompatible when used as cellular coatings and have around 1-2 orders of magnitude less substituted amino acids than the highly grafted silk ionomer species.64 The results of these studies indicate that the microcapsules have a relatively open porous structure that becomes denser at acidic pH, where some of the anionic charge can be reduced. In addition, the different processing strategies to produce the microcapsules lead to different pore structures, which play a critical role in determining the ultimate properties of the microcapsules.

Both poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) and poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) polymers selected for incorporation within TPUs of the present study are biocompatible and nonimmunogenic. So far, there have been several PCL- or PEG-based biomedical products for various clinical uses approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). (8, 9) PCL is one of the most promising synthetic polymers that can degrade in contact with microorganisms. (10-12) The related enzymatic hydrolytic degradation of PCL-based polymers has also been investigated, especially in the presence of ester-bond cleavage enzymes. (13-17) Lipases are one of the most popularly studied enzymes to catalyze the cleavage of ester bonds by transesterification, (18) although they do not occur naturally in the human body. Importantly, semicrystalline PCL blocks make the associated polyurethanes stiff and hydrophobic, limiting their compatibility with soft tissues and the range of potential applications. This problem might be overcome for water-contacting applications by introducing hydrophilic blocks such as poly(ethylene glycol), (19, 20) the approach adopted in our present work. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) is one of the most widely studied synthetic polymers used for designing hydrogels of use in the biomedical applications. The intrinsic hydrophilicity of PEG-based hydrogels repels nonspecific protein adsorption and resists bacterial and animal cell adhesion. (21-23) Their elastic and soft nature imparts to the TPUs low mechanical and frictional irritation when in contact with tissues and organs. However, PEG-based polyurethanes have generally exhibited poor mechanical properties. (20) The properties of these polymers can be improved by either blending (24) or copolymerization. (19, 25-29) Because of the combination of great advantages of PCL and PEG, PCL-PEG-based copolymers might have great potential application in biomedical fields including drug delivery, cell encapsulation, and tissue engineering. (26, 28, 30, 31) Indeed, Skarja and Woodhouse have developed a family of biodegradable segmented polyurethanes, which has potential for use in soft tissue engineering applications. (32-34) The hard segments of these materials are composed of a phenylalanine-based diester chain extender and lysine diisocyanate, whereas the soft segments are either a PEG or PCL diol. It was found that the degradation rate and mechanical properties of these materials could be optimized by blending the PCL-based and PEG-based polyurethanes. (24) Because of its vulnerability to hydrolytic and oxidative degradation, PCL-PEG-based copolymers have proven to be unsuitable for long-term implantation. In this manuscript, we attempted to overcome this limitation through incorporation of a biostable moiety, POSS, which we now describe. Polyhedral oligosilsesquioxane (POSS) is a class of hybrid molecules with an inorganic silicon-oxygen cage (Si8O12) and eight variable organic side groups pendant to each silicon vertex of the cage with the size of 1-3 nm. The silica-like framework renders POSS cages chemically stable, nontoxic, and mechanically robust. (35, 36) Our past work on POSS polyurethanes concerned microstructure-deformation studies, (37, 38) biodegradation, (39) controlled drug delivery, (40) biocompatibility, (41) and hydrogel formation. (42) Kannan et al. conducted in vitro hydrolysis and oxidation tests to assess the degradative resistance of polyhedral oligosilsesquioxane integrated poly(carbonate-urea) urethane (POSS-PCU). (43) Their studies revealed that all samples showed no significant difference in their compliance and elasticity after a 70 day hydrolysis and oxidation test, indicating striking biostability. The authors proposed that POSS nanocores covalently incorporated in PCU chains impart a type of “protective” or “shielding effect” on the soft phase, thereby preserving its elasticity and compliant properties in oxidation and hydrolysis. Polycarbonate-urethane itself, however, possesses a greater biostability than does polyether-urethane and polyester-urethane. (35, 44-46) How to change the more common polyether- and polyester-based urethanes from a biodegradable form to a biostable form by incorporation of POSS (or other means) has not yet been reported.
First published on 15th July 2015 This work evaluates the response of human aortic endothelial cells (HAECs) to thromboresistant collagen-mimetic hydrogel coatings toward improving the biocompatibility of existing “off-the-shelf” small-caliber vascular grafts. Specifically, bioactive hydrogels - previously shown to support α1/α2 integrin-mediated cell adhesion but to resist platelet activation - were fabricated by combining poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) with a 120 kDa, triple-helical collagen-mimetic protein (Scl2-2) containing the GFPGER adhesion sequence. Analysis of HAECs seeded onto the resulting PEG-Scl2-2 hydrogels demonstrated that HAEC adhesion increased with increasing Scl2-2 concentration, while HAEC migration rate decreased over this same concentration range. In addition, evaluation of HAEC phenotype at confluence indicated significant differences in the gene expression of NOS3, thrombomodulin, and E-selectin on the PEG-Scl2-2 hydrogels relative to PEG-collagen controls. At the protein level, however, only NOS3 was significantly different between the PEG-Scl2-2 and PEG-collagen surfaces. Furthermore, PECAM-1 and VE-cadherin expression on PEG-Scl2-2 hydrogels versus PEG-collagen controls could not be distinguished at either the gene or protein level. Cumulatively, these data indicate the PEG-Scl2-2 hydrogels warrant further investigation as “off-the-shelf” graft coatings. In future studies, the Scl2-2 protein can potentially be modified to include additional extracellular matrix or cytokine binding sites to further improve endothelial cell responses. An alternative approach involves harnessing the potential of host endothelial cells to migrate from graft-host anastomoses.9 In this approach, the graft luminal surface is generally modified to enhance endothelial cell migration.10 Previous efforts have often focused on using proteins from the blood vessel basement membrane, such as fibronectin and collagens I and IV, as coatings.11,12 However, many of these proteins3,4 and associated peptides - such as RGD13 - also support platelet adhesion until a confluent endothelium is established, rendering their use problematic for “off-the-shelf” applications. An ideal coating for “off-the-shelf” vascular prostheses would intrinsically resist platelet activation while supporting rapid endothelial cell migration from the anastomoses and the formation of a quiescent, luminal endothelial layer. The primary goal of the current study is to evaluate the capacity of a novel, thromboresistant biomaterial coating based on poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and collagen-mimetic proteins to support human endothelial cell adhesion, migration, and differentiation.
Functionalized OPF hydrogels were prepared and could be degraded by light. Over the past several decades, hydrogels have garnered substantial interest across a broad range of areas including food science, personal care, agriculture, and increasingly biomedical applications such as drug delivery, cellular therapy, wound healing, and device coatings [1], [2], [3]. They are characterized by their ability to retain significant amounts of water, making them attractive for use in water-rich environments such as the human body. By tuning their network structure and cross-linking mechanism, the mechanical properties of hydrogels can be engineered to match those of native tissues [3]. Hydrogels can be prepared from synthetic polymers including poly(hydroxyethyl methacrylate) [4], polyesters [5], poly(ester amide)s [6], [7], and poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) [8], [9], or biopolymers such as chitosan [10], alginate [11], collagen [12], or hyaluronic acid [13]. Oligo[poly(ethylene glycol) fumarate] (OPF) is one of the synthetic polymers that has been investigated for hydrogel formation. OPF hydrogels have been studied for applications such as cartilage tissue engineering [14], [15], bone repair [16], [17], [18], neural regeneration [19], [20], and drug delivery [21]. OPF can be synthesized through the reaction of fumaryl chloride with PEG in the presence of a proton scavenger [22], and cross-linked using chemical methods such as ammonium persulfate with N,N,N’,N’-tetramethylethylenediamine [23] or photo-cross-linked using a photoinitiator such as Irgacure 2959 [24]. The addition of PEG diacrylate (PEGDA) as a cross-linker reduces the cross-linking time [25]. PEG molar mass determines many of the properties of the resulting hydrogels such as the tensile and fracture moduli as well as the biodegradation time [25], [26], [21], [27]. Degradation of OPF hydrogels occurs relatively slowly, with mass losses ranging from 14 to 28 % after 12 weeks in vitro, depending on the PEG molar mass and PEGDA:OPF ratio [26].

Temperature-sensitive hydrogels are promising injectable materials for a wide variety of pharmaceutical and biomedical applications. The three-dimensional polymeric networks of the hydrogels are suitable for controlled drug release systems [1-4] and tissue engineering [5, 6]. Besides their good biocompatibilities, thermogelling hydrogels have the advantages of ease of application, localized delivery for site-specific action, a prolonged delivery period, and improved patient compliance. In recent years, a great variety of physically crosslinked amphiphilic hydrogels consisting of hydrophilic poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and biodegradable hydrophobic blocks have been reported in the open literature, such as poly(ethylene glycol)/poly(glycolic acid) (PEG/PGA) [7], poly(ε-caprolactone)/poly(ethylene glycol) (PCL/PEG) [8, 9], poly(lactide)/poly(ethylene glycol) (PLA/PEG) [10], and poly(ethylene glycol)/poly(lactic acid-co-glycolic acid) (PEG/PLGA) [11-13]. Among the hydrogels mentioned above, PLGA-PEG-PLGA has found extensive commercial use as localized delivery carrier for the anticancer drug pacilitaxel [14]. However, the main defect of this hydrogel is the generation of acidic products through the degradation of PLGA, which destroys the bioactivity of proteins and drugs. A great deal of attention has been paid to biocompatible hydrogels with hydrophobic poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) segments, as this segment releases fewer acidic units during the degradation process. However, the relatively high degree of crystallinity and the slow degradation rate of PCL chains limit their application. Jiang et al. recently reported a series of novel biodegradable hydrogels based on poly(ε-caprolactone-co-glycolide)/poly(ethylene glycol) [P(CL-GA)/PEG] and poly(ε-caprolactone-co-lactide)/poly(ethylene glycol) [P(CL-LA)/PEG] triblock copolymers [15-17]. The copolymerization of lactide or glycolide monomer with ε-caprolactone effectively accelerated the degradation rate of the hydrogels. The sol-gel transition behavior of these triblock copolymers could be controlled by tuning their chemical compositions and microstructures. However, the authors did not pay much attention to the crystalline behavior of the resultant sol solutions, and very little is known about the controllability of the stability of the sol. In fact, even though the low-temperature stability of sols of crystalline themogelling copolymers is a crucial factor in their practical utility, this stability has not been investigated. Poly(p-dioxanone) (PPDO), which has a much faster degradation rate than PCL, is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use as a biodegradable suture material [18]. The degradation time of PPDO is comparable to that of polyglycolide (PGA), and is shorter than that of polylactide (PLA). Based solely on the provided evidence, the biocompatibility mechanism of PEG coatings primarily involves:

1.  **Low nonspecific adsorption of proteins, cells, and bacteria:** PEG's hydrophilic nature and steric hindrance prevent non-specific binding of biomolecules and cells, reducing potential immune recognition and fouling [1, 6]. This is key to creating "stealth" surfaces that evade recognition by the immune system [2, 6].
2.  **Low toxicity and low immunogenicity:** PEG exhibits low toxicity towards mammalian cells and has minimal ability to provoke an immune response (low antigenicity and immunogenicity) [1, 2]. Its hydrophilicity contributes to this behavior [2].
3.  **Reduced interaction with blood components:** Due to its hydrophilicity, PEG coatings exhibit low interaction with blood components, contributing to enhanced blood compatibility (hemocompatibility) [2, 13]. This reduces thrombogenicity (clot formation).

Biodegradable polymeric materials have the developmental advantage of degrading predominantly by a simple hydrolysis reaction, producing predictable degradation products, and degrading through similar mechanisms whether evaluated in vitro or in vivo.60 In contrast, the development of a suitable metallic material for stenting applications, though promising,2 has been elusive. This may be due to the lack of suitable pre-existing materials, as well as the high cost and complexity of developing new materials. Metallic materials often corrode via complex mechanisms that produce a wide range of products, and the rates and products of corrosion can differ fundamentally between in vitro and in vivo conditions.61 This has made it difficult to translate success at the bench top into a successful stent. Consequently, the scientific and industrial community has engaged in more than a decade-long focus on Mg and Fe62 that has failed to realize the promise of acceptable fully bioabsorbable metallic alternative to the emerging fully biodegradable polymeric stents. Mechanical strength similarity to conventional stents allows clinicians to have reasonable deployment expectations when using a biodegradable metallic stent. Common bile duct (CBD) obstruction is a common disease occurring in hepatobiliary surgery, causing the thorniest issue for patients and surgeons. Implanting T tube drainage made of silicone rubber has widely been used to support CBD after removing the CBD stone, but it still has many complications during treatment [1, 2]. With the development of interventional therapy and materials science, various biliary stents are prepared for biliary stricture to prevent stenosis and support the reconstruction. Common materials including nitinol alloy, stainless steel and plastic, are used for biliary stents to guarantee enough supporting force with good bending and compliance properties [3,4,5]. These stents have good clinical efficacy but needed to be reserved in the body or removed by secondary operation [3]. Recently, as the application of biodegradable materials in vascular stents and orthopedic implantation, biodegradable biliary stents have emerged in bile duct therapy. Almeida et al. [6] investigated the reported data and found biodegradable versus multiple plastic stent implantation in benign biliary strictures reported lower complication rates, except for cholangitis and haemobilia. To date, studies on biodegradable biliary stent mainly focused on polymer materials such as polylactic acid (PLA) [7, 8], poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) [1], polydioxanone (PDO) [9], authorized by the FDA for clinical use. Gregory et al. [7] firstly evaluated the feasibility of PLA biliary stent in a porcine model, and the result showed the stent could remain patent up to 6 months, but the occlusion and migration remain concerns. Other disadvantages including long degradation time and insufficient strength also limit their application. Magnesium (Mg) is one of the most common metals in nature and also a constant element in the human body. In the past decades, Mg and its alloys have attracted continuously rising attention as biodegradable materials due to their good mechanical properties and biocompatibility [10]. The research of Mg alloys coronary stents has been the most popular field in medicine. The Mg coronary stents named Magmaris based on DREAMS 2 G from Biotronik Inc. obtained CE approval in June 2016 [11]. Different from vascular stents usually prepared by laser engraving, the braided technique has been applied for self-expandable metallic stents clinically during the development process of the non-vascular stent. Additionally, polymers are typically viscoelastic and can deform permanently over their lifetime when in use under stress. Although rarely mentioned in the stent literature, viscoelasticity is a disadvantage of using polymers for stent applications.
The main purpose of this study was to investigate the corrosion and mechanical properties of ZEK100 substrates modified by MGF-carrying multilayers, and study the biocompatibility of multilayers carrying MGF. Images observed by SEM, FTIR and AFM show that these uniform multilayers formed onto the substrates. However, cracks and convex particles on the surface exist, which was also seen in other studies of surface modification [13], [22], [23], [25], [34]. Since magnesium alloys are not as stiff as stainless steel or titanium alloys, convex particles may be generated for abrasion when polished by SiC papers [23], [25]. Cracks were probably produced by water desorption during the drying process [22], [34]. Multilayer-covered surfaces were relatively smoother [27], and small cracks and convex particles could easily be covered up by multilayer coatings, as evidenced in Fig. 3. Slight peelings are a disadvantage in reducing corrosion rate, which were observed on sample surfaces in vitro and in vivo. A reason for this is that each coated layer adhered to each other by weak electrostatic interaction [18], and another reason was the expansion of the coated layer when the modified layers absorbed water. As immersion time increased, multilayer-coats on the substrate would be completely corroded, and the ZEK100 alloy substrate would begin to corrode; which would lead to a downtrend in yield strength and ultimate tensile strength. However, this can continue to remain at > 85% of the mechanical strength after 7 days of implantation. Surface modification of AZ31B not only affected surface structure, but also helped improve one-point bending loads with the extension of immersion time [35]. In this study, fatigue life of coated ZEK100 is slightly larger than that of uncoated samples with 1 day immersion; and it could be deduced that the multilayer-coat can provide persistent protection and control the degradation rate of ZEK100. Similarly, Fu et al. [37] has investigated the ratcheting fatigue life of the AZ31 sheet without surface modification pre-corroded in PBS. These indicates that the pre-corroded damage could be defined as life reduction increases exponentially with immersion time, fatigue cracks observed from microscopic pictures would initiate preferentially from any surface pits (including corrosion pits), and life reduction considers the relatively deep pits at the crack initiation site on the ratcheting fatigue fracture surface. In other words, the pitting corrosion reduces the fatigue life of the ZEK100 magnesium alloy, as well as the AZ31 alloy, to some extent. In this study, the degradation rate of the ZEK100 sample was inhibited by surface modification, as shown in Fig. 5b and Fig. 8. Corrosion pits on the surface of coated ZEK100 magnesium alloy in Fig. 3f were smaller than that of uncoated ZEK100 magnesium alloy in Fig. 3e in tests in vivo. The crack initiation sites on the fracture surface of specimens with different immersion times of ZEK100 alloy could be observed in Fig. 9 in tests in vitro. It is found that fatigue cracks would initiate preferentially from the surface pits and corrosion pits on the fracture surface of coated ZEK100 magnesium alloy are less than those of uncoated ZEK100 magnesium alloy. Therefore, it is speculated that corrosion pits have significant influences on ratcheting fatigue, and surface modification makes valuable contributions to ratcheting fatigue life, indirectly. The corrosion rate of uncoated and coated magnesium alloy decreased as immersion time increased, probably due to the deposition of corrosion products that were covered or material composition changed on the surface during degradation, which protected the substrates against further corrosion, as some ions are released [9], [34], [36], [38]. In this study, multilayer-coated samples contain less cracks and particles on the surface than uncoated samples, as shown in Fig. 3a and c. Meanwhile, surface roughness value measured by AFM is reduced after surface modification, as shown in Fig. 4. The actual total corrosion area of the multilayer-coated substrate is less than that of uncoated substrates, which attributes to the relatively smooth morphology of the modification layer. Nguyen et al. [39] found that the decreasing surface roughness of pure magnesium helped to decrease the corrosion rate in Hank's balanced salt solution, since the actual total surface area exposed to the testing media decreased in lower rough samples; and a lower corrosion rate was expected. The existence of cracks has a disadvantageous effect on corrosion rate for anodic dissolution at the crack tip [40]. Therefore, it is speculated that the morphology of the surface is another important factor to control corrosion rate and match bone regeneration. In previous studies [21], [26], it is also known that the degradation rate could be controlled by surface modification.
The treatment of coronary artery disease has gone through three revolutions since the first plain old balloon angioplasty (POBA), which was performed in 1977 and published in the first volume of Lancet on Feb. 4, 1978.[1] Bare metal stents overcome the re-narrowing of coronary arteries after POBA,[2] but they show high incidence of in-stent restenosis in longer-term results, which promoted the development of drug-eluting stents (DES) as the second revolution.[3-5] However, the permanent presence of the metal implants may impair the physiological vasomotor and lead to chronic inflammation, thrombosis, late luminal loss, and neoatherosclerosis, as indicated by some experts.[6] As the third revolution, the biodegradable stents have the potential to circumvent these drawbacks owing to the temporary caging.[7-10] The company of Abbott Vascular pioneered the first biodegradable stent approved by U.S. Food and Drug Administration, yet the Absorb Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffold was withdrawn from the market mainly due to the increased rate of stent thrombosis and target lesion revascularization.[11-13] This is pertinent to the thick struts, which came from the lower mechanical strength of polylactide (PLA) compared to cobalt-chromium alloy, the currently main-stream raw material of coronary stent.[13, 14] Magmaris (Biotronik AG, Bülach, Switzerland), the latest generation of magnesium-based biodegradable stent, showed the safety and performance up to 12 months in BIOSOLVE-IV.[15] The struts are still thick (150 µm) mainly due to the lower mechanical strength of magnesium alloy,[16, 17] which was associated with high late lumen loss[18] and a long duration of dual antiplatelet therapy.[13, 15] Pure zinc and zinc-based alloys were also tried to make degradable vascular stents with good degradation performance.[19-22] Extensive investigations are still needed to meet the strict clinical criteria. While these previous efforts are great and both PLA, magnesium, and zinc stents have space to be further improved, the fourth alternative choice of raw materials will be helpful for research and development (R & D) of new-generation biodegradable stents appropriate for interventional treatments. Iron is of better mechanical properties than polymer and magnesium alloy as coronary stents, and its feasibility as a biodegradable stent material was preliminarily examined through the first implantation into the native descending aorta of New Zealand rabbits.[23] Compared with PLA and magnesium alloy, iron-based materials have the potential to make the struts as thin as the permanent DES, which may minimize blood flow perturbations, and reduce restenosis and thrombosis.[24] However, the biodegradation of iron is much slower than other candidates,[25] which inspired the development of alloying method[26-28] and nitriding technology.[29, 30] Nevertheless, the degradation period was still overly long, and some alloying elements, especially Mn, may be detrimental to cells.[31] To further shorten the biodegradation period, a metal-polymer composite strategy was proposed in our previous study.[32] The strategy was applied to fabricate a metal-polymer composite stent (MPS), which showed a satisfactory biodegradation rate and a promising efficacy in vivo. The manufacturing process of MPS and the percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) are schematically presented in Figure S1, Supporting Information. The effect of the metal-polymer composite strategy on the degradation of iron and in particular the corresponding biocompatibility evaluation will be investigated in the present article. It is well-known that an ideal biodegradable stent should not only have good mechanical properties and an appropriate degradation rate, but also keep a good biocompatibility. In light of fundamental research closely relevant to the potential clinical translation, iron-base biomaterials are faced with a critical argument about its possible cytotoxicity. Some in vitro studies have reported that the extracts of iron materials were non-cytotoxic to cells.[32-34] Furthermore, no thrombosis or pronounced inflammation and no systemic or local toxicity were observed in vivo studies, indicating the safety of iron-based biodegradable stents preliminarily.[30, 35, 36] However, a new issue has been raised up to focus on the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) during iron corrosion, which was ignored in the traditional cytotoxicity tests via extracts.[37] In 2020, a paper entitled as “Hydroxyl radicals and oxidative stress: the dark side of Fe corrosion” was published; Scarcello et al. kindly warned that the oxidative stress caused by iron corrosion was detrimental to endothelial cells in vitro[38] and rat aortic rings ex vivo.[39] This is a serious problem related to any effort of an iron-based biomaterial eventually implanted into body.
Historically, corrosion has been thought to be a critical issue that should be controlled to a level as minimal as possible for structural materials. In recent years, there has been a paradigm shift in thinking in the biomaterial community in terms of corrosion. There is now increasing interest in intentionally using a corrodible alloy in some medical device applications such as intravascular stents and orthopedic implants [1] because the use of biodegradable materials can avoid a second surgery. In this case, the human body must be able to deal with the corrosion products and their effects. There are three major groups of biodegradable metallic biomaterials: (1) iron and its alloys (Fe-Mn) [2-4], (2) magnesium (Mg) and its alloys [5-8], and (3) tungsten (W) [9]. Magnesium has attracted a great deal of interest due to its exceptional mechanical and physiological features. Physiologically, Mg2+ ions are a cofactor in many enzymatic reactions and essential for normal neurological and muscular functions. Also, the presence of magnesium benefits the mineralization process of bony tissue and is important to bone’s strength and health [10]. An adult human body contains approximately 30 g of magnesium in muscle and bone [11] and also need to take in 420 mg/day. From the perspective of physical and mechanical features, magnesium has good compatibility with human bone. For example, its density of 1.74 g/cm3 and Young’s modulus of 41-45 GPa are close to natural bone (1.8-2.1 g/cm3 and ~30 GPa, respectively). Advantageous over inorganic and polymeric biomaterials, Mg has much higher fracture toughness and yield strength. Even more important and attractive is its biodegradability. Current surgical orthopedics requires a secondary surgical procedure to remove the orthopedic plate, screw, or pin after the tissue has healed sufficiently. But if these orthopedic tools are made of magnesium, instead of stainless steel or titanium, then they can naturally degrade in, and be excreted from, the human body and therefore the secondary surgery can be avoided. The potential application of magnesium in orthopedics was realized in the early twentieth century. The first surgical attempt was reported by Lambotte in 1907 [12], but it was not successful because the pure magnesium metal corroded too rapidly in vivo, losing its mechanical integrity only 8 days after surgery and leaving hydrogen gas pockets beneath the skin. As such, the use of magnesium in orthopedic devices was quickly abandoned. Attempts at using magnesium were spurred again in the 1940s [12] and subsequently boosted in the early 2000s, in line with the advancement and development of magnesium technologies. The past few years have seen a big leap in the development of magnesium biomaterials [1, 13]. Magnesium metal stents (e.g. AMS, Biotronik GmbH) have moved to the clinical arena [4, 14, 15]. With the success of the clinical experiments, it is envisaged that biodegradable Mg will attract more academic investigations and capital investment.
The introduction of permanent metallic stents was a major advance over balloon angioplasty in the treatment of arterial diseases, being highly effective in preventing acute vessel closure due to balloon-induced dissection, and in reducing the rate of restenosis [1]. However, it has been suggested that the role of the stent is temporary and limited to the intervention and shortly thereafter, until healing and re-endothelialization of the vessel wall is achieved [2]. In fact, after six months arterial remodeling typically enters a stable phase where substantial scaffolding is no longer needed to prevent recoil [3]. Afterwards, the presence of a permanent stent, besides requiring a lifelong anticoagulant therapy, can lead to late thrombosis and chronic inflammation, and can hinder the lumen expansion associated with late vessel remodeling. Biodegradable stents have therefore emerged as one of the most promising approaches in obstructive cardiovascular disease treatment due to their potential in providing mechanical support while it is needed and then, once they are bioabsorbed, leaving behind only the healed natural vessel. This would allow the restoration of vasoreactivity and possibly vessel remodeling as well as to avoid the aforementioned concerns related with the presence of a permanent metallic implant [2]. In addition, biodegradable stents are particularly needed in the case of pediatric cardiovascular treatments where a permanent stent usually requires a second surgery since the target vessel grows with the child [3]. A number of biodegradable stents made of metallic or polymeric materials have been investigated over recent years [4, 5]. Mg alloys are by far the most investigated biodegradable metallic materials for intravascular stent development [6, 7]. The first metallic bioabsorbable stent implanted in humans was the Mg alloy stent studied in the ‘Clinical Performance and Angiographic Results of Coronary Stenting with Absorbable Metal Stents’ trial [8]. Aliphatic polyesters, such as poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA), poly(glycolic acid), poly(D,L-lactic-co-glycolic acid), and poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), have been widely investigated for biodegradable stents development due to their relatively long degradation rate and suitable mechanical properties [5, 9]. The Igaki-Tamai stent (Kyoto Medical Planning, Japan), the first biodegradable stent implanted in humans, consists of an extruded high molecular weight PLLA filament with a zig-zag helical coil design [10]. The stent received the CE marking in 2007 for the treatment of peripheral artery diseases, and recent clinical outcomes showed its long term safety as coronary scaffold that could disappear within three years [11]. The ABSORB Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffold based on PLLA (Abbott Vascular, CA) was the first bioabsorbable drug-eluting stent to have clinical outcomes similar to those following metallic drug-eluting stent implantation [12]. Other biodegradable stents that are currently under clinical investigation are the REVA Medical stent made of tyrosine polycarbonate (REVA Medical Inc., CA), the IDEAL stent made of a polyanhydride and salicylic acid (Bioabsorbable Therapeutics Inc., CA), and the novolimus-loaded DESOlve stent made of PLLA (Elixir Medical Corporation, CA) [8, 9]. Polymeric stents are generally composed by interconnected tubular elements with a zig-zag or sinusoidal structure. They are fabricated starting from a tubular body, obtained by injection molding or melt extrusion, whose wall is made porous by means of selective material removal through laser ablation, mechanical machining or chemical etching [3]. Alternatively, polymeric stents are made through melt extrusion of a monofilament that is then woven into a braid-like embodiment. Flege et al [13] recently reported on the development of stents made of PLLA or PLLA-co-PCL by means of a Selective Laser Melting technique. As highlighted by the authors, an additive manufacturing (AM) approach to stents fabrication allows achieving superior freedom in structural design and mechanical performance in comparison to conventional fabrication techniques. In fact, AM techniques allow fabrication of 3D objects with a predefined composition, geometry and size as well as a porous architecture characterized by a fully interconnected network of pores with customizable size, shape and distribution [14].
Among cardiovascular diseases, coronary artery disease is responsible for 18 million deaths around the globe [[1], [2], [3], [4]]. During various coronary artery treatments such as angiography, coronary stent implantation renders intra-arterial assistance [[5], [6], [7]]. For a stent to be ideal for clinical use, several fundamental merits are required such as mechanical strength, ductility, and biocompatibility [8]. Unfortunately, after stent implantation, a significant number of patients develop late restenosis [9,10]. Extensive anticoagulant medication is also not useful in the case of such patients. Non-degradable bare metallic stents (BMS) possess excellent mechanical properties with good biocompatibility but still, they cause late thrombosis and restenosis due to chronic inflammation and neointimal hyperplasia [11]. Drug-eluting stents (DES) are also employed which reduce thrombosis and restenosis in the early stages but in the latter stages due to the permanent implantation in the blood vessels, thrombosis and restenosis can occur after a year or two [[12], [13], [14]]. Biodegradable stents are a promising class to mitigate the shortcomings of the BMS and DES stents [15]. Magnesium and its alloys are an alluring class of metals for implants due to their biodegradable and mechanical properties [[16], [17], [18]]. After implantation, the spontaneous degradation and the resorption by the vascular tissue is a promising strategy. Despite the appreciable biocompatibility of the Mg stents, fast degradation hinders its vast clinical application [19,20]. For reducing the degradation rate, surface modification by surface coating is considered an efficient technique. Several surface coating techniques are used to achieve corrosion resistance, such as inorganic coating, chemical conversion, and organic coatings [[21], [22], [23]]. For a coating to be effective, it should be biocompatible and reduce the corrosion rate to an acceptable rate. Among the broad range of coatings, chemical conversion is considered an advantageous method offering simplicity, cost-effectiveness, and efficiency. Chemical conversion by treatment with hydrofluoric acid for the formation of magnesium fluoride (MgF2) improves the fast degradation of the Mg by reducing the corrosion rate [20]. Among the polymer coatings, Poly(l-lactide) (PLLA) and Polycaprolactone (PCL) are biodegradable polymers with good biocompatibility and excellent mechanical properties [20]. It has been reported previously PLLA has a better adhesion strength to the Mg substrate as compared to PCL [24]. However, the use of only polymer coating can have shortcomings such as acidic degradation products and undesired capillary pores that can limit the control of the degradation of Mg alloy. The acidic degradation products can also cause inflammation in the surrounding tissue environment of the implant [25]. The hydrophobicity of the polymer coating can hinder cell attachment [26]. HAp particles have high biocompatibility and due to the inorganic ions present in HAp, the degradation products are alkaline in nature. The hydrophilic nature of the HAp makes the cell attachment and proliferation favorable. If used alone on Mg substrate HAp coating can suffer fracture due to its brittle nature resulting in the lessen adhesion to the metal surface. Combining the polymer organic coating with inorganic HAp can assist to overcome the respective disadvantages while combining the advantages [18]. The inorganic alkaline degradation products can be neutralized by the polymeric acidic products and the intermolecular interactions between the different polymer layers and HAp can increase the adhesion strength of the coatings [27]. The degradation rate of the coating can be improved with increased bioactivity by combining polymeric organic coating with inorganic HAp.

Numerous examples of current usage of orthopedic implants include joints (hip, knee, ankle, and so on), bone spacers, or bone filling materials. In recent years, Mg-based biomaterial has received tremendous interest due to its excellent properties that are compatible with bone. To overcome these shortcomings, surface modification with biomolecules has attracted much attention. In healing bone defects, it is important to account for the degradation of scaffolds that have been used as implants to support the healing process. In order for bone ingrowth to take place, the degradation rate of the scaffolds should correspond to the rate of bone formation. Therefore, the ability to control the degradation rate of scaffolds is a key aspect and one of the advantages of using polyesters for scaffolding is that they offer more flexibility in controlling the degradation rate when compared to natural polymers. Moreover, it is necessary to take into consideration the change in scaffold structure over time as the porous structure evolves as the material degrades. Also, as mentioned earlier, aliphatic polyesters degrade via bulk erosion, which results in an accumulation of acidic byproducts and a reduction in pH, which can negatively affect nearby tissues. Therefore, it is important to evaluate the degradation rate and pH of the environment during the degradation process as well as to determine the structural changes that occur with scaffolds during this process. Previous studies have characterized the degradation of PLGA (50:50)/PCL scaffolds under physiological conditions.52 Polymeric scaffolds were reported to lose significant weight in dynamic conditions due to the rapid degradation of PLGA (50:50) over time, and once the PLGA(50:50) was fully degraded, degradation rate would slow down to match the rate of PCL.53 Additionally, their quantitative and qualitative SEM analyses showed that the microporosity of the scaffolds has evolved over time. In their proposed results, scaffolds containing two different polymers of PLGA (50:50) and PCL would allow for fine-tuning of the degradation rate of newly developed polyester-based scaffolds. In accordance with these results, the degradation rate of our scaffolds with PCL and PLGA (85:15) as slow-degrading components increased when PGA and PLGA (50:50) were added as fast-degrading components. It appears that adding the fast-degrading polyester to the slow-degrading polyester modulated the degradation rate of the newly formed polyester composite scaffolds. In addition, our SEM analysis indicated a consistent increase in the porosity of the scaffolds over the course of the degradation study as the fast-degrading component degrades. To address the issue of acidic environments after polyester degradation, each composite contained 20% TCP. It was shown in our previous study that the use of bioceramic TCP in composite scaffolds over 20% typically results in the separation of the polymer and ceramic phases and compromises the mechanical stability of the composite scaffold. According to our results, the addition of TCP to the compositions counterbalanced the acidic degradation of polyester composite scaffolds and increased the pH of degradation media. The results of our study are in agreement with those obtained by several other studies in which it was shown that basic degradation of ceramic particles can neutralize the acidic environment in which polyester degradation occurs.54-56 Overall, we were able to develop a polyester composite scaffold that exhibits mechanical properties similar to that of trabecular and cortical bone. The advantage offered by sintered microsphere is their pore interconnectivity and three- dimensional pore size despite that the porosity attained is less compared to other advanced techniques like electrospinning, rapid prototyping [11, 170]. Polymer sponge replication is one of the techniques used to produce porous three-dimensional ceramic scaffolds. In this technique, a polymer sponge composed of cellulose or polyurethane (template) is infiltered with ceramic (glass) slurry or suspension with certain viscosity. Susbequently, the ceramic slurry is allowed to dry and the polymeric template is removed by subjecting it to thermal degradation followed by ceramic sinteration. The sintering process helps in the formation of micropores and influences the mechanical strength of the scaffold. The developed ceramic sponge replicates the macrostructure and geometry of the original template [171, 172]. The scaffolds prepared by sponge replication has interconnected pore, controllable pore size but suffers with low mechanical strength which limits its application in load bearing defects [173]. The controlled porosity, along with the presence of bredigite, enhances mechanical strength, biocompatibility, and promotes the adhesion and proliferation of osteoblasts, rendering these freeze-dried scaffolds promising for applications in bone tissue engineering and repair [12]. An increase in porosity frequently results in a reduction of mechanical strength, as the area capable of bearing load is diminished; this correlation is generally characterized by a nonlinear nature. Characteristics such as pore size and morphology play a crucial role, with larger pore dimensions leading to a more pronounced loss of strength [22]. Porosity level will also enhance the degree of biocompatibility by providing an ideal environment for cell adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation in certain applications in bone and tissue engineering [23]. These support the implant's integration with the surrounding tissues because of better vascularization, with interconnected pore architectures allowing cell penetration, thereby improving the long-term biocompatibility of the implant [24]. On the other hand, excess porosity means a greater surface area, which may be more exposed to protein binding and bacterial colonization, promoting inflammation and implant failure. Pores size for biocompatibility differs for any particular application, but in the case of bone tissue engineering, 100-500 μm was found to be most optimal in facilitating sufficient ingrowth of bones [22, 24]. To address the challenges associated with bone tissue engineering, in this study, a multidisciplinary approach was employed to develop a novel scaffold for bone tissue engineering. The properties associated with biocompatibility and biodegradability concerning scaffold materials are of paramount significance, as they play a crucial role in establishing an environment that is conducive for the effective seeding of cells [25]. The scaffold was fabricated by combining three biocompatible and biodegradable materials: gelatin (Gel), polylactic acid (PLA), and bredigite. Gelatin, a denatured variant of collagen, is composed of a unique sequence of amino acids and is characterized by a high concentration of specific amino acids, including glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline, which closely resemble the structure of collagen [26]. Furthermore, gelatin exhibits properties similar to glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), allowing it to effectively mimic the architecture of the natural extracellular matrix (ECM) [26, 27]. In order to improve the mechanical characteristics of gelatin, PLA was chosen as a secondary component, recognized for its significant tensile strength and biodegradability properties [28, 29]. Additionally, bredigite, a mineral component, contributed to the scaffold's ability to form a strong bond with bone tissues. By strategically combining these materials, the researchers were able to create a highly functional scaffold that can potentially aid in the repair or regeneration of bone tissues [17-19]. In a study by Farzam Far et al., PLA/gel nanofiber scaffolds were formed using the phase separation method induced by heat and the electrospinning method. Combining platelet-enriched plasma with PLA scaffolds improved mechanical properties, porosity, cell attachment, and viability under laboratory conditions compared with pure PLA [28]. Nadi et al. developed a novel and functional scaffold by the PLA/ PCL composite polymers and strontium-doped bredigite nanoparticles that Ca was substituted by Sr, and the scaffolds exhibited the best potential to regenerate bone tissue [30]. The development of composite matrix scaffolds comprising a Gel/PLA composite reinforced with bredigite ceramic has been recognized for its advantages in bone tissue engineering. These scaffolds were fabricated and characterized, employing gelatin due to its biocompatibility and degradable nature, PLA for its biocompatible attributes, mechanical strength, and biological degradability, as well as bredigite for its robust formation of chemical bonds with bone tissues. This study ultimately assessed the scaffolds' bioactivity, biocompatibility, bonding capabilities, mechanical properties, and antibacterial effectiveness.

Based on the provided evidence, porosity significantly influences the degradation rate of ceramic/polymer composite scaffolds through several interconnected mechanisms:

1.  **Increased porosity accelerates degradation by enhancing fluid penetration and autocatalysis:** Higher porosity allows greater water penetration into the scaffold, facilitating hydrolytic degradation of the polymer matrix. This increased access also enables the accumulation of acidic degradation byproducts (common in polyesters like PLGA, PCL, PLA) within the pores, creating an autocatalytic environment that further accelerates degradation [1, 15].

2.  **Porosity evolution dynamically alters degradation kinetics:** As the fast-degrading component of a composite scaffold (e.g., PLGA 50:50) degrades, it increases the overall porosity and pore interconnectivity of the scaffold. This evolving porous structure further enhances medium penetration and the autocatalytic effect, leading to accelerated degradation. Once the fast-degrading component is depleted, the degradation rate slows to match the remaining slow-degrading polymer (e.g., PCL or PLGA 85:15) [1].

3.  **Lower porosity and smaller pore size decelerate degradation:** Scaffolds with lower porosity, smaller pores, or denser polymer networks (e.g., due to crosslinking or phosphorylation) limit solvent penetration and water absorption (swelling). This restricted access to water and reduced internal volume for acid accumulation slows down the hydrolytic degradation process [3, 7].

4.  **Porosity mediates the effect of ceramic additives on degradation:**
    *   Ceramic particles (e.g., TCP, HA, HNT) added to neutralize acidity or enhance bioactivity can alter porosity. Large particles (like β-TCP) can occlude pores, reducing pore size and potentially slowing degradation by limiting medium penetration [12].
    *   Conversely, the degradation of certain ceramics (e.g., bioactive glass) releases ions and increases porosity/nanoporosity over time, which can accelerate the degradation of the surrounding polymer matrix by increasing surface area and ion exchange [4].
    *   The presence of ceramics can also influence polymer chain packing and crystallinity at the interface, indirectly affecting degradation kinetics, though the specific effect depends on the ceramic type, particle size, and distribution [2, 12].

5.  **Porosity facilitates acid removal under dynamic conditions, mitigating autocatalysis:** High porosity and pore interconnectivity allow acidic degradation byproducts to diffuse out of the scaffold more readily, especially under dynamic fluid flow conditions. This removal counteracts the autocatalytic effect, significantly slowing down the degradation rate compared to static conditions where acids accumulate. The model in [15] confirms that high porosity combined with dynamic flow effectively reduces mass loss and molecular weight loss [15].

In summary, higher porosity generally accelerates the initial degradation rate of the polymer component by enhancing medium penetration and autocatalysis, while lower porosity slows it down. The dynamic evolution of porosity during degradation further modulates the rate. The interaction with ceramic additives adds complexity, as they can alter porosity, neutralize acids (reducing autocatalysis), or release ions that may influence degradation.

In healing bone defects, it is important to account for the degradation of scaffolds that have been used as implants to support the healing process. In order for bone ingrowth to take place, the degradation rate of the scaffolds should correspond to the rate of bone formation. Therefore, the ability to control the degradation rate of scaffolds is a key aspect and one of the advantages of using polyesters for scaffolding is that they offer more flexibility in controlling the degradation rate when compared to natural polymers. Moreover, it is necessary to take into consideration the change in scaffold structure over time as the porous structure evolves as the material degrades. Also, as mentioned earlier, aliphatic polyesters degrade via bulk erosion, which results in an accumulation of acidic byproducts and a reduction in pH, which can negatively affect nearby tissues. Therefore, it is important to evaluate the degradation rate and pH of the environment during the degradation process as well as to determine the structural changes that occur with scaffolds during this process. Previous studies have characterized the degradation of PLGA (50:50)/PCL scaffolds under physiological conditions.52 Polymeric scaffolds were reported to lose significant weight in dynamic conditions due to the rapid degradation of PLGA (50:50) over time, and once the PLGA(50:50) was fully degraded, degradation rate would slow down to match the rate of PCL.53 Additionally, their quantitative and qualitative SEM analyses showed that the microporosity of the scaffolds has evolved over time. In their proposed results, scaffolds containing two different polymers of PLGA (50:50) and PCL would allow for fine-tuning of the degradation rate of newly developed polyester-based scaffolds. In accordance with these results, the degradation rate of our scaffolds with PCL and PLGA (85:15) as slow-degrading components increased when PGA and PLGA (50:50) were added as fast-degrading components. It appears that adding the fast-degrading polyester to the slow-degrading polyester modulated the degradation rate of the newly formed polyester composite scaffolds. In addition, our SEM analysis indicated a consistent increase in the porosity of the scaffolds over the course of the degradation study as the fast-degrading component degrades. To address the issue of acidic environments after polyester degradation, each composite contained 20% TCP. It was shown in our previous study that the use of bioceramic TCP in composite scaffolds over 20% typically results in the separation of the polymer and ceramic phases and compromises the mechanical stability of the composite scaffold. According to our results, the addition of TCP to the compositions counterbalanced the acidic degradation of polyester composite scaffolds and increased the pH of degradation media. The results of our study are in agreement with those obtained by several other studies in which it was shown that basic degradation of ceramic particles can neutralize the acidic environment in which polyester degradation occurs.54-56 Overall, we were able to develop a polyester composite scaffold that exhibits mechanical properties similar to that of trabecular and cortical bone. The scaffolds were capable of developing a porous structure dynamically without compromising mechanical stability as the fast-degrading polyester components of the composite degraded slowly over time. Additionally, TCP, which mimics the structure of bone and increases the bioactivity of the scaffolds, was able to resolve the acidity issue related to the degradation of the polyester compound. It is essential that the scaffold in the BTE application be nontoxic to the cells and osteoinductive so that the MSCs can differentiate into preosteoblasts and initiate the formation of bone.
