The choice of PCL as the control group was based on its long-standing medical history as well as its low degradation rate that does not cause acidity over the course of the study. It was shown that cell attachment and proliferation were significantly greater on polyester composite scaffolds after adding TCP, as well as an increase in matrix mineralization and ALP production similar to the PCL positive control group. In the presence of TCP, cells were more viable and spread throughout the scaffolds compared to before TCP addition, confirming our original hypothesis that adding TCP neutralizes the acidity and enhances the biocompatibility of polyester composite scaffolds by neutralizing the acidity. It has been demonstrated that the addition of TCP and its controlled release by polyester degradation and formation of porous structures is extremely important, as scaffolds with TCP, particularly for PLGA (50:50)/PCL and PLGA (50:50)/PLGA (85:15), demonstrated a greater level of cell attachment and proliferation, ALP activity, and calcium deposition similar to the PCL control group without significant differences. The results of our study agree with those of other studies that indicated that adding hydroxyapatite (HA) to porous PLGA scaffolds results in a controlled release of HA and promotes superior bone marrow stromal cell adhesion, proliferation, and osteogenic differentiation compared with control groups.57 The expression levels of Collagen 1 (Coll 1) as an important component of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and bone sialoprotein (BSP) as a marker of mature osteoblasts were measured to further understand the osteochondral progression of hMSCs under osteoinduction. There are two types of proteins that make up the ECM which are collagens and noncollagenous proteins. Approximately 90% of the proteins in the bone matrix are collagens, mostly type I collagens. Noncollagenous proteins such as Osteopontin, Osteocalcin, Matrix gla protein, and BSP make up the bone extracellular matrix in lesser amounts but still contribute significantly to it.58 PLGA (50:50)/PCL and PLGA (50:50)/PLGA (85:15) composite scaffolds expressed high levels of both Coll 1 and BSP proteins after adding TCP, similar to the PCL control scaffold. According to our results, the addition of TCP to polyester composite scaffolds, with its porous structure developed as the fast-degrading component degrades, is effective for osteoblast maturation. Biomaterials used as a drug delivery vehicle or as a scaffold in tissue engineering must be biocompatible and biodegradable. It is also crucial that the degradation byproducts of the material are nontoxic and can be easily removed from the system. The in vivo evaluation of polymeric scaffold biocompatibility using animal models, particularly rats, has become a standard method for determining the tissue response to these scaffolds. As part of this method, histological examinations can be used to examine the inflammation of subcutaneous tissue and the thickness of the fibrous capsule, which are two of the most common host defense responses. In our previous research, we examined the biocompatibility of cellulose acetate (CA) as a natural polymer and compared it to PLGA, a synthetic polymer using a subcutaneous rat animal model. Histological and histomorphometric analysis revealed a higher foreign body response in PLGA after 8 weeks of implantation, while the immune response in CA was significantly lower.59 Our results showed that a change in the pH of the environment associated with the degradation of PLGA as an aliphatic polyester may cause an adverse immune response over time. In the present study, a polyester composite scaffold containing 20 wt.% TCP exhibited minimal tissue response, as indicated by thinner fibrous capsules and fewer macrophages than a composite without TCP. In addition, fibroblasts that produce new collagen and extracellular matrix were seen to increase significantly on polyester composite scaffolds containing TCP, confirming the effectiveness of the wound healing process.60 Based on this approach, we have demonstrated that adding TCP to polyester composite scaffolds significantly neutralized acidity of degradation byproducts and reduced foreign body responses as compared to the cases before adding TCP after 8 weeks of implantation, indicating a higher level of biocompatibility and a more successful healing process.
As noted earlier, bioactive glass is an ideal material for osteoconduction due to its ability to promote bone formation and degrade over time, releasing soluble calcium and silica ions in the process which are assumed to act as the activators of bone growth. Bioglass® is produced by a melting process, however scaffolds can also be formed using a sol-gel foam process which avoids any issues of crystallisation during sintering as with the melt-derived glasses and enhances the bioactivity of the resultant material [237-242]. It has been found that using a variety of particle size ranges and fibre diameters and foam textures allowed for the ideal dissolution properties of the bioglass to be attained [242-245]. The interconnected macropores (in excess of 100 μm) allow for bone ingrowth and the nanoporosity allows for the attachment of osteoprogenitor cells. In fact, there is evidence which indicates the biological and mechanical benefits of having a nanostructure in biomaterials since they are able to guide cell attachment, migration and differentiation [246, 247]. The formation of nanopores, such as those which are inherent to the sol-gel methods of glass fabrication, can be used to tailor the degradation process of the scaffold, since they dramatically increase the surface area available for cellular interaction [248]. However, as with CNTs, there remain concerns regarding the use of nanostructured materials in the body [249, 250]. As with bulk glasses and glass-ceramics, the development of glass-ceramic scaffolds are to try and overcome the limitations of glass scaffolds in terms of mechanical properties and to widen their applications beyond small defect sites and minor load-bearing applications [251-254]. These bioactive, biodegradable glass-ceramic scaffolds exhibit oriented microstructures and mechanical properties which can be tailored and are in the lower range for cortical bone along with controlled porosity [252-259]. The 3D foam-like glass-ceramic scaffolds are formed using polyurethane sponge as the sacrificial templates and silicate glass powders (produced via a melt-quenching process) as the final scaffold material. The scaffolds have great potential for bone reconstructive surgery, including load-bearing applications, due to the ease with which they can be produced and how their strength, bioactivity and bioresorption can be tailored. More recently, a study has been performed by this group observe the effect of adding silver ions to the surface of the scaffold to install antibacterial properties and broaden the effectiveness of the glass-ceramic scaffold [260, 261]. Alongside ceramic, glass-ceramic and bioglass scaffolds, composite scaffolds are also being investigated. Prior to the formation of composite scaffolds, degradable polymers were extensively researched for tissue engineering applications. They were selected due to their biological acceptance and controllable degradation rates. A recent review discussed the benefits and limitations of degradable polymer systems for use as scaffolds in tissue engineering [262]. The ability to seed and grow cells on the surfaces of such biodegradable polymers was shown to be vital to promoting tissue growth and bone remodelling. Therefore, in an attempt to mimic the natural system and provide enhanced bioactivity, biodegradation and mechanical properties, bioactive composite scaffolds based on bulk bioactive composites were developed [242]. Composites of degradable polymers reinforced with bioactive and biodegradable materials would ensure total resorption and replacement of the material by natural bone cells.

ans_rerank: Porosity significantly influences the degradation rate of ceramic/polymer composite scaffolds by modulating solvent penetration, surface area exposure, and degradation product diffusion. Higher porosity increases the scaffold's interaction with the aqueous environment, accelerating hydrolysis and mass loss due to greater water absorption and enhanced diffusion of acidic degradation byproducts [1], [5]. For example, chitosan/pectin cryogels with larger pores and higher porosity degraded faster due to increased solvent accessibility [1]. Similarly, dynamic degradation conditions combined with high porosity reduce autocatalytic effects by efficiently removing acidic monomers, further promoting degradation [5]. Conversely, reduced porosity from crosslinking or denser polymer networks (e.g., phosphorylated collagen/P-PCL scaffolds) limits solvent penetration and swelling, slowing degradation [2]. In composites like PCL/β-TCP, higher filler-induced porosity compromises mechanical strength but accelerates degradation in wet states due to aqueous media infiltration [7], [10]. Additionally, scaffolds incorporating fast-degrading polymers (e.g., PLGA) exhibit dynamically increasing porosity during degradation, which enhances hydrolysis rates [12], [15]. Thus, porosity directly impacts degradation kinetics by regulating environmental interactions and structural evolution.

question: What is the 'piezoelectric' property of PLLA and its biomedical relevance?
ground_truth: PLLA (in its shear piezoelectric form) generates an electrical charge under mechanical stress (piezoelectric coefficient d14 ~ 10 pC/N). This is relevant for bone scaffolds because natural bone is also piezoelectric. The stress-generated potential can stimulate osteoblasts and enhance bone growth, mimicking the physiological environment.

Besides naturally driven piezoelectric polymers, another class of biodegradable piezoelectric polymers is synthetically developed piezoelectric materials. Polylactic acid (PLA) and poly-l-lactic acid (PLLA) are two main synthetic biodegradable piezoelectric polymers that will be discussed in the next section, in addition to the other novel synthesized piezoelectric biopolymers. The PLA has unique piezoelectric properties as a replacement for the common inorganic and organic piezoelectric material.[140, 141] PLLA is another conformation of PLA containing l-stereoisomers. The piezoelectricity properties in both PLA and PLLA depend on crystallinity and molecular orientation. These polymers have a semi-crystalline structure with a natural chiral conformation that grants piezoelectricity. The electric dipoles of CO bonds with an aligned form and branched out of polymer backbone are responsible for piezoelectricity.[142, 143] The experiments revealed that the PLLA has piezoelectricity parallel to the z-axis with a d14 coefficient of 7-12 pC N−1.[144, 145] The stretching treatment in PLA and PLLA can orient the chains and enhance piezoelectricity. Smith et al.[146] measured the piezoelectric coefficient in the highly oriented nanowires grown in the anodized aluminum oxide (AAO) confined environment. The crystallinity of PLLA nanowires was improved by 70% with the nano-confinement method. In the measurements with the PFM, strong shear piezoelectricity was deflected from lateral signals along the nanowires. This deflection yields the value of d14 around 8 pC N−1. Curry et al.[22] fabricated a fully biodegradable piezoelectric sensor made by sandwiching the films of piezoelectric PLLA between molybdenum electrodes (Figure 4a). They studied the drawing effect on the piezoelectric properties of PLLA. The as-synthesized PLLA film shows three faces of (1 1 1), (2 0 0), and (1 1 0). As the drawing ratio increased, the (1 1 1) plane peak decreased in the PLLA X-ray diffraction (XRD) graph. This is reasoned by the transformation of the α phase of PLLA with the 103 helical conformations to the ß phase with the 31 helical conformations. The best piezoelectric property was obtained by the drawing ratio of around 2.5 to 4.5. According to this study, it was concluded that the CO dipoles could align uniaxially by drawing, hence effectively improving the piezoelectricity of PLLA. The alignment of PLLA could also be achieved with the help of electrospinning of aligned nanofibers, resulting in macro piezoelectricity. For instance, Zhu et al.[147] fabricated PLLA porous nanofibrous scaffolds with aligned morphology via melt drawing. They realized the piezoelectricity property in the nanofibers with the size 100 nm and 40 µm. Furthermore, the increase of piezoelectricity was observed with the increase of uniaxial force upon the nanofibers. In another inceptive study, Curry et al.[148] demonstrated a biodegradable device that worked as a force sensor for measuring physiological pressure and an ultrasonic transducer to assist drug delivery and blood-brain barrier opening. The biodegradable device was made of nanofibers of piezoelectric PLLA, PLA encapsulation, and molybdenum electrodes (Figure 4b). Wu et al.[149] fabricated an ultrasonic-driven biodegradable piezoelectric nanogenerator for sustainable electrical signal transmission. This device consisted of fully biodegradable piezoelectric poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV)/Poly (lactic acid) (PLLA)/potassium sodium niobate (KNN) as functional layer (Figure 4c). The voltage and current output levels were increased to 6 V, and 0.5 µA, respectively, by a 50% increase in KNN amount. Yousry et al.[150] developed a conformable shear mode ultrasonic transducer based on bioresorbable piezoelectric PLLA nanofibers. A wide range of frequency (500 kHz) was applied to evaluate the electromechanical responses over the macroscopic area of the transducer. The fabricated biodegradable ultrasonic transducer showed a high level of sensitivity in detecting imperfections in air and liquid. Further, the developed PLLA does not require electric poling to impart piezoelectricity because the shear mode originates from the chemical structure of PLLA itself. The shear mode ultrasonic transducer based on PLLA shows great potential for underwater structural health monitoring applications. Figure 4d schematically presents the underwater structural health monitoring technique with the help of ultrasonic shear waves utilizing shear piezoelectric ceramic-based transducers compared with transducers based on shear biodegradable piezoelectric polymers. The shear mode piezoelectric polymer-based transducers contain in-plane mechanical coupling, not needing electrical poling, are low profile, and shapes conformal; shear ceramic piezoelectrics are not shaped conformal, needed electrical poling, and have a high profile. Zhang et al.[53] demonstrated electrospun-based PDLA/PLLA nanofibers (Figure 4e, left) that improve filtration efficiencies for removing small particulate matter (PM). The surface charges generated from piezoelectric PLLA membrane (Figure 4e, right) with controllable porosity demonstrated great improvement in capturing small-sized particles (i.e., PM2.5). Additionally, they demonstrated the fabrication optimization parameters, such as solution concentration and electrospinning time to improve the quality factor, up to 4.6% compared to conventional 3 m respirator filters. Le et al.[151] fabricated a highly efficient, recyclable, self-sustaining, and humidity-resistant air filtration membrane utilizing biodegradable PLLA nanofibers with stable piezoelectricity and long-term biodegradability (Figure 4f). Based on the effect of aeolian vibrations, the self-charged PLLA nanofibers membrane (Figure 4g) permits the joined impact of mechanical sieving, and it increases electrostatic adsorption to eliminate particulate matter (PMs). In the current studies, researchers are developing synthetic biodegradable piezoelectric polymers utilizing natural piezoelectric materials. For instance, Yang et al.[51] demonstrated a self-assembly-based and wafer-scale approach to fabricate a PVA-glycine-PVA sandwich structure. Several examples of biodegradable piezoelectric materials derive from various sources, with different structures and degradation pathways. Generally, these materials can be divided into synthetic polymers and natural piezoelectric ones. The former include poly lactic acid (PLA) and poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA, a conformation of PLA containing only the L-stereoisomer), polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), poly-γ-benzyl-L-glutamate (PBLG), or poly-γ-methyl-L-glutamate (PMLG). PLA is synthesized by polycondensation of lactic acid (LA) monomers, or by ring-opening polymerization of lactides.[45] To obtain the pure L-stereoisomer (PLLA), the synthesis should start from the optically pure L-LA isomer; this is attained only when LA is synthesized by microbial fermentation. The piezoelectric properties observed in PLA and PLLA derive from their semicrystalline structure, characterized by a chiral conformation and the alignment of electric dipoles in the CO groups along the polymer backbone. In the thermodynamically stable α-form of PLA, the CO groups exhibit random orientation, resulting in negligible piezoelectric effects. Conversely, in the β-crystalline form, the CO groups align along the main chain, imparting piezoelectric properties to the material.[46] Achieving this orientation in PLA and PLLA necessitates specific processing techniques, such as thermal stretching or electrospinning, which promote the rearrangement of molecular chains along the stretching direction. PLLA exhibits piezoelectricity predominantly along the Z-axis, characterized by a d14 coefficient typically ranging from 9 to 11 pC N−1,[47] which is notably lower than inorganic piezoelectric materials. Nevertheless, PLLA continues to be extensively utilized in various biomedical applications owing to its biocompatibility and biodegradability. Furthermore, post-treatment procedures aimed at enhancing its molecular orientation and crystallinity can potentially increase its piezoelectric performance (d14 coefficient) up to 20 pC N−1. The piezoelectric properties of PLLA also depend on its optical purity and molecular weight. Tajitsu demonstrated that PLLA with a lower D-isomer content and high molecular weight might result in films with a higher piezoelectric response.[48] Similarly, Schönlein et al. showed that by increasing the D-content from <1% up to 12%, the d14 decreases from 3.7 ± 0.3 pC N−1 to 0.[49] PHB is a biodegradable polyester that belongs to the class of polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs), naturally occurring biopolymers synthesized by microorganisms under conditions of nutrient limitation.[50] The piezoelectric features of PHA-based materials stem from the presence of an asymmetric carbon atom linked to a polar oxygen group.[51] In the case of pure PHB electrospun nanofibers, the piezoelectric coefficients are ≈3.25 pC N−1 (d31) and 4.13 pC N−1 (d33).[50] The molecular weight of PHB impacts its piezoelectric properties; in fact, it has been observed that a decrease in the molecular weight from 803 to 102 kDa resulted in a lower number of piezoelectric domains in PHB films, leading to a lower piezoresponse.[52]

This paper presents for the first time that poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA) nanofibers can show the piezoelectricity along the fiber direction (d33) by using an electrospinning method. First, the electrospun fiber bundles are characterized by scanning electron microscope, X-ray, and piezoelectric coefficient measurements. The data show that the supercritical CO2 treatment can greatly enhance the piezoelectricity of electrospun PLLA fibers, which can be resulting from the increased crystallinity of the fibers. Later, it is found that the electrospun PLLA fiber can generate a current of 8 pA and a voltage of 20 mV by a simple push-release process. Further, a single PLLA fiber-based blood pulse sensor is also fabricated and tested and shows around a 2 pA output for blood pulse. Due to easy fabrication and relatively simple structure, this device enables a broad range of promising future applications in the medical sensor area. As a widely used biopolymer, poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA) based piezoelectric polymers have attracted a great deal of research attention due to their biocompatibility, flexibility, and relatively large piezoelectric coefficient.1-4 Previously, many researchers have utilized a uniaxial stretching method to process PLLA film and show piezoelectricity along the shear direction of PLLA film.5-7 Recently, we reported that electrospun poly(γ-benzyl-α, L-glutamate fibers can show piezoelectricity along the d33 direction and can be used in microphone sensor applications.8-10 In this paper, we report for the first time that the electrospun PLLA nanofibers can show piezoelectricity along the fiber length direction (d33) after electrospinning. Based on this property, electrospun PLLA fibers show a wide range of promising future applications in the areas of nanogenerators and diagnostic sensors. Since the 1990s, it has been found that, by using a uniaxial stretching method or a magnetic field, the main carbon chain of PLLA material can easily be oriented in a parallel or antiparallel direction to show piezoelectricity along the shear direction.11, 12 Recently, many researchers have used the electrospinning method to fabricate PLLA nanofibers for biomedical applications, such as scaffolding, tissue engineering, and filters.13, 14 In 2012, Sencadas et al. have studied the piezoelectric properties in a PLLA single fiber along the diameter direction of the fiber.15 However, the conformation structure of PLLA material mostly exhibits the α or β form, with a 103 or 31 helical structure, respectively.16-19 Normally, the two adjacent main carbon chain will arrange along the antiparallel direction. Due to the helical structure, the dipole components along the perpendicular direction of the main carbon chain will cancel out each other.19 Therefore, it is hard to exhibit piezoelectricity in PLLA material along the diameter direction and the piezoelectricity will only exhibit along the shear direction. In this paper, we report for the first time that the dipoles inside the PLLA nanofibers can be twisted toward the fiber direction using an electrospinning method. During the process, the shear force generated from a high DC electric field is applied to a PLLA polymer solution and all the dipole component along the main carbon chain can be aligned along the fiber direction during the electrospinning process. Therefore, the electrospun PLLA fibers will show the piezoelectricity along the fiber direction (d33).

The biomedical device can function as an actuator, pressure sensor, and other designs that collect bio-physiological signals and detect vital information.[213-215] Biomedical devices are in contact with external or internal tissues, and after their operation, they usually stay in the biological environment, which increases the concern about immunological toxicity or electronic waste. Recently, biomedical devices have been more sustainable and environmentally friendly than old-fashioned non-biodegradable devices. Decomposable piezoelectric-based devices can be designed based on biodegradable materials for advanced biomedical applications.[216-220] Biodegradable and piezoelectric polymers exhibit higher flexibility than inorganic materials; thus, they can show deformation under low forces. Due to this property, they can be utilized in applications where they should be conformally wrapped around the curved tissue for measurement. Besides, the biodegradability of the sensor is advantageous in acute and short-term biomedical applications (e.g., wound healing and bone regeneration). Curry et al.[22] fabricated a force sensor to detect bio-physiological pressures/forces with controlled biodegradability and piezoelectricity. Films of piezoelectric PLLA were made by hot compression molding followed by stretching/drawing and annealing for 8 h at 90 °C. In order to sharpen the device's piezoelectricity, the film of PLLA was cut at 45o angle, concerning the stretching direction. To fabricate a device based on a single layer of piezoelectric material, processed PLLA film was sandwiched between molybdenum electrodes. A sensor design based on multiple layers of processed PLLA is shown in Figure 4a. Deposition of the iron/magnesium combination was done on the film, and it was then folded over and compressed between the electrodes of molybdenum to achieve a multilayer design. After sandwiching the piezoelectric film between electrodes, rectangular sheets of Poly (Lactic acid) (PLA) with a thickness of 100 µm were utilized to cover the sandwiched area, and a PLA-based hot sealing bag and glue were used to seal the sheets. As demonstrated in Figure 6i, after keeping the sensor at an elevated temperature of 74 °C for 56 days, the sensor exhibited complete degradation. Implantation of a biodegradable piezoelectric PLLA sensor for detecting the diaphragmatic contraction pressure inside the intestinal cavity of the mouse is demonstrated in Figure 10a. A distinct pressure response was noticed when the mouse was conscious and breathing under a regular dose of anesthesia. The pressure response was utterly depressed after the mouse overdosed on anesthetics (Figure 10b). The developed device can measure pressure in the range of 0-18 kPa.

Based solely on the provided evidence, the piezoelectric property of PLLA and its biomedical relevance are as follows:

1.  **Piezoelectric Property of PLLA**:
    *   PLLA exhibits piezoelectricity due to its semi-crystalline structure and natural chiral conformation. The key mechanism involves the alignment of electric dipoles associated with the C=O bonds branching out from the polymer backbone. [1, 2, 3, 4]
    *   This piezoelectricity is primarily shear-mode, oriented parallel to the z-axis, characterized by the d₁₄ coefficient. Reported d₁₄ values range from 7-12 pC N⁻¹, 9-11 pC N⁻¹, or up to 20 pC N⁻¹ with optimized processing. [1, 2, 3, 4]
    *   The piezoelectric effect depends critically on molecular orientation and crystallinity. The thermodynamically stable α-crystalline phase (with 10₃ helical conformation) has randomly oriented dipoles and negligible piezoelectricity. Processing (like stretching or electrospinning) transforms it into the piezoelectric β-crystalline phase (with 3₁ helical conformation), where C=O groups align along the main chain. [3, 4]
    *   Uniaxial stretching (optimal drawing ratio ~2.5-4.5) or electrospinning aligns the molecular chains and C=O dipoles, significantly enhancing piezoelectricity. Higher optical purity (lower D-isomer content) and higher molecular weight also improve the piezoelectric response. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12]
    *   Unlike PVDF, stretched PLLA films do not require electrical poling to impart piezoelectricity; the shear mode originates inherently from its chemical structure after orientation. [1, 2, 6, 8]

2.  **Biomedical Relevance**:
    *   PLLA's biocompatibility, biodegradability, and inherent piezoelectricity make it highly suitable for transient implantable biomedical devices that degrade after fulfilling their function, avoiding long-term toxicity concerns or electronic waste. [3, 4, 10, 11]
    *   **Sensors:** Used to fabricate biodegradable force and pressure sensors for measuring physiological signals. Examples include sensors implanted in mice to detect diaphragmatic contraction pressure (measuring range 0-18 kPa) and blood pulse sensors. [10, 11, 5]
    *   **Transducers:** Developed into conformable shear-mode ultrasonic transducers. These are sensitive in air and liquid, enabling applications like physiological sensing (e.g., pressure measurement), drug delivery assistance (e.g., blood-brain barrier opening), and underwater structural health monitoring. Their flexibility allows conformal wrapping around curved tissues. [1, 2, 10, 11]
    *   **Tissue Engineering/Regenerative Medicine:** Piezoelectric PLLA-based scaffolds (including self-charged scaffolds and those combined with magnetoelectric nanoparticles) have been used to stimulate cell proliferation and differentiation (e.g., osteoblasts, neuronal cells) and induce tissue regeneration (e.g., skin regeneration), potentially leveraging interactions with cellular calcium channels. Biodegradability is advantageous for wound healing and bone regeneration. [13, 15]
    *   **Other Applications:** PLLA nanofibers are used in air filtration membranes for reusable, humidity-resistant face masks, leveraging piezoelectric charge generation to capture particulate matter (e.g., PM2.5, viruses, bacteria) via electrostatic adsorption and mechanical sieving, offering an eco-friendly solution. Afterward, their most recent and novel applications in physiological sensing, transducers, biomedical devices, and regenerative medicine are comprehensively discussed. The topics are outlined in Figure 1, where the review aims to understand the different categories of biodegradable piezoelectric polymers and their application in fabricating implantable devices for advanced biomedical applications. Filler-Enhanced Piezoelectricity of Poly-L-Lactide and Its Use as a Functional Ultrasound-Activated Biomaterial Due to their recyclability, biocompatibility, and biodegradability,1-4 Poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA) fibers and textiles have been widely used in the field of medical device,5, 6 smart wearable devices,7 flexible sensors,8 and so on. More attention has been paid due to their controllable mechanical, piezoelectric and wettability properties as the growing application of PLLA film materials.9, 10 Electrospinning is a simple and effective technique for the fabrication of membranes composed of submicron/nanofibers.11, 12 These fibers can make the membranes to realize unique properties, such as high porosity,13 large specific surface area,14 and good mechanical properties.15 The parameters of electrospinning process,16 such as spinning speed, applied voltage, fluid supply speed, conductivity, and polymer solution concentration,17 are significant for the characterization of nanofiber membranes. By the precise control of the parameters, the properties of electrospinning nanofibers can be optimized to meet the requirement of specific applications. These characteristics, piezoelectric properties, mechanical properties and wettability of PLLA nanofiber membranes prepared by electrospinning are affected by the parameters of spinning process. For example, the spinning humidity can affect the surface topography,18 and the spinning voltage can affect the degree of polarization,19 which can further change the piezoelectric properties. The concentration and molecular weight can be changed to tune the fiber diameter and roughness20 which are correlated with mechanical properties and wettability.21 However, the quality of electrospun fiber membrane is not only affected by the parameters in the electrospinning process, the solution parameters also play a key role. Together, these parameters determine the microstructure, physical properties, and performance of the fiber membrane for the final application.

The piezoelectric property of poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) arises from the alignment of electric dipoles, primarily from C=O bonds, within its semi-crystalline structure. Electrospinning induces longitudinal piezoelectricity (d₃₃ mode) by aligning dipoles along the fiber axis under high DC electric fields, overcoming the inherent dipole cancellation in helical conformations [1,2]. This contrasts with shear-mode piezoelectricity (d₁₄) in stretched films, where polarization occurs perpendicular to stress [5,6].  

Biomedically, PLLA's piezoelectricity enables:  
- **Implantable sensors**: Detecting physiological pressures (e.g., arterial pulse, diaphragmatic contraction) with sensitivities down to 0.2 kPa [3,10,12].  
- **Self-powered wearables**: Monitoring vital signs (e.g., pulse, muscle movement) without external power, leveraging mechanosensitivity up to 22 V/N [4,11].  
- **Tissue engineering**: Scaffolds with piezoelectric signals accelerate bone regeneration and wound healing by mimicking bioelectric fields [14,15].  
- **Air filtration**: Piezoelectric nanofiber masks capture particulate matter (PM₂.₅) via electrostatic adsorption, reusable after disinfection [14,15].  

Its biodegradability and biocompatibility ensure minimal toxicity, making PLLA suitable for transient devices like ultrasonic transducers and drug delivery systems [6,13,14].

ground_truth: A reduction in melt viscosity (or increase in Melt Flow Index, MFI) indicates a reduction in molecular weight due to thermal or hydrolytic degradation. Since viscosity is related to molecular weight by a power law, even a small drop in molecular weight causes a noticeable drop in viscosity, signaling process-induced degradation.

As a kind of linear aliphatic polyesters synthesized by the ring-opening polymerization of lactides, PLA is typically derived from corn starch fermentation,1 and has good mechanical properties, thermal plasticity, biocompatibility, and ease of fabrication.2 These characteristics enable PLA as a promising polymer for various applications.3 Another feature of PLA is the good safety upon exposure to heat. For example, it does not produce any toxic nitrogen oxide gases and only one third of the combustible heat of polyolefins is generated when it is burned, so it does not damage the incinerator and provides significant energy savings.4 However, the instable processability of PLA needs to be concerned, that is, thermo-oxidative, hydrolytic degradations, and so on. The instability of PLA usually leads to break the polymer chains, as a result to decrease its molecular weight.5 And it would further result in a deterioration of rheological properties, which should be avoided for a processing purpose, especially when high levels of melt viscosity and strength are required. For example, the viscosity and strength of material has significant influence on their final performance when they are in blow molding, blow film, extrusion, and foaming. As is well known, PLA has a very low viscosity and melt strength, so the fabricated films are far away from stability and close to rupturing during blow-film process; and the lower melt tension is not beneficial to obtain satisfying products during blow-molding process. To overcome such shortcomings, attempts to improve the melt rheological properties of PLA have motivated considerable research efforts. One of the most important techniques is increasing the molecular weight of PLA, which can efficiently improve the intrinsic melt intensity of PLA. However, the productivity would decrease for high molecular PLA because of the prolonged reaction time, and the degradation or the color changing is usually inevitable. Furthermore, some investigations on the free radical branching/crosslinking of PLA has been also carried out in the melt mixing process in an extruder or in a kneader with the presence of trace amounts of various peroxides (served as radical initiators).6-8 In these process, branching or crosslinking reaction of PLA molecule chain can happen to some extent because of the reaction of capturing hydrogen by peroxides. However, some of new problems would appear because of the high reactivity of peroxides, such as the excessive crosslinking reaction and the degradation of PLA, which is hard to avoid during such processing. Another method is incorporating some new functional groups onto the PLA backbone to improve its melt viscosity, which paves the way to prepare composites, coated items, and composites/alloys. For example, multi-isocyanate9 and multi-epoxide10 are often used to endow PLA functional groups through copolymerizing reactions during reactive extrusion process, but a good knowledge on the reaction and control of polymerization during manufacturing are necessary. However, the copolymerization reaction is often difficult to realize anticipative results because of the difference of reactive activity between lactide and copolymerizing ester, and the melt intensity of PLA can be seldom improved. Therefore, extensive investigations on polymer blend technology have been also carried out. Blending PLA with another immiscible or miscible polymer with higher melt viscosity is perhaps a less expensive and practical alternative way to prepare a variety of useful composites and alloys. Blends of PLA with PCL,11, 12 atactic poly[(R, S)-3-hydroxybutyrate],13 poly(ethylene succinate),14 hydrophilic poly(vinyl alcohol),15 poly(methyl methacrylate),16 poly(ethylene glycol),17 and poly(vinylphenol),18 have been investigated. Most of the above studies revealed that blending PLA with other polymers can substantially modify the mechanical and thermal properties, degradation rate, and permeability, but few distinct evidence of the improvement for melt viscosity can be found in these blends. Recently, Jiang et al.19 showed that the melt elasticity of the biodegradable PLA/poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) blends increased with the concentration of PBAT increasing via blending process, but the viscosity increase is limited. Carboxyl-ended polyester (CP) and solid epoxy (SE) have been widely used in polyester powder coating because they can form a crosslinking structure, and the viscosity of PLA will increase after in situ crosslink if CP and SE are added into the PLA matrix. In this article, CP and SE are used as the modifier of PLA to improve the melt rheological properties of PLA. Compared with the above-mentioned methods (increasing molecular weight, branching/crosslinking and incorporating new functional groups into PLA backbone), this method with CP/SE as the modifier has some outstanding advantages. For instance, the reaction temperature of CP/SE is close to the processing temperature of PLA; CP/SE has a high melt viscosity after reaction, and abundant functional end groups, which are easily accessible. With the unique crosslinking structure after reaction, CP/SE results in the different dispersion phase size and stereo hindrance for the linear polymer. Furthermore, the abundance of hydroxyl end groups attached to CS/SE may have some H-bonding interactions with PLA.20 Thus, it is reasonable to expect that the incorporation of CP/SE into PLA may bring about either the improved melt viscosity or the increased strength.
In this work, the influence of melt compounding and incorporation of talc on a commercial grade of poly (lactic acid) was studied. The neat material was mixed, for different backflow times, to monitor the effect of processing on this resin. The apparent viscosity of the PLA decreases with compounding time, as the material is subject to thermo mechanical degradation. The elastic modulus of neat PLA, was measured on injection molded dog shape tensile bars. The elastic modulus slightly increases with compounding time, probably because of the molecular weight reduction due to degradation. Concerning the incorporation of talc, it was found that it increases the viscosity measured during the compounding, but it also enhances the stability of the material viscosity during the mixing. Furthermore, the talc, acting as a nucleating agent, has a strong effect on crystallization kinetics, so that by adding 1 % of micrometric talc crystallization the half time reduces one order of magnitude with respect to the pure PLA processed in the same way.

The morphological changes of PLA and PLA/AES blends before and after annealing were analyzed using SEM analysis and correlated with the mechanical properties. Figure 4a,b shows SEM images (magnifications of 1000×) of fracture surfaces of PLA and PLA/AES blends. A distinct fracture morphology was observed between PLA and PLAT, indicating that the heat treatment affected the deformation mechanism. PLA fracture surface shows a smooth texture characteristic of a fragile material. In addition, well-defined and delineated striations are observed, with alternating smooth regions. Although PLA exhibits brittle behavior, the fracture aspect indicates some resistance to crack propagation. Contrastingly, the morphology of PLAT indicated a more homogeneous fracture, with no separation of smooth regions by striations. The PLAT deformation mechanism favored rapid crack propagation under mechanical impact stress, confirming the trend shown later in Figure 9. The annealing heat treatment of PLAT formed a structure with a high level of crystallinity and large spherulites, resulting in a smoother fracture surface. The higher crystallinity is particularly detrimental to the mechanical behavior on impact since the number of inter-spherulite binding molecules decreases as the size of the spherulites increases.59 As a result, crack propagation occurs more rapidly, confirming the lower impact performance of PLAT. Figure 4(c,e,g,i,k,m) shows the fracture surface of PLA/AES blends (70:30%) without annealing treatment as a function of DCP. The PLA/AES blends show phase separation, with AES particles dispersed in the PLA matrix. This morphology is typical of immiscible blends, even showing voids between phases that indicate pulled-out AES particles (see red circles). However, the existence of refined AES particles adhered to the PLA matrix indicates a partial affinity between these phases (see white circles). The affinity is probably due to the polar interactions of the AES acrylonitrile fraction with the PLA carbonyl. The acrylonitrile/carbonyl interaction provides some level of compatibilization through secondary interactions, which is crucial to strengthen the PLA/AES interface and contribute to toughening. The average AES particle size reduced as DCP concentration increased in the PLA/AES blend, probably due to crosslinking. The crosslinking of the PLA/AES blend promoted higher adhesion of the dispersed phase, which suggests a more prominent molecular entanglement between PLA and AES, as discussed in torque rheometry and MFI. However, the morphology of the PLA/AES/DCP blends revealed a critical DCP content to optimize wettability between PLA and AES, as seen in Figure 4k. Incorporating 0.8 phr DCP into the PLA/AES blend promoted the formation of a more stable morphology with refined, adhered, well-distributed, and dispersed AES particles. Meanwhile, the PLA/AES/DCP (0.8 phr) blend had a higher uniformity in the particle size of the dispersed phase and a marked void reduction. These observations evidence that the PLA/AES interface withstood and distributed stresses more effectively, indicating an optimized crosslinking process with 0.8 phr DCP. The compatibility within the PLA/AES/DCP (0.8 phr) blend revealed by the morphology of the fracture surface confirms the high impact strength and elongation at break results of this system, which were superior to the other materials (see Figure 8 and S2). Therefore, even though there is an increasing crosslinking reaction in PLA and AES with DCP presence, as evidenced by torque rheometry, there is a critical DCP content to form free radicals and optimize the degree of crosslinking.

Table 2 summarizes the relative viscosity of the as-received PLA and of all the investigated formulations. The relative viscosity of the as-received PLA is 2.5, in agreement with the datasheet provided by the supplier. All the formulations show a reduction in the relative viscosity after being processed by compounding extrusion. The measured relative viscosity varies in the range of 2.25-2.39. In particular, the formulation #4 that does not involve talc feature a relative viscosity of 2.31 (approximately 0.2 lower than that of as-received PLA). The relative viscosity of the formulation #4 is presumably affected by thermal degradation during compounding extrusion at high temperature. Degradation can reduce significantly the mean molecular weight of the PLA in it and, thus, cause the concurrent decrease in the relative viscosity of the formulation. The formulations #1, #2, and #3 that involve talc behave in the same fashion. The formulation #2 that involves talc and maleic anhydride (MAH) grafted PLA (PLA-MA) has the greatest relative viscosity after extrusion compounding. This result can be attributed to the effect of the expected interactions of the PLA-MA chain extender with the talc and Poly(Lactic Acid) (PLA). In fact, the chain extender is designed to lead to an increase in the molecular weight and/or promote branching of the polymeric chains.8 This can, in turn, determine an increase in the mean hydrodynamic volume of the PLA macromolecules in the solution and, therefore, the increase in the relative viscosity. The formulation #3 that involves talc and glycidyl methacrylate (GMA) grafted PLA (PLA-GMA) has a lower relative viscosity. This result can be ascribed to effectiveness of the PLA-GMA chain extender, which is probably less active to combine with both talc and PLA. The formulation #1 that involves talc alone features the smallest relative viscosity, this being ascribable to thermal degradation and lack of chain extenders to restore the initial molecular structure of the polymer. Barrier properties of the screw caps against UV-vis radiations were evaluated registering light transmission spectra on biodegradable screw caps by the use of UV-vis spectrophotometry (V670, Jasco, Easton, MD). The optical system includes a Rowland off-circle arrangement, a single monochromator, with a double beam type. The spectral bandwidth is 1 nm. The range of wavelength investigated was from 190 to 1,000 nm, with a scan speed of 1,000 nm/min, a slew speed of 24,000 nm/min, and a step of 0.5 nm. The analysis was conducted as a single measurement on a cap sample of each formulation. The top flat part of the cap was selected to cut out the slabs used as samples. All the investigated formulations were characterized by an equal ratio of PBAT to PLA. The concentrations of PBAT in the PLA were suggested by the general need to improve the flexibility of the material as much as possible, without becoming the prevalent material. Blend flexibility is of paramount importance in the injection molding of screw caps with “torn-off” ejection in order to avoid damage to the undercuts, specifically the flattening of the screw threads as mentioned in Section 1. During extrusion compounding, the three biodegradable blends were processed without any significant problem. The large presence of PBAT inside the formulations conferred higher elasticity to the molten materials, thus overcoming the typical brittleness of the as-is PLA. The elasticity of the molten PLA was particularly visible from the processing of AT1 formulation, where a continuous production was allowed without the rupture of the extruded string occurred. This behavior was observed even if no melt strength enhancer was added to the AT1 compound. This result is in good agreement with the experimental findings of Gu and coworkers.[20 ] They demonstrated that the extrusion of PBAT in blend with PLA would lead to a product characterized by a higher storage modulus, G′, indicative of a higher viscosity as well as a broader deformation range characterized by an elastic behavior over large processing ranges.[20 ] Moreover, an increase in screw torque was detected during extrusion compounding of the biodegradable blends herein investigated, more strictly related to the content of melt strength enhancer. In particular, the screw torque measured during compounding extrusion of the formulation AT1 was the lowest, while the screw torques measured during compounding extrusion of the formulation AT2 and AT3 were found to be progressively increasing. The increase in screw torque for the formulation AT2 and, even more, for the formulation AT3 is indicative of an increase in melt viscosity of the polymeric material. The found values are in accordance with the increase in the content of the acrylate-based chain extender for each formulation. Indeed, melt strength enhancers have the role of reacting and/or entangling to the main chain of PLA with the aim to enhance strength and thermal resistance of the molten polymer.[21, 22 ] Therefore, the higher is the concentration of the acrylate-based chain extender such as in the formulation AT2 and, even more, in AT3, the higher is expected the viscosity melt blend during compounding extrusion. Consequently, higher would be the resulting screw torque measured during compounding extrusion (Table 4). Pellets of AT1, AT2, and AT3 achieved by compounding extrusion featured a smooth surface. They were white in color (due to the massive presence of the TiO2 in the formulations), dense with sharp edges, without the occurrence of any defect, such as voids or bubbles, inside the plastic material (Figure 2). The three formulations exhibited a different behavior during processing by injection molding. Due to the difference in the concentration of the acrylate-based chain extenders, the process parameters for injection molding of the formulation AT1 were different from the conditions applied for the injection molding of AT2 and AT3. Specifically, the blends AT2 and AT3, being characterized by a higher concentration of the acrylate-based chain extenders, required a higher processing temperature (at least 10-20°C more, in each barrel section) and slightly longer cooling time (Table 3).

Mechanical Recycling of New and Challenging Polymer Systems: A Brief Overview Biobased and biodegradable bioplastics provide several possibilities for an improved end-of-life with respect to fossil counterparts,[1-3] because in many cases they can be mechanically or chemically recycled[4-6] and, when it will be no more possible, they can be composted (organically recycled) contributing to soil fertility. Hence, they offer a full recyclability.[7] PLA, being both biobased and biodegradable, is currently applied in packaging and tableware applications. Thus, investigating its recyclability by reprocessing is an interesting topic in nowadays research.[8, 9] In the Castro Aguirre et al. review[10] the end-of-life scenario for this polymer is considered in all its aspects, considering also environmental footprint and Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). Regarding the LCA approach applied to the polymer end of life, for both PLA and starch-based bioplastics and using different recycling methods (incineration, composting and anaerobic digestion) Piemonte[11] showed that, compared with the mechanical recycling process, the other methods, like chemical recycling, are clearly underperforming from the environmental point of view. It is reported that the main issue in mechanical recycling of PLA is the decrease in its molecular weight and the consequent worsening of its mechanical properties after several processing cycles, linked to its hydrolytic and thermal stability.[12] Elsawya et al.[13] indicated the hydrolysis during processing as the main issue also in the recovery and recycling of post-industrial scraps generated during the use of PLA in packaging molding. Badia et al.[14] evidenced that reprocessing of PLA induces also an increase in crystallization during cooling as a function of the injection cycles number. This behavior was explained by the higher chain mobility of shorter chains due to the occurring of chain scission during injection. Bruster et al.[15] studied the mechanical recycling of plasticized PLA by reprocessing. By a multiscale approach it was assessed that, in the case of five successive processing cycles including extrusion and compression-molding applied to a lab-developed grade of acrylated poly(ethylene glycol) (acryl-PEG) plasticized PLA, the tensile and impact properties significantly decreased. Therefore, in dependence of chemical structure, plasticizers can induce chain scission. More recently Beltran et al.[16] melt compounded and compression molded a commercial grade PLA without any additive, then subjected to different treatments simulating recycling and concluded that, despite the slight degradation of PLA, the impact of the different simulated mechanical recycling processes on the final properties is limited. Several methodologies can be adopted to recycle PLA, to obtain different final products. The melt recycling of PLA plastic waste to produce biodegradable PLA fibers by a melt spinning process was studied by considering melt spinning quality, mechanical, structural, thermal, morphological and dyeing properties of the PLA fiber samples.[17] Based on the achieved results, the melt spinning of PLA fibers from recycled wastes with acceptable properties is possible since the hydrolysis of PLA can be limited or overcome thanks to an accurate drying. Moreover the use of chain extenders is reported to modulate the melt viscosity of PLA and its blends, as shown by Najfi et al.[18] that investigated the effectiveness of three different chain extenders: polycarbodiimide(PCDI), tris (nonyl phenyl) phosphite (TNPP) and commercial epoxidized oligomers (Joncryl) in PLA and PLA-based nanocomposites containing 2 wt.% clay, in an attempt to control thermal degradation. The use of a commercial chain extender based on modified PLA resulted in an effective chain extension, but in a strong dependence on concentration and PLA features.[19] It was found that Joncryl was the most efficient chain extender among the ones used in this study. The possible use of biopolymers for controlling the melt viscosity of PLA was deeply investigated by Beltran et al.[20] that added silk fibroin or chitosan to PLA, observing an increase in intrinsic viscosity of the PLA. The authors evidenced that previously they have added halloysite modified with an aminosilane in PLA[21] and they have observed in the same way an increase in viscosity due to a similar mechanism. The addition of a nano-inorganic filler is thus suggested as an alternative route for both reinforcing and increasing the melt viscosity of PLA. Scaffaro et al.[22] have added nanostructured hydrotalcites to PLA, but its reinforcing effect was counterbalanced by the induced chain scission. The addition of clay[23] was reported to be effective for improving the PLA mechanical and barrier properties of PLA. Nevertheless, reprocessing the nanocomposite resulted in some chain scission. As a kind of linear aliphatic polyesters synthesized by the ring-opening polymerization of lactides, PLA is typically derived from corn starch fermentation,1 and has good mechanical properties, thermal plasticity, biocompatibility, and ease of fabrication.2 These characteristics enable PLA as a promising polymer for various applications.3 Another feature of PLA is the good safety upon exposure to heat. For example, it does not produce any toxic nitrogen oxide gases and only one third of the combustible heat of polyolefins is generated when it is burned, so it does not damage the incinerator and provides significant energy savings.4 However, the instable processability of PLA needs to be concerned, that is, thermo-oxidative, hydrolytic degradations, and so on. The instability of PLA usually leads to break the polymer chains, as a result to decrease its molecular weight.5 And it would further result in a deterioration of rheological properties, which should be avoided for a processing purpose, especially when high levels of melt viscosity and strength are required. For example, the viscosity and strength of material has significant influence on their final performance when they are in blow molding, blow film, extrusion, and foaming. As is well known, PLA has a very low viscosity and melt strength, so the fabricated films are far away from stability and close to rupturing during blow-film process; and the lower melt tension is not beneficial to obtain satisfying products during blow-molding process. To overcome such shortcomings, attempts to improve the melt rheological properties of PLA have motivated considerable research efforts. One of the most important techniques is increasing the molecular weight of PLA, which can efficiently improve the intrinsic melt intensity of PLA. However, the productivity would decrease for high molecular PLA because of the prolonged reaction time, and the degradation or the color changing is usually inevitable. Furthermore, some investigations on the free radical branching/crosslinking of PLA has been also carried out in the melt mixing process in an extruder or in a kneader with the presence of trace amounts of various peroxides (served as radical initiators).6-8 In these process, branching or crosslinking reaction of PLA molecule chain can happen to some extent because of the reaction of capturing hydrogen by peroxides. However, some of new problems would appear because of the high reactivity of peroxides, such as the excessive crosslinking reaction and the degradation of PLA, which is hard to avoid during such processing. Another method is incorporating some new functional groups onto the PLA backbone to improve its melt viscosity, which paves the way to prepare composites, coated items, and composites/alloys. For example, multi-isocyanate9 and multi-epoxide10 are often used to endow PLA functional groups through copolymerizing reactions during reactive extrusion process, but a good knowledge on the reaction and control of polymerization during manufacturing are necessary. However, the copolymerization reaction is often difficult to realize anticipative results because of the difference of reactive activity between lactide and copolymerizing ester, and the melt intensity of PLA can be seldom improved. Therefore, extensive investigations on polymer blend technology have been also carried out. This work investigates the effect of cellulose nanocrystal (CN) loading on the properties of polylactide/poly(ε-caprolactone) (PLA/PCL) (70/30) blend processed in a twin-screw extruder as a potential material that can be utilized in various applications where biodegradation is highly desired. The morphological analysis revealed a reduction in droplet size of dispersed PCL phase upon addition of CN at low concentrations (1 and 2 wt %) with maximum reduction at 2 wt % which led to maximum improvement in mechanical properties. The reinforcing effect of CN in increasing the DMA storage modulus of the prepared systems was noticed when CN concentration was increased. Further, CN enhanced the crystallization of PCL, whereas the cold crystallization of PLA remained the same with CN addition. Both melt strength and viscosity of PLA improved with the incorporation of PCL and CN. Blending of polymer materials to attain systems with enhanced properties has been a feasible strategy to improve properties that individual polymers possess and thus widening their utilization in various applications.1 Polylactide/poly(ε-caprolactone) (PLA/PCL) blend is a type of biodegradable blends that has received lots of attention because of the superior properties that the two polymers exhibit; in particular, both polymers are biodegradable-a property which makes them favorable for packaging and biomedical applications, and so forth.2-4 In this blend, PCL is mostly dispersed inside a continuous PLA phase to enhance its properties. These include enhancing its toughness, a reduction in brittleness, slow crystallization and biodegradation rates, poor thermal stability, and low melt strength, which restricts its foamability. PLA is a promising biodegradable polymer that is already available in the market to replace most currently used fossil-derived polymers such as polyolefins due to its environmental friendliness and biodegradability; hence, it is crucial to improve the mentioned properties by blending it with ductile and fast crystallizing polymers such as PCL.4-8 However, PLA/PCL blend has been shown to be thermodynamically immiscible over a wide range of composition, whereby both matrices exist in separate phases due to factors such as differences in molecular weights and viscosities, among others, and this usually leads to phase separation and thus poor properties and performance of the final system.9 Among the strategies mostly employed to improve interfacial adhesion between blend matrices, the addition of nanofiller materials becomes an effective route compared to utilization of copolymers which are expensive and only specific to individual blend systems.10-12 Even so, the localization of nanofiller materials in the blend matrices is still a challenge as they tend to localize either at the interface or selectively localize in one of the phases or reside in both phases depending on both thermodynamic and/or kinetic factors. The thermodynamic factors dictate localization when the filler has high affinity to either of the polymers while the kinetic factors control filler localization based on processing strategies employed during preparation, and also the viscosity differences whereby filler will localize in low viscosity phase.12, 13 Therefore, depending on their localization, the final morphology and properties would differ from one composite system to another. For instance, Kelnar et al.14 noticed localization of graphite nanoparticles (GNPs) in the PCL phase in PLA/PCL (80/20) blend. Selectively localized GNP in PCL phase could be the result of kinetic effects; that is, processing strategy employed during composite preparation whereby all the components were added simultaneously in the batch mixer; therefore, PCL that has lower viscosity and melts first masked GNP before it can disperse in PLA. Apart from the PLA/PCL blend system, the selective localization of filler particles has also been noticed in other immiscible blend systems such as PLA/PHBV blend. Mofokeng and Luyt5 observed titanium dioxide (TiO2) nanoparticles mostly dispersed in the PLA phase and also at the interface in 50/50 PLA/PHBV blends. In their case, although TiO2 was expected to localize in PHBV due to its low viscosity estimated from melt flow index, the localization in PLA phase was attributed to factors including crystallinity difference between PLA and PHBV and also high affinity of TiO2 to PLA as determined from surface energies. Filler materials typically localize in low viscosity phase to bring balance between the viscosities of blend polymers; however, such behavior was not observed in their case indicating that thermodynamic compatibility was predominant in controlling the localization of TiO2.

Based solely on the provided evidence, the reduction in viscosity of PLA during melt processing is indicative of:

1.  **Molecular weight decrease due to thermo-mechanical degradation and/or hydrolysis:** The viscosity reduction is primarily attributed to chain scission reactions (degradation) occurring during processing. This degradation reduces the average molecular weight of PLA, which directly lowers its melt viscosity [1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, 12].
2.  **Thermo-mechanical degradation:** Processing conditions like temperature and shear in the extruder cause mechanical chain scission and thermal degradation of the PLA polymer chains, leading to lower molecular weight and reduced viscosity [1, 3, 10]. Talc incorporation can enhance stability against this viscosity reduction during mixing [3].
3.  **Hydrolytic degradation:** Moisture absorbed by PLA before or during processing can lead to hydrolysis reactions, breaking ester bonds in the polymer chains, reducing molecular weight, and consequently lowering the melt viscosity [1, 10].

This viscosity reduction is a key indicator of PLA degradation during processing, negatively impacting its rheological properties and potentially the morphology and final properties of blends or composites [1, 2, 3, 10, 12]. Attempts to counteract this degradation and increase viscosity include using chain extenders (like PLA-MA, PLA-GMA, acrylate-based extenders, CP/SE) or nanoparticles (like talc) [2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12].

As a kind of linear aliphatic polyesters synthesized by the ring-opening polymerization of lactides, PLA is typically derived from corn starch fermentation,1 and has good mechanical properties, thermal plasticity, biocompatibility, and ease of fabrication.2 These characteristics enable PLA as a promising polymer for various applications.3 Another feature of PLA is the good safety upon exposure to heat. For example, it does not produce any toxic nitrogen oxide gases and only one third of the combustible heat of polyolefins is generated when it is burned, so it does not damage the incinerator and provides significant energy savings.4 However, the instable processability of PLA needs to be concerned, that is, thermo-oxidative, hydrolytic degradations, and so on. The instability of PLA usually leads to break the polymer chains, as a result to decrease its molecular weight.5 And it would further result in a deterioration of rheological properties, which should be avoided for a processing purpose, especially when high levels of melt viscosity and strength are required. For example, the viscosity and strength of material has significant influence on their final performance when they are in blow molding, blow film, extrusion, and foaming. As is well known, PLA has a very low viscosity and melt strength, so the fabricated films are far away from stability and close to rupturing during blow-film process; and the lower melt tension is not beneficial to obtain satisfying products during blow-molding process. To overcome such shortcomings, attempts to improve the melt rheological properties of PLA have motivated considerable research efforts. One of the most important techniques is increasing the molecular weight of PLA, which can efficiently improve the intrinsic melt intensity of PLA. However, the productivity would decrease for high molecular PLA because of the prolonged reaction time, and the degradation or the color changing is usually inevitable. Furthermore, some investigations on the free radical branching/crosslinking of PLA has been also carried out in the melt mixing process in an extruder or in a kneader with the presence of trace amounts of various peroxides (served as radical initiators).6-8 In these process, branching or crosslinking reaction of PLA molecule chain can happen to some extent because of the reaction of capturing hydrogen by peroxides. However, some of new problems would appear because of the high reactivity of peroxides, such as the excessive crosslinking reaction and the degradation of PLA, which is hard to avoid during such processing. Another method is incorporating some new functional groups onto the PLA backbone to improve its melt viscosity, which paves the way to prepare composites, coated items, and composites/alloys. For example, multi-isocyanate9 and multi-epoxide10 are often used to endow PLA functional groups through copolymerizing reactions during reactive extrusion process, but a good knowledge on the reaction and control of polymerization during manufacturing are necessary. However, the copolymerization reaction is often difficult to realize anticipative results because of the difference of reactive activity between lactide and copolymerizing ester, and the melt intensity of PLA can be seldom improved. Therefore, extensive investigations on polymer blend technology have been also carried out. Blending PLA with another immiscible or miscible polymer with higher melt viscosity is perhaps a less expensive and practical alternative way to prepare a variety of useful composites and alloys. Blends of PLA with PCL,11, 12 atactic poly[(R, S)-3-hydroxybutyrate],13 poly(ethylene succinate),14 hydrophilic poly(vinyl alcohol),15 poly(methyl methacrylate),16 poly(ethylene glycol),17 and poly(vinylphenol),18 have been investigated. Most of the above studies revealed that blending PLA with other polymers can substantially modify the mechanical and thermal properties, degradation rate, and permeability, but few distinct evidence of the improvement for melt viscosity can be found in these blends. Recently, Jiang et al.19 showed that the melt elasticity of the biodegradable PLA/poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) blends increased with the concentration of PBAT increasing via blending process, but the viscosity increase is limited. Carboxyl-ended polyester (CP) and solid epoxy (SE) have been widely used in polyester powder coating because they can form a crosslinking structure, and the viscosity of PLA will increase after in situ crosslink if CP and SE are added into the PLA matrix. In this article, CP and SE are used as the modifier of PLA to improve the melt rheological properties of PLA. Compared with the above-mentioned methods (increasing molecular weight, branching/crosslinking and incorporating new functional groups into PLA backbone), this method with CP/SE as the modifier has some outstanding advantages. For instance, the reaction temperature of CP/SE is close to the processing temperature of PLA; CP/SE has a high melt viscosity after reaction, and abundant functional end groups, which are easily accessible. With the unique crosslinking structure after reaction, CP/SE results in the different dispersion phase size and stereo hindrance for the linear polymer. Furthermore, the abundance of hydroxyl end groups attached to CS/SE may have some H-bonding interactions with PLA.20 Thus, it is reasonable to expect that the incorporation of CP/SE into PLA may bring about either the improved melt viscosity or the increased strength.
The low melt viscosity and melt strength of polyglycolic acid (PGA) severely limit its application. In this work, high melt viscosity PGA/PLA blends are prepared by reactive extrusion of bifunctional isocyanate (HDI) and multifunctional epoxy oligomer (ADR) as chain extenders. The use of hybrid chain extender (hCE) containing 2 wt% HDI and 1 wt% ADR results in a long chain branched/cross-linked structure, thus increasing melt viscosity more effectively than HDI or ADR alone. The complex viscosity, storage modulus and loss modulus of the PGA/PLA/hCE blends are significantly higher than those of the PGA/hCE.
