As the requirements for environmental protection are increasingly strict and petroleum-based polymers continue to rise in price, the biodegradable plastics has become a hot topic of common interest in academia and industry.1-4 Among the commonly utilized biodegradable plastics, polyester polymers such as polylactic acid (PLA) and poly (butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) have gained significant attention, however, their high cost and relatively low barrier properties have limited their widespread application. Polyglycolic acid (PGA), also referred to as polyethyleneglycolate or polyhydroxyacetic acid, is a biodegradable plastic with outstanding biodegradability and biocompatibility, as well as remarkable barrier properties.5-12 PGA has excellent temperature resistance and mechanical strength comparable to polyetheretherketone (PEEK).10 With the development of coal-based syngas to PGA technology, it is estimated that the production cost of PGA can be significantly reduced, which has a great competitive advantage compared with PLA and PBAT, and has a broad application prospect in the fields of biomedical, engineering plastics, food packaging, agricultural production, and so forth. However, PGA has not yet been mass-produced and used on a large scale, due to its poor processability. PGA is easily degraded at high temperature, and its thermal degradation temperature is very close to its melting point, resulting in low melt viscosity and melt strength during melt processing, and a narrow processing temperature window.6 Consequently, common plastic molding processes such as injection molding, extrusion, and blown film are not readily adaptable to PGA. To overcome these limitations for PGA, improved melt viscosity and melt strength is necessary.
Molecular weight decrease caused by thermal, hydrolytic, and mechanical degradation of PLA is a major concern during melt processing. Modeling and predicting degradation is essential to minimize material deterioration and material property changes. Current kinetic degradation models show potential to describe degradation, but they are limited to rheometry and focus on thermal and/or hydrolytic degradation only. There is no model yet that describes degradation during melt processing techniques such as injection molding or extrusion. The aim of this work is to establish a degradation model that predicts the molecular weight decrease of PLA throughout single-screw extrusion. A combination of experimental extrusion data and numerical simulations is used to establish the model. Subsequently, the model is experimentally validated to check its predictive quality. The results show good similarity between predictions and measurements for multiple process variables. The maximum deviation between both was found to be 5%. Combining experimental data with numerical simulations allows us to describe the extrusion process in an equipment-independent way, which is essential to use the model for different extruders or dies. Overall, minimizing degradation during processing will avoid the loss of valuable resources, materials, and time, and will result in obtaining high quality products. The sensitivity of the ester bonds in poly(lactic acid) or PLA is a major concern during processing, since polymer chains of molten PLA have the tendency to degrade [1]. The potential presence of moisture in the granules, combined with high shear stresses and temperatures during extrusion or injection molding, may result in hydrolytic, thermal, and mechanical degradation. Chain scission of the polymer chains, caused by the three types of degradation, leads to a decrease in molecular weight, depending on the applied process parameters [2-5]. The selection of process parameters is crucial to minimize polymer degradation, which is nowadays often based on experience by the process operator, recommendations on the technical data sheet of the material supplier or by trial-and-error. Generally, it is not investigated or known whether the selected process parameters result in degradation. Nevertheless, degradation may strongly affect PLA's material properties [2]. In the work of Teixeira et al. [6], the complex viscosity was reported to decrease from 2680 Pa s to around 1300 Pa s at the die end due to degradation during processing. A similar conclusion was reported by Benvenuta-Tapia and Vivaldo-Lima [7], where a decrease from 2300 Pa s for neat PLA to 330 Pa s was observed after processing PLA. Aside from rheological properties, also thermal properties are affected by processing PLA. Due to a decreasing molecular weight caused by degradation, the mobility of the polymer chains increases and allows faster crystallization. A decrease of the cold crystallization temperature from 103.0°C to 97.1°C and an increase of the crystallization temperature from 96.8°C to 100.2°C was reported in the work of Lv et al. [8]. Other researchers [9, 10] confirmed a change in the crystallization behavior. Also the mechanical properties are affected by degradation, such as a reported decrease in the stress at break from 66 to 25 MPa after repeated injection molding cycles [10], explained by a lower number of entanglements due to chain scission. The impact strength was also affected by degradation, as shown in the work of Zenkiewicz et al. [11] where a decrease of 0.19 kJ m−2 (7.4%) occurred in the first reprocessing cycle. Yellowing of PLA can also occur due to degradation, as reported in the work of Agüero et al. [12] by an increase of (blue-yellow value in LAB color space definition) from 10.75 to 20.59. In order to limit the change of PLA's properties and to obtain high quality products after extrusion or injection molding, it is essential to understand the severity of degradation during processing.
In this work, bio-based products composed of blends of a star-shaped poly(d,l-lactide) (star-PDLLA) and a conventional linear poly(l-lactide) (linear-PLLA) are produced by typical large-scale manufacturing techniques for thermoplastic blends. In the first case, the two polymers are blended through melt extrusion, producing pellets that are subsequently compression-molded into the final bio-based polymer films. Alternatively, the star/linear poly(lactide) (PLA) materials are developed by direct blending through injection molding, a process that generally applies after a preblending extrusion step to ensure proper mixing. Thermomechanical degradation induced by the different processes is evaluated, and the performances of the final star/linear PLA products are thoroughly compared. The effect of the short-branched, amorphous, star polymeric component on thermal, mechanical, and rheological properties of the conventional PLLA is comprehensively investigated, revealing that the star-PDLLA incorporation promotes the formation of a more flexible and tougher material with reduced capability of crystallization. Most importantly, star-PDLLA decreases the melt viscosity of the final material, while increasing the shear-thinning behavior, hence facilitating melt flow during manufacturing. Such properties lead to enhanced material ductility and processability, with respect to typically brittle and viscous conventional PLLA-based materials. Moreover, the tuning of final material performances can be achieved by simply varying the star-PDLLA content. Poly(lactide) is one of the most extensively investigated and utilized bio-based polymers of the last decades. This biodegradable thermoplastic polyester is now subject of significant industrial and commercial development by numerous manufacturing companies around the world, also thanks to recent advancements enabling its production from renewable stocks.[1] PLA exhibits many interesting properties compared to existing oil-derived commodity polymers, such as discrete tensile strength, stiffness, and biodegradability.[2, 3] However, although much progress has been made on PLA performances, its applicability on flexible products, both for packaging and biomedical field, is still limited due to several inherent drawbacks, such as brittleness, high melt viscosity, and poor impact resistance.[4] Conventional semicrystalline PLA (linear poly(l-lactide) (linear-PLLA)) is commonly processed at temperatures close to 200 °C, where chain scission and transesterification phenomena become significant.[5-7] PLA may also exhibit resistance to flow and color change through an injection-molding process due to the elevated melt viscosity at the applied manufacturing conditions.[8-10] Indeed, it has been demonstrated that bio-based polyesters, like PLA, undergo drastic degradation for every processing step they are subjected to, before getting to the market (i.e., from batch compounding of the raw material to the molding of the final commercial item).[9, 11] These complications generally cause loss of mechanical performances. Although a lot of research has been conducted on improvement of PLA performances through extensive use of both small molecules and macromolecules (e.g., plasticizers,[12, 13] polymeric tougheners,[14, 15] or nucleating agents[16, 17]), such modifications often drastically affect thermal stability, mechanical resistance, and, above all, biodegradability of the final material.[18] Indeed, in order to solve PLA disadvantages and maximize its applicability, it is essential to optimize its processing at high shear rates.[4, 9] Therefore, finding a proper green modifier to enhance ductility and ease the melt flow of conventional PLA would represent a versatile tool to improve its processability, preventing its typical deterioration during manufacturing, as well as final PLA-based product performances. An interesting industrially employed method to modify rheological properties of polymeric materials is the introduction of branching.[19, 20] This strategy has widely been used in the past for implementation of polyolefins processing[21, 22] and is now attracting attention for bio-based polyesters.[23-25] However, the information regarding combinations of different PLA architectures, which would ensure maximal compatibility between the blend components, is very limited, especially at relatively high-scale processing levels.[20, 26, 27] It has been shown that short-branched polymers present lower viscosities and improved melt elasticity than corresponding linear structures with comparable molecular weight (MW).[19, 28, 29] In particular, star-shaped macromolecular architectures, which consist of branched polymers with only one branching point, are characterized by very low capability of forming entanglements and extremely compact structures.[29, 30] Such well-defined polymer architectures can drastically enhance ductility and melt flow of conventional PLA, without altering the chemical nature of the material.[31] However, a high-molecular-weight PLLA is generally required to ensure sufficient structural strength.[32] Therefore, the incorporation of a star-shaped PLA with relatively short-chain branches to a conventional linear PLA matrix would decrease the overall melt viscosity, yet preserving the good original properties of the latter.[27, 33-35]
Although, processing of PLA-CNC nanocomposites by melt extrusion is a promising technique for nanocomposite fabrication at large scale, uniform dispersion of hydrophilic CNC into hydrophobic PLA matrix still remains a challenging task [17], [18]. In general, PLA is susceptible to thermal decomposition at elevated temperature during extrusion which leads to reduction in properties due to molecular weight reduction. At elevated temperature, segments of polymer chains start to separate and react with one another to change the physical and mechanical properties of material [19]. Hence the effect of CNC on thermal properties of PLA nanocomposites is important to understand processing of PLA. It is important to note that processing of PLA should be carried out without serious thermal degradation in order to make the nanocomposite suitable for packaging application with enhanced properties [20], [21]. In this study, CNC are fabricated using sulphuric acid (H2SO4), nitric acid (HNO3), phosphoric acid (H3PO4) and hydrochloric acid (HCl) based hydrolysis of native cellulose derived from filter paper. CNC from various types of acids have quite divergent characteristics such as morphology and aspect ratio. Both these parameters have significant role to improve the dispersion as well as tune the thermo-mechanical properties of the PLA matrix. The current work focuses on the degradation kinetics of fabricated PLA-CNC nanocomposites using TGA measured at different heating rate. The influence of different acid hydrolysed CNC on the degradation mechanism of PLA based nanocomposite is determined using Criado approach. Hyphenated TGA-FTIR is carried out to quantify the release of the volatile gaseous products during thermal decomposition [22]. Furthermore, this study will also provide enough information to determine which PLA-acid hydrolysed CNC based nanocomposite are most stable during melt processing without serious decomposition during extrusion.

Blending of polymer materials to attain systems with enhanced properties has been a feasible strategy to improve properties that individual polymers possess and thus widening their utilization in various applications.1 Polylactide/poly(ε-caprolactone) (PLA/PCL) blend is a type of biodegradable blends that has received lots of attention because of the superior properties that the two polymers exhibit; in particular, both polymers are biodegradable-a property which makes them favorable for packaging and biomedical applications, and so forth.2-4 In this blend, PCL is mostly dispersed inside a continuous PLA phase to enhance its properties. These include enhancing its toughness, a reduction in brittleness, slow crystallization and biodegradation rates, poor thermal stability, and low melt strength, which restricts its foamability. PLA is a promising biodegradable polymer that is already available in the market to replace most currently used fossil-derived polymers such as polyolefins due to its environmental friendliness and biodegradability; hence, it is crucial to improve the mentioned properties by blending it with ductile and fast crystallizing polymers such as PCL.4-8 However, PLA/PCL blend has been shown to be thermodynamically immiscible over a wide range of composition, whereby both matrices exist in separate phases due to factors such as differences in molecular weights and viscosities, among others, and this usually leads to phase separation and thus poor properties and performance of the final system.9 Among the strategies mostly employed to improve interfacial adhesion between blend matrices, the addition of nanofiller materials becomes an effective route compared to utilization of copolymers which are expensive and only specific to individual blend systems.10-12 Even so, the localization of nanofiller materials in the blend matrices is still a challenge as they tend to localize either at the interface or selectively localize in one of the phases or reside in both phases depending on both thermodynamic and/or kinetic factors. The thermodynamic factors dictate localization when the filler has high affinity to either of the polymers while the kinetic factors control filler localization based on processing strategies employed during preparation, and also the viscosity differences whereby filler will localize in low viscosity phase.12, 13 Therefore, depending on their localization, the final morphology and properties would differ from one composite system to another. For instance, Kelnar et al.14 noticed localization of graphite nanoparticles (GNPs) in the PCL phase in PLA/PCL (80/20) blend. Selectively localized GNP in PCL phase could be the result of kinetic effects; that is, processing strategy employed during composite preparation whereby all the components were added simultaneously in the batch mixer; therefore, PCL that has lower viscosity and melts first masked GNP before it can disperse in PLA. Apart from the PLA/PCL blend system, the selective localization of filler particles has also been noticed in other immiscible blend systems such as PLA/PHBV blend. Mofokeng and Luyt5 observed titanium dioxide (TiO2) nanoparticles mostly dispersed in the PLA phase and also at the interface in 50/50 PLA/PHBV blends. In their case, although TiO2 was expected to localize in PHBV due to its low viscosity estimated from melt flow index, the localization in PLA phase was attributed to factors including crystallinity difference between PLA and PHBV and also high affinity of TiO2 to PLA as determined from surface energies. Filler materials typically localize in low viscosity phase to bring balance between the viscosities of blend polymers; however, such behavior was not observed in their case indicating that thermodynamic compatibility was predominant in controlling the localization of TiO2.
However, it has been shown that initial filler morphology is not constant throughout processing, but it is prone to changes due to shear forces and high temperature.19 The extent of filler degradation in extrusion compounding, for example, was found to depend on process settings like degree of filling, screw design, screw rotation speed, and feed rate.20-25 While the influence of filler morphology on polymer properties, e.g., polymer rheology, was studied to a vast extent, there are only few studies that directly analyze the effect of polymer rheological properties, e.g., polymer melt flow rate (MFR), on wood filler size. Balasuriya et al.3 compounded wood flakes and HDPE with different MFR to study the effect on flake distribution and wetting by the matrix and to analyze the mechanical properties resulting thereof. Peltola et al.26 compounded wood fibers with polylactic acid (PLA) and PP and concluded that differences in fiber degradation result from the higher viscosity of the PLA matrix. Based solely on the provided context evidence, the 'burst release' phenomenon in drug delivery microspheres refers to:

1.  **An initial rapid release** of a significant portion of the encapsulated drug (often described as >50%) immediately or within a very short time period after the microsphere encounters a liquid medium (e.g., in vitro buffer or in vivo bodily fluids) [1][4].
2.  **Mechanism:** This rapid release is primarily attributed to:
    *   Drug molecules located on or very near the surface of the microspheres [4].
    *   Drug associated with easily accessible pores at the surface [4][3].
    *   Weak drug-matrix interactions allowing rapid diffusion, especially for hydrophilic drugs [8][12].
3.  **Contributing Factors:** Causes include surface characteristics, sample properties, drug-polymer interactions, and manufacturing parameters [1]. High porosity at the surface [6][7] and processing conditions leading to drug deposition on the surface are also factors [6][7].
4.  **Undesirable Consequence:** Burst release is generally considered problematic as it can lead to high initial drug concentrations (potentially causing toxicity) and insufficient drug release over the desired therapeutic period [1][2][12].
5.  **Mitigation Strategies:** Evidence discusses various approaches to reduce burst release, including:
    *   Polymer blending/composition (e.g., PCL/PEO) [1][11].
    *   Composite systems (e.g., microspheres embedded in hydrogels like PPP or alginate microspheres in PPP hydrogels) [2].
    *   Surface modification/coating (e.g., polymer surface modification, polyelectrolyte multilayer coating) [1][9].
    *   Crosslinking of the polymer matrix [8][12].
    *   Mineralization (e.g., calcium phosphate in hydrogels acting as crosslinkers and diffusion barriers) [3].
    *   Altering hydrophilicity [8].
    *   Incorporating inorganic particles (e.g., mineralized calcium silicate enhancing encapsulation and promoting zero-order release) [11].
    *   Affinity-based binding (e.g., heparin conjugation for growth factors) [9].
    *   Reducing surface drug content through processing modifications [6][7].

question: What is the 'hydrolysis half-life' of anhydride bonds compared to ester bonds?
ground_truth: Anhydride bonds are much more hydrolytically unstable than ester bonds. The half-life of an anhydride bond can be minutes to hours, leading to rapid surface erosion of polyanhydrides (days to weeks). In contrast, ester bonds (in PLA, PCL) have half-lives of months to years, leading to slower bulk erosion.

Hydrogels are highly hydrated polymeric networks that have been extensively researched for various biomedical applications. In particular, synthetic hydrogels can be designed to be nondegradable or degradable depending on the targeted application. The majority of hydrolytically degradable hydrogels are engineered to contain ester linkages located either in the cross-link or the backbone of the hydrogel. The hydrolysis of these ester bonds has been widely studied in the literature where the esters undergo different hydrolysis mechanisms at different conditions (i.e., neutral, acid and base). The rate of ester hydrolysis is both pH and temperature dependent. The hydrolysis rate has been shown to generally increase with the acidity or alkalinity of the environment.1 Also, it has been reported that heat can accelerate the hydrolysis rate by providing more energy to the reactants to overcome the activation energy required to initiate the hydrolysis reaction.2-4 Interestingly, although the esters undergo different hydrolysis mechanisms at different conditions, similar end products, a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, are obtained.4 The hydrolysis kinetics of ester bonds also vary depending on the chemical structure of the ester,5, 6 as well as other factors such as polymer crystallinity and wettability.7 It was reported that ester bonds associated with poly(lactic acid) (PLA) degrade much more rapidly than ester linkages of polycaprolactone (PCL).8, 9 Moreover, changes made to the polymer structure and size may also affect the degradation mechanisms. For example, bulk PLA has been shown to degrade in both acidic and basic environments, whereas PLA brushes only degrade in basic conditions.10, 11 Conversely, other studies of cross-linked polymers containing esters in the cross-link have demonstrated that their gels were nondegradable on the timeframes studied. Hennink et al. have reported that dextran hydrogels with high cross-linking density were resistive to hydrolysis despite having an ester group in the cross-links.12 Hydrogels formed from poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) conjugated with an ester containing methacrylate moiety were also shown to be hydrolytically stable over a period of several months.13, 14 One major advantage of hydrolytically degradable synthetic hydrogels is that the degradation rate of these gels can be tailored according to the targeted biomedical application. Previous studies have shown that hydrogels of tuned degradation profile can be engineered by varying the number of degradable linkages, macromer concentration and degree of cross-linking.15 Martens et al. successfully tailored the degradation of PVA gels grafted with ester acrylate groups from 1 to 12 to 35 days by varying the macromer concentration from 10 to 15 to 20 wt % respectively.15 Moreover, increasing the cross-linking density of the PVA ester acrylate gels from 0.3 to 0.64 mol/L by fabricating the gels using macromers of different molecular weights also increased the degradation time from 12 to 45 days.15 The ability to tune the degradation rate of these hydrogels is a major advantage in terms of designing tissue engineering matrices for various biomedical applications, such as drug delivery.16 For example, tailoring the hydrogel degradation also controls the drug release rate, which then permits stable clearance of the drug from the body without exerting too much stress on the kidney.17

4.  **General susceptibility**: Ester bonds are consistently highlighted as the primary site for hydrolytic scission in biodegradable polymers like polyurethanes and polyesters, being significantly more labile than urethane, urea, or ether bonds [1, 2, 10, 11, 12].

Hydrogels are highly hydrated polymeric networks that have been extensively researched for various biomedical applications. In particular, synthetic hydrogels can be designed to be nondegradable or degradable depending on the targeted application. The majority of hydrolytically degradable hydrogels are engineered to contain ester linkages located either in the cross-link or the backbone of the hydrogel. The hydrolysis of these ester bonds has been widely studied in the literature where the esters undergo different hydrolysis mechanisms at different conditions (i.e., neutral, acid and base). The rate of ester hydrolysis is both pH and temperature dependent. The hydrolysis rate has been shown to generally increase with the acidity or alkalinity of the environment.1 Also, it has been reported that heat can accelerate the hydrolysis rate by providing more energy to the reactants to overcome the activation energy required to initiate the hydrolysis reaction.2-4 Interestingly, although the esters undergo different hydrolysis mechanisms at different conditions, similar end products, a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, are obtained.4 The hydrolysis kinetics of ester bonds also vary depending on the chemical structure of the ester,5, 6 as well as other factors such as polymer crystallinity and wettability.7 It was reported that ester bonds associated with poly(lactic acid) (PLA) degrade much more rapidly than ester linkages of polycaprolactone (PCL).8, 9 Moreover, changes made to the polymer structure and size may also affect the degradation mechanisms. For example, bulk PLA has been shown to degrade in both acidic and basic environments, whereas PLA brushes only degrade in basic conditions.10, 11 Conversely, other studies of cross-linked polymers containing esters in the cross-link have demonstrated that their gels were nondegradable on the timeframes studied. Hennink et al. have reported that dextran hydrogels with high cross-linking density were resistive to hydrolysis despite having an ester group in the cross-links.12 Hydrogels formed from poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) conjugated with an ester containing methacrylate moiety were also shown to be hydrolytically stable over a period of several months.13, 14 One major advantage of hydrolytically degradable synthetic hydrogels is that the degradation rate of these gels can be tailored according to the targeted biomedical application. Previous studies have shown that hydrogels of tuned degradation profile can be engineered by varying the number of degradable linkages, macromer concentration and degree of cross-linking.15 Martens et al. successfully tailored the degradation of PVA gels grafted with ester acrylate groups from 1 to 12 to 35 days by varying the macromer concentration from 10 to 15 to 20 wt % respectively.15 Moreover, increasing the cross-linking density of the PVA ester acrylate gels from 0.3 to 0.64 mol/L by fabricating the gels using macromers of different molecular weights also increased the degradation time from 12 to 45 days.15 The ability to tune the degradation rate of these hydrogels is a major advantage in terms of designing tissue engineering matrices for various biomedical applications, such as drug delivery.16 For example, tailoring the hydrogel degradation also controls the drug release rate, which then permits stable clearance of the drug from the body without exerting too much stress on the kidney.17

The long-term goal of Langmuir monolayer degradation experiments is to predict the degradation kinetics of the corresponding bulk material. In theory, this is possible when the local water concentration inside the bulk material is known. Since the reaction rate is proportional to the water concentration, lifetime estimated from Langmuir monolayers need to be divided by the bulk water concentration to extrapolate to the situation in a bulk material. A typical water concentration for PCL degrading in an aqueous environment would be on the order of 1%.35 Then, the lifetime of an ester bond in bulk PCL as extrapolated from Langmuir monolayer experiments is 100 days at pH 2.5. A recent study found a lifetime of about 55 days for PCL films at very high pH.35 The comparable values hint that the degradation rate constants determined in monolayers are applicable to bulk materials, but to truly understand how the kinetic data from Langmuir monolayers can be applied to bulk materials, experiments comparing bulk degradation and Langmuir monolayer degradation kinetics over a range of different materials and conditions have to be carried out. For polyesters, which are probably the most extensively researched class of biodegradable polymer implant materials, enzymatic degradation is expected to take place at the material surface. There is a general agreement that enzymatic degradation of polyesters proceeds via a random fragmentation mechanism which is characterized by an S-shaped degradation curve as shown in Figure 3 and can be described by either Equation 1 or Equations 4-7. One noteworthy exception is poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB), which shows a degradation curve resembling a straight line, in analogy to the zero-order kinetics that are observed during thermal degradation of the polymer.36 A detailed quantitative model for the analysis of enzymatic degradation has been developed by combining surface adsorption, Michaelis-Menten kinetics and statistical fragment size distribution. For polylactide degraded by cutinase, the inverse of the observed, effective reaction rate constant was proportional to the inverse of enzyme concentration.34 The Langmuir monolayer proved to be an exceptional tool to gain insights into the interaction between the enzymes and the polymer chains. It was clearly shown that enzymes require a minimum packing density of the polymeric substrate to become active. Here, a lower threshold surface pressure was found for proteinase K degrading poly(l-lactide) (but not poly(d-lactide)) than for PHB which was degraded by an extracellular depolymerase.28 This was attributed to the greater hydrophilicity of poly(l-lactide) compared to PHB. Besides packing density, the impact of temperature and molecular weight on the random degradation of PCL has also been studied.29 An inverse proportionality between bond scission rate constant and molecular weight was found by fitting the degradation curve with Equation 1. Using the same analysis, a doubling of the bond scission rate constant was found when going from room temperature to 37 °C. This dependence, which is below van't Hoff's rule, underlines the importance to carry out degradation experiments at physiological temperature, since extrapolating from other temperatures may give misleading results. To further elucidate the mechanism of enzymatic degradation of polyesters, oligo(ε-caprolactone) was end-capped with phenylboronic acid. It was hypothesized that these end-caps can mediate a specific binding interaction with the lipase from Pseudomonas cepacia.33 Neither crystallization nor degradation rate in the late stage were affected by the end-caps. However, in the early stage, degradation was significantly retarded, and enzyme insertion was hypothesized due to the observation of an increase of the film area under isobaric conditions. Insertion of enzymes into polymer films was also found in other studies when degradation was either slow32 or inactive enzymes were used.26 This suggests that enzymes are also able to penetrate into the surface layer of bulk materials, with the thickness of the eroding layer expanding when degradation is slowed down. This hypothesis is supported by the observation of a porous surface layer during enzymatic degradation of certain materials.37
Another property that we can control with this modular polymer architecture is the NP degradation time. The degradation of these colloids is an important property because it affects their applicability. In fact, the progressive hydrolysis of the lateral ester bonds makes the polymer chains more and more hydrophilic, which may reduce the wettability from limonene, up to the point when the NPs disassemble destabilizing the Pickering emulsion. On the other hand, the degradation prevents the polymer accumulation in the environment, which is an urgent issue affecting the society. Therefore, the possibility of controlling the degradation time is of paramount importance to grant sufficient shelf life and avoid a premature emulsion destabilization without giving up the desirable polymer dissolution upon disposal. We tracked the degradation by monitoring the relative scattering intensity, i.e. the intensity of the light scattered by these colloids under accelerated degradation conditions (pH = 14) with respect to the value measured at time zero. The RSI is a function of the NP size as well as of their concentration in the medium.40,41 Therefore, it can be reliably considered as an indication of the block copolymer progressive dissolution and of the NP disappearance upon hydrolysis of the ester bonds. As expected, the RSI decreases with time, as clearly shown in Fig. S4a.† This decrease may be attributed to a reduction in either the NP size or concentration. However, caprolactone-based NPs are known to show a bulk-type erosion,38i.e. a degradation that involves the NP core, without affecting the size. This is demonstrated in Fig. S4b,† where we show that the NPs synthesized did not experience any change in their size during the degradation. Therefore, the decrease in the RSI was attributed uniquely to the progressive NP dissolution and consequent reduction in their concentration. For this reason, we evaluated the NP half-life as the time leading to 50% RSI. As shown in Fig. 1c, the half-life linearly increases with p at a fixed q, which is reasonable because of the higher number of hydrophobic units that need to be cleaved before reaching 50% RSI. Then, at a first glance, the degradation appears faster for NPs with q = 3. However, it should be considered that in this case, at a given p, the number of ester bonds to be cleaved in order to lead to the NP dissolution is much lower compared to the case q = 5. For a fair comparison, we then reported in Fig. 1d the half-life as a function of the total caprolactone units nCL = p × q. Here, it is evident that the NP half-life is a function not only of nCL, but also of how the caprolactone units are distributed within the polymer microstructure. Shorter lipophilic blocks composed of longer oligo(caprolactone) pendants (q = 5) degraded faster compared to longer hydrophobic blocks obtained with shorter macromonomers (q = 3). This may be attributed to the statistical nature of the hydrolysis reactions, which in the case of q = 5 can cleave longer oligomers leading to a faster reduction in the NP lipophilicity, followed by a more rapid water diffusion and hence dissolution. This unusual discovery allows decoupling the NP hydrophobicity (and in turn wettability) and degradation time by acting on the caprolactone distribution within the polymer chains. It is worth highlighting that the degradation rate could be kept low with this polymer architecture so that we do not expect influences over the emulsion stability as studied in the following, at least in the timescale of the experiments. It is worth highlighting that for all the combinations of n, p, and q, the NP morphology remained spherical, as confirmed by the TEM micrograph reported in Fig. 1e for 40EG4-30CL3 as an example and in Fig. S5† for other representative samples. Therefore, the modulation of the NP properties can be imputed only to p, n and q and could not be justified with a change in morphology.

It is well studied that polyester-based polyurethanes can be biodegraded by various bacteria and fungi, primarily through hydrolysis to the ester bonds, and in some cases secondary hydrolysis to the urethane bonds.5 Thus, biodegradable TPUs can be designed by incorporating chemical bonds that are susceptible to enzymatic hydrolysis. For biodegradation studies, we synthesized new TPUs (TPU1 and TPU4) using the formulations in Table 3 and subjected the materials to compost biodegradation in controlled environments. Biodegradation of polymers occurs through a combination of steps: the surface of the polymer is colonized by the surrounding microorganisms (i.e., compost microorganisms), often leading to physical fracturing of the surface, these microorganisms then secrete relevant hydrolase enzymes, which catalyze the hydrolysis of susceptible bonds within the polymer leading to lower molecular weight products in what is known as depolymerization and lastly, the lower molecular weight products are incorporated by the microorganisms into cellular biomass, as well as released as inorganic products.31 Under home-compost conditions at 45°C with 75%-85% relative humidity, we observed significant decreases in molecular weight of these polyester-polyol TPUs compared to a polyether-TPU control that is not expected to biodegrade due to the ether bonds, which are recalcitrant to biodegradation processes.5 Our findings indicate that these synthesized TPUs are susceptible to biodegradation under compost conditions (see the experimental section for detailed biodegradation procedure). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) results showed a change in surface morphology for degraded TPU1 and TPU4 compared to commercial polyether-TPU after 9 weeks, suggesting the first step in the biodegradation process-surface colonization and physical fracturing (Figure 6).

Tissue engineering scaffolds should provide mechanical support and physicochemical cues for the growth of cells to replace tissue [1]. Materials for such scaffolds should possess appropriate mechanical properties, chemical and biological compatibility and ideally should degrade in an appropriate time frame [1], [2]. Due to its biocompatibility, processability, and consistent degradation profile, polycaprolactone (PCl) has frequently been used as a long-term degradable implantable scaffold material for tissue engineering [3], [4], [5], [6]. The primary degradation pathway of pristine PCl is the hydrolysis of ester bonds leading to chain scission resulting in formation of shorter chains, oligomers and caproic acid [7]. This takes place in the amorphous bulk of the material and is dependent on its crystallinity and water transport into the material to enable hydrolysis [4], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12]. However, due to its semi-crystalline and hydrophobic nature, the rate of hydration and subsequent hydrolytic cleavage is low and hence the rate of degradation via this pathway is relatively slow (up to 4 years) [7], [10], [13]. Enzymatic degradation, on the other hand, occurs at the surface of the polymer with lipases and esterases attaching to the polymer surface before hydrolysing surface ester bonds in a much shorter time frame forming shorter chain polymers and oligomers. Degradation, while dependent on the enzyme used and the polymer composition and crystallinity, is generally complete after approximately 12 days and yields, among other fragments, ɛ-hydroxy caproic acid which, without clearance, can alter the pH of the host [14], [15], [16], [17], [18]. Tissue engineering of electro-responsive cells has been shown to be improved by electrical stimulation [19], [20]. The introduction of conducting fillers to such a well-studied tissue engineering matrix as PCl has been shown to result in conducting biocompatible composites which can be used to proliferate cells under electrical stimulation [21], [22]. However, the filler used must be biocompatible and have an appropriately low percolation threshold for conductivity so as not to adversely affect the degradation profile of the polymer scaffold. Graphene has shown promise as a filler for this application, as recent reports suggest it can enhance cell proliferation [23] and can be cleared by renal excretion, phagocytosis and/or endocytosis [24], [25], [26], [27]. In addition, the use of chemically converted reduced graphene oxide (CCG) has been reported to improve conductivities by orders of magnitude even at very low concentrations in a polymer matrix [22]. However, it is unknown what effects the addition of graphene would have on the degradation rates and products of a polymeric tissue engineering material.

question: How does 'blending' with Poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) affect the electrospinning of Chitosan?

The electrospinnability of chitosan is limited mainly because of its polycationic nature in solution, rigid chemical structure and specific inter and intra-molecular interactions [18], [19], [20]. Formation of strong hydrogen bonds prevents the free movement of polymeric chain segments exposed to the electrical field, leading to jet break up during the process [19], [20], [21]. Moreover, the repulsive force between ionic groups on the polymer backbone is expected to hinder the formation of sufficient chain entanglements to allow continuous fiber formation during jet stretching, whipping and bending, generally resulting in nanobeads instead of nanofibers [22]. Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) is a well-known solvent for the electrospinning of chitosan. It can form stable salts with chitosan which prevents interchain interactions, and also has a low boiling point (71.8 °C as compared to 118.1 °C for acetic acid), which is beneficial for faster fiber formation in the evaporation region of the electrospinning process [23]. Some papers report the preparation of pure electrospun chitosan nanofibers using TFA or its mixtures with dichloromethane (DCM) and trichloromethane (TCM) [24], [25]. However, TFA is environmentally harmful, very toxic and corrosive, which makes its use very limited from an industrial point of view for food and biomedical applications. A highly concentrated acetic acid aqueous solution (90 wt %) was also reported by two research groups as a successful solvent for the electrospinning of neat chitosan, using samples with degrees of deacetylation (DDA) of 54 and 75-85%, respectively [21], [26]. Electrospinning of chitin followed by deacetylation of the prepared nanofibers [22], [24], and co-axial electrospinning of chitosan with polyethylene oxide (PEO) are alternative proposed methods [27], however they present their own difficulties such as solubility and electrospinnablity of chitin or controlling adequately the co-axial electrospinning process. Finally, chemically modified chitosan has also been electrospun by some researchers, such as hexanoyl chitosan [28], [29], carboxymethyl chitosan [30], carboxyethyl chitosan [31] and quaternized chitosan [32], [33]. Among all of these approaches, the most successful and easiest method to improve the electrospinnability of chitosan is blending it with a second natural or synthetic polymeric phase. This co-spinning agent is usually an easily electrospinnable polymer such as PEO [7], [18], [34], [35], [36], polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) [19], [37], [38], [39], polylactic acid (PLA) [25], [40], [41], polyacrylamide (PAM) [42], [43], zein [44], [45], silk fibroin [46], [47] and collagen [48], which are all biocompatible and biodegradable and will not constraint the final applications of chitosan nanofibers. Brief descriptions of these various approaches have been recently reviewed elsewhere [49], [50], [51]. Depending on the second polymeric phase, type, content and developed morphology, physical and mechanical properties of composite chitosan nanofibers vary greatly. Integrity and stability of the fibers in different working conditions is another concern that should be taken into account for the final applications of chitosan-based nanofibers [52]. Generally, due to the outstanding electrospinnability of the selected second phase, a higher content of the co-spinning polymer leads to further improvement of chitosan electrospinnability. Normally, the second phase is added in the range of 20-90 wt%. Obviously, for applications that require a particular property of chitosan, such as antimicrobial properties, the lowest amount of added polymer is preferable. Bhattarai et al. [34] could reach a low amount of 10 wt% PEO in chitosan nanofibers by using dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and an aniogenic surfactant in an acetic acid aqueous solvent. Recently Zhang et al. [52] prepared chitosan-based nanofibers with 5 wt% of added PEO using ultra high molecular weight PEO along with DMSO as a co-solvent. Desai et al. also reported the formation of composite chitosan nanofibers having 5 wt% PEO [20] and 10 wt% PAM [43] by utilizing a special designed hot air assisted electrospinning unit. Finally, even though the preparation of chitosan-based nanofibers at high chitosan content has been achieved in the past years, several of these studies have been based on the use of harmful solvents such as trifuoroacetic acide (TFA) and dimethyl sulfoxane (DMSO) [34], [52]. Obviously, there is much remaining to be improved and clarified in the electrospinning of chitosan.

Lithium-ion batteries have been widely utilized as energy supplies for portable devices, electric vehicles, and wearable electronics due to their high operation voltages, long cycle life, and high energy density.1, 2 However, the intrinsically flammable liquid electrolytes and the formation of lithium dendrites result in the numerous safety hazards including fire and explosion, thus hindering their further widely applications.3, 4 In order to solve these problems, two strategies focusing on polymer electrolytes, including solid polymer electrolytes (SPEs)5-10 and gel polymer electrolytes (GPEs),11-14 have been proposed. Without the electrolyte solvent, SPEs are the ideal candidates except for their low lithium ionic conductivity (σ, 10−6 S/cm) at room temperature and high interfacial impedance.6-8 Besides, the widely reported lithium salts, LiTFSI and LiFSI, at present have been only used as additives in the commercial electrolyte because of their high cost. In contrast, GPEs could constraint the large amount of liquid commercial electrolyte into their polymer networks to provide lithium ion transport and good interfacial contact with electrode.15-17 High σ and lithium ion transfer number, electrochemical stability, tough mechanical properties, and stable interfacial properties toward lithium metal anode are the main concerns for designing GPEs structures. As widely acknowledged, the ethylene oxide unit is a typical structure studied for the lithium ion transport by inter/intra molecular polymer chain. Therefore, the design of polymer structures with ethylene oxide unit is still the main approach in the synthesis of polyethylene oxide (PEO) based GPEs. However, because of the strong solvation of carbonate ester and high dielectric constant, these PEO based GPEs usually show poor mechanical properties. Introducing of rigid acrylate monomers, cross-linking monomers, and reinforcements, such as poly (ethylene glycol) diacrylate,18 ethoxylated trimethylolpropane triacrylate,19 cyclic carbonate,20 and cellulose triacetate21 with (poly(ethylene glycol)) methyl ether methacrylate18 are extensively investigated. Obviously, high cost of Polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based functional monomers and unsatisfied mechanical properties are all the practical problems that should be solved toward the commercialization of GPEs. PEO, a cost-effective polymer, is rarely reported as GPEs because the pure PEO could become sticky in commercial electrolyte.22-26 In order to solve this problem, the plasticized quasi solid polymer electrolyte was proposed, nevertheless the high cost of LITFSI salts is undesirable.27-29 Blending with other polymers is simple and useful technique to improve the mechanical properties of GPEs with ethylene oxide unit, such as co-doping it with Poly(vinylidene fluoride-CO-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP)30 because of the good mechanical properties endowed by the semi-crystalline structure of PVDF-HFP and acceptable absorption of electrolyte.31 As the above discussed, great challenge is still encountered toward the practical utilization of PEO based GPEs, including the development of high cost-effective monomers/polymers instead of (poly(ethylene glycol)) methyl ether methacrylate and PVDF-HFP. Therefore, how to design a low cost and environmental-friendly method to improve the mechanical properties of PEO based GPEs is still a crucial problem.

Based solely on the provided evidence, blending chitosan with Poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) significantly improves its electrospinnability by addressing key limitations:

1.  **Overcomes poor inherent spinnability:** Chitosan itself has limited electrospinnability due to its polycationic nature, rigid chemical structure, and strong inter-/intra-molecular hydrogen bonding, which prevent sufficient chain entanglement and cause jet breakup, leading to beads instead of fibers [4], [8].
2.  **Improves solution properties & chain dynamics:** PEO, an easily electrospinnable polymer, enhances the solution rheology. It increases viscosity and entanglement density [9], [12], [13], while potentially reducing conductivity at higher PEO ratios [9]. This combination facilitates the formation of a stable jet during electrospinning.
3.  **Enables continuous fiber formation:** The addition of PEO promotes the formation of smooth, continuous, defect-free chitosan-based nanofibers, preventing bead formation [5], [7], [9], [13]. The required PEO content varies but is typically significant (e.g., 20-90 wt% [4]), though studies report achieving fibers with lower PEO content (down to 5-10 wt%) using specific solvents (e.g., DMSO, acetic acid) or setups [4], [13].
4.  **Allows use of less harmful solvents:** Blending with PEO enables electrospinning using less toxic solvents like aqueous acetic acid, avoiding the need for highly toxic solvents like trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) which are otherwise required for neat chitosan [4], [13].
5.  **Post-spinning considerations:** PEO can be removed post-electrospinning (e.g., by washing with water) to leave pure chitosan fibers, enhancing their aqueous stability [7].
6.  **Maintains functional properties:** Despite blending, the resulting chitosan/PEO composite nanofibers retain key chitosan properties like antimicrobial activity [5], [8]. Blending can also improve mechanical properties compared to pure chitosan nanofibers [8].

Polymer blending is an effective method for providing desirable polymeric materials with properties useful for the packaging industry. In the study reported, blends of chitosan/poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) were prepared in various weight ratios with and without glycerol. Line profile analysis of the X-ray diffraction patterns of these blended films was carried out. Microstructural parameters such as crystallite size and lattice strain were determined using paracrystalline modelling of X-ray data. These values were correlated with physico-mechanical and optical properties of the chitosan/PEO blends with and without glycerol to understand the holistic behaviour of the blends. Two prominent Bragg reflections at 2θ ≈ 19° and 23° were observed in the wide-angle X-ray diffraction patterns of the glycerol-based chitosan/PEO blended films of various ratios. Interruption of PEO crystallization with chitosan results in an amorphous polymer network and hence a reduction in crystallite size by almost 97.7%. For glycerol-based blends, the crystallite size/area decreases to 94.4% of the virgin crystallite size. In view of the recent interest in eco-friendly packaging materials, blends between biopolymers and synthetic polymers are of particular significance, because they can combine biocompatibility with good processability and mechanical resistance and can be used as biomaterials. One such blend is that of chitosan and poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO).1-4 Chitosan is a de-N-acetylated form of chitin, the second most abundantly available natural polymer obtained from the shells of crab, prawn, shrimp, etc. It consists mainly of β-(1-4)-2-amino-2-deoxy-D-glucose units and with occasional N-acetylglucosamine residues. Chitosan, a natural, non-toxic, biodegradable polymer,2 available commercially, has been used in a variety of applications. Chitosan can form transparent films, which may find application in a variety of packaging needs, as a result of intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Chitosan is soluble in aqueous solutions of organic and mineral acids under specific conditions. The mechanical and barrier properties of chitosan films can be controlled through choosing chitosan of appropriate molecular weight and an appropriate solvent system.5 PEO is water soluble and biodegradable. PEO has been extensively used in the biomedical field because of its excellent hydrophilic nature, high viscosity, ability to form hydrogen bonds with ether oxygen and biocompatibility. Based solely on the provided context evidence, blending chitosan (CS) with poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) significantly improves its electrospinnability by addressing key challenges:

1.  **Enables Fiber Formation & Improves Morphology:** Pure chitosan is difficult to electrospin due to its polycationic nature, strong intramolecular forces (hydrogen bonding), rigid structure, and lack of sufficient chain entanglement/elasticity in solution, typically resulting in bead formation or jet breakup instead of continuous fibers [5], [14]. Blending with PEO facilitates the electrospinning process, allowing the formation of smooth, continuous, defect-free nanofibers [1], [2], [6], [8]. PEO acts as a "co-spinning" or "carrier" polymer, enhancing chain entanglement and providing the necessary rheological properties (viscosity, elasticity) for stable jet formation [3], [5], [14].

2.  **Modifies Solution Properties:**
    *   **Viscosity:** PEO increases the viscosity of the chitosan solution, which is crucial for preventing jet breakup during electrospinning. Higher viscosity solutions exhibit longer stress relaxation times, stabilizing the jet [8], [10]. However, increasing chitosan content relative to PEO can significantly reduce viscosity, hindering spinnability [8], [10].
    *   **Conductivity:** Chitosan solutions typically have high conductivity due to charged groups. Adding PEO generally reduces conductivity [8], [10]. An optimal balance is needed: very high conductivity (high chitosan/low PEO) combined with low viscosity prevents smooth spinning, while sufficient viscosity (higher PEO content) allows spinnability even with lower conductivity [8], [10].
    *   **Solvent Compatibility:** PEO blending allows the use of less toxic solvents (e.g., aqueous acetic acid) instead of highly toxic/corrosive solvents like trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) required for pure chitosan electrospinning [2], [7], [14]. PEO improves chitosan's solubility and processability in common solvents [13].

3.  **Facilitates Intermolecular Interactions:** Hydrogen bonding occurs between chitosan and PEO, improving the compatibility and spinnability of the blend solution [5], [7], [13]. These interactions can interrupt chitosan crystallization, leading to more amorphous structures in films [13].

4.  **Enables Structural Control (Core-Shell/Microphase Separation):** Due to the poor miscibility of chitosan and PEO, electrospinning their homogeneous blend solutions can lead to fibers with internal phase-separated structures (core-shell with PEO core/CS shell or microphase-separated) depending on the blend ratio [4]. This structural control offers potential for tailored properties like drug release [4].

5.  **Post-Processing & Stability:** PEO can be selectively removed post-electrospinning (e.g., by washing with water after neutralizing acidic groups) to leave behind pure chitosan nanofibers or fibers with very high chitosan content, enhancing their stability in aqueous conditions [5], [6].

6.  **Limitation - PEO Content Requirement:** Achieving successful electrospinning typically requires a significant amount of PEO in the blend (often 5-90 wt%, though optimized ratios like 90:10 CS:PEO have been achieved with specific methods/solvents). Lower PEO content is desirable to maximize chitosan's inherent properties (e.g., antimicrobial activity) but is harder to spin [2], [6], [14].

The protocol of tensile tests under water conditions was elaborated to study the mechanical behavior of PBS/PBAT nanocomposites when wet and immersed in water, in order to simulate the conditions experienced by synthetic fishing nets throughout their use in seawater. In this section, all the samples in water conditions were drawn using a screw-action manual grip and were compared to those drawn in air conditions using the same grips. In order to achieve a better understanding of the mechanical behavior of our samples and their interactions with nanochitins and nanocelluloses, we will first discuss the shape of the curves obtained from the tensile tests. The tensile tests, under air conditions, curves for PBS, PBAT, PBS/PBAT blends and their nanocomposites are shown in Figure 4a. PBAT presents a curve that is characterized by a single yield at the beginning followed by necking and a long strain hardening with a slight increase in stress during polymer deformation, which ends with a fracture at around 300% strain. This behavior was also observed in the tensile tests under water conditions (Figure 4b). In the case of PBS, its mechanical behavior is a little more particular and unique. First, an initial yield is observed that is followed by a necking and a strain hardening of the material. Subsequently, a second yield and necking appear around 80% strain, followed by a long strain hardening before ultimate failure at 220% strain. This was also noted for the PBS/PBAT nanocomposites, which have a curve shape comparable to PBS. The second yield shifts toward approximately 120% strain for PBS/PBAT and toward 150% strain for PBS/PBAT/ChNCsLac1% and PBS/PBAT/NFCEster1%. Indeed, it is also noticeable that the failure stress of PBS/PBAT nanocomposites was higher than the initial yield stress usually accompanied by strain-induced crystallization, which would have aligned the crystallites in the direction of the strain [39]. The double yielding and necking phenomena have been explained by several authors by the fact that PBS crystallizes in two different crystal structures, the α and β forms, which appear under various conditions. For example, the α form is more general and appears when PBS is crystallized from the melt, while the β form is observed under a certain level of mechanical stress [36]. Liu et al. as well as Ichikawa and Mizukoshi have demonstrated the relationship between the crystal structure transition of PBS, as revealed by XRD analysis, and the mechanical behavior variations observed on its traction tests curves [40, 41]. Secondly, a unique stress oscillation phenomenon is observed which causes a cycle of stress drop and recovery. This behavior is more pronounced in the case of PBS/PBAT nanocomposites. Wan et al. reported the same behavior for compression-molded PBS samples drawn at a lower rate under 50 mm min−1 and also at a rate of 10 mm min−1 under different temperatures [42]. Their study presents a clear explanation for the occurrence of these self-stress necking oscillations on the tensile curves, which can be attributed to the local increase in temperature at the neck front of the samples, the crystallization induced by the orientation of the polymer chains or to the formation of cracks and micro-cavities which were observed on their drawn samples [42]. These cracks and micro-cavities were noticed in our PBS and PBS/PBAT nanocomposite drawn samples. The tensile tests curves in water conditions (Figure 4b) of neat polymers and their blends show almost the same behavior as in air with some changes in the second yield for the PBS/PBAT and PBS/PBAT/NFCEster1% blends, which appear in the same strain as PBS, while the second yield of PBS/PBAT/ChNCsLac1% has shifted to 120% compared to PBS which remains at 80% strain. The stress oscillation phenomenon is absent in the case of PBS, contrary to the PBS/PBAT blend and its nanocomposites where it appears periodically until the ultimate failure of the samples. Based on these tensile test behaviors, the variation of Young's modulus and elongation at break of the nanocomposites were also investigated under air and water conditions using screw-action manual grips (Figure 5). Firstly, both PBS and PBAT were tested to evaluate the impact of water penetration into neat polymer. Regarding PBS, considering the standard deviation of the measurements, the mechanical properties were not influenced by the presence of water. The presence of water in PBAT also led to a similar Young's modulus but an increased elongation at break by 24%-that is, 250% versus 310%, before and after immersion, respectively. It is obvious that the PBS/PBAT blend also increases both Young's modulus (+6%) and elongation at break (+11%) in water conditions. These results relate to those found in the literature, which demonstrate an improvement of the mechanical properties of PBS/PBAT monofilaments, notably in elongation at break, when used for the first time in water [17, 43]. In the case of PBS/PBAT/NFCEster1%, considering the standard deviation of the measurements, both Young's modulus and elongation at break remain constant in water conditions. Thus, the PBS/PBAT/ChNCsLac1% shows a slight decrease in Young's modulus (−10%) from 402 in air conditions to 364 MPa in water and a significant increase in elongation at break value (+52%) from 200% in air conditions to 304% in water. However, these values remain lower than those of PBS/PBAT blend and do not reveal a significant improvement of the mechanical properties of the blend by the addition of nanochitin and nanocellulose fillers. The presence of water generally acts as a plasticizer for many polymers, including PBS and PBAT, which reduces Young's modulus values, indicating a decrease in the stiffness of the materials. This was particularly evident for PBAT and PBS/PBAT/ChNCsLac1%. It also leads to an increase in elongation at break values that indicate an enhanced ductility that was shown in particular for PBS/PBAT, PBS/PBAT/ChNCsLac1%, and PBS/PBAT/NFCEster1%.
Elongation at break values have a significant reduction by at least of 86 %, with the addition of QH in the PLA/PBAT system. Contrary, at higher QH concentrations (15 wt%, 20 wt% and 30 wt%), an increase up to 13 % is observed, in comparison to the PLA/PBAT blend. The micrographs were obtained on a JEOL 6400 scanning electric microscope (SEM). The films were quenched and fractured in liquid nitrogen, and then adhered on the aluminum stubs. The cross sections of the films were coated with a thin layer of carbon prior to the observation. Poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) is a synthetic biodegradable polyester based on petrochemical sources. Thermoplastic starch (TPS) was used as an additive to prepare the PBAT/TPS blends in order to reduce the cost, and meanwhile to enhance the biodegradability. However, the mechanical properties of the PBAT/TPS blends tend to decrease due to the brittleness of TPS and the incompatibility between PBAT and TPS. Fig. 2 shows that the tensile strength and elongation at break of the PBAT/TPS blends depended on the content of TPS. With the increase of the TPS content, the elongation at break monotonically decreased. However, it is interesting that the tensile strength did not decrease but increased when the content of TPS was raised from 10 wt% to 30 wt%, reaching the maximum at 30 wt%. Above 30 wt% TPS, the tensile strength monotonically decreased. This phenomenon indicated that the variation of the tensile strength might be related to multiple parameters, and the content of TPS is one of the influencing factors. The SEM images of the PBAT/TPS blends with different contents of TPS (PBAT80/TPS20 represents 80 wt% of PBAT and 20 wt% of TPS) are shown in Fig. 3. When the content of TPS increased, the sizes of the dispersed TPS particles first decreased, then increased until TPS became the continuous phase (the content of TPS was over 50 wt%). This result suggested that the increase of tensile strength between 10 wt% and 30 wt% of TPS might be ascribed to the better dispersion and the smaller particle size of TPS in the PBAT matrix. However, the further increasing TPS above 30 wt% decreased the tensile strength. In our experiments, the PBAT/TPS blends containing over 50 wt% of TPS could not be blown into films because of the phase separation, and therefore, no data regarding mechanical properties were obtained.
PBAT is one of the most attractive additives to PLA, because it improves its flexibility and processability. PLA/PBAT compositions can be used in the automotive, agricultural, pharmaceutical and packaging industries [8]. As PBAT is a costly material, its blending is often required to limit the price [9]. Wang et al. [1] studied the PLA/PBAT blends prepared by in situ compatibilization reaction using ADR (multifunctional epoxy oligomer) as compatibilizer. Various ratios were tested, but in each case, the elongation at break was significantly (up to 579.9%) improved in comparison to the neat PLA. Ding and co-authors [10] fabricated tri-block copolymers of PLA-PBAT-PLA characterized by superior interfacial interaction, enhanced interpenetration and miscibility between PLA and PBAT resulting in higher elongation at break. Lyu et al. [11] dotted the PLA/PBAT blend for 3D printing with 10% of PLA-g-GMA (PLA grafted with glycidyl methacrylate) and measured the tensile strength and elongation at break for PLA70PBAT30 to equal, respectively, 42.6 MPa and over 200%. Sritham and co-authors [12] tested PLA/PBAT with different ratios of both polymers (from 10 to 40% of PLA) in terms of their tensile properties. Although the tensile strength remained similar for all blends, the elastic modulus slightly increased with the growing content of PLA. Simultaneously, the elongation dropped together with the higher content of PLA. TPS blends with PLA were reviewed by Zaaba and Ismail [13]. Thermoplastic starch is known to be another common material that can help to mitigate the brittle behavior of PLA. Nevertheless, the crucial limitation of this solution comes from the poor adhesion between the hydrophilic starch granules and hydrophobic polylactide. If needed, a similar approach may be undertaken as for PBAT-modification with compatibilizers, crosslinking agents etc. Moreover, the number of recycling (NOR) for PLA/TPS blends is limited as they are very sensitive to repeated processing, which ends up in deterioration of their mechanical properties [14]. There are also reported works on the manufacturing PLA/TPS-based composite materials, e.g., by joining them with cassava pulp (CP) [15]. CP-reinforced PLA/TPS composites can be readily subjected to injection molding. The most beneficial CP content was revealed to be 22.1% resulting in increased tensile strength (up to 354%) and Young’s modulus (up to 722%). Li and Huneault [16] proved that the addition of chain-extenders to PLA/TPS blends does not affect the tensile strength and Young’s modulus, nor the elongation. PLA/TPS mixture, due to its exceptional biodegradability, was chosen by Labus et al. [17] as a preferred material to be applied in the fabrication of long-term drug delivery systems (carriers). They can also be used in food packaging applications [18]. Przybytek et al. [19] found out that the joining of PLA with TPS and epoxidized soybean oil (ESO) enhances the elongation without comprising the biodegradability and compostability. There are also some attempts [20] at the creation of terpolymers, e.g., TPS/PBSA (butyl glycol ester copolymer)/PLA, where PLA is added to increase the compatibility of TPS/PBSA blends, maintaining them to be biodegradable. In the following paper, PLA base material was combined with plasticizing secondary polymeric compound: PBS or PBAT or TPS. Manufactured blends were characterized in terms of their tensile properties (tensile strength, elongation at break, yield strength and Young’s modulus). Selected processing parameters such as melt flow ratio (MFR) and melt volume ratio (MVR) were investigated in order to evaluate the possibility of utilization of the studied biodegradable compositions in common technologies, e.g., extrusion, injection molding or 3D-printing. The work was complemented with DSC test results identifying softening, glass transition, cold crystallization and crystallization temperatures of mixtures. Moreover, heat deflection temperatures for 1.8 MPa and 8 MPa (HDT A and HDT C) together with Vicat softening temperatures for two loadings of 10 N and 50 N (VST A and VST B) were tested. In order to facilitate the fabrication process no additional compatibilizers have been used. The paper gathers novel data concerning the influence of temperature on tensile properties, describing the materials’ stability under variable conditions.

As compared with pure PBAT, the tensile properties of the unmodified lignin (30 wt% HL) composites were significantly weakened, in which the elongation and tensile strength reduced from 828.7% and 23.0 MPa to 313.7% and 13.5 MPa, respectively. Their negative rates of change in elongation and tensile strength were respectively up to 87.6% and 45.2% at 40 wt% lignin loading. These results could be ascribed to the agglomeration of lignin, poor compatibility and weak interfacial interactions of lignin in the PBAT matrix, as confirmed by the SEM images of HL composites (Fig. 4b). By contrast, esterified lignin-based composites exhibited different improvements (especially in elongation) compared to HL-based composites. It was found that the elongation at break of the composites showed a dramatic enhancement with the extension of the incorporated aliphatic carbon chains. For LCL and OCL-based composites, the elongation at break first increased and then decreased with the augment of the lignin content (Table 2). The composites with 40 wt% loading of LCL and OCL both exhibited the highest elongation at break (up to 600% more), which was almost six times as compared with those of HL-based composites with the same content. Meanwhile, their tensile strength also showed relative ideal values (>13 MPa). Further increase of their contents (45-50 wt%) in the composites contributed to an obvious decline in ductility and tensile strength, which derived from the aggregation of lignin in the PBAT matrix. The distinctly improved mechanical performances of the composites implied that the soft segments of esterified lignins exhibited good compatibility and distribution with the PBAT matrix even with a high esterified lignin content (up to 40-50 wt%).18,22 As shown in Fig. 4b-f, the morphology images of the fractured surface from different composites show that HL had limited distribution and compatibility with PBAT since significant lignin agglomeration was visible. In contrast, esterified lignins showed evidently improved compatibility even under a high loading of 40 wt% (Fig. 4g-i). Additionally, it is necessary to investigate the interaction energy that can elucidate the physical or chemical molecular interactions in the prepared composite matrix. Furthermore, it was found that the addition of MAH into the composites played an important role in the improvement of mechanical properties (as compared to the control group in Table S4†), which served as a coupling reagent in the composite and further associated with PBAT and lignin polymer via new chemical bonds.13,43,44 Therefore, in this study, the esterification modification effectively enhanced the distribution and compatibility of lignin in the PBAT matrix, and also, the molecular mobility of composites was obviously improved. Meanwhile, the ingenious participation of MAH further reinforced the mechanical properties of the lignin-based composites. The polymer intermolecular diagrams for the present PBAT composite matrixes are presented in Fig. 5a. Fig. 5b compares the tensile strength and breaking strain of the prepared PBAT/lignin composites in this study with other PBAT-based composites. Previously, in most of the PBAT composites the loading of incorporated lignin was limited to 30 wt%, whereas the obtained PBAT/lignin composites here with higher lignin contents (40-50 wt%) exhibited a higher tensile strength (13.4 MPa) and excellent elongation at break (up to 618%). Due to the presence of the hydrocarbon side chains in the esterified lignin, more effective intermolecular bonds formed and facilitated better compatibility and distribution between lignin and PBAT (Fig. 5a), resulting in competitive mechanical properties of composites even when containing much more lignin.21,45 The desirable mechanical performances achieved in this study could meet the requirement (GB/T21302-2007) of laminated films and pouches for packaging, and these results provide valuable insight for the further development of lignin-based biodegradable composite materials. The preeminent UV-shielding of soft composite films is important for food or medicine packaging.18,46 However, the neat PBAT film shows no UV absorption performance, and the incorporation of the lignin polymer could artfully give the composites strong absorption performance for UV light.17,18 As shown in Fig. 6a, the high transmittance of UV was observed in the neat PBAT film, while all the lignin-based composites films exhibited much higher UV absorption. The admirable UV barrier properties were mainly attributed to the existence of abundant benzene rings and carbonyl groups in the composites.47-49 The composite film blended HL showed a higher broad shielding effect to UV and visible light than those of esterified lignins, which could be attributed to its aggregation during blending with PBAT and further impeded UV-vis light transmission. In addition, the dramatically decreased OH groups in esterified lignins also reduced the UV absorption of modified films. Nevertheless, with the increase of lignin loading, the UV-vis light was further shielded (more than 97%) and UV-A (320-400 nm) light was almost completely blocked. Here, the UV-shielding efficiencies of the prepared lignin-based films are comparable to those of the previous lignin-based composites films50 but better than those of PLA-lignin51 and nanocellulose-carbon dot composite films.52 Moreover, the stability of films under the longstanding UV irradiation was also previously confirmed to be stable.18 Due to the biodegradable characteristic of lignin and PBAT, their integration provided a feasible pathway for the production of biodegradable and UV-shielding composite films. In addition, the contact angle analysis of the composites showed that the incorporation of esterified lignin enhanced the hydrophobicity of composites (as indicated in Fig. S4†), which was in line with the aforementioned hydrophobicity of lignin preparations.
Figure 5a shows that the storage modulus of the PBAT/starch blends has a detectible increase with the addition of additives in the glass state (from − 60 °C to − 30 °C), indicating that the incorporation of additives plays a role in compatibilization. The pure PBAT exhibited an E' of 3213 MPa, while it increased to 4062 MPa with the incorporation of 35 wt% TPS. After the addition of TPS which was modified by MA and TC, the storage modulus up to 5000 MPa. The two additives as a compatibilizer entangled the molecular chains of PBAT and TPS, which limited the movement of continuous segments. After temperature rising above − 30 °C, the storage modulus of all samples decreased sharply, which was attributed to the Tg of PBAT. The storage modulus had dropped significantly as the temperature continues to increase. When the temperature approached rubbery region (above 40 °C), the storage modulus of PBAT/MA-TPS, PBAT/TC-TPS, and PBAT/MA-TC-TPS blends was reduced. After 40 °C, TPS began to be thermoplastic, the addition of MA and TC promoted the thermoplastic, which led to the reduction in storage modulus. When the temperature is over 95 °C, the rubbery region was ended with a sudden drop of storage modulus due to the melting of crystalline phase of PBAT. The glass transition temperatures (Tg) of the blends provided information on the miscibility of blends. The height of the tanδ peak was generally a measure of the damping nature of a compound. The two transitions of the neat PBAT were around − 18 and 42 °C in tanδ. The high magnitude at − 18 °C was related to the poly (butylene adipate) (PBA) segment mobility, and the low magnitude at 42 °C corresponded to the rigid aromatic domain of poly (butylene terephthalate) (PBT) segment [17]. These transitions were accompanied by a significant decrease in storage modulus at the same time. As for the PBAT/TPS blend, the tanδ curves display the different glass transitions of TPS and PBAT components, which are typically immiscible. One transition of PABT was around − 18.0 °C, and the another one of TPS dispersed phase was invisible. However, different additive types also affected the tanδ and modulus strength of the blends. In the presence of MA, the glass transition of PBAT decreased from − 18.0 to − 20.0 °C suggested that PBAT interacted with TPS at the molecular level. As for PBAT/TC-TPS, the tanδ value was higher than PBAT/TPS in the range of 0-88.5 °C. The Tg of PBAT was still clearly visible with its peak position reduced to − 20.5 °C. Interestingly, with the addition of TC, the peak value of TPS became visible with a value of 81 °C. The shifting is strong proof that TC can be used as a compatibilizer for PBAT and TPS. In the presence of both MA and TC, peaks of PBAT and TPS were both visible. The Tg of PBAT in the blends decreased from − 18.0 to − 21.0 °C. The lower Tg value for PBAT in PBAT/TPS compared to pure PBAT may be caused by the dispersion of the modified TPS in PBAT and steric effects which lead to an increase in the free volume. With the addition of MA and TC to the PBAT/TPS, the granule of starch becomes smaller and its dispersibility is improved, which increased free volume. So the Tg of PBAT reduced. The Tg of the TPS decreased from 81.0 to 76.5 °C which was consistent with the mixture was added TC only. The results suggest that both TPS and PBAT contributed to the elastic properties of the blends, TC and MA played the role of reactive compatibilization and the enhanced interfacial adhesion can effectively transfer the stress from the continuous PBAT matrix to the dispersed TPS phase. Tg of PBAT in the blend films was consistent with the results of DSC, which moved toward a lower temperature.
