Mechanical behavior of the slabs containing the reprocessed granules is comparable to results obtained for the slabs containing only virgin granules (R1 S and R2 S). The mechanical tests reveal a general increase in the maximum stress and deformation at break with the increase of reprocessed material. These variations could be attributed to the better homogenization of the fillers and additives in materials that involve multiple processing cycles. However, variations observed between the virgin compound-based slabs and the slabs containing reprocessed materials are limited. This result is in partial agreement with what has already been observed in the literature on multiple extrusion of formulations based on polylactic acid. The study conducted by Fazelinejad et al.30 on mechanical properties of a mixture of PLA with 30 wt% of chalk showed that up to six repeated extrusion processing cycles did not cause significant variations of the maximum stress, deformation at break and Young modulus. Zenkiewicz et al.4 studied the correlation between mechanical properties of PLA subject to repeated extrusion cycles. The researchers repeated the extrusion process of PLA in a co-rotating twin-screw system up to 10 times and observed that the extruded polymer after 10 extrusion cycles exhibited marginal differences in tensile test results with respect to the material subjected to a single extrusion process. The addition of the chain extender in the cast extrusion process of reprocessed compounds (R1 100CE, R2 100CE) determines an increase in elongation at break compared to the additive-free compounds (R1 100, R2 100) over 350%. With reference to the improvement of mechanical properties Arruda et al.24 demonstrated that PLA/PBAT polymeric binary blends with increasing Joncryl content exhibited an increase in elongation at break of 900% compared to the analogous mixture without chain extender. A similar effect has been observed by Veang et al.31 in a binary PLA/PBS blend. This improvement, visible on both formulations R1 100CE and R2 100CE, is attributable to the dual compatibilizing and dispersing effect given by the Joncryl additive, in accordance with what is reported in other literature studies. For example, the morphological analysis conducted by Cherykhunthod et al.32 demonstrated a finer dispersion of PBS in a polylactic acid polymer matrix following the use of Joncryl. Arruda et al.24 found the formation of a PLA-co-PBAT copolymer in a PLA/PBAT binary system. This copolymer served as a link between the main polymer phase and the dispersed phase, reducing interfacial discontinuities and improving PLA-PBAT compatibility. The creation of an interphase consequently caused an improvement in the mechanical, rheological, and morphological properties of the blends. The compatibilization action of the chain extender led to the formation of more continuous phases, and therefore, capable of more effectively transferring stresses from the rigid PLA structure to the flexible PBAT structure. Similarly, in this article, the increase in elongation at break is attributable to the improved compatibility between the rigid PLA phase and the plasticizing succinic acid polymer phase. The present study investigated the possibility of recovering post-industrial production waste. The effect of the recovery material has been studied both with reference to the twin-screw compounding process and, subsequently, to the cast extrusion process. In both cases, the influence of a chain extender additive featuring glycidyl methacrylate functionalities on the rheological and thermo-mechanical properties of the bioplastic material was evaluated.

Table 1 lists the tensile performances of neat PBAT and PBAT/PGA samples with various PGA contents, including tensile yield strength, tensile fracture strength, tensile modulus and elongation at break. The typical stress-strain curves of the samples were presented in Figure 1. As can be seen from Table 1, owing to its very low tensile yield strength and tensile modulus (7.67 and 62.6 MPa, respectively), coupled with a high elongation at break (>1000%), neat PBAT showed a very soft and ductility behavior. While introducing PGA with high tensile strength (>68.9 MPa) and tensile modulus (6.9 GPa)23 into PBAT matrix, the mechanical properties of the PBAT/PGA samples could be changed significantly. With an increase in PGA content, the tensile yield strength and modulus of PBAT/PGA samples gradually increased. While PGA content increased to 35 wt%, the tensile yield strength increased from 7.67 MPa of neat PBAT to 12.05 MPa. Meanwhile, the tensile modulus increased from 62.6 MPa of neat PBAT to 158.9 MPa. Compared with neat PBAT, the tensile yield strength and tensile modulus of PBAT/PGA (65/35) sample were increased by 57% and 153%, respectively. As we known, the tensile modulus and tensile yield strength are two important parameters for evaluating the resistance to deformation of polymer materials. Compared with neat PBAT, the enhancement in tensile modulus and tensile yield strength will allow the PBAT/PGA blend to meet wider application requirements while it is used as biodegradable packaging materials. However, it has to be mentioned that the tensile ductility of PBAT/PGA samples (in terms of elongation at break) decreased drastically with an increase in PGA content. For example, the elongation at break of PBAT/PGA (65/35) sample decreased from 1082.1% (neat PBAT) to 88.7%. Due to the significant reduction in tensile ductility, the stress enhancement effect caused by the orientation of macromolecule segments during the tensile stretching process was restrained greatly, as shown in Figure 1. As a result, the tensile fracture strength of PBAT/PGA (65/35) sample also decreased significantly from 25.74 MP (neat PBAT) to 13.17 MPa. SEM observation was conducted to research the microscopic morphologies of PBAT/PGA samples. The SEM photographs of cryo-surfaces for PBAT/PGA samples were shown in Figure 2. The sizes of PGA particles were measured using the particle size statistics software (Nano Measurer). Thus the ranges of particle size distribution and apparent number average particle sizes (app) of PGA for all the PBAT/PGA samples were shown in Figure 3. As can be seen from Figure 2, the PBAT/PGA blends exhibited a two-phase microstructure, where the PGA particles dispersed in PBAT matrix. The SEM observation confirmed that PBAT/PGA blends were incompatible. As PGA content increased from 5 to 15 wt%, the app of PGA particles increased from 1.77 to 2.59 μm. While further increasing the PGA content, the app of PGA particles remained almost unchanged along with an increase in number of PGA particles. For many incompatible polymer blends, the size of the dispersed phase tends to increase with the increase of the dispersed phase content, because the main mechanism that determines the shape development of the dispersed phase is the balance between breakdown and coalescence of the dispersed phase droplets. After reaching this balance, the trend that the dispersed phase size increases with the increase of dispersed phase content become less obvious.25, 26 For the PBAT/PGA blending system, when PGA content reached the threshold value of 15 wt%, the balance between breakdown and coalescence of PGA droplets could be achieved. According to SEM observation, with an increase in PGA content, more and more PGA particles formed in the PBAT matrix, which could greatly restrict the movement of PBAT chains and segments. Thus, it was beneficial to improve the tensile modulus and tensile yield strength of PBAT matrix. However, due to the poor interface compatibility between PBAT matrix and PGA domains, the elongation at break decreased significantly from 1082.1% (neat PBAT sample) to 88.7% with an increase in PGA content from zero to 35 wt%. Similar behavior was also reported previously for PBAT blends with other polymers, such as PLA, and EVOH etc. For example, Li et al.11 prepared PBAT/stereocomplex polylactide (sc-PLA) blends using sc-PLA as a reinforcing modifier. It was confirmed that the formed sc-PLA particles would enhance the tensile modulus and yield strength of PBAT. While increasing sc-PLA content from 0% to 30%, the tensile modulus and yield strength of the blend increased from 70.2 and 8.1 MPa for neat PBAT to 140.1 and 11.4 MPa, respectively. It was proposed by the authors that the increases of modulus and yield strength were the result of suppression of movement of the PBAT chains by the percolated sc-PLA particles network structure. However, when the sc-PLA content increased to 30 wt%, the elongation at break decreased largely from 1500% for neat PBAT to 114%. Elhamnia et al16 prepared PBAT/EVOH blends under various mixing conditions with different mixing times, rotor speeds and mixing temperatures. It showed that the tensile yield stress increased slightly from about 8.5 MPa for neat PBAT to about 11.0 MPa while increasing EVOH content from 0 to 30 wt%. However, compared with the high strain at break (780%) of neat PBAT, the strain at break of PBAT/EVOH (30 wt%) blend was halved. The decreased strain at break of PBAT/EVOH blend can be explained by the fact that stiff EVOH droplets hindered the elongation of PBAT chains by defects developed at the interface so that strain at break decreased and PBAT matrix could not undergo strain hardening.

Previous studies have conducted tensile tests on composites containing conventional clay, inorganic substances, or natural materials such as CNC, chitin, and lignin as fillers. The protocol of tensile tests under water conditions was elaborated to study the mechanical behavior of PBS/PBAT nanocomposites when wet and immersed in water, in order to simulate the conditions experienced by synthetic fishing nets throughout their use in seawater. In this section, all the samples in water conditions were drawn using a screw-action manual grip and were compared to those drawn in air conditions using the same grips. In order to achieve a better understanding of the mechanical behavior of our samples and their interactions with nanochitins and nanocelluloses, we will first discuss the shape of the curves obtained from the tensile tests. The tensile tests, under air conditions, curves for PBS, PBAT, PBS/PBAT blends and their nanocomposites are shown in Figure 4a. PBAT presents a curve that is characterized by a single yield at the beginning followed by necking and a long strain hardening with a slight increase in stress during polymer deformation, which ends with a fracture at around 300% strain. This behavior was also observed in the tensile tests under water conditions (Figure 4b). In the case of PBS, its mechanical behavior is a little more particular and unique. First, an initial yield is observed that is followed by a necking and a strain hardening of the material. Subsequently, a second yield and necking appear around 80% strain, followed by a long strain hardening before ultimate failure at 220% strain. This was also noted for the PBS/PBAT nanocomposites, which have a curve shape comparable to PBS. The second yield shifts toward approximately 120% strain for PBS/PBAT and toward 150% strain for PBS/PBAT/ChNCsLac1% and PBS/PBAT/NFCEster1%. Indeed, it is also noticeable that the failure stress of PBS/PBAT nanocomposites was higher than the initial yield stress usually accompanied by strain-induced crystallization, which would have aligned the crystallites in the direction of the strain [39]. The double yielding and necking phenomena have been explained by several authors by the fact that PBS crystallizes in two different crystal structures, the α and β forms, which appear under various conditions. For example, the α form is more general and appears when PBS is crystallized from the melt, while the β form is observed under a certain level of mechanical stress [36]. Liu et al. as well as Ichikawa and Mizukoshi have demonstrated the relationship between the crystal structure transition of PBS, as revealed by XRD analysis, and the mechanical behavior variations observed on its traction tests curves [40, 41]. Secondly, a unique stress oscillation phenomenon is observed which causes a cycle of stress drop and recovery. This behavior is more pronounced in the case of PBS/PBAT nanocomposites. Wan et al. reported the same behavior for compression-molded PBS samples drawn at a lower rate under 50 mm min−1 and also at a rate of 10 mm min−1 under different temperatures [42]. Their study presents a clear explanation for the occurrence of these self-stress necking oscillations on the tensile curves, which can be attributed to the local increase in temperature at the neck front of the samples, the crystallization induced by the orientation of the polymer chains or to the formation of cracks and micro-cavities which were observed on their drawn samples [42]. These cracks and micro-cavities were noticed in our PBS and PBS/PBAT nanocomposite drawn samples. The tensile tests curves in water conditions (Figure 4b) of neat polymers and their blends show almost the same behavior as in air with some changes in the second yield for the PBS/PBAT and PBS/PBAT/NFCEster1% blends, which appear in the same strain as PBS, while the second yield of PBS/PBAT/ChNCsLac1% has shifted to 120% compared to PBS which remains at 80% strain. The stress oscillation phenomenon is absent in the case of PBS, contrary to the PBS/PBAT blend and its nanocomposites where it appears periodically until the ultimate failure of the samples. Based on these tensile test behaviors, the variation of Young's modulus and elongation at break of the nanocomposites were also investigated under air and water conditions using screw-action manual grips (Figure 5). Firstly, both PBS and PBAT were tested to evaluate the impact of water penetration into neat polymer. Regarding PBS, considering the standard deviation of the measurements, the mechanical properties were not influenced by the presence of water. The presence of water in PBAT also led to a similar Young's modulus but an increased elongation at break by 24%-that is, 250% versus 310%, before and after immersion, respectively. It is obvious that the PBS/PBAT blend also increases both Young's modulus (+6%) and elongation at break (+11%) in water conditions. These results relate to those found in the literature, which demonstrate an improvement of the mechanical properties of PBS/PBAT monofilaments, notably in elongation at break, when used for the first time in water [17, 43]. In the case of PBS/PBAT/NFCEster1%, considering the standard deviation of the measurements, both Young's modulus and elongation at break remain constant in water conditions. Thus, the PBS/PBAT/ChNCsLac1% shows a slight decrease in Young's modulus (−10%) from 402 in air conditions to 364 MPa in water and a significant increase in elongation at break value (+52%) from 200% in air conditions to 304% in water. However, these values remain lower than those of PBS/PBAT blend and do not reveal a significant improvement of the mechanical properties of the blend by the addition of nanochitin and nanocellulose fillers. In fact, many factors can affect the mechanical behavior of these nanocomposites. The presence of water generally acts as a plasticizer for many polymers, including PBS and PBAT, which reduces Young's modulus values, indicating a decrease in the stiffness of the materials. This was particularly evident for PBAT and PBS/PBAT/ChNCsLac1%. It also leads to an increase in elongation at break values that indicate an enhanced ductility that was shown in particular for PBS/PBAT, PBS/PBAT/ChNCsLac1%, and PBS/PBAT/NFCEster1%.

Table 2 lists the tensile properties of the neat PBAT and lignin-based composites. As compared with pure PBAT, the tensile properties of the unmodified lignin (30 wt% HL) composites were significantly weakened, in which the elongation and tensile strength reduced from 828.7% and 23.0 MPa to 313.7% and 13.5 MPa, respectively. Their negative rates of change in elongation and tensile strength were respectively up to 87.6% and 45.2% at 40 wt% lignin loading. These results could be ascribed to the agglomeration of lignin, poor compatibility and weak interfacial interactions of lignin in the PBAT matrix, as confirmed by the SEM images of HL composites (Fig. 4b). By contrast, esterified lignin-based composites exhibited different improvements (especially in elongation) compared to HL-based composites. It was found that the elongation at break of the composites showed a dramatic enhancement with the extension of the incorporated aliphatic carbon chains. For LCL and OCL-based composites, the elongation at break first increased and then decreased with the augment of the lignin content (Table 2). The composites with 40 wt% loading of LCL and OCL both exhibited the highest elongation at break (up to 600% more), which was almost six times as compared with those of HL-based composites with the same content. Meanwhile, their tensile strength also showed relative ideal values (>13 MPa). Further increase of their contents (45-50 wt%) in the composites contributed to an obvious decline in ductility and tensile strength, which derived from the aggregation of lignin in the PBAT matrix. The distinctly improved mechanical performances of the composites implied that the soft segments of esterified lignins exhibited good compatibility and distribution with the PBAT matrix even with a high esterified lignin content (up to 40-50 wt%).18,22 As shown in Fig. 4b-f, the morphology images of the fractured surface from different composites show that HL had limited distribution and compatibility with PBAT since significant lignin agglomeration was visible. In contrast, esterified lignins showed evidently improved compatibility even under a high loading of 40 wt% (Fig. 4g-i). Additionally, it is necessary to investigate the interaction energy that can elucidate the physical or chemical molecular interactions in the prepared composite matrix. Furthermore, it was found that the addition of MAH into the composites played an important role in the improvement of mechanical properties (as compared to the control group in Table S4†), which served as a coupling reagent in the composite and further associated with PBAT and lignin polymer via new chemical bonds.13,43,44 Therefore, in this study, the esterification modification effectively enhanced the distribution and compatibility of lignin in the PBAT matrix, and also, the molecular mobility of composites was obviously improved. Meanwhile, the ingenious participation of MAH further reinforced the mechanical properties of the lignin-based composites. The polymer intermolecular diagrams for the present PBAT composite matrixes are presented in Fig. 5a. Fig. 5b compares the tensile strength and breaking strain of the prepared PBAT/lignin composites in this study with other PBAT-based composites. Previously, in most of the PBAT composites the loading of incorporated lignin was limited to 30 wt%, whereas the obtained PBAT/lignin composites here with higher lignin contents (40-50 wt%) exhibited a higher tensile strength (13.4 MPa) and excellent elongation at break (up to 618%). Due to the presence of the hydrocarbon side chains in the esterified lignin, more effective intermolecular bonds formed and facilitated better compatibility and distribution between lignin and PBAT (Fig. 5a), resulting in competitive mechanical properties of composites even when containing much more lignin.21,45 The desirable mechanical performances achieved in this study could meet the requirement (GB/T21302-2007) of laminated films and pouches for packaging, and these results provide valuable insight for the further development of lignin-based biodegradable composite materials. The preeminent UV-shielding of soft composite films is important for food or medicine packaging.18,46 However, the neat PBAT film shows no UV absorption performance, and the incorporation of the lignin polymer could artfully give the composites strong absorption performance for UV light.17,18 As shown in Fig. 6a, the high transmittance of UV was observed in the neat PBAT film, while all the lignin-based composites films exhibited much higher UV absorption. The admirable UV barrier properties were mainly attributed to the existence of abundant benzene rings and carbonyl groups in the composites.47-49 The composite film blended HL showed a higher broad shielding effect to UV and visible light than those of esterified lignins, which could be attributed to its aggregation during blending with PBAT and further impeded UV-vis light transmission. In addition, the dramatically decreased OH groups in esterified lignins also reduced the UV absorption of modified films. Nevertheless, with the increase of lignin loading, the UV-vis light was further shielded (more than 97%) and UV-A (320-400 nm) light was almost completely blocked. The tensile properties of PBAT processed by DCT are characterized and shown in Fig. 2a. The detailed tensile properties of all samples are summarized in Table S2. To minimize experimental errors caused by edge defects, tensile specimens were prepared from the central region of the film using a dumbbell-shaped cutter, as shown in Fig. S6b. From these tensile strain-stress curves, it can be seen that all samples show ductile fracture, and the failure occurs after yielding, indicating that the tensile behavior has not been affected. Moreover, as can be observed from Fig. S7, the tensile yield strength of the PBAT film obtained by DCT is higher than that of MCM, indicating that DCT effectively improves the ability of PBAT to resist deformation during the tensile process. While, for PBAT samples processed by DCT, the hardening behavior after yielding is significantly enhanced. Compared with the σ value of ∼19.68 MPa of MCM samples, the σ value of DCT-1.20 reaches 71.15 MPa, which is about 3.6 times that of MCM. Moreover, as Tpr increases from 0.00 to 2.10 s, the σ value of the samples first increases and then decreases, while the ε value first decreases and then slowly increases. Notably, DCT-1.20 reaches the lowest ε but is still greater than 600 %. Although the enhanced hardening behavior of PBAT after DCT treatment limits the deformation ability of the material, the material still maintains high flexibility and ductility. By adjusting the Tpr value, the tensile strength of PBAT can be regulated from 37.67 MPa to 71.15 MPa, and the toughness can be regulated from 174.07 MJ/m3 to 262.05 MJ/m3. The Tpr parameter in DCT can designed to process the target sample according to the mechanical property requirements of the films. In conclusion, we can realize the on-demand regulatable mechanical properties of high transparent PBAT by DCT. In another word, through using our novel DCT method, we are able to regulate the toughness and strength of a pre-prepared PBAT sheet on-demand, and may be potentially used in various applications that requires multi-type of biodegradable materials with different mechanical properties. In addition to static tensile analysis, we monitored the temperature-dependent mechanical properties through dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) of MCM, CM, and DCT-1.20 at temperatures ranging from −80 to 80 °C, as shown in Fig. 2d and e. The Tg of MCM, CM, and DCT-1.20 samples are detected as −12.21 °C, −6.59 °C, and −5.57 °C, respectively. This change in Tg indicates that DCT can regulate the glass transition behavior of PBAT and inhibit the movement of PBAT molecular chains, confirming the closer packing of DCT-1.20 [38]. The sharp decrease is due to the glass transition behavior of the sample. Detailly, the E′ of DCT-1.20 is smaller than that of MCM before the glass transition, indicating that our DCT-1.20 sample has lower stiffness than the MCM sample in the glassy state. However, after surpassing the glass transition, the E′ of DCT-1.20 is higher than that of MCM, indicating higher stiffness than the MCM sample in the high elastic state, consistent with the static tensile test results shown in Fig. 2a and b, which suggests that our DCT-PBAT is more capable for higher temperature applications. The tensile elongation (elongation at break) of PBAT varies depending on processing methods, blend compositions, and testing conditions. Reported values include:  
- **~400%** for pure PBAT under standard tensile tests [1].  
- **809–850%** (transverse/machine direction) for blown PBAT films [2][3].  
- **>1000%** (e.g., 1082.1%) in melt-processed PBAT [4][5].  
- **904%** for PBAT films prepared via hot-pressing [6].  
- **828.7%** for pure PBAT in lignin-based composite studies [10].  
- **1174.08%** for PBAT processed via melt-compression molding [14].  

Environmental exposure also affects elongation: PBAT shows **250%** elongation in air and **310%** in water [8][9]. The variability is attributed to differences in matrix continuity, phase compatibility, and testing protocols (e.g., humidity, orientation effects). For instance, blends with rigid additives (e.g., PGA) reduce elongation due to stress concentration [4][5], while water immersion enhances ductility via plasticization [8][9].

Nowadays, macromolecular design, blending, and additives are being considered to alter the conditions for biodegradation of synthetic polyesters.[38] In terms of polymer structure, the main factors affecting the abiotic and biotic degradation rate of polymers are the monomer structure, crystallinity, hydrophilicity, Mw, and density of the susceptible hydrolyzable chemical groups such as ester or ether. To increase the degradation rate, low crystallinity, low Mw, high density of ester groups (this means short-chains aliphatic monomers), and high hydrophilicity for microbial adhesion (associated with high surface roughness) are desired.[39] Abiotic methods to accelerate the biodegradation of biodegradable polymers include modifications of the bulk properties (Mw, crystallinity, increase of chain mobility, catalysis of chemical hydrolysis, among others), and surface properties (roughness, surface energy, and alteration of hydrophilic/hydrophobic balance). Besides these methods, reduction of the polymer size by mechanical action also allows the acceleration of biodegradation by increasing the surface area or surface-to-volume ratio available for water (abiotic) or biotic (enzymatic) attack. Treatments such as ultraviolet (UV) irradiation, plasma, microwave, alteration of the surface of the polymer by acidic/alkaline immersion, incorporation of specific additives (plasticizers or surfactants), copolymerization, reactive blending, composites, and nanocomposites have been reported to enhance biodegradation at some extent (Table 2). Since thermal properties of biodegradable polymers, reflected in transition temperatures such as glass transition temperature (Tg) and melting temperature (Tm), are expressed in a wide range, a pre-treatment of a mix of plastic waste involving the use of elevated temperatures presents some challenge. Temperatures around the Tg of PLA are already at the Tm of PHAs or PCL. It is conceivable that biodegradable polymers with low Tg and Tm have more susceptible biodegradable structures and higher biodegradation rates. However, other factors such as polymer crystallinity and surface properties also play a crucial role.

We recently developed a new class of biodegradable thermoresponsive polyesters (TR-PEs) based on N-substituted diol monomers. TR-PEs exhibited reversible cloud point temperatures (Tcp) between 0-50 °C and were shown to be non-cytotoxic. The synthesis of N-substituted diols and TR-PEs is highly modular, allowing for a wide variety of possible homo- and copolyesters. In this work, we report the synthesis and characterization of 20 homopolyesters in order to better understand the structure-property relationship of TR-PEs. UV-vis spectroscopy showed that the Tcp of TR-PEs was highly dependent on pendant group structure, such as secondary or tertiary amides, cyclic and linear groups, and substitution of oxygen atoms. Structure-Tcp analysis provides a correlation between Tcp and the number of heteroatoms relative to the number of carbon atoms in the pendant group thereby providing a rationale for the design of thermoresponsive polyesters with desired Tcp values. To demonstrate the expanded tunability of the TR-PE system, copolyesters bearing covalently attached ibuprofen were synthesized and shown to exhibit LCST behavior dependent on comonomer hydrophilicity. To demonstrate the feasibility of using sterilized silk fibroin solutions to cast lyophilized silk fibroin sponges, a set of protocols was developed to cast the sponges under sterile conditions. Silk fibroin sponges were cast from pre-sterilized silk fibroin solutions in sterile 24-well tissue culture plates in a laminar flow hood. Following freezing, scaffolds were placed in sterile autoclave bags and lyophilized. Scaffolds were water annealed in a glass desiccator, which was sterilized by autoclaving and placed inside a laminar flow hood. Finally, the mechanical properties of the silk fibroin scaffolds formed from 30-min boiling, 4 wt.-% silk fibroin solution that had been either sterile filtered or autoclaved were examined. This boil time and concentration was chosen as it is the commonly used to make silk fibroin scaffolds for tissue engineering applications. 54 Scaffolds were compressed under unconfined conditions using a 100 N load cell at physiological temperature and pH (37 °C, PBS). No difference in the shape of the strain-strain curve or compressive modulus was observed in scaffolds formed from filtered compared to unsterilized silk fibroin, but autoclaved silk fibroin resulted in significantly stiffer scaffolds compared to those formed from unsterilized or filter sterilized silk fibroin (Figure 2). Lower average molecular weight was expected to correlate with lower stiffness and strength; thus, it is possible that an increase in β-sheet content in the silk fibroin solution following autoclaving was responsible for these unexpected bulk material properties. Higher crystallinity has been shown to correlate with increased silk fibroin biomaterial stiffness.39 This is consistent with the findings by George et al.,47 who demonstrated that despite a shift in the protein size distribution toward lower molecular weight species, steam sterilization of pre-cast silk fibroin films resulted in increased material stiffness and strength, correlated with increased β-sheet content. The feasibility of casting sterile silk fibroin sponges from pre-sterilized silk fibroin solutions was demonstrated; however, the successful and cost-effective manufacture of silk fibroin-based medical devices and biomaterials will likely involve scaffold sterilization post-casting. Therefore, the effects of thermal (autoclaving and dry heat), physical (γ irradiation) and chemical (ethylene oxide and hydrogen peroxide plasma) sterilization protocols on the physical and biological properties of silk fibroin sponges were explored. Thermal sterilization protocols, in particular steam sterilization via autoclaving, are routinely used to sterilize medical devices made from metallic alloys, but are generally unsuitable for biomedical polymers and in particular proteins, causing major changes in mechanical and degradation properties.60 However, due to the unique mechanical and stability properties of silk fibroin, autoclaving has been routinely used to sterilize silk fibroin-based biomaterials, maximizing the β-sheet content and, thus, the stiffness and strength.39 γ irradiation is a routinely used sterilization protocol for a range of medical devices and biological molecules, resulting in sterilization via oxidation of biological tissue.60 However, it has been demonstrated to affect the physical properties of a number of synthetic and natural polymers, resulting in changes in molecular weight distribution, degradation, and mechanical properties.60 Chemical sterilization protocols are often employed as an alternative to thermal sterilization for materials that cannot withstand high temperatures.60 Ethylene oxide has, for many years, been the alternative sterilization method of choice as it is bactericidal, sporicidal, and virucidal via alkylation of a number of chemical groups in the nucleic acids of microbes, causing cell injury and death. However, ethylene oxide toxicity and suspected carcinogenicity make the risk of ethylene oxide retention in the sterilized material problematic and cause safety and environmental concerns in the facilities operating the sterilizer.60 Gas plasma using hydrogen peroxide has emerged as an alternative to ethylene oxide in many hospital and research settings, with less risk of severe or chronic toxicity compared to ethylene oxide.

As electronic devices become more multifunctional, miniaturized, and integrated, there is a greater demand for efficient thermal dissipation, which necessitates the use of thermally conductive materials. (1,2) Among the materials used for electronic packaging and thermal management, polymer-based composites have gained popularity due to their light weight, ease of processing, good insulation properties, and corrosion resistance. However, the rapid development of electronic devices in recent years has led to an increase in plastic waste resulting from disposal, which can seriously affect the environment. To address this issue, researchers have focused on minimizing the hazards associated with waste plastics while still meeting the performance requirements of electronic devices. (3,4) It has been suggested that biodegradable polymers may provide an alternative to traditional nondegradable plastics (e.g., petroleum-based plastics) to prepare biodegradable polymer-based composites that are both thermally conductive and electrically insulating. (5) Biodegradable polymeric materials possess environmentally friendly, renewable raw materials and biodegradability, making them an attractive alternative to traditional petroleum-based plastics. (6−11) However, most biodegradable polymers possess very low intrinsic thermal conductivity (typically between 0.1 and 0.5 W m-1 K-1), requiring further improvement. One effective approach to enhancing the thermal conductivity of biodegradable polymers is incorporating high thermal/conductive fillers through melt blending. (12) Commonly used thermal fillers include silicon carbide (SiC), (13,14) aluminum oxide (Al2O3), (15) aluminum nitride (AlN), (16) and boron nitride (BN). (17−19) Nevertheless, high filler loadings can negatively impact mechanical properties and impose processing difficulties. (20) An alternative solution involves using highly conductive fillers like carbon nanotubes (CNTs) (21,22) and graphene to achieve enhanced thermal conductivity at lower filler loadings, thus mitigating the negative effects of high filler content. However, this approach may affect the electrical insulation properties of polymers, such as high electrical conductivity or dielectric constants, while altering the thermal conductivity. Therefore, balancing thermal conductivity and electrical insulating properties and achieving biodegradable polymer composites with high thermal conductivity and excellent electrical insulation are challenging. Recently, researchers have reported the successfully construction of a segregated double-network structure, combining hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) coated on nylon-6 (PA6)/graphene nanosheets (GNPs) composite particles to form PA6/GNPs@h-BN composites with segregated double networks. (23,24) With a total filler content of 21 vol %, the composites exhibited a thermal conductivity of 2.69 W m-1 K-1 and good electrical insulation properties (4.13 × 10-9 S/m). It was confirmed that the h-BN segregated network maximizes the contact area by overlapping and interconnecting the fillers; in addition, the GNP fillers within the matrix increase the density of the thermal conductivity network and may serve as a bridge connecting the h-BN thermal conductivity networks, thus enhancing thermal conductivity properties synergistically. Furthermore, most highly conductive GNPs inside the matrix are blocked by the segregated h-BN fillers, which contribute to the composite’s good electrical insulation properties. Despite this success, a relatively high total filler content is still needed to achieve high thermal conductivity in this system, resulting in poor mechanical properties and high preparation costs, which emphasizes the need to study and optimize how composites with acceptable mechanical properties, high thermal conductivity, and good electrical insulation can be achieved with lower filler content. (25,26) To the best of our knowledge, there has been no research conducted on preparing biodegradable polymer composites with the combination of balanced mechanical performance, high thermal conductivity, and good electrical insulation properties by using the specific structure described above.
Microbial contamination and infection caused by pathogens are increasing global public health awareness. This issue is highlighted by the outbreak of Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic, which has caused more than 400 million confirmed cases and 6 million deaths worldwide. It is still increasing, causing immeasurable pain and economic losses [1]. The common way to prevent the proliferation of microorganisms and the spread of pathogens is disinfection and sterilization. It is well-known that the antibacterial agent is a core material, which can be divided into three categories: inorganic [2], organic [3,4,5,6,6], and natural antimicrobial agents [7, 8]. For the inorganic antibacterial agents, most of them are metal/metal oxide nanoparticles [9, 10], such as silver, copper, and zinc oxide. Their advantages are strong heat resistance, good antibacterial durability, and no drug resistance. However, complicated manufacturing processes, relatively expensive costs, and color issues restricted their applications. Commonly used organic antibacterial agents include aldehydes (ketones), phenols, quaternary ammonium salts [11], halides, thiophenes, biguanides, and diphenyl ethers. The advantages of organic antibacterial agents are wide range of sources, low production cost, fast sterilization rate, convenient processing, good stability, and their disadvantage is the poor heat resistance. The natural antibacterial agents such as chitosan, bacteriocin, lysozyme, plant essential oils are mainly obtained from animal or plant extracts or synthesized by microorganisms. The advantages of them are high safety, non-toxicity, good biocompatibility, and abundant resources. Their disadvantages are poor heat resistance, short pot life, and restricted production condition and equipment. As a kind of organic antibacterial agents, N-halamine antibacterial agents have higher stability, much stronger antibacterial efficacies, less harm to the environment, and easier use for antibacterial treatment on the surface of materials. It is generally believed that the sterilization mechanism of N-halamine antibacterial agents is that N-halamine molecules first contact the bacteria, and then the oxidized chlorines oxidize the receptors in the cell, thereby destroying the bacterial metabolism and killing them. At the same time, the bactericidal ability of N-halamines can be regenerated after rinsing with dilute bleaching water solution to convert the N-H bonds in the molecules into N-Cl ones [6, 12, 13].The immobilization of the antibacterial agent refers to the process of introducing the antibacterial groups to the surface of the material by physical action [14,15,16,17,18], such as van der Waals force or electrostatic attraction and covalent bond coupling. At present, the immobilization methods of N-halamine antibacterial agents mainly include physical modification methods represented by surface coating and blending, and chemical modification methods [18, 19] represented by surface electrophilic, nucleophilic reactions, and surface graft polymerization reactions [20,21,22,23,24]. When the material is modified by physical coating, the interaction force between the antibacterial agent molecules and the material is weak, the antibacterial agent molecules are easy to detach during use. When the material is modified by physical blending, most of the antibacterial agent molecules are deeply buried inside the material and are difficult to exert antibacterial effect, resulting in a relatively low utilization rate of antibacterial agents. In this paper, the chemical grafting method [25,26,27,28] was used to obtain modified film [29,30,31] materials with the superior stability of antimicrobial N-halamine groups and high-efficacy antimicrobial capacity. As conventional plastics for packaging, i.e., polypropylene, polyethylene, and other petro-sourced thermoplastics, full-biocomposites can be manufactured using industrial techniques such as compounding, mixing, extrusion, injection molding, compression molding, and resin transfer molding (RTM).9 Though depending on the studied matrix and the aimed application, and often for research purposes, samples are prepared by solvent casting in several studies.54-57 Among the disadvantages associated with classical thermal treatments, there is a risk of degrading both the bioplastic used as matrix and the lignocellulosic fibers. Indeed, most biopolymers are especially sensitive to temperature, their melting temperature being close to their degradation temperature (e.g., PHBV58). In the case of proteins, wheat gluten's degradation temperature is even below its melting temperature; therefore, such material has to be plasticized, generally with water and/or glycerol.59 Fibers are also sensitive to thermal treatments as degradation can occur that weakens the fibers. The inherent moisture that is naturally bound to the hemicellulose component can change depending on temperature and exposure time. Furthermore, heat-treated biomass is known to globally become darker and brittle, due to the loss of its tenacious and fibrous nature resulting from the decomposition of hemicelluloses and partial depolymerization of lignin and cellulose. Several publications have investigated these issues and have generally found that exposure to temperatures at or below 170°C did not have a significant effect on the strength of the fibers.60 Regarding fibers, processes involving shearing are also known to impact fiber length and morphology.61 Depending on the process, dispersion of the fibers within the composite might also be affected, thus impacts its mechanical and barrier properties.62 Finally, the feeding of melt extrusion equipments could be difficult with some fibers, as reported for flax or hemp fibers, thus imposing the use of a force feeder equipment.

Unfortunately, while terminal sterilization of the GelMA is a critical step for translational tissue engineering applications, it can potentially cause thermal or chemical modifications of GelMA. Thus, understanding the effect of terminal sterilization on GelMA properties is an important, though often overlooked, aspect of material design for translational tissue engineering applications. To this end, we characterized the effects of FDA-approved terminal sterilization methods (autoclaving, ethylene oxide treatment, and gamma (γ)-irradiation) on GelMA prepolymer (bioink) and GelMA hydrogels in terms of the relevant properties for biomedical applications, including mechanical strength, biodegradation rate, cell culture in 2D and 3D, and printability. Autoclaving and ethylene oxide treatment of the GelMA decreased the stiffness of the hydrogel, but the treatments did not modify the biodegradation rate of the hydrogel; meanwhile, γ-irradiation increased the stiffness, reduced the pore size and significantly slowed the biodegradation rate. However, ethylene oxide treatment significantly lowered the fibroblast viability in 3D cell culture. Furthermore, printability studies showed that the bioinks prepared from γ-irradiated GelMA had significantly reduced printability as compared to the GelMA bioinks prepared from autoclaved or ethylene oxide treated GelMA. The standard gamma-irradiation sterilization dose used in the industry for most combination devices that come in contact with skin or tissue is 25 kGy. This dose is considered sufficient for gaining a minimum of 10−6 sterility assurance level (6 log reduction). Use of an irradiation dose lower than the standard 25 kGy is of special interest in sterilization of medical devices, because of the damaging effect that this dose might have on physical-mechanical properties. During gamma irradiation at room temperature, the product temperature is elevated as a result of gamma ray absorption. For the sterilization of bioresorbable polymers, temperatures must be kept below the temperature at which changes occur in the polymer's molecular weight, in order to prevent degradation. For this reason, cooling the product to 0°C or less during irradiation is advised. This requires the use of cooling agents in the irradiation container to prevent heating to the critical temperature where molecular weight is affected. Various combinations of doses and temperatures can be employed to achieve product sterility without adversely affecting the product. The balance between the selected gamma radiation doses and the process temperatures allowing minimal damage is referred to as optimum sterilization.19 In the current study, the effects of gamma radiation on the physical and mechanical properties of our new biodegradable drug-eluting wound dressing were investigated. It is important to note that our new hybrid wound dressing, which contains the synthetic polymer PDLGA with the natural polymer collagen, combines the desired properties of both materials and therefore it is superior compared to other types of wound dressings. In addition, it releases antibiotics and pain killers in a controlled desired manner to the wound. Therefore, performing an appropriate sterilization process for this new system will enable to use it in the clinic. To demonstrate the feasibility of using sterilized silk fibroin solutions to cast lyophilized silk fibroin sponges, a set of protocols was developed to cast the sponges under sterile conditions. Silk fibroin sponges were cast from pre-sterilized silk fibroin solutions in sterile 24-well tissue culture plates in a laminar flow hood. Following freezing, scaffolds were placed in sterile autoclave bags and lyophilized. Scaffolds were water annealed in a glass desiccator, which was sterilized by autoclaving and placed inside a laminar flow hood. Finally, the mechanical properties of the silk fibroin scaffolds formed from 30-min boiling, 4 wt.-% silk fibroin solution that had been either sterile filtered or autoclaved were examined. This boil time and concentration was chosen as it is the commonly used to make silk fibroin scaffolds for tissue engineering applications. 54 Scaffolds were compressed under unconfined conditions using a 100 N load cell at physiological temperature and pH (37 °C, PBS). No difference in the shape of the strain-strain curve or compressive modulus was observed in scaffolds formed from filtered compared to unsterilized silk fibroin, but autoclaved silk fibroin resulted in significantly stiffer scaffolds compared to those formed from unsterilized or filter sterilized silk fibroin (Figure 2). Lower average molecular weight was expected to correlate with lower stiffness and strength; thus, it is possible that an increase in β-sheet content in the silk fibroin solution following autoclaving was responsible for these unexpected bulk material properties. Higher crystallinity has been shown to correlate with increased silk fibroin biomaterial stiffness.39 This is consistent with the findings by George et al.,47 who demonstrated that despite a shift in the protein size distribution toward lower molecular weight species, steam sterilization of pre-cast silk fibroin films resulted in increased material stiffness and strength, correlated with increased β-sheet content. The feasibility of casting sterile silk fibroin sponges from pre-sterilized silk fibroin solutions was demonstrated; however, the successful and cost-effective manufacture of silk fibroin-based medical devices and biomaterials will likely involve scaffold sterilization post-casting. Therefore, the effects of thermal (autoclaving and dry heat), physical (γ irradiation) and chemical (ethylene oxide and hydrogen peroxide plasma) sterilization protocols on the physical and biological properties of silk fibroin sponges were explored. Thermal sterilization protocols, in particular steam sterilization via autoclaving, are routinely used to sterilize medical devices made from metallic alloys, but are generally unsuitable for biomedical polymers and in particular proteins, causing major changes in mechanical and degradation properties.60 However, due to the unique mechanical and stability properties of silk fibroin, autoclaving has been routinely used to sterilize silk fibroin-based biomaterials, maximizing the β-sheet content and, thus, the stiffness and strength.39 γ irradiation is a routinely used sterilization protocol for a range of medical devices and biological molecules, resulting in sterilization via oxidation of biological tissue.60 However, it has been demonstrated to affect the physical properties of a number of synthetic and natural polymers, resulting in changes in molecular weight distribution, degradation, and mechanical properties.60 Chemical sterilization protocols are often employed as an alternative to thermal sterilization for materials that cannot withstand high temperatures.60 Ethylene oxide has, for many years, been the alternative sterilization method of choice as it is bactericidal, sporicidal, and virucidal via alkylation of a number of chemical groups in the nucleic acids of microbes, causing cell injury and death. However, ethylene oxide toxicity and suspected carcinogenicity make the risk of ethylene oxide retention in the sterilized material problematic and cause safety and environmental concerns in the facilities operating the sterilizer.60 Gas plasma using hydrogen peroxide has emerged as an alternative to ethylene oxide in many hospital and research settings, with less risk of severe or chronic toxicity compared to ethylene oxide.

Buy this article in print Gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) hydrogel scaffolds and GelMA-based bioinks are widely used in tissue engineering and bioprinting due to their ability to support cellular functions and new tissue development. Unfortunately, while terminal sterilization of the GelMA is a critical step for translational tissue engineering applications, it can potentially cause thermal or chemical modifications of GelMA. Thus, understanding the effect of terminal sterilization on GelMA properties is an important, though often overlooked, aspect of material design for translational tissue engineering applications. To this end, we characterized the effects of FDA-approved terminal sterilization methods (autoclaving, ethylene oxide treatment, and gamma (γ)-irradiation) on GelMA prepolymer (bioink) and GelMA hydrogels in terms of the relevant properties for biomedical applications, including mechanical strength, biodegradation rate, cell culture in 2D and 3D, and printability. Autoclaving and ethylene oxide treatment of the GelMA decreased the stiffness of the hydrogel, but the treatments did not modify the biodegradation rate of the hydrogel; meanwhile, γ-irradiation increased the stiffness, reduced the pore size and significantly slowed the biodegradation rate. None of the terminal sterilization methods changed the 2D fibroblast or endothelial cell adhesion and spreading. However, ethylene oxide treatment significantly lowered the fibroblast viability in 3D cell culture. Strikingly, γ-irradiation led to significantly reduced ability of the GelMA prepolymer to undergo sol-gel transition. Furthermore, printability studies showed that the bioinks prepared from γ-irradiated GelMA had significantly reduced printability as compared to the GelMA bioinks prepared from autoclaved or ethylene oxide treated GelMA. These results reveal that the choice of the terminal sterilization method can strongly influence important properties of GelMA bioink and hydrogel. Overall, this study provides further insight into GelMA-based material design with consideration of the effect of terminal sterilization. Export citation and abstractBibTeXRIS

As conventional plastics for packaging, i.e., polypropylene, polyethylene, and other petro-sourced thermoplastics, full-biocomposites can be manufactured using industrial techniques such as compounding, mixing, extrusion, injection molding, compression molding, and resin transfer molding (RTM).9 Though depending on the studied matrix and the aimed application, and often for research purposes, samples are prepared by solvent casting in several studies.54-57 Among the disadvantages associated with classical thermal treatments, there is a risk of degrading both the bioplastic used as matrix and the lignocellulosic fibers. Indeed, most biopolymers are especially sensitive to temperature, their melting temperature being close to their degradation temperature (e.g., PHBV58). In the case of proteins, wheat gluten's degradation temperature is even below its melting temperature; therefore, such material has to be plasticized, generally with water and/or glycerol.59 Fibers are also sensitive to thermal treatments as degradation can occur that weakens the fibers. The inherent moisture that is naturally bound to the hemicellulose component can change depending on temperature and exposure time. Furthermore, heat-treated biomass is known to globally become darker and brittle, due to the loss of its tenacious and fibrous nature resulting from the decomposition of hemicelluloses and partial depolymerization of lignin and cellulose. Several publications have investigated these issues and have generally found that exposure to temperatures at or below 170°C did not have a significant effect on the strength of the fibers.60 Regarding fibers, processes involving shearing are also known to impact fiber length and morphology.61 Depending on the process, dispersion of the fibers within the composite might also be affected, thus impacts its mechanical and barrier properties.62 Finally, the feeding of melt extrusion equipments could be difficult with some fibers, as reported for flax or hemp fibers, thus imposing the use of a force feeder equipment.

Based solely on the provided evidence, the sterilization method of choice for heat-sensitive biodegradable polymers depends on the specific polymer and desired properties, but chemical methods using hydrogen peroxide plasma or ethanol are generally preferred over thermal methods. Key findings include:

1.  **Autoclaving (steam sterilization) causes significant thermal damage**, including molecular weight reduction in alginate [12][13], pore collapse in membranes [9][10], and increased crystallinity/degradation resistance in silk fibroin [2][3][6][7][11].
2.  **Ethylene oxide (EO) is problematic due to chemical modifications and toxicity**. It esterifies carboxylic acid groups [1], leaves toxic residues that reduce cell attachment and proliferation even after degassing [2][3][6][7], and raises safety/environmental concerns [6][7].
3.  **Gamma (γ) irradiation causes molecular damage**. It reduces molecular weight (especially in polymers with high PEG content) [1] and accelerates degradation in silk fibroin through protein damage caused by free radicals [2][3][6][7]. While the standard 25 kGy dose is common, it damages physical-mechanical properties; using lower doses with cooling (≤0°C) during irradiation is advised to minimize degradation for bioresorbable polymers [4][5].
4.  **Hydrogen peroxide gas plasma (VHP) sterilization is effective with less damage**. It causes hydroxylation and hydrolysis [1], but pre-leaching (24-48h in PBS) effectively removes cytotoxic compounds, restoring cell proliferation on silk fibroin without significant impact on attachment or proliferation otherwise [2][3]. Compared to EO, it poses less risk of severe or chronic toxicity [6][7].
5.  **Ethanol treatment preserves structure better than autoclaving for silk fibroin**. While autoclaving significantly increases β-sheet content and reduces enzymatic degradation of silk fibroin scaffolds, 70% ethanol sterilization causes minimal changes to secondary structure, crystal size, and degradation rate [11].

Therefore, for heat-sensitive biodegradable polymers, **hydrogen peroxide gas plasma (with potential leaching)** [2][3][6][7] or **ethanol treatment** [11] are preferred methods as they cause less detrimental thermal and chemical modification compared to autoclaving, gamma irradiation, or ethylene oxide. The choice must consider the specific polymer chemistry and application requirements [1][2][3][6][7][11].

question: What is the 'critical solution temperature' (LCST) of PNIPAM and why is it relevant to biodegradability?
ground_truth: PNIPAM has an LCST of ~32°C. While not biodegradable itself, it is often grafted onto biodegradable backbones (like gelatin or chitosan) to create thermo-responsive hydrogels. The system is liquid below 32°C and gels at body temperature (37°C), useful for injectable scaffolds.

Biocompatible amphiphilic block and graft copolymers, in particular those comprising biodegradable sequences, have found over the last two decades great attention due to their potential applications as micellar drug delivery systems [1], [2], [3], [4]. Beside their biodegradability, an important feature for the biomedical applications is also represented by their responsiveness to different environmental stimuli, such as: temperature, pH, light, etc, which will trigger their colloidal properties and consequently the drug release [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. Among these smart copolymers, the temperature-sensitive polymeric systems are of practical interest as this feature is an important physiological factor in the human body. Moreover, some diseases are manifested by a local temperature change. Two types of thermo-sensitive polymers were reported up to now, ones which become molecularly dispersed in aqueous media only upon heating above a certain temperature, called the upper critical solution temperature (UCST), and others undertake a reversible coil-globule transition when they are heated above a critical temperature, so-called the lower critical solution temperature (LCST). Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) and the poly(N-vinylcaprolactam) (PNVCL) are among the most studied thermo-sensitive polymers having a LCST, near human body temperature [10], [11]. In comparison to PNIPAM, PNVCL is characterized by a higher biocompatibility as the hydrolysis of the amide group of the NVCL units does not produce toxic low molar mass amines [11]. In fact, PNVCL is a nonionic, water-soluble polymer, with low cytotoxicity and with LCST values in the range of 32-36 °C, as a function of the concentration and molar mass [10]. Thus, these features make PNVCL-based polymers very attractive for different applications in the biomedical field.
Stimuli-responsive polymers, intensively studied due to their physicochemical properties, are sensitive to external stimuli such as temperature,[1] which offer the possibility to develop non-invasive therapies, especially for biomedical applications.[2] For thermoresponsive polymers, a complicated interplay of physical-chemical effects leads to a sudden change of the solvation state of the polymer from solvent-soluble (usually water) to insoluble above a specific temperature, called lower critical solution temperature (LCST), which can be modulated by different parameters as the presence of salts,[3, 4] surfactants,[5] or variation of the solvents.[6-8] In this context, poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) is one of the most studied thermoresponsive polymers, owing to its LCST around 33 °C,[9] close to body temperature.[10-16] The LCST can be adjusted according to the final requirements through molecular features, but the addition of a second comonomer for preparing random or block copolymers can also introduce other kind of features.[17-23] Nowadays, the attention of the scientific community is focused on the preparation and development of hybrid materials based on smart polymers due to the versatility these systems can provide in numerous applications.[24, 25] Nevertheless, some shortcomings are associated with the preparation of these structures, such as being unable to avoid surface heterogeneity. Thus, the homogenization of the materials will be essential for controlling the final properties.[26] The use of some biopolymers, such as carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), can provide stability and homogeneity to the final material.[27] Also, the incorporation of biopolymers can provide additional functionalities, increase the surface area, and also respond to new environmental policies and regulations. These materials are usually biodegradable and can be obtained by sustainably. For instance, the incorporation of cellulose or its derivatives as a component of hybrid materials can provide multiple benefits such as enhanced mechanical properties and can reduce the final costs, as it is one of the most abundant natural polymers.[26, 28] On the other hand, other biopolymers like CMC are commonly used industrially due to their ability to act as a viscosity modifier or water-retention agent. The combination of some biopolymers with PNIPAM is relatively new, although there are some works published already. The significant part of these reports was mainly focused on chemical cross-linking,[29, 30] but physical cross-linking based on hydrogen bonding was not profoundly studied.[31-33] These published works used a different mixture based on glycol/water and methanol/water, where the physical-crosslinking was observed by intrinsic viscosity and rheology. The development of those structures could be useful for a new generation of drug carriers due to viscosity can be adjusted appropriately, and high viscosity values can be obtained.

The microgels show a great promise in bioseparation and many other fields. Recently, stimuli-responsive polymers have been investigated with a tremendous increasing frequency for their intelligent response to external stimuli, such as temperature, light and pH [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7]. In particular, copolymers based on thermally reversible poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) have attracted a tremendous interest because of their exponentially increasing application in the fields of drug delivery, cell separation, metal ion purification and fluorescence detection [8], [9]. That the amphiphiles possess lower critical solution temperature (LCST) is a rather general phenomenon. What previous studies have shown is that PNIPAM is hydrophilic existed as random, isolated and extended coils in water below the LCST (32 °C), whereas it is hydrophobic with the PNIPAM backbone undergoing the intrachain collapse prior to the interchain aggregation to form a molecular globule above the LCST [10], [11], [12], [13]. In addition, chitosan (CS) has attracted considerable attention as a naturally occurring polymer with fascinating properties of biocompatibility, biodegradability, nontoxicity and cationic properties [14], [15], [16]. Recent advances in copolymer fabrication such as micro-emulsion polymerization, coacervation and layer-by-layer self-assembly provide feasible approaches to prepare well-defined microgels with controllable shape and desirable stimuli-responsive characteristics [17], [18]. Till now, spherical copolymers with size from a few to several dozens of nanometers in diameter have been widely reported. However, the research on anisotropically distributed copolymers including ellipsoidal and rodlike particles is still rare. Dietsch and co-workers [19], [20] synthesized ellipsoidal hybrid magnetic microgels with thermally tunable aspect ratios and a spindle-shaped core in the centre of the microgels. However, to synthesize the spindle-shaped cores of the microgels, both complex multistep and advanced experimental skills were required [21]. Accordingly, one smart strategy with merits of simplicity, celerity and high accuracy to prepare shape-controlled stimuli-responsive microgels is urgently required.
Regarding crystallinity, Massardier et al. [70] and Woolnough et al. [71] indicated that amorphous regions are more accessible to biodegradation than the crystalline zones. PBS is a crystalline polymer that forms very stable crystals melting at 115 °C, which may explain its low disintegration. The addition of starch and the increase in its proportion decrease the crystallinity in both biphasic and triphasic blends. Furthermore, while the degree of crystallinity of PEB is higher than that of PBS, it forms smaller and less stable crystals due to its low molecular weight, melting between 56 and 62 °C. It is important to acknowledge a limitation of the ISO 20200 standard. The constant test temperature of 58 °C, while ensuring reproducibility, represents an idealized condition. This temperature is very close to the melting point of the PEB component, which likely softened its structure and facilitated microbial access, thus accelerating its degradation rate compared to the variable temperature profiles of real-world compost environments. Additionally, morphology may play an important role in the biodegradation process. Phase separation, with the consequent presence of pores and cracks, can favor the disintegration of a material. However, a more homogeneous distribution and a high concentration of the more biodegradable component promote a larger surface area for microbial attack [72,73]. This supports the increased degree of disintegration upon the addition of PEB as its plasticizing effect and affinity for starch promoted a better distribution of the CS phase, particularly at high concentrations. The formulation of starch-rich blends poses a significant challenge due to the inherent tendency of starch to agglomerate, its limited dispersibility, and its high viscosity, collectively compromising processability, morphological homogeneity, and ultimately, the overall performance of the resulting materials. The incorporation of PEB into PBS/CS/PEB ternary blends allowed obtaining a continuous phase with improved dispersion of starch by reducing interfacial tension, thereby facilitating the formation of more homogeneous structures. This is crucial for optimizing the balance between stiffness and flexibility in the blends, as an improved phase distribution contributes to enhanced mechanical strength and stability. However, the PBS content significantly influences the final phase compatibility. While the combination of PEB and CS improves structural cohesion at balanced ratios, excessive PBS in the blend can lead to incompatibility that compromises the material strength.
Thermally responsive hydrogel inks exploit temperature changes as a stimulus for sol-gel transition and swelling changes. This can be utilized in biomedical applications by raising the temperature from ambient to physiological. The majority of thermo-responsive polymers used in the development of biomedical hydrogel inks have a lower critical solution temperature (LCST) and construct a gel once heated.[191] In physiological applications, generally, LCST 30-37 °C is appropriate for sol-gel transition.[192] When an LCST polymer is in a state of dispersion within water, it experiences three types of interactions including interactions amongst polymer molecules, interactions between the polymer and water, and interactions between the water molecules themselves.[193] For polymers with LCST, an increase in temperature causes the system's free energy to be negative, making water-polymer association unfavorable and facilitating the other two types of interactions. In the thermodynamic relationship ΔG = ΔH-TΔS, this negative free energy (ΔG) is attributed to the higher entropy term (ΔS) concerning the increase in the enthalpy term (ΔH).[194], [195] At critical solution temperature, network formation is attributed to conformational changes, including coil-to-helix transition and polymer micelle packing.[196] On the other hand, some thermosensitive polymers, known as upper critical solution temperature (UCST) polymers, form gel below a certain temperature but are soluble above it.[197] However, they have been less explored for developing hydrogel inks for biomedical applications. PNIPAM, poly (N-isopropyl acrylamide), having LCST of 32-35 °C, is an effective material for developing hydrogel inks and the most widely-known temperature-responsive polymer. While thermal response is intrinsic in PNIPAM, covalent cross-linking is required to form a 3D hydrogel network.[198], [199] On its own, PNIPAM lacks the viscoelastic properties requisite for extrusion-based printing. As a consequence, it is frequently combined with other substances.[200] Bakarich et al., for example, printed a dynamic Alg/PNIPAM ionic covalent entanglement (ICE) gel ink to create a smart valve that regulates water flow. When exposed to hot water, the valve closed automatically, minimizing the rate of flow by 99 %, and opened when subjected to cold water (Fig. 6a). These 3D-printed actuating hydrogel constructs could be used in a diverse type of soft robotics and smart sensing applications that require close human interaction.[201] Another example of PNIPAM's temperature response was provided by Lewis et al. in the form of bioinspired, shape-changing structures. In this instance, cellulose nanofibrils were added for good mechanical properties, while laponite XLG (extra-large grade) acted as a viscosity modifier in the hydrogel ink and PNIPAM was used as a reversible thermal actuator in shape-changing constructs. Because of shear-induced cellulose nanofibril alignment in the printed direction, (i.e., along the length of fibrils) water-induced swelling was significantly less in the longitudinal direction than the transverse direction. The anisotropic swelling that resulted from using poly (N, N-dimethylacrylamide) (PDMAM) for printing was irreversible; however, using PNIPAM instead of PDMAM made the swelling temperature-reversible, meaning that the coil-to-globule conversion of PNIPAM above its LCST caused the material to return to a “flat” configuration (Fig. 6b).[202] Some examples of PNIPAM based thermo-responsive hydrogel inks are shown in the Table 2. Another example of a component for a hydrogel ink that responds to temperature is gelatin. It is a partially hydrolyzed collagen which in turn is found in skin, connective tissues, and bone marrow.[203], [204] It contains the arginine-glycine-aspartic acid (RGD) cell-binding peptide motif, in addition to the matrix metalloproteinase-responsive degradation motifs.[205], [206] Hence, it is a common substance in 3D printed soft tissues for encouraging cell growth and attachment. Billiet et al. took advantage of temperature-responsive behaviour of gelatin methacrylamide for DIW. They created a temperature-controlled system around the syringe to accomplish this, effectively raising the ink's temperature above the gelatin methacrylamide melting point. As a result, the ink had improved fluidity, which allowed it to pass through the nozzle and onto a platform with meticulously controlled temperature. The ink quickly underwent gelation after cooling, leading to quick solidification. The hydrogel inks were loaded with hepatocarcinoma cell line (HepG2) and the overall cell viability was affected by printing pressure and needle shape. Printed scaffolds with high cell viability (>97 %) exhibited a maintained expression of liver specific functions.[207].

Water transport is just as important as thermal management in interfacial solar-driven water evaporation.24 Therefore, it is highly necessary to choose the excellent carrier for interface solar-driven water evaporators. Currently, hydrogel materials have received considerable attention in solar-driven interfacial water evaporation because of their hydrophilic, porous structure and large specific surface area, which leads to their advantages in water absorption, water retention, water transport and photothermal conversion.25-28 In addition, hydrogels contain many hydrophilic functional groups such as -OH, -NH2 and -COOH, which endow hydrogels with broad application prospects as the carrier of solar evaporators.29,30 Thermoresponsive hydrogels are a type of intelligent hydrogel whose volume changes in response to external temperature changes.31,32 The thermoresponsive hydrogels generally have a critical transition temperature when the phase transition occurs, which can be divided into lower critical solution temperature (LCST) type and upper critical solution temperature (UCST) type according to their phase transition types.33,34 Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAm) hydrogel is a typical LCST hydrogel with a critical temperature of about 33 °C.35,36 The PNIPAm hydrogel exhibits thermoresponsive properties due to the coexistence of hydrophilic amide groups (-CONH-) and hydrophobic isopropyl groups (-CH(CH3)2) on its macromolecular side chains.37 When the temperature is below the LCST, the hydrophilic groups of PNIPAm interact with water molecules, forming a highly ordered solvation layer stabilized by hydrogen bonds, which results in an extended coil conformation.38 As the temperature increases beyond the LCST, the hydrophobic group interactions between and within PNIPAm chains intensify, leading to the disruption of hydrogen bonds and the formation of hydrophobic domains. Consequently, the mechanical contraction of the PNIPAm hydrogel leads to the release of a large number of water molecules when the temperature goes beyond the LCST. In this process, the polymer undergoes a conformational transition from a loose coil structure to a compact granular structure, accompanied by the expulsion of water molecules from the solvation layer, manifesting macroscopically as a phase transition, and demonstrating the temperature-sensitive characteristics of the PNIPAm hydrogel. Therefore, it is able to absorb a large amount of water when the temperature is below the LCST. When the temperature is above the LCST, mechanical contraction occurs due to the interaction of hydrophobic groups, resulting in good water release. This property enhances the water delivery capacity of the hydrogel to achieve a high water purification rate.39,40 However, the PNIPAm hydrogel is very fragile and has poor mechanical properties, and hence, it is not a perfect carrier for solar-thermal devices.41 In this work, we prepared a novel solar-thermal thermoresponsive evaporator based on a solution-processable fullerene derivative and a thermoresponsive double-network hydrogel composed of PNIPAm and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) (Scheme 1). The evaporator utilizes PCBM as the solar-thermal material. The results show that the PCBM powder exhibits light absorption in the range of 250-900 nm, and the photothermal conversion efficiency can reach 14.65% under 1.0 kW m−2 simulated solar irradiation. In addition, introducing PVA improves the mechanical properties of the PNIPAm thermoresponsive hydrogel. The hydrogen bonds in PNIPAm and PVA interact to form a double-network thermoresponsive hydrogel as the carrier, which not only improves the flexibility of the original single hydrogel and increases the water transport capacity of the hydrogel, but also retains the advantages of the original thermoresponsive hydrogel.42 Therefore, the PCBM solar-thermal thermoresponsive hydrogel (STT/H) can reach an excellent water evaporation rate of 1.46 kg m−2 h−1 under 1.0 kW m−2 simulated solar irradiation. It is worth noting that the surface temperature of the solar-thermal evaporator rises during the solar-driven water evaporation, forming the temperature difference between the solar-thermal layer and the cold water below. Based on the Seebeck effect, the waste heat generated during the water evaporation can be fully utilized by introducing a thermoelectric module into the evaporator. This method can effectively convert heat energy into electricity, which can improve the overall solar energy utilization and realize water-electricity cogeneration. Under 1.0 kW m−2 simulated solar irradiation, PCBM solar-thermal evaporator can simultaneously achieve a maximum output voltage of 57.9 mV and a water evaporation rate of 0.93 kg m−2 h−1. In addition, during the 10-day outdoor experiment, the PCBM solar-thermal evaporator maintained a stable water evaporation performance, with an average daily water productivity of 3.99 kg m−2. The thermoresponsive solar-thermal hydrogel based on solution-processable fullerene materials has pioneered a novel design strategy for interfacial solar-driven water evaporators, which improves the rate of solar-thermal water evaporation and promotes the development process of industrial application of solar-thermal water evaporators.
To explain observed low biodegradation rates of PLA in ambient conditions, it is often argued that the temperature of the degradation environment should exceed the Tg of PLA (∼58 °C) to enable hydrolysis of the polymer facilitating subsequent biodegradation [19,44]. Considering that in Fig. 10 the test temperatures are more or less the same and that the main differences between the soil and home composting environments are the inoculum and the (quantity of the) microbial population, there are apparently more factors involved that can enhance the biodegradation of PLA at ambient temperatures. This is affirmed by Han et al. [26] who recently reported that the biodegradation of PLA in home composting conditions was accelerated by blending it with amorphous polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA). Although more research is required to fully understand the underlying mechanisms, our results indicate that blending PLA with other readily biodegradable polymers can serve as a platform for development of plastic products that require a specific programmed biodegradation rate. Polymer blending is found to be an effective method to tailor the disintegration rate of PBHV, PBS and PLA in soil.
