Due to its biocompatibility, there is already a substantial number of articles dealing with the functionalization of HA to enhance its properties and to broaden its application possibilities [5,[7], [8], [9]]. In particular, it would be interesting to chemically modify HA so that it acquires a thermo-responsive character in water, going from a “sol” state at room temperature prior to injection to a “gel” state within the body. This would allow to apply HA as an injectable physical hydrogel [10]. Polymers displaying thermo-responsiveness in water are well documented in the literature. Two types of transitions are being studied: UCST (upper critical solution temperature) and LCST (lower critical solution temperature). In the case of the UCST, increasing the temperature is triggering the complete dissolution of the polymer in a given solvent (usually water), while the LCST is characteristic of the opposite behaviour, with the polymer being in solution at low temperature and separating into 2 phases by heating the polymer solution. It has to be stressed out the UCST and the LCST are respective transition temperatures which are specific for a given polymer-solvent composition, with the UCST being the maximum temperature where the polymer will fully dissolve in the solvent and the LCST the minimum temperature where the polymer will render the solution turbid through phase separation. In general, the clouding temperature, which varies with the polymer-solvent composition, is designated as a “cloud point” Tcp [11]. One of the most studied polymer displaying a LCST in water is poly-(N-isopropylacrylamide), known as PNIPAM, because of its interesting LCST around 32 °C and its clouding temperature not depending much on the polymer chain length [12]. PNIPAM is known to undertake a coil to globule transition when heated above its Tcp due to partial dehydration of the polymer chains. It has therefore been grafted on biopolymers like alginate and HA to devise physical hydrogels [13]. However, PNIPAM does not allow to tune the temperature of gel formation because of its set LCST. Recently, poly(2-alkyl-2-oxazoline)s (POxs), obtained through the living cationic ring opening polymerisation (CROP) of 2-alkyl-2-oxazoline, are receiving an increasing attention due to their biocompatibility and their tuneable physical properties (value of glass temperature, amorphous or semi-crystalline character, solubility) [14,15]. Indeed, the nature of the alkyl moieties greatly affects their characteristics, with notably side groups with two or three carbons leading to polymers with LCST behaviour [11]. POxs have already been used as such or in conjunction with poly(2-alkyl-2-oxazine) to design hydrogels with promising properties to be used as scaffolds for 3D cell culture [16,17]. However, they also display some drawbacks, as they are not biodegradable and their polymerisation can only be controlled when targeting short chains (DP < 100) [18]. Recently, new methods have been developed to grow longer POxs chains, however, they are thus far limited to poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) PEtOx [19] and poly(2-methyl-2-oxazoline) PMeOx, the latter being obtained through the post-functionalization of a deacetylated PEtOx chain [18]. It is thus of interest to rather graft short POx chains on longer biodegradable polymers, so that high molecular weight copolymers can be obtained while the graft can be eliminated through renal clearance after degradation of the backbone.

Polylactic acid (PLA) is a polymer with good thermal stability up to approximately 350°C, after which it decomposes rapidly. This is rather unexpected since the diffusion coefficient is usually lower for larger molecular entities. At concentrations equal or lower than 10 wt% (plots not shown) the ALG-g-PNIPAM-L copolymer solution exhibited a weak temperature dependence of its moduli and the G″ was higher than G′ in all temperature range investigated. At higher concentrations, 12 and 14 wt%, a more complex response was observed characterized by an Arrhenious behaviour at low temperatures and a thermothickening effect at higher temperatures. As can be observed, grafting of alginate with the thermo-sensitive PNIPAM short chains provokes remarkably different thermo-response at elevated concentrations. Two critical temperatures can be distinguished. The first temperature, which will be designated as Tass, divides the thermogram into two temperature ranges: bellow Tass both moduli decreases upon heating and under the same rate (Arrhenious behaviour). Above Tass, the storage modulus increases more sharply than the loss modulus crossing it at a given temperature. This is the second critical temperature (at the G′ G″ crossover) above which the elastic modulus prevails over the loss one which usually is related to the sol to gel transition and will be designated as Tgel. The first critical temperature Tass is a few degrees lower than the association temperature observed by light scattering at CP = 0.1 wt% (Fig. 4b), which is related to the LCST of PNIPAM, and it is weakly dependent on polymer concentration. Among the stimuli-responsive gels, thermo-responsive gels are the most studied.[11] These gels, which are mostly based on poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM), exhibit a change in shape and/or volume when exposed to sufficiently high temperatures. The research interest in PNIPAM stems from its ability to undergo a lower critical solution temperature (LCST) transition in aqueous media,[12, 13] close to body temperature. During this conformational change, which occurs at ≈32 °C, the polymer chains self-assemble to undergo a coil-to-globule transition, which is accompanied by a volume decrease as water molecules are shed from the macromolecular aggregates.[14] Despite the aforementioned desirable features, PNIPAM-based gels have a few drawbacks that limit their practical application. These include poor mechanical properties, low drug loading capacity, as well as rapid drug release, or the so-called “burst release” phenomenon, which is a direct consequence of fast de-swelling kinetics. Several strategies have been used to try and overcome this, including copolymerization of NIPAM with other monomers,[15-18] synthesis of interpenetrating networks (IPNs) with other polymeric components[19-21] and fabrication of nanocomposite hydrogels through incorporation of nanoparticles.[22-26] Cellulose is a ubiquitous natural polymer which is obtained from various sources including plants, algae, tunicates, fungi, and bacteria.[27] Nanocellulose, a nanoscale isolate of native cellulose, has recently attracted attention in biomedical applications owing to its excellent mechanical properties, versatility of post-isolation chemical modification, biodegradability, biocompatibility, and low toxicity.[28] This bio-nanomaterial, especially in its flexible nanofibril form (CNF), is employed as a reinforcing agent in the synthesis of mechanically-robust polymeric hydrogels.[29] The ability to precisely tune PNIPAM's LCST, to a much broader temperature range, widens the scope for its application in biomedical fields.[30] To this end, research has been conducted on thermo-responsive IPN hybrid gels based on PNIPAM and cellulose. A semi IPN is a hybrid gel where a linear polymer is physically entangled with a crosslinked network of another polymer, while a full IPN refers to a hybrid gel where two independently-crosslinked polymeric components are mechanically interlocked. In one study, the reinforcing effect of CNF was investigated when PNIPAM was synthesized via free radical polymerization (FRP) in the presence of CNF to form CNF/PNIPAM semi IPN gels.[31] The mechanical properties of the gels in the presence of CNF were markedly improved, and this was attributed to the good dispersion of the nanofibrils within the hybrids. The swelling ratio of the gels significantly dropped at the PNIPAM LCST, and the de-swelling profiles were similar despite different CNF contents in the hybrids. De-swelling kinetics were also studied at 50 °C by immersing the swollen gels in hot distilled water; de-swelling occurred instantly as the gels expelled almost all the water molecules within the first minute. Controlled tuning of the LCST was demonstrated by Li et al.[32] by synthesizing a thermo-responsive PNIPAM/hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC) hybrid gel via electron beam irradiation. It was reported that increasing the irradiation dose promoted a corresponding increase in the LCST of the PNIPAM network, which was attributed to increasing PNIPAM molecular weight. Increasing the HPC content also shifted the LCST of the hybrids to higher temperatures, albeit with reduced thermo-stiffening.

A semi IPN is a hybrid gel where a linear polymer is physically entangled with a crosslinked network of another polymer, while a full IPN refers to a hybrid gel where two independently-crosslinked polymeric components are mechanically interlocked. In one study, the reinforcing effect of CNF was investigated when PNIPAM was synthesized via free radical polymerization (FRP) in the presence of CNF to form CNF/PNIPAM semi IPN gels.[31] The mechanical properties of the gels in the presence of CNF were markedly improved, and this was attributed to the good dispersion of the nanofibrils within the hybrids. The swelling ratio of the gels significantly dropped at the PNIPAM LCST, and the de-swelling profiles were similar despite different CNF contents in the hybrids. De-swelling kinetics were also studied at 50 °C by immersing the swollen gels in hot distilled water; de-swelling occurred instantly as the gels expelled almost all the water molecules within the first minute. Controlled tuning of the LCST was demonstrated by Li et al.[32] by synthesizing a thermo-responsive PNIPAM/hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC) hybrid gel via electron beam irradiation. It was reported that increasing the irradiation dose promoted a corresponding increase in the LCST of the PNIPAM network, which was attributed to increasing PNIPAM molecular weight. Increasing the HPC content also shifted the LCST of the hybrids to higher temperatures, albeit with reduced thermo-stiffening.
Among these, thermogels that spontaneously solidify close to body temperature have garnered significant interest, notably because they do not require external stimuli or additional chemical agents such as toxic cross-linking compounds. Numerous thermogels have been explored as biomaterials. For instance, poloxamer and hyaluronic acid-derived hydrogels have been studied for postcesarean uterine scars, (9) while chitosan/B-glycerophosphate-based thermogels have been investigated for the osteogenic differentiation of dental pulp stem cells (10) or the osteoblastic MG-63 cell line. (11) Besides, poly-N-isopropylacrylamide (PNIPAM) has emerged as a valuable building block to elaborate thermogels. The transition of PNIPAM is related to a lower critical solution transition temperature (LCST): below 32 °C, PNIPAM is in coil, extended, and under a hydrophilic form, while when heated above its LCST, isopropyl hydrophobic interactions become predominant and a phase transition occurs. (12) The wide interest for this polymer, known since the 1960s, is largely due to the temperature stability of its LCST in aqueous solutions, mostly independent of concentration, pH, or ionic strength. (13) The hydrophobic association of PNIPAM blocks above the LCST combined with hydrophilic polymers possessing the ability to form hydrogels opens opportunities for thermogelling scaffolds. Numerous studies reported the in situ gelification of PNIPAM for osteoarthritis (OA) treatments using PNIPAM. Cartilage tissue engineering is a hot topic because of population aging and due to the low regenerative properties of this tissue. (14,15) Implantation of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) is a promising approach for cartilage regeneration since MSCs can be easily differentiated into chondrocytes and can secrete immunomodulatory factors. (16,17) PNIPAM was actually reported to preserve the chondrogenic phenotype of MSCs, but its transition is associated with a wide volume shrinkage. Copolymerization, for instance, with acrylic acid was shown to limit this phenomenon. (18) However, to ensure a high biocompatibility, PNIPAM was effectively combined with natural polymers such as gelatin, (19) chitosan/gelatin, (19) or chitosan/graphene oxide (20) to embed stem cells and applied to promote osteoinduction. Chitosan (CS), a deacetylated form of chitin, is one of the most widely used polysaccharides, owing to its biocompatibility, biodegradability, versatile properties, and availability. (21) However, because of limited mechanical properties and insolubility in water at physiological pH, this polysaccharide is often combined with other polymers. (22) The chitosan-PNIPAM (CS-PNIPAM) copolymer is one of the combinations to obtain a biocompatible thermosensitive gel and was already reported to preserve chondrocyte survival and phenotype and to offer a chondrogenic environment to MSCs. (23,24) PNIPAM-CS thus appears as an interesting chondrogenic vehicle for cells. However, femoral cartilage elasticity is quite high (elasticity around 300 kPa (25)) and relevant moduli for cell support are usually considered comprised between 150 and 1800 kPa. (26) PNIPAM-CS hydrogels are expected to present low mechanical properties due to their weak hydrophobic assembly and these hydrogels are not bioadhesive. (23) Therefore, their combination as a cellular vehicle with a robust scaffold is a promising alternative to provide an optimal environment for an MSC. In a previous study, we demonstrated the efficacy of collagen-based microbeads generated via microfluidics in facilitating cell adhesion and delivering TGF-β3 to induce MSCs’ in vitro and in vivo differentiation into chondrocytes. (27) To anchor the cells at the injection site, we propose the combination of these microspheres with a stimuli-responsive carrier. This carrier, a thermogel, was synthesized through the chemical conjugation of chitosan and PNIPAM. The investigation presented herein is thus centered on evaluating the copolymer’s performance as a potential cellular carrier. We first describe the copolymer synthesis procedure, then report on its rheological properties, thermal response, and stability in biological conditions, and finally give preliminary data regarding its ability to sustain MSC viability.
Smart or responsive hydrogels are those that possess the capacity to change their physical/chemical characteristics in response to various environmental factors, including temperature, pH, light, magnetic field, ionic strength, and other relevant variables [1]. This behavior is attributed to the presence of diverse functional groups and constituents within the polymers comprising the hydrogel [2, 3]. The term"thermo-responsive"refers to a class of polymers changing their solubility and, consequently, conformation versus the exposed temperature [4]. When the temperature changes above a certain temperature, i.e. the coil to globule transition temperature (Tcg), the conformational feature of the polymer chain changes from the coil to globule with a compact spherical shape. This conformation change considerably decreases the chain solubility in its media and causes polymer phase separation [5, 6]. This transition occurrence has a wide range of applications in drug delivery [7], tissue engineering [8], and biosensors [9]. Poly(N-isopropyl acrylamide) (PNIPAM) with a lower critical solution temperature (LCST) in the range of 30 − 32 °C is a proper thermo-responsive polymer candidate for biomedical applications [10, 11] because this temperature range is close to human body temperature. PNIPAM can be synthesized by free radical polymerization initiated by a redox system in aqueous or non-aqueous solvents [12, 13]. Potassium persulfate (KPS)/N,N,N'N'-tetramethyl ethylenediamine (TEMED) as an initiator/accelerator combination has been used for NIPAM polymerization in aqueous media [14]. To improve the efficiency of hydrogels in drug delivery systems, it is more important to prepare hydrogel structures that have a high degree of flexibility in controlling the release mechanism. Due to the complex conditions found in living organisms, the hydrogel system must be responsive to multiple factors at the same time [15, 16]. For this purpose, dual or multi-responsive hydrogels with interpenetrating polymer networks (IPN) and semi-IPN structures would be developed. For instance, the incorporation of thermo-responsive P(NIPAM-co-AA) chains in a pH-sensitive cross-linked hydrogel network would provide thermal and pH dual-responsive semi-IPN hydrogels. This hybrid hydrogel structure permits controlled drug release in response to both temperature and pH changes on/in the body [17, 18]. Additionally, the incorporation of some biopolymers, e.g. chitosan, in these hybrid hydrogels leads to desirable properties such as biodegradability and biocompatibility [19, 20]. Different hydrogel systems based on chitosan with semi-IPN structures with sensitivity to various stimuli such as pH and heat have been worked on recently [21, 22]. In this research work, poly (N-isopropyl acrylamide) (PNIPAM) and its linear copolymers with AA comonomer [P(NIPAM-co-AA)] as thermo-responsive polymers were synthesized. AA can be copolymerized with NIPAM to modify the LCST point of the thermo-responsive polymer exhibiting the pH-responsiveness behavior as PNIPAM shows [23,24,25]. Thereafter, the thermo-responsive copolymers were synthesized inside the pH-sensitive CC to prepare the final P(NIPAM-co-AA)/CC dual-responsive hydrogels with a semi-IPN structure. Thereafter, the GA as a drug was loaded inside the semi-IPN hydrogels. In addition, the influence of the P(NIPAM-co-AA) proportion on the swelling ratio, and the drug release rate of the resulting semi-IPN hydrogels was evaluated. As a hydrogel, this semi-IPN system has the potential to regulate the release of GA by changing the temperature and P(NIPAM-co-AA) proportion for transdermal applications.
Hydrogels have been studied as effective drug delivery vehicle for a long time and attracted increasing interests since the introducing of stimuli responsive properties.13-15 Incorporation of pH and temperature responses into one network endows the hydrogels with dually responsive properties, which provides versatile ways to control the drug release. Based on this concept, a variety of hydrogels being sensitive to both pH and temperature have been synthesized.16-19 Although there are many polymers responding to temperature change, poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) has been the most popular one used as the thermo-sensitive part due to its sharp phase transition.20 PNIPAM chain undergoes a reversible coil-to-globule transition at about 32°C (lower critical solution temperature, LCST), below which it is soluble in water and above which it precipitates out from the solution. Hydrogels made of PNIPAM exhibited unique hydrophilic/hydrophobic changes around the LCST of PNIPAM leading to the reversible swelling and shrinking behaviors, which can be used as effective trigger to modulate drug release.21-24 However, the most serious disadvantage is that PNIPAM hydrogels are not biodegradable. There have been many successful efforts to prepare PNIPAM-based biodegradable hydrogels by using biodegradable crosslinkers containing dextran or polylactide (PLA) units.17, 25, 26 To the best of our knowledge, there have been no pH-sensitive polypeptide-based crosslinkers employed to crosslink PNIPAM up to now. In view of these aspects, a promising strategy for designing biodegradable thermo- and pH-sensitive hydrogels was developed. In this work, PNIPAM was crosslinked by poly(L-glutamic acid) (PGA) modified with pendant double bond to endow hydrogel with both thermo- and pH-sensitive properties. PGA and its derivatives are most widely studied pH-sensitive polypeptides due to their biocompatibility and biodegradability.27-31 In our previous work, a series of thermo- and pH-sensitive hydrogels composed of PGA and poly(NIPAM-co-HEMA) (PNH) were synthesized through chemical coupling between the carboxylic groups in PGA and the hydroxyl groups in PNH.32 Although the hydrogels exhibited phase transition around the LCST reflected by optical transmittance change, their swelling ratios were not sensitive to temperature in neutral or basic media. To obtain hydrogels with improved thermo-sensitive properties, we design a new synthetic strategy, that is, copolymerized NIPAM with PGA macromonomer containing multiple 2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA) units at different feeding weight ratios using a photoinitiation technique. The hydrogels possessed similar structure with PGA/PNH hydrogels. However, their temperature-sensitive properties were quite different from PGA/PNH hydrogels due to the different crosslinking mechanism. The as-prepared hydrogels shrank at temperature above their collapse temperature (CT) and re-swelled when temperature was lowered to 25°C. And their pH-sensitive swelling behaviors were also examined at different temperature. Bovine serum albumin (BSA) were used as a model protein drug and loaded into the hydrogels. The pH and temperature depending release behaviors indicated promising application of these materials as controlled drug delivery vehicles. The microgels show a great promise in bioseparation and many other fields. Recently, stimuli-responsive polymers have been investigated with a tremendous increasing frequency for their intelligent response to external stimuli, such as temperature, light and pH [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7]. In particular, copolymers based on thermally reversible poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) have attracted a tremendous interest because of their exponentially increasing application in the fields of drug delivery, cell separation, metal ion purification and fluorescence detection [8], [9]. That the amphiphiles possess lower critical solution temperature (LCST) is a rather general phenomenon. What previous studies have shown is that PNIPAM is hydrophilic existed as random, isolated and extended coils in water below the LCST (32 °C), whereas it is hydrophobic with the PNIPAM backbone undergoing the intrachain collapse prior to the interchain aggregation to form a molecular globule above the LCST [10], [11], [12], [13]. In addition, chitosan (CS) has attracted considerable attention as a naturally occurring polymer with fascinating properties of biocompatibility, biodegradability, nontoxicity and cationic properties [14], [15], [16]. Recent advances in copolymer fabrication such as micro-emulsion polymerization, coacervation and layer-by-layer self-assembly provide feasible approaches to prepare well-defined microgels with controllable shape and desirable stimuli-responsive characteristics [17], [18]. Till now, spherical copolymers with size from a few to several dozens of nanometers in diameter have been widely reported. However, the research on anisotropically distributed copolymers including ellipsoidal and rodlike particles is still rare. Dietsch and co-workers [19], [20] synthesized ellipsoidal hybrid magnetic microgels with thermally tunable aspect ratios and a spindle-shaped core in the centre of the microgels. However, to synthesize the spindle-shaped cores of the microgels, both complex multistep and advanced experimental skills were required [21]. Accordingly, one smart strategy with merits of simplicity, celerity and high accuracy to prepare shape-controlled stimuli-responsive microgels is urgently required.
It is known that PNIPAM-based polymers are thermo-sensitive in aqueous solution presenting a lower Tcp as either the molar mass or the hydrophobic monomer content increases. Tcp is almost independent of concentration and chain length for PNIPAM based polymers with a molar mass higher than 50,000 g/mol [30]. On the other hand, low molar mass PNIPAM-based polymers show a Tcp which is a function of concentration and chain length [31]. In our case the Tcp of the PNIPAM-L and PNIPAM-H homopolymers were about the same, i.e. 36 and 35 °C respectively, showing that a decrease of molecular weight about 11.000 Da had negligible effect on Tcp. On the other hand, for the P(NIPAM-co-NtBAM) copolymer a remarkably decrease was observed, i.e. 10 °C for only 15 mol% hydrophobic enrichment of PNIPAM, showing that the tunability of Tcp is more effective by this way. Finally, the values of Tcp observed for the alginate-based graft copolymers are similar to the values of Tcp for the corresponding temperature sensitive polymer side chains grafted to alginate, within experimental error. The non-modified sodium alginate aqueous solutions are viscous without any sign of viscoelasticity (no entanglements) and exhibited Arrenious behaviour with temperature in all concentrations explored, up to 12 wt%. In order to detect the appearance of thermothickening behaviour of the alginate grafted samples, oscillatory shear experiments were conducted as a function of temperature starting with ALG-g-PNIPAM-L. In Fig. 5a, temperature ramp (heating rate 1 °C/min) of the storage (G′) and the loss modulus (G″), obtained in the linear viscoelastic regime at low frequency (0.1 Hz), are presented for several concentrations from 10 to 14 wt%. At concentrations equal or lower than 10 wt% (plots not shown) the ALG-g-PNIPAM-L copolymer solution exhibited a weak temperature dependence of its moduli and the G″ was higher than G′ in all temperature range investigated. At higher concentrations, 12 and 14 wt%, a more complex response was observed characterized by an Arrhenious behaviour at low temperatures and a thermothickening effect at higher temperatures. In Fig. 5b, the temperature effect on the dynamic moduli for the 12 wt% solution is compared with that of pure sodium alginate in order to underline the effect of grafting. As can be observed, grafting of alginate with the thermo-sensitive PNIPAM short chains provokes remarkably different thermo-response at elevated concentrations. Two critical temperatures can be distinguished. The first temperature, which will be designated as Tass, divides the thermogram into two temperature ranges: bellow Tass both moduli decreases upon heating and under the same rate (Arrhenious behaviour). Above Tass, the storage modulus increases more sharply than the loss modulus crossing it at a given temperature. This is the second critical temperature (at the G′ G″ crossover) above which the elastic modulus prevails over the loss one which usually is related to the sol to gel transition and will be designated as Tgel. The first critical temperature Tass is a few degrees lower than the association temperature observed by light scattering at CP = 0.1 wt% (Fig. 4b), which is related to the LCST of PNIPAM, and it is weakly dependent on polymer concentration. Thus, provided that LCST decreases with CP, it should reveal the onset of PNIPAM side-chain hydrophobic association, leading gradually to the formation of physical junctions of a reversible network.

The storage modulus (G′) and loss modulus (G′′) were monitored at 1 °C min−1 in the range of 20 °C to 45 °C. When the temperature exceeds 32 °C, the system loses its flowability, and the viscoelastic shear modulus increases by 2-3 levels of magnitude in the temperature range of less than 2 °C. The reversible curling/uncurling of the Zn2+/Fe3+(1:1)-SA-PAm/PNIPAm-HACC bilayer hydrogels have been used to lift and release an object in response to temperature. As shown in Fig. 10a, the curved Zn2+/Fe3+(1:1)-SA-PAm/PNIPAm-HACC bilayer hydrogel strips (Length × Width: 50 mm × 10 mm) can lift heavy objects with weights of 3.2 g and 3.8 g, respectively. This result indicated that the bilayer hydrogel has good load-bearing properties after bending. We also designed a four-arm gripper as a model demonstration of a soft robot, as shown in Fig. 10a. Fig. 10a demonstrates a series of processes for the Zn2+/Fe3+(1:1)-SA-PAm/PNIPAm-HACC bilayer hydrogel grasper to grasp and release the target object under temperature stimulation. The gripper is in the expansion mode when the temperature is below LCST. When the temperature is above LCST, the bilayer gripper bends toward the HACC side to capture the target. The results demonstrated that the reversible curling/uncurling performance of the Zn2+/Fe3+(1:1)-SA-PAm/PNIPAm-HACC bilayer gripper could be used to perform grasp-and-release activities, and it has the potential as an intelligent gripper. Based on the reversible curling/uncurling properties of Zn2+/Fe3+(1:1)-SA-PAm/PNIPAm-HACC bilayer hydrogels, we further fabricated a hydrogel actuator as a sensing element to turn on and off the circuit by controlling its temperature. Thermally responsive hydrogel inks exploit temperature changes as a stimulus for sol-gel transition and swelling changes. This can be utilized in biomedical applications by raising the temperature from ambient to physiological. The majority of thermo-responsive polymers used in the development of biomedical hydrogel inks have a lower critical solution temperature (LCST) and construct a gel once heated.[191] In physiological applications, generally, LCST 30-37 °C is appropriate for sol-gel transition.[192] When an LCST polymer is in a state of dispersion within water, it experiences three types of interactions including interactions amongst polymer molecules, interactions between the polymer and water, and interactions between the water molecules themselves.[193] For polymers with LCST, an increase in temperature causes the system's free energy to be negative, making water-polymer association unfavorable and facilitating the other two types of interactions. In the thermodynamic relationship ΔG = ΔH-TΔS, this negative free energy (ΔG) is attributed to the higher entropy term (ΔS) concerning the increase in the enthalpy term (ΔH).[194], [195] At critical solution temperature, network formation is attributed to conformational changes, including coil-to-helix transition and polymer micelle packing.[196] On the other hand, some thermosensitive polymers, known as upper critical solution temperature (UCST) polymers, form gel below a certain temperature but are soluble above it.[197] However, they have been less explored for developing hydrogel inks for biomedical applications. PNIPAM, poly (N-isopropyl acrylamide), having LCST of 32-35 °C, is an effective material for developing hydrogel inks and the most widely-known temperature-responsive polymer. While thermal response is intrinsic in PNIPAM, covalent cross-linking is required to form a 3D hydrogel network.[198], [199] On its own, PNIPAM lacks the viscoelastic properties requisite for extrusion-based printing. As a consequence, it is frequently combined with other substances.[200] Bakarich et al., for example, printed a dynamic Alg/PNIPAM ionic covalent entanglement (ICE) gel ink to create a smart valve that regulates water flow. When exposed to hot water, the valve closed automatically, minimizing the rate of flow by 99 %, and opened when subjected to cold water (Fig. 6a). These 3D-printed actuating hydrogel constructs could be used in a diverse type of soft robotics and smart sensing applications that require close human interaction.[201] Another example of PNIPAM's temperature response was provided by Lewis et al. in the form of bioinspired, shape-changing structures. In this instance, cellulose nanofibrils were added for good mechanical properties, while laponite XLG (extra-large grade) acted as a viscosity modifier in the hydrogel ink and PNIPAM was used as a reversible thermal actuator in shape-changing constructs. Over the past decade, increasing attention and efforts have been focused on the development of alternative energy sources and energy storage devices to alleviate the impacts of climate change and fossil fuel depletion. The development of practical energy storage devices for carrying and delivering the desired energy has turned into a priority to support the efforts to produce renewable energy from the sun and other renewable sources.6 Batteries and supercapacitors offer much higher cycling stability and power density, but suffer from low energy density.7 Furthermore, another trend is for flexible and wearable electronics, which are gaining significant importance due to their suitability for wide integration and their portability, with the added advantage of that they can undergo structural transformation to form supercapacitors, batteries, and flexible solar cells.8-10 Among the current strategies for energy storage in supercapacitors, high power and good cyclability are the two most desirable features. There are two different ways to store charge in a supercapacitor, via: a non-Faradaic double-layer electrostatic charging process or a Faradaic surface redox process. On the other hand, the lithium-ion battery (LIB) has also received widespread attention for large-scale power sources and energy storage devices, owing to its high power, high energy density, and long cycle life. There is an increasing demand for key LIB materials, especially separators, which serve the crucial functions of physically separating the anode and cathode while allowing the free flow of lithium ions.11,12 It has been recognized that the microporous structure and thermal dimensional stability of separators considerably affect the battery performance. Given the overwhelmingly growing demand for energy storage devices with high performance for portable electronic applications, lightweight, high power density, durable, and low-cost energy storage devices are the major targets. Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are an important energy storage technology due to their energy efficiency, high power density, and environmental friendliness.1 In the LIB system, separators play a vital role for they can provide physical separation between the electrodes to prevent short circuits and store enough electrolyte to allow lithium ions to pass through.2, 3 Although the separator is not an active component inside the battery, it directly affects the final cost, cycle life, electrochemical performance, and safety.4 Currently, commercially available separators include polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), or their composites.5 They have excellent chemical stability and good mechanical properties, but their poor thermal stability and low electrolyte wettability make them unable to meet the needs of high-performance LIBs.6, 7 The low affinity with the electrolyte has negative impacts on the migration number and migration efficiency of the lithium ions, and inevitably affect the overall electrochemical performance of LIBs.8 Moreover, a major hidden danger is the safety of LIBs for their poor thermal stability.9 Cellulose is one of the oldest and most abundant natural polymeric materials on earth.10 In contrast to polyolefins, the molecular chain of cellulose and its derivatives is rich in hydroxyl and carbonyl groups, so it has a good interaction with carbonate electrolytes.11 Moreover, the reported initial decomposition temperature of cellulose is approximately 270°C,12 much higher than the decomposition temperature of polyolefins,13 thus ensuring the safety of LIBs. As one of the most widely used materials in cellulose derivatives, cellulose acetate (CA) can easily form membranes, is biodegradable, and can be obtained from a wide range of raw materials.14, 15 In recent years, considerable work has been done to prepare CA-based separators, using CA as the skeletal of a multilayer or shell structure.11, 13, 16-19 In addition, the comprehensive performance of CA can be further improved by blending with inorganic nanoparticles. Huang et al.18 prepared a nanofiber membrane by coaxial electrospinning of a CA core and PVDF-HFP shell with excellent thermal stability (to 200°C) and electrolyte compatibility (355% electrolyte uptake). Wang et al.19 prepared a sandwich structure (PVDF|CA|PVDF) composite separator by layer-by-layer electrospinning technology with enhanced cycle stability (91.80% after 50 cycles). Boriboon et al.13 prepared a CA-based separator embedded with titania particles which retained its capacity with 79 mA h g−1 after 30 cycles and had excellent discharge capacity. However, the poor chemical stability and low mechanical strength of CA have always been a bottleneck restricting its application in the field of LIBs separators. Nanocellulose has been investigated as a promising green alternative to conventional energy storage materials.20, 21 Cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) have significant potential as polymer reinforcement due to their high aspect ratio and specific surface area, and excellent chemical, mechanical (120-150 GPa) and thermal properties (>270°C).22-24 Solubility, is an important parameter to measure the compatibility of substances, and plays a very important role in the processing, and modification of polymers.25-28 CNCs are poorly dispersed in hydrophobic polymer substrates while CA is compatible. Therefore, CNCs needs to be acetylated to have a polarity similar to CA so that the Flory-Huggins interaction parameter between the two is small enough to ensure the compatibility. Herein, acetylation modification was used as an intermediate process to prepare CNCs-enhanced CA separators through a phase separation technique. The process of acetylation makes CNCs change from hydrophilicity to hydrophobicity, so that they can be evenly dispersed in the CA casting solution. In addition, the deacetylation process removes the acetyl group from the CA and the acetylated CNCs (ACNCs) and forms a rigid network structure with hydrogen bonding, which further improves the chemical stability and mechanical properties of the composite separators. The whole process hardly affects the morphology of the CNCs or the pore structure of CA. Compared with PP separators, the composite separators exhibited an excellent overall performance such as high porosity, outstanding electrolyte uptake, enhanced mechanical properties, inherent excellent thermal stability, and improved ionic conductivity. This work sheds light on a simple method to prepare an environmentally friendly separator with a better and safer performance for LIBs and paves the way to the transformation of raw materials from petroleum to biomass resources.
Currently, the most commonly used commercial separator for ZIBs is the glass fiber (GF) separator, possessing high porosity and electrolyte wettability. However, its large pore size (micron scale) and irregular pore structure accommodate a large number of SO42− and H+ ions, triggering side reactions and non-uniform Zn2+ flux, thereby accelerating dendrite formation.9 Its poor mechanical strength renders it susceptible to penetration by Zn dendrites during repeated cycling, leading to internal short circuits and safety risks.10 Moreover, the production process of GF separators is relatively complex, raising environmental concerns. Recent studies reveal that surface modification of GF separators has proved to be a promising strategy for improving electrochemical properties, which can be categorized into three key aspects: first, modified surfaces with optimized pore structures and zincophilic functional groups effectively regulate Zn2+ flux distribution, thereby suppressing Zn dendrite growth; second, advanced coatings such as inorganic ceramic layers or polymer-based films demonstrate superior electrolyte wettability and serve as robust physical barriers to eliminate side reactions; third, the introduction of negatively charged functional groups through surface modification can repel SO42−, thereby reducing byproduct formation. However, their high cost and excessive thickness (typically >300 μm) hinder energy density and scalability of ZIBs.11 In recent years, biomass materials (e.g., cellulose, chitosan, chitin, and lignin) have emerged as promising alternative candidates for ZIB separators (Fig. 1b). Beyond their inherent biodegradability and sustainability derived from renewable sources, these biomass-based separators offer distinct advantages, including tunable microstructures and abundant functional groups, which collectively contribute to superior wettability, enhanced mechanical strength, and dendrite suppression. Specifically, their intrinsic polar functional groups (-OH, -COOH, and -NH2) provide abundant binding sites, thus reshaping the Zn2+ solvation structure and promoting uniform Zn nucleation/deposition.12 In addition, the hierarchical porous structures of biomass-based separators can effectively regulate Zn2+ flux, and targeted chemical modification of biomass materials can significantly improve their mechanical strength and electrochemical stability.13 Nevertheless, several challenges remain to be addressed for the practical application of biomass-based separators, such as ensuring sufficient mechanical strength, optimizing the pore structure for rapid ion transport, and maintaining compatibility with aqueous electrolytes. To our knowledge, recent reviews on separators of ZIBs provide a comprehensive overview of advanced design strategies focused on functionalized architectural design and chemical modification for dendrite suppression and interfacial stability enhancement. However, there is still a lack of comprehensive discussion regarding the advantages and challenges of biomass-based separators compared with GF separators, especially in terms of underlying mechanisms and large-scale applications. This review provides an in-depth examination of the recent achievements in biomass-based separators for ZIBs, highlighting fundamental requirements, structural configurations, preparation methods, and modification strategies. We also present the classification, summary, and discussion of biomass-based separator studies from the perspective of similar modification methods and operational mechanisms. Finally, the remaining challenges and future development directions of biomass-based separators for ZIBs are summarized and analyzed to promote further research and development for large-scale applications.

AbstractAqueous zinc ion batteries (AZIBs) have attracted increasing attention because of their high energy density, excellent safety features, and environmentally friendly properties. The separator plays a crucial role in the battery, greatly influencing its performance and stability. Therefore, the separator for AZIBs has attracted increasing interest in recent years. Glass fiber (GF) is the predominant separator material, and exhibits favorable hydrophilicity and remarkable ionic conductivity. Nevertheless, its internal inhomogeneous pore structure makes it difficult to achieve uniform deposition of zinc ions, while the GF separator is easy to pierce due to its inadequate mechanical properties. In response to these issues, cellulose materials have garnered significant interest owing to their exceptional hydrophilicity, cost-effectiveness, and widespread availability. This review summarizes the potential of cellulose separators to substitute GF separators for AZIBs because of their high porosity, ion mobility number, electrolyte wetting rate, and liquid absorption rate. Different methods for preparing cellulose separators for AZIBs and various strategies to enhance their performance are summarized. The future outlook of cellulose-based separators for ZIBs is also prospected. IntroductionThe increasing need for dependable power sources with substantial energy storage capacities is driven by the rapid development in the fields of electric vehicles and portable electronic devices. Rechargeable batteries offer a feasible solution for mobile electrochemical energy storage due to their high energy density, excellent charge-discharge performance, long cycle life, and minimal self-discharge rate. Among numerous batteries, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are widely recognized for their lightweight construction, portability, and superior energy density, and have become the primary option in portable batteries [[1], [2], [3]]. Nevertheless, there are quite a few challenges such as safety hazards, cost, and environmental impact in the manufacturing and utilization of LIBs [4,5]. Despite the long-standing dominance of LIBs in the market, the emergence of aqueous zinc ion batteries (AZIBs) has attracted considerable attention as a storage alternative, due to their exceptional safety features, cost-effectiveness, and environmentally sustainable characteristics. As shown in Fig. 1, the components of a battery consist of a negative electrode, a positive electrode, an electrolyte, and a diaphragm [6]. These components play unique roles during the battery's operation. The charging and discharging of ZIBs rely on the reversible insertion/removal of Zn2+ in the cathode material and the reversible dissolution/deposition of Zn2+ on the zinc cathode. The liquid electrolyte is the medium for transporting zinc ions in ZIBs, facilitating the migration of these ions between the cathode and anode. The separator effectively prevents direct contact between the positive and negative electrodes, facilitates the transport of Zn2+ ions through microchannels, and inhibits the formation of by-products such as zinc dendrites from redox reactions [[7], [8], [9]].During the charging and discharging process of ZIBs, Zn2+ are cyclically transferred to and from the negative electrode composed of zinc, and subsequently inserted and extracted from the positive electrode material [[10], [11], [12]]. Zinc metal is highly regarded as an excellent electrode material due to its cost-effectiveness, high theoretical capacity (820 mAhg−1), non-toxicity, and low redox potential (−0.762 V) [13,14]. Nevertheless, the service life of ZIBs is significantly impacted by zinc dendrites and side-reaction issues such as passivation, hydrogen evolution, and corrosion. Several strategies have been proposed to solve these issues, such as electrolyte modification [[15], [16], [17]], positive electrode protection layers [18,19], and zinc anode coating protection [20]. However, research is relatively limited on separators and their importance has been somewhat overlooked.Currently, GF is the predominant material used for separators in ZIBs due to its plentiful pores, hydrophilic properties, and superior ionic conductivity [21,22]. Nonetheless, the loose internal structure of GF separators leads to poor mechanical properties [23]. The inadequate mechanical properties of the GF separators, coupled with their considerable thickness, can have an unfavorable impact on the energy density per unit volume, the distance of ion transport, and the internal resistance of the battery [24]. Additionally, the non-uniform pore structure leads to the uneven distribution of Zn2+, causing dendrite formation and impacting the Coulombic efficiency (CE) and long-term stability of ZIBs. Therefore, novel separator materials are crucial to solving these problems.Currently, common polyolefin separator materials for ZIBs, including polyacrylonitrile (PAN) [25], polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) [26], and polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) [27] exhibit remarkable chemical stability and mechanical property. However, they are hindered by limitations such as low porosity and inadequate electrolyte wetting characteristics. As a result, these materials exhibit low ionic conductivity, which considerably restricts their applicability in zinc-ion battery (ZIB) systems. In contrast, as the most abundant biomass on earth, cellulosic materials present a promising alternative. Cellulose materials, known for their eco-friendliness, renewability, hydrophilicity, and cost-effectiveness, show great potential for application in ZIBs [28,29]. Cellulose has a high concentration of hydroxyl groups, enabling various chemical modifications such as esterification, oxidation, etherification, grafting, and others [[30], [31], [32], [33]]. Furthermore, the intermolecular bonding of hydroxyl groups on adjacent chains results in the formation of highly ordered crystalline regions, contributing to the exceptional mechanical strength of cellulose [34]. Consequently, separators fabricated from cellulose and its derivatives exhibit favorable physical and chemical properties.Cellulose-based separators have broad application prospects in ZIBs. However, there are few reviews summarizing the preparation of cellulose-based ZIB separators and their performance improvements. As shown in Fig. 2, herein, the preparation methods and commonly used materials for cellulose-based ZIB separators are introduced. The performance requirements of the ZIB separator and various strategies to improve the performance of the separator are reviewed. Finally, the challenges and future development directions of cellulose-based zinc-ion battery separators are proposed.

Cellulose, the most abundant biomass on earth, presents abundant hydroxyl groups, high mechanical modulus, and considerable porous surface, which are highly desirable for tackling the aforementioned issues. Over the past few decades, lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have attracted increasing attention because of their use in digital devices, electric vehicles, and large energy storage equipment due to their unique advantages, including high energy density, long cycle and calendar life, high efficiency, lack of memory effect, and environmentally friendly properties [1,2,3,4,5,6]. A lithium-ion battery consists of two electrodes, the cathode and the anode, which are physically separated with a polyolefin-based separator impregnated with electrolyte [7]. The battery separator, a porous polymer membrane, is known as a major component and plays a key role in lithium-ion batteries [8, 9]. It’s important role in the battery includes providing pathways for the ionic transportation from the electrolyte and the physical and electrical separation of the two cathode and anode electrodes, which prevents short circuit and leads to the safe operation of the battery. In this regard, the separator must have the following characteristics to satisfy these responsibilities: Proper wettability to the electrolyte is necessary to provide better ionic conductivity. The separator must have good mechanical strength to reduce the risk of short circuits and explosions. Furthermore, the thickness and porosity of the separator have a significant role in the ionic conductivity and energy density [10,11,12]. Commercial separators are about 20-25\(\:{\upmu\:}\text{m}\) thick and have 40% porosity [13, 14]. At present, polyolefin separators such as polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), and PP/PE/PP three-layer separators are widely used in commercial lithium-ion batteries due to their relatively good quality mechanical and electrochemical properties. These separators, however, also have some drawbacks. Poor polarity of these separators leads to the meager wettability of polar liquid electrolytes, which results in the inferior battery conductivity. In addition, due to the low melting temperature (135°C for PE and 165°C for PP), they suffer from severe dimensional contraction at higher temperatures, which leads to short circuits and safety problems for the battery [15,16,17,18,19,20]. To overcome the mentioned defects, some efforts have been exerted. A suitable method to improve the polyolefin separators’ characteristics, like thermal stability and mechanical strength, is to introduce ceramic nanoparticle coatings on their surface [21,22,23,24,25,26]. So far, various studies have been conducted to develop polyolefin separators by applying ceramic-based surface coatings. Yang et al. studied the boehmite (AlOOH) coating thickness of 1.15 \(\:{\upmu\:}\text{m}\) and found that the thermal shrinkage of the separator improved but the puncture strength and tensile strength were weakened [27]. Rahmani et al. modified the of a polypropylene separator by an electrospun coating layer of Poly(vinyl alchohol)‑SiO2 [28]. Wang et al. proposed \(\:\text{S}\text{i}{\text{O}}_{2}\)-coated PP separator to ameliorate the wettability, thermal shrinkage, and electrochemical performance of the separator [29]. Nahvi Bayani et al. prepared a composite separator by applying \(\:\text{A}\text{l}{\left(\text{O}\text{H}\right)}_{3}\) layer on the PP separator showed improved flame retardancy, thermal stability, electrolyte uptake, ionic conductivity and capacity retention after 100 cycles [30]. Shi et al. proposed an \(\:{\text{A}\text{l}}_{2}{\text{O}}_{3}\)-coated separator that had better thermal shrinkage than the pristine one, however, the ion conductivity through them dropped from 1.12 to 1 mS/cm [31]. First published on 18th February 2019 Lithium (Li) metal batteries have shown great promise for next-generation electrical energy storage due to the unique features of lithium metal like light weight, high specific capacity, and the lowest anode potential. Nevertheless, the uncontrollable growth of dendritic and mossy Li, resulting in a low coulombic efficiency and serious safety concerns, has hindered the practical application of rechargeable Li-metal batteries. Here we report an environmentally friendly nanocomposite separator, comprising polyvinyl alcohol and hydroxyapatite, which exhibits an outstanding Young's modulus and high mechanical flexibility. We show that this separator can efficiently suppress the growth of dendritic Li and enable a homogeneous stable solid electrolyte interphase. Compared to lithium metal batteries using a commercial polyolefin-based separator, cells using the reported nanocomposite separator demonstrate a superior electrochemical performance with a much higher coulombic efficiency during the charge/discharge cycling at a practical current density of 2 mA cm−2. This work indicates that nanocomposite engineering could be a promising strategy to develop stable, safe and sustainable Li-metal batteries. To date, plenty of efforts have been devoted to revealing the detailed mechanism of the Li dendrite formation. Chazalviel proposed that the large electric field caused by the anion depletion near the cathode could lead to the growth of Li dendrites.22 This theory indicates that electrolytes with high ionic conductivity and stable anion mobility are beneficial for preventing anion depletion, and thus to some extent relieving the generation of Li dendrites. On the other hand, it is recognized that as the Young's modulus of the separator is twice that of Li metal, the interfacial roughening could be mechanically suppressed.23 According to the abovementioned two strategies, many approaches have been proposed to build Li metal batteries with suppressed Li dendrite formation, for instance, using suitable electrolyte additives,24,25 solid phase electrolytes,26-28 network polymer electrolytes,29 organic or/and inorganic-coated separators,30,31 and three-dimensional current collectors.32-34 In recent years, constructing mechanical protective layers is of particular interest to impede the growth of Li dendrites and to achieve satisfactory coulombic efficiency. Cui fabricated a monolayer of interconnected amorphous hollow carbon nanospheres on a Li metal anode to isolate the Li metal deposition and facilitate the formation of a stable SEI layer.35 By the way, Cui also prepared a trilayer separator with a structure of polyethylene/SiO2 particles/polyethylene to delay the penetration of Li dendrites through the separator, thus prolonging the life of batteries.36 Hu designed a thermally conductive separator, mainly comprising of boron-nitride nanosheets, to improve the electrochemical stability of Li metal anodes.37 Additionally, Guo et al. designed an artificial Li3PO4 SEI layer to restrain the unfavorable reaction between the Li metal and the electrolyte and the dendritic Li growth in LiFePO4|Li systems.17 Nevertheless, in most cases, complicated processes (such as synthesis of templates or an artificial SEI layer and a complex manufacturing process), expensive instrumentation requirements, being time consuming and high cost of raw materials restrain the further practical application. Moreover, even with numerous efforts, the long-time suppression of dendritic Li growth at high current density (>0.5 mA cm−2) is still a challenging task impeding Li metal batteries from being commercialized in the market.

In recent years, various energy devices such as nanogenerators and supercapacitors have gained considerable attention, and with technological advancements, the demand for these energy devices has increased significantly. Traditional energy devices are predominantly composed of non-biodegradable materials and metals, leading to severe environmental issues: the non-degradability of these energy devices upon disposal results in environmental pollution; furthermore, these devices often contribute to the wastage of valuable metal resources [1]. To mitigate the negative environmental impact and meet the diversified functional requirements of energy devices, recent studies have turned their focus towards utilizing biodegradable polymers for the fabrication of energy devices. Energy devices based on biodegradable polymers can fulfill the original performance requirements during usage, maintain stability throughout their lifespan, and undergo chemical structure changes within a short period under natural conditions after use, resulting in performance degradation. Eventually, they can be completely decomposed into CO2 and H2O by environmental microorganisms, thus reducing their harm to natural ecosystems [2]. Moreover, energy devices fabricated using biodegradable polymers can meet the demand for multifunctionality, serving roles in energy provisioning [3], human health monitoring [4], [5] and smart wearables [6], [7], and other domains [8], [9], [10] as shown in Fig. 1. In the field of smart wearables, most electronic devices rely on external power sources, limiting the flexibility of wearable devices and leading to additional power losses [11]. However, employing flexible biodegradable polymer-based energy devices can convert the energy generated by human body movements into electrical energy through material properties such as piezoelectricity, frictional power generation, and electrostatic induction, thereby providing energy for smart wearable devices [12] (Fig. 1). Biodegradable polymers refer to a class of polymers that can be decomposed or degraded into CO2 and H2O by microorganisms or their secretions through enzymatic or chemical actions under certain natural conditions [13]. Biodegradable polymers can be classified into natural polymers and biocompatible synthetic polymers based on their sources, which can be regenerated into hydrogel, fiber, foam, film, tube, particle and other shapes (Fig. 1) [14]. Natural polymers primarily originate from renewable or biological resources such as animals, plants, marine organisms, and microorganisms, while synthetic polymers are chemically synthesized [15]. Natural polymers include polysaccharides such as starch, cellulose, chitosan, and its derivative chitosan, as well as protein-based polymers such as silk fibroin (SF), collagen, spider silk, and plant proteins. Biodegradable synthetic polymers typically contain ester, amide, or ether bonds and include polylactic acid (PLA), polycaprolactone (PCL), polyurethane (PU), polyethylene glycol (PEG), poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), polybutylene succinate (PBS), and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), among others [16]. Among these materials, the main polymers used for the fabrication of green energy devices are starch, cellulose, chitosan, chitin, silk fibroin, collagen, spider silk, soy protein from natural polymers, and PLA, PCL, PU, and PEG from synthetic polymers (Fig. 2). Most of the biodegradable polymers mentioned here are also bio-resourced, making them important for the sustainable society.
Supercapacitors (SCs) are promising energy storage devices in various applications requiring high power density, such as portable devices, hybrid power systems for electric vehicles, aircraft vehicles (UAVs, UGVs, etc.), and smart grids.1-3 The main components of SCs are electrodes (cathode, anode), electrolytes, and separators. To improve the performance of SCs, extensive work has been focused on increasing the specific capacitance of electrodes4 and widening the cell voltage by newly developed electrolytes and separators.5, 6 Synthetic polymer-based solid electrolytes or separators have been widely used in SCs, and their biodegradable alternatives from renewable sources have always been sought after because of environmental and economic concerns.7, 8 The major advantages of polymer electrolytes and separators are that they are flexible, easy to fabricate, free of leakage, nonvolatile, and low flammable.9 Much attention has been given to the development of high performance SCs by enhancing the ionic conductivity and chemical and electrochemical stability of polymer electrolytes and separators. The usage of different polymers or polymer blends that are well matched to electrodes enables one to widen the potential window and broaden the operating temperature range. The most widely used hydrogel electrolyte separator is the poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) for flexible SCs. Wan and his coworkers prepared a flexible and self-healable PVA hydrogel electrolyte crosslinked by hydrogen bonds for an SC with all-in-one configuration.10 A flexible sandwich-structured SC with a PVA/H3PO4-soaked cotton fabric as the electrolyte matrix and separator was reported for potential applications in smart textiles and wearable electronics.11 To improve the network structure and mechanical properties, cellulose/PVA composite gels are prepared as separators for quasi-solid state electrical double layer capacitors (EDLCs). Compared with the PVA gel, composite gels showed good cycling stability with capacitance retention of 88% after 1,500 cycles.12 A semi-interpenetrating polymer network (semi-IPN) based on poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) and noncrosslinked nitrile butadiene rubber system has been reported for high thermal and dimensional stability. The produced semi-IPN membranes exhibit an operating temperature range of from −80 to 120°C, which is wider than that of the classical cellulose separator.13 The SCs based on a porous polyacrylonitrile nanofibers separator14 and a crosslinked quaternized poly(arylene ether sulfone) membrane15 showed good cycle stability. These polymer electrolytes or separators are expected to meet the fundamental requirements to be ideal materials for energy storage devices with high energy/power density and good cycling stability. However, most of these materials are not biodegradable and environmentally friendly. Moreover, they are not manufactured from renewable sources.
It is critical to realize biodegradable and rechargeable batteries that are also flexible and safe for power supplies in vivo, yet they remain unavailable. Here, we discovered such a biocompatible battery by designing biodegradable fiber conductors incorporated with polydopamine/polypyrrole composite material as the anode and MnO2 as the cathode, biodegradable chitosan as the separator and body fluid as the electrolyte. It can be directly injected into the body mini-invasively and well integrate with biological tissues without inducing immune responses. It delivered a specific capacity of 25.6 mA h g−1 with a retention of 69.1% after 200 charge/discharge cycles to power various biomedical devices. For instance, it was demonstrated to effectively power biosensors in the body. After completing the mission, it could be biodegraded, eliminating the need of surgery to remove it. Here, we realized a biodegradable and rechargeable aqueous fiber battery by designing biodegradable fiber electrodes and a chitosan separator with body fluid as electrolyte (Fig. 1). Benefiting from the one-dimensional configuration and high flexibility, the fiber battery could be directly injected into the body with minimal invasion. It showed decent power capability and was demonstrated to successfully power a biosensor that detected pressure changes in vivo. After the use, it was biodegraded and the entire biodegradation process proved nontoxic and non-interfering with the body. The fiber power system was made from an aqueous sodium-ion battery by a facile and environmentally friendly process (Fig. 2a). As an essential component, conducting fiber was first prepared by sputtering a thin layer of gold (∼80 nm) onto a polyglycolic acid yarn (Fig. S1 and S2†), followed by twisting it into a bundle. Here, 10 yarns were used to fabricate a conducting fiber (Fig. S3†). The conducting fiber was then incorporated with polydopamine/polypyrrole and MnO2 as the anode and cathode, respectively. Both fiber electrodes were approximately 70 μm in diameter (Fig. 2b and d), and the active materials were uniformly and compactly attached on the surface of the conducting fiber (Fig. 2c and e). To prevent short circuits, biodegradable chitosan was used as the separator with decent ionic conductivity and controllable thickness (Fig. S4 and S5, Table S1†). Here, the fiber cathode was dip-coated with a layer of chitosan with a thickness of approximately 10 μm (Fig. S6†). A multi-layered coaxial structure was shared by the fiber anode and cathode (Fig. S7†).
The well-designed battery-grade separators generally rely on balancing several properties such as wettability, porosity and void distribution, thickness, electrolyte absorption capacity, dimensional thermal stability, mechanical properties, and flame retardancy. (9−11) The polyolefin separators currently leading the secondary battery market have outstanding advantages such as low cost, good mechanical strength, and flexibility. However, the inherent molecular nonpolarity of polyolefin separators and their low porosity due to dry and wet processing methods are not conducive to the absorption and wetting of liquid electrolytes by the separator. In addition, the poor thermal stability of polyolefin separators at higher operating temperatures (low melting point) and their own flammability causes them to be susceptible to shrinkage and decomposition, leaving SIBs at risk of short-circuit, fire, and even deflagration. (12−15) From the perspective of environmental protection and energy conservation, the extensive use of nonrenewable polyolefins derived from fossil fuels is undesirable. The cellulose, as a biodegradable and renewable natural polymer material, is widely found in the cell walls of plants in nature and is also the most abundant polysaccharide-based biomass polymer material on Earth. (16,17) Moreover, cellulose is a promising candidate separator material to replace polyolefins because of its abundant hydroxyl groups and dimensional stability at high temperatures. Based on the above advantages of cellulose, scholars have conducted in-depth research on the application of cellulose to sodium-ion battery separators, and a series of research results have been achieved. Chen et al. obtained a separator with high chemical stability, excellent thermal stability, and outstanding wettability (contact angle close to 0°) by modifying a flexible cellulose acetate membrane synthesized with an electrostatic spinning process. (18) Mittal et al. used biodegradable cellulose nanoparticles to prepare separators with a mesoporous hierarchical structure that exhibited a high liquid electrolyte uptake of 2985%, an ionic conductivity of 2.32 mS cm-1, and a Na+ transfer number of 0.637 and showed excellent electrochemical performance in SIB applications. (19) Lin’s research group successfully prepared cellulose filter paper-derived separators with high ionic conductivity, promoting Na+ transfer by coating cellulose filter paper with Zn5(OH)8Cl2·H2O particles. (20) However, based on the current research results, the cellulose-based separators are not perfect and still suffer from defects such as poor mechanical properties and flammability. Airlaid paper (AP) is an environmentally friendly material made from cellulose and polyester through dry molding technology without any binders or chemical additives. (21,22) It is widely used in industry and laboratories for its unique advantages, such as low cost, high porosity, excellent mechanical properties, and insulating properties. (23,24) Thus, we consider that separators composed of AP materials have significant potential to improve the electrochemical performance and ensure the safety of batteries. However, AP cannot be directly used as a separator since it has a large pore size and uneven pore distribution, which would lead to self-discharge or uneven current distribution in SIBs. In addition, the inherent flammability of AP causes difficulty for it to eliminate the safety risks of batteries. Therefore, in this paper, AP-based composite separators were developed by modifying the AP matrix with a noninflammable coating consisting of sodium silicate and hydroxyethyl cellulose. Sodium silicate is a low-cost inorganic binder and flame-resistant material that forms a strong foam layer against flames and can effectively hinder the spread of flames. (25,26) In addition, to increase the adhesion and flexibility of the coating, hydroxyethyl cellulose (HEC), a polymer binder with good bonding properties, was selected to be mixed with sodium silicate (NSIO) to prepare the NSIO-HEC coating. The NSIO-HEC coating material was anticipated to optimize the pore size and distribution while contributing to a range of physical and electrochemical properties of the separator after its introduction. Subsequently, systematic performance studies on the morphology and structural composition, wettability and electrolyte uptake, thermal stability and noninflammability, electrochemical properties, and battery performance of the separator were conducted, and the performance of the separator was analyzed and evaluated based on the results.
