As expected, without any treatment, a very long abiotic lag phase was observed for PLA at mesophilic conditions (37°C), indicating and reaffirming a very slow hydrolysis phase. This is depicted as negative mineralization over the test duration of 180 days. Improved CO2 evolution was observed for PLA when the compost was biostimulated with the addition of skim milk, gelatin, or ethyl lactate. This finding was corroborated by tracking crystallinity evolution and molecular weight changes. PLA biodegradation was accelerated to reach Mn ≲10 kDa (where the biotic phase is taken over to consume the PLA n-mers) by 15% by adding skim milk, 25% by adding gelatin, and 22% by adding ethyl lactate. This work opens the door to help biodegrade PLA in compost conditions by adding selected biostimulants.
Efforts by the National Organic Standards Board (NOSB) to update composting standards for bioplastics have established more precise guidelines for waste processing facilities, ensuring that certified bioplastics can be composted effectively without contamination, resulting in higher-quality compost [13]. This clarity benefits the agricultural sector, where compost enriched with bioplastic-derived material can be safely used as soil amendments. Another significant advancement is the development of bioplastics that biodegrade in diverse environmental conditions, offering solutions for applications where waste may end up outside controlled composting facilities, such as agricultural films and marine-based packaging. With enhanced breakdown rates and environmental compatibility, these bioplastic innovations support a more sustainable approach to waste management across various sectors. Recent advancements in the composting of bioplastics are summarized, demonstrating the benefits and limitations of bioplastics. Co-polyesters with tunable hydrolysis rates (PBS blends with starch) and enzyme-responsive polymers aim to reconcile biodegradability with environmental safety, an emerging innovation [116]. Enzymatic recycling utilizes polyester hydrolases (Thermobifida fusca cutinase) to achieve over 90% monomer recovery from PLA waste, providing a closed-loop alternative to traditional composting. However, scalability remains constrained by enzyme stability and cost, necessitating metabolic engineering of microbial strains for enhanced biocatalyst production. Composting advances bioplastic circularity, polymer design, microbial ecology, and policy fragmentation create systemic barriers. Future strategies must integrate lifecycle assessments (LCAs) to quantify residual toxicity, harmonize global standards for biodegradability, and prioritize polymeric structures that degrade predictably across environments, from industrial composters to marine ecosystems.
Biological waste treatments tailored for biodegradable plastics represent sophisticated end-of-life management strategies. These treatments can be implemented under aerobic conditions (with oxygen, such as composting) or anaerobic conditions (without oxygen, such as anaerobic digestion). Composting, which utilizes a diverse microbial community including fungi, bacteria, and actinomycetes, can occur at psychrophilic temperatures (below 35 °C for home composting) or thermophilic temperatures (50-60 °C for industrial composting) [11]. For example, kitchen scraps and garden waste are commonly composted in home settings, while large-scale operations might process municipal organic waste. This process reduces waste and produces valuable compost, rich in nutrients and beneficial for soil health. It can also be used in agriculture and landscaping. Similarly, anaerobic digestion, exclusively facilitated by bacteria, can be performed under mesophilic (below 35 °C) or thermophilic (50-60 °C) conditions. This method is often applied in wastewater treatment plants and livestock farms, where organic materials such as food waste, manure, and sewage sludge are digested [108]. The primary factor determining a bioplastic’s suitability for specific waste Management methods is its duration for complete degradation. International standards for biodegradability, such as those set by ISO and ASTM, define a Material as biodegradable if it fully decomposes within 56 days in aquatic environments or within two years in soil. However, these standards often rely on elevated temperatures that surpass typical conditions found in unmanaged natural environments, leading to a disparity between laboratory results and actual biodegradation in the real world. This highlights the importance of aligning biodegradation standards with actual environmental conditions when developing policies for managing plastic waste. Additionally, the design of plastic products must account for potential end-of-life scenarios, ensuring they align with the degradation timelines and processes of intended waste management systems. A cohesive strategy integrating policy, standards, and design is key to crafting practical and reliable solutions for bioplastic waste [101]. The study of biodegradation kinetics and carbon fate of bioplastics under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions offers valuable insights, but it also highlights critical limitations in their practical applications. While PHB and PHBV exhibit versatility by biodegrading under both conditions, PCL’s reliance on aerobic environments restricts its utility in anaerobic waste systems [99]. Integrating carbon balance analysis adds depth by tracking carbon sinks, such as gases, biomass, and soluble compounds; however, its complexity and resource demands may hinder scalability in industrial contexts. Additionally, the observed enhancement of mineralization rates with smaller particle sizes, though beneficial for assay duration, is impractical for real-world waste management, where uniform particle reduction is challenging and costly. Combining carbon balance with kinetic analysis provides a promising framework for testing and improving biodegradable materials, but the feasibility of implementing such rigorous methods at scale remains questionable. Addressing these challenges by focusing on scalable, realistic conditions and simplifying analytical methodologies will be critical to translating these findings into effective waste management solutions [99].
According to ASTM-D-6400, a biodegradable plastic is “a material whose decomposition is caused by naturally occurring microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, and algae”. This material, under certain environmental conditions, is designed to suffer a significant change in its chemical makeup. This leads to a loss of properties over a specific time frame that can be measurable by standard test methods that are appropriate for proper classification. To satisfy these conditions, a biodegradable plastic must demonstrate a satisfactory rate of biodegradation where at least 90% w/w of (i) the organic carbon in the whole component or (ii) each constituent making up more than 1% weight by dry mass is converted to carbon dioxide within 180 days, and other constituents making up less than 1% by mass but less than 5% summative, do not necessarily biodegrade. Composting (home or industrial) is one common pathway for biodegradation. Although not all bio-based plastics are biodegradable (e.g., bio-PE is not biodegradable but it is bio-based), all compostable plastics are biodegradable, whether fossil-based or bio-based. While home composting involves ambient temperatures of 25 ± 5 °C (ASTM 5810-2010), industrial composting is done at higher temperatures of 58 ± 2 °C and is in line with ASTM D5338-15, ASTM D6400, and ISO 14855-1, or ISO 14855-2 standards. The biodegradation behavior of PBAT has been thoroughly studied by researchers, showing that it satisfies the conditions of home, industrial composting, and soil biodegradation.[50, 133] There are two basic ways that degradation might take place in PBAT: i) enzymatically by naturally occurring bacteria, fungus, and algae; and ii) non-enzymatically such as thermal decomposition and hydrolysis of polymer chains as shown in Figure 10(1).[108, 134, 135] Being an aliphatic-aromatic biodegradable polyester, PBAT has two segments: the aliphatic segment - which promotes controlled degradation and the aromatic segment - which provides excellent physical properties due to its hard/rigid nature, making them recalcitrant to biodegradation.[50, 136] The ratio between the terephthalate and aromatic monomers, degree of crystallinity, presence of fillers, temperature, and media used for the enzymatic breakdown of PBAT are some of the critical factors that affect the rate of degradation of PBAT materials.[137]

Biodegradable Plastics: Standards, Policies, and Impacts Biodegradation under composting conditions is a process widely used as end-of-life (EoL) option for organic waste such as manure, food, and yard waste. The composting process allows the biological stabilization of organic waste, producing a stable material that can be diverted to agricultural activities at a large scale, urban areas at a smaller scale and also gardening at home.[1] Additionally, compostable plastic products, including packaging, can be collected and diverted along with organic waste. At present, although many materials are certified compostable, their biodegradation rate and disappearance in compost facilities may vary. Hence, the presence of compostable plastics during the collection of organic waste (mostly food waste and its associated packaging) has created a challenging situation for compost facilities since times required for ultimate biodegradation of biodegradable plastics may be longer than for organic waste such as food. Extensive research has been conducted at laboratory scales. Successful biodegradation of polymers in thermophilic simulated composting conditions has been reported, mainly for aliphatic and aliphatic/aromatic polyesters such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(hydroxybutyrate) (PHB), poly(hydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV), poly(hydroxyoctanoate) (PHO), poly(caprolactone) (PCL), poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), and natural polymers such as starch and cellulose.[2-5] However, laboratory studies involve mostly the use of polymers in their neat state (i.e., pellets, sheets, or films) or with one or two additives; whereas the final products to be discarded after post-consumer stage can be complex structures with several layers to fulfill product protection needs and consumer preferences. Furthermore, laboratory conditions offer a controlled environment where parameters, such as temperature, airflow, moisture content and even biotic population, are carefully tailored; and materials under biodegradation can also be conditioned to powder of homogenous thickness to make it the preferred substrate for the microbial population. However, in real conditions such as industrial or home composting facilities or soil environments, more variability is observed where a material under biodegradation may not be homogenous in type and shape, and they may not be the preferred available source of nutrients and energy for the microbial population.[6, 7]

Flow behavior of LDPE and its blends with LLDPE I and II: A comparative study Packaging polymers, particularly polyethylene films, have been considered to be the major culprit for causing the rising environmental pollution problem. These polymers, after completing their useful short lifecycle as packaging films, find their way to constitute the major fraction of solid municipal waste, where they refuse to degrade because of their hydrophobic nature. The problem aggravates due to the high molecular weight associated with these polymers. An acceptable solution to this problem is the use of oxo-degradable polyethylene, which first disintegrates to small pieces, thereby reducing their ubiquitous visual presence. In the process, their molecular weight is reduced and these become potentially biodegradable organics, which can be subsequently consumed by the microorganism to form biomass.1-3 Major strategies to facilitate the disintegration and subsequent biodegradation of polyethylene are mainly focused on the direct incorporation of carbonyl groups within the backbone of the polymer (ethylene CO copolymer)4 or by addition of certain pro-oxidants (Scott-Gilead Process) during the processing stage.5, 6 These pro-oxidants, in the presence of either light or heat lead to the generation of free radicals on the polymer chain, which further react with oxygen to form carbonyl groups through a series of reactions. These carbonyl groups, then undergo photochemical reactions (Norrish Type I, II, and III) to finally lead to chain scission and physical embrittlement.4 In the recent years, linear low density polyethylene (LLDPE) is fast replacing low density polyethylene (LDPE) as packaging films, because of its better mechanical properties and comparable cost. Keeping in mind the increased use of LLDPE, we felt the need of performing accelerated degradation studies on LDPE, LLDPE, and LLDPE -LDPE blends. As a part of our ongoing efforts towards development of oxo-degradable polyethylene, we have reported the pro-oxidative action of cobalt stearate on LDPE,7, 8 which first leads to the abiotic disintegration of the matrix. The degradation of these disintegrated films by bacterial consortium has also been reported.9 The effect of such pro-oxidants is expected to be less pronounced for LLDPE because of the lesser degree of branching in the polymer chain, therefore requiring higher concentrations of the pro-oxidant to reach the same level of degradation, which has been confirmed by our investigations.10 To avoid the slight bluish tinge in the films containing higher concentrations of cobalt stearate, the present investigation was performed on films containing manganese stearate which also belong to the broad category of pro-oxidants.11

Polyethylene has been widely applied in our daily life such as agricultural mulch film, disposal shopping bag, packaging film owing to its versatile, lightweight, durable, flexible and inexpensive qualities. However, the enormous increase in usage has also created many challenges associated with disposal and their impact on the environment because of their exceptional properties against degradation, resistance to peroxidation and biologically inert properties [1,2,3,4]. In order to reduce the accumulation of polyethylene in the environment, the new forms of plastic are required to be developed as quickly as possible. They must both retain all of the physical properties needed by the consumer and be easy degradable in the natural environment after disuse. Degradable plastic has been the research issue in order to solve the problem. Generally, degradable plastic are classified as photodegradable, thermo-degradable and biodegradable plastics. Photodegradable plastics have been studied extensively in recent years [5,6,7,8,9]. Photo-catalysts have been utilized to create photodegradable plastics. One of the most representatives is nano-TiO2 owing to its excellent properties such as inexpensiveness, photo-stability, non-toxicity and high photo-catalytic activity [10, 11]. Carbonyl compounds, hydroxide radical and other oxygen-containing groups are introduced into the polymer chain accompany with a decrease in molecular weight of polymer during the photo-degradation of TiO2-polymer [12,13,14]. This photooxidative process promotes the biodegradation or mineralization of the oxidation products of polymer. However, the photodegradable efficiency is strongly influenced by the irradiated light intensity, polymers’ exposed area and time. Oxidative degradation will be stopped immediately, while the waste polymer is buried by fresh waste and unable to be exposed to the sunlight. Thus, the degradable efficiency of photodegradable plastic is too low to be degraded completely. It is a major defect for photodegradable plastics [15, 16]. What is more, most of the photo-catalysts as hydrophilic inorganic particles have the poor compatibility with a hydrophobic polymer matrix. The polymer nanocomposite is difficult to form smooth surface without particle aggregates and/or agglomerates. This also causes an increase in cost and a decrease in photodegradable efficiency of the photodegradable film [17, 18]. In recent years, the study of thermo-degradable plastics has become a hot topic of research [19,20,21]. The mechanism of thermo-degradable plastics is adding thermo-degradable catalyst such as Co, Ni, Mn and Fe, transition metals, carboxylates and oxides into polymer. Roy et al. [22, 23] have reported ferric stearate, cobalt stearate and manganese stearate as effective pro-oxidants for polyethylene. Abdullah et al. have reported that the accelerating weathering degradation properties of polypropylene were improved by integration with cobalt stearate and ferric stearate as pro-oxidants [24]. But the degradable efficiency was low and the biodegradation behaviors of the residue of films were not involved.

Contextual caveats: biodegradability and land-use change While biodegradability is often promoted as a key sustainability advantage of bio-based polymers particularly for single-use disposable products, its environmental benefits are heavily conditional on proper disposal environments, such as industrial composting or anaerobic digestion facilities. In the absence of such controlled conditions, biodegradable plastics may persist, fragment into microplastics, and act as vectors for persistent organic pollutants and heavy metals through trophic transfer, thus posing substantive risks to both ecological systems and human health [120]. Additionally, many earlier assessments have overstated the carbon benefits of bio-based plastics by primarily accounting for carbon sequestration gains linked to land use, while neglecting the foregone carbon sequestration potential of pre-existing ecosystems. Notably, land-use change (LUC) emissions are frequently excluded from conventional LCA inventories, despite their critical influence. For example, reverting land to secondary forest can substantially decrease atmospheric CO₂ fluxes and deliver co-benefits for biodiversity and hydrological cycles. Products made from natural rubber are often vulcanized during the production to improve their strength and durability. Vulcanization improves the mechanical properties of the rubber at the expense of its biodegradability [4], [5]. Sulfur vulcanization and the presence of certain additives (such as antioxidants) in some of these products extend the duration needed for decomposition in the natural environment [5], [6]. Polyolefin plastics and metal complexes (such as Fe, Co, and Mn stearates) that serve as pro-degradant additives (PDA) or catalysts are frequently used to accelerate the natural degradation process of polymers [7]. The mechanism involved includes the absorption of UV light and oxidation, followed by the generation of unstable hydroperoxide that will subsequently dissociate to form a pair of free radicals responsible for the eventual disintegration of the polymer [8], [9]. The oxidation of the polymer also results in the formation of carbonyl groups in the hydrocarbon chain (Fig. 1A), making it more vulnerable to further degradation since these groups are photolabile and easily undergo photolysis via Norrish I and Norrish II reactions (Fig. 1B) [10], [11]. Given the current enormous volume of rubber usage, there is a need to consider the end-of-life treatment of rubber products, including ways to hasten its biodegradation in the environment. One viable strategy is the enhancement of oxo-biodegradable properties of natural rubber [4]. The introduction of oxo-biodegradable properties has been extensively studied in the plastics industry, evidenced by the high volume of patents and successful commercial products in the market with many positive results [12], [13], [14]. The most common approach to improving oxo-biodegradability is introducing a PDA in the polymers. The oxo-biodegradation of a polymer refers to a two-stage degradation process that begins with the oxidation of the carbon backbone of the polymer to form smaller fragments containing carboxyl, ester, aldehyde, and/or alcohol groups, followed by bio-assimilation of the oxidation products by microorganisms to produce carbon dioxide (CO2), water (H2O), and biomass. In the first stage of degradation, the oxidative breakdown of polymer to produce smaller and hydrophilic fragments is crucial to improve water wettability of the substrate, and molecules of the material must be sufficiently small for microflora, such as bacteria and fungi to assimilate carbon source in the substrate [15], [16]. This explains why most hydrocarbon thermoplastics, which are hydrophobic and usually produced with very high molecular weight, are bioinert. This could also explain the persistency observed in vulcanized natural rubber which is composed of poly(isoprene) chains connected by sulfur linkages [4], [5]. Over the past ten years, there have been reports of successful improvements in the oxo-biodegradability of plastics, particularly through the use of various PDA [17], [18]. Development of degradable polyolefin has attracted increasing interest due to their low price, useful properties, broad suppliers, and mature processing facilities and techniques. UV-oxidative degradation and blending with natural polymers can enhance their biodegradability.1-6 Oxo-degradation incorporates oxygen into the carbon chain and results in the formation of functional groups such as carboxylic or hydro-carboxylic acids, esters, aldehydes, and alcohols. This process can be accelerated by exposure of samples to ultraviolet (UV) light or heating. It is suggested that once the molecular weight of a polymer is significantly reduced during oxo-degradation, the oxidized products are deemed susceptible to further degradation by various micro-organisms, which assimilate the oxidized fragments and convert them into CO2, H2O, and biomass.7, 8 Photo-oxidative degradation is the process of degradation of the material by the action of light and the free radical chain degradation.9-11 Rate of abiotic oxidation of polyolefins is important as it determines the rate of subsequent biodegradation process. It has been reported that to achieve significant biodegradation in a reasonable time period, the average molecular weight of oxidized polyolefin should be less than 5000 Da.7, 8, 12-19 Transition metal salts and transition metal free systems have been widely used as prodegradants to accelerate the oxidation process of polyolefins, as the metal ions can absorb some of radiant energy and transform it to the polymer chain to accelerate its fragmentation. Various Fe and Co-based pre-degradants are commercial available in the market.4 Recently, it was found that hydrophilic polymers such as starch20-22 and cellulose23 play an important role in accelerating the degradation of polyolefin in a photo-degrading environment. It has been reported that addition of starch influence the molecule weight of low-density polyethylene (LDPE), resulting into significant reduction in the molecular weight of starch/LDPE blends on exposure to UV radiations.21 Raquez et al.22 studied degradability of LDPE using thermal analysis and scanning electron microscope (SEM) and found that oxidative degradations of oxo-degradable LDPE was enhanced with thermoplastic pea starch (TPPS) under UV-condition. Previous studies1, 24-26 have also shown that starch can accelerate the oxidative degradation of polyolefin blends and encourage their biodegradation by micro-organisms (bacteria, fungi, and algae)1, 24-27. However, there is no clear understanding of the mechanism by which starch influences degradation process of polyolefin-starch blends. To further explore the degradation mechanisms, it is important to study both chemical and physical changes in the interface between starch and polyolefin, and identify the stage at which acceleration starts.

ground_truth: In surface-eroding polymers (like Polyanhydrides), the drug is released proportionally to the mass loss of the polymer. As the polymer erodes layer by layer from the outside in, the drug entrapped in those layers is released. This allows for near zero-order (constant rate) release kinetics, which is difficult to achieve with bulk-eroding polyesters.

ans_raw: The drug release mechanism from a surface-eroding polyanhydride wafer is primarily governed by **surface erosion**, where hydrolytic degradation occurs at the polymer-water interface rather than throughout the bulk. The anhydride bonds in the polymer backbone hydrolyze faster than water penetrates the matrix, leading to layer-by-layer degradation. This results in a drug release rate proportional to the polymer's erosion rate, which is controlled by factors such as polymer structure, crystallinity, and pH [1], [6], [9]. Unlike bulk-eroding systems (e.g., polyesters), surface erosion minimizes **burst release** and maintains a steady release profile as the drug is exposed incrementally with each eroded layer [3], [6], [15]. The degradation products (e.g., diacids) are metabolized or eliminated, ensuring biocompatibility [1], [12].

Polyanhydrides are novel biodegradable polymers, and their surface-eroding property in aqueous medium makes them desirable for drug controlled release and functional soft tissue substitute.1-4 Polyanhydrides have been developed since 1980s' by the Langer's group.5 Since then, polyanhydrides of aliphatic and aromatic diacids have been extensively investigated as useful biomaterials for controlled drug delivery systems6, 7 because of their good biocompatibility and variable degradation properties. These advantages also make poly(CPP : SA) copolymers composed of 1,3-bis(carboxyphenoxy) propane (CPP) and sebacic acid (SA) good candidates for new drug delivery applications. Hundreds of polyanhydrides have been synthesized in the recent decades, but only poly(sebacic anhydride) and its derivations have been applied in controlled drug delivery system. For example, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved the application of poly(CPP : SA) in weight ratio of 20 : 80 to deliver the chemotherapeutic agent BCNU for the treatment of brain cancer.8 However, as polylactide (PLA) and polylactide-co-glycolide (PLGA) particles widely used in drug delivery, micro/nanoscaled particles fabricated with poly(CPP : SA) possessed hydrophobic surfaces that led to their rapid removal by the immune system and poor resuspension and aerosolization properties.9 In parallel, polymeric micelles formed by self-assembly of amphiphilic graft or block copolymers exerted many merits, such as biocompatibility, high drug-loaded amount, and markedly improved bio-distribution.10-12 Polymeric micelles have unique core-shell architecture consisted of hydrophobic segments as internal core and hydrophilic segments as surrounding corona in aqueous medium. Poorly water-soluble drugs can be solubilized within the hydrophobic core of the micelles and consequently, polymeric micelles can substantially improve the solubility and bioavailability of various hydrophobic drugs.13 Polymeric micelles were firstly introduced as drug delivery vehicles in the early 1980s by Helmut Ringsdorf.14, 15 Polymeric micelles must hold several specific properties before they can be used in biomedical field, such as biocompatibility, biodegradability, target specificity, and stability in the body. To date, biodegradable polymeric micelles have found increasing applications as nanoscaled carriers in drug delivery system as they can provide several advantages including escaping from reticuloendothelial system (RES) uptake, long circulation in systemic fluid, passive targeting into specific tissues, and simple sterilization.16 Drug targeting to tumors using ultrasound-activated polymeric micelles was also developed in previous reports.17-21 The simplicity of micelle formation by self-assembly of amphiphilic block copolymer molecules and drug encapsulation by physical mixing rather than chemical conjugation are of extremely attractive features. In this article, we synthesized a series of amphiphilic poly(PEG : CPP : SA) terpolymers containing of PEG, CPP, and SA via melt polycondensation. The two-component poly(CPP : SA) copolymers are biocompatible, biodegradable through surface erosion, and have gained increasing attention for sustained drug delivery applications. However, poly(CPP : SA) copolymers are hydrophobic, and their hydrolytic degradation need relatively long time, which results in the limitation of further applications in drug delivery system. PEG is a noncharged, hydrophilic, and nonimmunogenic polymer that possesses wide chemical, biomedical, and industrial applications.22, 23 It was reported that the incorporation of PEG could not only increase the hydrophilicity but also minimize protein adsorption and decrease nonspecific cell adhesion.24, 25 Many studies focused on the amphiphilic PEG-polyesters copolymers in expectation of achieving unique properties and corresponding applications.26, 27 In contrary to the PEG comprising the hydrophilic block, the CPP and SA chains were chosen as the hydrophobic blocks in the backbone of the amphiphilic poly(PEG : CPP : SA) terpolymers. The structure of these resultant terpolymers was investigated by 1H-NMR and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). The average Mw and its polydispersity index (PDI) were measured with GPC. Intrinsic viscosity ([η]) was determined by Ubbelohde viscometer. The crystallinity and crystallization morphologies were analyzed by XRD and polarization optical microscope (POM), respectively. The melting points of the distinct components in these materials were examined by differential scanning calorimeter (DSC). The water contact angle (CA) was measured to investigate their hydrophilicity.

In reservoir systems, the release rate is well established, and it is independent on environment, with advantage of keeping constant the concentration of drug inside the host body.3 The drug delivery from bulk-eroding or surface-eroding biodegradable or layer-by-layer14 systems are named of Chemically Controlled Systems, the drug may be uniformly distributed and immobilized in the matrix, and the release occurs by erosion of the matrix of the biomaterial. When there are covalent bonds between the drug and the biopolymer, the release will occur through the divisions of the connections formed through chemical reactions, usually enzymatic or hydrolytic degradation of the matrix.3 Most biodegradable polymers are designed to degrade as a result of hydrolysis of the polymer chains into biologically acceptable, and progressively smaller, compounds. Degradation may take place through bulk hydrolysis, in which the polymer degrades in a fairly uniform manner throughout the matrix. For some degradable polymers, most notably the polyanhydrides and polyorthoesters, the degradation occurs only at the surface of the polymer, resulting in a release rate that is proportional to the surface area of the drug delivery system. The drug can be dissolved, dispersed, or partially dissolved in the polymer matrix. The release of drug from stable polymers is based on diffusion, which can occur as either zero or first order kinetics. The release of drug from biodegradable polymers is predominantly a consequence of diffusion of drug molecule and simultaneous degradation of polymer matrix. In addition, there are multiple other factors that need to be taken into account when drug releasing devices are being developed.12

Recently, also poly(ester-anhydride) copolymers have been synthesized that combine the individual properties (such as biodegradation rate and mode) of these two classes of polymers [5], [14], [31], [32], [33], [34], [35].Previously we have described the synthesis of functional poly(ester-anhydride)s with allyl pendant groups, based on succinic acid. They were obtained by polycondensation of oligo(3-allyloxy-1,2-propylene succinate) terminated with carboxyl groups (OSAGE) [36]. Poly(ester-anhydride)s obtained from OSAGE exhibited rather fast degradation and weak solubility in organic solvents [36]. Solubility of polymers is a important factor influencing their application. For preparation of drug delivery systems the most commonly used organic solvents are dichloromethane and chloroform. Some difficulties concerning bad solubility of poly(ester-anhydride)s in chlorinated solvents were successfully solved by copolymerization of OSAGE with sebacic acid. Degradable polymers usually contain functional groups that are susceptible to hydrolytic degradation, such as ester, amide, carbonate, urethane or anhydride repeat units. In medical applications, different products require specific physical and mechanical properties, as well as tailored rates of hydrolytic degradation. For example, chronic implantable medical devices may need a degradation period extending over several years to fulfill their function effectively. Conversely, tissue engineering implants might need to degrade within a range from 1 week to several years. Polymers used in drug delivery systems should be designed to degrade over periods ranging from 1 day to several years, depending on the therapeutic requirements.1, 2 However, a significant challenge in using degradable polymers for medical devices lies in controlling the degradation time. Although various biodegradable polymers have been successfully utilized in clinical applications, no single polymer has yet emerged as the ‘ideal’ solution for all medical applications.3, 4 Polyanhydrides (PAs) are a class of biodegradable polymers characterized by the presence of anhydride linkages (COOCO) within their backbones. They degrade in vivo primarily through hydrolytic degradation, facilitated by their anhydride repeat units. PAs are known to degrade faster than polyesters, polyamides and polyethers,5 where their diacid degradation products can be metabolized and eliminated from the body. Due to their rapid degradation, PAs have been used in short-term controlled delivery of drugs or bioactive agents.6-9 It has been reported that the rate of water penetration into the PA matrix is slower than the cleavage of anhydride bonds, consequently classifying PAs as surface-eroding drug delivery carriers.10 In addition, the rate of drug delivery is significantly influenced by the polymer erosion rate, which is governed by factors such as polymer structure, crystallinity, pH of the release medium and the size and design of the device. PAs have been synthesized with a variety of backbones, including aliphatic, aromatic, unsaturated, aliphatic-aromatic, ester-anhydride, ether-anhydride, and amino-, glycol- or fatty acid-modified anhydrides, owing to the broad functionality of available monomer precursors.11 Various synthesis methods have been employed, such as melt condensation, ring-opening polymerization, interfacial condensation, dehydrochlorination and dehydrative coupling.12 For example, poly(sebacic anhydride) and glycol-modified poly(sebacic anhydride) have been synthesized from sebacic acid and excess acetic anhydride under melt condensation conditions for use as drug carriers.13 It was reported that the degradation rate and in vitro drug release profile of glycol-modified poly(sebacic anhydride) were slower than that of poly(sebacic anhydride) without glycol modification, due to the introduction of glycolate esters. Similarly, crosslinked amino acid-containing PAs were successfully synthesized for controlled drug release using either N-trimellitylimido-beta-alanine or N-trimellitylimidoglycine as a comonomer with sebacic acid, followed by crosslinking with 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylic acid.14 Another example involves the synthesis of poly(ester anhydride)s through the transesterification of ricinoleic acid and sebacic acid, followed by anhydride polymerization via melt condensation. These materials were found to be nontoxic and suitable for the development of biodegradable, drug-eluting devices intended for local delivery.15
Various strategies have been examined for preparing highly crosslinked biodegradable networks [6]. The most popular studied methods have been via free-radical curing with heat and/or radiation of hydrolytically degradable precursors containing acrylic [11], methacrylic [12], fumaric [13], maleic [14], or itaconic [15] double bonds. Among the curing methods, photo-initiated crosslinking has many advantages, such as fast crosslinking rates, mild reaction conditions and easy control of the reaction by controlling the light source [16]. However, for photo crosslinking, the viscosity of the crosslinkable material should be low. Thermal crosslinking is easily applied to materials that sustain heat and are highly viscous or even solid at room temperature. In addition, thermal crosslinking is suitable for very thick specimens or complex structures, where the absorption and scattering of the polymerising light is restricted [17]. Tailoring the degradation of biodegradable polymers is a key factor for several applications [16]. The degradation mechanism of biopolymers is commonly divided into bulk and surface erosion [18]. In bulk erosion, the degradation process proceeds homogeneously throughout the entire polymer sample, whereas in surface erosion, the degradation process occurs at the surface, and the sample decreases as the degradation proceeds [19]. In general, polyester networks show bulk erosion, whereas polyanhydride networks are commonly known to erode from the surface. The degradation mechanism and the rate of degradation can be controlled by the number and/or type (e.g., ester, amide, and anhydride) of degradable chemical bonds in each precursor, the molecular weight of the precursor, and the hydrophilic/hydrophobic nature of the precursors [16]. For example, Anseth et al. [17], [20] prepared crosslinked polyanhydrides and observed that the degradation time of these networks can be adjusted to between 2 days and 1 year by varying the network composition. The mass loss of these crosslinked polyanhydrides increased linearly with time, which supports a surface-erosion-type mechanism [21]. Previously, we have altered the degradation mechanism of crosslinked poly(ε-caprolactone) networks from bulk to surface erosion by adding anhydride bonds to the network precursors [22]. Because these poly(ester anhydride) networks rapidly eroded, for the next study, we slowed the erosion of the networks slightly by functionalising precursors with hydrophobic alkenylsuccinic anhydrides (ASAs) [23], [24]. In this work, our aim is to further slow the erosion of these functionalised poly(ester anhydride) networks by increasing the molecular weights of the precursors. Increasing the molecular weight of the precursor affects network properties, such as thermal transitions, hydrophobicity and crosslinking density, which all affect the erosion of the networks. The main objective of the present study was to slow the hydrolytic degradation while maintaining the surface erosion mechanism of the crosslinked poly(ester anhydrides). These types of surface eroding polymers are suitable for several medical applications, such as controlled drug delivery and tissue engineering.

In general, poly(ester)s are classed as bulk eroding since the diffusion of the surrounding medium into the polymer is faster than the rate of hydrolysis of the ester linkages. Drug-loaded implants can be applied directly to the site of resection, offering localized and prolonged drug release with minimal side effects caused by systemic administration. Implants made by biodegradable polymers provide a one-time administration of drugs without the need of removal by a second surgery, thereby attracting more and more attention in clinical settings.13-15 For example, Gliadel® Wafer made by carmustine-containing polyanhydride improves long-term survival among patients diagnosed with aggressive gliomas.16 The improved therapeutic efficacy might be attributed to the localized and sustained release of drugs, enabling a prolonged exposure of tumor cells to chemotherapy over multiple cell cycles, which has been proved to be more cytotoxic than most systemic administrated drugs that disrupt cell replication.13 Moreover, considering the need of breast tissue reconstruction for patients with mastectomy or excision, drug-loaded implants with the ability to provide mechanical support and to improve soft tissue regeneration may be promising as an adjuvant therapy for nonmetastatic TNBC. Polycaprolactone (PCL) is a well-investigated biomaterial and has been used as a scaffold for bone regeneration in clinics.17 PCL is an aliphatic polyester with a semicrystalline structure, low glass transition temperature (60 °C), and highly flexible mechanical properties.
